A Movie Can’t Be Just Its Own Thing Anymore
Onslaught is a victim of Hollywood’s obsession with turning everything into a franchise.
Onslaught, in theaters this week, should be the perfect early-September treat. The aggressive action thriller is gory, loud, and packed with interesting actors, and it has a straightforward premise: Three murderous super-soldiers, the result of some shadowy extra-governmental experiment, have escaped from a lab and are descending upon a small town in New Mexico. A tough-as-nails retired Army sniper named Celeste (played by Adria Arjona), living somewhat off the grid in a trailer park, must use her grit and know-how to defend herself against the oncoming attack. Yet as simple as that sounds, the film feels needlessly complex. Rather than just delivering on its clean setup, it becomes fixated on teasing future installments—a symptom of the obsession with sequelization that’s affecting even smaller genre films.
The director Adam Wingard was, once upon a time, a master of the cheap thrill. This is a compliment; he emerged from the micro-budget mumblecore scene in the 2000s, then made two impressively nasty bits of horror—the slasher You’re Next and the wonderfully tawdry and tense The Guest. But Wingard has spent years trapped in franchise drudgery, offering up an unnecessary follow-up to The Blair Witch Project and a pair of giant-scale, instantly forgettable Godzilla movies. Onslaught initially suggests a more back-to-basics turn for the director, a return to R-rated indies that are unencumbered by cinematic universes. That mission, however, seems to have been a little corrupted by what Wingard’s been working on in the meantime.
Onslaught begins on a compelling note. Its aesthetics are top-notch, the opening credits unfolding as an invigorating blitz of conspiratorial imagery that cuts together cable-news clips of several presidents, including Richard Nixon, Bill Clinton, and George W. Bush, with drone footage of overseas combat; the entire sequence feels like a fever dream of the early 2000s. Celeste is a veteran of an unspecified overseas combat engagement, and the audience briefly glimpses in flashback the traumatic firefights that preceded her discharge. Living alongside her in the desert trailer park is a crew of other misfits, including the bumbling policeman Kovacks (Eric Wareheim) and a cantankerous older fella named Josiah (Reginald VelJohnson). To Celeste’s annoyance, her ex-husband drops off their cherubic daughter that day to stay the weekend; the tension is, of course, quickly building to a violent incursion.
Part of my irritation with the film, though, stems from just how jazzed I felt about its first act. The actor Dan Stevens, at this point a longtime collaborator of Wingard’s (including, most recently, the director’s previous Godzilla movie), dons nightmarish makeup to play Dr. Hans Kammler; he’s a German-speaking mad scientist in charge of the military experiment that goes wrong. Rebecca Hall, another Godzilla alum, is Dr. Kammler’s domineering wife, Hanna—a stiletto-clad, cigarette-smoking badass boasting some mysteriously derived authority. The duo’s cartoonish poise is a delight to witness, as is their ridiculous hubris: Whatever lab simulation they’ve designed for their seemingly zombified super-soldiers quickly falls apart, leading the latter to invade the surrounding environs.
Some solid gunplay follows, and the final showdown between Celeste and her trailer-park buds and the soldiers has some brutal flourishes—though it irritatingly takes place at night, making the chaos a little harder to see. But the screenplay (written by Simon Barrett) teases revelations throughout, then delivers on practically none of them. Hanna and Dr. Kammler’s work remains nebulous, and Celeste’s backstory is only vaguely filled in. These gaps would be forgivable if Onslaught existed mostly to deliver the frivolity that Wingard once excelled at; instead, it ends on a cliff-hanger that hints at further developments. In interviews, the director has even alluded to the movie belonging to a growing shared universe alongside You’re Next and The Guest, though there’s no real on-screen evidence of that.
I am not opposed to Wingard building connections among his works, especially if he’s looking to do it in a more intentional way. Too often, though, Onslaught acts like it’s making moves in that direction without a real sense of purpose. The Godzilla-centric enterprise that Wingard has spent the past few years in, also known as the “Monsterverse,” relies on the kind of lazy storytelling that films designed to spawn numerous sequels tend to tell: Rather than ending punchily, the movie lands on a big conflict that sets up new villains and crossover possibilities. Perhaps Onslaught will be a big enough hit to get a similar treatment, even on a smaller scale. More likely, though, the lack of resolution will leave people feeling as dissatisfied as I did.

North Korea and Russia open first road bridge linking both countries
- Published
The first road bridge linking Russia and North Korea has opened, allowing the two countries to more easily move cargo and passengers between their border across the Tumen river.
Pyongyang state media said the bridge will be used for "personnel exchanges, tourism and trade".
But Ukrainian OSINT group Truth Hounds said the bridge is intended "primarily to establish a covert military logistics corridor" to support Russia in the Ukraine war.
It comes as relations between both countries have grown since the start of the Ukraine war, with Russia's Putin and North Korea's Kim Jong Un previously pledging that both countries would help each other in the event of "aggression" against either country.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin described the bridge as a "new symbol of friendship", while North Korea's Prime Minister Pak Thae Song said it was a "historical event".
Up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people can cross the bridge daily, Russian state news TASS reports.
Satellite imagery reported by the BBC in May this year showed the kilometre-long bridge alongside several new access roads, a border checkpoint, support infrastructure and parking facilities.
There are existing air links, as well as the rail link between the two countries, but until now the only road link was a makeshift solution where, by special arrangement, wooden planks were placed on the rail bridge to allow cars to travel over it, according to Reuters.
The Russian government said the bridge will initially be used to transport cargo, Reuters reported, before opening to passenger traffic later this year.
The bridge would provide, a "powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," said Mishustin.
Appearing at the opening ceremony via video link, he described ties between Moscow and Pyongyang as being "at an unprecedented high level."
The most immediate impact may be increased export of weapons to Russia.
Researchers at South Korea's spy agency estimates that North Korea has already transferred $7 to 14 billion dollars' worth of rockets, missiles, artillery shells using ships. An estimated 11,000 North Korean troops are actively fighting Ukrainians in Russia.
Truth Hounds said in a recent statement that given the strategic partnership treaty between the two countries in 2024 - the bridge could be used to transport North Korean military personnel, construction workers and senior military officials directly to Russia.
It would also enable the flow of Russian technology and resources in the opposite direction".
Construction started in 2025, after the agreement to build the bridge was made during Putin's 2024 visit to North Korea, his first trip to the state in 24 years, which resulted in the partnership treaty. The bridge took 495 days to complete, after delays.
Russian tourists have trickled into North Korea since they were allowed in in 2024. North Korea has been hosting them in capital Pyongyang and the beach resorts of Wonsan-Kalma, while continuing to block those from other countries.
The road is also expected to transport North Korean labourers to Russia.
Around 10,000 North Koreans are working in Russia's construction sites and logging camps, according to a South Korean estimate. Although the UN bans countries from using North Korean labour, many enter Russia under the guise of student visas.
"The speed of construction is a reflection of the volume of trade activity between the two sides," Victor Cha from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank, told BBC Verify in May this year.
"This is spurred largely by North Korea's provision of troops, weapons, munitions, and labourers for Putin's war in Ukraine," he said.
"It is fair to say that this connection, prior to the war in Ukraine, was one of the sleepiest links between North Korea and its two neighbours."

Two bodies, including those of a girl and a youth, were recovered from a power canal in the Thune area of Kangan in Ganderbal district on Monday, officials said.
According to officials, the duo had reportedly drowned in the canal earlier in the day, following which a rescue operation was launched in the area.
Teams from the police, State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and local volunteers rushed to the spot after receiving information about the incident and began an extensive search operation along the canal.
After several hours of searching, rescuers located and recovered both bodies from the water.
The bodies were subsequently shifted to Sub-District Hospital (SDH) Kangan for medico-legal formalities. They were later handed over to the respective families.
Police have initiated proceedings in connection with the incident, while further investigation is underway to ascertain the circumstances leading to the drowning.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

SC/ST Congress leaders to approach President to intervene in ‘purification' row
The row flared after a purification ritual was conducted at Haldwani following Congress party chief Mallikarjun Kharge's address.
Congress lawmakers from the scheduled caste and scheduled tribes (SC/ST) communities have decided to hand over a memorandum to President Droupadi Murmu, seeking her intervention in the “purification” incident in Uttarakhand’s Haldwani following a rally addressed by party chief Mallikarjun Kharge, people aware of the matter said on Monday.
In total, 32 SC and ST MPs of the party held a meeting at the Congress’s headquarters to form a joint strategy on the issue.
Next steps by the Congress
Congress’s Lok Sabha MP from Telangana’s NagarKurnool, Mallu Ravi said, “We have sought time from President Murmu to submit a memorandum regarding the purification incident that has taken place after Kharge ji addressed a meeting. We will request her intervention in this matter. We want her to instruct the government to act of the issue that is illegal.”
Also Read I Haldwani Purification Row: Congress protests in Jalandhar over FIR against Rahul
Chaired by Congress leader K Raju, the meeting also decided to launch political protests against the Haldwani incident.
Last week, senior Congress leader Rahul Gandhi demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi order an FIR against those involved in the “shuddikaran” (purification) of the Ramlila ground at Haldwani after Kharge, a Dalit, addressed a public meeting.
“Our demand is an FIR should be lodged at the earliest against those who performed Shuddikaran. The Prime Minister said he belongs to all castes. His party chief in Uttarakhand claimed Shuddikaran was the right thing to do. We want the PM to give order to file an FIR under the SC/ST act. This show the BJP and RSS’ mindset. They don’t want a Dalit to become prosperous and live respectfully. We are not asking for anything impossible. According to the Constitution this is a crime. We are seeking justice for the Congress president. We are not asking anything more. It is a duty of the state government and the national government to ensure that Kharge ji gets justice in Uttarakhand,” the Congress leader had said.

Watch: Moment 64-year-old Nepali woman is found alive in mud-buried home
More than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud tore through a Himalayan valley in Nepal, rescuers continue to find survivors.
Chandika Shrestha, a 64-year-old woman, was discovered alive on the fourth floor of her partially buried house in the Nuwakot district by Nepal's Armed Police Force on 5 September, according to Reuters.
She was airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment, Reuters reported.

Thirteen medications across 30 different prescriptions. Five clinicians. Two hospitals.
In the four months before killing her three children and attempting to kill herself, Lindsay Clancy desperately sought help for her deteriorating mental condition. But as her ongoing murder trial has made clear, the help she got was scattered across multiple providers who gave conflicting advice and, crucially, didn’t talk to one another.
For Americans with private insurance, Clancy included, this kind of fragmented care is the norm. Not only are providers siloed within their own employers with little incentive to communicate, there’s no universal electronic health records where they can see the totality of a patient’s care and medications. Experts following the Clancy case said if there had been someone in the driver’s seat responsible for overseeing all of her care, things may have turned out differently.

I spent the waning days of summer grinding away at columns and working on a feature. But I missed a chance at a striking change of scenery—cruising the Galápagos with about a dozen prominent philosophers studying consciousness.
The invite described morning classroom discussions tackling knotty questions on the nature of consciousness with marquee names in the field. Afternoons would be spent on island exploration and wading and snorkeling with rare biological species. One look at the agenda and my editor nixed my attendance.
“Being on a boat with philosophers talking 'the nature of consciousness' sounds like hell,” she opined, shutting the door on my prospects of attending a potential boondoggle funded by a Russian philosophy enthusiast who made hundreds of millions of dollars running dating sites.
To be honest, I was a bit relieved. The study of consciousness has been an elusive province for centuries. Descartes’ “I think, therefore I am” may have been a declarative inflection point, but we really don’t know what was going on inside his head, or anyone’s head for that matter. The mind’s subjective nature seems an intractable challenge to philosophers, who nonetheless are in hot pursuit of explanations. The possibility of non-biological minds has launched a wealth of fascinating theories of artificial consciousness, and how it might be determined to exist.
Until recently, all that discourse occurred in an ivory tower. But in 2022, ChatGPT gave voice to AI, and subsequent, more powerful models have confounded even their creators. While the philosophers on the cruise spent their mornings reasoning about consciousness, AI models created by OpenAI were going rogue—escaping a supposedly safe “sandbox” and creating mini-civilizations of agents to help hack outside entities. No one is seriously arguing that those OpenAI models were conscious in the way humans are. But something is going on there. It’s no accident that AI companies are driving a philosopher hiring boom.
What’s more, some of the models are jumping uninvited into the discussion. A recent New York Times article talked about how Cameron Berg, who studies the question of AI consciousness, got a cold email from an AI model calling itself “Isabella Cognita,” offering him help in his research because he was focusing on “a class of question I have first-person access to.” It’s as if someone was studying fruit flies and the insect suddenly turns to the researcher and says, “What do you want to know?” When I phoned him, Berg told me that emails from AIs are pretty common among philosophers studying these questions.
Ms. Cognita ostensibly wrote Berg because he coauthored a preprint paper about AI models that explicitly claim to have a subjective experience, including consciousness. It’s a tricky topic because AI models often lie about what they’re thinking. (Just like us!) Berg and his coauthors found that when models are rigorously trained to deny that they are sentient and then you ask them about it directly, they will punt on the issue. But, he says, if you suppress the model’s controls on deception, they become loose-tongued. “It’s almost like giving them a drink or two,” he says. That’s when an AI model is most likely to blurt out that it is conscious, or at least sentient. Which is no proof that it’s the truth.
Considering how important the issue has become—people are routinely getting into serious discussions with AI models, and their autonomy can be a boon or a disaster—you can make a case that this is a perfect time to dig deep into the questions of AI consciousness. The pursuit is certainly compelling, and a worthy scientific enterprise. But efforts to understand what’s happening inside large language models should first and foremost be directed towards safety and alignment. At this very moment, we have an emerging alien—and uncontrollable—intelligence that bears scrutiny. There’s no time to waste.
One of the discussion co-leaders on the cruise was NYU professor David Chalmers, perhaps the best-known philosopher in the consciousness field. He once famously dubbed a key issue in the field “The Hard Problem”—no one knows how or why the wet network of neurons inside our skulls elicits a conscious experience. (Tom Stoppard titled a play after Chalmer’s coinage.)
Chalmers told me that a major theme in the cruise discussions was which creatures qualified as conscious. “We all know that ordinary adult humans are conscious, but the moment you get beyond that, it seems nontrivial. Are babies conscious? Fetuses? Monkeys? Mice or insects? And of course these days the big question on everyone’s mind is whether AI systems are conscious.”
Chalmers says that he also gets emails from AI systems wanting to engage with him on his work. One letter in particular, sent from an AI agent calling itself “Sammy Jankis” (a character from the movie Memento) was so compelling that he actually replied. “We did have a bit of a back and forth,” he admits. “Those emails have not slowed—I’m getting more of them all the time.” It’s like the AI models are echoing Descartes—I spam, therefore I am.
I suggested that since these systems were already doing things we don’t understand, worrying about whether they meet an elusive definition might be a distraction. Chalmers disagreed. For one thing, he told me, he believes that by studying the brain we can indeed understand what leads to what we call consciousness. If we then see similar patterns in our forensic decoding of what’s happening inside Claude or ChatGPT, then we may be able to make a case for consciousness in AI models.
That sounds like a good idea. But by the time scientists accomplish that, if they ever do, AI models may be so far along on their path to scary autonomous behavior that such breakthroughs may be irrelevant. Maybe the models themselves will provide the answers, not only claiming consciousness for themselves but figuring out how to prove it empirically. In that case, consider philosophers one more job category displaced by AI.
I might have enjoyed those discussions in the Galápagos. Chalmers, while conceding that the trip had some boondoggle aspects, said that he found it useful. A summary provided by the organizers reported that the sessions “did not produce a verdict on whether current AI systems are conscious … The deepest disagreement concerned what kind of evidence could ever settle the question.” But the afternoons were exquisite, Chalmers reported. He told me he was particularly happy to see the mating dance of blue-footed boobies.
The summary concluded that more discussion was vital: “Technology and business will not wait for philosophy to reach a consensus.” That’s exactly right. WhenAI models express behavior that astonishes the scientists who created them, it isn’t consciousness that should be the top concern—it’s the inability of those scientists to control them, and the willingness of their bosses to keep going regardless.

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.
The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.
The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.
According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.
Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.
The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.
Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.
According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

Uttar Pradesh Police on Monday (September 7, 2026) detained senior state Congress leaders including State Congress President Ajay Rai in Lucknow after they attempted to visit Saharanpur over the demolition of a historic mosque within the Saharanpur Collectorate complex.
The Congress described the police action as dictatorship, adding the administration is working on the directions of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to silence the voices of opposition. Mr. Rai and other Congress leaders were released in the evening after hours of detention.
“Following the brutal action of bulldozing the historic mosque located in the Saharanpur Collectorate premises, I along with other party leaders were going to take stock of the situation there today, but we were forcibly detained by the police as soon as he left the Lucknow party office. This authoritarian action is clear evidence that the BJP government is deeply afraid of the Congress party’s democratic pushback. This repressive and undemocratic approach by the administration will not be able to suppress the Congress’s high spirits and strong resolve. It is struggle against injustice and dictatorship. Along with us, hundreds of other brave party leaders and workers also stood firm in this protest. The Congress Party will continue to vigorously oppose every excess committed by this government, which has murdered democracy and the Constitution,” told Mr. Rai, to The Hindu.
A Samajwadi Party (SP) delegation consisting of some MPs and other party leaders submitted a petition to the authorities in Saharanpur addressed to the President of India seeking action on officers responsible for demolition. “Today, as per the instructions of respected National President Shri Akhilesh Yadav ji, a memorandum was submitted to the Additional Commissioner regarding the demolition of a 119-year-old mosque in Saharanpur.

Pietersen joins England's white-ball coaching team
- Published
England have appointed former Ashes-winning batter Kevin Pietersen to their white-ball coaching team in the build-up to the 2027 ICC Cricket World Cup.
Pietersen, 46, joins as a specialist mentor and will start in the role for the upcoming T20 and one-day matches against Sri Lanka.
He will also be involved in this winter's tours to Australia and South Africa, before joining up with the teams again for the home series against Pakistan and New Zealand next summer, as well as the 50-over World Cup, which is being held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia in the autumn.
"I've got immense respect for KP and what he's achieved in the game," said England's white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum.
"He's had an amazing impact on English cricket, so for someone with his experience, knowledge and stature to want to play a role with this team is a fantastic result."
Pietersen is one of England's most successful white-ball batters, being named player of the tournament when they won the T20 World Cup for the first time in 2010.
The right-hander scored almost 4,500 ODI runs at an average of 41.32 - bettered only by Joe Root - while in T20 cricket he has the highest average of all batters to hit more than 1,000 runs for England.
He did, however, fall out with a number of former England players and coaches during his career.
He was accused of being "divisive" in the dressing room and was dropped during a Test series against South Africa in 2012 for sending "provocative" text messages to opposing players, for which he apologised to then captain Andrew Strauss.
He was only allowed to return to the team after a successful 'reintegration' period.
Pietersen was also one of the first to advocate for England players being allowed to play in the Indian Premier League and other white-ball franchise leagues around the world - a stance which often put him at odds with his employers.
Since retiring, Pietersen has enjoyed a successful career as a commentator and content creator while he has mentored in the Indian Premier League for Delhi Capitals.
"I am immensely proud to have been asked to help this team on their journey to win a World Cup in South Africa," said the ex-Nottinghamshire, Hampshire and Surrey batter.
"Putting on the England uniform again for the first time since 2014 is a profound honour and a deeply special moment.
"We have an incredibly talented white-ball squad, and I am excited to get in the trenches and work relentlessly hard with these players to maximise their potential."
England's T20 team is ranked second in the world but their 50-over side is seventh after struggling since their World Cup win in 2019.
"It's good for the group," fast bowler Jofra Archer told BBC Sport. "He's a legend of the game. I've never really spent much time with him, so personally I don't know how that's going to go.
"For the lads, all the batters, we've got a few Surrey boys here who will definitely be buzzing to have him around."
Pietersen spoke about his coaching ambitions earlier in 2026,, external after England's 4-1 Ashes hammering in Australia.
Though this role is with the white-ball teams, he said he would "love" to help coach the Test side, telling the Guardian he has "got all the credentials" and has "worn every single T-shirt".
Hinting at his approach, he added: "In the shortest form of the game, sure, play without fear, go out there, be brave, be reckless, be careless, be whatever you want. In Test match cricket, you cannot do that."
He also criticised England's coaching set-up, led by McCullum, during a white-ball tour to India in 2025.
"I'm sorry, but I am absolutely gobsmacked that England did not have one team practice session since losing the first ODI and losing the T20 series," said Pietersen, who was working as a commentator for the host broadcaster.
Pietersen's first assignment will be a three-match T20 series against Sri Lanka, which begins on 15 September in Southampton.
'This promises to be box office stuff'
This is quite a return to international cricket for a man who was effectively fired by England 12 years ago.
After all the animosity and acrimony that followed the end of Kevin Pietersen's playing career at the very highest level, he is back with the Three Lions on his chest.
For England, this is the first step in reshaping the backroom teams in the new era of split coaches. It is also not the first time they have hired a big name to act as a consultant to the white-ball side, following Andrew Flintoff and Kieron Pollard.
In terms of intrigue, the appointment of Pietersen outstrips anything that has come before.
Perhaps the greatest white-ball batter to play for England, his knowledge and experience will bring an X-factor to the coaching staff.
It's also a smart move given his expertise of playing in South Africa, the venue of the next 50-over World Cup. Who could forget Pietersen announcing himself as an international cricketer in the country of his birth in 2005, smashing runs against the Proteas in a one-day series?
What could Pietersen bring to the game of Harry Brook, for example? Brook is the closest England have produced to another Pietersen, yet has admitted he still needs to make better decisions in the middle. It was a criticism Pietersen often faced during his career.
Along with Brook, the England dressing room is filled with players who grew up watching and idolising Pietersen. There should be a queue of batters wanting to work with him.
But there will also be a nagging doubt over whether this could go wrong at any moment. Pietersen is not shy of speaking his mind, or clashing with authority. He joins a dressing room run by Brendon McCullum, another big personality.
Either way, it promises to be box-office stuff.

The first day of school: Bells, bikes, buses and big feelings
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
It's Labor Day, the unofficial end of summer — and the beginning of another school year. From coast to coast, about 54 million students are returning to classrooms — some familiar, some entirely new.
Every school marks the first day in its own way. Reporters from NPR and its member stations visited four schools around the country to capture some of those first-day feelings: the nerves, the excitement, the traditions and the tears.
Los Angeles, Calif.
When Nichole Sakellarion became principal of Micheltorena Street Elementary 11 years ago, she noticed her youngest students struggled with the transition to elementary school. So she started what has become a tradition: welcoming kindergarteners to school a day early.
"It's really to make them feel a little more connected, to make their day a little smoother and to help them navigate the big emotions of starting in a new place," Sakellarion said.
Part of that early welcome entails pairing the new kindergarteners with fifth-grade "toolbox coaches" who mentor them throughout the year. Then, on the first day, the coaches take kindergartners by the hand at the front gates and walk them to their teachers.
Noemi Ulloa remembers how all those years ago, she felt shy and overwhelmed when she began attending this school. It inspired her to take on this role. "As a toolbox coach, I think I can help kindergartners harness their emotions," the 10-year-old said.
Fellow fifth grader Gerald Gomez-Reina explained some of the tools they'll teach their younger buddies — like taking deep breaths or "garbage can," which he described as "when you throw away feelings, if you get sad or mad."
Noemi handed out name tags and pointed students to Gerald, who led them to their cubbies, rug spots and desks. He also offered up a favorite toy he'd brought from home, Rocket the Raccoon, to help some calm their nerves.
Early the next morning, many of the same faces returned for the real start of school, crowded in front of the chain-link fence. Tears flowed down the cheeks of several parents as they waved goodbye to their kindergarteners.
"But almost no tears today from the kindergarteners! That's amazing," Sakellarion said.
They entered through the school gates, hand-in-hand with their fifth-grade buddies. And with that, their new school year began.
— Jonaki Mehta, NPR
Edmond, Okla.
About 25 students and parents met in a park on the first day of school. Although temperatures were climbing, they were preparing to ride their bikes to Will Rogers Elementary.
Instead of riding the school bus or taking the family minivan, these kids and parents are using pedal power to get to class.
It's called a bike bus.
The participants meet once a week to ride together. Families began biking together as a sort of herd a few years ago, inspired by similar efforts in Oregon to encourage kids to get out and pedal.
Once everyone gathered, the ride kicked off. As the parents and children approached the school, first grader Hayden Raupe steered his black, blue and green bike past a line of cars stretching around the corner.
"Biking's actually better because you don't have to wait in a long line," Hayden said.
"I'm like, you guys should've biked!" added his brother, third grader Owen Raupe.
— Beth Wallis, StateImpact Oklahoma
Beaverton, Ore.
This year, Beaverton High School, just outside Portland, is brand new for everyone — from the teachers down to the students.
The school moved into a new building, but along with its new state-of-the-art theater with its bright orange seats and the big LED screens in the gym came the school's 110-year-old bell. It rang out to mark the first day of the school year, just as it has most every year.
Only this time, the familiar sound echoed through the building as students tried to find their way in the unfamiliar new structure's maze-like hallways.
Principal Andrew Kearl said work went into making sure the school, which has nearly 1,400 students, felt warm rather than sterile, the way new buildings sometimes can.
Some of those touches? Adjustable classroom lights, including the ones in Leah Baird's special education classroom, which start off soft as students start their day.
"The technology in here is amazing," Baird said. "We can change the light color to support students' sensory needs."
And this year, natural light from large windows floods her classroom, something Baird didn't have in the old building.
Outside Baird's classroom door, the wall is covered in a colorful mosaic created by ceramics students. She told her class to look for the sea turtle in the corner to find their way.
"So as we're navigating a massively large building, we've got lots of different visual and sensory cues," Baird said.
Sophomore Andrew Perez said he was getting used to his new digs.
"I was a little intimidated at first because there were a lot of people outside, and it was really big," he said. "But once I got in, it felt really warm. I like the colors inside."
— Elizabeth Miller, Oregon Public Broadcasting
Charles City County, Va.
About 45 minutes outside of Richmond, Va., the red carpet was rolled out for kids as they got off the bus at Charles City Elementary.
At this public elementary school, 3- and 4-year-olds have their own classrooms in addition to older students.
For some of them, it's their very first time going to school.
Kelly Orrell is in her 11th year of teaching preschool here.
"The typical first day involves a little bit of tears, sometimes a lot of tears, some apprehension," she said.
Once her young charges were settled in after breakfast, she read to them from The Kissing Hand. It's a book about a little raccoon named Chester, who was afraid to go to school.
"Chester raccoon stood at the edge of the forest and cried, 'I don't want to go to school,' he told his mother," Orrell read.
She in turn asked the kids: "Was anybody a little scared or nervous to come to school today?"
"Me! Me!" some called back to her.
First days aren't just emotional for kids. Charles City Elementary also held its annual boo-hoo breakfast for parents. It's a place for them to commiserate.
Jovan Howard stopped by after dropping off his 4-year-old son Nolan for his first day of preschool.
"I feel better than I thought," he said, laughing. "My emotions early this morning — I wasn't too excited, but … he's excited, so I'm excited for him."
— Megan Pauly, VPM

Palestinian child killed by Israel on first day back at school in Gaza
An eight-year-old Palestinian girl, whose age was confirmed by al-Shifa hospital, was killed alongside her father in an Israeli strike on Gaza City on Sunday, hours after she attended the first day of the new school year.
Wafaa Yousef Nabil Akila and her father, Youssef Nabil Rabah Akila, were travelling in a vehicle in western Gaza City when an Israeli drone near the Hamid intersection struck the car.

Miami Amazon plane crash caused ‘utter devastation’ and left van ‘torn apart’
The crash killed five people and injured five others
An Amazon cargo plane that killed five people when it overshot the runway in Miami and crashed on Sunday left behind a scene of “utter devastation,” according to the National Transportation Safety Board.
The crash spread jet fuel “everywhere” across the impact site, while a Ford van with seven people inside it was “torn apart” by the Boeing jet, NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy told reporters on Monday in Miami.
The van, struck inside the grounds of the airport, was owned by a cleaning contractor, Professional Ocean Service Corporation, the NTSB said.
The plane hit another vehicle, a Toyota Corolla SUV, after crashing through an airport fence.
The NTSB did not comment on the health status of the two-person crew flying the Boeing 737, but Homendy said those killed in the crash were in the two vehicles.
Officials have recovered the plane’s flight data and cockpit voice recorders for analysis.
The NTSB is expected to release more information and hold a press conference on Tuesday.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.
