When Apple debuts the next generation of iPhones this week, they’re likely to come with an unwanted change: a higher price tag. A price hike from the supply-chain powerhouse would be the clearest sign yet that soaring memory costs have become unavoidable — with no end to the memory crunch in sight.
Why the iPhone is about to get more expensive
Soaring RAM costs are driving up prices across the tech industry. It may take years to settle down.
Why the iPhone is about to get more expensive
Soaring RAM costs are driving up prices across the tech industry. It may take years to settle down.
Call it “chipflation” or “RAMageddon.” The shortage is reversing a decades-long decline in memory costs that helped make consumer electronics more powerful without making them dramatically more expensive. The terms “memory prices” and “memory shortage” appeared in 473 company transcripts last quarter, according to data provided by AlphaSense. The entire industry is seemingly working on the problem. And yet, we’re years away from seeing it fixed.
The common wisdom is that AI is at fault: The technology isn’t just contributing to higher energy prices and layoffs; it’s also helping drive up the cost of everything from smartphones to game consoles.
But the shortage was brewing well before ChatGPT took off — and was then amplified by AI’s unending hunger for RAM. The current market is the product of a complicated and very profitable reshuffling of the memory industry within a system that was already failing to keep up.
“We need to build more wafer capacity,” Manish Bhatia, president and COO of Micron — one of the three largest memory manufacturers — told The Verge. “[It’s] a very different challenge for the industry than it had been for many years before, where technology alone was able to keep up with the demand.”
For years, memory manufacturers could increase production by fitting more chips onto each wafer. But those gains were shrinking and taking longer to achieve. In 2021, even as pandemic-era electronics demand surged, Micron concluded that the problem was more fundamental: Technological advances alone would no longer create enough capacity to keep pace with long-term demand. Manufacturers would have to process more wafers — and build enormous new facilities to do it.
Then the memory business collapsed. Pandemic-era purchases of computers, tablets, and phones had pulled demand forward; consumer spending weakened, and manufacturers were left with excess inventory. They lost money and slowed their expansion plans.
By the time the market began recovering, generative AI had unleashed a wave of demand far larger and more memory-intensive than manufacturers had ever anticipated.
The memory business is also extraordinarily concentrated. Three manufacturers account for about 90 percent of the market, according to Counterpoint, leaving the world dependent on a handful of companies to divide limited capacity between AI infrastructure and consumer devices. Counterpoint estimates that Samsung controlled 39 percent of the memory market in the second quarter of 2026, followed by SK Hynix at 26 percent and Micron at 25 percent.
The memory inside your phone or computer broadly falls into two buckets. DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory, temporarily holds the information a device needs while opening apps, loading webpages, or running software. NAND flash memory provides longer-term storage for things like photos and files.
“It’s not as simple as saying data centers are consuming RAM. The RAM is not the same.”
Inside AI data centers, specialized processors rely heavily on a form of DRAM called high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.
“It’s not as simple as saying data centers are consuming RAM,” David Naranjo, associate director at Counterpoint, told The Verge. “The RAM is not the same.”
By stacking memory chips together and using advanced connections and packaging, HBM can move enormous quantities of data to and from those processors much faster and more efficiently.
It’s more difficult to produce, but also more lucrative to sell. Deep-pocketed AI chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD and tech giants like Meta and Microsoft have an insatiable need for it to power their AI systems — and are more than happy to pay.
HBM also consumes significantly more manufacturing capacity than conventional DRAM. Memory chips are made many at a time on large, circular silicon wafers. Because a finished HBM product stacks multiple, larger chips together, it requires considerably more silicon. Micron estimates that producing a given amount of HBM requires roughly three times as many wafers as producing the same amount of conventional DRAM.
The incentives increasingly favor AI. Rather than guessing how many phones or laptops will sell a year from now, memory makers can lock in multiyear commitments from some of the world’s richest companies.
“We have been engaging in discussions with customers, prioritizing those who can guarantee committed future captive demand,” Jaejune Kim, Samsung’s executive vice president of memory, said on the company’s last earnings call.
AI is also increasing demand for conventional DRAM. Phone and PC makers want to run smaller AI models directly on their devices, requiring more sophisticated conventional memory — and more of it. Future models may need substantially more memory than their predecessors to support those capabilities.
“The three big memory guys, they’re just basically allocating the capacity that they have to these companies.”
“As AI spreads across various services such as search, coding, and productivity tools, the scope of demand is widening from a memory perspective,” said Song Hyun-jong, president of SK Hynix, another of the big three memory manufacturers, on the company’s most recent earnings call. “We are witnessing a structural shift in demand where both AI memory and conventional memory are growing together.”
Samsung and Micron have both said they remain committed to conventional DRAM. Micron’s Bhatia told The Verge that it still accounts for most of the company’s wafer capacity. But limited supply, surging demand, and AI customers willing to make long-term commitments have made it extraordinarily lucrative to cede space to HBM.
SK Hynix posted a record 76 percent operating margin last quarter, up from 41 percent a year earlier, while Micron’s adjusted gross margin hit a record 85 percent. Samsung’s semiconductor profits, meanwhile, jumped roughly 250-fold from a year earlier.
“It’s more profitable,” Naranjo said. “The three big memory guys, they’re just basically allocating the capacity that they have to these companies.”
Counterpoint estimates that DRAM prices for smartphones increased roughly 56 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to a quarter earlier, and grew around 83 percent in the second quarter. For 16GB of DRAM for a smartphone, Counterpoint estimates that it cost roughly $42 in the second quarter of 2025 and about $181 a year later — an increase of more than 300 percent.
Those aren’t necessarily Apple’s prices — few companies have more leverage with suppliers — but the figures show how dramatically the component costs of building a high-end phone have changed.
The obvious solution is to make more memory. The problem is that it takes years to accomplish — even if you’re working fast.
Micron is currently demonstrating just how much work “more” entails.
In July, the company poured the first concrete for its planned manufacturing complex near Syracuse in upstate New York. Once completed, the site will contain 2.4 million square feet of cleanroom space, making it the largest semiconductor manufacturing site in US history by that measure — and Micron’s largest facility anywhere in the world.
Those cleanrooms where the chips are made will occupy only a fraction of the entire build, which is roughly the size of 350 football fields.
“By the time we’re done, we’ll have built probably 15 to 20 million actual square feet of building space to support the 2.4 million square feet of cleanroom,” Bhatia told The Verge. In one of Micron’s fab designs, the cleanroom occupies just one floor of a five-story building.
Micron doesn’t expect meaningful output until 2030
The remaining space will house a vast network of water-treatment, power, air-handling, and utility-distribution systems needed to keep it running.
Even though Micron reached the concrete pour ahead of schedule, it still took more than two years. The company began permitting after its CHIPS Act grant for New York was confirmed in March 2024, broke ground in January 2026, and poured concrete about six months later.
The physical construction unfolds in three broad stages. Preparing the ground can take six to nine months, Bhatia said. Building the concrete structure and facade can require another 18 months. But the most complicated stage comes after the building is standing: installing the vast network of mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and piping systems required to operate a semiconductor fab.
Those systems must turn an enormous industrial building into an environment where a single microscopic particle doesn’t land in the wrong place and ruin a chip.
Bhatia offered a sense of the precision required:
“Imagine trying to build all of New York state and not have any ants anywhere in the entire state,” he said. “That’s what we’re trying to do on every one of these wafers, and we do it over and over again.”
Completing the building still doesn’t produce memory. Micron expects to activate and test essential systems like power, water, and ventilation at the end of 2028, then spend 2029 moving in manufacturing equipment and beginning pilot production. The company doesn’t expect meaningful output until 2030. Even on an accelerated timeline, the journey from permitting to production will have taken roughly six years.
The company’s new Idaho fab is further along and is expected to begin wafer output in mid-2027.
Micron is spending enormous amounts to move the process along more quickly, roughly doubling its capital expenditure from a year earlier to exceed $25 billion this year.
Even with that investment, Micron can’t identify a clear point at which supply will catch up because demand continues to grow almost as quickly as manufacturers can expand.
“We’ve said that right now it’ll be beyond 2027, and we don’t see when it closes just because demand continues to grow so fast,” Bhatia said.
Counterpoint doesn’t expect capacity to catch up with demand until late 2027 or early 2028 in the best-case scenario. The market data firm IDC similarly expects the shortage to last through 2027 and well into early 2028 before there is meaningful relief.
PC and smartphone makers can’t absorb component costs that have multiplied several times over indefinitely. They can raise prices. They can make fewer devices. They can put less memory in them. Or they can focus on more expensive devices with enough profit margin to absorb the added cost.
Citing soaring memory costs, Microsoft recently raised Xbox prices by another $100 to $150, leaving some models as much as $300 more expensive than at launch. Microsoft also raised the price of some Surface Pro laptops and tablets by $500 over their original starting price. Meta, meanwhile, added $100 to the cost of its Quest 3 headset.
Apple is perhaps the most revealing test case because it should be among the companies best equipped to withstand the shortage. Its scale gives it extraordinary leverage with suppliers, and its customers have historically proved willing to pay premium prices. Yet Apple has already raised prices across its lineup of Macs and iPads.
Now attention is turning to the iPhone.
Rather than releasing its full lineup at once this fall, Apple is expected to introduce the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max alongside its first foldable iPhone, while holding the standard iPhone 18 and refreshed Air until spring 2027, according to Bloomberg.
Tim Cook described memory pricing as a “100-year flood”
That leaves Apple’s fall lineup concentrated heavily at the most expensive end of the market — exactly where it has the most room to protect its margins. Counterpoint’s supply-chain tracking shows Apple preparing roughly 10 percent more iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max units for September through December than it allocated to the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max during the same period last year.
On Apple’s last earnings call, the company forecast slower growth due partly to worsening supply constraints, including for memory chips, and said higher memory costs had directly reduced its gross margin. Then-CEO Tim Cook described memory pricing as a “100-year flood,” citing “exponential increases” that had caused Apple to raise prices.
The iPhone 18 Pro could start at $1,299, according to The Wall Street Journal’s calculation based on estimates from TechInsights that factor in component costs and attempt to minimize margin reductions. That would be $200 more than the iPhone 17 Pro. Samsung and Google have each raised the starting prices of some new phones by $100 this year, though several also come with more storage.
Apple may be better positioned than most companies to pull off higher prices. Its installed base, tightly integrated ecosystem, and loyal customers make its phones behave more like luxury goods than interchangeable electronics. The company has already gained market share by keeping its prices steady while lower-end competitors raised theirs. In places like China, the world’s largest smartphone market, it almost became common sense to opt for a premium iPhone when lower-cost alternatives were selling for nearly as much.
For other manufacturers, the options are worse.
Counterpoint and IDC are already seeing smartphone companies reduce expected shipments while shifting toward more expensive models. If they can’t sell as many phones, they can at least try to extract more revenue from each one.
That means more OLED displays, AI features, larger memory configurations, and other upgrades that can justify higher prices. As a result, revenue for PCs and smartphones could actually remain flat or even rise as unit sales decline.
In other words, AI isn’t just making electronics cost more. The memory shortage is changing which electronics companies bother making in the first place.
Eventually, more supply should arrive.
Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron are all investing heavily in additional manufacturing. But because new facilities take years to build, that spending won’t bring immediate relief.
SK Hynix is investing 600 trillion won in its Yongin Semiconductor Cluster, a massive complex south of Seoul first announced in 2019, and has accelerated its target for completion from 2045 to 2033. The company says it will double its capacity within five years but still expects demand to outpace supply through 2030.
Samsung and SK Hynix also plan to invest a combined 800 trillion won, or about $588 billion, in four new memory-chip factories in southwestern South Korea, according to The Wall Street Journal. Micron’s New York and Idaho projects are part of the more than $250 billion it says it will spend on US manufacturing and research through 2035.
A potentially important fourth player is also emerging in China. CXMT is building additional fabs, though its technology isn’t yet considered as advanced as that of Samsung, SK Hynix, or Micron. Apple is currently testing CXMT chips but would need approval from the Trump administration to do business with the company.
The other possibility is that supply won’t have to catch up because demand will collapse first. If the AI investment bubble bursts, memory manufacturers could suddenly find themselves facing very different economics.
For now, that remains hypothetical. The long-term contracts AI companies have signed with memory suppliers make the immediate future easier to predict.
“2027 is pretty locked and loaded,” Naranjo said.
Counterpoint and IDC expect price increases to slow from the breathtaking pace of the past year to single or low double digits. But slower increases aren’t the same as falling prices.
“Not to say prices will come down to 2025 levels, but the price increases will stabilize at a new normal,” Nabila Popal, a senior director at IDC, told The Verge. That new normal is “at least triple what they used to be.”
New fabs still take years to come online, while AI data centers and increasingly sophisticated consumer devices continue to require more memory. And manufacturers have little economic incentive to prioritize cheaper consumer electronics over customers willing to pay handsomely and commit years in advance.
Naranjo’s forecast was blunt.
“It’s not a happy ending anytime soon.”

A 27-second long video has gone viral on social media over the past week. The clip shows a mob, predominantly comprising men, kicking and attacking a woman in the middle of a busy street, while police personnel in the vicinity do little to nothing to prevent the attack.
The X user, Vikas Pokhariyal (@vikasindiafirst), posted the clip on August 31, claiming that a female Hindu teacher had been attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh. At the time of this article being written, the post had been reshared over 3000 times. (Archive)
Female Hindu teacher attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh pic.twitter.com/DQnvCjN8FK
— Vikas Pokhariyal (@vikasindiafirst) August 31, 2026
Pokhariyal later posted a reply to his tweet, attempting to correct his earlier claim. “Correction: The woman was reportedly assaulted by shopkeepers and salesmen after she complained about the shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law,” the tweet read.
Another X user, Deepak Sharma (@SonOfBharat7), posted the same clip, with a seperate claim that in Bangladesh, a Dalit teacher had allegedly offered water to an upper-caste Muslim child, following which she was chased down in the streets and thrashed. (Archive)
दलित मुश्लिम एकता 🔥
ऊँची जाति के मुस्लिम बच्चे को प्यास लगने पर
अपना पानी पिलाने वाली दलित शिक्षिका को सड़कों पे दौड़ा दौड़ा के कूटा…
मामला बांग्लादेश के ढाका के कुफ़न्ना इलाके का
जय जय भीम + मीम… जिओ शेरों ✊ pic.twitter.com/Iew8np2MDG
— Deepak Sharma (@SonOfBharat7) August 31, 2026
X user Yati Sharma (@yati_Official1) further amplified similar claims. (Archive)
बांग्लादेश में दलित हिंदू महिला शिक्षिका पर मुस्लिम कट्टर पंक्तियां द्वारा हमला। pic.twitter.com/W3ClKFtOFJ
— Yati Sharma (@yati_Official1) August 31, 2026
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claims surrounding the viral clip, Alt News broke it down into keyframes. A reverse image search on one keyframe led us to a news report published by the Bangladeshi news portal BD News 24 on August 30.
According to the report, the incident took place at Bangladesh’s Rajbari clothes market, on August 29. The victim in the video is reportedly a female shop owner, who managed her own clothing shop in the market for 12 years. She had allegedly found that one of her female employees had started working in a different shop on August 22. In response, she dismissed the worker from her role at the shop and asked her collect payment in the following month.
Further, another news report published by The Dhaka Tribune on August 30, identifies the female shop owner as one Zakia Sultana, and the ex-employee as Shahana Parveen Bristy. In another report by the outlet Ajker Patrika, Sultana accused Bristy of turning up at her shop with 15-20 men on August 23 and intimidating and verbally abusing her.
This prompted Sultana to launch a protest at the clothes market on August 29 afternoon, along with her female employees. Enraged by this, several shop-owners from the Rajbari clothes market then attacked her, in the presence of police officers who had turned up at the spot to offer her protection, the report states. However, in the video it is visible the that men continue to kick and attack Sultana despite police presence.
We also found a video report from BBC News Bangla, uploaded on August 31, which shows recorded evidence of the attack.
News reports from Bangla TV, Views Bangladesh, and Jago News 24, dated September 1, also reveal that three people have been arrested in relation to the violent attacks on Sultana, as recorded in the viral video.
In conclusion, the viral clip which shows a woman being violently attack is indeed from Bangladesh, but the woman seen in the clip is Muslim, thereby refuting any allegation of a communal angle at play.
Further, the reason for the attack arises from a business dispute as reported by several credible news outlets, thus the aforementioned claims, including that Sultana is a Dalit teacher who was beaten up for offering water to a Muslim child or that she complained about the other shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law, are false and misleading.

Tata Consultancy Services’ (TCS) data centre subsidiary, HyperVault, and its partners will invest up to ₹70,000 Cr to build and operate a large-scale AI data centre campus in Hyderabad with a capacity of up to 1 GW capacity. In a filing with the exchanges, TCS said that it has secured 264 acres of land in Hyderabad to develop the facility. Once completed, the campus aims to offer high-density, liquid-cooled compute workloads for frontier AI companies and hyperscalers. The project will be executed in phases according to the market demand. Once fully developed, the campus will likely rank among India's largest AI infrastructure sites, incorporating green energy and water-neutral design principles. As per the IT giant, the project will also generate several thousand direct and indirect jobs in the region. “HyperVault advances TCS’ infrastructure-to-intelligence strategy by bringing together AI-ready infrastructure with our cloud, engineering, enterprise transformation and AI capabilities,” said TCS managing director and CEO K Krithivasan. TCS established HyperVault in October last year to build AI-focussed data centres across India. In November 2025, the IT giant also brought in global investment firm TPG as a major investor and strategic partner to scale the new data centre subsidiary. At the time, the two companies said that they would invest up to ₹18,000 Cr (about $2 Bn) in a mix of equity and debt over the next few years in order to set up HyperVault’s data centres. Notably, HyperVault has also partnered with AI juggernaut OpenAI to build the latter’s AI infrastructure in India. TCS’ latest move underscores a broader shift among India’s legacy conglomerates, who are now building the local AI infrastructure layer. For instance, HCLTech has partnered with portfolio startup Sarvam to set up an AI data centre in Odisha, while L&T also has set up its Vyoma.AI subsidiary to build data centres and AI infrastructure. The Adani Group has also joined hands with US-based manufacturing company Jabil to build AI data centre infrastructure in India. Meanwhile, Reliance plans to invest up to ₹10 Lakh Cr in AI over the next seven years, including setting up a 168 MW AI-enabled data centre in Gujarat’s Jamnagar.

Germany's far-right achieves an electoral breakthrough in key state election
Germany's far-right party wins landslide victory but falls short of outright majority
BERLIN — Germany's populist, far-right Alternative for Germany party has declared victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt after more than doubling its share of the vote in the first of several regional elections this fall.
Falling just shy of an absolute majority, it's not yet clear whether the AfD will be able to govern the state of Saxony-Anhalt. But the outcome is already causing a political earthquake.
According to preliminary final results, the AfD won 43.8% of the vote — its strongest performance in any German state election, which puts the far-right party within reach of power for the first time since the time of Nazi Germany.
The center-right Christian Democratic Union more than halved its share of the vote, falling to a historic low of 17.2%. The centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) received 9.3%, the Greens 8.9%, and the Left party 8.6%.
All of these parties refuse to form a coalition with the AfD. But the AfD can come to power with the help of BSW, a small, anti-immigration, left-wing populist party. BSW got 5.3% of the vote on Sunday, potentially giving it enough seats to form a parliamentary majority with the AfD — something the party has not ruled out.
AfD's candidate for state governor, Ulrich Siegmund, said the result "sends a very clear signal to Berlin: this is the end of the line; people don't want to go on like this." 
"They want their good, old, secure Germany back," Siegmund told German public broadcaster, ARD.
Christian Democrat candidate Sven Schulze took to the stage on Sunday evening to congratulate the AfD on its win. While polls had shown the AfD with a comfortable lead for weeks, the CDU fared worse than predicted.
Whether Schulze will attempt to cobble together a "firewall" coalition — a platform by Germany's main political parties to keep the AfD out of government — is unclear. Such a strategy would require the Christian Democrats and others to work with the far-left party, Die Linke — something the conservatives refuse to do.
Addressing supporters, Schulze sounded resigned.
"Some say this is a dark day for Saxony-Anhalt. I say this is democracy," he said.
Alice Weidel, co-chair of AfD at the federal level, told public broadcaster ZDF that the CDU will never win another election. She said the AfD is seeing "explosive growth" across the country.
In Saxony-Anhalt, that growth is down to 35-year-old Siegmund, a former marketing executive and a salesman who, observers say, showed a knack for packaging his party's policies in positive slogans and pop-star-like appearances at campaign events and on TikTok.
His personable and amiable style is uncharacteristically upbeat for the AfD and he distinguishes himself from others in the party for being more happy-go-lucky than angry.
Germany's domestic intelligence classifies the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt as extremist. Its regional platform is the party's most radical and is seen by the AfD as a blueprint for the rest of Germany.
If Siegmund ends up as state governor, he will be privy to foreign and domestic intelligence, which is a major concern for the other parties considering the AfD's push to revive relations with Russia. Several state interior ministers from Germany's other 15 states say they are already preparing to meet separately.
At the top of their platform agenda is what the AfD calls its "remigration" policy, which promises mass deportations. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD on Sunday night, Siegmund spelled out the policy in more detail.
"Remigration is far more than just deportation," he said, adding that "remigration applies to anyone who does not contribute to society." He included Ukrainian refugees without jobs.
The AfD also wants to segregate refugees and disabled children in schools and revamp the curriculum to focus on what it refers to as a "more positive" teaching of Germany's history.
After the results, Siegmund declared: "We have made history in this country."
"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," he told supporters, "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."
On Sunday evening, President Trump posted a screenshot of the projected election results on Truth Social. Trump's post was shared by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who described the result as a "historic win."
The AfD has called for an end to support for Ukraine and seeking to revoke the refugee protections currently granted to Ukrainians.
Also among those hailing AfD's success was Tesla CEO Elon Musk. In response, Siegmund thanked Musk for his "support" and "clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time."
But neighboring Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk took a very different view, posting on X that "in Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany."
France's Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, described the election results as a "grave moment in Europe."

Who are the AfD? Germany’s far-right party on the brink of power in key state
The success of the far-right AfD is a ‘final warning’ to democratic parties, the winner of Germany’s election warns
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won an historic victory in state elections in the east of the country, delivering a fresh blow to Friedrich Merz’s ailing government and paving the way for the party to trial its radical policies.
The anti-immigration, pro-Russia AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, official results showed, falling short of an absolute majority with 39 of the 83 seats, while support for Merz’s CDU slumped to just 17.2%.
Both France and Poland reacted to the election results with alarm, while Russia’s presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev hailed an “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”.
The AfD was only formed in 2013 but is already the country’s most popular party at the national level. It has sought to secure a foothold for advancing its agenda, which includes heavy restrictions on immigration, better ties with Russia, and leaving the euro.
Leadership in Saxony-Anhalt could see sweeping reforms around migration, education, culture and family, offering a preview of the AfD’s plans for the country ahead of the 2029 national elections.
Alice Weidel, co-leader of the party at the national level, presented Sunday’s result as a milestone and said her party aimed to win at least 40 per cent in the upcoming federal elections.
What is the AfD?
The party Alternative for Germany (AfD) was first set up in 2013, with its initial manifesto focusing solely on dissolving the Eurozone and opposing bailouts for countries struggling with the debt crisis.
Founded by breakaway members of the conservative CDU party, it was initially dubbed a “party of professors” and veered away from harsh anti-migrant sentiment, crafting a reputational shield against accusations of extremism.
However, a series of leadership changes saw the party veer further into a hardline territory marked by its anti-migrant and anti-Islam stance, and rooted in nativism, following successes in regional elections.
Earlier this year, the party revealed some of its proposals for governance in a lengthy ‘programme’ for Saxony-Anhalt, detailing plans to clamp down on immigration, restore ties with Russia and support families of German origin.
The party outlined plans for a task force to expedite deportations, while the children of refugees would be placed in separate classes at schools.
They also said schools would be banned from flying rainbow flags, with the national flag raised daily instead. Schoolchildren would follow a curriculum built around a ‘patriotic cultural policy’ and be expected to sing the national anthem at school events.
An AfD state government would advocate for removing war refugee status for Ukrainians in Germany as long as the conflict remains concentrated in eastern Ukraine, arguing they should seek refuge in western Ukraine.
Since 2023, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency BfV has listed AfD as a suspected extremist organisation which requires surveillance, while classifying its youth wing Young Alternative as extremist.
The country’s mainstream parties have all refused to work with the AfD as part of a Brandmauer, or ‘firewall’, against the far-right. But none currently appear to be able to muster the popular support to defeat the party on their own.
What has AfD said about Islam and Nazism?
While it ostensibly began as a ‘party of professors’, by the time of the 2017 election - which saw the party enter the Bundestag for the first time with 12.6 per cent of the vote - AfD’s manifesto was claiming that “Islam does not belong in Germany”.
The party said that Germany’s Muslim population posed “a great danger to our state, our society and our system of values”.
The more recent proposals for Saxony-Anhalt promised an AfD state government would exhaust “all legal avenues” to limit Islamic expression.
The AfD dismisses accusations of extremism as scaremongering and an insult to the party's millions of supporters. But party members have shown sympathy for Germany’s Nazi past.
Bjorn Hocke, AfD’s leader in the eastern state of Thuringia, has twice been fined by a court for using the banned slogan “Alles für Deutschland” (Everything for Germany) during public speeches, which was engraved on the daggers of Nazi SA Stormtroopers.
Mr Hocke, whose branch won in state elections last September – marking the first such far-right victory in post-war Germany – has also described Berlin’s Holocaust Memorial as “a monument of shame”, and has called for a “180-degree turn” in how Germany remembers its past.
Alexander Gauland, an AfD co-founder and former leader, has claimed that Germans should “have the right to be proud of the achievements of the German soldiers in two world wars”.
The AfD’s rhetoric on immigration has also increasingly tested the boundaries of Germany’s post-war society.
Mass protests broke out in early 2024 amid calls from parliamentarians to ban the party, after a bombshell investigation exposed a secret meeting with far-right extremists in Potsdam to discuss the mass deportation of foreigners and “non-assimilated” Germans should the AfD win power.
But while AfD politicians initially denied the reports as a smear, the party began actively campaigning for “remigration” – deportations – just weeks later.
How has support for AfD grown?
Despite the efforts of the mainstream parties to contain the rise of the AfD, the party has gone from strength to strength in recent years.
The party won just 4.7 per cent of the vote in their first federal election in 2013. That had climbed to 12.6 per cent by 2017, before falling to 10.4 per cent in 2021, and then doubling to 20.8 per cent last year.
At the state level, victory in Saxony-Anhalt this weekend illustrates the simultaneous drop in support for Merz’s party on the centre-right, which has led the state for 24 years.
The AfD claimed 43.8 per cent of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago. Turnout was very high at 77.8 per cent and the party appeared to have won over many people who did not vote last time around.
Once previously the party won a state election in neighbouring Thuringia but did not end up governing, as a CDU governor took power with a minority government.
CDU state candidate Sven Schulze attributed part of his party's poor performance over the weekend to developments in Berlin, where Merz — the most unpopular chancellor in German history — is struggling to revive Germany's sluggish economic growth.
Merz faces more state elections in the coming weeks and into next year, though he hopes his mix of reforms and higher spending in some areas will revive growth in Europe's largest economy.
The euro was little changed in Monday trade but analysts are closely monitoring the surge in support for far-right parties across Europe, noting that the AfD wants to take Germany out of the common currency.

South African among workers abducted after attack on hunting camp in Mozambique
A South African national was among a group of workers abducted in Mozambique during an attack by insurgents on a hunting camp, South Africa’s foreign ministry said on Monday
JOHANNESBURG -- A South African man was among a group of up to 20 workers abducted in Mozambique during an attack by insurgents on a hunting camp, South Africa’s foreign ministry said Monday.
The Department of International Relations and Cooperation said the 30-year-old man was among five South Africans working at the wildlife reserve who were caught up in last week's attack. Of the other four, two had returned to South Africa, and two remained safe in Mozambique.
“Embassy officials are working with Mozambican authorities and are monitoring the situation and developments in Niassa Province,” the department told told The Associated Press.
Three U.S. citizens are thought to have been evacuated from the area.
The attack is thought to have been carried out by militants linked to the Islamic State group, which launched an insurgency in neighboring Cabo Delgado province in 2017.
The U.S. Embassy in Mozambique, which acknowledged the attack in a statement, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Local police said at least 11 people, including children, were abducted during the attack on the town of Marangira, in Niassa province. It wasn't immediately clear why there was a discrepancy in the number of people abducted between South African and Mozambican authorities.
Police spokesperson Osvaldo Mahando told local media that one person was killed, another slightly injured, and vehicles were burned in the attack.
Security forces were patrolling nearby forests, he said.
The insurgency has destabilized northern Mozambique, killing thousands and forcing more than 1 million people to flee their homes, according to the United Nations. The militants have also carried out attacks in the neighboring Niassa and Nampula provinces.
Mozambique’s state news agency, Agencia de Informacao de Mocambique (AIM), reported that the attackers looted and burned a hunting camp and damaged a health center, police post and telecommunications tower.
Citing provincial government figures, AIM said the attack forced thousands to flee and about 2,000 people were initially given shelter.
The attack prompted the U.S. Embassy to advise Americans to avoid the Niassa Special Reserve and areas near the Niassa-Cabo Delgado border.
Peter Bofin, a regional expert at the conflict monitoring group Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the latest attack marked the group’s first incursion into Niassa since May 2025.
Although Bofin said the raid was probably an isolated operation rather than evidence of a sustained presence in Niassa, he said it demonstrated the militants’ mobility.
“The ability of one group of ISM (Islamic State Mozambique) fighters to enter Niassa and undertake that attack highlights that ISM still has an advantage in maneuverability in rural areas,” he said.
Bofin said the camp offered an opportunity to seize supplies and strike an important economic target, undermining confidence in the government’s control of the region.

Bleecker Street has released a teaser-trailer for Alex Gibney’s highly anticipated documentary Musk, and it’s not a flattering portrait of the SpaceX, Tesla, Starlink honcho and X owner.
Yes, the teaser begins with voices of some people heaping praise on Elon Musk – one idolator roaring he’s “the greatest capitalist in history!” But those encomiums are quickly followed by harsher appraisals from Musk observers: “He’s chaotic, random, capricious,” says one. Another offers, “He is manifestly cruel and selfish.” Yet another observes, “In a science fiction novel, he would not be a hero.”
Watch the teaser-trailer above.
Watch on Deadline
Gibney’s film, which premieres Tuesday at the Venice Film Festival, clocks in at just under 4 hours. He and Musk have already tangled on the X/Twitter platform, with the mega-billionaire branding him a “douche.” (To which Gibney amusingly retorted, “Douché.”). Leaving epithets aside, what can be said about Gibney is that he is one of documentary’s most respected figures, and the Oscar-winning director of Taxi to the Dark Side, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief, Steve Jobs: The Man in the Machine, Zero Days and many other documentaries.
RELATED: Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews
It’s perhaps worth noting that Gibney enjoys the backing of a multi-billionaire too – Wendy Schmidt, who bought a controlling interest in Gibney’s production company, Jigsaw Productions in 2025.
After Venice, Musk heads to the Toronto Film Festival. Bleecker Street plans to release it theatrically on October 16, with HBO debuting the film on premium cable and the HBO Max streaming platform after that. The documentary is expected to make a strong bid for Academy Award recognition.
RELATED: Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews
In 2024, Gibney appeared on Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast and gave us something of a preview of the film.
“He is a larger-than-life figure,” he said of Musk. “People have their opinions about him, but I think the challenge… is to bring something that people don’t expect to find, something in the material that’s hiding, some stuff that’s hiding in plain sight, which is what I’d say we are finding that I think will be surprising for folks. And it’s not just like, is it Elon thumbs up or Elon thumbs down? I’m not really interested in that kind of formula, douche or not. But it’s more like, what do we really think about how he operates? And I’m pretty confident that what we’re coming up with will be illuminating and also kind of formally innovative. We’re really going to have fun with this.”
Watch the teaser-trailer for Musk above.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

Can Kane buck history and win Ballon d'Or?
- Published
With the Ballon d'Or shortlist to be announced tomorrow, Harry Kane heads the field as the bookmakers' favourite after a prolific season for club and country. History, however, suggests football's biggest individual prize is rarely decided on goals alone.
Since the Ballon d'Or was first awarded in 1956, performances in the game's biggest competitions have consistently shaped the outcome.
World Cup years, in particular, have followed a remarkably clear pattern and recent editions have shown just how difficult it is to win the award without lifting a major global or continental tournament.
Once the nominees are announced, an international jury of specialised journalists will cast their votes, with one representative per country from the men's top 100 having their say.
So, can Kane, who has never finished higher than 10th in the battle to be the world's best player, become one of the rare exceptions?
- This could be year I win Ballon d'Or, says Mbappe 
  - Published3 hours ago
- 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it 
  - Published3 days ago
The World Cup effect
Created by France Football journalist Gabriel Hanot, the Ballon d'Or was first presented in 1956, with England's Sir Stanley Matthews the inaugural winner. Originally voted for by journalists, the award was restricted to European players until eligibility was expanded to all nationalities in 1995.
Raymond Kopa became the first Ballon d'Or winner in a World Cup year after helping France reach the 1958 semi-finals. To mark the award's 60th anniversary in 2016, France Football revisited every pre-1995 edition, external. Its retrospective review concluded Pele would have claimed the award after inspiring Brazil to their first World Cup triumph at the age of 17.
Four years later, Josef Masopust officially won the Ballon d'Or after captaining Czechoslovakia to the World Cup final. Again, France Football judged Brazil's Garrincha to have been the standout performer after leading his country to successive World Cup titles.
It reached the same verdict for Pele in 1970 after he inspired Brazil to a third World Cup crown. By then, a clear pattern had emerged. Bobby Charlton (1966), Paolo Rossi (1982), Lothar Matthaus (1990), Zinedine Zidane (1998), Ronaldo (2002) and Fabio Cannavaro (2006) all won the Ballon d'Or after lifting the World Cup.
Even among the official exceptions, players still tended to enjoy deep runs at the tournament. Johan Cruyff collected the Ballon d'Or after leading the Netherlands to the 1974 World Cup final, while Luka Modric repeated the feat with Croatia in 2018.
World Cup success has never been an absolute requirement. Kevin Keegan won the 1978 Ballon d'Or despite England failing to qualify for the World Cup, although France Football later concluded Argentina striker Mario Kempes would have been the deserving winner after finishing as the tournament's top scorer and helping the hosts lift the trophy. The publication reached the same verdict for World Cup winners Diego Maradona in 1986 and Romario in 1994.
France Football's review ultimately reinforced the World Cup's influence on the Ballon d'Or. In essence, had the prize always been open to players from all countries, each South American World Cup-winning side between 1958 and 1994 would have supplied the winner.
The biggest prizes matter
The World Cup is not the only competition to shape Ballon d'Or voting.
Recent history suggests success in one of football's biggest tournaments has become almost a prerequisite. Only four of the previous 19 Ballon d'Or winners failed to lift either the Champions League, World Cup, European Championship or Copa America during the year of their triumph.
Those exceptions underline just how extraordinary Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo had to be. Messi won despite Argentina's quarter-final exit at the 2010 World Cup, and again in 2012 and 2019 without lifting a major international or continental trophy.
Ronaldo also prevailed in 2013 after Portugal failed to progress beyond the World Cup play-offs, thanks largely to another remarkable individual season with Real Madrid.
Conversely, Wesley Sneijder's treble with Inter Milan and run to the 2010 World Cup final, Franck Ribery's role in Bayern Munich's 2013 treble and Mohamed Salah's record-breaking 2017-18 season all proved insufficient when voters favoured different narratives.
Rightly or wrongly, modern Ballon d'Or voting has consistently rewarded football's biggest occasions. That presents Kane with another obstacle.
Unlike Ronaldo in 2014 or Luka Modric in 2018, he cannot point to Champions League glory as Bayern Munich's European campaign ended in the semi-finals against eventual winners Paris St-Germain.
Nor is he alone, with Erling Haaland, Kylian Mbappe, Michael Olise, Declan Rice and Jude Bellingham all potential rivals and attempting to buck one of the award's strongest recent trends.
Why Kane's case is different
History points towards major honours being important to winning the Ballon d'Or but Kane's 2025-26 season suggests this may not be a typical race.
The England captain scored 73 goals for club and country - 61 for Bayern Munich and 12 for England - in a season in which Bayern won the Bundesliga and DFB-Pokal and England finished third at the World Cup.
Among players representing clubs from Europe's top five leagues, only Messi has scored more goals for club and country in a single season, the Argentine striking 82 times for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane's tally places him ahead of Bayern great Gerd Muller (72 in 1972-73), Cristiano Ronaldo (66 in both 2011-12 and 2014-15), Ronaldo (66 in 1996-97), Haaland (64 in 2022-23) and Luis Suarez (64 in 2015-16).
Kane or Spain?
Voters might face a familiar dilemma.
Rodri appears Kane's strongest rival. The former Ballon d'Or winner was arguably Spain's standout performer throughout the tournament, collecting the Golden Ball after helping his country secure a second World Cup title.
Lamine Yamal also added a World Cup winner's medal to a season in which he helped Barcelona reclaim La Liga, although it was teenage team-mate Pau Cubarsi who claimed the Fifa Young Player Award after a series of outstanding performances.
Mbappe and Messi are also expected to feature prominently. Mbappe finished as the World Cup's top scorer with 10 goals, while also claiming the Champions League Golden Boot and La Liga's top scorer trophy, despite France falling short of the final and Real Madrid ending the season without a major honour. Messi, meanwhile, captained Argentina to a second successive World Cup final and at the age of 39 scored eight goals during the tournament.
Should Kane prevail, he would become only the fifth Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or after Matthews, Charlton, Keegan and Michael Owen. He would also become the first player representing a Bundesliga club to lift the trophy since Matthias Sammer in 1996.
History suggests the odds remain stacked against him but few players have entered a Ballon d'Or election with stronger individual credentials.
Voters must now decide if one of the most prolific goalscoring seasons of the modern era outweighs football's biggest prizes, and if Kane can join one of the most exclusive groups in Ballon d'Or history.

While scrutinising caste status, the authorities must adopt a lenient approach and not expect a Scheduled Caste (SC) or Scheduled Tribe (ST) member to prove their case like an ordinary citizen, observed the Kerala High Court.
The Division Bench of Justices A.K. Jayasankaran Nambiar and A.K. Preetha held that the authorities should look at the overall circumstances, including the extension of social security benefits to other family members and extended family.
V. Balan of Thrissur, a retired postal assistant, had approached the Division Bench challenging the order of a Single Bench, which had held that he had not provided enough evidence to back his claims regarding his caste status.
He obtained regular appointment as postman in 1980 under the ST quota based on a caste certificate issued by a tahsildar showing him as belonging to the Malai Pandaram community. During his service, a Vigilance inquiry was conducted into the genuineness of his caste status at the request of his employers, the postal service. The inquiry concluded that Mr. Balan belonged to the Pandaram (Veera Saiva) community, part of the Other Backward Classes, and not the Malai Pandaram community, as he claimed.
The report submitted to the Scrutiny Committee for Verification of SC/ST Claims declared that his family members would not be eligible for benefits reserved exclusively for ST members.
While considering Mr. Balan’s petition against the committee’s action, the single judge held that the Vigilance report was filed after a detailed anthropological study, and there was no scope to interfere.
Mr. Balan argued before the Division Bench that the committee initiated proceedings against him without considering his detailed objections, and that the documents which were used to determine his caste status were never provided to him.
The court said that the denial of constitutionally guaranteed privileges to members of SC/ST communities must only be in exceptional cases of apparent fraud that is established through material independently available to the State, including proof of the alleged fraud, if any, committed by the authorities who issued the caste certificate based on which the person concerned obtained the service benefits.

The U.S. Postal Service said on its website that it handles prepaid and stamped mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services.
In September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that adding postage to a prepaid mail-in ballot would "force" the U.S. Postal Service to treat it as first-class mail, a service that allows postcards and small envelopes to be delivered in one to five days.
The claim circulated as states began sending out mail-in ballots for the 2026 midterm elections, despite the Trump administration's ongoing court battles to enforce an executive order that would restrict voting by mail.
One Threads user who shared the claim wrote:
By adding a 1st Class Postage Stamp to your postage prepaid ballot, it will then force USPS to handle it as 1st Class Mail, instead of Bulk Mail! SHARE EVERYWHERE!
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true.
The claim was false. According to the USPS, the service always handles mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services. In other words, adding additional postage will not expedite the delivery of a standard mail-in ballot.
The USPS included the following message on its webpage about "Election Mail" (emphasis ours):
Mailpieces containing a completed ballot are handled as First-Class Mail® service, regardless of whether they are prepaid by election officials or mailed with a stamp affixed by the voter. The only situation where a completed ballot is not handled as First-Class Mail is when the voter opts to pay for a premium service like Priority Mail® service or Priority Mail Express® service.
Who pays postage on a mail-in ballot varies by state. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan, nonprofit organization that represents lawmakers in the 50 U.S. states, 19 states and Washington, D.C. require local election officials to pay postage while voters in other states must pay.
In a June 2026 FAQ, the USPS said its policy directs employees to deliver ballots with insufficient postage and attempt to recoup the payment from the local election board.
Mail-in ballot return deadlines vary by state. The USPS advises that voters mail their ballots "before Election Day, and at least one week prior to the deadline by which your completed ballot must be received by your election office."
Voters can check deadlines for returning mail-in ballots with their local election office. Some states also allow voters to deliver completed ballots to drop boxes that are emptied by election officials, which eliminates the need to use the postal service to vote.
At the time of this writing, the Trump administration sought to implement new federal regulations on mail-in ballots that could require states to submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal and follow a uniform envelope style. In an August 24, 2026, opinion, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to proceed with implementing the proposed regulations but did not rule on whether they were legal.
The Associated Press reported that "legal wrangling" continued over Trump's executive order in lower courts. Therefore, it was unclear at the time of this writing if, or how, the proposed changes to mail voting would affect the 2026 midterm elections.
Despite having previously voted by mail himself, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized mail voting, including after he lost the 2020 presidential election.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Every year, the question returns: Has Burning Man lost its edge?
First tech billionaires turned the desert oasis into their playground. Then the festival's younger crowd began to thin. Burning Man has been deemed uncool by Gen Z: In 2025, 10% of surveyed attendees were in their 20s, down from more than 30% in 2015.
And still, an estimated 70,000 made the pilgrimage to Black Rock City this year, braving dust storms and the logistical gymnastics of surviving for a week in the desert.
Maybe Burning Man is no longer the cutting-edge counterculture experiment it once was. But the art cars still rolled, the costumes still glittered, and the playa still became home to a group of revelers unlike any other. These photos offer a glimpse of what it looked like in 2026.
Additional reporting by Katherine Li.
For decades, a city has risen at summer's end on a remote stretch of Nevada desert.
Burners call this temporary metropolis 'Black Rock City.'
Roughly 70,000 people were expected to attend the art and music festival this year.
They hauled the food, water, shelter, and supplies needed to survive a week.
The 'mutant vehicles' were a sight to see.
Rain and heavy winds forced the gates closed on the first day.
Mud has dogged the festival in recent years.
These resourceful burners got creative with their footwear.
The weather didn't appear to dampen the mood.
Some of the fashion channeled 'Dune.'
Goggles were a practical accessory.
The Man structure rose above the Cryptomeria, a treehouse-like pavilion at the center.
Art installations took shape across the playa.
'Titantic's End' showed two halves of a massive ocean liner sinking into the dry lake bed.
Gazelle Dasti's artwork, 'Zarvan,' links Persian culture and the idea of endless time.
Burners escaped the heat under an acre-wide canopy at the festival's center.
Organizers issued a new rule this year.
Smart glasses were allowed. But wearers needed to ask permission from anyone who might appear in the recording.
A Burning Man Project spokesperson told Business Insider that its privacy and consent rules are not new, but that it recently updated its guidance to explicitly include smart eyewear as the technology has evolved.

Held from 15 June 2026 to 30 June 2026, Drug-Free India Awareness Quiz 2.0 and 1 July 2026 to 15 July 2026, Drug-Free India Awareness Quiz 3.0 received an overwhelming response from citizens across the country. A total of 17,345 participants joined the quiz contests, showcasing their commitment to learning about the dangers of drug abuse, reporting drug trafficking on MANAS Helpline 1933 and understanding how they can seek timely support, guidance, and rehabilitation assistance through the helpline.
The quiz aimed to empower citizens with the right information, bust myths about drug addiction, and promote a collective responsibility to fight against drugs.

A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found.
Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.
These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.
There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.
“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.
“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”
Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground.
More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.
Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week.
After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
The death toll from the unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 people are missing.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.
New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.
In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.
“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …
“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”
| US access to Australian defence facilities |  | 
|---|---|
| Access level | Facilities | 
|---|---|
| United States-controlled facilities with Australian access | 17 | 
| Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access | 24 | 
| Australian facilities with US military access | 51 | 
| Australian facilities with US corporate access | 18 | 
| Australian facilities with no significant US access | 41 | 
| Australian facilities with US access unresolved | 17 | 
‘Aligning ourselves completely’
The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:
- 
  Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.
- 
  Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.
- 
  Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.
- 
  Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.
Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.
Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.
Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.
Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.
Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.
Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.
Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.
The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.
Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.
The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.
The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.
Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.
“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.
“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”
Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.
“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”
There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.
Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.
“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”
‘Waltzing its way into a war’
At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.
Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.
“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.
Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.
Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.
“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”
Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.
The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.
But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.
The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.
Australians’ fragile faith
Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.
But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.
A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.
Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.
Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).
Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.
Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).
More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.
This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.
“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”
Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.
“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.
“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”
Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.
“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”
She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.
“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”
Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.
“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.
Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.
“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.
“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”
Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”
- 
  The Australian bases & US involvement database is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

Iran-US war latest: Tehran vows to extend ‘exclusion zone’ near Strait of Hormuz after US strikes on tankers
Centcom denies Iran's claims of successful attack on a US military vessel as a ‘total lie’
Iran has said Tehran plans to establish an “exclusion zone” outside the Strait of Hormuz targeting vessels it believes are attempting to transit the strategic waterway.
The new head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, said the zone would be declared in the coming days and would stretch for some distance on either side of the Strait "begin[ning] from the line of the US naval blockade".
It comes as the US and Iran have traded strikes on ships, the latest round of attacks since the conflict flared a week ago after a period of relative calm.
US Central Command said it struck three Iranian oil tankers, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near the nation’s oil export hub, after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against US military vessels in the region, and later said it targeted three tankers that Tehran claimed were on unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three US-linked vessels in other areas.
Iran's claims to have successfully struck an uncrewed US military vessel were a "total lie", however, according to a Centcom spokesperson.

The chancellor has warned that the Budget in the autumn could be tough, as Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East affects the British economy.
