In Summary
- The Live 780NC are the latest headphones in JBL’s premium mid-segment Live series of wireless ANC headphones.
- Featuring a different design from their predecessors as well as some flashy colors, the JBL Live 780NC boast good mainstream sound as well as a number of smart features.
- Priced officially at Rs 15,999 (but available at lower prices), the JBL Live 780NC are one of the best pairs of headphones one can get for about Rs 15,000 in the Indian market.
They let you not only pump up the bass or turn up the treble of the audio playing on them but can also add bass and treble to your voice and the person you are talking to during phone calls. They come with good ANC that adjusts itself to your surroundings and come with very good battery life. Get them in orange, and you can be assured of being the center of attention in every room. All this at a price of USD 199/Rs 15,999. But can these features (and many others) and that price tag help the JBL Live 780NC become the perfect headphones for those who want a lot of sound and smarts, without parting with a truly premium price?
Table of Contents
JBL Live 780NC Looks: Comfortable and delightfully colorful
The JBL Live 780NC can look smart or spectacular depending on the shade you choose. We got the very elegant Black ones, which are at home everywhere, from cafes to campuses to corporate offices, but the Purple, Green, or Orange will definitely turn heads, thanks to their unusually bright shades. They follow the classic over-ear headphone design, with a band connecting two earcups, but look different from their predecessors, the Live 770NC.
The headband of the Live 770NC was of the same thickness throughout, whereas the band of the Live 780NC becomes thinner as it nears the earcups, giving it a sleeker and more contemporary look. There is plenty of cushioning on the earpads as well as the headband. There’s plenty of JBL branding too, which appears on the earcups and headband, but as the lettering is in the same color as the headphones, it does not get overwhelming. The earcups have left and right printed inside them, which is always better than having tiny letters on the frame.
The right earcup has the sliding on/off and connectivity button, as well as a button for switching between ANC and Ambient Aware mode, as well as a Type-C port. The volume controls are on the left earcup. The outer part of the right earcup is also a touch panel. There is no 3.5 mm audio jack, but a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable in the box lets one use the headphones with a device with a 3.5 mm audio jack.
The headphones are mostly made of plastic but have metal hinges, and best of all, fold all the way inwards, making them very easy to bunch up and carry. There is a rather basic cloth bag in the box, which is not as good as a case but should suffice for most of us. At 260 grams, the JBL Live 780NC are not exactly super light (the Sony WH-CH 720N are the bosses there at 192 grams), but not uncomfortably heavy either. We have worn them for 3-4 hours without ever feeling too burdened. All the padding in the ear cushions and headband makes them very comfortable to wear, and the clamping force is just right – tight enough to let us move our head without making the headphones wobble, and loose enough to never make us feel squeezed in the head.
The JBL 780NC have a very solid and substantial feel to them. But they come with no dust or water resistance, so we would advise due caution while using them in the gym or using them for running sessions.
JBL Live 780NC Specs and Features: An impressive feature list
The JBL Live 780NC come with a very good spec and feature lineup. Sound is handled by 40 mm drivers, which deliver the famous mainstream JBL Signature Sound. Also on board are support for high-quality LDAC, adaptive ANC, six microphones (most headphones in this price have four), spatial audio, and a number of smart features, such as ear detection (audio pauses when you remove the headphones) and an AI-trained algorithm for clearer calls.
On the connectivity front, they come with Bluetooth 6.0, multi-point connectivity, and support for Auracast (so one can listen to public broadcasts and announcements wirelessly). They also boast a battery life of 80 hours (without ANC) and support fast charging. There is no charging cable in the box, though one does get a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable and a basic cloth carry bag. On the software side, the headphones work with the JBL Headphones companion app, which gives one access to a number of features as well as detailed equalizers and regular software updates. For their price, the JBL Live 780NC are pretty well stacked in the spec and feature department.
JBL Live 780NC Controls and Interface: Buttons for some, touch for others
Connecting the JBL 780NC is as simple as putting them in pairing mode (just slide the on/off button towards the Bluetooth icon) and selecting them on the other device’s Bluetooth device list. To experience all their features, however, one should also connect them via the JBL Headphones app, which is available for both iOS and Android. While connecting the headphones is simple, the app takes some time to recognize them every time it connects to them, which can be a little irritating.
The JBL Live 780NC controls are a blend of physical buttons and touch, although the touch works only on the right earcup. A single tap on the earcup pauses audio and also resumes playing it; a double tap takes one to the next track; a triple tap takes one to the previous track, while tapping and holding accesses the voice assistant. A double tap can also enable one to take or end a call, while tapping and holding rejects an incoming call. One can customize the touch controls to an extent, and add options to access equalizer settings and spatial audio, although there is no way to access ANC or volumes through touch – those are accessed through buttons on the earcups.
The combination of touch and buttons controls works well enough, once one gets the hang of them – we kept forgetting that touch worked only on the right earcup, and ended up tapping the left one initially, out of habit.
JBL Live 780NC Performance: Super audio, decent ANC and great smart touches
Most users will love the warm and detailed sound that the JBL Live 780NC deliver. While there is an emphasis on bass, it does not overwhelm the vocals. Those who want a sharper sound can tweak the equalizer in the app (move it to ‘Jazz,’ we suggest) to enhance treble, but most users will love the sound of these headphones right out of the box. Enabling spatial audio makes the sound a little more airy, although the absence of head tracking gives one much more of a “sitting in a room with the music” feels. There are three kinds of spatial audio – Movie, Music and Game – and although there is not much difference between Movie and Game, Music is rather different and seems to add slightly more detail to the sound. One can also use the Person-fi feature to let the app personalize a sound signature for it, although we were not too convinced by it.
The app allows one to tweak the sound significantly. LE Audio makes a huge difference to audio quality whenever supported (although turning it on and off requires restarting the app), adding greater detail and depth to sound. One can also choose from six equalizer settings – a relatively plain Studio, a thump-friendly Bass, a rumbling Club, a boosted bass Extreme Bass, a mids-stressing Vocal, and a treble-oriented Jazz. There is also the option to completely come up with one’s own EQ setting under the My EQ option. Most mainstream users will prefer the Bass setting, while purists will like either Studio or Jazz. One can also adjust the balance of sound between the right and left earcups, although we found no reason to do so.
The JBL Live 780NC are perfect for mainstream audio, whether one wants to listen to pop, trance or rock, or watch a film, play games or just lend an ear to podcasts. At their price, they are perhaps the best-sounding wireless ANC headphones out there.
JBL Live 780NC ANC and calls: Super sound over calls, decent sounds of silence
The JBL Live 780NC come with adaptive ANC. You can either specify the level of ANC you want using a slider, or enable Adaptive ANC and let the headphones decide the level. We suggest simply keeping it at maximum. Noise canceling on the headphones is good for their price. Of course, one does not get the kind of ANC that comes on Sony and Bose flagships; the Live 780NC do enough to dull a lot of the traffic sound, kill the hum of the Metro, and can even make a noisy cafe a little quieter.
Call quality is where the Live 780NC shine. Not only do they handle calls very well, with very good levels of clarity, but the app even lets you adjust the tone of the person you are speaking to and your own voice as well. You can actually add more bass or treble to both sides of the conversation on the JBL Live 780NC. The headphones are also able to keep out a fair bit of the ambient noise – we have used them on auto rickshaw rides, with the person we are speaking to not even realizing that we are in the midst of noisy traffic. That AI algorithm for clear calls definitely helps.
JBL Live 780NC Battery life: Charge them once a week only!
JBL claims that the headphones come with 80 hours of battery life without ANC and 50 hours with ANC. We mostly used them with ANC – it does not affect audio quality, apart from making it a little more bass-y – and got a comfortable 40-45 hours of battery life (we admit to hearing them at slightly higher volumes). In practical terms, charging them once easily got us through close to a week of hectic use, where we used them for everything from making calls to listening to music to watching videos, shorts, and reels to playing games. That makes them great daily drivers.
The headphones charge off their USB Type-C port and take about two hours to charge from empty to full. They also come with a fast-charging function that gave us about four hours of audio listening after being charged for five minutes. One can tweak the power settings for the headphones to switch off automatically after 30 minutes, an hour, or two hours, to further conserve power. There is no charging cable in the box, but any Type-C charging cable should work just fine with it.
JBL Live 780NC Review Verdict: In a zone of their own in the Rs 15,000 segment
The headphones are priced at Rs 15,999, but are often available at lower prices (they are available on Amazon India at Rs 14,999 even as this is being written). Their closest competitors are the Sony ULT Wear, which are now available at close to Rs 15,000 but have a very bass-centric sound. The ULT Wear have better ANC than the Live 780NC, but the Live 780NC beat them easily in terms of call handling. offer almost double the battery life and also have a more elegant and foldable design.
Audio purists might like the sound of the Sennheiser Accentum Plus, which are available for Rs 13,999, but they lose out to the Live 780NC in ANC, call quality, and battery life. Those looking for head-turning headphones might also be tempted by the Nothing Headphone (1), which come with a transparent-ish appearance and very good audio quality (if one is ready to spend time adjusting the equalizer), but are more expensive at Rs 17,999, and again, do not match the Live 780NC in ANC and battery life.
We would say that they are comfortably the best all-round mainstream ANC headphones you can get for around Rs 15,000. They deliver decent ANC, very good audio, and excel in calls and battery life. Get them in orange, purple, or green, and they are a sight for sore eyes too!

Jakarta airport and others reopen after volcanic ash crisis in Indonesia
Hundreds of thousands of travellers have been stranded since Saturday’s eruption of Mount Anak Krakatoa
Indonesia’s main airport and several other air travel hubs reopened early on Tuesday after days of closure due to ash from a volcanic eruption, the Transport Ministry said.
The ministry wrote on Instagram that the airport serving the capital Jakarta and four others near the city or around the island of Java are now operating again, as the air safety crisis that left hundreds of thousands of travellers stranded subsides.
Mount Anak Krakatoa, about 150km (93 miles) from Jakarta, erupted on Saturday, spewing a fountain of lava and a plume of volcanic ash.
Eight airports halted operations over the weekend after ash was detected in their airspace, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights and leaving more than 340,000 passengers stranded, the Transport Ministry reported on Monday.
Early on Tuesday the ministry posted on Instagram that Jakarta’s airport and four others are up and running again.
Jakarta’s main airport wrote on Instagram that “following the current volcanic eruption activity of Mount Anak Krakatoa, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has resumed flight operations”.
Earlier, the airport closures had been repeatedly extended.

Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
- Published
Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.
It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office.
In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated".
Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.
According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".
The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.
Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing.
He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation.
Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country.
In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap.
Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union.
Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption.
Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.
Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.
A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked.
In an interview with the BBC last month, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the president needed to be asked about his awareness of potential corruption among his closest team.
"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions," he said.
During his time in office, the 35-year-old was credited with heading a drive against corruption.
Since his dismissal in mid-July, after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces, he has been outspoken against what he has called a "systemic crisis of governance" in Ukraine.
However, he has emphasised that he has no evidence that Zelensky is personally involved in corruption.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity," Federov told the BBC.

Nathan Fielder teases Elizabeth Holmes documentary with eyebrow-raising trailer

If you were wondering what possible antics Nathan Fielder has been up to after watching the latest season of The Rehearsal, we have your answer.
The Vancouver-born comedian, writer and director released a teaser late Sunday for his next project, a documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes who was famously convicted of fraud in 2022 after her company claimed to have created a type of blood testing that could screen for hundreds of diseases with small amounts of blood.
Fielder's film, titled You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.
Oppenheim's previous works include Spermworld (2024), an FX-produced doc about sperm donors and Some Kind of Heaven (2020) about a Florida retirement community.
Fielder grew to fame with Nathan For You, a series on Comedy Central in which he gives horrible business advice to entrepreneurs. Previously he won (and baffled) Canadian hearts and minds with his appearances on CBC's This Hour Has 22 Minutes, in field segments titled "Nathan On Your Side" in 2008 and 2009.
You Can See Everything is being distributed by Gen Z favourite A24. The trailer features the company's signature high-saturation colour grading and overall eeriness.
It includes a roughly-one minute close-up conversation between Holmes and Fielder. The two intensely gaze at each other, as Holmes says, "Why would I deceive you? There's no — there's no reason for me to do that."

On the rainy morning of August 26, the front courtyard of District Women Hospital in Maharashtra’s Amravati district was crowded with politicians, reporters and bystanders. Amid them stood 30-year-old Swapnil Borde. His bottle-green shirt hung limp with sweat, while his red-rimmed eyes brimmed with tears.
He is the father of one of the three newborns who died after a fire broke out in the four-storey Special Newborn Care Unit and Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) on the third floor of the maternity hospital around 3.15 a.m. on August 24. Thirty-six babies were rescued and shifted to nearby hospitals, according to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar. Two sustained burn injuries, says Amol Narote, medical superintendent of the government-run super-speciality hospital. Preliminary investigations indicate that a ventilator sparked the fire.
Also Read : Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar fire: 58 rescued, including nine newborns in blaze at hospital
Swapnil’s newborn was of low weight and had breathing issues, so was put on a ventilator two days before the fire.
“Gora bala kala kela. Ek minta pan nahi tambaycha ikde, khup bekar jhala ahe, pan mala ajun majhya mulachi janiv hote (My fair baby was turned black. I don’t want to be here even for a minute, but I still feel the presence of my child here),” says Swapnil, who works as a delivery person.
He adds, “This was the first baby in my family in this generation. It took us four years to conceive him. I took him in my arms only after he died.”
Outside the NICU, the empty fire extinguishers lay on the floor, while the soot-covered room, guarded by the police, continued to be frequented by people. Among them were members of a State-level investigation committee, Amravati MLC Pravin Pote and Achalpur Bharatiya Janata Party MLA Pravin Tayde. Former Leader of the Opposition in the Maharashtra Assembly and Congress leader Vijay Wadettiwar also visited the hospital. The parents of the other two newborns who died in the August 24 fire came from Achalpur and Paratwada, 50 km from the hospital.
Established in 1938, the hospital is one of Amravati’s major government maternity hospitals. It also caters to Wardha, Yavatmal and Washim districts. Primary healthcare centres and sub-district hospitals across Amravati, including Melghat, a tribal-dominated region, refer critical pregnancies here. The hospital was formerly known as Dufferin Hospital, named after Lady Hariot Dufferin, who established the Dufferin Fund in 1884 to provide medical aid to women in India.
Investigation underway
District Civil Surgeon Dr. Vinod Pawar, who is in charge of the maternity hospital, says, “Around 3.15 a.m., my staff in the NICU heard an explosion from the ventilator and saw fire coming out of it. They alerted the fire department and me simultaneously. Our priority was to rescue the babies.”
Dr. Pawar has submitted the fire-audit-related documents to the investigation committee. The police, meanwhile, have registered an accidental death report.
Maharashtra Minister for Public Health and Family Welfare Prakash Abitkar formed a seven-member committee headed by Public Health Commissioner Sanjay Katkar and directed it to submit its report within eight days. He said the committee’s findings would be made public and responsibility fixed.
On August 26, Mr. Katkar and the committee visited the spot and questioned the nurses who were present in the NICU at the time of the incident. The CCTV footage was also handed over to the committee, which comprises officials from the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, AIIMS and the Directorate of Medical Education and Research. It has been tasked with examining ventilator and electrical faults, the fire-audit history and administrative lapses. The report was due on August 31 but has not yet been released.
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced ₹5 lakh in compensation for each family that lost its newborn in the fire and directed that the treatment of injured infants be fully covered by the government.
Of the 36 newborn babies, 11 have been admitted to Dr. Panjabrao Deshmukh Memorial Medical College (PDMMC), 10 to Hope Hospital, eight to Murkey Hospital and two to Parijat Hospital. Five were discharged with their mothers.
Survivors’ accounts
Radhika Yehkade, 19, was the last to deliver her twins before the fire. They were born around 2 a.m. on August 24 and kept in the NICU.
“I had a difficult pregnancy. I was in the hospital the week before my delivery. I am unable to let go of the voices in my head. Nurses shouting, ‘Help,’ people screaming, ‘Fire, fire.’ I am unable to make peace with the fact that my babies’ lives would have lasted only for two hours,” says Radhika, whose twins were admitted to PDMMC.
Radhika’s mother, Phula Shanware, 55, also an eyewitness, adds, “The smoke was dense; the fire brigade reached in time but took almost an hour to take water pipes to the third floor.”
Talking about her daughter, Phula says, “She had a tough pregnancy; we are daily wage earners and have already spent ₹80,000. We have been far from our house in Achalpur for almost 10 days.”
Another woman, Arti Kharale, 27, narrated her story. “When I saw my daughter, she smelt of wet ash. My heart sank when I heard about the fire,” says Arti, who lives in Amravati city. She says this was the second such fire in the hospital. The last, as reported by the media, was in September 2022.
Fifty-three-year-old Asha Dharse’s daughter delivered her baby at PDMMC. Chatting with other women, she says, “In June, I removed my daughter’s name from Dufrin because my cousin said they are negligent. Chutney, bhakri bhetel, pan aulad nahi, navas karava lagto (We will earn food, but not the baby).”
Yogesh Savarkar, 24, is waiting outside the maternity room at PDMMC, where his daughter and wife have been transferred. Recalling the night of the incident, he says he was among the first parents who barged into the room to rescue the infants.
He narrates, “The flames were soaring, wires were sparking, black smoke was coming out of the broken windows, and the equipment was burning. When I entered, I saw three children covered in black powder. One child had burns on his face. We rescued them first.”
Mr. Savarkar is also from Achalpur and came to the maternity hospital on August 17.
Maharashtra’s fire audits
Chief Minister Fadnavis has raised concerns over the hospital’s mandatory fire audit. A fire audit is a systematic inspection of fire safety readiness, assessing electrical load, wiring safety, overloaded circuits, faulty switchboards, and equipment prone to sparking or overheating, such as ventilators, oxygen concentrators and compressors.
According to data from Maharashtra’s Public Health Department, of the 530 government hospitals across the State, 528 have completed fire audits. As many as 442 hospitals have fire safety systems fully installed, while only 372 hospitals hold a fire no-objection certificate (NOC). This means nearly 30% of government hospitals do not have fire NOCs.
In Amravati alone, 18 government hospitals were audited, of which 16 received the NOC. Meanwhile, in Wardha and Gondia districts, 11 hospitals were audited, but none received the NOC. In Beed district in the Marathwada region, 18 hospitals did not receive NOCs.
On August 25, the Public Health Department announced a State-wide fire and electrical safety inspection of all government, private and charitable hospitals. Minister Abitkar had said, “If discrepancies are found in the audit, then they are to be rectified. Every hospital will appoint a nodal officer for fire safety, who will review fire audits, electrical safety, fire-fighting systems, emergency evacuation arrangements, staff training, and mock drills, and submit compliance information to senior levels.”
Initial warning
Records show that the Dufferin Hospital Authority had flagged concerns over the fire safety systems. A letter dated June 29 stated, “The hospital had obtained a fire NOC valid from June 22, 2025, to June 21, 2026. Before this validity period lapses, a registered licensed agency must conduct a fire safety audit, and Form B must be submitted to this office — so the fire NOC renewal proposal can then be forwarded to the Fire Department of Amravati Municipal Corporation.”
A follow-up letter was also written to the Public Works Department on July 17, reminding it to arrange a fire safety audit. “The fire NOC is an essential document for the hospital, and if its validity period lapses, the possibility of legal complications arising during an emergency cannot be ruled out,” the second letter stated, urging immediate action. The letter was marked to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar and health services in the Akola division. Mr. Yerekar has not responded to The Hindu’s query regarding the action taken after receiving this letter.
Meanwhile, hospital staff and patients said this was the second fire incident in the last five years. “We learnt from our mistakes in the 2022 fire. That is why we have been extra careful with fire audits,” says an official from the Amravati maternity hospital. According to hospital authorities, a ventilator in the NICU had also caught fire then, causing minor injuries to two newborns.
The ventilators in both cases were supplied by Schiller Healthcare, which has been called for the investigation. An official said a committee will be set up to create SOPs for the procurement of medical equipment.
Courage under fire
Outside the NICU, the smell of smoke lingered. In the corridor, kaksh-sevikas (nursing attendants) were waiting for their turns to appear before the committee as part of the investigation. Among them was Surekha Dhanvijay, 45, one of the four attendants present in the NICU, who witnessed the fire and called for help. “The moment I heard the explosion, a huge flame burst out. With our bare hands, we tried to douse the fire near the cradle and take a baby out.”
“I have only one regret: that we couldn’t save those three children,” says Kirti Ghanvir, 45, another nursing attendant. Showing her fire burns and blisters, Ms. Ghanvir adds, “I had to feel around in the burning cradles to see if there was a baby. When I found one, I grabbed it.”
In the meantime, they informed others in the hospital, who rushed to help. “Most of us wrapped blankets around ourselves, broke the glass and entered, rescuing babies,” says Lalita Lasbe, 35.
The sevikas say they do not want any appreciation as they consider this part of their jobs, but appeal to the government to increase their salaries. They say they currently get ₹8,000 a month and are hired on contract, so their salaries barely increase.

The National Film Awards ceremony is set to move out of Delhi for the first time in its 72-year history. The 72nd edition of the awards will be held in Ekta Nagar, Gujarat, on September 22, with President Droupadi Murmu scheduled to present the honours, officials said on Monday.
72nd National Film Awards to be held in Gujarat; President Droupadi Murmu to present honours on September 22
The venue shift marks a departure from a long-standing tradition. The first National Awards were presented in 1954 at Vigyan Bhawan in Delhi, which has hosted the ceremony on several occasions over the years. This year, the awards will instead be presented in Ekta Nagar, formerly known as Kevadia.
Ekta Nagar is home to the Statue of Unity, the world's tallest statue dedicated to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Standing 597 feet tall, the monument was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in 2018.
Article 370 leads this year's winners
The winners of the 72nd National Film Awards were announced in July, with Article 370 emerging as the Best Feature Film. The film's lead actor Yami Gautam was also named Best Actress for her performance.
Malayalam superstar Mammootty and Bollywood actor Kartik Aaryan will share the Best Actor honour. Mammootty has been recognised for his performance in Bramayugam, while Aaryan won for his role in Chandu Champion.
Actor-filmmaker Randeep Hooda has also earned recognition at this year's awards. He has been named the Best Debut Director for Swatantrya Veer Savarkar, his directorial debut based on the life of Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.
Kalki 2898 AD and Captain Miller among major winners
Nag Ashwin's Telugu science-fiction epic Kalki 2898 AD will receive the Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment award.
Meanwhile, Tamil film Captain Miller, directed by Arun Matheswaran and starring Dhanush, has been named the Best Feature Film Promoting National, Social and Environmental Values.
The ceremony on September 22 is expected to bring together several of the year's biggest winners as the National Film Awards begin a new chapter by moving the prestigious event outside Delhi for the first time.

Tiranga Yatra at 13000 Feet- National Pride Celebrated in Tawang’s Border Villages
The spirit of patriotism reached the high frontiers of Arunachal Pradesh as the Chuna and Mago Sector Vibrant Villages in Tawang district hosted a Tiranga Yatra at an altitude of nearly 13,000 feet. The event brought together local communities, the civil administration, Panchayati Raj representatives, and security forces in a celebration of national unity and pride.
The program was organized as part of the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign and commemorated 150 years of Vande Mataram, connecting the national celebration with the people living in one of India’s most remote border regions.
A Community Celebration at the Frontier
The Tiranga Yatra was organised by the Jang Sub-Divisional Administration in collaboration with the Indian Army, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), BJP Mandal 3-Mukto, and residents of Chuna and Mago.
The yatra was flagged off by the Zilla Parishad Chairperson, in the presence of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Assistant Commissioner, Panchayat representatives, Heads of Offices, senior personnel of the Indian Army and ITBP, and local residents.
The participation of people from different sections of the community reflected the spirit of collective responsibility and the strong bond between frontier communities, the administration, and the forces serving in the region.
A 300-Meter Tricolour Across the Mountains
The highlight of the celebration was the carrying of a 300-meter-long National Tricolour from Chuna to Mago village.
Against the backdrop of the Eastern Himalayas, the Tricolour made its way through the high-altitude terrain, turning the yatra into a memorable expression of national pride. The event was further enriched by a band performance by students of Higher Secondary School Jang, whose participation brought the enthusiasm of the younger generation to the celebrations.
Honouring India’s Frontier Communities
Events such as the Tiranga Yatra also highlight the important role of Arunachal Pradesh’s border communities in the country’s frontier landscape. Villages such as Chuna and Mago are located in challenging high-altitude terrain, where communities continue to live, work, and contribute to the social and economic life of the region.
The participation of villagers alongside the Indian Army, ITBP, civil administration, and Panchayati Raj representatives demonstrated the importance of community participation in strengthening the social fabric of the border areas.
The event also complemented the broader objective of the Vibrant Villages Programme, which seeks to improve infrastructure, connectivity, livelihoods, and public services in strategically located border villages while strengthening their connection with the rest of the country.
The Tricolour at the High Frontiers
The Tiranga Yatra at Chuna and Mago was more than a ceremonial event. It brought the national spirit directly to communities living at one of India’s highest and most remote frontiers.
The sight of a 300-meter Tricolour moving through the Himalayan landscape served as a powerful reminder of the unity that connects every part of the country, from its cities and towns to its most distant border villages.
At nearly 13,000 feet, the celebration reflected the resilience of Arunachal Pradesh’s frontier communities and the enduring spirit of national unity.

All humans must be treated equally. That is a moral and constitutional position. It is not a scientific position because science does not carry moral or constitutional authority.
The normative system laid out in the ‘Manusmriti’ expresses the ‘principle’ that the birth of a person says something essential about who that person is supposed to be, with persons born into specific social categories to be assigned a place in the division of labour and a set of permitted relationships and social rights. Modern constitutional thinking is radically different. Per the Magna Carta, the English Bill of Rights and the constitutional democracies of today, individuals possess rights that depend on more than their place in a social hierarchy. After all, the fundamental rights of the Indian Constitution are attached to persons and citizens, not to inherited social functions.
Yet a poster that turned up at IIT-Mandi on September 4, 2026 said the role of “Brahmanas” is to “spread god’s message”, that of “kshatriyas” to “protect society and spirituality”, of “vaishyas” to “drive economy, support others”, and of “shudras” to “serve higher classes”.
Science, which underlies the technologies the IITs are primarily concerned with, offers another conception paralleling the constitutional view, rooted in a different kind of authority.
The authority of science
While some defenders of the caste system have claimed that it is based on inherited biological differences, the system is really the cause of the differences, rather than their inheritor. The human organism develops as its genes interact with its environment, and caste-based discrimination affects these environments. Studies on the social determinants of health have revealed caste-related inequities in healthcare and access to healthcare while social epigenetics has found that social circumstances can induce biological changes via mechanisms that affect the way genes are regulated.
People of Black African heritage and Indigenous peoples in Asia, say, have non-identical genomes for this reason. By applying science’s methods, we know the differences between these peoples do not excuse a caste-like system. Instead, the differences in these people’s social circumstances through history — including societies of which they were part practising a hereditary, hierarchical system at any point — affected the way they developed.
In a landmark 2009 study, geneticists reported that most present-day Indians descended from two differentiated ancient populations, which mixed extensively before endogamy took root, and present Indian groups contain mixes of these ancestries. The team also said there are substantial genetic differences between various communities today thanks to a long history of endogamy. Other studies of Indian populations have also reported strong founder effects (when a new population emerges from a small group of individuals and inherits the lack of genetic diversity) due to endogamy. The genome does not announce that these people were ordained to marry one another but records the fact that they elected to do so for reasons beyond scientific wisdom.
The human nervous system is also very plastic: it constantly rewires itself in response to every experience in a life-long process. Not everyone is good at everything, but plasticity means the neurological system develops together with each human’s environment, interests, temperament, and individual choice, giving rise to a variety of abilities among people.
No matter how well-equipped, the practice of science could never say whether all humans are equal. That is a political and ethical proposition it cannot test or prove. However, it does say that all humans are members of one species, that their development is shaped by their experiences, and that social environments can become embodied.
Just as caste constrains the plasticity of the human brain, it also constrains the human capacity for culture. Homo sapiens can accumulate knowledge and pass it on so that other H. sapiens do not have to learn from scratch. Caste-based discrimination, however, restricts the spread of knowledge and narrows the social range over which one of the defining capacities of our species can operate — as if a student’s ability to solve a differential equation has anything to do with the ritual status of their ancestors.
This clash of possibilities is what makes the appearance of a message reinforcing the caste system at a centre of scientific learning particularly tragic.

Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.
The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.
“I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.
Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.
Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.
But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.
In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”
As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.
On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.
Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.
In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”
It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.
However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

In a major breakthrough, the U.K. has recognised India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme as a qualifying criterion for pricing relief under its carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), a move that would reduce the tax burden on domestic exporters, an official said on Monday (September 7, 2026).
In a communication addressed to the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Ministry of Power, the U.K.'s HM Treasury confirmed that the CCTS has been included in the U.K.'s published indicative list of overseas carbon pricing schemes assessed as qualifying criteria under a provision of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Calculation of CBAM Rate and Determination of Carbon Price Relief) Regulations 2026, the official said.
The move is important as the Commerce Ministry was pursuing the matter with the U.K. for long.
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) has been notified by India with the objective of reducing, removing, or avoiding greenhouse gas emissions from the Indian economy by pricing such emissions through the trading of Carbon Credit Certificates.
The financial support for implementation of the CCTS would be met by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency from fees and charges collected from entities under the scheme and its own resources.
The official said the U.K. government had included the scheme in its indicative list as a qualifying carbon pricing mechanism under Britain's CBAM.
With this recognition, U.K. importers of eligible Indian goods covered under CBAM will be able to seek carbon price relief corresponding to the effective carbon price borne by those goods under the CCTS, subject to satisfying the evidence and verification requirements prescribed under U.K. law.
"This will reduce the effective CBAM liability on Indian goods, directly benefiting Indian exporters to the U.K.," the official said.
The recognition follows sustained technical-level engagement between the two governments on the design and implementation of the CCTS.
The recognition reflects the U.K. CBAM's core principle of avoiding double taxation on goods that have already borne an eligible carbon price in their country of origin.
Going forward, cooperation on carbon market design and implementation will continue through the U.K.-India Energy Memorandum of Understanding and the Partnership for Market Implementation.
The two governments are also committed to continued dialogue on carbon pricing, including on the interaction between the CCTS and U.K. CBAM rules, further strengthening India-U.K. engagement.
However, the amount of relief that can be claimed will depend on the effective carbon price to which the goods in question have been subject.
A liable person for U.K. CBAM will still be required to satisfy the applicable evidence and verification requirements.
India and the U.K. have implemented a comprehensive economic and trade partnership on July 15.
Merchandise trade between the two countries stood at $25.1 billion in 2025-26, while bilateral services trade reached $35.4 billion in 2024.

U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner land for talks in Kyiv after meeting Putin in Moscow
KYIV, Ukraine — U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push for peace after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Their trip follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, seeking to revive peace talks during escalating aerial attacks by both sides.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday that Kyiv is ready for a "constructive" discussion with U.S. representatives.
"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared," he said in a post on Telegram.
Washington's push to end the fighting has lost momentum, with the United States focused for the past six months on the Iran war. The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was in January when they also held talks with Putin at the Kremlin.
No breakthroughs in Moscow talks
Saturday's meeting in Moscow lasted more than three hours behind closed doors and ended without announcements of any breakthroughs. Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, described them afterward as constructive, frank, and useful but didn't discuss specific outcomes.
While Moscow offered its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, Ushakov said, the talks were not purely focused on the war in Ukraine.
"Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," he said.
Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire
The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.
Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks take place. Still, the two traded fire overnight into Sunday, officials said.
Russian attacks across multiple Ukrainian regions killed one person and injured at least 10 others overnight into Sunday, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
In Zaporizhzhia, drone strikes killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three people, while a drone damaged an apartment building, injuring seven people, in the Khmelnytskyi region.
Ukraine's air force said Sunday that it intercepted 82 drones out of the 108 launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.
In Russia, a man was killed and a woman seriously wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a vehicle, local authorities in the Belgorod border region said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Sunday that its air defenses overnight shot down 258 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the waters of the Black and Azov seas.
Mixed hopes on the ground
In Kyiv on Sunday, dozens gathered for a nationwide 9 a.m. moment of silence honoring Ukraine's fallen soldiers, a daily ritual held in cities across the country.
Among them was Nataliia Lipei, 67, whose son Viktor was killed in December 2022. Despite a health condition, she has traveled from city to city to take part, and she said she hopes the talks in Moscow and Kyiv will finally bring an end to the war.
"I hope these steps and these meetings will definitely produce results, because there has been so much bloodshed and so many deaths here that we have to stop all of this," she told The Associated Press.
Not everyone shared her hope for the talks. Oleksandr Pastukhov, 27, a video editor who joined the commemoration, was skeptical the envoys' visit would change anything.
"We've already seen delegations like this come here before," he said. "We've seen this so-called ceasefire for three days, which ended after just a couple of hours, and now we're supposed to naively think that two people will come and change something."

‘Israel’s military gave me just minutes to leave my apartment before it was bombed. I’m lucky to be alive’
Neveen and Mohammed had recently married and were hoping to get their life back on track after nearly three years of Israeli attacks. But in the space of just minutes, those hopes were once again shattered, Alex Croft reports
Just after midnight, Neveen Abu Hatab and her husband Mohammed were awoken suddenly by the sound of shouting from their neighbours.
The panicked screams would save their lives. Shortly after they fled their Gaza home with just a work laptop, an Israeli missile reduced the building to rubble.
“I cried uncontrollably because I lost everything in an instant, for no reason at all,” Neveen says, speaking of the moment she saw footage of her new home in the Zeitoun neighbourhood the burning on social media on Thursday 30 July.
The destruction of the house was heartbreaking for the couple, who had recently married and hoped to get their lives back on track after nearly three years of a brutal Israeli bombing campaign.
Israel has continued launching attacks on Gaza and seized more territory since a ceasefire deal was agreed last October, killing at least 1,222 Palestinians during that time, according to figures from the Gaza health ministry.
Meanwhile, Hamas has stated that it will disarm, but only if Israel ends “all forms of aggression” against it and withdraws its forces from Gaza.
The Israeli military said it killed two Hamas commanders in its overnight strikes on 30 July. Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that three Palestinian citizens were killed in the Gaza City strikes overnight, and another 21 killed across the Strip by Israeli shelling and gunfire after dawn.
Asked for comment about the strike on Neveen’s home, the Israeli military said it had “struck in several areas in the Gaza Strip and dismantled four Hamas weapon storage facilities”. They claimed the facilities held “Kalashnikov guns, explosive devices, additional ammunition and military equipment”.
“The weapons were intended to harm Israeli civilians and IDF troops operating in the area of the Yellow Line and were dismantled to eliminate the threat,” it added.
The prospects for the a second phase of the truce look bleak, after Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a 15-point document put forward by Donald Trump earlier this year, declaring Israeli forces would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas was disarmed.
For Neveen and Mohammed, both aged 28, the possibility that there will be no immediate end to the ongoing military strikes in Gaza, has shattered their efforts to rebuild their lives amid the rubble.
She recalls details of the night of the attack tearfully during an interview with The Independent.
“I grabbed my personal bag and work laptop, then we left to get away from the apartment unless than 10 mins before it was targeted,” she recalls.
“We spent the night at my husband’s family home, where I still am to this day. We were shocked later to find out the missiles had rained down on the buildings, burning and fully destroying our apartment.”
The Israeli military added that it takes “great measures to mitigate harm to the civilian population” and that it “works to distance civilians from combat zones and areas where military activity is expected, by issuing advanced warnings and calls to move to safer areas”.
Neveen and Mohammed had waited for years to get married and buy their first home, as the war in Gaza raged. Over nearly three years, the Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza health ministry, during a bombardment and invasion it launched after the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October in which militants killed 1,195 people, according to Israeli tallies.
“We have not even been married for four months,” says Neveen. “We were postponing our wedding until the Gaza war ended. We finally got married dreaming of stability, only to feel that everything we tried to build was shattered once again, resetting us back to zero.”
“We decided to set up our home despite resources being so scarce.”
With no sign of a stable political future for the Strip, the outlook for Palestinians in Gaza remains bleak.
Former British prime minister Tony Blair, whose role in the Gaza “Board of Peace” has grown in recent months, has been drafted in to try and fast-track the peace process.
Along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, he met with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday, for a nearly-four-hour meeting aimed at saving the 15-point roadmap for peace in Gaza.
But the talks failed to make a breakthrough on the stalled deal, after Netanyahu reiterated the Israeli stance that there will be no progress on the deal or on Israel’s withdrawal from the enclave before Hamas disarms.

While warning that breaching the 1.5°C global warming limit would bring irreversible losses that no adaptation initiatives could undo, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) on Wednesday (September 2, 2026), for the first time, set out a detailed “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway.
This is a route under which the world overshoots the 2015 Paris Agreement’s central goal — limiting the rise in average global temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels — which a UNEP report said was now unavoidable, but holds the peak as low as possible and then brings temperatures back down below the limit by the end of the century.
The report, Limiting Overshoot, released in Nairobi, said global warming would cross 1.5°C “in the next few years”. Even a scenario in which every country delivers on its national climate plan and net-zero target puts peak warming at 1.8°C, it said. According to the report, current policies point to a rise of about 2.6°C by 2100, with a range of 1.9–3.6°C. The pathway, the report said, "is by no means an acceptable or preferred pathway; it is simply the best remaining option."
The diplomatic grounds for that framing were laid at the 30th UN Climate Change Conference, COP30, held in 2025 in Brazil’s Belém, where the consensus “Global Mutirão” decision became the first COP text to concede that a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C limit was likely, given how fast the remaining carbon budget was being spent. At the conference, countries also committed, for the first time, to limiting the size and duration of the overshoot and to closing adaptation gaps, which would require deep, rapid and sustained emission cuts.
Given that cuts alone will no longer suffice, a steep scaling up of nature-based removals such as large reforestation programmes was needed, COP30 CEO Ana Toni said in a statement. UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres also released a statement, saying, “This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead. We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition."
Compounding costs
The UNEP report suggested that time spent above 1.5°C carries compounding costs such as faster sea-level rise, coral reef collapse, glacier loss exceeding a quarter of global mass by 2100, declines of up to 14% in global food production by 2050 without effective adaptation, and rising odds of irreversible tipping points in the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and the Amazon.
Moreover, it gets harder to roll back the effects of a tonne of emitted carbon. The report computed that every five years of continued high emissions adds roughly 0.1°C to peak warming. Reversing that same 0.1°C afterwards means pulling about 220 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide back out of the atmosphere over and above whatever is still being emitted. Very broadly, a single large tree growing for about 30 years can cut out only a tonne of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide removal, the report stresses, is needed in addition to, not instead of, emission cuts, and can credibly cool temperatures back to the 1.5°C limit only if peak warming stays well below 2°C. Even the most optimistic scaling up of emission cuts is unlikely to reverse more than a few tenths of a degree this century, the report underlined.
UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen was explicit that the report is not a concession. “Let’s be very clear, the 1.5 target is still the goal. But now we need to approach it differently from above,” she said.
The report arrives at a moment of uncertainty over whether countries will cut emissions at all. The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, formally exited the Paris Agreement earlier this year and has also announced its withdrawal from the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the Green Climate Fund. Separately, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the conflict in West Asia has produced what the International Energy Agency calls the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, with output from affected countries down more than 14 million barrels a day. Sustained high energy prices could push governments toward coal and other short-term fossil responses.
Methane targets
The report, in a first for the UN, placed significant stress on methane, which currently contributes about 0.5°C of warming. Cutting it is described as the most effective way to slow warming in the near term. Human activity currently puts out roughly 350–400 million tonnes of methane a year, mostly from fossil fuel operations, livestock, rice paddies, landfills and wastewater. When modellers build the pathways that underpin net-zero targets, they typically assume that about half of this gets cut by mid-century through “cheap, technically easy” interventions such as plugging leaks and venting from oil and gas. But the other half, roughly 150–200 million tonnes a year still being emitted in 2050 from agriculture and waste, is harder to cut; though shaving 60–70 million tonnes from it could reduce temperature rise to the same extent as removing 220 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Over 155 countries have joined the Global Methane Pledge to cut anthropogenic methane at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030. India, China, Russia and Iran remain outside it.
The UNEP report co-author Richard Betts of the University of Exeter said, “It is a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world."

Zheng wins set from 5-0 down again to stun Swiatek
- Published
Zheng Qinwen won a set from 5-0 down for the second match in succession as she extended her fantastic US Open run by beating former champion Iga Swiatek to reach the quarter-finals.
Zheng, the reigning Olympic champion and former world number four, dropped outside the world's top 100 earlier this year while struggling to regain her best form following elbow surgery in July 2025.
The 23-year-old from China had trailed Madison Keys 5-0 in the deciding set of their third-round match on Saturday before winning seven successive games to secure her spot in round four.
And Zheng was 5-0 down in the opening set against Poland's eighth seed Swiatek, but won 13 of the next 16 games on Arthur Ashe Stadium to set up a quarter-final against second seed Elena Rybakina, who sped past former champion Naomi Osaka.
The second set was on serve until the seventh game, when Zheng crushed a powerful backhand return winner to secure a crucial break, and she broke again two games later to complete a 7-5 6-3 victory.
This latest win - her seventh in a row in New York having come through three rounds of qualifying - will put her back to the brink of the top 50.
"The more matches I play, the more rhythm I have on court," said Zheng.
"People have asked me if I'm tired and when I arrived I was not tired at all. I felt really pumped for my match, trying to reach better levels here and enjoy this fantastic stadium."
Elsewhere, French Open winner Mirra Andreeva recovered from losing the first set to Austria's Anastasia Potapova to reach the last eight in New York for the first time in her career.
The year of the qualifier?
Zheng's only win in eight previous meetings against Swiatek was in the semi-finals of the 2024 Olympics on her way to singles gold in Paris.
Former world number five Daniela Hantuchova told BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra: "She [Zheng] is starting to be very dangerous for the rest of the players left.
"I don't want to say she's playing the best tennis out of everyone, but if you have Iga Swiatek panicking on the other side of the court, not knowing what to do, that says a lot."
The most recent qualifier to reach this stage of the women's draw at the US Open was Great Britain's Emma Raducanu, who went on to win the title in 2021.
And Zheng is not the first female qualifier to perform well at a Grand Slam in 2026 - Poland's Maja Chwalinska, who began the French Open at 114th in the world, lost to Russian teenager Andreeva in the final at Roland Garros.
Swiatek 'started making mistakes' after fast start
For Swiatek, 25, a fourth-round exit is a disappointing end to her Grand Slam season, with a quarter-final appearance at the Australian Open her best result.
She was beaten in round four of the French Open, while the defence of her Wimbledon title ended in the third round.
It means that, for the first time since 2021, Swiatek will end a year without winning one of the sport's four majors.
Swiatek, who received treatment to her left thigh when leading 2-1 in the second set, had entered the US Open in excellent form by winning the WTA 1000 event in Toronto and getting to the semi-finals in Cincinnati, while she had progressed through to round four without dropping a set.
Reflecting on losing the first set to Zheng, Swiatek said she simply missed too many shots after going 5-0 up.
"My focus was the same as always," said the six-time major winner. "I wanted to play the same as always. [I] just started to miss too much, wanted to adjust it, but nothing kind of worked at that point.
"I knew I was going to have another chance and I wanted to use it, but I missed them all."
She continued: "I wouldn't say it had anything to do with mentality. It was more that I started making mistakes from easy balls and Qinwen stopped doing mistakes. She played the balls better."
Andreeva through against 'warrior' Potapova
Andreeva, 19, was severely tested by Potapova until the 24th seed injured her knee in what proved to be the final game of their match on Louis Armstrong Stadium.
Potapova seemed to twist or hyperextend her knee while attempting to hit a ball on the run from the baseline and Andreeva was across quickly to check on her grounded opponent.
Potapova returned to the court after receiving treatment but lost the remaining points in her service game, confirming her exit from the tournament.
Fifth seed Andreeva, who won 5-7 6-4 6-3, said: "Anastasia is my good friend and seeing what a battle we had and seeing her fall like that in the last game, it's not easy.
"I told her that she's been playing amazing and having one of her best seasons. I'm sure she'll come back even stronger - she's a warrior and an even better fighter than me."
Andreeva will play either Coco Gauff or Iva Jovic, who play their all-American fourth-round match in Monday's night session, in the quarter-finals.

US President Donald Trump has shared an AI-generated image depicting himself day trading Intel stock from $20 to $95, while claiming he has made “Hundreds of Billions of Dollars” on stocks and other holdings for the United States.

The latest post comes amid scrutiny of Trump-linked investment activity and his public comments about companies whose shares have subsequently moved sharply.
Government filings with the US Office of Government Ethics have reportedly shown accounts tied to Trump building positions in Intel and Dell Technologies before public posts about the companies.

Some of Trump's posts portrayed countries, territories and even celestial bodies as US possessions.

More than six months after the US and Israel launched what they called “major combat operations” in Iran, there has been little indication that either side is preparing to return to negotiations. Iran's economy has reportedly contracted during the conflict, while inflation has surged to historic levels.

King Charles clarifies Harry and Meghan’s status after UK return
Palace letter confirms couple will not use royal titles or receive state-funded security for private work
Britain’s King Charles has reiterated that Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, remain non-working members of the royal family following their return to the United Kingdom.
A letter sent on behalf of the king to senior government officials said the couple will continue to refrain from using their royal titles as they have done since stepping back from official royal duties in 2020.
Any charity work the couple undertakes will be carried out in a private capacity and operational security decisions are matters for the relevant police agencies, the letter adds.
The letter was sent by the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the royal household, to senior officials in the government and military, as well as lord lieutenants, the king’s personal representatives around the country.
“To help avoid doubt or confusion, The King has directed that [this] information be shared,” the letter says.
While the communication simply confirms that Harry and Meghan’s status remains unchanged, the decision to send the letter and release it publicly shows the concern among some palace observers that the couple’s status could allow them to become a sort of parallel royal court, competing with working members of the royal family.

As students head back to school, parents have all the usual worries about their kids, like remembering to pack lunch and making it to the bus stop on time. But parents of immunocompromised kids have a new one: How to deal with the resurgence of measles.
Cases of the highly transmissible disease have reached a 35-year high in the US, with nearly 3,000 confirmed infections in 2026 so far. The first two measles-related deaths of the year were recorded in Pennsylvania, right as the school year is getting going. With vaccination rates dropping across the country, parents of kids who aren’t able to get vaccinated or don’t mount a strong enough immune response due to weakened immune systems are weighing whether it’s safe enough to go to school.
Victoria Schiano, national community engagement coordinator for Little Lobbyists, a nonprofit that advocates for children with complex medical needs and disabilities, says the return of measles is “absolutely terrifying.”
While it’s not known exactly how many US children have compromised immune systems, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that 2.6 percent of children are immunocompromised. Immune deficiencies can have genetic causes or secondary reasons, such as chemotherapy for cancer treatment.
Schiano’s kid is among them. Her 10-year-old has mitochondrial disease. The family lives in Chester County, Pennsylvania, which has the second-highest number of measles cases in the state right now. Schiano has been closely monitoring the vaccination rates in her son’s school district, which have dipped below the 95 percent threshold needed for community protection against measles. Measles is breaking through in places where vaccination has dropped below that threshold. In neighboring Lancaster County, for example, just 87.6 percent of kindergartners are fully vaccinated against measles and 83.3 percent of seventh graders are.
Her son can’t be vaccinated, and he receives weekly infusions of immunoglobulin—concentrated antibodies from donated human blood plasma—to help his body fight infections.
“Measles is dangerous for anyone, but for him, this absolutely could be life or death,” she says.
The virus can cause severe, life-threatening complications such as pneumonia and brain swelling. Measles can also wipe out the body’s memory of past infections—a phenomenon known as immune amnesia—leaving people susceptible to other diseases.
Her son already wears a mask and uses a plexiglass screen at school, and the family is diligent about handwashing. Now, Schiano says they’ve had to make the difficult decision to limit her son’s time with friends and after-school activities like karate. She says it’s hard as a parent to balance his quality of life with his safety.
“He just wants to play and to do all the things that he sees other kids doing,” she says.
Her son did online school for a time during Covid-19, and she says she’s prepared to take him out of school if there’s even one confirmed measles case. That comes with a different set of risks, though. During the pandemic, remote learning was associated with an increase in social isolation and behavioral and mental health issues among students.
Amalia, a parent in South Carolina who asked to go by a pseudonym for privacy reasons, has already chosen to keep her 16-year-old son home this year and do online schooling due to concerns about measles. Her son has immunoglobulin A deficiency, in which the body doesn’t produce enough of an antibody found in mucous membranes, body fluids, and digestive tracts that help fend off germs.
“Even if there’s just a flu going around, he gets sicker than the average kid will,” she says.
Her son was able to get the measles vaccine, but doctors monitor his antibody levels regularly to check for waning immunity.
She lives in Spartanburg County, where measles broke out earlier this year and caused nearly 1,000 cases and 21 hospitalizations. About 91 percent of those cases were among children and teens, and most were among those who were not fully vaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. Even though there was a 94 percent increase in the number of vaccines administered during the outbreak in Spartanburg County compared to the year before, she still wasn’t comfortable sending her son back to school.
“Covid happened, and then measles happened, and we just feel like it's not going to be the last time,” she says. “If it's not measles, it's going to be something else because rates for other vaccines have fallen, too.”
Before this year, her son shared a classroom with other students who have special accommodations. But outside of that setting, Amalia says it has been difficult for him to make friends because of his medical condition. She says it’s hard to talk to other parents about vaccination status because it can be such a hot-button issue. The family is thinking about moving because of what she views as an anti-vaccination sentiment in the community as well as “hostility” toward masking that she’s encountered.
“Some people don't want to take ownership of the responsibility of public health,” she says. “I think it's something we're supposed to share across humanity. It's not supposed to be carried by one person.”
Cortney, another South Carolina parent of an immunocompromised kid, says the state’s measles outbreak was highly concerning because the family needed to travel near the epicenter for medical appointments. Whereas before they might stop in town to eat lunch or do some shopping, they ended any unnecessary stops. “We planned to drive directly into that county, we go only to the doctor, and we leave,” Cortney says.
Her 17-year-old daughter Grace’s condition means that rhinovirus—the cause of the common cold—led to her getting hospitalized. During Covid, Grace and her brother were homeschooled, and that is something mother and daughter considered again for Grace’s senior year.
“At the end of the semester, we're going to reevaluate and see where things are,” Grace says.
Even though she is immunocompromised, Grace doesn’t wear a mask at school because of fear of being bullied. Cortney says her family’s preference would be to mask while in public, but she’s concerned about being ostracized. “You worry that your family could be targeted,” she says. “It’s unfortunate that we have to think about that.”
