The Federal Communications Commission yesterday urged a court to dismiss a Disney lawsuit and let the FCC continue a proceeding that could end in the nonrenewal of ABC’s broadcast licenses.
Meanwhile, two watchdog groups and individual viewers of ABC stations are trying to intervene in the lawsuit, saying they are worried Disney will agree to a settlement with the FCC that isn’t in the public’s interest. Disney opposed the motion, and a judge will have to decide whether the groups and individuals can act as intervenors in the case.
Disney sued the FCC on August 18, saying the agency is waging a “campaign of censorship” to retaliate against ABC for speech that President Trump doesn’t like. As the lawsuit gets underway, Trump continued his attacks on the media last weekend by demanding that the FCC punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in his election endorsements.
The FCC filed a motion to dismiss the Disney lawsuit yesterday, defending the early license review that it ordered for the eight broadcast stations owned by ABC. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has threatened ABC over jokes made by Jimmy Kimmel and political content on The View, but the FCC claims the early license review is strictly about other matters and that no decision has been made.
FCC says Chairman Carr is “open-minded”
The FCC filing in US District Court for the District of Columbia said the proceeding is only about “allegations of unlawful discrimination” related to Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policies. The FCC wants the court to toss the lawsuit entirely, or at least deny Disney’s request for a preliminary injunction that would halt the license review pending the outcome of litigation. The FCC said:
The Commission’s Chairman has repeatedly emphasized that, although the allegations against Disney are serious, he and the agency remain “open-minded,” have “not made a decision,” and are “going to follow the facts and the law wherever they [lead].” And the renewal process in progress does not abridge or otherwise affect Plaintiffs’ rights. Licensees with pending renewal applications are entitled to continue operating without interruption during the license period for the duration of the renewal proceeding—even were it to result in a hearing. In fact, even if the Commission were to deny the stations’ applications, their licenses would remain in effect for however long they might wish to seek judicial review.
The FCC alleged that Disney’s responses to the commission’s investigative inquiries “were deficient and nonresponsive,” necessitating the order for an early license review. The agency also said the district court lacks jurisdiction because FCC orders are reviewed by circuit appeals courts.
“Granting Plaintiffs’ request would mean taking administrative processes off the table before the Commission has seen and analyzed the voluminous evidence,” the FCC said. “This would only hobble the Commission’s efforts to investigate and resolve serious allegations that Disney has engaged in unlawful discrimination, and from otherwise ensuring that Disney’s stations are serving the public interest. Plaintiffs, in return, would only free themselves from the burdens of proving their case in administrative proceedings.”
In exchange for licenses to use spectrum, “Congress has required broadcasters to operate in the public interest,” the FCC said. “To foreclose the Commission from using all the tools at its disposal to investigate whether Plaintiffs are meeting their statutory and regulatory duties would seriously harm both the government and the public.”
Watchdogs and viewers don’t want Disney to settle
Disney argued that the license review is inhibiting its right to free speech. The proceeding could “mir[e] ABC in years of costly litigation, with the threat of adverse action ever present and with every editorial judgment shadowed by the prospect of provoking the Administration into further retaliation,” the lawsuit said.
Disney said ABC is being harmed by the license review during the run-up to this year’s elections. “Plaintiffs must make editorial judgments about how to cover the election in the shadow of a threatened corporate death sentence, and the Commission has every incentive to let that threat loom as long as possible. Nor can that harm be undone after the fact,” Disney said.
In the meantime, there is a dispute between Disney and groups that want to be part of the case against the FCC. Frequency Forward and the Media Action Center filed a motion to intervene in the lawsuit, saying they want to prevent a settlement between Disney and the FCC. The two groups were joined in the motion to intervene by 18 individuals who are viewers of their local ABC stations.
“Proposed Intervenors are FCC watchdog non-profits and regular viewers of ABC stations in their home markets who are harmed by the FCC’s actions and face further harm to the extent the Plaintiffs continue to succumb to the agency’s pressure, possibly by negotiating a settlement which limits the content provided by the ABC stations,” Frequency Forward and the Media Action Center told the court.
Although Disney and ABC are advocating for their First Amendment right to be free of governmental interference, “their corporate interests may not necessarily align” with the interests of viewers and the advocacy groups, the filing said. In December 2024, ABC agreed to a $15 million payment to settle a lawsuit that Trump filed over statements made by George Stephanopoulos.
Disney says it will “vigorously” fight censorship
Disney opposed the motion in a filing yesterday, saying the “proposed intervenors lack a legally protected interest because the harm they invoke is harm to Plaintiffs, not to themselves. And the broader injury they claim on behalf of the viewing public is a generalized grievance shared by all viewers, which cannot support intervention.”
Disney said that it, ABC, and the ABC-owned stations “have every incentive to protect their own right to be free of unlawful retaliation” and will “vigorously contest Defendants’ unlawful, speech-suppressing conduct.” Disney said the groups and individuals can instead file an amicus brief to make their views known to the court “at the appropriate stage in the litigation.”
Art Belendiuk, a lawyer for the groups seeking to intervene, said in a statement provided to Ars that they will continue making their case to the court.
“The FCC’s pressure campaign against Disney has already forced the company to compromise its reporting and programming, as it outlined in its lawsuit, harming countless viewers across the United States. While Disney can argue that our interests are aligned, that may not always be true,” Belendiuk said. “Disney has a legal and fiduciary obligation to its shareholders, and its corporate interest is in preserving its licenses. My clients are fighting in the public interest to protect and preserve the integrity of the First Amendment. The American people deserve a seat at the table, and we are confident that the judge will agree.”
Disney acknowledged in its lawsuit that it changed coverage because of the FCC’s actions. With The View facing a separate FCC proceeding related to the equal-time rule, “ABC must now evaluate any invitation to a political candidate for its potential consequences, including whether it might later be cited by the Commission as a basis for non-renewal in the Stations’ impending license renewal proceedings,” the lawsuit said. The View hasn’t aired any interviews of political candidates since the FCC began the proceeding that could revoke the show’s bona fide news exemption to the equal-time rule.

The liver is a large, forgiving organ, but tumours can grow deep within it, spread across both its halves, or take root in a liver already scarred by disease. Up until recently, cutting out the cancer was often impossible without leaving too little healthy liver behind to keep a person alive. Today, however, a growing field known as transplant oncology is changing that.
What happens
Instead of trying to cut the cancer out of the liver, doctors remove the entire diseased liver and replace it with a healthy one. The most common type of liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), is frequently multifocal, meaning it appears in several places at once. A transplant solves both problems in a single operation: it removes every tumour, eliminates the scarred field that keeps producing them, and restores completely normal liver function.
The central challenge of transplant oncology has always been selection. Donor livers are precious and scarce, and a transplant only makes sense if the cancer is unlikely to return. What increasingly matters is a tumour’s biology: how aggressive it is, how it behaves, and how it responds to treatment. This shift is the heart of modern transplant oncology. Teams now weigh blood markers such as AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) and PIVKA-II, patterns seen on PET scans, and the tumour’s grade under the microscope.
One of the most powerful tools in this field is downstaging, which means deliberately shrinking tumours until a patient who was previously ineligible becomes a candidate for transplant. A cancer that shrinks and stays quiet is showing favourable biology. One that keeps growing despite treatment reveals itself as too aggressive for a transplant to help. Roughly half of appropriately selected patients can be successfully downstaged, and those who are then transplanted after a mandatory observation window do strikingly well.
Expanding limits
While HCC remains the main indication, transplant oncology is expanding into cancers that were, until recently, considered off-limits. Bile duct cancers (cholangiocarcinoma) are a prime example. For certain patients with tumours at the junction of the bile ducts that cannot be removed surgically, a rigorous protocol combining chemotherapy, radiation, and careful staging before transplant has produced survival rates far beyond what surgery alone could achieve.
Beyond HCC and bile duct cancers, this treatment modality is also relevant to several other complex liver tumours, including intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and cancers that metastasise to the liver, such as colorectal liver metastases and neuroendocrine liver metastases. In children, it also plays an important role in the treatment of paediatric liver cancers, including hepatoblastoma, HCC, and hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
Two lives, one principle
A 54-year-old man with chronic liver disease arrived with two hepatocellular carcinomas involving the right lobe of the liver. Owing to the underlying chronic liver disease, he was not a suitable candidate for bridging therapy. As his tumour markers were within normal limits, and a PET-CT showed no evidence of extrahepatic disease, his 45-year-old wife came forward as a living donor and donated her right lobe. He then underwent a successful living donor liver transplant, made an uneventful recovery, and is now five months post-transplant with excellent graft function and no evidence of disease recurrence. This case highlights another important indication for liver transplantation, where it offers a curative treatment for patients with both decompensated chronic liver disease and underlying liver cancer.
Another patient, a man in his fifties, had liver cancer that had grown into a major blood vessel. Rather than turning him away, his team treated the tumour with targeted local therapies and precision radiation, watched his tumour markers fall steadily to normal, and confirmed the cancer had responded before proceeding. Nearly two years after his transplant, he remains cancer-free.
Transplant oncology has therefore shifted the question from “can this tumour be removed?” to “does its biology make a new liver worth giving?” As selection grows more precise, more patients who were once told nothing could be done, are finding a real path to cure.
(Dr. Jayanth Reddy is lead consultant - HPB & liver and pancreatic transplants at Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, Bengaluru. jayanth.reddy@manipalhospitals.com)

The Best Monitors for the Mac
Featured in this article
The Mac Mini is back. And so is the Mac Studio. They’ve been nearly impossible to buy for most of 2026 thanks to the rising demand for running AI models locally. Prices have risen, yes, but when new models go on sale in late September, they’ll finally be out in the wild. And with that, you’ll want a decent monitor to match.
Whether you need something basic or you're a content creator looking for a high-end display, one of these monitors I’ve tested below should do the trick. They’ll work with any Mac, not just the Mac Mini.
Be sure to check our Best Apple Desktops, Best MacBooks, Best Monitors, Best Monitor Arms, and Best Gaming Monitors guides for more.
Updated September 2026: I’ve oriented this guide toward monitors that work with any type of Mac (not just a Mac Mini), and I’ve added a number of monitors I recently tested, such as the BenQ MQ270S, Apple Studio Display XDR, and Asus ProArt 27 QD-OLED. I’ve also added some recommended new monitor arms from my recent batch of testing.
What to Look For in a Mac Monitor
Just about any monitor can work with a Mac. It doesn’t need to be made by Apple or have any official certification. There’s a case to be made for using a cheap 1080p monitor, but most Mac users will want something a bit more premium. As you can see from options like the Dell 27 Plus 4K, that doesn’t have to mean overly expensive. Either way, here are the four elements to consider when shopping for a good monitor to go with your Mac.
Size and resolution: 27- and 32-inch monitors are the most common sizes these days, but there are larger options. I would also consider a 34-inch ultrawide monitor if you like the wider 21:9 aspect ratio with the curved shape. With Apple, resolution is king. There's a reason it invests so much in high pixel density for every screen it sells, even in midrange options like the MacBook Air. Pixel density is what gives a screen its sharpness, and you need a lot more pixels when they're stretched across a large external monitor. If you want to keep fidelity up, I wouldn’t buy anything less than 4K, and bumping up to 5K or 6K on a 32-inch monitor can be helpful. Read more to learn the details on the funky way macOS handles resolutions and scaling. You should also consider the refresh rate: a 120-Hz refresh rate is what the MacBook Pro supports, offering smoother animation, especially in games.
Adjustability: Apple monitors and iMacs aren’t exactly known for adjustability. They often have none at all, and cost more when they do. That isn’t the best for your posture and ergonomics. Famously, the discontinued Pro Display XDR charged an extra $1,000 for a Pro Stand with proper adjustability (now a $400 add-on for the newer Studio Display XDR). For ergonomics, the top of the screen you're working on should be as close to eye level as possible, and that ranges depending on someone’s height. If a monitor doesn’t have height adjustability, you’ll need a separate monitor stand or arm. Beyond height adjustment, many monitors also have stands that can swivel, tilt, and rotate, all of which matter when using multiple monitors. This is also needed if you want to use a second monitor vertically, which has become increasingly popular.
Ports: Even the cheapest monitors will always have HDMI, which is all you need to connect directly to a Mac Mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, or MacBook Pro. Some monitors have USB-C that supports video, which will let you connect to one of a Mac’s Thunderbolt ports. The Mac Mini comes with three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an Ethernet jack. The Mac Mini Pro model has the same ports, except three of them support faster Thunderbolt 5 instead of 4. You’ll need to use at least one of these Thunderbolt ports to connect more than one external monitor. These monitors also tend to have other ports, such as USB-A. These can be useful, as the Mac Mini doesn't have any on its own.
Image quality: Apple prides itself on the image quality of its Macs, so in the case of the Mac Mini, you’ll likely want to get something worthy of your Mac. This is especially important for content creators, photographers, and designers. So, consider a monitor’s brightness, color accuracy, color coverage, and contrast. While some IPS displays offer decent color and contrast, mini-LED or OLED displays will guarantee better image quality. These also have significantly higher peak brightness in HDR content, which really brings games and movies to life.
How Many Monitors Can a Mac Mini Support?
The latest Mac Mini with the M6 chip can support up to three external displays, using the three Thunderbolt ports or one HDMI port on the back. Regardless of the resolution (up to 8K) or refresh rate (up to 240 Hz), if you're just plugging in a single monitor, any one of these ports will do. Use whichever your monitor has or whichever is the most convenient. But when you need multiple displays, that's where things get complicated. Here's a table explaining the differences.
| Mac Mini Model | One Display | Two Displays | Three Displays | 
|---|---|---|---|
| M6 | Up to one 8K display at 50 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz | Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz and one display up to 5K at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI) | Up to two 6K displays at 60 Hz or 4K at 165 Hz and third display up to 5K at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI) | 
| M5 Pro | Up to one 8K display at 50 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz | Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz and one display up to 5K at 120 Hz or 4K at 200 Hz | Up to three 6K displays at 60 Hz or 4K at 165 Hz | 
| M4 | Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 4K display at 240 Hz | Up to one 6K display at 60 Hz and one display at 4K at 144 Hz | Up to two 6K displays at 60 Hz and one 5K at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI) | 
| M4 Pro | Up to one 8K at 60 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz | Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz and one 6K at 60 Hz or 4K at 144 Hz | Up to three 6K displays at 60 Hz or three 4K displays at 144 Hz | 
| M2 | Up to one 6K display at 60 Hz or 4K at 60 Hz | Up to one 6K display at 60 Hz and 5K display at 60 Hz (using Thunderbolt) or 4K at 60 Hz (using HDMI) | Not supported | 
| M2 Pro | Up to one 8K display at 60 Hz or 4K at 240 Hz | Up to two displays at 6K at 60 Hz or one display at 4K at 144Hz | Up to two 6K displays at 60 Hz and one display at 4K at 60 Hz | 
| M1 | 4K display at 60 Hz | One 6K and one 4K at 60 Hz | Not supported | 
Why Macs Don't Run 4K Resolutions Natively
When you plug in an external 4K monitor to a Mac of any kind, it will look good. The icons, text, and UI elements look sharp and not overly small. But open up the Display menu in System Settings, and you'll find that it’s not actually rendering at the full resolution of 3840 x 2160. Instead, it'll default to a much lower resolution to achieve that scaling. In fact, this happens even on the integrated display of a MacBook Air, which defaults to 1470 x 956 instead of the native 2560 x 1664. No doubt, this is one reason macOS defaults to hiding the list of resolutions and instead just asks the user how large they want the text to appear.
I won’t get into the rather complex reasoning behind this, but know this: the resolution you see in the macOS display settings doesn't appear to be that resolution. That's what Apple's Retina Display branding is all about: preserving clarity. And when you plug in an external monitor, macOS will maintain that priority of clarity at the expense of native resolution.
That said, there are a few resolutions and screen sizes that are best optimized for macOS’ proclivities. Namely, it's 27-inch monitors with a 5K resolution (5120 x 2880), which gives you exactly twice the resolution of 1440p and produces an extremely sharp image without messing up the scaling. That doesn't mean 4K monitors won't work or aren't worth the money; just don't expect things to work exactly how they do when connected to Windows.
Mac Mini or iMac?
If you haven’t already bought your Mac Mini, you might be wondering if it's a better deal than the iMac. After all, both are desktop Macs with similar specs and performance. The M6 Mac Mini starts at $899, which gets you 16 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage. The M4 iMac, on the other hand, costs $1,499. It has an older processor, but comes with the same memory and storage, a built-in 24-inch display with 4480 x 2520 (4.5K) resolution, a 12-megapixel webcam, a mouse, a keyboard, and some decent speakers. For the $600 difference, you either get a computer with a newer processor but no display or accessories, or an all-in-one that's ready out of the box.
It's hard to quantify, though, as there aren't any 4.5K monitors out there. The 24-inch monitor size has largely disappeared, except for ultra-budget displays or professional esports gaming monitors. However, you can certainly buy a quality 27-inch 4K monitor for less than $500 (and a 5K variant for not much more), with money left over to add on peripherals such as a webcam or computer speakers. So, in terms of cost savings, grabbing the Mac Mini is a smart move. You're paying extra for the iMac’s convenience of it being an all-in-one system.
More Great Mac Accessories
Kit out your Mac with these other accessories, and make sure to check out our Best Mac Accessories guide for more.
Satechi Mac Mini M4 Hub Stand for $75: Very few products are designed specifically for the Mac Mini, which is what makes this USB hub and stand from Satechi so special. It gives you forward-facing USB-A ports and an SD card slot, plus an enclosure for an NVMe SSD drive to expand a Mac Mini's integrated storage.
Herman Miller Flo Single Monitor Arm for $305: You’d better have a nice monitor if you’re even considering this monitor arm, which is one of the most expensive I’ve ever seen. But after testing it, I have to say I was impressed by what it offers. Most monitor arms share a lot in common, but this one uses an innovative mechanism that attaches the back of the screen in an entirely different way, resulting in a remarkably smooth sense of motion. It’s not for everyone, but it definitely won me over.
Logitech MX Master 4 for $120: The Logitech MX Master mouse has been a mainstay on the desks of Mac users who are serious about productivity and comfort. The latest version isn’t a major overhaul, but it makes tweaks to modernize the design, using better materials, haptics, and a new thumb rest button. But everything that made the MX Master series so great is still here.
BenQ Ergo Arm for $150: This is my favorite monitor arm. I’ve tested a bunch recently, and I really like the complete package of the Ergo Arm. The white color is nice, and while it’s extremely sturdy and can handle just about any monitor (no matter how large), it doesn’t feel as clunky as some other monitor arms I’ve tested. Extra features like the included reinforcement plate to prevent damage to your desk also sweeten the deal.
Harber London Leather Desk Mat for $239: If you’re looking to upgrade the look and feel of your desk and complement your Mac Mini, a desk mat goes a long way. It’ll endure some wear and tear on your desk, but this high-end leather option from Harber London has the quality to last many years of use. And yes, it’s gorgeous.
Hemudu Monitor Stands for $30: If your monitor doesn’t have proper height adjustment, elevating it is key to keeping it at eye level. There are tons of different options out there, but this affordable monitor stand is especially nice for those setting up two monitors side by side.

Steinem led a CIA-backed organization that reportedly recruited young Americans to disrupt Soviet Union-supported festivals and share alternatives to communist ideas. She maintained through her life that her involvement with the CIA was an innocent arrangement and claimed in a 1967 New York Times article that the CIA never asked her to report on other Americans or foreign nationals.
After American journalist and feminist activist Gloria Steinem died at age 92 on Sept. 3, 2026, a rumor spread online that she once worked with the CIA.
Social media users on X, TikTok and Reddit claimed she was a CIA "asset," "cop" or "operative," or that she led an organization that was actually a front for CIA operations.
Steinem repeatedly and publicly acknowledged working with the CIA. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, she ran the Independent Research Service, a CIA-backed organization that recruited young Americans, reportedly to disrupt Soviet Union-supported festivals and promote alternatives to communist ideas.
As such, we have rated this claim as true.
Whether she actively spied for the CIA is unclear. In 1967 news articles, Steinem insisted she was never asked to pass information to the CIA.
Steinem admits involvement after exposé
"This was the organization that made life so miserable for the organizers of the communist-leaning world youth festivals in Vienna in 1959, and in Helsinki in 1962," the 
According to a 2016 New York Times article about Steinem, after the Ramparts issue ran, Steinem publicly acknowledged to the Times and The Washington Post that the CIA was a major financial backer of the Independent Research Service.
While the Times said the Independent Research Service simply received financial support, the Post said Steinem "worked closely with the Central Intelligence Agency" and "had great praise for the CIA agents whom she collaborated with."
"I found them liberal and farsighted and open to an exchange of ideas," Steinem said, according to the Post. "I never felt I was being dictated to at all." Steinem told both newspapers that very few people involved in the Independent Research Service knew of the CIA's involvement.
The Post's article also quoted another director of the Independent Research Service, Dennis Shaul, who said, "The Helsinki Festival was a disaster from their (the Communist world's) point of view, and I think we can take a good deal of credit for that."
In March 1967, Steinem appeared on a CBS documentary, "In the Pay of the CIA: An American Dilemma," to tell her story about her time taking "secret CIA funds," per a CBS news release archived in the CIA's public records.
A clip of her interview in that documentary appears to be available on YouTube. In the clip, she acknowledges working for the CIA and, again, says the CIA did not interfere with her point of view.
"I had the conventional liberal's view of the CIA as a right-wing incendiary group, and I was amazed to discover that this was far from the case, that they were enlightened, liberal nonpartisan activists," she said (at 2:17).
We reached out to CBS to ask for an official copy of the documentary and await a response.
Steinem responds to feminist 
In 1975, Redstockings, a radical feminist group, attacked Steinem's involvement with the CIA and called Steinem's insistence that she was never asked to gather information for the CIA a "serious lie."
"The Report on the Vienna Youth Festival, published with her name on it as Director of the Independent Research Service, contains 13 pages devoted solely to biographies, political affiliations, and even pseudo-political analyses of individuals from all the countries participating in the festival," Redstockings wrote.
Redstockings also said it questioned Steinem's motives for entering the women's movement and was "suspicious of her sudden rise to prominence as a 'women's liberation leader' at a time when, unlike other prominent women's liberationists, she was active in no women's group, she had not written a feminist book, won a Congressional seat or played a superb game of tennis."
The New York Times reported in 2016 that Steinem said the criticism from other feminists "hurt more than anything."
"They never called to ask me what I did," she said.
In the same 2016 article, Steinem maintained that her relationship with the CIA was innocent.
"It's so interesting now, because the initials C.I.A. will make people believe anything," she said. "It just wasn't like that. It just was so uncontrolled. As I remember saying at the time, if this was our grandmother's money we'd be doing the same thing."

Littler beats Humphries to win Czech Open

Luke Littler overcame defending champion Luke Humphries to claim the Czech Open title in Prague.
World number one Littler was playing in his first European Tour event since the Belgium Open in March, and beat Krzysztof Ratajski, Danny Noppert as well as Michael van Gerwen on his way to the blockbuster final.
He was trailing 4-3 against world number two Humphries, who saw off Andrew Gilding, William O'Connor and Gerwyn Price, before a four-leg burst put the 19-year-old Littler 7-4 in front.
Humphries reduced the deficit to 7-6 but failed to level the match as he missed with two darts at double 16 in the 14th leg.
Littler capitalised by taking out 39 for a win which secures his place at the European Championship in Dortmund in October.

"It's good to be back and I'm back with a bang.
"These long days are worth it, especially lifting the trophy."
Littler, who is attempting to complete the calendar sweep of ranking events in 2026, added: "I think I've secured my place in Dortmund - Dortmund is the one I'm chasing."
Humphries was aiming to win the Czech Open for a fourth time and third occasion on the trot.
"I was going to pull out Thursday, and I made the final, so I can't be too upset with myself because I did really well," he said.
"I never give up, especially in finals. I know that Luke is obviously going to throw everything at me.
"Hopefully over the next four months, I push him. If he does the clean sweep, he has to do it the hard way."

A shift swap on 9/11: The story of the World Trade Center restaurant staff who lost their lives
A new documentary retells the story of the World Trade Center’s iconic top-floor restaurant, Windows on the World. For the surviving staff, its legacy rests not on how it ended but on the workplace they created for 25 years before that tragic day, Jasmine Fernández writes
Sekou Siby was supposed to be working the morning shift on September 11, 2001. Instead, he swapped with a young co-worker from Ecuador, taking the afternoon slot.
The decision left him one of the survivors of Windows on the World, the World Trade Center’s legendary top-floor restaurant.
Now, as the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks approaches, the story of the venue and its staff is being retold through the eyes of the workers who made it run.
Directed by Oscar nominees Betsy West and Julie Cohen, the new documentary short “Top of the World”, airing Monday night on CNN, offers an intimate look at the fine-dining institution that operated for 25 years, 1,300 feet above Manhattan.
Getting a job at Windows on the World, the country’s highest-grossing restaurant packed with celebrities, tourists and New York power brokers, was seen as a coup among those recently arrived in the United States.
When American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower between floors 93 and 99, all escape routes below the restaurant were instantly severed. Of the nearly 3,000 lives lost across the country that day, all 170 people at the restaurant died - 79 employees and 91 guests.
For the surviving staff, the legacy of Windows on the World rests not on how it ended but on the workplace culture they created for 25 years before that tragic day.
Conceived by renowned restaurateur Joe Baum to help revitalize a financially struggling New York in 1976, Windows on the World quickly became a cultural landmark.
Occupying the 106th and 107th floors of the North Tower, the restaurant functioned as a quarter-mile-high theater, brought to life through design work by architect Warren Platner and Milton Glaser, the revered graphic designer behind the “I Love New York” logo.
Anchored by a 107th-floor bar, a glass-enclosed “Cellar in the Sky” and a menu refined by head chef Michael Lomonaco, the venue generated more revenue than any standalone restaurant in the nation.
“Everybody knew what Windows on the World was, right there at the top of the World Trade Center,” Lomonaco says, during the CNN Films and TIME Studios short film. “We were the highest-grossing restaurant in America. It was glamorous.”
The workers came from more than 60 countries — Ecuador, Mexico, Peru, Ghana and Bangladesh, to name a few. For many, Windows on the World was their first real foothold in America. The restaurant’s 450 employees built a tight-knit community. They picked up phrases in new languages, joined for soccer matches on days off and explained cultural traditions to one another — like why Muslim staff fasted during Ramadan.
“We're all children of immigrants, whether it’s this century or two centuries ago,” Lomonaco says. “The immigrants who worked at Windows, I mean, they came from all over the world-and they found a job in the most glamorous, glorious place in New York City.”
Siby came to the United States from the Ivory Coast in 1996 when he was 31 years old. “I thought, America is really the country of freedom,” Siby recalls in the film.
He got his start through his roommate, Abdoul Karim Troare, a fellow West African immigrant who was a banquet cook at Windows on the World. Troare helped him land a job as a prep cook, where Siby spent his early days peeling carrots, potatoes and, at times, 200 pounds of onions, until his eyes burned.
On the floor, hostess Nathalie Tolentino saw life at the restaurant from a different angle. After studying hotel management in Peru and moving to New York with her family to escape political violence, she landed a job as a hostess at Windows on the World. Her exceptional work ethic soon led to an offer from ownership for a management role.
The film opens on archival home video of Tolentino giving her grandmother a tour, in Spanish, through the dining space, showing off the floor-to-ceiling views the restaurant offered.
“For me, coming from Peru, it was just learning from the best,” Tolentino says in the film. “Living in Lima was chaos, especially during the worst era of terrorism in Peru.”
September 11, 2001
On the morning of September 11, 2001, New York City shone beneath bright, clear skies. At Windows on the World, 79 staff members and 91 guests were on the 106th and 107th floors, preparing for breakfast service and a financial technology conference hosted by the London-based Risk Waters Group.
Siby was off that morning because of a shift swap. Moises Rivas, a 29-year-old cook and immigrant from Ecuador, had asked Siby to cover his Sunday shift so he could perform with his band on Saturday night without having to wake up for a 5 a.m. call.
In return, Rivas offered to work Siby’s Tuesday morning slot. Siby agreed. Rivas, a husband and father of two young children, reported to work in his place that morning.
Lomonaco also survived due to a chance delay on the lower level before heading up to the restaurant.
“I parked my car in the garage,” Lomonaco says. “There was an event that morning, a breakfast meeting. I could have easily gone up to my office, but instead I went in to the eyeglass shop to get my glasses adjusted.
“There was an ophthalmologist right there in the building on the lower level. I was sitting in the office. He had just examined my eyes, and I felt the building shake.”
Siby was at home when his phone rang. It was the wife of Troare, the friend who’d helped him land the job. She told him to turn on the TV, and he watched as smoke poured from the North Tower, where Troare, Rivas and dozens of his colleagues were working.
“The entire morning crew, all the people that you used to play soccer with, they were all gone,” Siby recalls in the film. “Why them? Why not me?”
Three weeks after the attacks, Siby’s wife gave birth to their daughter.
“Taking care of a baby helped me occupy my mind and gave me a reason why God saved my life,” Siby says.
In the days that followed, surviving staff members and management scrambled to locate missing staff and support their relatives, setting up an emergency hotline out of a temporary union office.
“We gathered as a group to identify our friends and colleagues that we lost,” Lomonaco says in the film.
Because many of the workers were immigrants, communication was complex. Tolentino stepped up to answer the phones, serving as a vital link for Spanish-speaking families calling from throughout New York and across Latin America as they searched for news of their missing loved ones.
For Siby, losing his friends shifted his focus to organizing. He went on to earn an MBA and a doctoral degree in business administration, and he helped found Restaurant Opportunities Centers United, a national advocacy group for restaurant workers.
Decades later, when reflecting on the tragedy in conversation with Lomonaco, Siby speaks to the heavy, singular trauma borne by the survivors.
“We lose all those people in one day,” Siby says. “That’s not the kind of experience that normal, regular people experience in their life.”
Lomonaco agrees, emphasizing that the absence of their colleagues remains a permanent part of their lives.
“There was nothing ever like Windows on the World,” Lomonaco says as the film closes. “There will never be anything like Windows on the World.”
The film premieres Monday, September 7, at 8 p.m. Eastern Time on CNN, airing again three hours later for West Coast viewers, before streaming the following day on CNN digital platforms.

Swiggy’s subsidiary, Swiggy Networks Ltd, has entered a share acquisition agreement with B2B ecommerce unicorn Udaan to acquire Swiggy-owned retail distribution platform Lynk in a share-swap transaction valuing the business at ₹500 Cr.
Under the deal, Swiggy Networks will transfer its entire shareholding in Lynks Logistics Ltd to Trustroot Internet Pvt Ltd (TIPL), Udaan’s Singapore-based parent entity.
“During the financial year ended March 31, 2026, the said business contributed revenue of ₹668 Cr, representing 2.90% of the consolidated revenue of the company. The net assets attributable to the said business were ₹500 Cr as at March 31, 2026, representing 2.73% of the consolidated net worth of the company,” Swiggy said in its filing with the exchanges.
In return, TIPL will issue 1.67 Lakh Series R CCPS to Swiggy Networks at an issue price of $314.40 apiece. The shares, worth $52.37 Mn, will give Swiggy a roughly 2.8% stake in Udaan.
Swiggy will also invest ₹75 Cr in primary capital in TIPL for an additional 0.4% stake, taking its total shareholding in Udaan to about 3.2%.
The acquisition is expected to be completed by October 22, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals.

Nawazuddin Siddiqui recently reflected on the years of perseverance, theatre training and limited opportunities that shaped his journey as an actor which primarily started with Sarfarosh. In a conversation with Shekhar Suman, the actor spoke about the uncertainty he experienced while trying to find substantial work, while maintaining that he never doubted his abilities as a performer.
Nawazuddin Siddiqui on his Sarfarosh debut: “For those 40 seconds, I had enough confidence that people will only watch me”
Siddiqui explained that his determination came from having committed himself entirely to acting. Recalling the mindset that helped him navigate the difficult phase of his career, he said, “It was that we had no other option. Nor did we keep one. It was an absolute do or die. It was do or die. It was like we will only do this, even if it takes 50 years, if we are at it. Yes, we will stay at it. There was a stubbornness and belief too. There was a belief that the day we get it, we will show them that day. That was there. The belief was there because you had practiced so much on acting. Yes, yes absolutely. So there was not even a slight doubt about this thing. But with me, there is no doubt about the skill, the doubt is whether I got the opportunity or not. Yes, now of course I got it.. in Sarfarosh, I got a 40-second role. 40 seconds, yes, so for those 40 seconds I had enough confidence that when my 40 seconds come, I will bring everything to a halt, people will only watch me.”
The actor’s reference to Sarfarosh highlights how he approached even a brief screen appearance. Rather than viewing the limited duration as a reason to hold back, Siddiqui saw those 40 seconds as an opportunity to put his years of preparation into practice.
His comments also draw a distinction between confidence in one’s abilities and the availability of opportunities. According to Siddiqui, the uncertainty during his early years was not about whether he could perform, but whether he would get the chance to demonstrate what he had learned through years of theatre and training.
Siddiqui eventually went on to take on a range of supporting and lead roles, becoming known for performances across Hindi cinema and streaming projects. His latest reflections offer a look back at the mindset he maintained before wider recognition came his way.
For the actor, the journey involved continuing to pursue acting despite the absence of immediate opportunities. His recollection of the 40-second role in Sarfarosh underscores how he approached even smaller parts with the same conviction he had developed through years of preparation.

A clever technique used to hide malicious prompts in attacks on AI agents has been adopted by spammers to evade filters on email platforms that are designed to flag unwanted messages used in mass campaigns.
The technique is broadly known as ASCII smuggling. It gained attention two years ago as a means of making a class of AI attack known as prompt injections more stealthy. Malicious instructions embedded in emails or other untrusted content to be processed by an LLM aren’t written in ordinary text. Instead, they’re rendered by a special range of Unicode tags. For example, the tag point U+E0041 mirrors “A,” and U+E0061 mirrors “a.”
No longer just for obscuring prompt injections
The block of 128 tags mimics a portion of the American Standard Code for Information Interchange almost perfectly, with one major difference: the characters they encode are readable by computers but, by design, are almost completely invisible to humans. By expressing the malicious prompts in these tags, LLMs detect the instructions, but people reading the email never see them. There’s much more about ASCII smuggling here.
Earlier this year, Microsoft started seeing a massive increase in spam messages that used the technique. Beginning on one day in early February, the number of ASCII smuggling signatures detected by Microsoft Defender for Office spiked from roughly 21,000 per day to more than 1.3 million. Within four days, signature detections jumped to 2.5 million. The deluge persisted for months and then fell off sharply in mid-May.
“Because tag characters are invisible to humans but exist at the text-processing level, the same property that makes them useful for smuggling instructions into a model also makes them useful for obfuscating keywords before a detector evaluates them,” Microsoft explained Thursday. “The intent is inverted, but the mechanism is similar, and a user’s suspicions are not raised.”

Pope returns to sanctuary where he prayed after election and unveils a fresco depicting the event
Pope Leo XIV has returned to a sanctuary where he prayed just after his election
GENAZZANO, Italy -- Pope Leo XIV returned Monday to a sanctuary where he prayed just after his election and revealed a permanent sign of his devotion to the place: a fresco depicting him praying that now adorns an upper cornice of the basilica.
Leo unveiled the portrait before celebrating Mass with his fellow Augustinian brothers at the Sanctuary of Our Mother of Good Counsel in the medieval village of Genazzano south of Rome. He joins a handful of past popes whose visits to the sanctuary were commemorated with portraits that adorn its walls, going back to Pope Urban VIII in 1630.
Leo visited the sanctuary on May 10, 2025, just two days after his election and in his first outing as pope. The former Robert Prevost had been there many times before, since the place has special significance for the pope's Augustinian religious order.
The sanctuary is managed by Augustinian friars and has been a place of pilgrimage since the 15th century. Leo’s namesake, Pope Leo XIII, elevated it to a minor basilica and expanded the adjacent convent in the early 1900s.
Leo referred to that 2025 outing during his homily at the basilica Monday, which commemorates the birth of Mary. Leo recalled what he wrote then in the sanctuary's guest book.
The new pope wrote at the time that he felt the “need and profound desire” to come to the sanctuary after his election to pray before the Madonna of Good Counsel “who has accompanied me all my life with her maternal presence, with her wisdom and example of love for her son who is always the center of my faith.”
Leo and the Vatican are stepping up activities now that summer lull is coming to a close. The Holy See’s typically busy autumn conferences and audiences are taking shape, and Leo is gearing up for a trip to France at the end of the month and his much-awaited trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November.

President Donald Trump doesn't want one particular Canadian aircraft crossing over into the US.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump wrote: "No more selling Bombardier in the United States! Their products aren't good enough."
Trump said that if the company wants business from the US, it needs to build its jets in the US. Bombardier, an aircraft manufacturer based in Montreal, makes business and private luxury jets.
US federal agencies such as the US Air Force and the Federal Aviation Administration were previously reported to have Bombardier aircraft in their fleets. Representatives for the White House did not respond to a query from Business Insider on whether any federal agencies are canceling orders with Bombardier after Trump's announcement.
Bombardier wrote in a statement on its website on Monday, without any reference to Trump's post, that it's a "strong contributor" to the American aerospace industry, creating "tens of thousands of jobs across the United States."
The statement said that Bombardier's American workers are based across the US, with sites in Kansas, Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, Washington, D.C., and New Jersey. It has "overall direct employment presence in more than 20 states," Bombardier said.
The company said it also uses American-made aircraft components in its manufacturing, like engines, wings, and avionics. Its supply chain includes 2,800 American companies across 47 states, it added.
"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its U.S. employees," the company said in the statement. "Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers, and the communities in which we operate across the country."
Trump's post comes as trade tensions between the two neighbors flare. Canada's latest round of tariffs went into effect on Tuesday, imposing 50% duties on hundreds of US goods, including cheese, honey, and aluminum foil. These levies are a retaliatory response to the 50% tariffs the US imposed on Canadian products such as dairy, alcohol, and electronics.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
- Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark 
  - Published7 June
- Antonelli says he still has questions to answer 
  - Published11 June
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Why a famous Montreal sandwich shop has been forced to swap its soda
Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has stopped serving the iconic US-made black cherry soda that has been a fixture at the restaurant for decades.
The sandwich shop had struggled to maintain supply of the cola for the last eight years as the distributor cut back production due to the rising cost of aluminium.
But it didn't expect the cans to vanish permanently. Now it has switched to a locally-made version, which the venue's customers have largely embraced.

Expressing grave concern over the high prevalence of child marriages resulting in underage pregnancies and deliveries in the State, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (September 7, 2026) said that the State had recorded nearly 60,000 underage institutional deliveries in the first six months of 2026.
Details of underage institutional deliveries from January 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 had been obtained from the State Health Department, and the numbers were alarming, Mr. Adhikari said.
“As a result of the previous government, we are now number one in two criteria across the country — marriage of girls below 18 years of age, and deliveries before 18 years of age. These numbers are so high that there aren’t enough jails in which to put these people,” the Chief Minister said, addressing media persons at the State Secretariat.
Mr. Adhikari read out the provisions of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, adding that the law prohibited marriage with a child below 18 years of age. In such cases, “Police action will be initiated and arrests will be made,” he said.
The Chief Minister emphasised that the practice of child marriage could not be allowed to prevail, and the State Health Department would issue a show-cause notice to the offenders, especially the husband, who would have to provide documentary evidence within a month that both he and his ‘wife’ were adults in accordance with the law.
“If he fails to do so, the DGP (Director General of Police), who is sitting right next to me, will take action as per the law,” Mr. Adhikari said. The State government would stop delivering benefits under all Central and State government welfare schemes to these families, he said. Action would be taken against the priest and qazi who solemnised the marriage, and against other family members, he added.
Sharing district-wise details of cases of underage pregnancies, the Chief Minister said 12,847 institutional childbirths by underage girls were recorded in Murshidabad district alone, followed by South 24 Parganas at 4,178.
West Bengal has recorded the highest number of child marriages over the past few years, despite schemes rolled out to keep girls in schools. According to the Sample Registration Survey report published in September 2025, West Bengal recorded 6.3% of females getting married before the age of 18 years, whereas at the national level, 2.1% of females got married before the age of 18 years. Murshidabad remains a hotspot for child marriages. About 55.4% women in the district aged 20 to 24 years said they were married before the age of 18 years, according to the National Family Health Survey-5.
Experts working on the ground, however, say that child marriage is a complex issue involving not only parental or social pressure but also cases of elopement, and minor grooms. They warn that the arrest of husbands may result in placing a strain on already marginalised families, and impact marital relations adversely.

- Onimusha: Way of the Sword's Mask puzzle is located in Underground Laboratory Level Three at the Nijo-jo Castle.
- This puzzle appears in Chapter 11, "What Lurks in the Shadows".
- You can solve it by shooting the third mask -> fourth mask -> first mask -> second mask in this order with your bow.
Like any Capcom title, Onimusha: Way of the Sword has multiple puzzles throughout Miyamoto Musashi’s journey to stop the Malice from spreading across Kyoto. While fairly straightforward, the Mask puzzle is one of the more confusing puzzles in Chapter 11, “What Lurks in the Shadows,” where Musashi explores Nijo-jo Castle in search of Okuni’s friend, Hinagiku. So, here’s how to solve the Onimusha: Way of the Sword Mask puzzle.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword Mask Puzzle Solution Explained
The mask puzzle in Onimusha: Way of the Sword appears after Dyoko sends you on a hunt to find one of the keys to the Underground Laboratory Door. You’ll come across it after opening two doors held shut by red strings, shortly after finding the Level Three Spirit Mirror, as shown in the image above.
When you enter the puzzle area, you’ll find four masks hanging from the ceiling by threads. The same four masks are also displayed on the walls on either side of the entrance, lit up by four spotlights from above. To solve the puzzle, you need to fire arrows in a specific order to remove the Unsettling Mask ahead.
Figuring out the masks’ order is easy. Walk out the entrance and examine the masks’ shadows on the wall. You’ll notice that each mask has a specific number of holes. Count the holes to find out the masks’ order, then fire your arrows accordingly. If you’re still confused, here’s the correct order to solve the Onimusha: Way of the Sword Mask puzzle:
| Order | Mask | 
|---|---|
| 1 | Third mask (white mask with eyes closed and smiling) | 
| 2 | Fourth mask (red mask with eyes open and green details) | 
| 3 | First mask (yellow smiling mask with purple details) | 
| 4 | Second mask (purple mask with eyes and mouth open) |

A video purporting to be the first-ever helicopter view of Mount Kailash in Tibet is being shared on social media (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of Mount Kailash in Tibet, filmed from a helicopter.
Fact: The viral video is not of Mount Kailash, but of Mount Assiniboine in Canada. China has closed the airspace around Mount Kailash, and helicopters are completely banned from flying there. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using the keyframes of the viral video led us to photos showing the same mountain on various photography and tourism websites, where it was identified as Mount Assiniboine in Canada. We also compared the mountain seen in the viral video with available photographs of Mount Kailash and found that the two mountains are clearly different.
Additionally, videos filmed by tourists visiting Mount Assiniboine can be viewed here and here. These videos also feature the lake seen in the viral footage. On the other hand, the Government of China has prohibited planes, helicopters, and drones from flying over Mount Kailash, located in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. As the airspace around Mount Kailash is closed for security and religious reasons, tour operators in neighbouring Nepal offer special Kailash Darshan charter flights. These flights operate at around 27,000 feet within Nepali airspace, allowing pilgrims to view Mount Kailash from a distance without entering Tibetan airspace.
To sum up, a video of Canada’s Assiniboine Mountains is being shared as a view of Mount Kailash.

A team of Indian researchers has produced the first comprehensive molecular and functional profile of the venom gland of Stegodyphus sarasinorum, a colonial spider species found across the Indian subcontinent, to identify numerous proteins and small molecules that could serve as promising leads for future drug discovery.
Published in Springer Nature’s peer-reviewed, open-access journal Scientific Reports, the study identifies bioactive compounds associated with anti-cancer, antimicrobial and immune-related functions, while also demonstrating that venom gland extracts can kill cancer cells under laboratory conditions.
The researchers caution, however, that the findings represent an early stage of biomedical research and require extensive validation before any clinical application becomes possible.
Lead researcher A.P. Ajay Kumar of the Department of Zoology at Sree Neelakanta Government Sanskrit College, Pattambi, led the multidisciplinary study.
Unlike most spiders, which are solitary hunters, S. sarasinorum lives in permanent colonies, constructs communal silk nests and captures prey cooperatively. It is among only a small number of permanently social spider species known worldwide, thereby making it an important model for studying both spider behaviour and venom biology.
Although spider venom has long attracted scientific interest for their diverse biological activities, this is the first study to comprehensively analyse the molecular composition of the venom gland of this species using an integrated multi-omics approach, the researchers emphasise.
The research team combined transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and Confocal Raman Spectroscopy to examine the spider’s venom gland in great detail. Their analysis identified 31 protein components through transcriptomic profiling and 32 proteins through proteomic analysis. In addition, Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS) detected 81 metabolites, including amino acids, biogenic amines and organic acids to provide a detailed molecular inventory of the venom gland.
To investigate the biological activity of these molecules, the researchers tested venom gland extracts against Dalton’s Lymphoma Ascites (DLA) cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The extracts exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, meaning that higher concentrations destroyed a greater proportion of cancer cells.
The findings suggest that the venom gland contains molecules with anti-cancer potential, the experiments were conducted only in cultured cells. Nonetheless, further studies involving additional cancer models, healthy cells, animals and eventually clinical trials will be required before any therapeutic use can be considered.
Among the most significant discoveries was the identification of several protein families that are already known for their biomedical relevance. These include hemocyanin proteins, which are known to stimulate immune responses and have attracted considerable interest in cancer immunotherapy research. The study also detected U12 and U20 lycotoxins, peptide molecules that can disrupt the membranes of bacteria and cancer cells, making them promising templates for the future development of antimicrobial peptides and targeted anti-cancer compounds.
The experimental work was carried out by research scholar Veena Venugopal, with contributions from collaborators from Calicut University, S.N. College, Nattika, St. Joseph’s College, Devagiri, PSG Institute of Advanced Studies, Coimbatore; GITAM University, Andhra Pradesh; and Ajman University, UAE.

A Delhi court on Monday (September 7, 2026) remanded Hindutva influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj to 14 days in judicial custody in connection with the alleged assault of the father of a student during a protest at Jantar Mantar in July organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
Additional Sessions Judge Saurabh Pratap Singh Laler of the Patiala House Courts passed the order after Mr. Bhardwaj was produced before the court following the completion of his one-day police custody.
The court had remanded him to police custody for a day on Saturday (September 5). He will be produced before the court again on September 21.
Mr. Bhardwaj was detained in Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh, on Friday (September 4), a few hours after the CJP held a demonstration outside the Parliament Street police station demanding his arrest in connection with the alleged assault.
The Delhi police subsequently added provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and criminal intimidation to the FIR registered against Mr. Bhardwaj over the alleged assault of the minor activist’s father. A separate case under the POCSO Act has also been registered against him.
Mr. Bhardwaj came under scrutiny after a video podcast in which he claimed to have “cracked the skull” of the student’s father during the demonstration went viral. He also claimed during the interview that he had political connections that helped him avoid arrest.

The September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks plunged the US into fear and uncertainty, but they also produced extraordinary acts of courage. Among them was the story of Heather Penney, a young F-16 pilot who was prepared to sacrifice her life to defend Washington, D.C.
Penney was 26 years old and serving as a first lieutenant with the D.C. Air National Guard when the attacks unfolded. After watching the hijacked planes crash into the World Trade Center, she and other airmen realised Washington could be the next target.
“We knew the world had changed and we knew we needed to get airborne,” Penney recalled, ABC7 News reported.
But the fighter pilots had to wait for orders before launching. By the time the Pentagon was struck, Penney said frustration was growing among those who knew they needed to protect the capital.
“It was shortly after the Pentagon was hit that we finally got a call from the Secret Service telling us to get airborne,” she said.
Penney and her flight lead, then-Colonel Marc Sasseville, scrambled to their F-16s. However, the jets were not armed with missiles.
Penney said the lack of ready aircraft was partly a consequence of changes made after the end of the Cold War, when many US alert units had been shut down.
Their mission was to search for an airliner that could potentially be heading toward Washington at low altitude.
“We would do what was necessary to protect and defend,” Penney said.
With no missiles available, Penney and Sasseville devised a desperate plan: they would use their fighter jets to intercept and destroy a hijacked aircraft by crashing into it.
“[Sasseville] would ram his jet into the nose of the aircraft, and I would ram mine into the tail,” Penney recalled.
At the time, the pilots did not know the details of United Flight 93 or what had happened to the passengers aboard the plane.
“Had [Sasseville] and I been successful, it would have been a suicide mission. And you're willing to do it,” Penney said.
Penney remained airborne for roughly three hours but did not know the flight number or the fate of United 93.
Only after landing did she learn that the aircraft had crashed in Pennsylvania before she and Sasseville were ordered into the air.
“By the time [Sasseville] and I were given the order to launch, we would have been too late,” she said. “Flight 93 crashed maybe half an hour, 20 minutes before we launched.”
The passengers of Flight 93 had fought back against the hijackers, ultimately preventing the aircraft from reaching its intended target.
One of the pilots who later flew to assist Penney over Washington was Dan Caine, who went on to become chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Later that day, Penney and her flight lead escorted Air Force aircraft back into Washington as President George W. Bush prepared to address the nation.
Now retired from the Air Force as a major, Penney says the true heroes of September 11 were the passengers who fought back aboard Flight 93.
“What [Sasseville] and I were willing to do is what the passengers on Flight 93 actually did,” she said.
Twenty-five years after the attacks, Penney said Americans should remember not only the tragedy but also the unity and courage that emerged in its aftermath.
“It's also to remember how we came together as a nation,” she said, urging Americans to remember “the best of who we can be” and carry that legacy forward in honour of those killed on 9/11.
ABC7 News reported on Penney's recollections as the US approaches the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.
