It's been a full two years since the National Association of Realtors settled multiple class-action lawsuits related to commission fees in real estate transactions.
Homebuyers and sellers rejoiced knowing that a commission fee — which was normally 6% split between the buying and listing agent — was no longer baked into their bottom line. Anecdotally, both parties have saved thousands of dollars, but so far, not much has changed.
Data from Redfin shows that buyer's agent commissions fell from 2.43% to 2.36% from Q1 2024 to Q3 2024. However, by Q2 2025, they ticked back up to 2.43%.
A February 2026 survey of 533 real estate agents by Clever Real Estate found that the total commission on a real estate transaction is about 5.7% — not too far from the former standard of 6%.
Still, there are people who have found success without using a traditional real estate agent. Vicki Lynn used Homa, an AI-powered buying platform, to buy a home in Florida without an agent. Lynn was turned off by the high fees and slow response times, so she opted to have AI write a contract for her.
Homa charged her a flat fee, and she saved about $7,000.
In the post-NAR world, the landscape hasn't changed dramatically, but a handful of startups want to give buyers and sellers a few different options.
Below are nine startups that are trying to save home sellers money by shaking up the role and pay of the traditional real estate agent.
Dan Latu contributed to a previous version of this article.
Beycome
Beycome aims to be a one-stop shop for homebuyers and sellers who prefer not to use real estate agents.
Founder Nico Jodin started Beycome in 2020 after having a rough experience buying a home in Miami. He wanted his company to focus on the people at the center of the transactions.
"We didn't develop our technology for real estate agents," Jodin told Business Insider. "We didn't develop our technology for brokers. It's for you."
Beycome has helped close on over 18,000 homes and has saved users $212 million in commissions and fees, according to Jodin. Buyers using Beycome can expect the company to act as a broker during transactions. While they will collect the commission fee from the seller, they credit the buyer after taking 1%.
"You can use this credit to cover your closing costs, or you can use this money to buy interest points on your mortgage to reduce the cost of your mortgage," Jodin said. "It is really money that we credit to you, and you do what's better for you."
Clever Real Estate
Though Clever Real Estate has been around since 2017, the flat-fee movement only started hitting its stride recently.
An early adopter of flat-fee rates, Clever Real Estate works with full-service real estate agents, but instead of negotiating a fee, it's set at 1.5%. Founded in St. Louis, Clever Real Estate expanded nationwide in 2019 and works with brokerages like Keller Williams, RE/MAX, and Century 21.
For agents who are skeptical, Clever Real Estate cofounder Luke Babich said that as more consumers realize they don't have to pay the standard 6%, some concessions will have to be made — so you might as well keep your transaction volume up.
"Real estate transactions have gotten a lot more efficient," Babich told STLPR. "It's a matter of time before there's price pressure, and they have to start bringing these rates down. What Clever gives them is a way to tap into discount, to grow their business with a dependable supply of customers, a series of introductions every month that they can count on."
Since its founding, Clever Real Estate has worked with over 251,000 clients, facilitating more than $16.8 billion in real estate transactions, it said. The average customer saves about $7,000 by not going the traditional commission route.
Galleon
Think Craigslist, but for homes — that's the idea behind Galleon.
Galleon is an off-market, for-sale-by-owner residential marketplace that lets homeowners name their prices to see if any buyers bite.
"We believe that there should be a free and open consumer-led marketplace," Amanda Orson, the CEO and founder of Galleon, told BI.
While similar to platforms like Zillow and Redfin, Galleon removes brokers and agents entirely — a move the company said can save sellers $30,000 or more, presuming a typical 6% commission.
Galleon doesn't post days-on-the-market data for its listings, which Orson said gives sellers "no incentive not to try" going without a broker. On traditional platforms, a high days-on-the-market figure on a listing might lead prospective buyers to think a property is either priced too high or that something is wrong with it.
Creating a listing on Galleon's app or website is free.
For $299, sellers can upgrade their listings with professional photography, a digital yard sign with a QR code so sellers don't have to post their phone numbers publicly, and featured placement on Galleon's website for added visibility.
For those wanting more support, Galleon's $899 package includes tools like a scheduling calendar for inspections and appraisals, an offer management dashboard, in-app e-signing, and access to legal support — all aimed at simplifying the sales process and cutting down out-of-pocket costs for the seller.
"We don't think there is a future without agents," Orson told BI. "We think that there is a minority of people who want to be able to transact without one. That's who we're here to support."
The platform is free for home buyers and available nationwide.
Homa
Former Zillow senior product director Arman Javaherian noticed that homebuyers were already putting in a lot of work when searching for a home, so he planned to reward them for it.
"One thing I saw is after talking to hundreds of these homebuyers over the years was that a lot of these homebuyers are going on Zillow and finding the homes and doing a lot of legwork themselves," Javaherian told Business Insider. "They would constantly tell us, 'Why are these agents coming in and making $20,000 or $30,000 for a little bit of work at the end of the process?'"
Javaherian, along with the help of cofounder Federico Campeotto, launched Homa in May 2025 with the goal of building an all-in-one platform for homebuying powered by AI. It's currently only operating in Florida, but has plans to expand to California and Texas in early 2026.
Homa has two offerings: Homa Pro and a free version. The difference between the two offerings is that Homa Pro charges a flat fee of $1,995 to the buyer in transactions where a selling agent is involved, which is most of the time. If no agents are involved, Homa doesn't charge anything.
Javaherian said his company's AI arm is what sets it apart from other platforms.
"Homa is helping come up with the offer price, it's helping analyze the disclosures, the inspection reports," he said. "Homa helps them see the home immediately, and it also helps them draft the offer."
Listwise
Listwise isn't trying to push real estate agents out of the picture — its aim is to help home sellers find the right one.
The platform, aimed primarily at sellers, uses an incentive-based commission model designed to boost competition between agents and improve transparency for home sellers.
Here's how it works: On Listwise's digital platform, sellers share the commission amount they're willing to pay a listing agent and what they're looking for in one — including number of years of experience, importance of local market knowledge, or whether they prefer someone from a big-name brokerage or a smaller local firm. Sellers also propose how much they are willing to pay the buyers' agent.
Listwise then matches the sellers with qualified listing agents in its network who meet those preferences.
Each listing agent then bids for the listing by submitting a personalized offer that includes their commission charge. If a seller chooses one of those agents and the home sells, that agent pays Listwise a referral fee or commission for helping them win the business.
Off-Markt
Alison Bernstein first got the idea for a real estate app when a friend sent her a fitness influencer's Instagram video.
Bernstein liked the flow of the influencer's apartment and messaged her directly to see if she'd be interested in selling. They ended up closing an off-market deal. Bernstein then found an off-market buyer for her own apartment.
It inspired her to create an Off-Markt, an app with an Instagram-like interface that lets homeowners show off their spaces and attract prospective buyers year-round — without ever formally listing them.
"The consumer should own the story of their home. They should own that digital footprint," Bernstein, who is based in New York City, told Business Insider.
On Off-Markt, a user creates profiles for their home. They can post photos showing off the best features of their property. Bernstein's hope is that homeowners feel like they can "own the narrative" of their space and better attract future buyers.
"The average consumer is very savvy," Bernstein said.
Real estate agents create a profile on the app for $50 a month and offer their services to users who might need extra help.
Off-Markt declined to share how many homes and cities are currently listed on the site.
Redy
Josh Altman, a real estate agent featured on "Million Dollar Listing Los Angeles," cofounded Redy in 2020 to encourage transparent competition among agents.
On Redy, agents compete for the opportunity to sell your home by offering incentives like a "cash bonus" and competitive commission prices.
"For the first time, sellers get paid cash to pick an agent; as a result, agents are directly invested in the sale," Altman said in a 2024 press release. "All agents have the opportunity to own local seller listings, which will, in return, help them own the local market they operate in and level the playing field for listings. When you own local seller listings, you own your local market."
Kenneth Bloom, who used Redy to sell two homes in Michigan, told BI in 2024 that he appreciated having agents come to him. Otherwise, he said, he would've had to do a lot of legwork to find the right person to sell his homes.
He said he was able to find an experienced agent who was familiar with his area and could get his homes sold fast, which was a priority for him. He ended up finding a buyer for one of the homes in one day through the agent he found on Redy.
Bloom said he received a $1,200 cash bonus for the first house he sold through Redy and $1,040 on the second. He estimated he saved nearly $10,000 on broker commissions between the two transactions.
Ridley
When the tech entrepreneur Mike Chambers wanted to sell his Boulder, Colorado, home in February, he didn't see the point in using an agent.
He described his five-bedroom, four-bathroom home as a "turnkey house in a desirable neighborhood." He wasn't sure how much an agent would have to do besides uploading the home's photos online and unlocking the door for tours.
So Chambers listed the home himself for $2.725 million and started an Instagram called @realtorshateme to document his for-sale-by-owner adventure. The account, which has nearly 18,000 followers, quickly drew the ire of local Boulder agents. Chambers told BI he saw videos of agents on social media saying they wouldn't take clients to his house.
Chambers found an out-of-state buyer through Instagram, but his family ultimately decided to pull their house off the market and stay in Colorado.
The experience opened Chambers' eyes to the possibilities of — and appetite for — a broker-less way to sell your home.
Enter Ridley, a new app that's set to launch by the end of May. It will offer homeowners a suite of AI agents who can help people who want to list their property for sale by owner, or FSBO.
"Technology has basically made almost every step of this process more efficient, and there's been no reflection in the price or in the costs associated with these transactions to reflect that," Chambers said.
The AI agents can do things like write a listing description or book photographers. Sellers would pay a one-time fee of $999 or $1,999 to add an on-call lawyer.
"A product like this that empowers consumers to take control of this process and save lots of money is really good," he added.
Turbohome
Turbohome is a real-estate brokerage that pays agents a salary rather than a more typical commission-based compensation and gives buyers the option to pay a flat fee.
"They have healthcare, they have a salary, and they have consistent work," Ben Bear, Turbohome's cofounder and CEO Ben Bear, said of his agents.
"It's appealing for people who just like working with clients without that pressure of knowing how they're going to pay their next rent check," he told BI in 2024.
Instead of paying a percentage commission, buyers pay a flat fee to the Turbohome agent — between $5,000 and $10,000 — and the commission given to the agent is then credited to the buyer.
Turbohome's site has a "cash back calculator" that shows buyers their refund based on a home's price. For example, a buyer would be refunded $35,000 on a $1.5 million home purchase.
Arnab Dutta used Turbohome to buy a home in the Bay Area in 2024 after trying the traditional route without success in years past, and his offer beat out other offers because he said the seller didn't have to pay his agent's commission, he previously told BI.
Turbohome launched in 2024 and had raised $3.85 million as of March. The brokerage currently operates in California, Texas, and Washington.

In the wake of the passing of Dolly Parton in August 2026, a story we previously debunked in December 2025 about Parton opening an animal sanctuary resurfaced. Parton's real acts of charity were well documented throughout her career, yet this false story still made the rounds.
This was a type of claim we refer to "glurge," a term originating in the 1990s that we've defined as "a sentimental or heart-rending story that undermines its own inspirational message by distorting — or ignoring — the facts."
Tales like the one about Parton's supposed animal shelter would indeed be inspiring ... if they were true.
These stories often recirculate when a celebrity makes real headlines for something unrelated — and the spread of generative artificial intelligence tools that can fabricate text and realistic images makes it harder than ever to sort through the noise and find the truth
We dug into the Snopes archives to collect 15 false stories about celebrities doing (fake) acts of kindness.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

Some of the hottest software this year revolves around capturing voices. Whether it’s the sharp dictations of Wispr or the always-listening ears of Granola, voice-centered software currently feels inescapable. Voice dictation is getting so sharp, in fact, that I often write drafts in my notepad and then dictate aloud to my laptop.
Some prognosticators have declared this to be a dramatic end-of-the-keyboard moment, where legions of white-collar workers will soon be quietly whispering into desk microphones rather than clacking away at keyboards. I disagree, but I do think these changes could upend how customers give feedback.
I rarely email customer support unless something substantially negative has happened and I’m fishing for a refund. I’m much more open to giving feedback by blabbering for 20 seconds into my phone, good or bad, than I am to waiting on hold for who knows how long until someone answers.
“In the last two years, we hit a tipping point,” says Karan Gupta, CEO of Voicebox, a startup designed to collect feedback via voice. “That voice could now be accurate. It could be fast.” His previous startup also relied on voice technology—an app called Alice designed for secure transcription.
Giving feedback through Voicebox is simple. Shoppers can scan a QR code or tap their phone to an NFC chip posted in a store and then say whatever they want. The feedback is automatically transcribed and sent to the company’s dashboard, with a sentiment analysis. Companies can also follow up over email, if needed. Voicebox has partnered with airport terminals so that travelers can give their two bits about bathroom messiness or gate directions.
Gupta wants this type of feedback to extend beyond corporate experiences. Earlier this year, Lena Dunham held an event in San Francisco for her book Famesick and flashed a Voicebox QR code on the screen. Numerous attendees gave feedback, sharing emotional messages about how they empathized with her medical journey. He sees this as an example of the public wanting to share more feedback more easily on topics they feel passionate about.
As part of this larger vision, Voicebox recently launched its “directory,” so feedback can be sent in from anywhere and, in future iterations, users can discover what other people are saying publicly about a specific business. I could give a quick opinion about my haircut on my way out of the barbershop by just whispering into my phone, or share advice for future visitors about navigating some hospital’s parking situation.
The directory expands Voicebox’s potential from a customer-complaint vehicle centered around business needs into something more like Google Maps, with crowd-spoken reviews. This voice-centric approach mirrors other popular software trends, where the future of dictation feels so natural that using your thumbs to tap away on a smartphone may feel cumbersome and outdated.
After chatting with Gupta, I opened the Voicebox directory and searched for, well, Voicebox. It was time for my voice to be heard. Though I’m still waiting for the couple sitting next to me at the airport to leave so I don’t feel awkward about whispering into my phone.

In a time when many film and television productions shoot in other states or countries despite having their roots of development in Hollywood, 20th Century Studios has taken a big swing with its upcoming feature Whalefall, which arrives in theaters October 16.
Starring Austin Abrams, Josh Brolin, Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy and Emily Rudd, the film adaptation of Daniel Kraus’ book shot in a couple California locations — from Monterey to San Pedro — before finishing up at Radford Studios, where Deadline visited set during production last September.
Executive producer Doug Merrifield, whose credits stretch from 2023’s Candy Cane Lane and The Shallows (2016) all the way back to associate producer on 1993’s Free Willy, revealed that he compared schedules and budgets in both California and Louisiana as shooting locations side by side before production began.
Watch on Deadline
“On paper, Louisiana was a little cheaper — six figures cheaper, not seven figures cheaper — but at the end of the day, we were able to convince 20th Century that the best creative teams are here for this kind of picture,” Merrifield told Deadline a little over a year ago. “To their credit, even though it was a little more expensive to make the movie in California, they agreed to do that.”
Merrifeld added that — at the end of the day —should the film have shot in New Orleans, the cost comparison would have been a wash if not more expensive, once specialists were brought in.

“We had the ratio between the cost above the line, below the line, and then visual effects with Guillaume [Rocheron]. In California, you don’t get an incentive on above the line, but we had enough in post and visual effects to offset the loss of what we didn’t get from above the line,” Merrifield continued.
The visual effects, set design and other “specialty skills” in Merrifield’s words were important in a story with a premise like Whalefall’s, where Austin Abrams’ character spends an hour in a whale’s stomach after diving deep in the ocean looking for his father’s (Josh Brolin) remains. Said whale stomach models were built by the Wētā Workshop in New Zealand, but the head, throat, esophagus and larynx were constructed in California because they were too big to ship to set in time. The 12-foot-tall 18-foot-long whale head was manufactured by StudioArt & Technology.
“It’s so unfortunately rare to have the opportunity to shoot here, that when people know that a movie’s shooting in L.A., that is their first choice,” said producer on the Imagine Entertainment side of things, Allen Mendelbaum. “They can come home at night, see their families and everything. Why not? I think we’re really punching above our weight in this movie, because the crew is as good as it gets.”
For 50 days — which later turned into 62 — of filming, with a cast of 11 and a crew of 180 plus 409 background players, the film received nearly $11 million in tax credits on $50M total qualified expenditures. For the crew members living in the valley, including director Brian Duffield, production at Radford Studios was a huge plus, especially with stacked stage levels for easy access when shifting between shooting environments like the tank that simulates the ocean Jay (Abrams) dives in and then the whale’s head, throat and stomach, where he spends most of his time in the story.
“We originally were looking at L.A. Center, which was sort of a split [geographically]. [Radford] made us a great deal. And the fact that we had all these four stages [during production.] The tank [was] on 17, we had all the [whale] stomachs on 16, and then we had our special lead throat, and the 360 rigs on 12 across the way,” Merrifield said. “We were fortunate that it is at this time we were able to make such a good deal. But unfortunately, it is because it’s so slow right now.”
Whalefall benefited from a $330 million round of funding that preceded the newly approved expansion of the California Film & TV Tax Credit program, which included a total of $750 million in incentive funding.

“I’ve seen, where it’s started [to] already help the increase to television. For features. ultimately, if we want more feature work here, we’re going to have to have some sort of ATL (above the line) incentive credit, which you don’t get here right now. So if you have a big above the line, it doesn’t make sense to shoot here,” Merrifield who worked on the Free Willy films in Mexico City, shared.
With a smaller cast, Whalefall could make production in California work, but for other major projects with heavy-hitting stars attached, above-the-line costs are a different story.
“Things take time to trickle down, but I think in a year, we’ll have a much better idea how the new, increased incentive here has helped, not only television, but I’m hoping, in features,” Merrifield added.
California is currently in the middle of both film and television application cycles for the state’s tax credit program. Applications close in September for feature films and independent productions, while the window for television series runs into October. Though production in California remains low, several other projects that have benefited from the California Film Commission’s incentive will release this fall alongside Whalefall.

Mid-March 2026, The Pitt, High Potential and Season 2 of Bill Lawrence’s Rooster comedy were among 14 small-screen projects to receive tax credits.

The high-end watch world has an understandable affection for Casio. You can easily rock an iconic, brightly colored F-91W in any meeting with a luxury brand, and you'll get nods of approval. It is, after all, the watch that has graced the wrists of Barack Obama and Napoleon Dynamite.
If not the F-91W, you'd be on similar safe ground sporting the famous “CasiOak” that many G-Shock fans love because of its more than passing resemblance to Audemars Piguet's Royal Oak, which was recently given a similarly affordable makeover by Swatch with the Royal Pop. First introduced in 2019, the wallet-friendly G-Shock GA-2100 earned the nickname largely because of its octagonal case shape, and it is considered by some the definition of attainable luxury.
Now, however, it appears Casio has something genuinely new for the G-Shock line. Leaked on Notebookcheck and Instagram, the upcoming GMC-2500 and GAC-2500 series echo the CasiOak's links to high-end brand AP with more than a passing resemblance to Patek Philippe's Nautilus thanks to prominent shoulders on either side of the case.
Casio did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.
In 1972, legendary watchmaker Gérald Genta suggested an angular stainless steel watch design to Audemars Piguet with a high-end movement inside that would, perversely, be more expensive than gold dress watches. The Royal Oak, and the idea of the luxury sports watch, was born. In 1976, Genta repeated the trick for AP's main competitor, Patek Philippe, to create the now equally famous Nautilus.
According to Notebookcheck, the GAC-2500 series is a resin analog lineup supposedly built from the DNA of the DW-5000C, the very first G-Shock made back in 1983. Stainless-steel versions will be labeled the GMC-2500 series. So far, nicknames like the “CasioNaut” and “CasioTilus” are already being thrown around on Instagram. The leaked four resin colorways in November are expected to be white, black, green, and yellow, and the price is estimated at 20,900 Japanese yen (about $134) each. The metal versions will supposedly retail for about $320.
Another striking aspect of the CasioNauts, one that helps the comparisons with Patek even further, is that the watches are fully analog, a rarity in a G-Shock. The brand has always had a digital display somewhere on its main ranges, just like the CasiOak does.
A two-eye dial layout means a small seconds subdial on the left and a date window on the right. A Shock Resist mark is on the tail of the seconds hand. These pieces apparently have Casio's Magnetic Holding Structure, so the hands aren't fixed to a shaft but are instead held magnetically in place. When the rugged watch takes a severe smack, the hands can absorb the impact and won't break.
The metal GMC-2500 dimensions are supposedly 46.7 x 43.8 x 12.9 mm (H x W x D), with the GAC-2500 a shade thinner at 46.7 x 44.5 x 12.7. It looks like the metal versions will offer a choice of colors, along with the bracelet or strap options. The rumored release date for all of the CasioNauts is November, so set your watch.
According to legend, the inspiration for the Nautilus shape was the portholes on transatlantic ocean liners, and the idea struck Genta while he was having dinner at a hotel. Genta supposedly saw Patek executives sitting in a corner on the opposite side of the restaurant. It took him just five minutes to sketch the watch that would later become an icon.

Prashanth Fertility launched ‘Prashanth Fertility at Home’, an initiative to provide select IVF-related support services at patients’ homes across Chennai.
The service is aimed at helping patients maintain continuity during fertility treatment, particularly those who may find it difficult to make frequent visits to the fertility centre because of work and other commitments.
Under the initiative, a dedicated team will provide services such as injection administration, eligible monitoring, follow-ups and treatment coordination at home, while patients continue to remain under the supervision of their treating fertility specialists.
A dedicated vehicle and team will operate across Chennai. Patients can schedule eligible services through the Prashanth Fertility app, which also allows them to manage appointments, follow-ups and treatment-related medical records.
Speaking at the launch, actor Khushbu Sundar, the chief guest, highlighted the stigma and emotional challenges associated with infertility and fertility treatment. She said couples often have to navigate not only the physical and financial demands of treatment, but also social expectations and questions around parenthood.
Samhitha Moturi, Director, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said fertility treatment involves multiple appointments, medication schedules, monitoring and follow-ups, and repeated travel to a fertility centre can be an additional challenge for couples. “The initiative has been conceived to take appropriate, clinically supervised aspects of care closer to the patient,” she said, adding that reducing practical barriers could help patients stay on track with treatment.
Geetha Haripriya, Chairman, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said the initiative was intended to make fertility care “more accessible, more personalised, and more connected to the patient”.
The service is currently available across Chennai. Patients can contact the 24x7 helpline 044-2888-2888 for details about eligibility and scheduling.

In 2026, people online repeatedly shared a tale framed as a true story about a heroic dog receiving an award for its military service at the Pentagon. For example, one Facebook post (archived) included an image depicting a dog with the right side of its face scarred — apparently K9 Valor — receiving the Congressional Medal of Honor.
The text of the post read:
This is K9 Valor. He saved 47 soldiers. He survived a suicide bomber, then went on to stop three more, fighting tooth against knife. In the end, he placed himself between an explosion and his handler.
The blast shattered half his face. He lost his left eye and ear. He was flown to Germany, where surgeons worked to rebuild his jaw.
At the Pentagon, he was honored with a standing ovation that lasted over eight minutes.
A true American hero
This story (archived) appeared numerous times (archived) on Instagram (archived), X (archived) and Reddit (archived). The same account that shared the above Facebook post in June reposted the story (archived) nearly a month later and again the following month (archived). Snopes readers sent us emails asking whether it was true.
A version of the story shared on LinkedIn (archived) went into more detail than the others. That post described the dog, K9 Valor, being wounded by a suicide bomber at Kabul International Airport on Aug. 26, 2021. Even after being injured, Valor supposedly warned soldiers of a second bomb just in time for them to avoid the blast, and then charged and kill three insurgents trying to shoot wounded survivors. According to the post, Valor became the first dog to receive the Congressional Medal of Honor in May 2023.
This story, however, was fabricated out of whole cloth. There is no evidence of a K9 Valor present at the Kabul Airport suicide bombing or of a dog being awarded the Congressional Medal of Honor. Therefore, we've rated this claim as false.
Since even the less detailed versions of the claim shared an image of a dog receiving the Congressional Medal of Honor, Snopes first searched if a "Valor" or any other dog has received the medal. The Congressional Medal of Honor can be identified by its light blue ribbon with 13 stars and the unique design of the medal itself.
A recipient search for "valor" on the Medal of Honor Museum website returned no results. A dog doesn't appear among the Congressional Medal of Honor Society's list of recipients who received the award for serving in Afghanistan. A list of "firsts" among Medal of Honor recipients did not identify a first dog to have received an award.
A blog post from the Congressional Medal of Honor Society said it welcomed just two new members to its ranks in 2023. Neither received the award in May and both were humans.
The organization Animals in War and Peace awards service animals medals for their duty, often in war. While many of its recipients are Belgian Malinois dogs like Valor apparently is, none of the organization's award recipients have stories about suffering wounds from one bombing and immediately saving soldiers from a second. Its award ceremonies typically occur in March, not May, and at the U.S. Capitol, not the Pentagon.
Immediately after the suicide bombing at Kabul International Airport, U.S. officials reportedly believed a second bombing occurred nearby. The U.S. Department of Defense clarified the following day that it no longer believed there was a second explosion, and instead the attack was carried out by a single suicide bomber.
That would mean the events as described in the LinkedIn post couldn't have happened, since there was no second bomb from which to save 47 soldiers.
Snopes has sent U.S. Central Command an email asking whether any dog with a similar story to the one here was present at the 2021 Kabul bombing. We will update this story if and when we receive a reply.
Images show signs of AI generation
The images shared with the posts showed signs of being generated or edited using artificial intelligence tools.
Some readers may have already noticed one piece of evidence: Even though the posts say Valor lost his left eye, the dog in the image used in the Facebook post above appears to be missing its right eye.
In another version of that same image, an insignia that doesn't match any used in the U.S. military is visible on the arm of the service member's jacket. His insignia shows four evenly spaced chevrons pointing up, but across the U.S. military the fourth line in insignias are separated from the others by a space and curve downward.
A Google SynthID check, a tool that checks for hidden watermarks Google AI adds to images and video, found that all or part of that image was edited or generated by Google AI.
Additionally, various posts used AI-generated images of different dogs that are supposedly K9 Valor. For example, the more detailed story from the LinkedIn post included an image of a different dog with both ears still present, despite Valor allegedly having lost his left ear. Again, a Google SynthID check found that the image was edited or generated by Google AI.
Snopes previously reported on this claim in June and July 2026. We're reporting on it again due to continued interest in the claim.

Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
His life as a writer and farmer was informed by a simple, clarifying idea: Forget tomorrow, and work toward what is good today.
Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach. When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing. Berry didn’t have a cellphone. He didn’t use email. He didn’t even have a computer. He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light. And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk.
I knew this already, of course. Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention. He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him.
The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf. This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s. Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring. After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request. He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post.
A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr. Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone. He asked me to call him back.
When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter. I’d asked him to take part in “By Heart,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook. He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World, contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way. It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.”
He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk. So I did. And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since.
I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible. Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written. Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorrow” seemed to better describe the ethos of Berry’s longtime nemeses: coal-industry strip miners, big agribusiness, the global financial system.
It was also an odd choice for someone who seemed so concerned about the excesses of modern life. Berry struck me as someone who absolutely would fixate on the general worsening direction of things. Fretting about the future is a favorite preoccupation of the conscientious. Berry occasionally admitted to his own worried state of mind on the page, including in one of his best-known poems: “When despair for the world grows in me,” he wrote, “I wake in the night at the least sound / in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be.”
Nevertheless, in the part of his book that he asked me to read, he wrote, “Taking thought for the morrow is, fairly predictably, a waste of time.” He insisted that what we call “the future” is a flimsy and insubstantial thing at best—a phantom we obsess over that never really arrives, or never arrives in the way we imagine. “Most of the bad possibilities I have worried about have never happened,” Berry wrote. “By taking thought for the morrow we have invested, and wasted, a lot of effort in preparing for morrows that never came.”
Obsessing about the future, he argued, also has devastating moral consequences. It allows people to avoid engaging with the urgent realities of the present.
I don’t know whether Berry, given his extremely offline lifestyle, ever learned about doomscrolling—the way social media can serve as a collective orgy of dread. But he’s right that, when people become too obsessed with a future that may or may not befall them, they tend to turn their back on the moment they’re in. “The time is coming when it will be too late to save the world. Oh, oh, oh,” he wrote, lampooning the handwringer in so many of us. “If that is the way our minds are afflicted, we and our world are dead already. The present is going by and we are not in it.” As I see it, this was the core purpose of Berry’s work: He dared his readers to live in a way that honors the situation at hand, at this very second.
That mandate suffused everything he wrote about. He exhorted readers to enjoy the food on their plates, to bear witness to the places that surround them, and to revel in shared experience with the people in their orbit. Honoring the present was a joyful thing for Wendell Berry. It was also a form of rewarding but very difficult work. It meant slow, careful deliberation about the things he was willing to let into his life, whether that was a new piece of technology or a request from a journalist.
And it meant searching for ways to disentangle himself, by turns and sometimes painfully, from destructive systems. The moral goal of a human being, he often argued, should be to do less harm right now. When one of his most famous essays, 1987’s “Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer,” resulted in astonished and outraged letters from readers, Berry replied by writing, “I did not say that I proposed to end forthwith all my involvement in harmful technology, for I do not know how to do that. I said merely that I want to limit such involvement, and to a certain extent I do know how to do that.” This response boils down to a simple, radical worldview: We must seek to understand the harms caused by the systems we’re implicated in, then strive to become less reliant on them.
Berry was no purist. He understood that no 20th- or 21st-century American can live a wholly blameless life. He lamented needing to drive a truck, the unavoidable, occasional use of gas-powered equipment on his farm. He knew that his ancestors had enslaved their fellow human beings and that he, in direct and indirect ways, had benefited from that obscene bondage. “I am owned by the blood of all of them,” he wrote in an early poem, “My Great-Grandfather’s Slaves.” “We cannot be free of each other.”
Moral blamelessness isn’t possible. But Berry’s larger point was that people should strive for something better, here and now. As he put it in Our Only World, with his trademark aphoristic brilliance: “Maybe we could give up saving the world and start to live savingly in it.” This reframes Jesus’s “sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” as a simple, clarifying injunction: Forget the future, and work toward what is good today.
I did speak with Berry a second time. We talked a little while about the Sermon on the Mount, but I didn’t get him to agree to a formal interview. I could tell he wanted to help me, to be a sport. Still, I sensed something else nagging at him: the irresistible presence of the now. He was here, living on this Earth. He had land to tend to, animals to care for, a wife to love, books to write—more than 50 of them, by the end. Maybe someday, in some dimly glimpsed future, he would find some more time to talk with me. But right then, at that moment, there was just too much to do.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
- Published
Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction.
A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive.
A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box.
It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades.
For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.
But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock.
The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members.
Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition.
This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari.
"They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC.
If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins.
It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts.
A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect.
At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC.
They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure.
Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month.
Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party.
The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year.
The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle.
In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it.
The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government.
Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP.
He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP.
But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party.
This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot.
Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic.
Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible.
He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness.
"We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there.
"If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again."
Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late.
With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them.
Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

The 958 candidates recommended by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) in the 2025 Civil Services Examination (CSE) are now in limbo over their service allocation and the starting date of their foundation course. While the course was expected to begin in August, several candidates told The Hindu they have received no communication regarding the way forward.
The delay follows the Centre’s application to the Supreme Court asking permission for the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) to allocate services without implementing the court’s March 11 Rohith Nathan judgment. That ruling found the DoPT was incorrectly excluding certain Other Backward Classes (OBC) candidates from reservations by concluding they belonged to the creamy layer based only on their parents’ salary income. The court directed corrective measures within six months. The CSE 2025 results were declared on March 6, days before the Rohith Nathan judgment.
Candidate uncertainty
Now, while the Supreme Court is set to hear the Centre on September 17, candidates recommended for the Civil Services told The Hindu they have “no idea” what their future pathway looks like.
One candidate said, “The foundation course has obviously not started. I have received no communication from the DoPT or the academy about when the foundation course will start. There was a schedule that said it was to start on August 24 tentatively, but since the Supreme Court became seized of the matter, we have not heard anything”.
Another candidate said that they have not been able to see any updates regarding the next steps on the website of the DoPT or the website of the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration, where they will be trained.
A third candidate said that they are now waiting to see how the next hearing in the Supreme Court goes. “I believe the government is also waiting for the Supreme Court,” the candidate said, adding that since the court is going to look at the issue of service allocation, no news of the foundation course can be expected until then.
Income test issue
The Centre’s application to the Supreme Court said it would be unfair and “against the principles of natural justice” if the judgment’s reading of the income test is applied to the service allocation for the CSE 2025 batch, because it would affect anyone who did not apply or could not qualify under the OBC category based on the pre-Rohith Nathan understanding of the income test.
It further said that the CSE 2025 batch was expected to start their foundation course by August-end and continue service allocation based on the pre-Rohith Nathan understanding of the income test, which the Supreme Court ruling had described as a practice of “hostile discrimination”.

The DSA’s Problem Isn’t ‘Media Training’
Authoritarian extremists are speaking for American socialists, and a lot of people don’t like what they say.
American socialists are convinced that they have a media-training problem.
In the past year, members of the Democratic Socialists of America, the country’s largest leftist organization, have won electoral victories in places such as New York City and Michigan, drawing a spotlight that the group has struggled to handle.
Last month, the DSA’s co-chairs, Megan Romer and Ashik Siddique, gave several high-profile interviews that even many of their most fervent supporters agree were disastrous. The two leaders struggled to give straight answers to simple questions, and they defended outlandish policies, such as abolishing prisons and police. They seemed to present socialists exactly the way their opponents caricature them: as extremist, unserious, and unprepared.
In damage-control mode, many of DSA’s defenders on social media are repeating the phrase media training as though it were a mantra. If only the group’s leaders had been better prepared to deal with media outlets, the thinking goes, they would have avoided this train wreck. The DSA’s communications director, Priscilla Yeverino, recently told Axios, “Our leaders aren’t politicians. They’re working-class people and new to doing media.”
The idea that the DSA’s troubles on prime-time television are a technical matter solvable by the right training is surely comforting, but it is also wrong. The group has a bigger problem: It is led by unpractical extremists whose views are a far cry from those that its electorally successful figures, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, espouse.
This disconnect is partly explained by a sharp division within the DSA. One wing engages in mass politics and includes AOC, Mamdani, and other socialists committed to democratic principles. The other wing is sectarian and extremist: It evinces little commitment to democracy and includes open admirers of Hamas, the Iranian regime, and historical dictators such as Mao Zedong. If the interviews with the DSA’s co-chairs were embarrassing, that’s a result not of a lackluster media performance but of the actual positions the group has embraced.
A closer look at the interviews confirms this. Romer, who belongs to the sectarian wing, evidently did not know what the 2000 Camp David Summit was and could not say what “taxing the hell out of millionaires,” as she demanded, would look like in practice. When asked about authoritarianism in Cuba, she praised the country’s constitution and suggested that Americans should learn from it.
Maybe media training could have taught Romer what happened at Camp David and what a tax policy might entail. It still wouldn’t have made the pro-authoritarian politics she shares with her faction of the DSA more palatable. In December, Romer’s Red Star caucus, a self-declared Marxist-Leninist faction of the DSA, posted quotes from a speech by Mao in “celebration” of the Chinese Communist leader’s 132nd birthday. Members of the faction study the works of Mao and the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin as part of their political education. Red Star has declared its unequivocal sympathy for Hamas and praised the “good judgement” of “our socialist siblings” in Palestine for working with the Islamist organization and “external groups like Iran, Hezbollah, and Ansarallah under a principle they call unity of the fields.” In other words, Red Star is an admirer of Iran’s notorious “Axis of Resistance.”
That Romer wouldn’t critique authoritarianism in Cuba is not a lapse but an expression of her faction’s politics. Red Star’s stated policy couldn’t be any clearer about this: “To publicly critique a government or movement that stands in opposition to the American government is to do the U.S. State Department’s work for them, from Iran to Palestine.”
In other words, any state or group that opposes the American government should be beyond criticism. Liberation, the DSA’s “Marxist-Leninist-Maoist caucus,” likewise declares the United States to be “not a nation” but a “prison-house of nations, with the Euro-Americans being the jailer.”
Unlike Romer, Siddique belongs to the mainstream wing of the DSA, but he is bound by the group’s statements and broader culture. The sectarian wing currently dominates the DSA: The group’s convention in Chicago last year rejected a resolution opposing “all governments that engage in the repression of democratic rights.” Thus, when asked repeatedly what he thought of Fidel Castro, whom the DSA had praised in an earlier statement, Siddique awkwardly referred to “inequality in the United States” and criticized U.S. policy—deflecting the question and offering sound bites instead of engagement, much as an establishment pol might do.
This pro-left-authoritarian orientation explains why DSA electoral observers shamefully reported no fraud when they were dispatched to monitor the electoral sham organized by Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in 2024. Those results were so bogus that even the left-wing governments of Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay couldn’t accept them. Yet at a DSA session on the subject, a pro-Maduro organization’s assessment that Venezuela’s electoral system was “one of the very best in the world” was presented as fact, as was the false claim that Venezuela’s main opposition candidates were “fascist.”
The two wings of the DSA are committed to wildly different methods. Mamdani governs New York City partly as a technocrat, and AOC has sought to influence the Democratic Party from within. One of the DSA’s sectarian factions, by contrast, recently suggested that socialist lawmakers “should do everything in their power to disrupt any Congressional business that does not benefit the working class or advance the socialist program.” They should, it went on, “creatively abuse their powers to make it difficult to conduct legislative business,” for instance by packing the galleries of Congress with hecklers. This faction seems to view elected lawmakers as “tribunes” for the socialist movement rather than as people who, you know, make laws.
The sectarian wing got the DSA to drop its endorsement of AOC and refuse to support Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Red Star argued against endorsing AOC unless she withdrew her support for Joe Biden (then the Democratic nominee), and it refused to fundraise for the Democratic leadership or central congressional campaign. But ultimately, the DSA dropped AOC on the grounds that she was not sufficiently anti-Israel—a singular obsession of the sectarian wing. (The foreign-policy section of the DSA’s political platform discusses the details of only one country’s politics, and that’s Israel and Palestine, in which it calls for the self-determination of Palestinians without making a similar provision for Israeli Jews.)
For all of the extremist wing’s influence, however, my years of research into the group suggest that the DSA’s members are mostly not members of any caucuses. The average DSA member probably has more in common with AOC than with Mao or Hamas, and the nonsectarians seem especially dominant in the group’s large urban chapters—such as in New York City, where the DSA has more than 15,000 of its approximately 120,000 members. More than 80 percent of DSA members in the Bronx and Queens voted in 2024 to endorse AOC. The sectarian wing came to control much of the organization’s leadership by manipulating internal processes, which is one reason it opposes organizational referenda and other one-member-one-vote procedures.
The DSA’s mainstream wing includes thinkers who are committed to democracy, critical of authoritarianism (including that of socialist regimes, past and present), and who reject some of the signature policies of the sectarian wing, such as police abolition. These figures have been vocal in response to last month’s media fiasco.
Eric Blanc, a labor historian at Rutgers, sharply criticized Romer for “falling into a trap being set by the establishment,” which seeks “to paint DSA as extreme.” Like others in his wing, Blanc advocates for adopting a Nordic-style social democracy as a step toward overcoming capitalism. This position is also shared by the Jacobin founder and former DSA Vice Chair Bhaskar Sunkara, whose 2019 Socialist Manifesto explores Swedish social democracy in envisioning a socialism for the 21st century.
Reacting to the DSA’s recent media debacles, Ben Burgis, a philosopher and Jacobin writer, opined: “We don’t do ourselves any favors by refusing to say anything too negative about left-wing dictatorships targeted by US foreign policy,” especially “if we’re trying to argue that the failures of authoritarian state socialism in the twentieth century shouldn’t mean that capitalism is the best humanity will ever be able to do.” The group has failed to reassure its critics of its commitment to multiparty democracy, Burgis added.
Thinkers in this wing of the DSA take seriously the imperative to reconcile socialist commitments to economic justice with democratic and liberal values. Burgis, Sunkara, and the economist Mike Beggs have co-authored a forthcoming book called The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World, which attempts to offer a “realistic model” of a post-capitalist economic system. Drawing on the work of the liberal philosopher John Rawls, as well as detailed economic research, the book takes the Soviet Union to task for a “record of systematic economic failure, not just political repression” and suggests a model that mixes social ownership with a significant role for the market. It also engages the arguments of well-known critics of socialism, such as Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises. This work puts the flippancy of Romer’s “taxing the hell out of millionaires” comment to shame.
But if the likes of AOC, Sunkara, Burgis, and Blanc wish for the American public to give their notions of an economically rigorous and democratically committed socialism a chance, they need to break with the fans of Mao and Hamas. So long as they share an organization with the DSA’s sectarians, they can’t complain when the media associates the DSA—and American socialism—with the extreme positions that it formally adopts and that its leaders espouse. No amount of media training can solve that.

Dr Imran Majid, Director of the Cutis Institute of Dermatology, Srinagar, has been conferred the prestigious Dr Mulekar Oration at the National Conference of the Association of Cutaneous Surgeons of India (ACSI) held in Goa on September 5, 2026.
The distinguished academic honour recognises Dr Majid’s longstanding and significant contributions to the field of vitiligo research and vitiligo surgery.
Dr Majid delivered the oration titled 'My Journey in Vitiligo Research and Vitiligo Surgery,' in which he shared his several-decade journey in the field, encompassing clinical research, innovations in vitiligo treatment, targeted phototherapy and surgical techniques for repigmentation.
Dr Majid is regarded as one of the prominent dermatologists in India working in the field of vitiligo.
His academic and clinical work has focused extensively on improving outcomes for patients with vitiligo, including the use of targeted phototherapy, medical therapies and surgical repigmentation procedures.
With more than 100 research publications and around 2000 citations, Dr Majid has made notable contributions to academic dermatology and is recognised for his work in vitiligo and dermatosurgery.
The honour marks a significant milestone in his career and brings national recognition to the contributions from J&K in the field of dermatology and vitiligo care.

Every morning, many of us drink one or two cups of coffee and feel good, refreshed, and ready for the day. Some of us drink one or two more cups at work before lunchtime. Some use pure coffee while others add chicory to it. We prepare the powder using a filter, add milk and sugar, and take a swig.
While many Indians have a fondness for coffee, almost everyone in the U.S. and Europe drinks coffee, and more of it, every day.
Now, what are the effects of drinking coffee? How many cups per day? Should it be black coffee or can it include milk and sugar? And how does this affect our health? These are some questions that have been on our minds — and for which research has offered contradictory answers in the past. Fortunately, a new publication, titled ‘Caffeine and Cardiovascular Disease: A Scientific Statement from the American Heart Association’, may clear some doubts. The authors of the statement analysed several studies that examined the effects of caffeine, the active molecule in coffee that stimulates the brain and the central nervous system and encourages the body to produce and use more energy.
The statement reported that moderate caffeine intake, especially through coffee, may lower the risks of type-2 diabetes, stroke, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation. However, high doses, especially from energy drinks, may harm cardiovascular health, and unfiltered coffee can also raise LDL cholesterol levels.
Data from the Nurses Health Study at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Harvard Medical School and an analysis of 3 lakh people from the U.K. Biobank and Health Canada have indicated that drinking four cups a day may lower the risk of developing cancer, type-2 diabetes, heart diseases, and age-related disorders like dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. However, analyses also suggest that it would be prudent for pregnant and lactating women to limit their coffee intake to three cups a day.
Drinking hot black coffee is recommended, with little or no additives like sugar or milk. However, a group from Copenhagen, Denmark, pointed out in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Science in 2023 that adding milk to black coffee can be good as milk contains antioxidants, minerals, and vitamins and allays the bitter taste.
Chicory-blended coffee
Many people in South India prefer to have pure coffee, i.e. with no additives like chicory, which comes from a perennial herbal plant with coloured flowers. This herb contains no caffeine but a polysaccharide called inulin, which supports digestion and can help control blood sugar.
The benefits of a coffee and chicory blend and their implications for nutrition and health implications were discussed in a recent review paper by a group led by Pushpa S. Murthy at the Central Food Technology and Research Institute, Mysuru, published in the Journal of Food Science and Technology. Chicory contains several compounds that help protect the liver from inflammation, shield the stomach from damage, and may help defend against cancer. Adding chicory to coffee also improves coffee’s fragrance and taste.
The optimal blend of coffee and chicory was suggested to be 70:30 or 60:40, coffee to chicory, to strike a balance between taste and benefits. In fact, most coffee sellers across India have these ratios, unless of course a customer asks for ‘pure’ coffee. This writer himself used to prefer pure coffee until he read the review article by the Mysuru group!

This fall, 54 million K-12 students are headed back to the classroom for another year of lessons in all the classic subjects: math, English, history, biology. But there’s another subject that’s been sneaking into school curricula: plastics.
A new report from the nonprofit Plastic Pollution Coalition documents the many ways the plastics industry has been inserting its agenda into classrooms across the US—including through lesson plans and worksheets, hands-on science experiments, and a program called “PlastiVan” that travels from city to city teaching students about “the contribution plastics make to modern life.”
Industry interests offer these resources to teachers for free or for cheap, according to the report. The materials tend to highlight the necessity of plastics while downplaying their significant downsides to human health and the environment.
“When that information is provided to kids, it obfuscates the true impacts of plastic pollution,” said Madison Dennis, senior policy and advocacy manager for Plastic Pollution Coalition and one of the report’s main authors. Besides harming marine life, plastics can expose people to hazardous chemicals, clog storm drains and contribute to flooding, and release planet-warming greenhouse gases. The Plastic Pollution Coalition is calling for stricter school policies against the use of industry-sponsored learning materials.
The report lays out four case studies of plastics industry “propaganda” for schoolkids. One involves the Society of Plastics Engineers, or SPE, a trade group that recently became a division of the Plastics Industry Association. SPE’s lesson plans include activities like a “plastic scavenger hunt,” which aims for students to “understand that plastics are ubiquitous and their importance to society and their personal life.” A video titled “Your Bottle Means Jobs” explains how plastics recycling supports local employment.
Another case study highlights the American Association of Chemistry Teachers, an initiative of the Dow Chemical Company. One of the association’s lesson plans teaches elementary and middle school students how to compare the strength of various types of plastic bags that can be found in a grocery store. After a brief experiment, the lesson invites them to “pretend [they] are an employee for Dow Chemical Company” and are designing a plastic bag for a customer.
While many of the materials claim to support STEM learning objectives, they do so while promoting familiar industry talking points, emphasizing the affordability and safety of plastics. Some acknowledge plastic pollution as a serious problem, but they blame irresponsible consumer behaviors and, instead of recommending less plastic be produced, propose more recycling as the primary way to address it.
In reality, only 9 percent of all plastics are recycled worldwide, and scientists have repeatedly warned that recycling will be unable to keep up with projected growth in plastic production. Investigative reporting has shown that industry groups knew this decades ago, but promoted recycling anyway in order to defuse growing concern over plastic pollution.
Wendy Johnson, a science education specialist at the National Center for Science Education, said the industry’s lesson plans and worksheets don’t reflect good pedagogy. Materials claiming to be aligned with state-level STEM standards don’t say which standards they support, or how they’re aligned. Lesson plans instruct students to read teachers’ notes, or list industry-specific vocab terms like “stretch blow molding” or “thermosetting.”
“By using all of these technical terms, it’s tricking people into thinking … that they’re doing science,” Johnson told Grist. What the materials really teach, she said, is “ideological perspectives about the economy,” like the desirability of cheap consumer goods.
“It’s so clear that the purpose isn’t to make really clear, easy-to-use materials,” Johnson added. “The idea isn’t to teach,” but to get industry talking points into classrooms. The report documents plastics propaganda finding its way into schools since at least the 2000s. Between 2009 and 2011, for example, a plastics trade group lobbied the California Department of Education to add a section on “The Advantages of Shopping Bags” to the state’s high school textbooks. The PlastiVan initiative has been ongoing since 2011, and SPE claims it’s reached over 132,000 students in total.
Plastic Pollution Coalition suggests that the problem is particularly significant in schools located near petrochemical facilities. In Beaver County, Pennsylvania, for example, Shell operates a 386-acre plastics production complex and has invested millions of dollars in the development of plastics-related curricula and recycling programs, both for grade schoolers and for community college students. It has also donated hundreds of backpacks filled with school supplies, and bought one school a basketball court—seemingly in exchange for incorporating plastics recycling into the curriculum.
Shell didn’t respond to Grist’s request for comment. Neither did SPE, the American Association of Chemistry Teachers, nor the school district in Beaver County.
The report hints at a broader problem with STEM education in US public schools. Teachers often lack the time and money needed to design their own curricula, or to buy high-quality materials and lesson plans needed for in-class labs or science projects. When vested interests come along offering support—whether it’s the tobacco industry, the junk food industry, the pesticide industry, or the fossil fuel industry—it can be hard to say no.
“As a teacher, I’m always looking for free stuff,” said Suzie Hicks, a K-8 environmental educator in California who consulted on the Plastic Pollution Coalition report. Hicks said their education and background make them comfortable vetting materials for greenwashing—but that’s likely not the case with most teachers.
Dennis recommended that school boards adopt policies banning educational materials sponsored by the chemical, fossil fuel, and plastics industries. She also emphasized the need for better school funding more generally, so that teachers and districts aren’t so desperate for ready-made learning materials.
One way to achieve this would be to eliminate tax breaks for petrochemical processing and plastics production facilities, which deprive communities of much-needed cash.
Katie Allen, executive director of Algalita, a California-based environmental nonprofit that develops educational materials on plastic pollution, pushed back against the idea that schools should ban all industry-sponsored content.
“Once you start banning one thing, where does it end? What I want to do is give educators the benefit of the doubt and allow them to make their own decisions,” she told Grist. She argued that teachers should be trusted to properly contextualize industry materials—and that they could even use them to teach critical-thinking skills.
That said, there are plenty of educational materials on plastics that are developed by nonindustry sources. Algalita, for instance, offers free lesson plans on topics like plastic garbage patches in the oceans and biomagnification—the phenomenon where plastics build up inside sea creatures as you move up the food chain. The Story of Stuff, another nonprofit, offers a broader high school curriculum focused on the costs and consequences of producing consumer goods—including those made from plastics.
Those learning materials still come from organizations with an agenda. But Hicks argued they’re more trustworthy, since nonprofits usually aren’t trying to sell something.
Another option is for teachers to simply design their own curricula. That’s what Jacqueline Omania, a recently retired elementary school teacher in Berkeley, California, did in 2015. She turned her classroom into a zero-waste laboratory, and each year for 11 years, Omania and her students developed a set of zero-waste classroom agreements, vowing to minimize their plastics use—by swapping individual glue sticks for a communal tub of glue, for example—while also advocating for more systemic change, like by campaigning for a policy requiring Berkeley restaurants to stop giving out single-use plastic foodware.
“There are so many challenges in the world, but plastic is something tangible,” Omania said. “It’s right there in front of them, and they can see the difference that they’re actually making through their actions.”
