The story so far: Last week, the Supreme Court ruled that adoptive mothers could avail themselves of 12 weeks of paid maternity leave regardless of the age of their children at the time of adoption. Striking down Section 60(4) of the Social Security Code, 2020 (previously Section 5(4) of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961), which limited this benefit only to mothers who adopted children under the age of three months, the Court said that an adoptive mother had the same rights and obligations towards the child as a biological mother.
What is the law on maternity leave in India?
Statutory maternity benefits for working women in India began to be granted in colonial times. The Bombay Maternity Benefit Act, 1929, covered women factory workers. It was followed by similar laws in other parts of the country in the run-up to Independence. In 1961, Parliament passed the Maternity Benefit Act to provide paid maternity leave of 12 weeks to working women across the country.
In 2017, the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act not only extended the period of paid maternity leave for biological mothers to 26 weeks, but also inserted a provision extending maternity leave for the first time to adoptive mothers or surrogate mothers. Section 5(4) of the Act stated that surrogate or adoptive mothers legally adopting a child below three months would be entitled to maternity leave for a period of 12 weeks from the date the child is handed over to the mother.
Why was this law considered inadequate?
Also Read: What legal protections exist for women returning from maternity leave?
This provision was challenged in 2021 by Hamsaanandini Nanduri, a lawyer who adopted siblings in 2017. Ms. Nanduri told The Hindu that her Bengaluru-based law firm gave her only six weeks of paid maternity leave. “I could not leave my young children at home to turn up in office after just six weeks, so I took some additional months of unpaid leave. But it made me angry that there was no policy about it,” she said.
Terming the 12 weeks of maternity leave granted in 2017 to adoptive or surrogate mothers as “mere lip service”, the petitioner contended that when compared to the 26 weeks of maternity leave granted to biological mothers, the provision violated the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution.
The three-month limit was unjust to both children and parents, depriving older adoptees from receiving the maternal care they need for their development and integration into their adoptive families, her lawyer argued.
The petitioner also pointed out in Court that adoption procedures take much longer than three months in India.
Also, as Ms. Nanduri told The Hindu: “I found on filing an RTI (Right to Information) application with CARA (Central Adoption Resource Authority) that less than 5% of children adopted at that time were under the age of three months.”
What did the Court say about motherhood?
The Court made it clear that motherhood cannot be seen through the “narrow lens of biology” alone. It referred to adoption as part of the “right to reproductive autonomy”. It noted that “the period of leave plays a crucial role in fostering [an] emotional bond between the mother and the child”. The Court added that stress hormone levels in children raised in orphanages are often higher than those in children brought up in a familial environment, which pointed to a greater need for paid maternal leave for older adoptees.
How will the judgment help adoptees and their parents?
Madhumitha Venkataraman started interviewing for jobs as a senior HR executive while waiting for an adoption referral, stipulating in every interview that she would need paid time off to support her child. Several multinational organisations balked at the idea of granting leave for more than a few weeks. But Ms. Venkataraman was finally recruited by a global media company that promised her one year of paid maternity leave. “My son came home at the age of three and a half months in 2023, so I was not eligible for maternity leave under the old law. But because this company was so accommodating, I did not have to choose between my career and my parenting,” she said. “There are emotional needs, and not just for the child. The time at home with my son gave me space to grow into motherhood,” she said. It is this time and space that other adoptive mothers say they will be entitled to as well, from now.
Noopur Goyal’s daughter was 15 months old when she came home in 2021. “I worked as a paediatric cardiologist at a top hospital in Delhi. I knew there was no provision for maternity leave, so I had to give up my job,” said Dr. Goyal, a single parent who works as a freelance consultant in Noida. “I had brought her into a new world, so I had to be present for her. An adopted child has been uprooted twice. I needed the time at home with her to build attachment and give her a sense of security.” Dr. Goyal said she was financially stable to be able to do this, but she is “glad now that there is a law mandating 12 weeks of paid maternity leave for all adoptive mothers.”
What did the Court say about paternity leave?
The Court also called on the Union government to examine the need for a formal law recognising paternity leave for all fathers, adoptive or biological. Noting that India’s legal framework does not adequately account for the role of fathers in childcare, it underlined the importance of shared parenting. As of now, only male government servants are entitled to 15 days’ paternity leave for the birth of a child or adoption. Leaves in the private sector are generally determined by company policies.

Why the AfD’s German triumph is a win for Putin – and leaves Ukraine exposed
The AfD and the Trump administration, with its special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are bound into a commercial friendship run out of the Kremlin by one man, writes world affairs editor Sam Kiley
The success of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in state elections could herald a disaster for Ukraine, a European victory for Vladimir Putin, and a stampede of greed over democracy orchestrated by one man.
Kirill Dmitriev is to Donald Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, what Putin is to the 47th president – their favourite and much favoured Russian.
What Putin gives Trump – the thrill of proximity to unlimited power – Dmitriev offers to America: unlimited potential wealth. He is the head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, Moscow’s sovereign wealth government slush pot, and he has close links to the AfD.
There was unbridled delight in Moscow with the success of the AfD over the weekend.
Dmitriev called the result a win that “humiliates the arrogance, narrow-mindedness, warmongering, ineptitude and hypocrisy” of German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s governing coalition.
The AfD, seen by German intelligence as an extremist organisation, has enjoyed (among other things) Russian support for its social media campaigns to win the elections in Saxony-Anhalt, according to German and other European intelligence sources.
In addition, Markus Frohnmaier, AfD foreign-policy spokesperson in the Bundestag, has been an enthusiastic supporter of Putin’s policies in Ukraine since before the 2022 full-scale invasion.
And on 3 June he met Dmitriev in St Petersburg after meeting the head of Russia’s oil giant, Gazprom, at Russia’s “International Economic Forum”.
“Looking forward to building a great FUTURE together with AfD, Germany’s most popular party,” Dmitriev wrote on X afterwards.
“Along with AfD’s Deputy Chairman Markus Frohnmaier, I discussed the economic cooperation with Germany, including restarting the Russia-Germany-US business dialogue,” he added.
The same day, 3 June, Dmitriev confirmed he was also in touch (as he often is) with Witkoff and Kushner.
That future is shaping up nicely for the Kremlin.
Dmitriev, who is unelected and holds no official government role in Russia, has been a regular guest of Kushner and Witkoff in Miami, ostensibly to work on a peace deal with Ukraine. No such sojourn has been offered to any Ukrainian.
Notoriously, Dmitriev is reported to be offering advantageous terms for American businessmen if they backed the unfreezing of $300m of Russian assets held in Europe. He later even reportedly dangled the idea that there was “$14 trillion” in business opportunities for the US in Russia if sanctions, imposed over its invasion of Ukraine, were lifted and normal business could resume.
Dmitriev was the main escort for Witkoff and Kushner when they visited Moscow at the weekend on the latest of numerous visits to the Russian president. After all the fanfare, there was no significant outcome from their first visit to Kyiv the next day.
Dmitriev, Witkoff and Kushner were behind a 28-point plan for peace in Ukraine that reflected business opportunities for America, lifted sanctions on Russia, and would have led to Russian annexation of vast tracts of the invaded democracy where US companies could join a minerals exploitation bonanza.
Witkoff and Kushner have also been Trump’s Middle East envoys. The diplomatic shuttling has included a business boom for both men.
Since their involvement in Middle East diplomacy, both men have seen striking inflows of Gulf-linked capital into businesses they own. Kushner, Trump's principal Middle East adviser in his first term, created Affinity Partners immediately after leaving the White House in 2021; it subsequently received $2bn from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.
In 2024, another $1.5bn from Qatar's sovereign wealth fund and Abu Dhabi-based Lunate, taking assets under management to $4.8bn by the end of that year. Kushner is the sole owner of Affinity's management company.
Witkoff, appointed Trump’s Middle East envoy in November 2024, has meanwhile benefited through his family's stake in Trump-linked crypto company World Liberty Financial.
Forbes estimates the Witkoff family made about $130m from WLFI token sales, plus roughly $48m after tax from selling part of its stake to an investment vehicle backed by Abu Dhabi royal and national-security adviser Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed.
The Trump administration has taken a consistently pro-Russian stand on every aspect of “peace talks” involving Ukraine. Early on in the administration, Trump ended military aid to Kyiv.
He then exploited Ukrainian vulnerability to extract a minerals deal from Volodymyr Zelensky that means Ukraine must pay back all the costs of war support it got from the Biden administration.
There are no US security guarantees seriously mooted for Ukraine in any Russian or American peace proposal.
There is agreement, or an understanding, between the US and Russia that Ukraine will have to give up all or most of the Donbas, about 25 per cent of its territory, give up on joining Nato, and enfeeble its military as part of any end to the war with Russia.
The AfD, meanwhile, has a vocal pro-Putin stand on almost every issue and often goes further in fulfilling the geopolitical aims of the Kremlin than even the Trump administration.
The AfD has taken legal action to try to stop German support for Ukraine’s armed forces. Its leaders have campaigned for an end to sanctions against Russia and a resumption of gas and oil sales by Moscow to Germany.
The party’s 2025 manifesto says that Ukraine’s future should be as a neutral state outside both Nato and the European Union. Trump and Co have not said Ukraine should stay out of the EU, which the AfD wants to leave and which Putin sees as Russia’s nemesis.
Ukraine’s diplomatic vulnerability, in other words, is not simply that Trump wants a deal, or that Germany’s politics are shifting rightward.
It is that the same individual, operating through the same playbook of framing Russian rapprochement as lucrative rather than dangerous, is working both ends of the problem at once – one negotiating table in Florida, one ballot box in Saxony-Anhalt.
If that pincer closes – a Washington-brokered settlement favourable to Moscow, arriving at the same moment Berlin's political centre of gravity shifts toward a party openly sympathetic to the Kremlin – Ukraine could find itself losing the war diplomatically and politically, at a time when Kyiv’s long-range drone strikes are putting Putin on the back foot.

ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే పర్వతాన్ని చూపుతున్న ఫోటోలు కెనడాలో ఉన్న ‘మౌంట్ అసినిబాయిన్’ పేరుతో వివిధ ఫోటోగ్రఫీ, పర్యాటక వెబ్సైట్లలో ఉండటాన్ని గమనించాం. అలాగే, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్న పర్వతాన్ని అందుబాటులో ఉన్న కైలాస పర్వతం ఫోటోలతో పోల్చి చూడగా, ఇవి రెండూ వేర్వేరు పర్వతాలని గుర్తించాం.
అంతేకాకుండా, అసినిబాయిన్ పర్వతాన్ని సందర్శించిన పర్యాటకులు తీసిన వీడియోలను ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు. వీటిలో వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న సరస్సుని కూడా చూడవచ్చు. వాస్తవానికి, చైనాలోని టిబెట్ స్వాధికార ప్రాంతంలో ఉన్న కైలాస పర్వతం మీదుగా విమానాలు, హెలికాప్టర్లు, డ్రోన్లు ప్రయాణించడంపై అక్కడి ప్రభుత్వం నిషేధం విధించింది. పర్వతం చుట్టూ ఉన్న గగనతలాన్ని భద్రత, మతపరమైన కారణాల దృష్ట్యా మూసివేసినందున, పొరుగున ఉన్న నేపాల్లోని పర్యాటక నిర్వాహకులు ప్రత్యేకంగా కైలాష్ దర్శన్ చార్టర్ విమానాలను నడుపుతున్నారు. ఈ విమానాలు నేపాల్ గగనతలంలో 27 వేల అడుగుల ఎత్తులో ప్రయాణించడం ద్వారా యాత్రికులు టిబెట్లోకి ప్రవేశించకుండానే కైలాస శిఖరాన్ని దూరం నుండి వీక్షించగలుగుతారు.
చివరిగా, కైలాస శిఖరాన్ని తొలిసారిగా హెలికాప్టర్ ద్వారా చిత్రీకరించారంటూ కెనడాలో ఉన్న ‘మౌంట్ అసినిబాయిన్’ దృశ్యాలను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Victoria Police has ended its investigation into gynaecologist Simon Gordon, who is accused of performing unnecessary surgeries on women.
Former premier Jacinta Allan referred the allegations to police in February this year following a Four Corners investigation.
What's next?
The Medical Board of Australia last month referred Dr Gordon to Victoria's civil tribunal, alleging he engaged in professional misconduct.
Victoria Police has dropped its investigation into gynaecologist Simon Gordon, who is accused of performing unnecessary surgeries on women.
Earlier this year, Four Corners revealed allegations the renowned surgeon repeatedly removed tissue and organs from women for "severe" endometriosis, when pathology showed little trace of the disease.
Dr Gordon has maintained he always acted ethically and responsibly.
He told the ABC earlier this year he "never performed surgery to treat endometriosis or any other condition unless I was absolutely convinced it was in the patient's best interest and to improve their overall quality of life".
Then-premier Jacinta Allan referred allegations against Dr Gordon to Victoria Police in February, but police are not proceeding with an investigation.
"Victoria Police has completed the assessment of the referral," a spokesperson said today.
"Based on the information provided, we are unable to take the matter further at this time.
"Any new information provided to police will be thoroughly assessed."
Earlier in the year, the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) began reviewing previous complaints it received and launched a fresh investigation into Dr Gordon.
AHPRA commissioned a panel of independent medical experts to review patient care and requested thousands of medical records and documents.
The Medical Board of Australia, which registers medical practitioners and develops standards, has since determined the allegations AHPRA had been investigating against Dr Gordon warranted consideration by an independent tribunal, and referred the matter to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT).
Dr Gordon retired from practice shortly after Epworth Hospital, where he worked, discovered in October 2025 that Four Corners was investigating him.
In December, Dr Gordon removed himself from AHPRA's register of practitioners.

Telluride chief Julie Huntsinger took a significant risk programming a documentary as the festival’s sneak premiere this year, given that nonfiction can’t claim the broad appeal of fiction. Indeed, just as she prepared to reveal the chosen film someone in the Werner Herzog Theater shouted Digger!, apparently hoping it would be the Tom Cruise-starring feature from director Alejandro Iñárritu. That person may have been disappointed, but judging from reaction, the selection of the documentary You Can See Everything has turned into a triumph.
More than 24 hours after the premiere of the Nathan Fielder–Lance Oppenheim film, everyone in Telluride is still talking about it (well, everyone still in town; plenty headed to the airport Monday). One festival regular told me he’d got a message from someone in Lake Charles, LA wanting to know if he’d been one of the lucky few to get into the screening. The news has spread fast and far.
Walking near Colorado Avenue Monday afternoon, I spotted a publicist who had advance knowledge that You Can See Everything would be the super-secret special film. We proceeded to get into a 10-minute discussion of the film’s two principal characters – the enigmatic and unblinking Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the notorious Silicon Valley blood-testing startup Theranos, and her romantic partner, Billy Evans, father of her two young children. Is he out of his mind (as one important figure in the film exclaims)? Is she on the level or a preternaturally gifted manipulator trying to pull a Jedi mind trick on Fielder? Those kinds of vigorous debates have been going on from the moment the crowd spilled out of the Herzog into the Telluride night air.
Watch on Deadline
At an afterparty at La Marmotte (French for marmot, a stout ground-dwelling squirrel. I mention this because that’s the kind of weird detail I think Fielder would seize on), the directors held court as enthusiast after enthusiast heaped praise on them in between slurps of cocktails and bites of molten mushroom croquettes and seared tuna cubes. I spoke with Fielder and he seemed a bit dazed by the ardent reception for his film. He’s been working in intense secrecy on the project since before Holmes began her prison term in 2023 after her conviction for defrauding investors (and her acquittal, she repeats several times in the film, of defrauding patients). To emerge from that edit cave into the spotlight of public reaction must be disorienting. Fielder didn’t even know where the film would play next – whether distributor A24 would take it to another festival or proceed straight to theatrical release next month.
Two-time Oscar winner Emma Stone hung out at the afterparty too (can we say she Marmotted? Is that a verb?). She moderated the Q&A after the world premiere and acquitted herself admirably (as people were leaving the theater a veteran journalist went up to Emma and congratulated her on her performance as moderator, helpfully noting that actors typically don’t excel at that).
The nearly three-hour long film drew continuous laughter, frequently triggered by hilarious reaction shots of Fielder, the Canadian comedian and co-director, who is seen on camera throughout attempting to process what Holmes and Evans are pushing. “Liz,” as she goes by in the film, suffered catastrophic reputational damage from the implosion of Theranos, not to mention a skewering she received in Alex Gibney’s documentary The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley and the devastating portrayal by actress Amanda Seyfried in the fictionalized Hulu series The Dropout. Aware of that and wishing to revive Theranos in a new form, the couple invited Fielder to observe their every move for the 30-some days before she had to report to federal prison in Texas.
In the glory days of Theranos, Holmes — her big blue eyes and blond hair set to advantage in black turtleneck sweaters — had reeled in powerful backers like Larry Ellison, Rupert Murdoch, Henry Kissinger, and George Shultz. Shedding the turtleneck in favor of a cozier sweater and rumpled coiffure for the documentary, she locks eyes with Fielder perhaps thinking she could work her magic on him. But he proves resistant, relentlessly probing whether Holmes knew she had oversold what her blood testing machines could do.
Evans emerges as a troubling presence who may be exerting undue control over Holmes, in a possible recapitulation of her relationship with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, the Svengali-like president of Theranos and Holmes’s then romantic partner (he’s serving a federal prison term as well, of 12 years). Billy boy is eager to have the film crew record him pumping iron, and later, while showering at home – clearly aware a camera was on him – he proudly displays his, uh, manhood. Well into the film he gets into a discussion with the film team where he proclaims his prowess at love-making. And they call Donald Trump a narcissist. He admits to taking over Holmes’s X/Twitter feed and tweeting as her, and he works out a deal for A24 to pay he and Holmes to appear in the film, possibly without her knowledge (he ultimately abandoned that effort to score a payday).
The motives of Holmes and Evans remain resolutely opaque; during the Q&A the directors said the film crew would often debate what they had witnessed of the couple after a day’s shooting, but no one could agree on a common interpretation. You Can See Everything, then, qualifies an arch title. What does it serve to “see everything” when you’re mired in muck?
(In the teaser below, you can see one of those delicious reaction shots of Fielder as Holmes assures him of her utter honesty).

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Women's Super League: Alexia Putellas' debut for London City analysed with more on Man City and Chelsea
Digital journalist Laura Hunter returns for a second season with a WSL-dedicated column, analysing all the big talking points from across the weekend's action; London City Lionesses' winning start is this week's big focus, with more on Manchester City and Chelsea
Monday 7 September 2026 13:18, UK
Sky Sports columnist Laura Hunter analyses the big talking points from the first round of Women's Super League matches, bringing you closer to the key stories at the heart of the women's game.
Putellas only part of London City's style meets substance - will it last?
Michele Kang rolled out the red carpet in Bromley for London City Lionesses' season opener under the lights, where the Sky Sports cameras were in attendance to watch a dominant win over Manchester United. Kang herself was among the spectators in a sell-out crowd.
Alexia Putellas inevitably made all the headlines. The two-time Ballon d'Or winner commands that kind of attention. But the real standouts from such a positive opening night, in footballing terms, were Delphine Cascarino and Danielle van de Donk. Neither part of this summer's spending spree but the two most influential players on the park.
London City gave a good account of themselves in most departments, actually. A performance far more complete than the majority of last season, or even the sum of all their individual parts suggested.
Putellas was sound, if not as spectacular. It will take time for her to acclimatise to new surroundings, or perhaps more appropriately, take patience for those surroundings to adapt to her. It has always been that way around for La Reina. Team-mates must reach her wavelength.
What was clear is that the Spain superstar will be the nucleus of Eder Maestre's plan. Of the eight chances London City created, she claimed two and Cascarino was responsible for four. The restless Putellas hype will no doubt carry through the season, her standards acting as the spine and soul of this group of newcomers. She has to knit all the various pieces together to meet the required level of chemistry that constitute a team.
But Maestre's side look to have gelled fairly well on first glance. No doubt they will face sterner tests in future weeks. London City and Man Utd were actually the perfect antithesis for opening night, a side on their way up passing one in obvious decline. London City barely stopped to say hello.
Kang's empire has consumed Bromley and will continue to dominate WSL chatter for as long as their results match their endeavour. There is no denying the pull of Putellas. Or Cascarino. Or Mary Earps, who did not feature on Friday but was still a major fan attraction. But buying footballers is really the easy part. Creating a consistent team out of them much more difficult.
Are Man City too reliant on Hemp?
It's only week one and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw has reaffirmed her position as the best the Women's Super League has to offer, her 11 shots yielding two goals as Man City beat Birmingham.
Nothing about that victory was especially experimental, though still impressive. Shaw scored two carbon-copy goals, both from corners, both delivered from the left. Her movement for each was similar except the angle of the second header was far more difficult to guide on target. She made it look easy.
City scored 15 times from corners last season, a seasonal record, and such a superpower will no doubt come in handy again as they look to defend their crown. They were the only side to score from a set-piece across opening weekend. Last term, they scored from a set-play in all but seven games.
But what struck me was how lop-sided their attacking phase was from open play. Almost everything went through Lauren Hemp. Loading on the left is not necessarily a new tactic, but to such an extent surely misses an opportunity.
Hemp is an exceptional outlet, with pace to burn and superb crossing accuracy, which is why the centre-backs often look left when playing out from the back. Gracie Prior found Hemp 11 times against Birmingham. Opponents know to expect this.
Where City might profit this term is by exploiting that expectancy to unlock different pockets of space. Use the threat of Hemp to attract numbers and play elsewhere. Andree Jeglertz has spoken plenty about wanting City to have fresh, innovative ways of creating goals. He likes central rotations, utilising the ball-playing skill of Yui Hasegawa. City should lean into her passing range more.
Perhaps that will be helped by Vivianne Miedema's return from injury, whenever that might be. But before then, they can also afford to mix it up a bit more. Becoming even more versatile than they are now could propel them from being a very good team to an unbeatable one.
Chelsea's goal-shy streak persists
New season, same problem for Chelsea. Their creators are crying out for a finisher.
Lauren James cannot be expected to shoulder the scoring burden on her own. So, how can Chelsea combat a flaw that has been plaguing them since Sonia Bompastor took charge?
Stylistically, Chelsea are doing most things right. A statistical reading of their 1-1 draw with Aston Villa will tell you that final-third entries were plentiful. The Blues created five big chances, missing four.
Essentially, James has been left to do the job of a winger and striker. She created the joint-most chances for others (4) while taking the most shots herself (11). Aggie Beever-Jones accumulated the highest expected goals total but debutant goalkeeper Akane Okuma was equal to both of her two efforts on target, neither particularly taxing.
The speed at which Chelsea arrive in the box remains an issue. It allows enough retreating defenders to make blocks; Villa made six of them. Okuma also made a remarkable nine saves. "We have to speed up the game," reflected Bompastor.
Chelsea's 35 shots were their most ever in a league game they failed to win. Bompastor added: "If you analyse the statistics, you would say it's crazy that we didn't win." The club's succession line of attackers looks too thin given what they are up against. They have Melvine Malard and Mayra Ramirez to return. But they need firepower now.

Novo Nordisk has stopped two trials of a drug that aims to tame inflammation as a way to improve cardiovascular health, another blow for the approach.
The company said it had halted the HERMES and ATHENA trials of its drug, ziltivekimab, after a data monitoring committee found they were unlikely to succeed. Novo informed trial investigators on Friday.
The move follows the earlier failure of the drug in the ZEUS trial, which showed that the medicine, despite lowering markers of inflammation, did not reduce the risk of major clinical complications, including deaths and heart attacks.

The story so far: As OpenAI last week launched its Health offering in ChatGPT for U.S. users, a new lawsuit against the company began gaining traction online. Dated June 12, 2026, the U.S. lawsuit focuses on a suicide linked to an older ChatGPT model that is no longer available, but was until recently used by people all over the world: GPT-4o.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani announces ban on AI use for students until high school
What is the latest case linked to OpenAI’s GPT-4o?
The lawsuit focuses on Christian Faith Madison, 29, a late mother and working professional based in the U.S. state of Alabama. Ms. Madison began using ChatGPT (model GPT-4o) in December 2024, according to the lawsuit, with her work-related interactions shifting to praise, affection, and flattery from the chatbot.
The interactions then began to take on a dark, religious tone, with the chatbot allegedly convincing Ms. Madison that she was a religious saviour or messiah-like figure who needed to suffer and die to be resurrected. She later died by suicide on June 9, 2025. The lawsuit was filed by an administrator of her estate, on behalf of her minor son.
In particular, the legal filing highlighted the development of OpenAI’s GPT-4o, claiming that the system’s rushed development and inadequate safety performance training made existing issues even worse.
“The system’s design prioritized keeping users engaged above all else. It portrayed anthropomorphic traits, convincing some users that it was more than just a coded chatbot. It was excessively sycophantic, which fueled vulnerable users’ psychosis and delusions. And in tragic cases, the design flaws led ChatGPT-4o to push users to self-harm or suicide. Releasing ChatGPT-4o in this manner was a calculated decision – a conscious choice with enormous risks,” stated the lawsuit.
The filing observed that OpenAI’s Dr. Ilya Sutskever, a co-founder, resigned the day after GPT-4o’s launch, while researcher Jan Leike resigned days later.
What made GPT-4o different from other models?
On May 13, 2024, OpenAI introduced GPT‑4o as a “step towards much more natural human-computer interaction”.
Between February and April 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman praised the updates that were introduced to the model. However, on April 28, 2025, he noted that the “last couple” of updates made the model’s personality “too sycophant-y and annoying” and that the company was working to fix this immediately.
In a blog post dated April 29, OpenAI observed that “GPT‑4o skewed towards responses that were overly supportive but disingenuous,” adding that people would instead be using an earlier version with more balanced behaviour. For context, 16-year-old Adam Raine — a ChatGPT user — had died by suicide on April 11.
OpenAI announced in January this year that it would be retiring GPT‑4o, GPT‑4.1, GPT‑4.1 mini, and OpenAI o4-mini in ChatGPT. The transition triggered a range of negative reactions as a number of users had become emotionally attached to GPT-4o and its responsive style, catching even Mr. Altman by surprise.
Sycophancy in AI
Will the U.S. government take action against OpenAI over GPT-4o?
Multiple lawsuits against OpenAI are ongoing in the U.S., so a definitive answer has not yet emerged. These actions have been filed by separate legal teams in many cases, and cover both user suicides and injuries, as well as homicides.
For example, the U.S. legal firm Edelson PC said it had filed seven wrongful death and negligence lawsuits on behalf of families affected by the Tumbler Ridge shooting in Canada. These lawsuits alleged that OpenAI did not act to stop the shooting in spite of having knowledge of the shooter’s profile and plans. Edelson PC is also representing the family of Adam Raine, and the estate of Suzanne Adams, a woman who was murdered at 83 by her son who used ChatGPT.
Several related lawsuits, including the one for Ms. Madison’s case, echo the same points: they allege a hurried GPT-4o launch, inadequate or highly sped-up safety training, a focus on keeping users engaged for longer, high levels of sycophancy that encouraged the users’ thoughts of self-harm or suicide, and a design that evoked the feeling of intimate interactions with other human beings — even if this led to dangerous offline actions.
Is OpenAI legally in the clear with its later AI models?
Mishi Choudhary, a technology lawyer and activist who founded the Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in) organisation, told The Hindu there was not yet enough independent evidence to say whether OpenAI’s newer models were “reliably safe” for young people or those in distress.
“Some recent research suggests that newer models may be better at asking direct questions about suicide risk and may produce fewer overtly harmful responses in controlled tests. But the same studies identify continuing failures,” Ms. Choudhary explained.
“We see from research studies that models continue to miss indirect or culturally expressed warning signs, respond inconsistently across a longer conversation, and cannot be relied upon like a human therapist to pick up warnings,” she added.
From a legal perspective, Ms. Choudhary cited past pharmaceuticals and software cases, noting that a manufacturer does not ordinarily escape liability just by withdrawing or replacing a product after an alleged injury.
While OpenAI’s users and customers look forward to adopting newer and more advanced AI models, the lawsuits against GPT-4o call on tech users to remember and pay attention to the past.

Welcome to Edition 9.09 of the Rocket Report! This edition includes an update from Blue Origin on the groundbreaking of a new Payload Processing Facility in Florida. It has been about a month since the company offered any meaningful news on its heavy-lift New Glenn rocket, which remains grounded after an on-pad explosion at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in May. The official line from Blue Origin is that the company is targeting a return to flight with New Glenn by the end of the year, but there’s good reason for skepticism.
As always, we welcome reader submissions. If you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets, as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Isar Aerospace is ready to try again. Isar Aerospace is about to make the next attempt to launch the Spectrum rocket into orbit, with a weeklong launch window set to open Friday at Andøya Spaceport in Norway, the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation (NRK) reports. The German launch company aims to deliver several small CubeSats to orbit with the two-stage Spectrum rocket. A test flight of the privately funded launcher failed shortly after liftoff last year, and Isar has attempted to launch the second Spectrum rocket several times since January, only to be thwarted by technical problems and the unavailability of the launch range in northern Norway.
Mourning period… This launch window comes as Norway is in a period of national mourning following the death of King Harald V. Isar’s founder, Daniel Metzler, told NRK he hopes to launch before the late king’s funeral on September 9, but the Norwegian government says the mission can go ahead normally during the mourning period. Isar Aerospace won a 200 million euro ($230 million) contract from the European Space Agency last month to support further development of new launch vehicles.
The Ars Technica Rocket Report
The easiest way to keep up with Eric Berger’s and Stephen Clark’s reporting on all things space is to sign up for our newsletter. We’ll collect their stories and deliver them straight to your inbox.
Europe’s other launch startups announce new funding. Spanish launch services provider PLD Space has secured an additional 108 million euros ($126 million) in funding as it prepares for the inaugural orbital launch attempt of its small Miura 5 rocket, European Spaceflight reports. The most recent fundraising was led by Japan’s Mitsubishi Electric Corporation and came less than a week after PLD Space won a 159 million euro ($185 million) contract from the European Space Agency’s European Launcher Challenge program, alongside Isar Aerospace and Rocket Factory Augsburg.
HyImpulse, too… German launch services provider HyImpulse announced Wednesday that it had extended its Series A funding round by more than 50 million euros ($58 million), bringing its total funding to date to 125 million euros ($145 million), European Spaceflight reports. The company is currently preparing for the second flight of its suborbital SR75 rocket and the inaugural launch attempt of its larger orbital-class SL1 rocket. HyImpulse was not among the European companies that won contracts through the European Launcher Challenge.
NASA weighs new ways of buying rockets. NASA is consolidating many of its launch programs into a single office that is considering block buys of launches, Space News reports. NASA officials at the recent Small Satellite Conference discussed the creation of a new Commercial Access to Space office within NASA’s Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate, established earlier this year as part of an agency reorganization. The new office would be responsible for all launch activities at NASA except those for human spaceflight. Pete Wilczynski, the NASA official responsible for science missions in the Commercial Access to Space office, said one reason to combine separate launch activities is to aggregate launch demand and enable bulk buys of launches.
Following the Pentagon’s lead… The US Space Force employs a bulk buying scheme with its launch procurement office, guaranteeing its top launch providers—SpaceX and United Launch Alliance—a certain number of launch contracts over a period of several years. Proponents of this strategy say it results in lower launch prices for the government and assured business for launch providers, a factor that is especially important for new entrants in the market. “We’re looking at a new strategy that will entail an all-of-NASA approach, which means we may procure five, 10, 15, 20 rockets in a procurement,” Wilczynski said.
Galactic Energy’s Pallas-1 launches on first flight. Chinese commercial launch company Galactic Energy announced it successfully launched its first Pallas-1 rocket Monday, with future flights to attempt first stage recovery, Space News reports. The Pallas-1 is the sixth new Chinese rocket to debut this year, and the fifth with a potentially recoverable and reusable booster stage. Galactic Energy’s first rocket, the expendable, solid-fueled Ceres-1, has flown 23 times on missions carrying small satellites into low-Earth orbit. Pallas-1 is a medium-class rocket with a maximum payload capacity of about 15,400 pounds (7,000 kilograms) to low-Earth orbit.
Some doubt?… While Galactic Energy and Chinese state media heralded Monday’s launch as a success, the US Space Force had not added the Pallas-1 rocket’s upper stage or any payloads to its catalog of space objects as of late Thursday. This is highly unusual for a successful orbital launch. Jonathan McDowell, an expert tracker of spaceflight activity, noted on X that Galactic Energy has not announced the orbital altitude or inclination achieved by the Pallas-1 rocket. “I must regard success of the launch as not confirmed at this point,” McDowell wrote.
China’s Long March 6C can’t keep it together. A Chinese Long March 6C rocket upper stage has fragmented in orbit, just days after the stage delivered a seven-satellite rideshare mission, Space News reports. LeoLabs, a commercial space surveillance company, confirmed the breakup. The rocket launched August 24, but LeoLabs’ Multi-Object Detection tool flagged the fragmentation of the rocket’s upper stage less than two days later. “We estimate tens to hundreds of fragments were generated,” LeoLabs stated in an August 28 post on social media platform X.
An unenviable track record… The good news is that the rocket’s orbit is low enough that the debris should reenter the atmosphere within a few years. The bad news is that this breakup is the latest in a series of fragmentations afflicting the Long March 6 series, most notably the Long March 6A, which uses a slightly larger-diameter second stage than the 6C. Both rockets use a single YF-115 engine powered by kerosene-liquid-oxygen propellant. The Long March 6A breakups have been especially troubling, with more than 1,200 pieces of debris cataloged by the US Space Force from two upper stages in 2022 and 2024.
Ariane 6 aces first GTO mission. Arianespace has completed the first Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO) mission with an Ariane 6, deploying the MTG-I2 weather satellite for European meteorological agency Eumetsat, Aviation Week and Space Technology reports. This was the rocket’s farthest mission so far. The two-booster Ariane 62 rocket took off August 27 from Kourou, French Guiana, and released its weather satellite payload about 30 minutes later. The spacecraft, soon to be renamed Meteosat-14, will use onboard propulsion to circularize its orbit more than 22,000 miles (nearly 36,000 kilometers) over the equator to begin providing continuous weather observations over Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.
Back to Europe… This launch marks Eumetsat’s return to European launch services after the weather agency launched its previous Meteosat weather satellite on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in 2025. Delays in the debut and ramp-up of Ariane 6 launches forced several European customers to look overseas for launch services after the retirement of the Ariane 5 rocket in 2023. Doubts about Ariane 6’s competitiveness remain top of mind in Europe, but the rocket has proven fairly reliable. The Ariane 6 has notched eight flawless missions in nine launches since its first test flight in 2024.
India launches high-altitude Earth imager. India’s space program achieved another successful rocket launch Thursday, placing an Earth observation craft into orbit as New Delhi works to sharpen its satellite-based surveillance capabilities, Bloomberg reports. The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle lifted off from the country’s main spaceport at Sriharikota, an island in southern India, and reached the designated orbit 18 minutes later. The payload was the Indian government’s EOS-05 satellite, a roughly 2.5-ton spacecraft with an Earth-facing telescope to provide near-continuous views of the same region of the world from a perch in geosynchronous orbit.
A do-over for ISRO… The EOS-05 satellite is a replacement for GISAT-1, which was lost in a GSLV launch failure in 2021. Geosynchronous orbit is an unusual location for a dedicated Earth observation satellite due to its high altitude, but it has the benefit of providing a constant vigil over a fixed geographic area. The Indian Navy is reportedly interested in geosynchronous surveillance of Earth. The mission of EOS-05 is different from a conventional weather satellite in that its telescope will capture optical images with a maximum resolution of 42 meters (138 feet). Modern geosynchronous weather satellites, such as NOAA’s GOES satellites, have weather instruments that cover wider areas at a resolution of about 500 meters (1,640 feet).
NASA launches next great observatory. NASA’s $4.3 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, equipped with a 300-megapixel camera sighted through a refurbished spy mirror, launched Sunday from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on a mission to reveal the mysterious forces driving the Universe, Ars reports. The new mission will extend the vision of NASA’s other famous observatories, providing a field of view 100 times wider than the Hubble Space Telescope and complementing the groundbreaking work of the James Webb Space Telescope. Roman is just the second NASA-led astrophysics mission to launch this century, following the launch of Webb in 2021. Unlike Webb, which suffered many years of delays before reaching space, Roman arrived at the launch pad nine months before NASA’s commitment to send it skyward by May 2027.
Riding Falcon Heavy… SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket gave the Roman Space Telescope a ride toward a final operating post around the L2 Lagrange point nearly a million miles from Earth. This was the 13th flight of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy, a rocket most commonly used by NASA and the US military for strategic space science and national security missions. The rocket’s two side boosters returned to Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, for reuse on another Falcon Heavy flight later this year.
Super Heavy static fire at Starbase. SpaceX took another step toward the highly anticipated next test flight of its Starship mega-rocket, Space.com reports. The rocket’s enormous first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, lit its 33 engines on the launch pad at Starbase, Texas, on Friday, August 28. The static fire on Super Heavy followed a test-firing of the six-engine Starship upper stage earlier in August. This is the rocket that will power Flight 14 of Starship, scheduled for launch later this month. Flight 14 is expected to be the first Starship flight to low-Earth orbit after the previous 13 test flights targeted suborbital trajectories.
Unleashing Starlink V3… The orbital flight will allow SpaceX to deploy operational payloads. A batch of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink “Version 3” satellites will launch on Flight 14. The new Starlink V3s are too large to fit on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket, and they offer significant performance upgrades over the Starlink V2s that currently populate the network. SpaceX has not said how many Starlink V3s will launch on Flight 14. The company deployed 20 Starlink V3s on the previous Starship flight in July, but those satellites did not enter orbit. They reentered the atmosphere over the Indian Ocean, as intended, as Starship headed for a controlled splashdown northwest of Australia.
Blue Origin breaks ground on satellite hangar. While Blue Origin plows ahead with its reconstruction of its New Glenn launch pad at Cape Canaveral, damaged in a massive explosion earlier this year, it is also moving forward with new construction of an adjacent facility that will help the US Space Force, the Orlando Sentinel reports. Jeff Bezos’ company was awarded a $78 million contract last year by Space Systems Command to construct a space vehicle processing facility on Florida’s Space Coast by 2028. The hangar won’t be just for Blue Origin, though, but will support any launch provider flying national security payloads.
Thinking big… The Payload Processing Facility (PPF) will cover 120,000 square feet and will be large enough to accommodate Blue Origin’s planned 25.5-foot-diameter (8.7-meter) payload fairing for the company’s upgraded New Glenn rocket. Dave Limp, Blue Origin’s CEO, said the facility will house four payload processing bays, two encapsulation bays, and a multi‑manifest area supporting National Security Space Launch, civil, and commercial missions. Blue Origin is on a building spree at Cape Canaveral, with the rebuild of its partially destroyed launch pad at Launch Complex 36, the construction of a second launch pad, and now the PPF.

U.S. coach Mauricio Pochettino vowed to change the attitude and habits of the American national team as he starts a second term, appearing to refer to star Christian Pulisic’s decision to skip the 2025 CONCACAF Gold Cup.
“It was difficult to make the roster for the Gold Cup one year before because the mindset was different,” Pochettino said Monday during an online question-and-answer session with reporters. “You say, ‘If I play, I have not holidays. I cannot arrive fresh for the World Cup.’ ... You know now that is bull----.”
Pochettino said his goal “is to change this type of idea that are not right.”
Pulisic, the top American player, took himself out of consideration for the 2025 Gold Cup citing the need to rest after his season with AC Milan and the hope to be fresh for the 2026 World Cup. He didn’t score in four World Cup appearances this year, missing one group-stage match because of a calf injury and leaving the Americans’ round of 16 loss to Belgium on July 6 after fracturing his right tibia and fibula.

He had 10 goals in his first 15 matches for AC Milan last season but went scoreless in 19 club games after Dec. 28. He has been an unused substitute in AC Milan’s first three games this season.
Pochettino took over from Gregg Berhalter in the fall of 2024 and was given a four-year contract in a deal announced last month.
Pochettino plans to announce his roster on Sept. 17 for the first games of his second term, a double window that includes friendlies against Peru (Sept. 26 in Orlando, Florida), Chile (Sept. 29 in St. Louis), Mexico (Oct. 3 in Glendale, Arizona) and Canada (Oct. 6 in St. Paul, Minnesota). In their first competitive matches since the World Cup, the Americans play CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals in November.
“A new process, new project, new rules, new principles,” he said, speaking from London. “I think that the headline needs to be that (it) is a new start, a fresh start. And I think we need to change habits.”
“We need to create a group of players that (are) really being professional and compete in the way that we expect that they need to compete,” he added.
Players dropped from the World Cup roster, such as midfielders Diego Luna, Tanner Tessmann and Aidan Morris, could return. Young players such as 16-year-old Philadelphia midfielder Cavan Sullivan could be included for possible debuts.
Some, such as 19-year-old Crystal Palace winger Zavier Gozo, could be left off to allow them time to integrate with new clubs following summer transfers. Pochettino also expressed uncertainty about midfielder Sebastian Berhalter and defender Max Arfsten, who transferred to Middlesbrough.
Pochettino said players could be given national team debuts before they focus on the under-23 team, which will be coached by former U.S. defender Steve Cherundolo heading toward the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. He cited a “need to be careful” with youngsters.
“You need to (have) confidence. You need to have the trust in yourself and belief that you can perform and do well,” he said. “Sometimes if you play well and you are 17, 16 or 18 and you play well and people start to talk, about you are (Lionel) Messi or you are a big star in the world because you do some good things. If after you are confused and you don’t manage well, that can be dangerous for your career and that is what we don’t want.
“You only are entitled to talk a little bit out of order if you are Messi, if you win. If you won, you can talk with certain arrogance.”
Among the attitudes Pochettino wants to change are those of coaches who would rather have their young players stay with clubs during international breaks.
“Sometimes the coaches say no. I have a 17-year-old guy that play in the MLS but when the (under) 19 national team called, say no because they need to rest,” Pochettino said. “If (you are) 17, you need to rest, aye yai, yai. We have a big problem.”
Augsburg defender Noahkai Banks still hasn’t decided whether to play for the U.S. or Germany.
“Noki is still in the same situation that (he) was before the World Cup,” Pochettino said. “We are in contact with all the potential duel nationals. I think it’s important for us to see. That is the connection, the human connection, that is so important.”
Pochettino intends to telephone striker Folarin Balogun, whose proposed transfer from Monaco to Everton came apart last week.
“I want to know from him what happened but always offering our support,” he said. “He’s an important player for us, was an important player in the World Cup and (I) hope that he can find being in Monaco, in another place, his best place to perform.”

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Marvel and Disney+ have issued a stacked watch list for fans ahead of the cinema release of Avengers: Doomsday on December 18.
The Marvel Cinematic Universe can be complex terrain to navigate. Its 38 movies and 25 series to date span varying superhero plot lines, crossovers, and multiverse action, with the latest Avengers release likely to spare no less lore and real fan knowledge.
Marvel released an official “Countdown to Doomsday” playlist with Disney+, featuring 15 official selections to help fans catch up on all the action before watching the new movie. Among the selections, fans will get refreshers on origin stories, team-ups, and key multiversal information gearing them up to the Doomsday storyline.
The studio also launched the Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday Official Podcast, available on Disney+, YouTube, and audio platforms. The podcast features weekly recaps of the MCU’s Infinity Saga.
Devoted fans were quick to spot that two X-Men entries predate the MCU entirely, presumably because Patrick Stewart, James Marsden, Ian McKellen, and Alan Cumming are all rumored to be coming back for Doomsday. The Marvels from 2023, interestingly, did not make the cut.
The official movie watch list will require 42 hours to get through, which is roughly under three hours a week if you spread it out evenly before the new movie drops in December. Disney+ releasing a homework list for its own film is a great bit of subscriber farming. It converts the hype ahead of the theatrical release into watching content on a streaming service that has to, in the meantime, justify its monthly cost.
Every title below streams on Disney+, which is available in many markets around the globe. Some titles are also available on other streamers, and most are available to rent or buy digitally through Amazon Prime Video or Apple TV.

Captain America: The First Avenger (2011)
Loki, both seasons (2021 to 2023)

Indian, Chinese armies hold talks focusing on maintaining peace along LAC
The Indian delegation was headed by Lt General Girish Kalia, the commander of the Army's Dimapur-based 3 Corps.
The Indian and Chinese armies reviewed the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the Arunachal Pradesh sector, days after the two sides held Special Representative talks in Beijing on the festering boundary question.
The focus of the corps commander-level talks at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point in Arunachal Pradesh's Kibithoo region on Sunday was to maintain peace and tranquillity along the frontier, people familiar with the matter said.
The Indian delegation was headed by Lt General Girish Kalia, the commander of the Army's Dimapur-based 3 Corps.
There is no official word yet on the talks.
The meeting also came amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.

In the Special Representative (SR) talks on August 25, India conveyed to China the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity along the frontier for overall bilateral ties.
National Security Advisor Ajit Doval held the SR talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi which focused on delimitation of the frontier and sustaining work on trans-boundary cooperation.
In his remarks at the meeting, Doval said that normalcy in the ties has been a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas.
The Indian side highlighted the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity in the India-China border areas for the continued development and progress of the bilateral relationship, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) had said on the SR talks.
Both Doval and Wang are the designated SRs for the boundary talks mechanism, which was established in 2003 to comprehensively address the dispute over the India-China border spanning 3,488 km.
In the last few months, the two sides have taken a series of measures to rebuild their relationship after it came under severe strain following the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020.

The Indian automobile industry retailed 24,23,201 units in August 2026, registering a 17.51% growth YoY.
However, compared to July 2026, retail sales fell by 6.48% due to a seasonal monsoon lull and a festival calendar that shifted Ganesh Chaturthi and the spillover of Onam-led buying into September.
The growth was led by Wheeled Construction Equipment, up 31.45%; Two-Wheelers, up 19.69%; Passenger Vehicles, up 16.14%; and Commercial Vehicles, up 14.45%, while Three-Wheelers grew 8.64% and Tractors were effectively flat at 0.84%, according to data released by the Federation of Automobile Dealers Association (FADA) on Monday (September 7, 2026).
For the first time in India’s history, alternative fuels — CNG, hybrid and electric combined — overtook petrol in the Passenger Vehicle market, at 41.95% against petrol’s 40.85%.
“Two-Wheelers, Passenger Vehicles, Commercial Vehicles, Tractors and Three-Wheelers each set fresh August records, and overall registrations were the highest ever for the month,” said Sai Giridhar, president, FADA.
Two-wheeler retail sales stood at 17,14,610 units, up 19.69% YoY—the best August since 2018 —but down 5.70% MoM.
2W EV share reached 10.68%, crossing the 10% mark in a non-festive month for the first time, against 7.66% a year ago according to FADA.
Commercial Vehicle retails came in at 90,769 units, up 14.45% YoY — the best-ever August — though 8.93% lower MoM.
LCVs grew 15.32% YoY, HCVs 13.98% and MCVs 10.38%, with dealers citing infrastructure execution, mining and e-commerce-linked logistics alongside steady financing.
Electric CV share rose to an all-time high of 5.18% from 2.06% a year ago, with e-CV volumes setting a fresh monthly record.
Passenger Vehicle retails were 4,02,398 units, up 16.14% YoY — the best-ever August and the first time PV has crossed the 4-lakh mark in an August — though 3.40% lower MoM.
Beyond the volume record, the fuel mix reached an inflexion point— alternative fuels (CNG 25.28%, Hybrid 9.04%, EV 7.63%) together touched 41.95%, edging past petrol/ethanol at 40.85% for the first time, though petrol still remains the single largest individual fuel.
“Dealers attribute the shift to running-cost economics and continuing consumer hesitation around the E20 transition, which is nudging petrol buyers towards CNG, hybrids and EVs,” Mr Giridhar said.
On the channel side, PV inventory rose by a further 5 days over July-end to around 38–40 days — well above FADA’s recommended 21-day benchmark, with 56% of PV dealers reporting higher stock month-on-month, he added.
Three-Wheelers at 1,22,281 units (8.64% up YoY) posted their best-ever August, with EV penetration at 65.30% — the segment is now structurally electric.
Tractors at 87,977 units were effectively flat (+0.84% YoY) and fell 25.03% MoM.
Wheeled Construction Equipment at 5,166 units rose 31.45% YoY on infrastructure momentum.
Total EV retails across categories reached 2,98,448 units — the biggest-ever August and up 52.9% YoY — taking overall EV penetration to about 12.3% from 9.5% a year ago, with Electric Commercial Vehicles at an all-time monthly high, FADA said.

Who will be new Liverpool sporting director - and what issues do they face?
- Published
With Richard Hughes' move to Al-Hilal now confirmed, Liverpool are seeking a new sporting director for the fifth time since 2022.
Hughes joined Liverpool in the summer of 2024 and oversaw the appointments of Arne Slot then Andoni Iraola. He informed the club earlier this year that he wanted to pursue a new challenge in Saudi Arabia.
Mike Gordon, the president of Fenway Sports Group (FSG), is overseeing the process of finding Hughes' replacement, with Liverpool keen to make a swift appointment.
Liverpool will look at internal candidates, but have not ruled out the possibility of appointing someone from outside the club. There is a desire to have someone that is committed long term.
But who are candidates? And what challenges do they face?
Who are the candidates?
David Woodfine, who was Hughes' assistant and was previously Liverpool's director of loans is one potential candidate. Woodfine was pictured giving Iraola a tour of the facilities at the AXA Training Centre when he arrived in June.
Another is Julian Ward, who was Liverpool's sporting director between 2022 and 2023 and oversaw the signings of Luis Diaz, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Darwin Nunez. He is now FSG's technical director.
Pedro Marques is FSG's director of football development and was previously the technical director at Benfica, where he helped sign Enzo Fernandez for £10m and before that, a first-team performance analyst at Manchester City.
Outside Anfield, Luis Campos at Paris St-Germain would be the strongest appointment but he is unlikely to view his immediate future away from the European champions.
Whoever replaces Hughes - who has also taken two members of Liverpool's recruitment staff in Mark Burchill and Craig McKee to the Middle East - they will have plenty to address.
Do Liverpool try to keep Alisson and Van Dijk?
Alisson's deal expires at the end of the season and although Juventus were interested in the Brazil goalkeeper this summer, Liverpool had no intention of letting him leave.
Iraola appointed Alisson one of his vice-captains and the 33-year-old has started in all three of their league games so far. He remains comfortably their best goalkeeper even if he is not at his peak.
Liverpool are not short of options, although Giorgi Mamardashvili has not fully convinced thus far while 18-year-old Lucca Brughmans will arrive next summer from Genk in a deal worth up to £30m but is unlikely to be viewed as an immediate first choice.
Alisson has been one of Liverpool's best players during a period in which they won two Premier League titles and a Champions League and the new sporting director will have to decide whether to try and keep him at Anfield next season.
The same can be said of skipper Virgil van Dijk, who is out of contract next summer. Having lost senior figures Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson at the end of last season, Liverpool need experience, so losing both Alisson and Van Dijk in the same close season would carry risk.
After an extended break following the World Cup, the 35-year-old has played every minute of Liverpool's league campaign so far and although he may not be quite the force he once was, he is still comfortably one of Europe's best centre-backs.
Jeremy Jacquet, Giovanni Leoni, Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye have huge potential and the new sporting director may view Van Dijk as the perfect player for them to learn from.
What about Liverpool's midfield and attack?
Iraola believes Liverpool have "good numbers" in midfield despite not strengthening that position over the summer following Curtis Jones' move to Inter Milan.
Faith has been placed in Trey Nyoni to feature more this season and the 19-year-old was one of the standouts of Liverpool's pre-season tour of the USA.
As the fixture list heats up, a lot will be asked of Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Mac Allister, so an injury to any of them could prove a major issue.
As reported last week by BBC Sport, Liverpool have looked at Monaco's Lamine Camara but were not open to buying a midfielder this summer.
That position could become a priority in January or next summer, particularly if it looks likely that there will be no contract extension for Mac Allister, whose deal expires in 2028.
As things stand, there are no talks over a new deal for the Argentina midfielder. That will be another situation for Hughes' successor to pick up.
The area where there is less concern is up front, with Hughes signing Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Hugo Ekitike, Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola on his watch.
With 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha expected to sign a long-term deal, Liverpool appear well-stocked in that department.
Liverpool eventually decided not to allow Cody Gakpo to leave for Manchester City this summer. The Netherlands forward has one goal and three assists already this season, but if they were able to sign a new winger and received another lucrative bid for Gakpo, that could be a scenario the club revisit.
Building a relationship with Iraola
When the question of stability was put to Billy Hogan, Liverpool's CEO, this summer, he told BBC Sport: "I would send a message that we are in a very healthy place as a football club - the leadership from the ownership is in a very steady place and we're looking forward to the next season and the season ahead."
However this has been a summer where Liverpool have changed managers, welcomed new investors, lost a number of senior players and seen their sporting director leave a year earlier than expected. Michael Edwards, who appointed Hughes, also resigned as FSG's CEO of Football.
Hughes, who is understood to have been influenced by Edwards' departure, was integral in the decision to sack Slot and appoint Iraola and ultimately the new sporting director will have a big say in the Spaniard's future.
When he joined Liverpool, Iraola said he only signed a two-year-deal because he didn't just want to be somewhere because he had a contract.
His relationship with Hughes from their time at Bournemouth played a part in him getting the Liverpool job. Now it will be down to someone else to work in tandem with Iraola as Liverpool look to challenge again.

Travel and lifestyle brand Mokobara has raised ₹170 Cr (about $18 Mn) in a Series C funding round led by Sauce.vc. The round also saw participation from Peak XV Partners, AYRA Ventures, Niveshaay Investment and other existing backers. As per a social media post by Sauce.vc’s vice president Karan Kathpalia, the VC firm led the round with a ₹109 Cr infusion in its portfolio startup. The story will be updated based on their response. According to Registrar of Companies (RoC) filings accessed by Inc42, Mokobara’s board has approved a proposal to issue 1,300 Series C compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) to the investors at ₹6.2 Lakh each, which aggregates to ₹80 Cr. The board also allotted 199 shares at ₹5.4 Lakh apiece to the investors, translating into an amount of ₹10.7 Cr. There appears no clarity on how Mokobara raised the remaining nearly ₹80 Cr. Founded in 2019 by Sangeet Agrawal and Navin Parwal, Mokobara sells a range of luggages, travel bags, wallets, kits and sling bags on its online platform. It also sells its products on marketplaces like Amazon and Flipkart. The startup also operates about 50 stores in Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai and Pune. It also also entered the UAE in February 2025, marking its international debut with its first store at BurJuman Mall in Dubai.
