The funding comes at a time when India’s luggage market is witnessing strong growth, driven by rising travel, premiumisation and a shift towards branded products. As per a report, the homegrown luggage industry is projected to become a ₹26,700 Cr opportunity by 2028.

Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019 as doctors seek new, effective treatments for younger patients with obesity, according to a study published on Friday.
The study, which included more than 3.5 million children aged between eight and 11 years with obesity but not diabetes, found that prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs rose from 0.03% in 2019 to 9.3% as of June.
Although the drugs are not approved for use in children under 12 years, clinical guidelines allow the medications to be used for obesity in children as young as eight years old in certain cases.
94% of the children prescribed GLP-1s had severe obesity, and about 65% had at least one related condition, such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and sleep apnea.
Overall, 20,282 children received GLP-1 drugs during the study period - most often, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy. Doctors also prescribed Novo's Saxenda and Eli Lilly's Zepbound.
While the absolute numbers of children under 12 receiving GLP-1 treatment is still low, the study shows that GLP-1 use is accelerating rapidly, said lead investigator and obesity medicine specialist Dr. Babak Orandi of NYU Langone Health.
Orandi added that long-term safety monitoring is needed to ensure the drugs remain safe and effective.
Children living in higher-income communities were 55% more likely to be prescribed the medicines, suggesting emerging disparities in access, according to the study published in the journal Pediatrics.
"Physicians and health policymakers alike have a responsibility to ensure ... these valuable and sometimes costly treatments become available to more than those who have access to health insurance and can afford to visit pediatric clinics," said Allan Massie, co-author of the study and associate professor of surgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.
Researchers used Epic Cosmos, a national electronic health records database encompassing more than 300 million U.S. patients. Epic had no role in the study.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

- Snopes previously investigated a variation of this claim in 2018 and 2026. We found then and now that Oliver said in a 2011 TV program that beef trimmings used for a product he called "pink slime" were "not fit for human consumption." We found no evidence that he specifically called McDonald's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic," as the posts suggested.

- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether Oliver has ever called the fast food chain's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic" or whether McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver and are waiting for responses.
A claim (archived) circulated on Facebook in August 2026 that fast food chain McDonald's lost a lawsuit against the TV chef Jamie Oliver after Oliver proved its food was "unfit for human consumption" because it was "highly toxic."
For example, one Facebook user wrote:
McDonald's loses lawsuit against chef Jamie Oliver, who proved that the food they sell is unfit for human consumption because it is highly toxic.
Chef Jamie Oliver won a lawsuit against the world's largest fast-food chain. Oliver demonstrates how hamburgers are made.
According to Oliver, fatty cuts of meat are "washed" with ammonium hydroxide and then used to fill the hamburger patties. Even before this process, the TV presenter says, this meat was unfit for human consumption.
Oliver, a radical activist chef taking on the food industry, says: "We are talking about meat that is sold as dog food and then served to humans. Aside from the quality of the meat, ammonium hydroxide is harmful to health." Oliver calls it "the pink slime process." What sane person would put a piece of meat soaked in ammonium hydroxide into a child's mouth?
Similar claims circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim, which we previously reported on in July 2026 and January 2018.
The claim contained three parts: that McDonald's sued Oliver, that Oliver made the comments about "pink slime" and that Oliver's alleged comments were specifically about McDonald's.
We found no evidence in online searches (archived, archived, archived) that McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver. AFP Fact Check reported in December 2021 that Oliver had never taken legal action against McDonald's.
According to an excerpt of a 2011 episode of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," Oliver said that the meat used to produce a specific type of beef product that the celebrity chef called "pink slime" was "not fit for human consumption."
McDonalds reportedly ceased using "pink slime," which is also known as Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, in their food in 2011, as we noted in 2018 when we fact-checked a previous version of this claim. Oliver did not mention McDonald's specifically in excerpts of the 2011 episode of "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" that Snopes reviewed.
However, because we could not access a full version of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question to see if it mentioned McDonald's, we leave this claim unrated.
Snopes contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver, whether Oliver had ever proved McDonald's food was "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic" and to ask whether McDonald's used Select Lean Beef Trimmings in 2026. We await replies to our queries.
Oliver's allegations
In the first episode of the second season of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," in which Oliver attempted to reform school lunches and fight obesity in the U.S., the celebrity chef held a demonstration where he showed children and adults where on a cow different cuts of meat came from.
According to a segment of the episode (archived) that an internet user uploaded to YouTube in 2016, after spray-painting prices on a live cow to show where various cuts were found, Oliver then addressed what happened to the remainder of the animal.
He said (time code 00:01), "The public loved seeing that, that, equalling a steak. They never for a minute thought I would clear all the meat and cuts away and introduce them to a new world of food. It's called pink slime."
Oliver added (time code 00:12), "When you've broken down a whole beast, you're left with trimmings. You know, in my industry, we call those trimmings [BLEEP]."
Speaking to a crowd of people, Oliver described the trimmings used for "pink slime" as (time code 00:36) "not fit for human consumption."
Oliver went on to say that processing plants took trimmings that were "not fit for human consumption," separated the meat from the fat, killed harmful bacteria using ammonium hydroxide and sold the end product, which he called "pink slime," as human-grade food. Ammonium hydroxide is a watery solution that can be used to regulate acidity in food or in hair dye or cosmetics.
In an excerpt from the program included in a 2012 CBS report, Oliver said (time code 00:32), "We're taking a product that would be sold at the cheapest form for dogs, and after this process we can give it to humans."
(Snopes could not locate a complete video of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question. The clips we have found online appeared genuine and did not indicate any signs of possible manipulation.)
FDA says ammonium hydroxide 'generally safe'
Around 11 months after Oliver's episode discussing "pink slime" aired, the American Meat Institute President J. Patrick Boyle issued a statement to say that Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings was "a safe, wholesome and nutritious form of beef" that helped prevent food waste by utilizing trimmings that would otherwise go to waste.
The institute is a trade association that represents processors of meat and poultry.
Boyle's statement said, similarly to Oliver's demonstration, that processing Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings involved first separating the meat from the fat and using "food grade ammonium hydroxide gas" to destroy bacteria before blending the product into foods like ground beef.
However, he denied claims that the trimmings used to create Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings were not edible. The statement said:
Some recent media reports created a troubling and inaccurate picture, particularly in their use of the colloquial term 'pink slime.' The fact is, BLBT is beef. The beef trimmings that are used to make BLBT are absolutely edible. In fact, no process can somehow make an inedible meat edible; it's impossible. In reality, the BLBT production process simply removes fat and makes the remaining beef more lean and suited to a variety of beef products that satisfy consumers' desire for leaner foods.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which regulates ammonium hydroxide use in food, says the ingredient is "generally recognized as safe." This was also the case when we last reported on these claims in 2018.
In sum ...
While Oliver did call the cuts of meat used for Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings "not fit for human consumption" and claimed (time code 00:59) the product was "admitted to being in at least 70% of ground beef products" in a 2011 program, the episode excerpts Snopes reviewed did not show him specifically accusing McDonald's of using the product or calling the fast food chain's products toxic.
McDonald's said in a 2013 statement it had not used Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings in its products since 2011.
We found no evidence that McDonald's had lost a lawsuit involving Oliver since then. Given the prominence of McDonald's and Oliver, such a lawsuit would have been widely reported by reputable sources. That was not the case.
While the FDA generally recognizes ammonium hydroxide, which is used to process Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, as safe, reporting by the publication Food Safety News claimed that fast food giants like McDonalds, Taco Bell and Burger King had all stopped using the product by January 2012.
Both ABC, which broadcast Oliver's program, and Oliver himself have faced lawsuits over their coverage of the product.
ABC settled out of court in 2017 in a $1.9 billion defamation lawsuit brought by Beef Products Inc., a producer of Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, over Oliver's program and other stories the network had reported about the product in March and April 2012.
A man who Beef Products Inc. laid off after negative press heavily affected the company's sales sued Oliver, ABC and other defendants in 2012. He dropped the case in 2013.

Peace talks rich in symbolism but fundamental differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
- Published
The talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion.
The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago.
The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday.
You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making.
Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell.
And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe.
But fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield.
The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded.
Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army.
After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult".
Witkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there.
But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that.
So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead.
Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic.
Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long.

Lewis Hamilton called for written rules of engagement with Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc after the duo’s crash at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza on Sunday.
The seven-time champion tangled with his partner at Turn 2 and put a wheel into the gravel, which resulted in him losing places and dropping to tenth at the end of the first lap.
Leclerc, whose race came to an early end after a crash into the barriers, admitted that the pair had races too hard in the opening corners.
Hamilton managed to claw back places but could not keep up with the pace of the Mercedes-powered cars, ending up sixth at the chequered flag. He now trails race winner Kimi Antonelli by 76 points.
“We’re just not executing as well as we can. Not as well as the other teams are. But we were at other points in the season,” Hamilton told reporters.
“I think it comes down to rules of engagement. When I was at Mercedes we had written rules of engagement. And we never really had it too bad.
“There was a moment, maybe with me and Nico (Rosberg), a couple of times. But more often than not, it was good. Here, there are no rules. And I think that’s something that needs to probably change.”
Hamilton said he felt “massively gutted” for fans of the Scuderia who had turned up in record numbers.
“I think today we just lost so much ground to them (Mercedes) on points, and it’s far too late for those decisions to come,” said Hamilton.

From match point to US Open exit - lucky loser denied history
- Published
France's Arthur Gea was one point away from being the first lucky loser to reach a Grand Slam quarter-final - but three hours later he was out of the US Open.
Gea, 22, was unable to convert a match point in a third-set tie-break against Dutch opponent Botic van de Zandschulp, then could not serve out victory in the fourth set of a gruelling fourth-round contest.
Van de Zandschulp took full advantage to escape from the jaws of defeat, going on to secure a 3-6 6-7 (0-7) 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (7-3) 6-4 win after five hours and 13 minutes - the fourth longest match on record at Flushing Meadows.
World number 87 Gea was not ranked high enough for the main draw when the US Open entry list was finalised, meaning he had to go through qualifying instead.
Seeded first, he lost to American Nishesh Basavareddy in the third and final round but earned a reprieve when 2022 finalist Casper Ruud withdrew injured on the eve of the tournament.
Gea took full advantage by beating Argentina's Juan Manuel Cerundolo, Zachary Svajda of the United States and another American Michael Zheng to reach the last 16.
But he could not find a way past 70th-ranked Van de Zandschulp, who said he had "no clue" how he completed a "crazy comeback".
After becoming the 13th lucky loser to be eliminated in the fourth round of a Slam, Gea will receive $480,000 in prize money - a considerable increase on the $66,000 which he thought he was taking home from qualifying.

Zverev unsure 'what to do' after finishing before midnight
Van de Zandschulp's reward for reaching the second US Open quarter-final of his career is a meeting with German top seed Alexander Zverev.
Zverev, 29, had a rare finish before midnight in New York when he beat Italian 21st seed Luciano Darderi 6-2 6-2 7-6 (7-3) to reach the last eight.
Zverev's previous three matches finished at 1:55am, 2:15am and 1:09am.
"I don't know what to do with myself because it's before midnight - I might go back to the practice courts or go to a bar," Zverev joked.
On whether he wants to play Van de Zandschulp in Wednesday's night session, the French Open champion added: "I will request the night match for sure.
"I've rented this court out from 11pm until 2am for two weeks so I hope they will continue putting me on at [night] time."
Earlier on Monday, Belgium's Alexander Blockx said he was "really close" to retiring injured against Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo before playing on to reach his first major quarter-final.
Blockx, seeded 28th, fought through rib pain to win 6-3 4-6 7-5 7-5, becoming the first Belgian man to make the last eight in New York.
"It was really tough from the beginning of the match. I was struggling a lot, especially while serving. It kept getting worse throughout the match," said 21-year-old Blockx.
"I was really close to retiring, to be honest. I was just hanging in there, but if I would have lost the third set, I think the chances were really high of me retiring.
"I'm glad that I kept on playing."
Presuming he is fit enough, Blockx will play Russian world number 50 Karen Khachanov in the quarter-finals on Wednesday.
Khachanov, 30, fought back to win 7-5 4-6 6-7 (6-8) 6-1 6-4 against 14th seed Learner Tien, ending the American's attempt to put four home men in the quarter-finals for the first time since 1995.

Among a flurry of posts this weekend, Donald Trump revealed the service dress uniform designs for his Space Force.
Without additional comment, the president shared photos and an overview of the uniforms on Truth Social, which include in their color palette “space gray” and “midnight black” as well as knee high leather boots and snazzy epaulettes. The overview indicated the ensemble was “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper uniform.”
The admission is a bit of a shocker, not just because Trump loves winners and the critically-panned 1997 Paul Verhoeven film was a flop, but also because it was a satire of fascism. In his review at the time, Roger Ebert noted the picture’s “quasi-fascist militarism,” while admitting that those aspects were leavened a bit by “an element of sly satire.” But, for Ebert, that was not enough. “We smile at the satirical asides, but where’s the warmth of human nature? The spark of genius or rebellion? If Star Wars is humanist, Starship Troopers is totalitarian.”
As for the costumes themselves, Ebert was only slightly less critical. He calls them “a cross between Buck Rogers and the Archie comic books.”
Watch on Deadline
Trump has seemingly drawn inspiration from movies and television before for his newest branch of the United States Armed Forces, which he created in 2019. When the president unveiled the logo, science fiction fans almost immediately called out the similarity to that worn by Captain Kirk and other Starfleet officers in Gene Roddenberry’s enduring, space faring sci-fi franchise. Star Trek legend George Takei even weighed in, telling Trump to give the source material its due.
In 2020, then-Vice President Mike Pence celebrated the one year anniversary of Trump’s new branch by announcing that — as those serving in the Navy are known as sailors and those in the army are known as soldiers — “henceforth, the members of the United States Space Force will be known as ‘guardians.’”
The announcement drew a quick reaction from Guardians of the Galaxy fans, who thought there might be an unacknowledged connection between the film series and the new name.

A rumor circulated in early September 2026 that incarcerated people in the state of Oklahoma were contracted to work for a call center company that handled telemarketing for a conservative super PAC.
Users on social media shared the rumor, with some claiming the Oklahoma Department of Corrections earned $10 per hour from the vendor but that prison laborers were getting paid only $2 per hour.
The rumors circulated as the United States approached the Labor Day holiday, which has celebrated the labor movement since the late 1800s.
The claim was true, according to a service contract between the state prison department and telemarketing company HBW Leads, embedded below.
The document originated in reporting by Oklahoma Watch, a nonprofit investigative journalism outlet, which published the article on Aug. 24, 2026.
One current inmate, Steve Wilbanks, was named as a source. Snopes confirmed Wilbanks was a prisoner at the James Crabtree Correctional Center in Helena and has been in state custody since 2015. Oklahoma Watch cited three other inmates used as sources anonymously.
According to the report, inmates earned $2 per hour at call centers located at four state prisons: James Crabtree, Mabel Bassett in McLoud and Lexington Correctional and Joseph Harp, both in Lexington.
According to the service contract, tasks inmates could perform were:
1. outbound calls related to marketing lead generation; and
2. conducting or assisting with political opinion polling, subject to applicable laws and regulations.
The contract further says Oklahoma Correctional Industries, a division of the Oklahoma Department of Corrections whose website says it "employs offenders who lack marketable job skills," would earn $10 per hour of work per inmate. However, the contract states the corrections department can "withhold up to but not to exceed 80 percent of the wage rate per inmate hour worked," which matches the rates reported.
The Oklahoma Watch piece stated:
BW Leads agreed to pay the Department of Corrections $10 per inmate hour worked. Prisoners employed at the call centers earn $2 per hour, plus possible bonuses for generating leads or completing surveys.
The remaining $8 per hour is allocated as overhead for Oklahoma Correctional Industries, a self-supporting sub-entity of the Department of Corrections that provides work programs and job training to inmates.
We reached out to the Oklahoma Department of Corrections for further comment on the report. We also asked for the specific reasoning behind inmate pay structure and why telemarketing doesn't appear on the list of services provided by Oklahoma Correctional Industries. We'll update this article if we hear back.
HBW Leads' website identified the Oregon-based company as generating "insurance leads" gained through telemarketing on behalf of the clients who hire them. The website said, "Our lead specialists spend, on average, 4-7 minutes with each potential prospect asking them a series of qualifying questions on your behalf."
HBW Leads made no mention of political calling on its website, but a subsidiary company operating out of Toledo, Ohio, Visible Trends, specializes in "polling, fundraising, legislative outreach, or GOTV," referring to get-out-the-vote efforts.
A business search on the Ohio Secretary of State's website confirmed Visible Trends to be registered by HBW Leads in January 2025.
(Ohio Secretary of State)
One of Oklahoma Watch's sources said some of the statements they read during their telemarketing jobs specified that the calls were paid for by conservative super PAC Make Liberty Win, whose website described them as specializing "in mobilizing voters to engage in primary and general elections through direct voter contact."
An FEC filing (archived) showed at least 38 payments totaling more than $400,000 from Make Liberty Win to Visible Trends between from March 2026 and June 2026, the same term length shown in the service contract between HBW Leads and the corrections department.
Though it was clear the Oklahoma Department of Corrections and HBW Leads had established a contract to use inmates as telemarketers, Snopes couldn't independently verify whether the inmates made political calls on behalf of Make Liberty Win specifically.
Oklahoma Watch's reported one of its sources said they made political calls that resembled push-polling, in which the caller purports to be asking survey questions but actually aims to influence voters, a practice generally frowned upon in campaigning.
We reached out to Make Liberty Win to ask whether it was aware of Visible Trends using prison laborers and will update this article if we hear back.
Oklahoma Watch reported that the super PAC's executive director, Barrett Young, told the outlet that the group was unaware of the use of prison labor and has since canceled the contract for performance reasons.

The Meaning of the Lindsay Clancy Mistrial
Everyone has a theory. But what if this case means nothing at all?
During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word. She has been on display for the entirety of her livestreamed trial, sitting in her wheelchair beside her lawyer at the defense table. At one point, when the prosecution walked the jury through the children’s autopsy reports, she hunched over, racked with sobs, crying out, “I can’t do this!” But mostly, Clancy has remained silent and wide-eyed, her gaze wandering around the courtroom as though searching for something.
The judge in the case has just declared a mistrial because the jury has been unable to reach a unanimous verdict. But the viewing public, in the absence of Clancy’s own explanation of her experiences leading up to and after the killings, has projected its own ideas onto the case and rendered its own verdict. Some people have interpreted Clancy’s trial as a referendum on women’s postpartum mental health. Others have developed elaborate conspiracy theories maintaining that Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick, is actually the guilty party. Still others have construed Clancy’s story as evidence for their own niche political beliefs.
These are all comforting narratives, in some sense, because they imply an underlying logic that imbues the events with meaning and provides a road map for catharsis. Yet the jury’s inability to arrive at a verdict makes plain that a careful evaluation of the facts does not yield an easily intelligible conclusion. The reality may be darker and more despairing: that something so dramatic and destructive could, in the end, mean nothing at all.
As Clancy’s trial has progressed, dozens of women wearing pink have appeared at organized rallies outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, holding signs signaling a kind of support for her. “Any one of us who have dealt with mental health, anxiety, depression, postpartum—I think we just know that any one of us could be sitting in her chair,” the organizer of a recent event billed as an opportunity to “stand in peace for Lindsay” told a local news outlet.
There is something inherently unsettling about any public expression of support for a confessed killer, but these gatherings and their associated social-media movements have not seemed aimed at improving Clancy’s odds of success in court. Instead, these demonstrations suggest that Clancy has for some women become a symbolic figure: the devoted but suffering mother martyred by the relentless, punishing demands of her children’s early years and left to suffer by a flawed and fractured health-care system. Many women have felt overwhelmed to the point of drowning in the months after giving birth, and many have sought help but failed to receive it. Clancy’s case, in her supporters’ imagination, appears to be the sum of all those biological and social hazards. What happened to Clancy, in this view, was predictable, and thus preventable.
That’s a tidy narrative about what took place in Duxbury that night in 2023, when Clancy strangled her three young children to death, then attempted to end her own life by swallowing prescription drugs, slashing her neck and wrists, and then jumping out of a window. A possible upshot of this view is that it may raise awareness about the inadequacy of treatment options for postpartum mental illnesses—to the degree that raising awareness about any given issue ever meaningfully changes anything. And some elements of it seem inarguably true, such as the idea that Clancy’s psychiatric care was woefully uncoordinated. But this theory also has the odd effect of making Clancy the star of her own murder trial, for whom the viewer at home may be encouraged to root, which risks eliding the gravity of what she did.
Simultaneously believing that someone is relatable and vulnerable and that they are nevertheless guilty of and accountable for heinous crimes is, however, cognitively tricky. I suspect that that tension is the origin of a similarly enormous groundswell of conspiracy theorizing about Clancy’s case that has pervaded social media. Although those theories vary, they generally maintain that Clancy is factually innocent of the killings and that her ex-husband is instead guilty of murdering the children, attempting to murder Clancy, and framing his ex-wife for the deaths. Proponents typically cite as proof any number of purported facts presented at trial, such as that Clancy’s fingerprints weren’t found on the exercise bands used to strangle the children, or that her core body temperature upon her arrival to the hospital called the prosecution’s timeline of events into question. Clancy is, in these tellings, a victim of spousal abuse akin to torture, whose partner cruelly exploited her postpartum suffering in order to dispose of his family.
That, too, is a tidy story with symbolic significance: For those who deny her guilt, Clancy’s life and fate become a nightmare of female subjugation. This view morphs a reasonable claim that Patrick ought to have been more attentive to Clancy’s deteriorating mental state into a much stronger insistence that he is in fact fully culpable for what happened, having carefully plotted the entire sequence of events. Clancy’s story, then, becomes a parable about male violence against women.
Yet this embrace of Clancy as the true victim of her crimes has triggered an online backlash on the political right that maintains that liberal-female support for Clancy is a naked expression of latent female tendencies toward violence against children and an indication that liberal women are unstable and dangerous. (This despite the fact that women actually have varying views on the case, and that men kill the majority of children murdered in the United States.) That thinking also mistakenly takes Clancy to be a representative Everywoman, this time standing in for the threatening volatility of liberal women writ large.
All of these views of Clancy’s case strive to make sense of her alleged crimes: This trial must mean that mothers in America are crucially underserved, or that men in America are chauvinistically exploitative, or that women in America are secretly a danger to themselves and others. Some of those readings are more compelling than others, but they all seem to overemphasize what is generalizable about the case while understating what is unique, particular, and hyper-specific about what happened. The broader the statements about this case are, the less they have to do with the events as they really occurred.
Clancy’s experience was inarguably extreme. If, as the defense claims, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, it was an ultra-rare expression of an already uncommon condition. Her psychiatric care was, per a subsequent malpractice lawsuit, allegedly mismanaged, and the severity of her purported adverse reactions to widely used medications was highly unusual. She was undoubtedly suffering in the months leading up to the murders, and it’s possible that the right degree of support could have prevented what happened, but it’s likewise true that nobody could have reasonably predicted what happened. More than any general theme or idea, Clancy’s crimes seem to have hinged on a moment of catastrophic dysfunction. Life, in the end, defies a great deal of neat storytelling.
For the past several weeks, Clancy’s case has been heard in the court of public opinion. At this point, people seem desperate for answers about why these deaths happened and what they mean, or at least a guarantee that something we’ve learned from this case will prevent similar tragedies from happening in the future. Many such onlookers have hoped that the trial verdict will supply such insights. This hope now appears to have been in vain.
Prosecutors in Clancy’s case must now decide whether to retry her, negotiate a plea deal, or drop the charges altogether. No matter what they choose, this case will continue to frustrate those trying to make sense of it.
Clancy herself, with her haunted, bewildered gaze, seems to already understand what her well-meaning supporters and their opponents can’t yet come to terms with: There is no making sense of what happened, and no greater wisdom to learn from it. At the core of all of this is a void, and nothing emanates from it but the assurance of everlasting pain.

Rajouri, Sept 7: A startling incident has come to fore in Rajouri where a newborn baby allegedly died during delivery while the mother is battling for life and has been put on ventilator support at Government Medical College (GMC) Rajouri.
The woman, whose identity has been withheld, is a resident of Mammankote in Chassana tehsil of Mahore sub-division of Reasi district. She had been brought to GMC Rajouri for delivery.
According to the woman’s family, she was allegedly taken from the hospital to a private room outside the hospital premises by a female nursing staffer, an ASHA worker and another woman on the pretext of facilitating a normal delivery.
"We were waiting for delivery of baby when the nursing staff and others approached and lured us." they said.
The family alleged that complications developed during the delivery in the private room, following which the newborn died, while the woman’s condition deteriorated due to excessive bleeding and she was subsequently shifted for critical care at GMC Rajouri.
Speaking about the incident, the woman’s husband alleged that the nursing staffer, ASHA worker and another woman had persuaded them to shift to the private room for delivery.
He alleged that complications arose during the process, resulting in the death of the baby, while his wife is now battling for her life.
The husband has demanded strict punishment against those found responsible for the incident.
Meanwhile, Rajouri Police, in an official statement, said it had taken cognisance of a written complaint received at Police Station Rajouri regarding the circumstances surrounding the stillbirth of the newborn.
Police said the involvement of two individuals, including a woman employee of GMC Rajouri, had surfaced in the case.
A case, FIR No. 465/2026, under Sections 106(1)/3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), has been registered at Police Station Rajouri, and investigation is underway.
The police investigation is expected to establish the circumstances leading to the newborn’s death and determine the role, if any, of the persons named in the complaint.
Meanwhile, the Government Medical College and Associated Hospital Rajouri has constituted a four-member inquiry committee to conduct a detailed probe into the death of a newborn baby of a woman from Chassana, Reasi, amid allegations regarding the involvement of hospital staffers in the incident.
The order, issued by Principal GMC Rajouri Prof. (Dr.) A.S. Bhatia on September 7, stated that the inquiry committee was constituted in view of a viral video circulating on social media regarding the death of the newborn of Sushma Devi, wife of Ragveer, resident of Chasana, Reasi, and allegations regarding the involvement of staffers from GMC & AH Rajouri.
The committee has been tasked with enquiring into the matter in depth and recommending further action. It has been directed to submit its report to the Principal’s office within three days.
The committee comprises Dr. Shamim Ahmed, Medical Superintendent, as Chairman; Dr. Chander Sheikhar, HoD Obstetrics and Gynaecology, as Member; Dr. Vidushi Badyal, HoD ENT, as Member; and Hanan Shawl (JKAS), Administrative Officer, as Member Secretary.
The development comes amid allegations by the family of the woman that she was taken to a private room outside the hospital for delivery, following which complications allegedly developed, resulting in the death of the newborn while the mother’s condition remained critical.
Meanwhile, Rajouri Police has already taken cognisance of a written complaint regarding the circumstances surrounding the newborn’s stillbirth and registered FIR No. 465/2026 under Sections 106(1)/3(5) of the BNS at Police Station Rajouri. The police investigation is underway.
The hospital-level inquiry is expected to ascertain the circumstances surrounding the incident and examine the alleged involvement of hospital staffers before recommending further action.

Germany’s far-right AfD hails unprecedented election win: 3 scenarios for what happens next
The pro-Russian AfD could become the first far-right party to take control of a regional parliament in Germany since the Second World War. Their victory creates a large political headache for the country’s leaders, report Chris Stevenson and James C Reynolds
The results from Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt regional election are likely to be a major political headache for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) have governed the eastern state for more than 20 years.
Sunday evening’s exit poll showing the far-right, pro-Russian, Alternative for Germany (AfD) potentially gaining 44.5 per cent of the vote is beyond the 40 per cent recent opinion polls had been showing and well in excess of the 20.8 per cent the party secured in 2021. Mr Merz’s CDU fell to 18.5 per cent in the exit poll from 37.1 per cent in 2021. The CDU currently leads a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the free-market Free Democrats (FDP).
About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents. Participation was at a record high of 76.5 per cent.
AfD had been looking to secure an absolute majority of above 50 per cent, to ensure they could try and implement their own radical agenda.
So what happens now?
1. AfD seizes power
If AfD were to take control of the regional parliament, they would be the first far-right party to have power in either a regional or the national parliament since the Second World War. If this were to happen, what is known in Germany as the “firewall” – where parties create coalitions to keep far-right parties from power – would be breached for the first time.
AfD has been clear about what it would do if it were to take power. It seeks to restrict immigration, quit the Euro and restore ties with Russia as most of Europe rallies around Ukraine.
Based on the party’s “Vision 2026” election manifesto, victory in Saxony-Anhalt could invite sweeping reforms around state policy on migration, education, culture and the family.
Under Germany’s federal system, state governments sit in the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, and also have wide powers in education, domestic security and culture.
An AfD-led state would launch a crackdown on migration, with a task force set up to coordinate quicker deportations.
The children of refugees would be placed in separate classes at school to prevent what the party claims are “stresses” on the other children from being around different cultures.
Meanwhile, children with disabilities would no longer be taught in the same classroom as those without, instead being sent to new schools.
Schools would also be banned from flying rainbow flags, and the government would exhaust “all legal avenues” to limit Islamic expression.
The party has claimed greater acceptance of what it offensively labels as “sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles” has contributed to sinking birth rates and promises to aggressively promote “traditional” family structures consisting of a mother, father and children. An AfD government would see major changes to the school curriculum around a “patriotic cultural policy”, extended to raising the German national flag daily and singing the national anthem at school celebrations.
It would also advocate for removing war refugee status for Ukrainians in Germany as long as the conflict remains concentrated in eastern Ukraine, arguing they should seek refuge in western Ukraine.
The current structure of the public broadcasting system would be dismantled and funding withdrawn for some cultural institutions.
In terms of domestic security in Saxony, AfD in the state is assessed by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency as a “far-right extremist” group, which would create concerns about the intelligence AfD would be able to see if it was in charge of the regional parliament.
However, AfD will likely need the support of another party, depending on how many smaller parties pass the five per cent threshold needed to get seats. In Saxony-Anhalt, all the parties except the small far-left BSW party have ruled out joining a coalition with AfD.
If some smaller parties do not pass the threshold though, it would make AfD’s job easier, as it would make the chance of a coalition against it less likely.
The party will talk to any sensible party with whom it can find common ground on policy positions, said AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel after the exit poll
2. The CDU pulls together a coalition
The CDU has been hit hard, but may yet be able to pull together a “firewall coalition”. That is what happened in the state of Thuringia in 2024, where AfD gained more than 30 per cent of the vote, but not enough for an absolute majority.
However, American think tank the Brookings Institution believes this will be difficult. “The task of organising a CDU-led governing majority faces almost insurmountable difficulties,” it said in a recent briefing note, exacerbated by the CDU’s ruling out of any coalition with the staunchly socialist party Die Linke (The Left). With exit polls predicting a 9.4 per cent share of the vote for The Left behind the CDU’s 18.4 per cent, the party leadership has indicated it would be open to an arrangement formalising support for a CDU-led government over AfD. But the CDU faces internal divisions over a possible alliance with a party on what it regards as the far left.
Mr Merz said ahead of the election last Sunday that they would “assess the situation in light of the election results” and “do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt from falling into the hands of the radicals”.
State premier Sven Schulze congratulated AfD in the wake of the exit poll and acknowledged the result showed it was the strongest party. If AfD is unable to rule outright, it could trigger a protracted process of coalition building by mainstream parties who are determined to keep a party under investigation for right-wing extremism by Germany’s domestic intelligence service.
3. The German government takes a hit regardless
However the political wrangling in the wake of the Saxony result ends up, it is clear that the manner of AfD’s win is important for their national standing and a blow to Mr Merz’s coalition government.
Nationwide, AfD has swollen to become the most popular party, polling at 29 per cent, while Mr Merz has become the most unpopular chancellor since the founding of the Federal Republic, with 85 per cent of voters dissatisfied.
Lars Klingbeil, co-leader of Germany’s centre-left SPD party and vice chancellor in Mr Merz’s governing coalition, said after the exit poll that the result of the Saxony-Anhalt state election is a signal for Berlin politics. The result is a reason to reflect on the federal government’s policies, Mr Klingbeil told public broadcaster ZDF. “And rest assured, that is what we will do.”
Mr Merz has already sought to create a harder line on immigration, in a move designed to try and stem the rise of AfD. There will no doubt be a greater push from AfD to try and move the needle on national policy, while their pro-Russia stance could be an issue when it comes to European support for Ukraine, given the nation has previously been accused of moving cautiously when it comes to handing Ukraine weapons to fight off Russia's invasion.
Mr Merz will face an increasing level of political pressure about his own job and government, something AfD will be all too happy to try and press home in both future regional elections and the wider national polls.

Six years ago Sony and Bose were in the middle of a noise-canceling battle, with each new model of headphones better than the last. In the fall of 2020, Sony released the WH-1000XM4 headphones to wide acclaim. They sat atop best headphones lists for years, thanks to their great sound, competitive ANC, and compact size, until they went out of stock. Now Sony has brought them back, with minor improvements, as the WH-1000XM4C.
Six years later, Sony revisits its legendary XM4 headphones
After the WH-1000XM4 were discontinued in 2025, Sony is bringing them back as the WH-1000XM4C.
The XM4C look identical to the original XM4 (although they now have a lavender option), with the same hinge design and ability to fold up. It’s a compact design that Sony moved away from when it released the XM5 in 2022, and then returned to (although not quite as compact) with the XM6. But it’s not just the look that’s returned. The XM4C still use the same QN1 processing chip and four microphones for ANC. That design is showing its age: The XM5 still used the QN1, but had eight mics. Last year’s XM6 have 12, plus the new QN3 chip.
Sony did update the XM4C’s sound profile to bring it in line with current models, and the headphones have a 10-band EQ in the Headphones app, instead of the 5-band on the XM4, plus a gaming preset. The XM4C also support Bluetooth 6 instead of 5. Surprisingly, the battery performance on the new headphones is slightly worse. Sony claims the XM4C get up to 27 hours of use with ANC on as opposed to 30 hours previously. Not a huge difference, and still more than enough for a cross-country trip.
The XM4C will be available later this fall for $300, which is $50 cheaper than the XM4 when they first came out (and $100 cheaper than the XM6 are now), but more than they could be found for before being discontinued.
I have loved the Sony XM4 since they came out, and still have my pair hanging on the side of my desk. Beyond nostalgia, though, I’m confused why they’re coming back. A review sample of the XM4C arrived at my door while I was writing this, so some deeper investigation will be coming soon. But the headphones industry has moved forward in the past six years, and I’m not sure there’s a need to go back. And the XM5, while they don’t fold up as nicely as the XM4C, are excellent headphones and currently available for $200 (though that price may be an effort to clear out inventory ahead of the XM4C).
Alongside the XM4C, Sony released the next generation of two of its less-expensive midrange and entry-level headphone lines: the WH-CH730N and WH-CH530. They both get the same 10-band EQ upgrade and gaming EQ preset as the XM4C, and the CH730N will now fold up into a more compact form.
The two headphones also get a boost to battery life according to Sony: The CH730N get up to 50 hours with ANC, and the CH530 get up to 55 hours (there’s no ANC on the CH530). A new safe mode in the app allows a user to limit the max volume output of the headphones. It’s a nice addition for parents looking to protect their kids’ hearing, although there’s no way to lock the limit once it’s been set.
The WH-CH530 come in black, cobalt, mint green, white, pink, and coral and cost $70. For $180, you can get the WH-CN730N in black, blue, oat, white, or pink. Both headphones are available now.
Sony is also doing a partnership with Hello Kitty. Bundles include headphones — the WH-1000XM6, WH-CH730N, or WH-CH530 available in black or pink — a Hello Kitty-shaped carrying pouch, and Hello Kitty-branded bag. The bundles will be available in limited supply later this year on the Sony website only.

The Last Thing Teenagers Will Let You Teach Them
An interesting shift happens when a kid is learning to drive, and you’re both inside a box with your fear, moving 40 miles an hour.
A strange thing happened to me in a deserted parking lot on a recent Sunday morning: My 16-year-old daughter actually asked me a question.
I was telling her everything I know about reversing a car without the help of a backup camera. “First turn your whole body, shoulders rotated, right hand on the back of the passenger seat, until you’re looking out the rear window at the world behind you.” Her hands were on the wheel. Her phone was face down in the cup holder. She turned her body the way I’d suggested and nudged the wheel to the left, and the car floated backward in a woozy arc that wasn’t quite what she’d intended. “Wait,” she said. “Do I turn with both hands? Did I do that wrong?”
I want to stop here, because I don’t think I can convey just how unusual such an exchange is these days—her listening to me and asking for help. Sometime in the past year, she stopped wanting anything from me other than my credit card and maybe my nicest suede boots. She definitely stopped wanting my instruction, my opinion, my take on anything, having concluded that she already understands pretty much everything.
The talking is what I have missed. For 14 or 15 years, my daughter narrated in a fire hose of chatter—to me, to her father, to whoever. So much talking: about why the sun sets, the kid she was mad at, the plot of a show she was three episodes into, how she wanted to decorate her room. Around the start of high school, the talking thinned out, siphoned almost exclusively to her friends. Nothing announced the change. It went the way a baby tooth goes, loose for a while and then simply absent.
When she got a learner’s permit, some measure of talking reappeared. It wasn’t fully restored, exactly, but confined within one small, sealed space that moves. Inside the car, she knows she doesn’t know: In no version of parallel parking can she wing it without asking for tips from someone who has done it 10,000 times. Learning to drive is something she cannot fake her way through.
This wobbly uncertainty, this return to a kind of innocence, is the rarest condition in a 16-year-old, and it lasts about as long as a learner’s permit does. So my daughter asks, and listens, and we manage to simply talk in some of the ways we haven’t in a long time: about what her friends did over the summer, which kid at the pool where she lifeguards asked her if she could babysit them. For an hour at a stretch I get a version of my daughter that I had filed away as gone for good.
But this is also, in some ways, the worst hour of my week, because the terms of a driving lesson are the exact inverse of the many other kinds of lessons that came before it. Everything else I ever taught my daughter, I did with one hand on the thing: I steadied the tail end of the bike, I held the knife and moved her fingers back from the blade, I grasped her hand crossing Seventh Avenue for so many years that my palm still expects to find hers at intersections. In the car, though, she has the wheel, and I have the fear. My only instrument is my voice, which is not connected to anything that stops the car.
Parents say they’re letting go or loosening the reins or handing over the keys, as if adolescence were a series of small, deliberate releases, each one manageable. Then you hand over the actual keys, and the metaphor becomes a physical arrangement staged on a public road at 40 miles an hour, at which point it breaks. First there is supervised driving, and soon there is nothing. In between, the passenger seat is one of the few places on Earth where a parent gets to occupy two conditions at once: maximum proximity plus zero control.
I have thought about this a lot from that seat, just 18 inches from my daughter, slowly understanding that being nearby was never the same as keeping her safe. Ever since she was born, I had assumed that being close to her was a form of protecting her. I could catch her if she slipped. In the car, that assumption comes apart, and all I can do is sit there with my fear.
What surprised me is that the fear runs both ways.
For the first time in years, my daughter is frightened of something in front of both of us rather than scared of something I might do to embarrass her—that is, afraid of me. That distinction turns out to be enormous. Since she hit adolescence, her anxiety, in my presence, has generally been about whether I would say something wacky (yes!), make a dumb joke (also yes!), or exist too loudly in a space containing her peers (duh). I have been the weather she is bracing against. But in the car, we are braced against the same thing, and it is outside the windshield. A massive truck backs out without looking; a cyclist suddenly appears. We both suck in air at the same instant, and her hand and my hand tighten—hers on the wheel, mine on nothing.
Coming to a stop at a red light, she sees me sending a text from the passenger seat. “I can’t understand how anyone texts and drives,” she says, almost bewildered, the way a fifth grader might talk about someone doing calculus in their head. At that moment, she is using every part of her brain to keep a two-ton object between two painted lines, and the idea that a person could do this and tap out a message strikes her as physically impossible. I agree with her, but what I don’t say is that practicing will help her rethink this. Competence makes the risk available. One day she will be good enough at driving to consider being more careless about it.
As she improves and gains confidence, the driving, for her, slowly grows less frightening and more thrilling. She presses the accelerator, her foot more sure, and we both know that she is on the edge of a huge new expanse of freedom and change—that driving lessons are not about a test to pass but a way to get farther than she has ever gotten on her own. The shared fear is temporary, and I can already feel the expiration date on it.
Some Sunday soon, we’ll have our last lesson. And what I’ll miss isn’t the driving; it’s the asking—the tacit admission that she doesn’t know everything—and how she lets her guard down while she’s admitting it. When the questions end, she’ll be very much on her way, and I’ll be the boots and the credit card again, which, I remind myself, is part of the assignment too.

Tamil Nadu recorded nearly 45,000 fewer births in 2025 than the previous year, with the number of births falling by 5.3% from 8.47 lakh in 2024 to 8.02 lakh, pointing to a continuing decline in births in the State.
The decline comes against the backdrop of a long-term fall in fertility in the State. In 2026, five lakh-odd births were recorded so far, according to Civil Registration System data.”
While the decline in births reflects a broader demographic transition, with implications for the workforce and ageing population, experts say greater attention must be paid to education, childcare, social security, elderly care and standard of living.
T. Sundararaman, former executive director, National Health Systems Resource Centre, said the total fertility rate among women of reproductive age fell below the replacement level of 2.1 in Tamil Nadu nearly 20 years ago. “We continued to have a positive population growth rate because of population momentum. We have now moved beyond this phenomenon and a decline in the population is likely to occur,” he said.
S. Irudaya Rajan, chairperson, International Institute for Migration and Development, Thiruvananthapuram, pointed out that Tamil Nadu is better placed compared with Kerala, which has recorded around three lakh births.
“There will be no short-term impact. The State government can focus on creating a productive, healthy population of eight lakh-plus by investing in quality education over the next 20 to 25 years. The focus should be on quality rather than quantity,” he said.
“First of all, there is no need to worry about the low fertility rate or the decline in births,” Padmavathi Srinivasan, independent research consultant in demography, said, adding: “This opens up opportunities to increase and improve the standard of living and enable people to better access the State’s resources. The State government should seize this opportunity and capitalise on low fertility.”
Observing that politicians would worry about what would happen to the State’s labour force, she said, “but this is the time to focus on education and employment opportunities. Tamil Nadu is a prosperous State, but this prosperity needs to translate to better living standards.”
“It would be an injustice if the State focussed on increasing fertility and channelled government funds towards it. Rather, it should focus on the existing population, especially the youth. The State should pay attention to the foundations, such as quality education and the nutritional status of children. There are still pockets of people living in poverty, those who have no access to opportunities and have not benefitted from the State’s economic growth.”
Financial incentives to reverse low fertility rates have never worked, as evidenced in many developed countries, she said, asking: “So, why go down that route, when there are much more pressing issues we need to tackle.”
Professor Rajan said the State government’s “Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam”, under which one-gram gold rings will be gifted to babies born in government hospitals, is unlikely to help increase births. Increasing maternity leave to women government employees for a third child cannot be considered a meaningful incentive, he believed.
Policies alone will not help much. At best, they may add another 5,000-odd births, he said. “Children are assets, but when you ask couples today, many consider them liabilities. This mindset should change. Increasing the fertility rate is not simple, given factors such as delayed marriages. To motivate young couples to have children, we need out-of-the-box, innovative ideas.”
Priority areas
Professor Sundararaman said increasing longevity means that there will be more people aged 65 or 70 and above. “At the same time, we will have less working age population and a larger elderly population that needs to be cared for. This has already happened in most developed countries that have stronger social security systems and better elderly care,” he said.
“I am less worried about productivity and more concerned about social security and elderly care. We need policies that anticipate these changes,” he added.
Efforts simply to increase childbearing are unlikely to work. What can make a difference is providing child care support for the first two children, he said. “We need to have innovative thinking and creative community-based efforts for elderly care. Our priorities should include elderly care, social security, child care support, good quality primary education and measures that make it easier for working women for childcare. Funds should be better utilised to establish facilities, such as creches for working women,” he added.
