Rescuers search for people trapped in a New Delhi building collapse as death toll rises to 6
Search and rescue teams are combing through the debris of a collapsed building in New Delhi as the death toll has climbed to six
NEW DELHI -- Search and rescue teams combed through the debris of a collapsed building in New Delhi on Monday as the death toll climbed to six, officials said.
The five-story building, which housed a boys’ hostel, collapsed on Sunday in Satya Niketan, a densely populated neighborhood known for its private student accommodations near a Delhi University campus.
Police, firefighters and crews from India’s disaster response agency continued their search for a second day as earthmovers cleared debris and sniffer dogs worked the site to help rescuers reach those still trapped inside.
Rescue crews pulled at least 12 people from under the rubble, Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta told reporters at the site on Monday. About 80% of the debris had been cleared and only rubble from the basement remained, she said, adding that six people died and six others were injured in the incident.
According to residents, the building was at least 55 years old and had been under renovation for months before reopening to tenants, mostly students, in August despite work remaining unfinished.
Prakash Chand, a resident, said laborers were in the basement carrying out digging work when the building collapsed.
Preliminary findings suggest water accumulation in the basement and ongoing repair work on the aging building may have caused the collapse, Gupta said.
She said the government will draft a policy that would require periodic structural audits and safety certificates for buildings used by the public, including student accommodations, nursing homes and schools. “No public activity will be permitted” in buildings that fail to comply, Gupta said.
Building collapses are a recurring hazard in parts of India during the June-to-September monsoon season, when heavy or prolonged rain can weaken older structures.

Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of 'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
- Published
Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.
Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.
He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.
A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification".
"Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal who had committed war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity," the EU said in a statement.
"Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries," the statement said.
Serbia has been a candidate to join the EU since 2012, even though membership talks have recently stalled.
Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.
During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people.
Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation.
Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils.
Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported.
The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him".
Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on.
Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine.
Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.
In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags.
Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.
On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade.
For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war.
A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade.
Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said.
"He should be remembered only as a butcher."
Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail.
The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors."
Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said.
"It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past."

Google-backed spacetech startup Pixxel has raised $100 Mn (about ₹945 Cr) in its Series C funding round co-led by Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund Temasek and UK-based spacetech investor Seraphim. New investors 360 ONE Asset and IMM Investment also participated in the round, along with existing backers Radical Ventures, growX ventures, and others. The latest investment takes Pixxel’s total funding to $195 Mn. The startup said that the Series C was the single-largest funding round raised by a spacetech company in India. However, it did not disclose the valuation at which the funding was raised. The Bengaluru-based startup will use the fresh capital to expand its satellite sensing capabilities, further develop its Earth intelligence platform Aurora, deepen its work on sovereign space systems, and increase its satellite manufacturing capacity. Pixxel said it would widen its sensing capabilities through its upcoming Honeybee constellation, high-resolution optical imaging satellites, and other technologies. Aurora will act as the software layer combining data captured by these satellites to generate insights for governments, businesses, and research institutions. The startup will also ramp up production at Gigapixxel, its satellite manufacturing facility in Bengaluru. Inaugurated in 2024, the facility was designed to handle more than 20 satellites simultaneously and manufacture up to 40 satellites a year. “Years ago, we set out to build a health monitor for the planet. Hyperspectral imaging gave us a fundamentally new way to see Earth. This new investment gives us the scale to turn that vision into planetary infrastructure,” Pixxel founder and CEO Awais Ahmed said. Beyond Hyperspectral Imaging Founded in 2019 by BITS Pilani alumni Ahmed and Kshitij Khandelwal, Pixxel started by developing hyperspectral Earth observation satellites. Unlike conventional imaging satellites, hyperspectral satellites capture light across a large number of narrow wavelength bands. This allows them to identify materials and changes on the Earth’s surface that may not be visible in ordinary satellite images. The data can be used across agriculture, mining, oil and gas, environmental monitoring, defence, and disaster management. Pixxel currently operates six Firefly hyperspectral satellites and claims that they form the world’s highest-resolution commercial hyperspectral satellite constellation. The first three Firefly satellites were launched aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-12 mission in January 2025, marking the deployment of India’s first private satellite constellation. The startup has secured contracts from NASA and the US National Reconnaissance Office, besides winning multiple iDEX challenges from India’s Ministry of Defence. It has also been selected to lead the development of India’s first public-private Earth observation satellite constellation under IN-SPACe. The proposed constellation will comprise 12 satellites carrying different types of imaging sensors. Besides Earth observation, Pixxel has partnered with AI unicorn Sarvam to develop Pathfinder, a 200-kilogram orbital data centre demonstration satellite. Pixxel will design, launch, and operate the satellite, while Sarvam will enable AI training and inference in orbit. Pixxel’s fundraise comes amid growing investor interest and commercial activity in India’s private spacetech ecosystem. In May, Skyroot Aerospace raised $60 Mn at a pre-money valuation of $1.1 Bn, becoming India’s first spacetech unicorn. It followed this by completing the country’s first private orbital rocket mission in July, placing customer payloads into low-Earth orbit using its Vikram-1 launch vehicle. Besides Pixxel and Skyroot, startups such as Agnikul Cosmos, Digantara, Bellatrix Aerospace, GalaxEye, Dhruva Space, and SatSure are building capabilities across launch vehicles, satellite manufacturing, propulsion, space situational awareness, Earth observation, and downstream analytics.

On Thursday, Elon Musk’s X won a court order blocking Operation Bluebird from launching a new app taking over the Twitter name.
In his opinion, Chief Judge Colm Connolly explained that Operation Bluebird was unlikely to prove that X had entirely abandoned the Twitter name. Therefore, X was likely to succeed on trademark infringement and dilution claims tied to the platform’s former name.
Most compellingly, X argued that it still uses the Twitter name in the current listing for the X app in Apple’s App Store. In the first sentence of that listing, written in the same size font as the rest of the text, a single clause clinched the early court win for X by stating, “Welcome to X (formerly known as Twitter).”
X’s legal director, Naser Baseer, testified that X “deliberately” added that clause “to ensure that people who were searching for the Twitter app within the App Store, as well as people who were searching for the Twitter app outside of the App Store, would find the Apple app link and have an understanding that this is one and the same app, same platform,” Connolly said.
Additionally, survey evidence showed that people still think Twitter’s a “famous” brand, and X showed that despite wiping the name from its platform, the company still “takes advantage” of the “goodwill” that the “commercially strong” initial brand maintains by associating X with Twitter in the App Store, Connolly wrote.
“By virtue of the parenthetical, the listing is telling customers that what they knew as Twitter is now X and can be accessed by downloading the X app from the Apple App Store,” Connolly said.
It may also strengthen X’s case that twitter.com redirects to x.com, but Connolly did not yet have to weigh that question. Because X could be irreparably harmed if Operation Bluebird benefits from using the Twitter name at X’s expense, Operation Bluebird will be blocked from using the name until litigation is resolved, Connolly ruled.

In a statement sent to Ars Technica, the Pentagon said that the document, titled “Clinical Guidance for Health and Human Performance Optimization,” had been temporarily rescinded on September 3 to allow for updates.
“The Department remains committed to addressing hormone deficiencies, protecting the long-term health of its Service members, and enabling peak operational performance,” the Pentagon said. An interim guidance remains in effect, and “the final clinical guidance will be issued shortly,” it added.
The Pentagon declined to provide more information regarding what was being updated about the guidance and why it needed to be updated so quickly after its release.
Reuters reported that the rescinded guidelines called for men aged 30 and older to be screened through a questionnaire that could then trigger a blood test for testosterone levels and, if needed, testosterone hormone therapy. Women were also to be screened through a questionnaire, which could lead to treatment for hormonal imbalances.

Deepinder Goyal’s wearable startup Temple has released its first validation study, with researchers finding that its proprietary brain flow metric broadly tracked changes in cerebral blood-flow velocity recorded using transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasound. However, the study, published as a preprint, involved only 23 healthy adults and has been submitted for peer review. TCD is a non-invasive ultrasound technique used to measure the speed and direction of blood flow in the brain’s major arteries. The study compared Temple’s metric with blood-flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery rather than directly measuring total or absolute cerebral blood flow. Researchers compared Temple’s wearable with TCD during two activities designed to produce changes in cerebral blood flow – stationary cycling and a shift from standing to lying down. Data from 20 participants was analysed under each protocol. Temple’s brain flow metric registered a median within-subject correlation of about 0.8 with middle cerebral artery blood-flow velocity across both activities, according to the paper. Goyal said in a post on X that the result demonstrated that Temple could track changes in brain blood flow that conventional heart-rate measurements might miss. During the postural test, participants’ heart rates declined when they lay down, while cerebral blood-flow velocity increased. Temple’s metric moved in the same direction as the Doppler reading despite the opposing change in heart rate, the researchers found. “Any device that only measures heart rate would have gotten this completely wrong,” Goyal said. The findings suggest that Temple’s wearable can follow the direction and pattern of short-term changes in cerebral blood-flow velocity under controlled conditions. They do not establish that the device can accurately measure absolute cerebral blood flow or diagnose medical conditions. The paper also said further studies involving other measurement techniques and cerebrovascular challenges would be needed to determine whether Temple’s brain flow metric specifically reflects cerebral activity and to establish potential clinical applications. Goyal acknowledged the limited scope of the research, saying it involved one study, two interventions, and healthy adults. He added that further validation studies of Brain Flow and Temple’s other proprietary metric, Entropy, were under way. The startup is also offering to loan its devices to qualified researchers seeking to independently test its metrics, Goyal added. Temple’s Wearable Bet Temple is developing a wearable device intended to continuously track signals associated with cerebral blood flow. It describes its device as a product that will measure “brain flow” – the blood flow to the brain. Unlike conventional consumer wearables that primarily monitor metrics such as heart rate, blood oxygen levels, and sleep, Temple is betting on measurements taken from the side of the head. Temple raised around ₹493 Cr earlier this year from investors including Peak XV Partners, Steadview Capital, NK Squared, and Goyal. The round reportedly valued the startup at about ₹1,700 Cr (about $204 Mn). Its valuation subsequently nearly doubled to $375 Mn as part of an ESOP liquidity programme for early employees. Last month, Goyal said Temple had reduced the size of the wearable to less than half that of the earlier version. The startup is preparing to open preorders and expects to begin shipping the device before the end of 2026. Temple also recently acquired London-based longevity medicine practice Longevous for an undisclosed amount, adding clinical and scientific expertise ahead of the wearable’s launch.

In Summary
- The Poco M8x is the latest phone from Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, and is targeted at the budget segment.
- The phone is the first in the Indian market to come with the new Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also boasts a massive 7900 mAh battery.
- At Rs 20,999, the Poco M8x packs a punch in everyday use. It cuts some corners in the display department, but remains a very good option for those wanting reliable performance on a budget.
Even as smartphone prices head north, a new budget contender has entered the Indian smartphone market. Xiaomi’s sub-brand Poco has launched the Poco M8x 5G. With a starting price of Rs 20,999, the smartphone is the first in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also packs in a huge 7900 mAh battery. It also packs in some good specs and some decent ones, but is that enough to help it deliver a performance that can make it stand out in a segment which is not as spec-forward as it once used to be? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Poco M8x Appearance and Design: Premium looks even at a budget price
The Poco M8x may be a budget smartphone but does not look like it. We received the Leather Green variant, and it is, without a doubt, the best-looking version of the device. There are plain-ish black and blue colors on offer too, but the combination of muted gold and that vegan leather back makes the Leather Green look very good indeed.
The back has a rectangular camera unit with rounded sides. This is slightly raised and comes with a matte gold finish and a shiny metallic gold outline around it. There are two large, dark camera lenses arranged vertically on the left side of the camera unit, while the flash is encased in a long, vertical pill-shaped island on the right. The Poco badge appears on the lower portion of the back, which is covered with textured green eco-leather goodness. This not only helps the phone stand out from the usual budget segment crowd but also keeps scratches and smudges at one arm’s distance. We are guilty of packing multiple gadgets in the same bag compartment, which often roughs them up, but the Poco M8x still looks brand new in spite of many such crowded trips.
The front of the phone is more regular-looking. It is all about a tall display, surrounded by bezels which can be termed “thick” now, for those who notice them. There is a punch-hole notch in the middle of the top of the display, which is home to the front camera. The sides of the phone also come in the same gold shade as the camera unit and house ports and buttons. The left side of the frame is completely plain, while the right side carries the volume rocker and the power/lock button, which doubles up as a physical fingerprint scanner as well. While it has been written off in almost every other smartphone segment, you do get to see the mighty 3.5 mm audio jack in the budget segment. The Poco M8x comes with one right on top of the phone, although the trademark IR blaster has been skipped. The base holds the hybrid SIM card tray, along with a USB Type-C port and a speaker grille.
The Poco M8x is a big phone, and this is immediately noticeable – it is 170 mm tall and 78.4 mm wide. It is relatively slim at 8.8 mm, but at 232 grams, it makes its presence felt both in hand and in pocket. While the phone feels very good in hand, one needs both hands to use. It is a pretty sturdy customer too – it comes with an IP64 rating which provides some dust and water resistance, while the screen has Corning Gorilla Glass 7i protection.
Poco M8x Spec sheet: Fit for its segment
Its design may look more premium than its price, but the Poco M8x’s spec sheet slots very well in the budget segment, or rather the new budget segment that has been defined by increasing component prices. It is the first smartphone in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor. This is paired with 4 GB and 6 GB RAM and 128 GB storage, which can be expanded up to 2 TB using a microSD card.
The display on the phone is big – a 6.9-inch HD+ LCD display (yep, those have made a comeback) with a 120 Hz refresh rate. There are two cameras on the back of the phone, one being the main 50-megapixel sensor and the other an “auxiliary” one, while the one on the front for selfies and video calls is an 8-megapixel sensor.
One of the major spec USPs of the Poco M8x is its battery. The phone comes with a large 7900 mAh battery, with support for 45 W fast wired charging and 22.5 W reverse wired charging as well. The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 out of the box with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3 on top of it, with a promise of 4 years of OS and 6 years of security updates. In the sound department, it features stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack as well. Since it has an LCD display, the fingerprint scanner is on the side. All in all, these are good specs for the price the Poco M8x charges.
Poco M8x Performance: A consistent daily driver
The Poco M8x delivers the performance its spec sheet promises. The processor and RAM combination is budget-level, and the phone manages to get through everyday smartphone tasks with ease. Jumping from one app to another, social media scrolls, messaging, emails, photography, and calls are all handled without strain. Casual games like Tetris and Subway Surfers run with ease too. The phone is not designed to handle high-end games – we tried Genshin Impact, and not surprisingly, the experience was laggy even with tweaked settings.
The display is big, and the 120 Hz refresh rate does make the process of scrolling on social media a pretty smooth one. However, it is an LCD display with HD+ resolution, which makes the content feel a little less sharp, even though the colors do seem quite vibrant. This, combined with stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack, makes the Poco M8x a good device for those who like to watch content on their smartphones.
We had said waaay back in 2020 that the real home of a fingerprint scanner is on the side of the phone, so the fingerprint scanner placed on the side of the Poco M8x is something we actually liked. It worked smoothly and was easy to access. There is the option of using face unlock as well, which turned out to be impressively accurate and speedy, although it is supposed to be less secure than the fingerprint scanner. Call quality was good, and we did not face any abrupt call drop issues. In short, the Poco M8x is a terrific daily driver, handling everyday life and delivering entertainment with ease.
Poco M8x Cameras: Good main and selfie camera for the price
The Poco M8x comes with a 50-megapixel main sensor on the back paired with an auxiliary lens. The daylight performance of the main camera is pretty good. It captures basic shots well, with a decent amount of detail. The colors look a little muted as compared to the natural settings, but still turn out good enough for a quick social media post. You get a 2x digital zoom, which basically crops an image. The details do get compromised here, but it comes in handy when you need a closer look. The camera, however, struggles a bit if you push it out of its comfort zone.
It struggles to capture macro photos – you have to keep your hand very (very) steady to get a decent photo, and the portrait mode on the phone did not really add a lot of visible difference – the bokeh added was very light and almost negligible, which was disappointing. The low light performance of the phone is nothing too special either. As the light dims, details take a hit, and the colors remain muted here as well. There is a night mode which makes results a bit better, but low-light pictures in general take a second to process, and it is very important you keep your hands very steady for that second (there’s no OIS, remember). The phone comes with a number of modes like Document, Dual video, and Pro, that give users more shooting options and utility.
The front camera also performs surprisingly well for a modest-sounding 8-megapixel shooter, in terms of both color and detail. With beauty mode off, it can capture skin texture well, and colors seem good too. The portrait mode on the selfie camera actually delivers deeper bokeh than what we got from the primary camera. It does not catch edges very well (blurred out my ear once), but the photos are good enough for social media posts. There are a number of beauty filters, all of which do their job well. However, it follows the path of the primary camera and struggles with details and color in low light. The primary camera is capable of capturing full HD videos at 30 fps. Videos also turn out well in daylight but get noisy in low light. All said and done, we were actually surprised by the cameras on the Poco M8x, which performed well beyond our expectations (we still don’t know what difference the auxiliary camera makes, though).
Poco M8x Battery: Where the phone is BOSS
This is one department where the Poco M8x shines most brightly, and how. The phone comes with a massive 7900 mAh battery, and it is safe to say it just keeps going on and on. The combination of a low-resolution display, an efficient everyday processor, and a big battery is a terrific one. The Poco M8x comfortably lasted for two days of hectic usage, with hours of Instagram scrolls, YouTube, and some Modern Family episodes here and there, emails, messaging, WhatsApp, calls, sessions of Tetris, and some photography. The phone handled it all like a champ.
With a bit of careful usage, we even got it to last the third day. It is safe to say this is perhaps the best battery performance we have experienced in this segment. The phone comes with 45 W fast charging support and a 45 W adapter in the box, which took about one hour 15 minutes to go from 20 percent to full. But so big is the battery that even a 30-minute charge session can easily give you a full day’s battery. And as it comes with a 22.5 W reverse charging feature as well, it can double as a power bank for your other devices, including smartphones and wearables. This is pretty much the battery boss of the segment.
Poco M8x UI and software: A mixed bag of functionality and third-party apps
The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 with Hyper OS 3, and on budget devices, Hyper OS is a bit of a mixed bag. The first thing that hits you when you fire up the phone is the large number of third-party apps. It is a little overwhelming – there are even multiple casual games of the same type. Although there are also popular apps like Instagram, YouTube, YouTube Music, and LinkedIn, the interface can seem very crowded. Thankfully, these can be uninstalled, and we recommend doing so.
Now on to the good bits. HyperOS is otherwise quite functional and customizable. There are a number of personalization options – from icons to fonts, to themes and wallpapers; you can personalize them all to your liking. There are also features like interconnectivity that allow you to connect your device to other Xiaomi products and carry out functions over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and you can also link your device to a Chromebook.
There are some basic AI features on the phone as well – Google Gemini for writing and other assistance, and features like Circle to Search. Of course, given its specs, we do not recommend pushing the phone too hard in the AI zone. Finally, the phone has an array of accessibility features (divided into general, vision, physical, and hearing), which aim to make the experience smooth for all users. Get rid of the bloatware, and the Poco M8x’s UI experience can be a pleasant one.
Poco M8x Price: In line with the new budget zone
The Poco M8x comes with a starting price of Rs. 20,999 for its 4 GB/ 128 GB version, while the 6 GB/ 128 GB version is priced at Rs. 22,999. Keeping in mind the rising prices of smartphones, the Poco M8x is quite fairly priced for the specs it offers. It does face competition, though.
One of its most notable competitors is the Samsung Galaxy M17, which starts at Rs 17,999 and comes with triple cameras on its back (50 MP+ 5 MP+ 2 MP), a 13-megapixel front camera, and most notably, a Super AMOLED Full HD+ display with a 90 Hz refresh rate. That said, its display and battery (with no charger in the box) and its Exynos 1330 processor are a step behind the Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 on the Poco M8x. There is also the Moto G37 Power 5G, which starts at Rs 19,999 and is powered by MediaTek Dimensity 6400, and has RAM that goes up to 8 GB, but comes with a smaller display and battery and also starts with a 4 GB/ 64 GB version.
Poco M8x Review Verdict: The big battery boss of the budget segment
For its starting price of Rs. 20,999, the Poco M8x is a pretty budget smartphone. It mainly shines in two areas: design (Green Leather variant) and battery. It also does well in other departments, and we can see many people liking its large display, good speakers, and main and selfie cameras (in good light conditions). It also delivers very consistent everyday performance and comes with a very functional OS as well. All of which make it a great option for those who are looking for a good-looking but reliable device with days of battery life.
- Leather Green design stands out
- Good main and selfie cameras
- Great battery life
- Handles everyday tasks well
- Big display and screen combo make it great for consuming content
- Relatively low-resolution HD+ display
- LCD display, rather than an AMOLED one
- Portrait shots from the main camera are disappointing
- Bloatware in the UI

Thanks to their ability to provide a smooth ride and quiet powertrain with ease, electric vehicles are a true shoo-in for the high-end luxury automotive segment. Rolls-Royce has the Spectre, Cadillac’s Celestiq is taking bespoke to a whole new level, and Mercedes has given the EQS the full Maybach treatment. From Volkswagen Auto Group, Bentley is just about to debut its 2027 Torcal, a spacious SUV that shares a platform with the electrified Porsche Cayenne.
Bentley’s Torcal EV tries to balance authenticity with fake V8 sounds
The British automaker is on the hunt for a new demographic with its first electric vehicle.
I recently got a quick ride in a heavily camouflaged preproduction Torcal as a way to experience it before its official debut toward the end of this month. Between this brute’s spacious interior, supple ride quality, and focus on craftsmanship in the digital age, all signs point to it not just being a viable competitor in the segment, but also characteristically Bentley.
When I say heavily camouflaged, this not only covers (pun intended) the Torcal’s exterior, but the interior as well. Thick black cloth was draped over most of it, to the point of the engineers punching holes in the cloth for proper seatbelt usage. The exterior was rather deceiving, too; apparently they affixed false body paneling under the wrap so as not to fully spoil its overall shape and profile. Upon first glance, it seemed like Bentley took a page from Lucid’s Gravity by making it wider at the front than at the back—in the name of teardrop-resembling aerodynamics—but Martin Page, the Torcal’s product line director-slash-chauffeur for my ride, assured me that what I was seeing (or rather, trying to see) wouldn’t be production.
However, this enabled me to zero in closer on what I could feel and hear. Whether up front or in back, the Torcal is amply spacious, even though it’s noticeably smaller in size and shape than Bentley’s current Bentayga. Page explained the great lengths that engineers reached to ensure it had an isolating and tremendously smooth ride. Running off-the-shelf two-chamber air suspension — common in the rest of the brand’s lineup — would seemingly suffice with an EV’s inherently good chassis balance, but engineers took it a step further by carefully altering the flow of oil through its adaptive dampers. This means that the jump in ride and handling between Comfort and Sport modes is much more discernible. No matter the mode, it rode incredibly smoothly. Heavy focus was paid to the Torcal’s alignment, too, with steering that returns to and maintains center as confidently as possible.
Diving deeper into signature Bentley characteristics, developing the best simulated engine note was high on the list of priorities. Inspiration came from the brand’s V8-powered Turbo R of the 1980s, except the track itself was recorded by a musician’s drum beat and mixed accordingly, rather than simply churned out from a synthesizer.
“What we wanted to do throughout the car is maintain craftsmanship, not only in the materials but also in the way we execute the digital aspects,” Page shared.
“What we wanted to do throughout the car is maintain craftsmanship, not only in the materials but also in the way we execute the digital aspects.”
— Martin Page, Torcal’s product line director
The reasoning behind this lies in hearing subtle imperfections, much like one would from an analogue internal combustion powertrain. Going one step further, the Torcal’s throttle tuning seemed to mimic a torquey V8 with progressive power delivery. In light of this, Page added that with this sound turned on, it gives occupants auditory cues to tie to the vehicle’s torque delivery, which is known to help reduce motion sickness. The sound has not yet been finalized and is still being finely tweaked at the time of this writing.
I got a peek at the digital instrument cluster and center infotainment screen — Page had to observe the speed limit, after all. The image these display in the background is of a fine crystal decanter hand-cut by Cumbria Crystal with light shone through it. In Page’s words, this shows the natural refractions and reflections that you get from every one of the cuts. It’s another indication of the brand’s focus on craftsmanship in the digital age, albeit a subtle one.
It’s also worth pointing out that Bentley takes net environmental impact seriously. “In this car we take sustainability to another level, we have clear targets for circular material and green aluminum,” Page shared. “The door cards are made with a natural fiber — not injection-molded plastic — that’s fully recyclable and fully sustainable.”
Then, Bentley is working with fellow UK company Fox Brothers to offer a Merino wool interior option, not just as a lesser-taken route for comfort (Volvo’s done well with wool, too) but also as a sturdy, renewable material that will hold up to automotive use. Finally, the assembly plant in Crewe, England, has tough requirements for green energy use (namely solar) and other renewable practices.
Output, battery, and charging specs are not carved into stone just yet. Power will be north of 800 hp and 700 lb ft of torque, and curb weight is estimated to be nearly 6,000 lbs. Page was quiet about battery size (though, expect it to mirror the Porsche’s 108 net kWh unit), and the targeted range is over 370 miles. With a peak charging rate of 400 kW, the brand is aiming for a 10–80 percent top-up in under 20 minutes, with 100 miles tacking on in as little as seven.
“We’re trying to be authentic in the whole experience,” Page summed up as we headed back to the parking lot where I met him.
The approach with the Torcal is to make a great Bentley first, and in the process of doing so, a great EV. It combines some already hashed-out tech from Volkswagen, but the brand is hoping its focus on craftsmanship and fine-tuning will attract discerning, well-heeled potential customers who want an electric luxury vehicle. Pricing hasn’t been announced yet, but it will be interesting to see how the Torcal is received after its full official unveiling.

A video (here & here) claiming to show the bodies of victims who died in the Nepal flash floods on 26 August 2026, is circulating widely on social media. Let’s examine the veracity of this claim.
Claim: Video showing the deceased victims during the flash floods that struck Nepal on 26 August 2026.
Fact: This video is unrelated to the Nepal floods. It is a staged video shot for entertainment purpose by an Instagram creator. The Nepal floods occurred on 26 August 2026, but this video was uploaded on 03 August 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is misleading.
A reverse image search of the keyframes from the viral video revealed that the same video (archive) was uploaded to Instagram on 03 August 2026 by a content creator named Simran SK. This confirms that the video has no connection to the Nepal floods, as it was uploaded well before the actual disaster took place.
A closer review of Simran SK’s Instagram account indicates a pattern of uploading comedy and scripted videos. We also found other scripted videos (archive) on the account featuring individuals pretending to be dead. Furthermore, during the Assam floods in July 2026, another scripted video from this very account was falsely circulated as a real incident. Our previous fact-check article regarding that instance can be read here.
To sum it up, a scripted video is being falsely shared as genuine footage of deceased victims from the 2026 Nepal floods.

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.
A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.
The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.
The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.
The People’s Insurance Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish its capital.
The initiative could help bolster state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.
The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.
“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.
Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.
The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.
The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corp and its subsidiaries.
The two lenders said the proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans on state banks to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

Ecclestone stopped by police for taking shotgun into Portugal
- Published
Former Formula 1 boss Bernie Ecclestone has denied being arrested at an airport in Portugal after arriving with a shotgun he intended to use in a clay pigeon shooting competition.
Ecclestone, 95, said he was stopped and questioned by four police officers and customs officials at the Tires Aerodrome in Cascais on Monday after arriving from Switzerland.
The British businessman told the Press Association he had to "surrender" the weapon he travelled with as he did not have the right documents to correctly import it.
Ecclestone, who was in charge of F1 for nearly 40 years until 2017, said the Portuguese police were "very helpful" and rejected reports he had been arrested.
"I was going to take part in a clay pigeon shooting competition in Portugal," said Ecclestone.
"I went to see the police and said, 'What can I do for you?' And they said, 'We would like some information on this gun you brought in'."
Ecclestone added he had already taken his shotgun from England to Switzerland and said he anticipated no problems as the airport officials know him "very well".
However, on arrival he was questioned by police for about an hour and was asked to hand over the weapon as he did not have the official documents to bring it into the country.
The incident marks the second time Ecclestone has encountered airport issues regarding firearms. In 2022, he was arrested in Brazil for illegally carrying a gun while boarding a private plane to Switzerland and was ordered to pay 6,000 Brazilian reals (£1,000) to the local authorities.

Grindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.
The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.
The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.
According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.
Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.
The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September.
"While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.
The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.
'Significant distress'
The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.
It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.
People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.
Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.
She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".
Two data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.
The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.
It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.
Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.
It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.
The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community".
"Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

The deadliest ever Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now claimed the lives of more than 3,000 people, according to the latest official toll released on Wednesday.
The epidemic, which has hit the conflict-hit east and northeast of the country, has caused 3,007 deaths and infected 6,186 people, the Congolese National Institute of Public Health said.
The fatality rate is 48.6%. A total of 1,409 people have been reported to have recovered, it added.
Ebola, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and causes haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa in the last 50 years.
The worst outbreak previously recorded in DR Congo left nearly 2,300 people dead from 3,500 reported cases between 2018 and 2020.
The current outbreak originated in the remote northeastern province of Ituri and is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is currently no approved vaccine or treatment.
The virus has spread to six provinces and is ravaging areas where the presence of the Congolese state is weak and insecurity is widespread due to the presence of armed groups.
The health response lacks sufficient resources and has been overwhelmed by the surge in cases, while there has been widespread mistrust in parts of the community.
Several treatments and vaccines are being tested against the Bundibugyo strain. Approved vaccines are only effective against the Zaire strain, which is responsible for the largest-known Ebola outbreak to date.
The World Health Organization has in the meantime recommended the implementation of a phase three clinical trial using the Ervebo vaccine deployed against the Zaire strain.
WHO experts are still unclear as to whether Ervebo protects humans against Bundigbugyo but initial data suggests that it could offer a degree of protection.
A batch of 16,250 doses for use by frontline medical personnel arrived in DR Congo at the end of last month and vaccination began shortly afterwards in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province in the northeast.

Whatever happened to the U.S. campaign to ban child marriage?
Our team of global health reporters has covered child marriage –- when one partner is under age 18. The United Nations calls it a "human rights violation," citing a litany of concerns for child brides: "early pregnancy and social isolation, interrupting her schooling, limiting her opportunities for career and vocational advancement and placing her at risk of domestic violence." Yet every year, the U.N. estimates that 12 million girls become child brides.
Child grooms, the U.N. further notes, may be forced into "an adult role for which they are unprepared," with pressure to drop out of school and support a family.
The U.N. has set the goal of ending child marriage by the year 2030.
This year there are new efforts to make child marriage illegal — a bill introduced by U.S. legislators in July and a resolution adopted by the U.N. General Assembly on September 4 establishes November 27 as the International Day to End Child, Early and Forced Marriage. As part of our "Whatever happened to …" series, we asked contributor Kamala Thiagarajan to examine the ongoing effort to end this practice.
Over the next week, we'll be looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
Nations around the world are seeking to meet the U.N. goal of ending child marriage by 2030.
Since 2021, countries as diverse as Sierra Leone, England, the Philippines and the Dominican Republic have been passing legislation to set the marriage age at 18, with no exceptions.
In the United States, the current push for a national law is controversial — some have criticized provisions in the proposed legislation, and others oppose it altogether.
And legislation is not necessarily the solution. In India, marriage under age 18 is illegal, yet the latest National Family Health Survey conducted in country found that one in five women ages 20 to 24 married before turning 18. UNICEF estimates that at least 1.5 million girls under the age of 18 are married in India each year.
The U.S. effort
On July 16, U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin and Sens. Dick Durbin, Brian Schatz and Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Child Marriage Prevention Act, a federal bill aimed at combating child marriage.
This legislation would push states toward a nationwide minimum marriage age of 18. "In 34 states, including Wisconsin, child marriage is legal. Many of these marriages are between young girls and adult men. It's time we end this predatory practice," Moore said in a statement emailed to NPR. "I know that advocates have pushed for reform at the state level, which has led some states to change their laws. This federal legislation would help bolster and support those efforts, including helping states get the data to understand its prevalence in their jurisdictions and then take action to address it."
In announcing the bill, its four congressional cosponsors cited data showing that more than 314,000 minors were legally married in the United States between 2000 and 2021, including girls as young as 10. The figures, compiled by child-marriage advocacy groups from state marriage records, indicate that most of the underage girls were married to adult men.
Unchained At Last, a nonprofit worked to end forced and child marriage in the U.S., estimates that at least 66,415 of these marriages — about one in five — occurred when the bride was at an age when sexual relations would be considered a crime (the age varies from 14 to 18 depending on the state). In roughly 90% of that subset, according to the organization's founder, Fraidy Reiss, marital exemptions in state statutory-rape laws shielded the adult spouse from prosecution. Married minors may also face legal barriers to hiring an attorney, filing for divorce or obtaining protection from abuse.
The Tahirih Justice Center, an organization with a long history of advocating for survivors of forced and child marriage, has been a key partner in developing and supporting this legislation.
"The one thing we hear all the time from places — Cameroon, Guatemala, you name it — is: 'It makes my work harder when a politician can say to my face, the United States allows child marriage, so why should I do anything?' The best thing that we can do to help the global movement is to get our house in order," says Casey Carter Swegman, director of public policy at Tahirih.
Swegman says that a child's apparent consent does not necessarily mean that the decision to marry was made freely. "A 15-, 16- or 17-year-old who has been pressured and coached by family members may tell a judge that she consents because refusing could expose her to punishment or violence at home," she says. This is especially troubling, Swegman says, when pregnancy, potential evidence of sexual abuse, is treated as justification for allowing the marriage to proceed.
"A child is coming before your court pregnant by an adult person — that should be a red flag for statutory rape, not a green light for marriage," she says.
Although the proposed bill has won support from many child-marriage advocates, others have questioned whether its provisions go far enough and warn of possible unintended consequences that it has overlooked.
"If I could heart a provision of this bill, it would be [the proposal] to provide financial incentive to states that have banned child marriage — that I can get behind," says Reiss. "While I applaud Congress for introducing and considering legislation to combat child marriage at the federal level, I am appalled that two sections of the Child Marriage Prevention Act would make a mockery of the bill's title."
Section 6, she says, would provide federal grants to states to "study" child marriage instead of banning it. "If states are given money to examine something that's a human rights violation instead of banning it outright, it would be devastating," says Reiss, who says she was forced to marry at age 19.
Section 10 would allow some minors as young as 16, whether in the United States or abroad, to qualify for a U.S. spousal visa under certain circumstances. This would actually encourage a particularly heinous form of child marriage, says Reiss: the trafficking of minors to the U.S. under the guise of marriage, and it would discourage U.S. states from setting their marriage age at 18, no exceptions. "If the bill were amended to set the spousal visa age at 18, it would be a 'game-changer' by sending a clear message to states and halting legal trafficking," she says.
And there is opposition to the very idea of the bill. In some states, Oklahoma and Missouri, for instance, Republican lawmakers have opposed state bans on child marriage, arguing that such restrictions constitute government overreach and interfere with parental authority.
In 2024, in an interview with the Missouri Independent, Republican state Rep. Dean Van Schoiack called a proposed ban "government intrusion in people's lives." Asked what would be lost if 16- and 17-year-olds could no longer marry, he replied, "Liberties that people currently have."
How the U.S. bill compares to other global efforts
As Congress prepares to debate the U.S. bill this fall, other countries have already adopted more sweeping national restrictions. The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2024 in Sierra Leone sets 18 as the minimum age of marriage without any exceptions for parental consent, religious marriage or pregnancy. Section 15 declares that any child marriage contracted after the Act took effect to be void. The legislation even penalizes people who facilitate or attend a child marriage.
In November 2024, Columbia, where 23% of girls are married before they're 18, passed a law banning such marriages outright. In a similar move, on Sept. 25, 2025, Bolivia banned child marriage without exceptions, removing provisions allowing 16- and 17-year-olds to marry with parental consent or judicial approval.
But laws are not always a solution. In many countries in sub-Saharan Africa and in India, there are national laws banning child marriage but weak enforcement often limits their effectiveness.
"In countries like India, child marriage persists despite strong laws due to deeply ingrained cultural factors, making solutions very complex," says Renu Singh, executive director of Young Lives India, a research program that studies how poverty and inequality shape children's lives as they grow into adulthood.
The Young Lives study began in 2002, in India, Ethiopia, Peru and Vietnam.
In India, Young Lives has followed 3,000 children in the southern Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana — from childhood into their late 20s. Researchers have repeatedly interviewed them and their families about education, health, employment, marriage, fertility, household circumstances and personal aspirations. They found that many of the children they'd followed married early.
Working with India's National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, they analyzed 2011 Census data to map child marriage at the state and district levels. That research reported 12.1 million marriages involving people below India's respective legal marriage ages (21 for boys and 18 for girls) and identified hotspots that could help the government target interventions.
"We found that there were so many varied and complex reasons driving these marriages," says Singh. "It wasn't just low-income groups who got their children married off." Some parents, she says, who were deeply concerned about the safety of an unmarried daughter, saw marriage as a security net. Young Lives found that girls with older brothers were more at risk of being married early because of the social custom of giving dowries — when the bride's family gifts the bridegroom's family money at the time of marriage. In a household with a boy and a girl, the girl was married especially early, so that her older brother could get married too.
"Boys were often married off early as well, especially if the family wanted to get dowries for their sons to offset the financial losses they faced when they gave their own daughters away in marriage. And this was the case across all income groups," says Singh.
India's national law has helped establish that child marriage is unacceptable and punishable, Singh says — but lasting change also requires communities to stop accepting and supporting the widespread practice.
NPR has reported on how this practice unfolds in India: "Our parents just hold the weddings in secret," a 16-year-old told our correspondent. "At night - very rushed." Our story continues: "She was married when she was 9 years old. A bunch of other girls nod. They were all married around that age, too. A shy girl in a pink T-shirt says she didn't even understand what was happening at the time."
For legislation to be effective, Singh says, parents, relatives, religious leaders and others must no longer regard an early marriage as normal, protective or beneficial for a girl.
"The U.S. also has major issues with deeply entrenched gender roles, with patriarchy, with extreme — I would say almost obsession over the control of female sexuality. These are the [reasons] the social pressure for this practice continue," says Swegman. In addition to a national law, it's clear that attitudes must change too. "This requires belief and behavior change, services, support, thoughtful conversations on the community level," says Swegman.
The campaign for stronger laws in the United States is a part of a growing international effort to move child marriage higher up the global political agenda.
One of the key figures behind the U.N. resolution declaring a day "to end child, early and forced marriage" is Bhuwan Ribhu, a lawyer and the founder of Just Rights for Children, a child rights network. Just Rights for Children has filed 60 Public Interest Litigations in India that would reframe child marriage as child rape, securing legal protections for the young women.
"Establishing an official International Day to End Child, Early and Forced Marriage gives us an annual platform to hold governments accountable and enforce laws that protect children. Now is the time to build on this commitment and end child marriage by 2030. Today, the world has spoken in one voice: the crime of child marriage must end," Rhibu says.
Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times, The British Medical Journal, the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.

Ukraine-Russia war latest: Two killed in Russian ballistic missiles attack on Kyiv day after Trump’s envoys leave
Russian ballistic missiles rain on Ukraine just a day after US peace envoys held a press conference in Kyiv alongside Zelensky
Russian air strikes have killed at least two people and injured seven others in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv this morning, officials said.
The attacks came just a day after US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held peace talks with Volodymyr Zelensky and left the Ukrainian capital.
During their visit to Kyiv, Donald Trump’s peace envoys were confronted over their talks with “war criminal” Russian president Vladimir Putin.
In a news conference in Kyiv alongside Volodymry Zelensky on Sunday, Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon asked whether Putin was deceiving the US president.
“You have met with President Putin very often. Does it seem to you that Putin has been deceiving you all this time?,” he added according to the Kyiv Post.
“And finally, don’t you find it disgusting to sit at the same table with an international war criminal, the executioner of the Ukrainian people, who is personally responsible for the tragedy in Ukraine?” he added.
Zelensky held talks with Witkoff and Kushner on Sunday, after their three-hour talks with Putin in Moscow on Saturday. He lauded their “very substantive” conversation and said Ukraine was ready for trilateral talks involving Russia, the US and Ukraine.
Burnham and Trump discuss working towards Ukraine-Russia ceasefire
Prime minister Andy Burnham spoke with US president Donald Trump yesterday, with the two leaders agreeing on "the need to continue working towards a ceasefire" to end Russia's war in Ukraine, Downing Street said.
"The Prime Minister reiterated the UK's support for Ukraine and for recent US-led peace negotiations," a Downing Street spokesperson said.
Burnham and Trump also discussed the Middle East, with Burnham "stressing the importance of the two-state solution, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon", the spokesperson added.
Monday's call comes after US peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday, having spoken with Russian president Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday.
Two killed and seven injured in Russian missile attack on Kyiv
Russian air strikes have killed at least two people and injured seven others in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv this morning, officials said.
The attacks came just a day after US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held peace talks with Volodymyr Zelensky and left the Ukrainian capital.
Russia says external power at Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant restored
Off-site power at the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine has been restored via the Ferosplavna power line, Russia's Rosatom state nuclear corporation said.
The plant has been without external power since 20 August and has relied on emergency diesel generators to cool its vital safety systems.
A local ceasefire brokered by the International Atomic Energy Agency took effect on Saturday to allow repairs to restore external power.
The IAEA later confirmed the restoration in a post on X, citing its chief Rafael Grossi.
The plant is operating as normal, Rosatom chief Alexei Likhachev said in a statement.
Ukraine's prosecutor general resigns citing political conflict
Ukraine's prosecutor general on Monday announced that he has offered his resignation citing political reasons, in the latest sign of disunity in the senior ranks of the Ukrainian ruling elite.
“This is a political decision, and I have made it consciously. I do not want the position of Prosecutor General to be used as an instrument of political confrontation,” Ruslan Kravchenko said in a statement on Telegram late on Monday, without elaborating.
Kravchenko thanked president Volodymyr Zelensky and Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, and asked them to accept his resignation.
Ukraine's anti-graft agencies, the NABU and SAPO, said last week they had uncovered a criminal organisation dealing with fraudulent call centres which was allegedly arranged by an official within the Prosecutor General's Office.
Kravchenko has denied he was involved in the alleged scheme.
“My position regarding the accusations remains unchanged,” he said in his Telegram post.
Kravchenko's resignation offer follows other changes among top officials in Ukraine as it continues to battle Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv as Trump's envoys leave
Russia resumed airstrikes on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv in the early hours today, shortly after the departure of US peace negotiators, attacking the city with ballistic missiles and injuring six people, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
People were also trapped in a residential building and there were fires across Kyiv, Klitschko said, after what he said were Russian ballistic missile strikes.
A five-storey apartment building and a three-storey residential block were damaged by falling debris, the Kyiv Military Administration said on Telegram separately, asking people to seek shelter.
As explosions were heard in Kyiv, neighbouring Poland, a Nato and European Union member, began military aviation operations to protect its airspace against a risk of violation, its armed forces said on X.
Russia resumed attacks on its smaller neighbour after US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner left following a meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday.
Drones hit civilian infrastructure in Russia's Saratov
A Ukraine drone attack has hit civilian infrastructure in the Russian city of Saratov on the Volga river and injured some people, regional governor Roman Busargin said this morning.
The Saratov region is home to a large oil refinery run by state oil company Rosneft, as well as a number of other industrial and military facilities.
Russia to strip contract soldiers of one-off payment if laws violated at home
Russia's defence ministry wants to claim back part of a one-off payout from contract service personnel found guilty of criminal offences at home, a document showed, amid increasing cases of domestic violence among those fighting Russia's war on Ukraine.
Russia does not disclose official statistics on domestic violence committed by its service personnel but independent media, citing military courts data, reported hundreds of such cases, including murders, since the start of the 2022 invasion.
Russia provides a minimum one-off payment of 400,000 roubles (£3,418) for soldiers signing at least a one-year contract to fight in the war with Ukraine that Moscow calls "a special military operation".
In practice, one-off payouts may reach a few million roubles per soldier, depending on the region, in addition to a monthly salary.
Russia is also reducing sentences for those serving time in prison in exchange for signing up for the war, among other benefits, as it seeks to bolster army numbers.
Russia has seen a rise in domestic violence as fighters return home for leave, and the defence ministry wants to claim part of the one-off payments "in order to increase the motivation of military personnel to comply with the law", in case of a criminal offence, a draft law published on Monday showed.
If active contract service members are found guilty of a criminal offence which does not imply a prison sentence, they should pay back a portion of the one-off payout based on the months of the service left, the document showed.
Moscow criticises deployment of US missile system to Norway
Moscow has lashed out at the deployment of an advanced US missile system to Nato member state Norway, saying on Monday it dealt a further blow to the prospects for US-Russia talks on strategic nuclear stability.
Reports in the US said Washington had delivered a missile system to Norway that used Mk-41-style launchers capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said the deployment posed a threat because the launchers could be used to fire missiles capable of reaching a substantial part of European Russia, including Moscow.
"Steps such as the deployment in Europe of U.S. ground-based intermediate-range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation 'reset to zero', to put it mildly, the conditions for constructive dialogue with the US on strategic issues," the ministry said in a statement.
It added that Russia would pay "particular attention" to the deployment sites and command-and-control centres of US missile systems and that they would become targets in the event of a military conflict.

Editorial: Putin has no interest in peace – and Trump is falling into his trap
Steve Witkoff is the real estate guy with zero diplomatic experience who Donald Trump appointed in 2024 as his personal “peace emissary”. Jared Kushner is the president’s son-in-law, but did at least play some role in one of President Trump’s few foreign policy achievements – the Abraham Accords process that promised to deliver some stability to the Middle East during the first Trump term. As a team, they have enjoyed little success in securing the “settlement” to the war in Ukraine that Mr Trump so desires.
There is little reason to suppose that their latest exercise in shuttle diplomacy will succeed where their previous efforts failed. Indeed, the prospects for an end to the war, let alone one that will prove just and lasting, are as dismal as at any time since Vladimir Putin launched his ill-fated “special military operation” more than four and a half years ago – its duration now longer than the Soviet Union’s four-year “great patriotic war” against Adolf Hitler. Just as in that epoch-defining conflict, it is the civilian population of Ukraine that will face some of the harshest consequences as winter approaches.
Before the Witkoff-Kushner double act set out for Moscow and Kyiv, Mr Trump expressed his usual confidence in the pair – he could hardly do otherwise – and declared that “we have an idea for peace”. This idea remains opaque. Yet, for a change, this may be more than the usual self-flattering bluster. After a period when, easily bored, Mr Trump lost interest in the region (the situation in Iran didn’t help), this unexpected flexing of US power comes as a surprise.

The French space agency Centre National d’Etudes Spatiales (CNES) said that it is not perturbed with the back-to-back failures of Indian Space Research Organisation’s (ISRO)’s workhorse rocket, the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), and has complete trust in its Indian partner.
The PSLV is scheduled to launch the Indo-French TRISHNA (Thermal Infra-Red Imaging Satellite for High-resolution Natural Resource Assessment) mission next year which is a collaborative endeavor between ISRO and CNES.
“There is always a risk with launches and we know the risks. You must trust your partners and trust is very important in space cooperation because we do difficult things together and to do difficult things you trust each other. ISRO is a huge space player in the world, they know what to do. So we trust them for the launch and the satellite also,” Lionel Suchet, Chief Operating Officer, CNES told The Hindu.
The PSLV had suffered two setbacks. On January 12, 2026, the PSLV-C62 mission carrying the EOS-N1 earth observation satellite failed to finish its intended trajectory after an anomaly was detected during the end of the third stage of the launch vehicle. On May 18, 2025, while ISRO attempted to launch the EOS-09 satellite aboard the PSLV-C61 mission, it couldn’t complete it. It was also due to an anomaly in the third stage of the rocket.
“Setbacks sometimes happen with vehicles and we are not responsible for the launch but we trust our Indian partners ISRO in particular to launch the mission with the vehicle (PSLV),” said Christophe Venet, Director of Europe and International Affairs, CNES.
ISRO and CNES are jointly developing TRISHNA which is engineered to deliver high spatial and high temporal resolution monitoring of earth’s surface temperature, emissivity, and biophysical and radiation variables for surface energy budgeting at regional to global scale.
According to ISRO, this mission addresses critical water and food security challenges, focusing on the impacts of human-induced climate change and efficient water resource management through evapotranspiration monitoring.
The satellite will have two primary payloads, the Thermal Infra-Red (TIR) payload, developed by CNES and the Visible - Near Infra-Red - Short Wave Infra-Red (VNIR-SWIR) payload, developed by ISRO.
“The mission will be launched next year and the French instruments have been delivered to India. They are currently being integrated, we are having regular technical exchanges with our colleagues at ISRO and everything is looking pretty fine as of now,” Mr. Venet said.
(The reporter is in Paris at the invitation of France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs to cover the International Space Summit)
