- An August 2026 U.S. Department of Health and Human Services report claimed that "watchdog analyses tracking" had determined more than 5,500 minors had undergone "sex change surgeries" from 2019 to 2023.
- The "watchdog analyses tracking" references an anti-LGBTQ+ group that inflated the data by counting a vast number of procedures entirely unrelated to "sex change surgeries," including hair removal, surgical removal of excess eyelid skin and bladder drainage. These procedures were counted in the "sex change surgery" statistic as long as the patient had a gender dysphoria diagnosis or a psychiatric condition related to crossdressing (which is different from being trans). As with any other person's healthcare, there are many reasons why a trans person may need these procedures that have nothing to do with being trans.
- Credible data indicates that gender-affirming surgeries are rarely performed on minors, and most minors who receive them are not actually trans, but cisgender boys getting chest reductions. A peer-reviewed study from Harvard University researchers in 2024 determined that in 2019, only 85 trans minors received gender-affirming surgery and most of them were age 15 to 17. The Harvard study found no gender-affirming surgeries conducted on children under 12.
In August 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services under U.S. President Donald Trump released a report alleging that according to "watchdog analyses tracking," more than 5,500 minors had undergone "sex change surgeries" from 2019 to 2023.
Here's what Page 9 of the report says (emphasis ours):
Watchdog analyses tracking billed charges for minors from 2019 onward estimate almost $120 million in total hospital and clinic billings nationwide, encompassing over 5,500 surgical procedures and 8,500 courses of hormones or blockers. 
(14) 
(14) "What We Found," Stop the Harm Database, accessed March 12, 2026, https://stoptheharmdatabase.com/about/. ($119,791,202 in total submitted charges; 5,747 minors had sex change surgeries; 8,579 minors received hormones and puberty blockers).
Social media users across Facebook repeated the supposed statistic and cited the report, including Republican U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger, a pharmacist from Tennessee (screenshot). Similar posts included a video of Adm. Brian Christine, assistant secretary for health at HHS, who claimed that there were more than "5,500 sex-rejecting procedures" performed on minors (screenshot). Snopes readers searched the website to investigate the legitimacy of this statistic.
The HHS report pulled this number from a database of supposed surgeries created by Do No Harm, an advocacy group that opposes gender-affirming care for trans minors and diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in medicine. The Southern Poverty Law Center, a civil rights organization that tracks extremist organizations, has designated Do No Harm as an anti-LGBTQ+ hate group.
Do No Harm's methodology report lists insurance codes — standardized codes insurance companies use to describe various health care procedures and treatments — that the organization used to come up with the statistic. However, a Snopes review of the report found that many of these codes are entirely unrelated to "sex change surgeries," thus contradicting Do No Harm's claims.
Furthermore, both a peer-reviewed study from Harvard University researchers and a Reuters analysis found far lower rates of gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors. In truth, for minors, these surgeries are exceedingly rare and occur only among older teenagers.
As such, we have rated this claim as false.
A spokesperson for Do No Harm, Caroline Anderegg, said in an email that answers to our questions could be found on Do No Harm's methodology page and report. Anderegg did not return a follow-up inquiry noting that the methodology report and page did not answer our questions about what insurance database the group used and how the group filtered the insurance codes to ensure the data included only "sex change surgeries."
Methodology doesn't hold up to scrutiny
Do No Harm's website for its "Stop the Harm Database" claimed that between 2019 and 2023, "5,747 minors had sex change surgeries."
However, its methodology report said Do No Harm included insurance procedure codes for treatments that do not change a person's sex, including electrolysis for hair removal, bladder drainage, "removal of excessive skin of upper eyelid" and more (pages 17 through 20). These procedures are also not necessarily for gender-affirming care more broadly and can happen for many different reasons.
Do No Harm said it included these procedure codes only when connected to a patient with a gender dysphoria diagnosis or transvestic disorder, a psychiatric condition where a patient experiences clinically significant distress or impairment due to sexual arousal while crossdressing (Page 17).
However, a gender dysphoria code merely indicates that the patient is transgender, not that the procedure was done specifically to alleviate gender dysphoria, said Kellen Baker, senior adviser for health policy at the Movement Advancement Project, a nonprofit think tank known for tracking LGBTQ-related laws and policies.
"I really cannot underscore to you how irregular the Do No Harm analysis is," 
There are many reasons why a trans patient might receive any number of these procedures that are unrelated to being trans. For example, a trans child could have a urine obstruction and need bladder drainage, or require excess skin removal for droopy eyelids impairing their ability to function.
Furthermore, some of the codes, such as codes for intersex surgery, are used for intersex people, not transgender people. Intersex people are born with a variety of different sex characteristics that do not fit typical binary ideas of male or female bodies. Intersex infants and children in the United States sometimes receive surgeries, either for medical necessity or, more controversially, to align their bodies with more "typical" traits.
Baker also pointed out that Do No Harm claims to use "an all-payer claims database" — a database with every open and shut insurance case — but 
Gender-affirming surgeries rarely performed on minors
There are very few studies on the number of gender-affirming surgeries done on minors, largely because the surgeries themselves are so rare, Baker said.
However, Harvard researchers published a peer-reviewed study in 2024 that analyzed 2019 insurance claim data and found no incidences of a child under 12 receiving a gender-affirming surgery.
Out of a total of about 22 million minors sampled, the study found only 85 instances of a minor undergoing a gender-affirming surgical procedure in 2019, with 82 of those instances involving chest-related procedures, presumably either a chest reduction or breast tissue removal, commonly known as top surgery. The vast majority of those instances involved teenagers ages 15 to 17.
The study also found that far more cisgender boys — those who align with their gender assigned at birth — received gender-affirming chest reductions than transgender boys. Cisgender boys often receive these chest reductions because of gynecomastia, or physically harmless enlarged chest tissue that can affect their self-esteem and mental health.
Snopes reached out to the Harvard researchers involved in the study for their thoughts on the Do No Harm database and did not immediately hear back.
In 2022, Reuters, a credible news source, analyzed data from Komodo Health — considered the most complete health insurance database available — and found 238 mastectomies, or top surgeries, in 2019, 256 in 2020 and 282 in 2021 among trans minors. The analysis also found 56 genital surgeries among patients ages 13 to 17 with a prior gender dysphoria diagnosis from 2019 to 2021.
However, the Reuters analysis did not appear to separate out trans youth who received these surgeries due to health issues unrelated to gender identity, unlike the peer-reviewed study from Harvard researchers.
Furthermore, any increase in gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors has likely reversed due to the rise in anti-trans health care policies across the country and on the federal level, Baker said.
The bottom line
The data HHS cited in its report comes from an anti-LGBTQ+ group that used faulty analysis to inflate data on gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors.
It's more accurate to say that from 2019 to 2023, more than 5,500 minors, many of whom had a gender dysphoria diagnosis at one point in time, received various procedures for any number of medical reasons, the vast majority of which were unrelated to being trans.
Peer-reviewed research suggests that gender-affirming surgeries among minors are incredibly rare and usually involve cisgender boys undergoing chest reductions.

Ex-Louisiana mayor released after serving 90-day sentence for raping teen boy at pool party
Judge Kent Savoie acknowledged that he made mistake in sentencing of former DeRidder Mayor Misty Roberts, but denied request to amend ruling
A former Louisiana mayor, Misty Roberts, is out of jail after serving her 90-day prison sentence for raping a 16-year-old boy during her tenure.
Roberts, 44, finished her term on Monday, a week after the judge who presided over her case rejected a request from prosecutors to force her to serve a more severe sentence, according to KPLC.
Judge Kent Savoie said he based Roberts' sentence on more than 30 cases that culminated in plea deals. However, Roberts did not take a plea — she was convicted in a jury trial.
Savoie has acknowledged that he made a mistake in basing his sentencing on cases that ended with plea deals, but did not opt to amend his sentencing after the ruling.
“I asked someone to get me a list of cases similar,” he said during a court hearing on August 31. “I made an assumption, and that assumption was wrong. I was wrong in that respect.”
Had she not been given the lighter sentence, she could have faced up to 17 years in prison following her conviction for statutory rape.
According to prosecutors, she raped the teenage victim at a pool party at her home in July 2024. She was serving as the mayor of DeRidder at the time of the incident. She resigned just days before her arrest.
The victim was a local high school student who was friends with Roberts' son.
Her sentence was met with frustration by some community members who thought she was getting off without a proper punishment.
“When it comes to children, we should use the fullest extent of the law. There are no excuses when it comes to our children," DeRidder resident Karin McGee told local broadcaster KALB.
Another resident, Ryan Clark, called the 90-day sentence "an insult."
In addition to the jail time, Roberts was also ordered to pay $5,000 in fines, submit to regular drug screenings, register as a sex offender, and undergo psychotropic and psychological therapy.
If she violates her release conditions, she will be forced to serve two suspended five-year prison sentences concurrently, according to the ruling.
During her sentencing on June 9, Roberts addressed the judge and said she was at fault for what happened.
“I blame myself then, I blame myself today and I will blame myself for the rest of my life. I let a lot of people down, and I am the only person responsible for that," she said, according to KPLC.
She said she hit "the absolute floor" the day she committed the crime, and called herself an "embarrassment."
“What an embarrassment I’ve been to this city,” she said. “I’ve made a mess of all of this, but it certainly was not my intent.”
During victim impact statements, the victim's mother called Roberts "a predator with hair extensions, high heels [and] Botox" and warned her to "stay the hell away from my family," according to the broadcaster.
Beauregard Parish District Attorney James Lestage said the prosecution did what it could to put Roberts away for longer.
“We’ve done our part. We’ve done what we could to present the evidence to protect and represent the victims. I think the jury saw that. The jury convicted her. We argued for the maximum sentences, which we feel are appropriate," he said, according to KPLC. "I don’t think the sentence that was imposed reflects the severity of the crimes. It doesn’t, in my opinion, represent the values of Beauregard Parish."
Roberts' defense attorneys, Adam Johnson and Todd S Clemons, said their client would adhere to all of her post-release conditions.
"She was sincere, strong, and apologetic for her actions in her address to the Court today and we believe that also had a real impact on this outcome," they said.
Roberts also apologized to the victim's family.
“I can’t give back the high school days … I can’t take away the embarrassment that so many mean people on the internet have put them through," she said.

Approximately one in eight girls/women, experienced rape or sexual assault before turning 18, according to UNICEF 2024 estimates. Global estimates have also documented substantial sexual abuse among boys. Child sexual abuse is predominantly seen as a social evil and crime against humanity, but it is equally a serious public health problem. Yet our response understandably revolves around the perpetrator. Was the crime reported? Has the accused been arrested? Will the prosecution succeed? What punishment will follow?
For the young person or child, however, punishment of the offender does not reverse what has happened. There may be physical injuries to treat, infections to prevent, pregnancy to consider and psychological wounds that may surface immediately or years later. Healthcare must begin even if justice is delayed.
The first contact with the healthcare system is crucial. Depending on the nature and timing of the assault, the child may require treatment for physical injuries, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, and assessment of the risk of HIV. When indicated, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should be started as early as possible and within 72 hours. Emergency contraception can be offered to girls at risk of pregnancy who present within 120 hours. Hepatitis B and HPV vaccination, STI prophylaxis or treatment and pregnancy-related care may also be required. This is why medical examination after sexual assault cannot become merely an exercise in collecting evidence for a criminal case. Evidence matters, but the survivor is also simultaneously a patient sitting in front of the doctor.
Unseen injuries
The immediate psychological response to sexual abuse may include fear, confusion, shame, anger, numbness, disturbed sleep or silence. A child may not even have the vocabulary to explain what has happened. The first psychological intervention, therefore, is not necessarily psychotherapy, but safety. The child must be protected from further abuse, listened to without blame and helped to regain a sense of security and normalcy. Repeatedly asking the child to recount traumatic details can itself cause distress.
While some children recover with family support and appropriate care, others may develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, nightmares, intrusive memories, hypervigilance or dissociation. Self-harm, suicidal thoughts, eating disorders, substance misuse and behavioural problems can also occur. Longer-term difficulties may involve self-worth, emotional regulation, trust, intimacy and relationships.
Experiencing trauma does not automatically mean developing a psychiatric disorder. Outcomes vary with age, developmental stage, duration of abuse, relationship with the perpetrator and support following disclosure. This is why every survivor should receive a baseline mental health assessment covering mood, sleep, behaviour, schooling, relationships, self-harm and suicidality. Its purpose is not to label the child as mentally ill, but to establish a clinical reference point from which recovery or emerging difficulties can be followed.
Trauma over time
Sexual abuse is also not invariably a single traumatic incident. For most children, particularly when the perpetrator has regular access or authority, abuse may recur for months or years. What clinicians encounter may therefore be the cumulative effect of repeated exposure.
Even after the abuse stops, recovery is not governed by a calendar. Memories, family responses, seeing the perpetrator, investigation and court proceedings can reactivate distress. Childhood is also the period during which emotional regulation, self-concept and ideas about safety and relationships are developing. Trauma occurring during these formative years can become entangled with these processes.
Healing consequently means more than making traumatic memories disappear. It means helping the child resume development. Returning to school, playing, sleeping normally, rebuilding relationships and recovering a sense of safety and control can themselves be important parts of recovery.
Paths to recovery
Treatment must be individualised. Supportive psychotherapy and counselling may be sufficient for some. Children with significant symptoms require assessment by trained mental health professionals. Cognitive behavioural therapy helps identify connections between thoughts, emotions and behaviour and develops healthier ways of responding to distress.
For children and adolescents with post-traumatic stress symptoms or PTSD, trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, or TF-CBT, is an important evidence-based option. It can teach skills to manage anxiety, gradually and safely process traumatic memories, challenge beliefs such as self-blame and help restore normal functioning.
Other interventions, including interpersonal psychotherapy for appropriate emotional disorders and EMDR for PTSD, may have a role depending on clinical assessment. The principle is that every survivor deserves an assessment and access to care, but not every survivor needs the same treatment.
Families matter
Recovery also rarely happens in the consulting room alone. A supportive, non-offending parent or caregiver can be one of the child’s greatest protective resources. Families need guidance on how to respond to disclosure, avoid blaming or repeatedly questioning the child, recognise warning signs, and restore ordinary routines without pretending that nothing happened.
Where safe and appropriate, caregivers can participate in trauma-focused therapy. They, too, may require psychological support. A parent discovering that their child has been sexually abused may experience guilt, anger, helplessness and enormous distress. Helping the caregiver can indirectly strengthen the child’s recovery.
Building capacity
This requires more than appointing counsellors. The system needs to facilitate frontline doctors, paediatricians, gynaecologists, nurses and counsellors to provide immediate trauma-informed care. District services need access to clinical psychologists and psychiatrists, with clear referral pathways for children requiring specialised interventions. The healthcare providers themselves also need protection. Listening repeatedly to accounts of sexual violence can result in secondary or vicarious trauma. Supervision, manageable caseloads, debriefing, peer support, and periods away from continuous trauma work should be built into services rather than regarded as luxuries.
Eventually, the success of our response cannot be measured only by whether justice was set in motion: it is whether the infection was prevented, whether reproductive healthcare was provided, whether the child’s mental health was assessed, whether treatment was available when needed, whether the family knew how to support the child, whether the child returned to school and, ultimately, whether that child was able to move forward.
A humane health system must, at first, ask what needs to happen for the child, while law simultaneously addressing what needs to happen for justice.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

'We're not robots' - why US Open men's contenders have tumbled
- Published
Talent, athleticism and commitment are not nearly enough to become a Grand Slam singles champion.
Possessing the confidence that you can beat anyone on the biggest stage - where the eyes of the world are fixed on you and there is no place to hide - is arguably the most important characteristic a player can have.
Unwavering belief. Or, as former US Open runner-up Taylor Fritz describes it, delusion.
Fritz is one of the current crop of leading men yet to get his hands on one of the sport's major prizes. The world number 10 is also one of the guys who has blown what looked like a golden opportunity to win this year's US Open.
With Jannik Sinner missing through injury, and Carlos Alcaraz making his comeback from his long lay-off, it felt like a tournament where the leading seeds could capitalise.
Instead, six of the top 10 perished by the fourth round at Flushing Meadows - including Fritz, who squandered a two-set lead against Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo in round three.
Former champion Daniil Medvedev's fourth-round exit on Sunday means the only top-10 players remaining are top seed Alexander Zverev, defending champion Alcaraz and eighth seed Ben Shelton.
"It shows you how even the circuit is, how tight every match is, how difficult it is to win matches," said 24th seed Cerundolo.
"Anything can happen right now."
The dominance of Sinner and Alcaraz - who have won 10 of the past 11 Grand Slam men's singles titles between them - adds to the pressure.
Speaking to the Guardian, external earlier this year, 28-year-old Fritz said he believes he will feel an "emptiness" at the end of his career if he does not win a Grand Slam title.
World number two Zverev finally landed his first major at this year's French Open, but revealed afterwards he "could not sleep" and was "not eating" during previous Slam fortnights because of nerves.
Once he released the pressure valve, the 29-year-old German went on to reach the Wimbledon final - where he played freer but still lost to Sinner - and remains in the hunt at the US Open.
Zverev is scrambling through his half of the draw despite being far from his best, but the spectre of Alcaraz - who is getting better with every win - looms large.
"The two-horse race between Sinner and Alcaraz is not healthy for the tour," former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"With every win, Alcaraz is becoming more of a favourite. Four months off, no matches and he could win the US Open."
Are there other reasons behind early exits?
Pressure is not the sole reason for the leading seeds tumbling in New York.
One argument is that the current top 10 - Sinner and Alcaraz aside - is weaker than it has been for a while.
Illness, injuries and fatigue also contributed at the final major of a demanding season.
Fourth seed Novak Djokovic's ageing body let him down in his shock first-round exit, while third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime put his second-round loss down to suffering dizziness.
Fifth seed Flavio Cobolli said he lacked energy in a third-round defeat, which he attributed to his volume of matches and New York's sapping heat.
Cincinnati champion Arthur Fils lost a tough opener against former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas, while teenager Rafael Jodar - who has played more than 50 matches in his first full season on tour - looked drained during his first-round exit.
"The season is long. I think all the guys who performed well in the preparation tournaments have it more difficult here," said Belgium’s Alexander Blockx, who knocked out French Open finalist Cobolli.
"We're all human. We're not robots. Every week is difficult. Especially at a Grand Slam where it gets even more physical.
"Mentally you have to really stay in it."
The calm amid the chaos - but anyone can also win women's title
The chaotic nature of the men's draw has been a sharp contrast to the calm of the women's.
Eleven of the top 16 seeds reached the fourth round, led by two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka and Australian Open winner Elena Rybakina.
Neither dropped a set on their way to the last 16, while American pair Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff - seeded third and fourth - progressed without any serious scares.
French Open winner Mirra Andreeva and Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova ensured the top six seeds remained unscathed.
Two-time major finalist Karolina Muchova, Ukraine's Elina Svitolina and 2025 US Open runner-up Amanda Anisimova were the first top-10 seeds to be eliminated when they lost in the third round.
"It is great for the women's tour to have so many people who could possibly win," added Cash.
"Anyone can win at any time - doesn't that make it exciting?"
The past seven Grand Slams have produced seven different winners - a stark contrast to Sinner and Alcaraz's dominance - and leads to a school of thought that the current crop of top stars feel less burden than the men.
Everyone in the top 10 is a reigning Slam or WTA 1,000 champion, underlining their ability to triumph on the biggest stages.
The four leading players locked in a battle at Flushing Meadows for the top ranking adds another element to the dynamic.
Sabalenka has been the world number one for the past two years, but has recently suffered a dip of form which leaves her position under severe threat.
Rybakina is guaranteed to overtake Sabalenka if she reaches the semi-finals, while Pegula and Gauff could pounce if they win the title.
"Looking at the difference between the points in the top 10 compared to the men, you can see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.
"Everyone has been very consistent and makes it hard to a certain extent [to win a Slam].
"But then you know there's not one or two super dominant players where you feel like they have to lose in order for you to have a chance."

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Pam Manfredo Curtis, author of "Origin of a Leader." It has been edited for length and clarity.
It's no surprise that we often make choices based on how we were raised. I can see it in my own life: my mom was a school psychologist. I went into psychology, too, and married a man who is also an industrial and organizational psychologist, like me.
In our field, there's a lot of focus on empathy, tuning in to others, and helping them understand why they show up the way they do. Oftentimes, the answer lies in childhood.
I know that might sound like psychological gobbley gook, or Freudian hogwash. I've had clients tell me that. But after working with me, they realize that emotions are data. Leaders and companies can use that data to excel — and that emotional information is becoming more important than ever in the age of AI.
Parents worry about the wrong things
Parents often worry about the little mistakes they make. The moment when you raise your voice, or say the wrong thing, can haunt you. Luckily, those aren't usually the things that stick with our kids over time.
What matters more is our parenting patterns. Children pay attention to how we build relationships, express love, and deal with conflict. Those teachings will stay with them long into their adulthood and career.
Teaching kids to name emotions is key
I often ask the executives whom I coach how they are feeling. Their response is usually the same: "Fine."
I sometimes want to yell, "Fine is not an emotion!" Once, I was working with an executive of a well-known company, asking him again and again how he was feeling, and he answered, "Fine. Fine. Fine." One day, he said "sad," and I thought "woohoo. There's something I can work with."
The greatest executives I work with are able to tune into and name the emotions they're feeling. They understand why they're feeling the way they are, and can tell others. This is important data for them and their company — and something that can't be replicated by AI. Teaching children to recognize their emotions will equip them for the C-suite — or any other career.
Check in with head, heart, and hands
In all my meetings, I typically start by asking people to check in on their heads, hearts, and hands. Your head tells you what you're thinking. Your heart is about what emotion you're feeling and why: for example, I feel nervous because I'm not sure what to expect. Your hands represent the physical — time constraints, hunger, or distracting muscle tension.
Sharing what's in our heads, hands, and hearts builds trust. Once you've become vulnerable, there are no hidden agendas. It's a great practice to do with kids, to help them connect with their emotional state.
Point out strengths — even in challenging situations
The environment in which children are raised shapes them as adults. A person raised in a stable home with high expectations and lots of love will likely become good at nurturing others. Even psychologically complex or traumatic environments can give rise to strength. An abused child who had someone advocate for them often becomes a fierce advocate for others, for example.
Each situation, and how a person responds to it, is unique. I always tried to let my children know what I thought was beautiful about them. I highlighted their strengths and validated their worries while pointing out what I really admired about them.
Giving children agency and helping them feel heard will strengthen their ability to move forward, even in the face of difficult emotions or circumstances.

Health minister Kenichiro Ueno, who oversees the Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), said the fund is still considering whether a review of its asset allocation is needed.
The fund “decided in March that there wasn’t a need for it, but my understanding is that it’s continuing to consider the matter in an appropriate way,” Ueno said at a regular news conference in Tokyo on Tuesday. He also said that the investment environment hasn’t diverged too much from the GPIF’s assumptions for its portfolio.
The GPIF’s allocation decisions are closely watched by traders around the world due to its mammoth size, overseeing about ¥318 trillion ($2.1 trillion) in assets at the end of June. That means that on paper a 1 percentage-point change in allocations can translate to more than ¥3 trillion in fund flows.
The pension fund now tries to hold 25% each of four asset classes in its investment portfolio — domestic bonds, overseas debt, Japanese shares and foreign equities. But analysts have said that after surges in Japanese bond yields in past months, there’s scope for GPIF to expand its allocation target for domestic bonds.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama have also called on Japanese pension funds to park more funds in the home market.
GPIF’s management committee convened on Aug. 21, its first publicly announced meeting during the holiday month in seven years. The gathering spurred speculation that the fund may change its allocation.

A horror story of sorts is unfolding in the United States. It goes like this: AI has made it so effortless to access information, and short-form video has made it so easy to entertain ourselves, that nobody reads anymore.
It shouldn’t feel impossible to finish a book
Screens have atrophied our reading muscles. Here’s how to get them back.
If you’re familiar with this tale, it’s possible, ironically, that you read about it. A viral Atlantic story from earlier this summer put a chilling headline on trend: “The End of Reading Is Here.” Teachers and professors, the magazine reported, don’t even bother assigning entire books to their students, because excerpts are good enough to prepare for standardized texts. The piece said we’re living in a “postliterate era.”
This is a cultural crisis, yes — but for a lot of us, it’s a personal one. We’re all short on time, and we’d like to read more, but the ascendancy of attention-stealing tech companies has made it feel like we have less of it.
“Reading was and is a crime of opportunity,” said Leah Price, a professor of modern book history at Oxford and the author of What We Talk About When We Talk About Books. “The limiting factor isn’t reading matter, but reading time.”
Key takeaways
- Reading is changing, not dying. The bigger problem is competition for people’s time and attention.
- Print offers productive difficulty. E-readers and audiobooks make reading easier, but the friction of print promotes deeper comprehension.
- Leisure reading should be fun! It’s totally fine to peek at the ending, skip boring parts, or just give up on boring books.
Losing the reading habit is especially bad because it’s a healthy practice in a world obsessed with self-improvement. Studies suggest that reading is an astonishingly good mental exercise, as well as a very accessible one. Reading, especially leisure reading, can improve your language skills. It exposes you to new knowledge and ideas. Reading can help relieve stress, anxiety, and insomnia. It can make you more empathetic and combat cognitive decline. Reading is absolutely great for kids. Reading, perhaps above all, also happens to be fun.
There are, I’m happy to say, some bright spots in this story — and some helpful news.
There’s evidence that reading isn’t over. It’s just changing. A 2025 Pew study found that the number of Americans who say they read books has remained roughly the same in recent years, although the way that they read them is changing. The vast majority of books read in the United States are print, but a growing number of people are reading e-books and listening to audiobooks. The number of print books sold is actually growing on the backs of the science fiction and self-help genres. The number of e-books and audiobooks borrowed from their local libraries, meanwhile, topped 820 million last year, a new record. There’s no shortage of books to read. And it’s never been easier to access any book you want in your preferred format.
The other bit of good news is useful to you: Reading is like a muscle. Even if you feel like your ability to pore over a book has atrophied, that muscle is still there, ready for exercise. The more you do read, the more your vocabulary improves, the more you learn, and the more you’re able to put new information in context. In other words, the more you read, the better you get at it. And probably as a result, the less appealing algorithmic feeds become.
It’s one of those personal habits that extends beyond your own life, too. Becoming a better reader is good for American society. The nation’s founders believed that an informed citizenry was necessary to preserve democracy — and to prevent tyranny. A nation of people passively flipping through 10-second videos on a smartphone or bedrotting with a streaming show can be informed in a sense. You might want to be a better American.
The big question, then, is: How does one become a better reader in an era that increasingly appears to be postliterate? Actually, there are some interesting insights — and ironically, some technology — that can help.
Reduce friction
One thing that keeps a lot of people from reading is simply friction. Reading can be hard — or at least effortful — for a lot of different reasons.
For me, I hit friction every time I pick up all 1,300 dense pages of The Power Broker by Robert Caro. It’s the weight of a doorstop in my hands, as I struggle with the context of mid-century New York bureaucratic history, ultimately unsure if I’ll live long enough to reach the end of the book. Reading is full of friction, and finding ways to reduce friction is one way to read better.
Technology is good at this. Just take the growth in e-book popularity as proof. Whereas people over 65 have historically read more than young people, more than 40 percent of young people have read an e-book in the past year, according to an April Pew study. You can’t blame them. Once you get used to the lack of pages and paper, e-readers are incredibly convenient. The classic Kindle Paperwhite is more portable than a doorstop, and you can keep an entire library on something the size of a side plate. It’s even waterproof, or at least more waterproof than paper. More advanced devices, like the Kobo Libre Colour, offer color e-ink displays and the ability to scribble on the page.
What turned me into a Kindle enthusiast is the existence of Libby, an app that lets you check out e-books from your local library. From the comfort of the New York City subway, I can find, borrow, and download just about any book I’d ever want and start reading it in a matter of seconds. You might call this a frictionless experience. The raw simplicity of the device also means that I can’t easily navigate away from the book to check my email or start doomscrolling.
Audiobooks open up another avenue: the ability to read a book while doing something else, like chores or driving. You might disagree on whether listening to an audiobook counts as “reading,” but there’s evidence that people can comprehend and retain information from audiobooks equally as well as they can from printed material. Audiobooks can even make difficult language more accessible for more readers.
There are drawbacks, too. Audiobooks force you to listen at the speed of the narrator, although you can probably speed it up or slow it down in increments. And it’s difficult to go back and review the text or to skip ahead, which is also true for e-books. This spatial component of reading is something that printed books will always have going for them. Rereading text can improve comprehension, and the spatial nature of books makes it easier to find certain passages. Just think about that effortless feeling of flipping back toward the beginning of a book for that really juicy section. That’s not easy to do on a Kindle or with an e-book.
There’s an interesting paradox here: In order to become a better reader, you need to reduce enough friction that you read more. But you also need to preserve certain kinds of friction that help you fully appreciate what you’re reading.
Embrace useful friction
There’s a good reason your teachers and professors assigned hard books when you were in school. “Learning only happens when there is some cognitive friction, if you’re actually grappling with the ideas,” said Daniel Willingham, a psychology professor at the University of Virginia.
Reading difficult text, scribbling notes in the margins, rereading the difficult text, taking breaks to think about it — this friction-full process leads to deeper comprehension. Certain inconveniences that come with reading print books, including turning physical pages and navigating the spatial elements of the object, invite you to do the mental work that promotes learning. Screens, with their lack of friction, may actually make it harder to comprehend what you’re reading.
The advantage of print is small but meaningful. A 2018 meta-analysis of nearly two decades’ worth of studies showed that paper-based reading had a slight advantage to screen-based reading when it came to comprehension, especially when dealing with informational texts, rather than narratives. Another meta-analysis published a year later suggested that readers were more efficient when reading on paper and, interestingly, seemed to have a more accurate awareness of how well they understood the text. In other words, when you read on your phone, you might think you’re absorbing more than you actually are.
There are other drawbacks to reading on screens. Scrolling alone is bad for comprehension, according to yet another meta-analysis, because it basically forces us to lose our place on the page. There’s also been research into how reading on screens demands more of our cognitive resources than reading on paper, perhaps because the technology requires the reader to process more information, leaving them with a little less gas in the tank to actually comprehend the text. But again, plenty of studies show that the difference in how well we comprehend information by reading on screens versus print is small.
What’s perhaps more meaningful are the vibes we bring when we approach a medium. We’ve been trained to read on screens a certain way, according to Naomi Baron, a professor emerita of linguistics at American University. From the early days of Google, screens became places where we searched and scanned for information, quickly clicking through to the next page in pursuit of an answer. That’s a far cry from the millennia-old tradition of poring over printed manuscripts.
“We got used to thinking a digital device is that which one doesn’t concentrate on,” Baron said. “One keeps moving like a shark. … Print is a medium that encourages stopping.”
It turns out two things can be true. Indeed, keeping a smartphone next to you while you’re trying to read a book is an invitation to distraction. You may also feel like your attention span is already shredded, probably thanks to your smartphone. You just have to be more intentional about your attention and harness your focus. Taking breaks can help restore your attention stamina, especially if you do so in nature. Try reading a book for a few minutes every day, and you’ll soon find that you can read for longer. The next thing you know, you’ll have read a book.
Let’s not lose the plot here
Some people read to learn. Others read because their job demands it. The luckiest of us read for fun. Some people read to escape or to imagine. And depending on your purpose, you might choose a different approach or device to stuff that text into your brain.
If you’re simply trying to become a better reader, it doesn’t matter how you do it.
You should keep reading, again, because reading more makes you better at reading. If you’re trying to learn, printed books can facilitate that, but you can also learn quite a bit by listening to an audiobook. If a Kindle and a library card can unlock all the hard sci-fi and fantasy your eyes could ever consume, go for it and enjoy.
Part of what keeps some people from reading, I have to imagine, is the preconception that reading needs to be difficult to be rewarding. And as many teachers and professors will point out to you, navigating your mind through the difficult text can be especially rewarding, since that friction leads to better comprehension and learning. Still, you don’t need to read everything like you’re trying to get a good grade.
“There are no rules about leisure reading,” Willingham told me. “You can peek at the end. If you’re not enjoying a book, drop it. You can do whatever you want. The whole point is for you to have fun.”
You should read material that feels magnetic to you, that keeps you coming back for more. If reading is going to have any chance of competing with TikTok, it needs to be interesting and compelling, regardless of how literary or sophisticated you might think reading needs to be. You should read books, longform articles, and blog posts on whatever medium makes sense in that moment — and whatever medium makes it easy to keep reading.
That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t try to read the big difficult, doorstopper-sized classics, though, if that’s important to you. Just think twice about using AI to summarize what you’re reading. It’s tempting to ask ChatGPT why Anna Karenina is a classic — I just did, and ChatGPT says “psychological realism, moral complexity, continuing relevance” — but it’s not fun.
Using AI as a reading partner may help initial understanding of reading material, but old habits like note-taking better promote engagement and long-term comprehension. Pia Kreijkes, senior researcher at Cambridge University Press & Assessment and author of a study on this topic published earlier this year, is worried about young people leaning on AI to do more of the cognitive lifting that reading requires.
“Given that children are already on a trajectory of declining reading frequency and enjoyment, and that reading skills are also declining, we should be very concerned about this,” Kreijkes said. “The more we use AI to reduce our reading effort, the more likely reading skills are to decline.”
After all, if the kids stop reading, there’s not a whole lot of hope for future generations to be readers of books. If we let technology remove too much friction from our pursuit of knowledge, we will lose the plot entirely and slide into the postliterate horror so many people are currently afraid of, AI-dominated dystopia and all. When you put it that way, though, this is also a great premise for a sci-fi novel.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has distanced itself from the hooliganism at the Anandabazar Patrika (ABP) office in Kolkata on September 1, with state spokesperson Debjit Sarkar asserting that BJP was not involved in the incident and that “wearing saffron could not be a political identity”. “I don’t know who all went there. Wearing saffron cannot be a political identity. If any particular person is identified, the party can comment on it. Our party does not condone attacks on any place. We don’t know who went there, but our party was not involved,” he said.
A group of saffron-clad men shouted slogans and painted the walls of the ABP office in Kolkata saffron on Tuesday, days after West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari had demanded an apology from the daily for describing the violence at Jadavpur University on July 19 and 20 as “gerua gundami” — or “saffron hooliganism”.
When Alt News examined the footage of the raid on the ABP office closely, we identified three men with direct BJP links leading the group. One, Pramod Dubey, was seen addressing the crowd. He is a BJP worker. The other, Suraj Verma, another BJP worker, was seen painting a pillar on the left side of the main gate, and the third, Ravi Gupta, the president of Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha (BJYM) Uttar Howrah 1 Mandal, was also in the group.
See the graphics below:
Both Dubey and Verma’s social media profiles have ample proof of them being active BJP workers for years. In the following photo posted by Verma on Facebook on August 20. Dubey is tagged in it.
Pramod Dubey: BJP Worker from Howrah
Pramod Dubey was seen speaking to the gathering outside the ABP office on September 1.
On his Facebook page, he has photos with several BJP MPs and MLAs, including Sanjay Bhatia, Rakesh Singh, Kartik Maharaj, Rudranil Ghosh, Krishnendu Mukherjee and Sanjay Singh.
His Facebook and Instagram accounts contain multiple posts in which he addresses the public against the backdrop of BJP Uttar Howrah’s banner, speaking on a range of political issues.
Following the ABP incident, Dubey posted a video with the caption, “today we painted Anandabazar Patrika office”.
In another reel that he shared, Dubey responded to Alt News’s investigation into the incident at ABP office with communal slurs directed at its co-founder, Mohammad Zubair. Here, too, he is seen sitting in front of a BJP North Howrah banner.
Alt News found that in 2021, Dubey was reportedly shot at during a clash between BJP and TMC workers. On January 23, 2021, the official X account for BJP Howrah Sadar shared a post identifying Dubey as their party worker.
Suraj Verma: BJP Worker from Howrah
Another individual identified at the scene was Suraj Verma, who describes himself in his Facebook bio as a “BJP Youth Leader” from Howrah.
He was seen smearing saffron paint on a pillar at the ABP office.
He shared the video himself with the caption, “ABP Group still hasn’t apologised for its hurtful “SAFFRON TERROR” headline on the ABVP protest at Jadavpur University. Today, we painted ABP’s office walls SAFFRON…”
Verma’s social media profiles also contain photographs documenting his association with BJP leaders, including his photos with BJP MP Sanjay Bhatia and West Bengal PWD minister and Kulti MLA Dr Ajay Kumar Poddar. His Instagram timeline also has his photos where he is wearing a membership card issued by Anjani Putra Sena, a Hindutva outfit.
Ravi Gupta: BJYM Howrah North-1 President
Alt News also identified Ravi Gupta, president of BJYM Uttar Howrah Mandal 1, among the group present at the ABP office.
Gupta went live on Facebook from the site on September 1, recording the protest and the act of Suraj Verma painting the building’s pillars saffron.
On August 6, BJP Howrah Sadar on its official Facebook page shared a list of the names of BJYM office bearers from the district. Ravi Gupta is named as the president of Uttar Howrah 1 local committee.
Gupta’s social media profiles contain photographs with senior BJP figures, including West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and the MLA from the Howrah Uttar constituency, Umesh Rai.
Taken together, these pieces of evidence confirm that the raid on the Anandabazar Patrika office at Prafulla Sarkar Street in Kolkata on September 1 was led by BJP workers.

Trump mocked over his new design for Space Force uniforms: ‘The evil bad guys from Star Wars’
The uniforms were inspired by Starship Troopers, a 1997 space epic about a future Earth governed by a fascist regime that wages war against giant alien bugs
Donald Trump has been mocked over his new design for Space Force uniforms, with social media users comparing them to the costumes worn by sci-fi villains – and even Nazis.
The president raised eyebrows Sunday after posting a graphic of a “next generation” design for Space Force uniforms that includes a sleek, charcoal-colored collared jacket and pants with a black belt, black boots and a matching cap. There’s also the Space Force Delta symbol on the collar, sleeve patch, belt buckle and the front of the cap.
The graphic says the design is “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper uniform. Modernized for the guardians of the space domain.”
Starship Troopers is a 1997 space epic — directed by Paul Verhoeven, who grew up in Nazi-occupied Netherlands — about a future Earth governed by a fascist regime that wages war against giant alien bugs. Some social media users picked up on the inspiration behind the uniforms, while others compared them to other space films.
“Designing the Space Force uniforms to look like the evil bad guys from Star Wars, who are led by an elderly, power hungry tyrant, who lose, repeatedly, is a bit too on brand, no?” healthcare advocate Melanie D'Arrigo wrote on X.
An independent military history author who goes by ChrisO_wiki shared a GIF of a scene from the 1987 Star Wars parody film Spaceballs, and wrote, “Ah yes, I see the source of inspiration for this uniform.”
“This is the kind of design costume designers make to tell you who are the bad guys in a space movie,” menswear writer Derek Guy posted.
Speaking on Starship Troopers, Jonah Goldberg, the editor-in-chief at The Dispatch, a digital media company focused on politics and culture, said, “My concern is whether these guys understand the point Verhoeven intended in Starship Troopers.
“The thing is I don’t know what would be worse: whether they got it or didn’t.”
A political X account that goes by Wu Tang is for the Children sarcastically wrote, “No Nazi vibes here.”
Several conservative voices also chimed in, noting the similarity to Star Wars uniforms.
Christian broadcaster Erick Erickson called the uniforms, “A cross between Star Trek in the symbols and Imperial Forces from Star Wars.”
Jennifer Zilla, who identifies as a “conservative critic,” said she was “entirely on board with Space Force and the new Space Academy coming and everything we’re doing in space and President Trump.”
But she admitted that the new design was “the uniform of the Imperial Army from Star Wars.”
“Aka the people Darth Vader works for. Emperor Palpatine’s people. I’m not saying don’t use it I’m just pointing out that’s what it is,” she wrote.
It’s unclear if Trump will actually push to change the design of Space Force uniforms or if the graphic was just part of one of his regular social media sprees.
The Independent has reached out to the Space Force and White House for comment.

Black boxes recovered from Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami
5 people were killed in Sunday’s crash. Investigators will seek to determine where the plane landed and why the pilots did not abandon the landing
Investigators with the US National Transportation Safety Board said on Monday they had recovered the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder from an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran the runway and crashed while landing in Miami on Sunday, killing five people on the ground.
NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said the two devices, commonly referred to as the black boxes, were being returned to the agency’s headquarters in Washington on Monday night for evaluation.
The 32-year-old Boeing 767-33A, operated by Miami-based 21 Air LLC, overran the runway by some 396 metres (1,300ft) and crashed into two vehicles on the ground: an Econoline van on the airport grounds carrying seven people from an airline cleaning crew and a Toyota SUV that was driving on a road beyond the perimeter fence.
The two people aboard the plane, the pilot and co-pilot, survived and had yet to be interviewed, Homendy said in a press conference.
Five people were injured, three of them critically, officials said on Sunday.
Homendy, leading a team of 32 investigators at Miami International Airport, briefed reporters on the early stages of the investigation but said a probable cause of the accident would not be determined until the end of the investigation.
The NTSB was still recovering and recording evidence, and crews were still removing jet fuel from the scene and aircraft, keeping two of the airport’s four runways closed. Although the airport halted all flights immediately after the crash, flights had resumed by Sunday evening.

- There are a total of two bosses that players can fight in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4.
- Each boss drops a Mythic/Legendary variant of a weapon and Gold Bars, along with some healing items.
- Epic will add more bosses to Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 as the season continues.
Geno has employed bosses in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 to do his bidding, and their locations have been revealed for everyone to challenge. They are infused with dark energies, which make them a tad difficult to face in combat, but are worth challenging for rewards. That said, here are all Fortnite boss locations in Chapter 7 Season 4 and how to defeat them all.
All Boss Locations in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4
At the time of writing, there are only two bosses whose locations have been revealed on the Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 map that can be challenged and defeated for rewards. They are:
- Doctor Eggman: Found in Green Hill Zone POI
- Hush: Found in Reality’s Reign POI
They have fixed spawn areas, which means you won’t need to look for them elsewhere. Here are all the possible boss locations in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 marked on a handy mini-map:
Keep in mind that while Fortnite Boss spawn area locations in Chapter 7 Season 4 are fixed, they do move about a bit. That said, let’s talk about each boss, how to defeat them, and what rewards they’ll drop once defeated.
How to Defeat Doctor Eggman Boss in Fortnite
Doctor Eggman is the stronger of the two bosses in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4, and his location is perhaps the most active region to land in. He can be found in the Green Hill Zone POI on the eastern edge of the region and next to Geno’s Machine Landmark (spire in the center of the map).
We recommend using the Fortnite Mega Buster when engaging to keep a safe distance. Moreover, with this being one of the most active Fortnite locations in Chapter 7 Season 4, you won’t just be dealing with the boss. Expect to face other players as well.
Doctor Eggman has two attacks in Fortnite: one that shoots projectiles in a fast-moving horizontal arc, and a slam attack that does AoE damage. His health pool is also quite vast, so bring plenty of ammo. When defeated, you will get a Fortnite 1-Up Token alongside other rewards, such as:
- Midas’ Masterpiece
- Sonic Power Sneakers
- Chug Jug
- Ammo
- Gold Bars
We recommend looking for a Golden Fishing Spot in Fortnite to get good gear before trying to engage Doctor Eggman. This will let you inflict the maximum amount of damage in the shortest possible time frame.
How to Defeat Hush Boss in Fortnite
Hush is the weaker of the two Fortnite bosses in Chapter 7 Season 4, and while her location is easy to find, it’s a hot-drop POI, and as such, you will need to be careful. You’ll find her patrolling the road to the south of the Reality’s Reign POI, just outside a little outpost.
As you engage her in combat, she will activate a boost. This allows her to move faster and deal quite a bit of damage. Also watch out for Tetris Rift items she throws to protect herself. However, with her health pool being rather small, you won’t have trouble eliminating her. When defeated, she will drop the following items from the Fortnite loot pool:
- Enhanced Assault Rifle
- Tetris Rift
- Gold Adventure Sprite
- Gold Bars
- Ammo
We recommend keeping a pair of Fortnite Sonic Power Sneakers in your inventory, just in case you need to retreat or rotate if things get too difficult. Also, if you get a Gold Sprite, we highly recommend that you extract it as soon as possible.
That’s all you need to know about the locations of all bosses in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4. We will update the list if and when Epic Games adds more bosses to the island. Until then, go and try your luck against Geno’s lackeys.

John Ternus faces the tough task of balancing Steve Jobs’ product-first innovation with Tim Cook’s business success. As Apple’s new CEO, he must revive innovation, fix its AI struggles, manage rising costs, and keep Apple at the top.
It is September, and around this time of year my stories usually start with “Tis the iPhone season” (not kidding, you can check). While the new iPhones are still coming early in September, this story is not about the iPhone but rather about the people behind it, or rather Apple in general.
After 15 years of taking care of CEO business, Tim Cook finally bid farewell to Apple. On his last day in the role, on 31 August 2026, he penned an emotional memo addressed to “Team”. Cook has not cut ties with Apple completely but will now serve as the Executive Chairman of Apple’s Board of Directors.
John Ternus has taken over the reins as Apple’s new CEO. He has been with Apple since 2001 and has climbed the corporate ladder, all the way from being a member of the product design team to the CEO position in 2026. In case you do not know him well, we got you covered.
A full circle moment for Apple
This change in command feels like Apple’s life has come full circle. The company was started/ headed mainly by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, who were known as product people through and through. It seemed to be teetering on the verge of closing down when Jobs returned to turn it around in 1997. He was succeeded by Tim Cook, who, as Jobs himself mentioned, is “not a product person” but focused more on scaling the business and made Apple the first trillion-dollar company in the world under his tenure. And now Cook has given the Apple empire to Ternus to take care of.
Many believe Ternus has been handed a golden spoon— Jobs laid the groundwork in his second coming, made products that became aspirational and industry benchmarks, and then Cook followed by scaling the business in a way no one had ever imagined could be done. Many think Ternus can just pass his tenure enjoying the fruits of their labor.
I respectfully would like to disagree. If anything, I believe he has an uphill battle in front of him.
From Jobs to Cook – from being insanely innovative to being a world champ
Steve Jobs focused on products and features that were not created to blend in. Under him, Apple’s product portfolio was slim and streamlined. People who have recently started following tech may find it hard to believe, but under Steve Jobs, Apple back then was generally launching just one iPhone a year. Just one. The idea was to focus on user experience, bringing out products that made the lives of its users easier, developing interfaces that would make using a device a simple process – in short, innovation that would make a difference. Apple was actually ‘thinking different’.
Under Tim Cook, that rulebook was respectfully thrown out of the window. Whatever Jobs did, it seemed Cook was doing the opposite. From launching just one iPhone a year, Apple started to launch multiple ones, sometimes more than once a year. It also had multiple watches, earbuds, headphones, iPads, iMacs, MacBooks, Mac Minis, HomePods, and, believe it or not, even a cleaning cloth (there are two generations of it now). It is safe to say Apple’s product portfolio expanded (some would say “exploded”) under Tim Cook.
It may have gotten extremely hard to keep track of all of Apple’s products, but under Cook, Apple became the most valuable company in the world. During his time as CEO, Apple’s shares went up a whopping 2,275 percent! When Cook gained control in 2011, Apple was valued at USD 350 billion (a very healthy number), and with his strategy of diversifying the portfolio and expanding into new markets, Cook took Apple all the way up to a valuation of USD 5 trillion, becoming only the second company in history to do so (Nvidia was the first).
Jobs and Cook thus both played very vital but very different roles in making Apple what it has become today. One focused on innovation, the other on expansion.
Ternus has got some big shoes to fill
Now, Ternus has stepped into the CEO’s role, and he has some really big shoes to fill. Not just in terms of his immediate predecessor, but the one before him too.
Let me explain: Ternus is a product person, and for all these years when Cook was in the office, many Apple purists were disappointed by his constant efforts to make the brand more mainstream. Cook’s efforts were not about making the brand more accessible or democratizing it (even though the number of Apple products has vastly expanded, they still remain premium), but were more about relentlessly releasing products and their variants. While this did increase Apple’s revenues and profits exponentially, many believed it had deflected the brand from its core values, the values Jobs believed in: innovation, user experience, and product design. According to many critics, Apple’s designs became repetitive, software became buggy, and its innovation arc felt more like a flat line of late, with the odd bump here and there.
So naturally, now that Ternus has assumed office, this lobby has new hope. Hope that perhaps as a “product person,” he will take Apple back to what they insist were its ‘golden days’ under Jobs. That he will channel all of Apple’s energy into making more innovative products and not just products that seem to exist to make numbers.
What this lobby, however, forgets is that Jobs is not the only legacy Ternus has to live up to. Cook may have done things very differently (some might say he really did ‘think different’ but in a different sphere of business), but under his leadership Apple soared and found its way to the top. Today, it stands at the very pinnacle of the tech world; some would even say it is the most important company in the world. While topping this would be difficult, Ternus can certainly not let it slide off this pedestal.
Now it’s Ternus’ turn to think different
This means John Ternus basically has to find a balance between the Jobs method and the Cook method or come up with something completely new. And that too at a very difficult time for the industry. With demand for memory driving up prices of all things tech – smartphones, laptops, computers, hard drives – it will be a challenge for Ternus to manage prices, even while bringing in the big sales numbers that many now associate with Apple. There is also the matter of Apple’s struggle with AI for the past couple of years, which has become quite a spectacle, one which Ternus needs to solve as soon as possible.
Many would kill to be in Ternus’ position, as it seems like the guy has got it all made and simply has to carry it forward, but if you ask me, I do not envy him his place or task. He has to deal with the shadows of two illustrious predecessors and an industry crisis, as well as a deeply polarised community, apart from, of course, intense competition from the likes of Microsoft, Google, Meta and Samsung. To be fair, it was not easy for either Jobs or Cook. Jobs took over Apple in 1997, with many confident that the company would not last another year. When Jobs passed away in 2011, an equally large number of people felt that a non-product person like Cook would not be able to succeed. Both of them defied their detractors and added a new dimension to Apple in different ways. It is Ternus’ turn to put his own spin on Apple. It will not be easy. Will he, too, Think Different, differently? Only time will tell.

KFC appoints first-ever ‘global chief brand officer’ as fast-food chain faces fierce competition
KFC announced a rebrand effort in June that involved new menu items and a refreshed logo
KFC has appointed its first-ever global chief brand officer as the fast-food chain looks to make a comeback amid fierce competition.
Amy Ellis Durini — a longtime executive at KFC’s parent company, Yum Brands — was appointed to the role, effective November 1, the company said in a press release.
Durini will lead global brand strategy and oversee brand, loyalty, retail and new concept development and innovation. Her appointment to the role comes amid efforts to modernize the KFC brand and help improve the fried chicken chain’s positioning among competitors.
While the chain is successful overseas, its U.S. arm has been attempting a comeback, looking to rival competitor chicken chains like Raising Cane’s and Chick-fil-A. The chain announced a rebrand this June that includes new menu items and a new logo as part of an effort to lure back those customers.
The new logo features Colonel Sanders sandwiched between “KFC” in the shape of a chicken bucket.
The company said it was looking to make its logo feel “more relevant, more expressive, and more in tune with modern culture” while “keeping it’s “iconic ‘Finger Lickin’ Good’ ethos,” according to a statement.
The rebranding effort also included changes to stores and a revamped menu that features more boneless chicken, more than 20 new flavors of dipping sauces and a variety of drinks.
The new dips range includes flavors like include “Chimichurri Ranch” and “Hot Honey Habanero.”
KFC, which has 34,000 locations globally, is also joining scores of other fast food restaurants in expanding its drink selection.
The new drink line, available under the sub-brand Kwench by KFC, includes “Boba Refreshers,” sparkling lemonades and iced coffees.
The offerings are already available in some U.K. and Ireland locations and will expand from a pilot program to permanent menu items in Australia and Canada sometime this year. It was not immediately clear when they would arrive in the U.S.
Establishing global chief brand and marketing officer roles is one way companies attempt to bring consistency to their operations, Restaurant Dive reports.
Valier Kubizniak has acted as KFC’s global chief marking officer since 2022 and has been working on KFC’s most recent overhaul, according to the report.
In addition to KFC’s revamp, Yum Brands just finished selling Pizza Hut for $2.7 billion, concluding years of struggles for the pizza chain.

Trump envoys confronted over Putin talks during Kyiv visit: ‘Don’t you find it disgusting?’
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were confronted by Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon
Donald Trump’s peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been confronted over their talks with “war criminal” Russian president Vladimir Putin.
In a news conference in Kyiv alongside Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday, Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon asked whether Putin was deceiving the US president.
“You have met with President Putin very often. Does it seem to you that Putin has been deceiving you all this time?,” he said according to the Kyiv Post.
“And finally, don’t you find it disgusting to sit at the same table with an international war criminal, the executioner of the Ukrainian people, who is personally responsible for the tragedy in Ukraine?” he added.
Zelensky held talks with Witkoff and Kushner on Sunday, after their three-hour talks with Putin in Moscow on Saturday. He lauded their “very substantive” conversation and said Ukraine was ready for trilateral talks involving Russia, the US and Ukraine.
The US president is expected to speak to Putin and Zelensky over the phone on Monday.
Zelensky urged all sides to “keep diplomacy going” in a post on X on Monday, after a fresh round of talks between US envoys and negotiators in Kyiv and Moscow.
"Our partners know what can bear fruit and what must bear fruit ahead of winter. We are coordinating our next steps. We are preparing the next meetings and communications," he said.
He said there were three rounds of negotiations held, with representatives from France, the UK and Germany also joining, adding that he had a “separate tête-à-tête with [US envoys] Steve [Witkoff] and Jared [Kushner] to discuss the day’s outcomes”.
Meanwhile, Moscow said on Monday that it had not ruled our the potential resumption of peace talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine, but said it was too early to say what form these talks might take.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov made the comments when asked about a weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv by Witkoff and Kushner.
He said the Kremlin did not rule out a phone call between Putin and Trump to discuss the US envoys' trip.
But he added that Moscow had not heard anything about the meetings between US envoys and Ukrainian officials in Kyiv on Sunday.
"As for the resumption of the trilateral format, you heard the statement from Kyiv yesterday,” Peskov told reporters. “Mr Kushner made such statements. We, too, do not rule out the resumption of this trilateral format, but it is still too early to speak of the venue and exact dates.”
He added: "Undoubtedly, any attempts... represent a small step towards peace, and we truly hold the peace-building efforts of the American negotiators in very high regard. President Putin himself has said that he holds President Trump’s efforts in high regard, and that he is grateful to President Trump for his commitment to this path towards peace.”

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

Diet Sabya (@dietsabya), the anonymous Indian fashion watchdog, spills the tea on his current obsession: “Gathering by Haider Saleem is a very under-the-radar, slow-fashion brand that not enough people know about. There’s a lingering notion that Indian menswear-forward brands have to look a certain way or that they somehow can’t occupy the same conversation, say as The Row or Lemaire. Gathering proves otherwise. The clothes have this organic ease to them: earthy tones, flattering cuts, natural fabrics, with much of the dyeing done traditionally in Jaipur. The sort of brand you want to gate keep until everyone discovers it and you can say: “Oh, I’ve known them for ages.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing

The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM Cares), set up during the coronavirus pandemic, had a balance of £647m (Rs 8,452 crore) at the end of the 2025 financial year, prompting questions about why such a large sum remained unused instead of being put towards relief work. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata party, countered the charge in a debate on Times Now, saying the PM Cares fund provides for long-term rehabilitation instead of immediate relief during disasters.

For choreographer and director Usha Jey (@usha_jey), learning bharatanatyam at the age of 20 was a way to connect to her culture. Jey, who is French and of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, has since developed her own movement language. Hybrid bharatham, as she calls it, fuses the Indian classical dance form with hip-hop but is careful to retain the integrity of both. There is an interplay of abandon and elegance in her choreographic works. Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan features in her latest video, Hide N Seek. Directed by Jey and her longtime partner, Gavin Emishka, the film is a striking visual treat featuring two dance forms in fluid negotiation.
