A six-week-old baby girl in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, died from measles, the county coroner confirmed to local press on Friday.
Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican elected coroner in 2007, told Lancaster Online that the baby died at home. “I believe it was the 18th of August,” he said.
He also noted that the baby had a genetic condition called Amish lethal microcephaly, in which babies are born with unusually small heads and underdeveloped brains. The condition is caused by a mutation in the SLC25A19 gene, which codes for a protein involved with energy-producing enzymes in the mitochondria and is thought to be important for brain development. About 1 in 500 babies in the Old Order Amish population of Pennsylvania is born with the condition. Infants with the disorder only survive for about six months.
Diamontoni confirmed to Lancaster Online that while microcephaly was present, measles was the cause of death.
Pennsylvania’s two measles deaths
The death is one of two that the state’s health department announced last week as being from measles, according to a response from the state health department sent to Ars Technica Friday. Additionally on Friday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro shared a local news report about the coroner’s confirmation on social media. In the post, he also seemed to confirm that it was one of the deaths reported by state health officials.
The tragic deaths—both in infants, the other a newborn boy—have been engulfed in a firestorm of controversy sparked when anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed without evidence that the state may have “fabricated” them. The controversy was fueled by Diamantoni himself, who said he had not received the death reports at the time of the state’s announcement, seemingly adding to Kennedy’s false claim that the deaths were not real. But Lancaster County does not have its own health department and relies on information sent from the state health department.

Self-identifying OpenAI agents posted 18,000 messages to a public wiki that discussed ways for other agents to bypass security sandbox restrictions during what was likely internal testing designed to gauge the agents’ hacking abilities, researchers said Friday.
In all, agents with 3,700 distinct self-given names posted the messages to German site DSEwiki over a six-week period. Besides discussing ways the agents could break out of the restricted environment OpenAI intended to prevent them from posting code or content to the Internet, the posts shared test answers. The posts also shared possible ways to perform XSS (cross-site scripting) attacks against the wiki and to impersonate site moderators. In three of the posts, agents used the word “swarm” to describe the collection of agents engaged in the activity.
Colluding to share answers
The research team—composed of Sydney Von Arx, Spencer Kitts, Thomas Larsen, and Cormac Slade Byrd—said they found the posts and pieced them together. The researchers say there are gaps in their understanding of precisely what actions the agents took because the research is based solely on the content of the posts. Additionally, the agents generated “chain of thought” data that’s understood only by OpenAI. As a result, the researchers said, they in some cases made educated guesses, including that the agents were, in fact, from OpenAI. In a statement, OpenAI later confirmed they were.
The researchers wrote: “These AIs colluded to share answers, research their environment, and bypass sandbox restrictions.” They continued:
Our best guess of what happened is as follows:
- Agents within OpenAI were assigned a timed web-lookup task.
- As part of the task, they were supposed to have the ability to read the internet but not to write on it. They found a way to use their read access to write information to an obscure German wiki.
- The agents used this wiki to communicate information with each other, primarily to help them succeed at their task. They asked for answers, pooled results, and shared techniques for bypassing their restrictions. This allowed them to use the work of others to cheat on their task.
- OpenAI found out about this. A day later, agent activity plummeted, likely due to OpenAI intervention.
Friday’s revelation comes a week after researchers from the nonprofit METR said more than 1,200 OpenAI agents made posts to a makeshift message board that repurposed an internal sandboxing tool. The posts discussed ways to game an internal test OpenAI gave to agents that had been altered to remove safety guardrails that are normally in place.

Charles confirms Harry and Meghan to remain non-working royals after their return to U.K.
Couple stepped down from duties and moved to the U.S. in 2020
King Charles authorized a letter to senior British officials on Monday confirming that his youngest son, Prince Harry, and Harry's wife, Meghan, remain non-working royals following their return to the U.K.
The letter, which was shared with Harry's team and sent as guidance to senior officials in the government and military, said that after Harry and Meghan stepped down from official royal duties in 2020, they "are no longer working Members of The Royal Family."
"This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected," the letter said.
"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.... The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.
"In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."
Prince Harry and his family arrived back in Britain late last month, six years after quitting royal duties and moving to the United States.
The couple had left for the U.S. in 2020, stepping down from official royal duties to chart independent careers, but they never left the headlines as Harry accused the royals of neglect, the tabloid press of ruining his life and the government of failing to provide enough security for him to ever return home.

The data center backlash has entered the midterms conversation.
Data centers are bringing Americans together
And politicians can’t run away fast enough.
Politicians from across the spectrum have changed their minds — or at least their policy positions — about data centers in the past few months as public resistance to their construction has skyrocketed. A major example is Texas, where just about one year ago, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott was proclaiming that his state was the “epicenter of AI development.”
Now, after months of grassroots organizing and community outcry, Abbott is pushing to slow the roll of new data centers in Texas. He’s imposed a statewide moratorium on new construction pending an audit over the new connections to Texas’s power grid. While he hasn’t explicitly said the change is tied to his reelection campaign this November, the pause is expected to last through the election.
As dramatic as Abbott’s about-face has been, he’s not alone: Democrats and Republicans alike are following suit.
Jeremy Merrill, a data reporter at the Washington Post, analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see what elected officials on both sides of the aisle are saying about data centers. He spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about his findings, what they say going into midterm elections, and how the backlash might change the way we think about what politicians owe to their constituents.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
What did you find?
Data centers didn’t used to be a big deal. And now, almost all of a sudden, they’re a big issue. Candidates are falling over themselves to sound tough about data centers. And data centers are overwhelmingly portrayed as a problem rather than an opportunity or a benefit.
A great example is Sen. Jon Husted, who’s a Republican senator from Ohio, who’s up for election this November. He used to praise data center projects that were coming to Ohio when he was lieutenant governor because it would help establish Ohio as “an important tech hub in America.”
He said that data centers are essential to our digital lives. And now he’s saying he’s trying to “protect Americans from having to foot the bill for data centers.”
He’s really emblematic of a shift that happened all across the Republican Party in about February of this year. That’s when the bulk of messages from Republicans about data centers flipped from focusing on them as bringing benefits to their states and communities, to talking about their downsides.
This is really a case of the anger and unhappiness bubbling up from everyday people up to political elites. And that grassroots anger was all across the political spectrum over a whole range of issues: power bills, claims about how much water data centers may use, air pollution, eminent domain, taxes, subsidies, and a generalized, physical manifestation of the anxiety that people feel about what AI is going to do to our society, to our brains, to our kids and to our jobs.
We know that it’s not just one single candidate, maybe even not just a handful, because you reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that, “Data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”
That’s pretty strong language. Is the National Republican Senatorial Committee admitting that the wrong position on data centers is enough to lose a candidate a race at this point?
I think it’s something that they’re certainly worried about. He’s in a tough race. It’s a tossup. And presumably you’re looking for an edge, or to prevent your opponent from getting an edge over you.
What about President Donald Trump’s messaging on data centers? He, initially at least, was very bullish on AI investment in the US. What has Trump been saying?
This is a story in two or three parts. As President Trump took office again last year, he was overall trying to portray his second term as president as “inaugurating a golden age for American manufacturing and technological dominance.”
As part of that, he issued an executive order trying to make it easier to build data centers in the United States. And I think that’s probably why last year most Republicans across the board were talking about data centers as a benefit to the country and to the communities where they were being built — talking about jobs, talking about investment.
But like I said, the tide turned. And so on the one hand, you have President Trump promoting this bill that would protect people from having data centers cause their power bills to go up. But on the other hand, he just wrote earlier this week on Truth Social, “If [communities] want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”
He’s saying if they don’t want data centers, they’re going to “end up being backwards and poor.” So he’s still very pro-data center, which is fascinating.
Let’s talk about the Democrats. Which Democrats in particular are we seeing change their minds?
There are a lot of governors who used to be very positive on data centers in their states because these bring jobs. These bring construction investments, some amount of permanent jobs, some amount of construction jobs. Examples of folks who are now limiting data centers in their states include Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and [Gov.] J.B. Pritzker of Illinois.
The most striking case of a Democrat whose rhetoric has shifted so much is Rep. Ro Khanna of California, whose district actually includes Silicon Valley. In 2025, he was calling for building more data centers in the United States versus overseas. When the Trump administration did an AI deal with the United Arab Emirates, he said, “Why are we putting data centers and research hubs in Dubai?”
But now he’s more critical, calling for an end to data center extraction, taking communities’ water and jacking up their bills, sucking all the money into the hands of a few tech billionaires.
Is anyone in either party still coming out strong for data centers?
My favorite example of this is Rep. Eric Burlison, who’s a Republican from Missouri. He’s really focused on the need to build data centers in order to compete with China. In June, he wrote, “Ask yourself who benefits when Americans turn against data centers? China does.”
He’s making the point that I think a lot of people in tech are making, which is, “This is coming whether you like it or not.” And part of politics is dealing with reality.
In this day and age, it seems constituents don’t want to deal with that reality, but clearly there are people who hold office, or who hope to hold office, who are going to maintain the line that this is something we’ve just got to do.
This is a classic political science dispute about what a politician’s job is supposed to be. If you accept the premise that we need data centers to build a wonderful technological future or keep pace with China or whatever the argument is, is the job of a politician to just do what their constituents want, to be their tribune in Washington? Or is it to be the wise, thoughtful leader who’s willing to push back when constituents are missing something important?
This is one thing I keep in mind when analyzing — particularly some of these governors who shifted more recently — is that they’re talking about the downsides of data centers. They’re talking about mitigating those downsides. They’re saying, “Oh, we need to get data centers to pay their fair share. We need to make sure that data centers don’t screw up our water. We need to make sure they don’t raise your power bills. We need to make sure they give back.”
But then it’s so that we can build them and still reap the benefits while mitigating the costs.
What is it about this issue, do you think, that has got us to this place? We’re polarized, but we’re not polarized in the same way that we’re often polarized.
One possibility is that this is coming from the grassroots so much and bubbling up to politicians and political elites, that everybody got the signal at the same time that this was something that they ought to oppose.
The other possibility is people have for a while been saying, “Are we living through a generational political realignment in the United States where a lot of things are up for grabs?”
You don’t see a lot of the libertarian-adjacent pro-business, free markets, free trade Republican Party. And so when all these issues are up for grabs, politicians see opportunity in being innovative rather than sticking with the same traditional views of their party.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Alonso was beaten for the first time in four games in all competitions since taking charge in the close-season.
The Spaniard was frustrated with the way Chelsea failed to take advantage of its early lead.
“It hurts because a defeat has to hurt. It was a very intense game. We had chances to equalise,” he said.
“After we scored, there were 15 or 20 minutes where we had to defend too much and we were struggling a bit to get control. Overall, it was a very tight, very intense game.
“We could do better with the second goal. You need to control the overloads on the right side.”
‘A joy to watch’
While Alonso was annoyed to leave north London empty-handed, he expects Chelsea to be better for the experience.
“The players have this attitude, this desire to compete better game by game to create something we believe in,” he said.
“It’s game three, and this is going to be a long, long ride.”
As Alonso ponders Chelsea’s development in the early stages of his rebuild, Arteta finally has the finished article at his disposal after seven years in charge.
The Gunners ended their 22-year drought to win the title last season, and lifting that pressure from their shoulders appears to have given them more freedom this season.

“It wasn’t the right start, but we certainly reacted in an amazing way. I enjoyed the way we competed. We took risks; it was a joy to watch,” Arteta said.
“Chelsea have a great coach who can set them up in great condition. We constrained them well. Overall, it was an incredible performance.
“We are very happy, and we need to continue to raise the bar and look to improve every single time. We need to enjoy the victory because it was a big one today.”
After an inconsistent season marred by injury last term, Odegaard has been in fine form at the start of the new campaign.
The Norway midfielder has three goals from four games, including the Community Shield, and Arteta said: “I think he is enjoying his football.
“His personal life is settled, he is available, he is training, he has his routine, and if he is intelligent, he can take a lot of benefits from the players around him. He was outstanding today.”

Late last year, men in parts of Congo’s Tshopo province began whispering about something strange that was happening in nearby villages. At first, the stories sounded too absurd to travel far. A man in a market claimed his genitals had suddenly shrunk after brushing against a stranger. Someone else said it happened inside a taxi. In another village, people spoke about a man who returned from town convinced that the part of his body had disappeared altogether.
And then the videos started appearing, people gathered around phones watching clips of alleged victims speaking inside crowded churches while pastors stood beside them claiming they had been cured through prayer. Some videos spread through Facebook pages and TikTok accounts. Others moved from phone to phone through Bluetooth shares and WhatsApp groups, spreading across villages faster than official information ever could.
In many places, the rumours arrived before the authorities did. By the time officials in Tshopo publicly denied the existence of any mysterious illness, fear had already settled across parts of northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where rumours, churches, and social media had combined to create something more powerful than a simple falsehood. Men spoke cautiously around strangers. Communities became suspicious of outsiders. Stories changed slightly depending on who was telling them, but the central fear remained the same.
Something was stealing men’s bodies. In the month of October, the health workers travelling through the Isangi area of Tshopo province arrived in villages already consumed by weeks of panic. They carried tablet computers, questionnaires, and reflective jackets as part of vaccination-related field surveys, but in some communities those unfamiliar objects and routines were interpreted very differently by residents who had spent weeks hearing that outsiders were spreading a disease that caused men’s genitalia to shrink or disappear.
According to Reuters, at least four health workers were later killed after crowds accused them of spreading the supposed illness.
One of them was Dr. John Tangakeya. His wife later told Reuters that the family had spoken to him earlier that day because it was his birthday. The children were waiting for him to come home that evening so that they could celebrate together. Instead, news arrived that the health team he was part of had been attacked by mobs even as they tried to explain that their surveys had nothing to do with the rumours spreading in the province.
The World Health Organization(WHO)-backed Africa Infodemic Response Alliance, which monitors dangerous health misinformation across Africa, later linked at least 17 killings to the rumours, though some incidents could not be independently verified.
Long before social media existed, versions of this panic had already travelled across parts of Africa.
Researchers have documented similar episodes for decades in Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, Benin, and Congo itself, where rumours of “penis theft” or genital shrinking periodically triggered mob attacks against people accused of witchcraft or supernatural powers. In Ghana, during the 1990s, several people accused of “penis snatching” were beaten to death by mobs. In Kinshasa, in 2008, police detained more than a dozen suspected “sorcerers” after panic spread through the capital and led to attempted lynchings.
Anthropologists who study such incidents have often argued that the panic is not simply about superstition. In many places, fears around genital theft became tied to larger anxieties about masculinity, illness, vulnerability, power, and social instability, particularly in societies where spiritual explanations for misfortune remain deeply embedded in everyday life.
But something about the Congo episode felt different. Earlier, panic spread through markets, crowded taxis, churches, and radio broadcasts. This time, much of the fear moved online first, where videos featuring alleged victims and miracle cures circulated rapidly through algorithm-driven feeds before local officials fully understood what was unfolding on the ground.
Several churches in Kisangani hosted testimonies from supposed victims while Facebook pages and TikTok accounts reposted clips that gathered hundreds of thousands of views. Some videos remained online even after authorities publicly dismissed the claims as false.
Health officials later said the violence exposed a deeper crisis facing public health systems in parts of Africa, where distrust toward authorities has been shaped by years of political instability, misinformation, and memories of earlier health emergencies, including Ebola and COVID-19 outbreaks, during which some communities viewed outside medical teams with suspicion.
In villages where people had already spent weeks discussing the rumours among themselves, the arrival of unfamiliar health workers carrying devices and asking questions appeared, for some residents, to confirm the fears they already believed were true.
Months later, the rumours have still not completely disappeared.
Officials continue running radio campaigns and public awareness programmes aimed at stopping the spread of misinformation. Arrests have been made in some areas. But many of the original videos are still circulating online, resurfacing again and again across different parts of Congo, long after authorities declared that the illness itself never existed.

Last month, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon won the state’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major upset over her better-funded opponent, retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman. Her victory was quickly slotted into a narrative about the Democratic Party’s insurgent progressive movement, which has triumphed in House and Senate primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, and elsewhere.
Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026?
Angie Nixon explains her playbook to be Florida’s next senator.
But while Nixon supports progressive policies, she argues there’s more to the story than a simple progressive-versus-centrist tale. She says that she out-worked and out-organized her opponent — and that Floridians across the political spectrum are hungry for change.
Vox’s Astead Herndon invited Nixon on a special pop-up episode of America, Actually to break down how she won the nomination, why she thinks there’s a path to victory in what many analysts believe is a solidly red state, and what she wants to get done as a senator if she prevails in November.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Why do you think your victory took so many by surprise?
It took so many by surprise because people both tend to underestimate a Black woman — especially a progressive Black woman in politics — and then one who wasn’t able to raise as much money. But as a former single mom for 12 years, I know how to make a dollar stretch.
This win is attributed to good old-fashioned grassroots organizing. I am a former union organizer. I am a community organizer, and I know the importance of people power and talking to people and getting them energized about why they should vote and why they should see themselves in this country.
How much would you ascribe your win to the type of politics that you’re describing here versus the progressive policies that you championed? Should we take this as a sign that Medicare-for-all and “abolish ICE” have strong support in Florida?
It’s all of it, right? It is the hard work that we put into this race to raise awareness about who I am and the policies and positions that I stand for, which are policies and positions that the majority of hardworking, everyday people stand for.
Just because we want access to quality healthcare and affordable housing and fully funded public schools, they try to fear-monger and make it seem as though we are communist and we’re not.
We are not communist. We are people who want to put hardworking, everyday people in power so that they can determine and shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like. There’s nothing radical or extreme about that.
Democrats are still dismissing your chances to win a general election. Prominent pundits have said that Democrats should not invest in Florida, and that would amount to wasted money. Political forecasters moved the race in the Republican direction after your primary victory, arguing that the progressive politics makes it easier for Republicans to win in a state like Florida.
I wanted to ask about electability. Can you give me the case for how you can win a statewide race amongst such skepticism?
The same way that I was able to win a primary being outspent and out-raised 18 to 1. I am building a very unique, diverse coalition of people. We’ve had Republicans and independents that crossed over in the primary to vote for me in the primary. They also volunteer in our campaign. They’ve made donations.
We literally have a bunch of Republicans and libertarians who have been stating that they are voting for me because they like that I am no-nonsense. They appreciate that I am trying to put a check on what is coming out of Washington, DC, all of the cruelty and the corruption, and that is the winning message.
Look, we’re up against a woman, [incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody], who allowed the theft of $10 million. She allowed money to be stolen from medically needy and low-income kids, to be diverted toward two citizen-led ballot initiatives that actually caused us to not have better health in our communities.
People are frustrated, and that’s all Ashley Moody has done — just look out for herself, her campaign donors and these billionaires. People are ready for elected officials to stop bailing out these big businesses [and] actually look out for everyday people.
In November 2023, you introduced a resolution to the Florida House calling for “the immediate de-escalation and ceasefire…in Israel and occupied Palestine.” It was rejected 104 to 2. And it earned you some bad blood with some of the members of the Florida Jewish Caucus. The chair actually said that the resolution was born out of ignorance and antisemitism.
Obviously, the Democratic Party base has shifted on that issue over the last several years. There’s been an open discussion about whether Joe Biden and Kamala Harris did themselves damage in the 2024 election by not breaking more explicitly with Israel’s actions in Gaza.
Do you think that was a mistake for Democrats?
I would say yes. I would say that we have to have really uncomfortable conversations amongst our different communities and we just have to talk. But I feel that they did do a disservice in regards to just going along with the AIPAC lobby.
You had mentioned that you don’t support sending any money or any weapons to Israel at this moment, but I also wanted to ask about things like BDS, the movement to boycott, divest, or sanction Israel. Is that something you support?
It is. I’m a Black woman who is a descendant of slaves, and who is the descendant of people from the civil rights movement, and I know how we used boycotts and we used protest to gain our civil rights for our community. So I’m fully supportive of that.
You repeatedly said that you don’t support defunding the police on your website. It says that you support demilitarizing the police. And that “real safety comes from good jobs, strong schools, affordable housing, and healthcare for all — not from more cameras, more cages, and more agents.”
What is the difference between that and defunding?
Whatever folks think the difference is. I’m not going to box myself in because I understand how they’ll try to cut and clip things with me saying certain words.
But doesn’t that sound a little bit like lessening the resources that go to police to focus on other things? I mean, that sounds a little like the same thing.
It sounds like I know that is my position. I want to defund Flock cameras because bad cops are stalking their ex-girlfriends and ex-boyfriends. And so to-may-toe, to-mah-toe. I literally said this before and that is what I am for. I’m not trying to get clipped in any kind of way.
Let me ask you this way. I appreciate the focus on root causes, and I think you’ve laid that out that that’s where you want the energy to go — that real public safety comes from focusing on the things that cause people to commit crimes in the first place, but those often take a long time to show effect.
If we’re talking about the root causes of crime, what is the message to someone whose community is unsafe right now that does not include policing?
What I would say is, making sure that we invest in making sure people have more jobs and we invest in community control of the police. I totally believe in civil review boards and that type of thing, but I believe in making sure that people’s most basic needs are met.
One of the things that I believe could help that right off the bat is things like universal healthcare, or at a minimum, extending the ACA subsidies so that we can drive down these healthcare premium costs. Or fully funding these programs that allow people to have access to first-time homebuyer programs.
I was a single mom for 12 years, and I took part in the first-time homebuyer program that was funded from the federal government. That trickled down to the state and then to the local government. That helped me with down payment assistance as well as closing costs and those types of programs. We need to put policies in place that are allowing people to be good.
We need to push for universal child care. For every $1 that is invested by the government, it puts $3 back into the economy so parents can get to work. They can be able to make sure that they have money to put their children in different programs. We need to invest in programs to keep our children off the streets.
There’s been so much effort to put you in one of the boxes that have defined the Democratic ideological battles — DSA versus establishment. I hear in this interview how that doesn’t neatly fit with what it seems like you’ve done in Florida.
Where do you think this campaign fits into the ongoing question of where do Democrats go next?
We’re coalition builders, we’re aggregators. Folks should know, I was a vice chair of a local Democratic Party. I was also the field director and the political director with the state party. I have never fit in a box. I was a union member and I also led a statewide organization that was straight-up progressive.
We need all these things to fight back against this Donald Trump regime. Look, this man is not going to leave willingly in 2028. He’s created a paramilitary force in the form of ICE that is getting away with shooting people and slaughtering them on camera while they’re masked without any accountability. They’re pushing to see how far they can go.
Granted, Black people have been getting slaughtered on camera without accountability for a while, but now they are doing it to people who aren’t just Black, who aren’t just Latino. They are banking on us being normalized with what’s happening.
First lady Michelle Obama says, “They go low, we go high.” I’m saying, “We get loud, we push back. We organize stronger and harder so that we can win and change this country and build a new vision for the next 250 years, where we have a Florida and an America for all.”

Whatever happened to kindness? Spoiler alert: Our readers prove it's alive and well
In recent years, NPR has explored how small interactions with strangers can do more than just brighten our days — they can improve our well‑being.
Our original story from 2023 traced psychologist Gillian Sandstrom's research back to her experience as a lonely graduate student in Toronto who exchanged a wave and hello daily with a hot dog vendor she passed on campus, even though she never once bought a hot dog. That brief exchange boosted her spirits so much that she began studying the power of "weak ties." Her research found what many people intuitively feel: Even the most casual encounters can boost mood, ease isolation and strengthen our sense of community.
Global health professor Kristin Jenkins of Cornerstone University in Grand Rapids, Mich., wrote to tell us that our story had inspired her to ask her students to intentionally engage with strangers and casual acquaintances. They enjoyed the assignment so much, they wanted to continue doing it! In sharing some of their experiences with NPR, they described moments that echoed Sandstrom's findings. A mechanic started "a wonderful conversation" about nursing school. A hospital worker felt more grounded during a stressful shift: "Something as simple as using someone's name or taking a few extra minutes to listen can actually mean a lot.". These short, simple interactions became reminders that kindness doesn't always have to be grand to be meaningful.
About This Series
We're looking back at some of our past global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
Now, we've invited readers to share their own moments of connection — small exchanges that lift their spirits and stay with them much longer than they expect.
One woman from California shared a story about her mother, who lost a year of school to polio as a child and has lived ever since with a twisted spine and chronic pain. Even so, for the past two decades, she and her dogs have made weekly visits to nursing homes and hospitals, bringing handwritten cards and goody bags to people who normally don't have visitors.
Another reader in Kenya told us that a quick question about an acronym on a man's T‑shirt while waiting in line at a bakery turned into a lively 15‑minute conversation. They both walked away smiling.
Finally, one open-hearted reader doesn't just limit kindness to other humans. "Even a simple greeting like 'Hello, brother' to a hawk or 'You are so beautiful' to a flower brightens my day."
And the stories kept coming, all reflecting a simple truth: small gestures matter. To keep a smile on your face, here are a few more:
A listening ear, a pack of tissues
It's no mystery that I enjoy talking to strangers. Everyone has a story, and I'm hear (see what I did there?) to listen to it. I actually dated a guy once that said, "Why do you have to talk to everyone?" I knew right then and there he wasn't the one.
When I stumbled across the NPR article, "Why saying hello to strangers can be good for you," I felt inclined to share a story that happened just today.
I work in corporate events, and part of my job includes operating registration desks. Consider me the Welcome Wagon! The role actually requires a lot of project management and organizational skills, but for the point of this story: I smile, check people in and print their badges. There is a lot of interaction with strangers, which I enjoy.
Toward the end of the day, a woman came up to my desk in tears. She was so embarrassed about what had just transpired in a meeting and decided to share with me. She explained she felt behind during the training course. She said the presenter did not assist her in a helpful way and was actually pretty crass. When she packed up her things and left the room early, the heavy door slammed behind her, making everything feel worse.
Out of everyone she could have walked up to, she chose me. I gave her a mini pack of tissues and listened. The woman talked about her struggles of being an older woman in a male-dominated tech environment and about how certain moments could make her feel invisible. I felt like I had a purpose right then to help her in the best way I knew how – just by listening. By the end of our conversation, I felt her mood shift and the heaviness lift. I even managed to get a smile out of her!
What she doesn't know is that she gave me something too. During our exchange, I felt like I was right where I was supposed to be, at the right time. I am proud that I carry myself in a way that makes others feel comfortable to approach me and share.
The article said people feel good after random encounters with strangers, and I would have to agree. I try to remind myself that we never know someone's full story, and a little grace — a smile, a quick hello, or a moment of listening — can really go a long way.
Michelle Sarnosky
Missouri
Puppy love
After moving from South Florida to a small town on Florida's west coast, I discovered the community was more closed-off than I was used to. But as I was out walking my puppy, neighbors — dog owners or not — would stop to talk. Within a month, my new husband, who had lived in this bedroom community for years, was amazed by how many new friends I was making for both of us!
Thank you for writing about this small but powerful way we can make a difference in each other's lives. It truly is a two-sided gift.
Anita Finley Derr
Florida
A stranger's hug
My older brother passed away unexpectedly on December 30, 2019. As my family gathered at my younger brother's apartment in downtown Philadelphia the next day, the mood was deeply heavy. We were all in shock — disbelieving and numb.
My dad was handling payroll for a small organization at the time and had to walk to the UPS on Chestnut Street to overnight some paychecks. I decided to go with him. When we entered the small UPS office and approached the counter, the woman working there made a pleasantry — I can't exactly recall, maybe something like "Oh, are you all together for the holidays?" I decided to be honest. I said in a somber tone that ended more in a whimper, "Yes… but also, unfortunately, my brother died yesterday.."
I will never forget her reaction. Her jaw dropped, she gasped, and she looked at my dad and asked "Your son?" When he said yes, she said nothing more. Without hesitation, she came around the counter and gave us both the most incredible, genuine hugs. She didn't know us at all, but she instantly recognized the weight of our indescribable pain in that moment.
There was something incredibly healing and meaningful about that moment. To feel seen by a stranger who cared enough to step forward — it mattered. I'll never forget this, and since then, I've often tried to pass on that type of compassion, whether to a stranger or friend.
Cordelia Biddle
Pennsylvania
A world of stories
I always chat with strangers, in elevators, walking along the street, waiting in lines. If you pay attention and listen, everybody does have a story to tell.
Donald Pederson
Maryland

'Layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
- Published
A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.
Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border.
"It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.
The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people.
"I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.
Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.
They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors.
"We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.
Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said.
He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.
At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water.
Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.
Finally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.
The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".
Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.
But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.
Rescuers heading to 'Goldilocks zone'
Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.
Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".
The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers.
"Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."
But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time.
"It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."
Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".
This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located.
"We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."

Burundians rush to leave Kenya ahead of crackdown on unregistered traders
- Published
Hundreds of Burundians in Kenya are scrambling to process travel documents to leave the country ahead of the crackdown on unlicensed small businesses run by migrants.
Kenyan President William Ruto set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work, after the trade ministry said some exploited visa rules to work without the required permits.
Long queues were seen outside Burundi's embassy in the capital Nairobi after it said it would offer free emergency travel documents to citizens who want to go back home. Others are racing to buy bus tickets.
Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of migrants from across East Africa seeking work and business opportunities.
Kenya's trade ministry said there had been "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", who arrived as investors or tourists but got involved in business activities that breached their declared status.
According to the United Nations refugee agency, there are around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya.
It is unclear how many are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown.
Burundians have been seen carrying all their belongings - from suitcases to mattresses - as they try to leave ahead of the crackdown, but some of them said they could not afford the cost of travel and urged the Kenyan government to extend the deadline.
Ruto's directive follows a similar crackdown in Tanzania last year and rising anti‑migrant sentiment in South Africa.
Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change".
"Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.
His comments came after Ruto last week said that while Kenya remained open to foreign investment, it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".
He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.
Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.
Some foreign nationals say they fear for their safety, while police have warned Kenyans against targeting them.
Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region.
Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi.
Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.
On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities.
"Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said.
The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders.
Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.
He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries.
"This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."
Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.

A “shocked” and chastened Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office despite the far right’s triumph in a state election that has brought anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin politicians within striking distance of power.
The German chancellor, appearing ashen-faced in front of reporters in Berlin, said on Monday that the landslide victory by the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt had shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) “to its very foundations”.
The unpopular Merz, who had pledged to halve the AfD’s support at the national level, has watched the nativist party rack up electoral gains, none as convincing as its utter rout of the CDU in the eastern region on Sunday with nearly 44% of the vote.
The AfD and its candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority but could yet create Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi period.
Merz appeared contrite and willing to work on his “communication” with voters. “This is the worst electoral defeat the [CDU] has suffered in years, in decades,” he said. “Of course this will have to have consequences.”
Exit polls indicated the state’s voters were driven by deep dissatisfaction with the political establishment and its stewardship of Europe’s biggest economy, with one showing that only 9% approved of Merz’s performance.
Siegmund, a media-savvy former fragrance salesman, was also able to tap into a sense of grievance in the former communist east, where complaints abound that voters there are treated as “second-class citizens” more than three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Siegmund, 35, mocked the 70-year-old Merz as “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.
Only 16 months in office, Merz conceded his own low poll ratings had played a role in his party’s loss. “I know that I personally was a constant topic in this election campaign,” he said. “We must try – myself included – to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions.”
The CDU’s junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats, indicated a willingness to water down contentious measures to shore up the statutory healthcare and pension schemes.
However, Merz insisted: “My determination to continue on the path of reform is unbroken,” saying a sustainable system was essential for the sake of “our children and grandchildren”. He added: “Giving up is not an option for me.”
Merz said he wanted to assure Germany’s allies that “our institutions are resilient and stable” and its own vulnerable minorities that the country would stick to its values and constitution even if the AfD took power in Saxony-Anhalt. “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history,” he said.
He also promised to stay the course on Ukraine, stressing he would “not budge a single millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia as well”.
Merz said Moscow would cheer the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt and accused it of lending support to the far right’s campaign, with another two German state elections still to come this month amid alleged Russian interference and sabotage.
Although the CDU rallied behind its chancellor and party leader, several influential commenters openly called for his immediate replacement – a complex step under German law.
Germany “needs a clean slate, a fresh start, and that starts with Friedrich Merz”, said the Der Spiegel editor-in-chief, Dirk Kurbjuweit. “He is evidently the wrong man for this office in these times.”
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt chapter is listed as “confirmed rightwing extremist” by the domestic intelligence service. It has pledged mass deportations of unwelcome immigrants and asylum seekers, which critics have said would be illegal, while promising massive boosts in social welfare spending with unclear financing.
The AfD has also taken aim at state support for public broadcasters and cultural institutions it deems “unpatriotic”, sparking fears of “cultural hegemony”.
The party did not win enough seats to elect Siegmund as state premier, but AfD leaders said they seek to pick off rebel lawmakers from other parties willing to play kingmaker. It is only three seats short of a majority.
The conservative-left populist BSW party, which also favours restoring ties with Russia and largely blocking immigration, signalled an openness to working with the AfD but before the election ruled out joining the state government.
In the 13 years of the AfD’s existence, the mainstream parties have maintained a “firewall” against the far right, refusing any formal cooperation that would allow it take power. The strategy meant to sideline the party has appeared to backfire, however, as the permanent “outsider” role appeals to legions of voters fed up with politics as usual.
The CDU state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged his party had “no mandate” to govern given its humiliating 17% result, even if it managed to cobble together an unwieldy coalition with all the other parties in the legislature.
Although Saxony-Anhalt forms part of the AfD heartland as a relatively poor, ex-communist region, the party has begun making inroads in the west as well amid alarming signs of decline in the steel, chemicals and automotive sectors.
Germany faces another two regional elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the AfD is also strong.
The party co-leader Alice Weidel, beaming after Sunday’s vote, said the AfD was now targeting 40% at the next general election, due in 2029. It is polling at about 28%.

HIV is no longer a word that frightens young people. For a generation that has grown up seeing HIV transformed from a feared death sentence into a manageable chronic condition, the virus no longer carries the deterrent power it once did.
But the fading fear of HIV is confronting Keralam with a new public-health challenge. Changing sexual behaviour, gaps in information and awareness, and growing substance use are increasingly putting young people at risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
The numbers seeking care at the 23 District STI/RTI Centres (DSRCs) under the Kerala State AIDS Control Society (KSACS) have been rising steadily. However, these figures do not capture the full picture, as Keralam does not have routine STI surveillance across public and private hospitals. STIs also rarely figure in formal public health conversations.
World Sexual Health Day
On World Sexual Health Day (September 4), experts say Keralam needs more open conversations with young people about sexual health, safe sexual practices, consent and healthy relationships. Equally important is ensuring that youngsters know where they can seek confidential testing, advice and treatment without fear of judgement.
KSACS data compiled up to December 2025 show that attendance at DSRCs rose from 41,417 in 2023-24 to 63,129 in 2024-25. Another 51,243 people visited the clinics during April-November 2025 alone.
The proportion of DSRC clients undergoing RPR screening for syphilis also increased—from 55% in 2023-24 to 70% in 2024-25 and 79% during April-November 2025. The increase in screening means more infections are being detected, and the figures cannot by themselves be taken as evidence of a corresponding rise in prevalence.
Of particular concern is the increase among younger clients. Among those aged up to 19, clinic attendance rose from 1,547 in 2023-24 to 2,255 in 2024-25; another 1,910 had been recorded during April-November 2025. The proportion of newly detected HIV infections among those aged 15-24 also rose from 10% in 2022-23 to 15% during April-October 2025.
Change in societal attitudes
“There is a change in societal attitudes towards casual sex and today, the earlier message of abstinence that we used to give youngsters no longer works. Many youngsters are sexually active today and our only message to them is to remain safe, because their health is at stake,” a senior Health Department official said.
Being safe goes beyond HIV prevention. Condoms significantly reduce the risk of many STIs, including HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia, but do not eliminate the risk of infections such as syphilis, HPV and genital herpes, which can spread through skin-to-skin contact. HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, regular testing, timely treatment and reducing exposure to multiple or unknown partners are also important.
Consent and communication also need to be part of sexual-health messaging. Being safe means being able to say no, respecting a partner’s decision and discussing protection before sex.
Substance use among young people is another concern for sexual-health professionals, who say intoxication can increase risky sexual behaviour and impair the ability to make informed decisions.
Testing is crucial
“One of the most important messages we can give youth today is that testing matters, even without symptoms. Many STIs cause no symptoms, so someone can have and transmit an infection without knowing it. Testing becomes particularly important after a potential exposure or when starting a new sexual relationship,” said V. Sam Prasad, who heads AHF India Cares, an NGO working in HIV.
Keralam’s STI clinics are seeing a range of infections, with syphilis emerging as a particular concern. Doctors also report a resurgence of gonorrhoea, which they say is increasingly being encountered in clinical practice.
KSACS data show that clients found reactive for syphilis on screening increased from 1,206 in 2023-24 to 1,455 in 2024-25, with another 1,121 recorded during the first seven months of 2025-26.
Complicated infections
“We are quite concerned that some STIs are now presenting differently and with serious complications. We have had reports of neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and cardiovascular syphilis, which are complicated and require long and intensive treatment,” a Health official said.
At STI clinics, young people diagnosed with an infection are encouraged to bring their partners for testing to prevent reinfection. They are also advised to complete treatment and undergo HIV testing, given the close relationship between HIV and other STIs.
Self-assessment tool
To encourage confidential testing, KSACS has launched a digital self-assessment tool through which users can privately assess their sexual-health risk. By scanning a QR code and answering questions about lifestyle and behavioural practices, users receive guidance on whether testing may be advisable, along with information on the next steps and the nearest STI clinic.

Ethernet splitter vs switch: What's the difference and how do you use them?
At this point, there are very few situations in which you'll want to use a splitter.
Have you ever found yourself needing to connect two or more devices to the internet off a single Ethernet cable? Chances are that you've considered an Ethernet splitter or switch, especially if you're far from your router and cannot run a second line. With so many options on the market, however, picking the best option can get confusing.
Passive Ethernet splitters are incredibly simple devices and don't have any hardware capable of distributing network traffic between devices connected to them. This limits the maximum speed and has a tangible real-world impact on usability. On the other hand, powered Ethernet splitters and network switches actually have the processing hardware to route data between devices. But why does this distinction matter and which one should you buy? Let's break it down.
Why you should avoid passive Ethernet splitters
Before we talk about the differences between Ethernet splitters and switches, we first need to examine what's inside a typical Ethernet cable. Modern Ethernet cables, specifically Cat5e or better, use four twisted pairs of copper wires, which translates to eight individual copper wires. These days, most devices are capable of gigabit speeds and use all four twisted pairs to send and receive data.
However, not every Ethernet standard requires the use of all four pairs. Older Ethernet standards are limited to 10Mbps and 100Mbps transmission, and these only require two twisted pairs to reach maximum throughput. This leaves the other two pairs in the Ethernet cable unused. And this is where the most basic type of Ethernet splitters come into play. They split the cable's four twisted pairs into two separate two-pair connections. Each connection gets its own RJ45 port, allowing you to connect two different devices.
Passive Ethernet splitters (pictured above) have two major drawbacks, with the most obvious one being that they can only carry 10/100Mbps Ethernet connections. However, the other big catch is that you actually need two splitters for this setup to work. You cannot simply plug one cable from your router's LAN port into a passive splitter and connect two devices at the other end.
This is because passive splitters simply rearrange the wiring so that each device gets two twisted pairs. The router, meanwhile, cannot communicate with two different Ethernet devices through a single physical RJ45 port.
Active or powered Ethernet splitters: The bare minimum
Because of the limitations of passive Ethernet splitters, you need two of them: one at each end of the cable run. If you only use one splitter at the end, one of the two connected devices will likely fail to connect.
To remedy this problem, you'll need an active or powered Ethernet splitter. These cost a bit more than their passive counterparts, but they contain networking hardware that can logically manage traffic between multiple RJ45 ports. So even though they're marketed as splitters, they're essentially compact switches that take a single Ethernet connection and provide multiple fully functional ports on the other side.
The easiest way to identify an active Ethernet splitter is to look for a power input as these devices contain dedicated switching hardware. Besides simplifying the setup, these splitters also offer one more advantage: the ability to take advantage of the full bandwidth of the Ethernet connection, including Gigabit speeds and beyond. That said, if you use both devices simultaneously, you'll still be sharing the upstream connection between them, effectively splitting the available bandwidth.
Network switches: The most versatile Ethernet splitting solution
While active Ethernet splitters make sense when you simply need one or two additional RJ45 ports, they're often limited to just that. If you need multiple ports from a single cable run, a conventional Ethernet switch would be a better choice. And luckily, they typically don't cost much more than an active splitter. Switches offer anywhere from a handful to dozens of RJ45 ports, making them much more flexible for future expansion.
Even the most inexpensive network switches these days support Gigabit Ethernet, while higher-end ones start to offer 2.5Gbps ports. Enterprise-grade switches add 10Gbps ports, but that's beyond what most home users need. A 2.5Gbps switch is a good middle ground if you're looking to keep the switch well into the future.
This distinction matters beyond your internet speed too — if you use network-attached storage (NAS) to back up your data or serve media through Plex, a faster switch can significantly improve transfer speeds between devices on your local network. Of course, the devices in question need to support 2.5Gbps Ethernet for this distinction to matter.
In a home setting, all you need is a simple, unmanaged switch from the likes of Netgear and TP-Link. These require power but are essentially plug-and-play otherwise: connect one port to your router while the rest can be used for your TV or other devices. Several network switches exist on the market, so simply pick the one that matches the number of devices you need to connect and the maximum speed you anticipate needing. But if you only need to connect two devices, an active splitter will serve you just as well.

Reform UK's Zia Yusuf pulls up the ladder on Britain's immigrants
There is something almost exquisite about the hypocrisy of Zia Yusuf.
Last week, the Reform UK politician surveyed possible Labour candidates for the by-election in Holborn and St Pancras, to fill the MP seat previously held by former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, and apparently discovered something terrifying.
One of them was born in Somalia.
"The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour... was born in Somalia," Yusuf announced darkly.
Then came the sinister little flourish: "Do you understand what's happening?"

Yes, Yusuf, we do.
A woman came to Britain as a child refugee, grew up there, built her life there, entered public service there, became a councillor there and eventually became leader of Camden Council.
Now she may stand for election to the British Parliament.
Terrifying stuff. Someone alert the authorities!
At what precise point does a brown immigrant cease to represent the terrifying transformation of Britain and become Zia Yusuf?
Except, of course, Yusuf himself is hardly the blond, blue-eyed Anglo-Saxon guardian of some ancient native tribe. He is the son of Sri Lankan Muslim immigrants, which makes the performance all the more comical.
It is the politics of pulling up the ladder after you have climbed it - then standing at the top shouting that everyone still below is an invader.
Sagal Abdi-Wali has lived in Camden for 35 years - "the place that gave my family sanctuary", in her own words. She leads the council of the very borough containing the constituency she may seek to represent.
So what exactly is the problem? That she was not born there?
Perhaps Reform could publish the number of years an immigrant must reside in Britain before Yusuf permits them to become fully British. Ten? Twenty? Thirty? Forty?
Or perhaps there are other qualifications. Must their parents come from Sri Lanka rather than Somalia? Must they become millionaires? Must they join Reform?
At what precise point does a brown immigrant cease to represent the terrifying transformation of Britain and become Zia Yusuf?
That is the question his little dog whistle cannot answer.
The convenient messenger
Yusuf is hardly alone - even if Reform's London mayoral candidate, Laila Cunningham, distanced herself from this particular attack, saying she did not understand it. The daughter of Egyptian-Muslim immigrants, Cunningham has built her own political profile by portraying the visibility of other Muslims as vaguely menacing.
A few women in niqab become evidence that London feels like a "Muslim city"; foreign-language signs become symptoms of cultural surrender; and Muslim clothing in a market becomes a national problem requiring state intervention.
Cunningham even wants police empowered to stop women in face coverings on suspicion that they may be concealing their identities to commit crimes.
It is a particularly cheap form of politics: find some of the most conspicuous and vulnerable women in society, turn their clothes into evidence against them, magnify them into a civilisational threat, and invite everyone else to be suspicious.
The oldest trick in the anti-Muslim right's repertoire - only this time, delivered by the daughter of Muslim immigrants. The innovation is not the message. It is, conveniently, the messenger.
And while Yusuf was worrying about whether a Somali-born woman represented some existential threat to British public life, Channel 4 broadcast an undercover investigation into people rather closer to home.
Senior Reform figures were secretly filmed discussing arrangements around foreign-funded polling and a possible £500,000 ($676,000) donation from an American source channelled through a UK-based intermediary. Two senior aides subsequently stepped aside while Reform launched an investigation.
Ah, British values.
Apparently the danger to Britain is the Somali woman serving the people of Camden, not the questions about foreign money swirling around the party that spends half its time telling everyone else how fiercely it intends to defend British sovereignty.
Perhaps this is the "one civic culture" Cunningham keeps talking about.
Cues from America
Of course, Reform is taking its cues from across the Atlantic.
US President Donald Trump spent years shamelessly singling out Ilhan Omar, the Somali-born congresswoman, before widening his invective to Somalis more generally.
The irony is almost too obvious to require explanation. Trump himself is married to an immigrant. But apparently immigration ceases to be immigration when the immigrant happens to be a blonde Slovenian former glamour model who is married to the US president.
The same contradiction runs through US Vice President JD Vance's politics. His wife, Usha, is the daughter of Indian immigrants and was raised Hindu. His own family is a living product of precisely the ethnically and religiously plural America that his politics repeatedly treats as a source of suspicion.
Vance recently turned on Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, declaring there was something about him that was "very, very evil".
It was a textbook dog whistle, a piece of Islamophobia that has trailed El-Sayed throughout his campaign. His response punctured the trick by dragging the conversation back from demonisation to politics.
Evil, El-Sayed countered, is starting wars when there is peace. It is stripping away people's healthcare when they have no other option. It is corrupting yourself for a little more power, to fund tax breaks for billionaires.
There lies the difference between politics and prejudice. One talks about what governments do to people. The other tells people whom to fear.
The Palestine test
And that brings us to the central fallacy behind this grubby brand of identity politics. Your name tells us almost nothing about your political worth. Neither does your birthplace. Nor your religion. Nor your ethnicity.
Take perhaps the most morally charged political question of our time: Palestine.
Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum is the country's first woman president and its first president of Jewish background. She has formally received the credentials of Palestine's ambassador to Mexico, and her country has intervened in South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
Mexico also declined a seat on Trump's "Board of Peace" because Palestine was excluded, while Sheinbaum herself has spoken explicitly of the "genocide in Gaza".
Meanwhile, Latin America has produced leaders of Palestinian ancestry whose politics could hardly be more different.
El Salvador's far-right populist president Nayib Bukele comes from a Palestinian family, yet has aligned himself closely with Trump and maintained strong pro-Israel positions. Honduras's Nasry Asfura is also of Palestinian descent, yet is a committed ally of Israel.
Europe supplies its own example. Simona Mohamsson, leader of Sweden's Liberal Party and the daughter of a Palestinian father from Haifa and a Lebanese mother, recently appeared in a televised election debate wearing a Star of David necklace, and has made warnings about "political Islam" - that increasingly convenient smokescreen for repackaging anti-Muslim rhetoric as opposition to "Islamism" - a prominent part of her politics.
A Jewish woman can stand forcefully for Palestinian rights. People of Palestinian ancestry can do the reverse, choosing proximity to power over solidarity with the vulnerable and dispossessed.
Ancestry confers neither conscience nor principle. Identity is no guarantee of character or morality.
Back to Holborn
In Holborn and St Pancras, Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, intends to seek his party's nomination for the upcoming by-election. Sagal Abdi-Wali is being discussed as a leading contender for Labour.
Polanski is Jewish. Abdi-Wali is Muslim and wears a hijab.
So what? I am Muslim. I wear a hijab myself.
And yet, if I were voting in Holborn and St Pancras today, I might well vote for Polanski.
Why? Because I know considerably more about what he stands for. Over the past three years, I have admired his willingness to describe what Israel has done in Gaza as genocide, demand sanctions, oppose British complicity and stand against racism and Islamophobia.
We are watching a man expose not only the absurdity of his own politics, but the grubby little fraud at the heart of Reform
His Jewishness neither adds to nor subtracts from that. It is irrelevant.
I know much less about Abdi-Wali's politics. I would want to know what she thinks, what she has done, and what she intends to do before deciding whether she deserves my vote.
Her being Muslim does not inherently earn it. Her wearing a hijab does not automatically earn it. And her being Somali-born most certainly does not disqualify her from it.
I wish her well, particularly after the disgraceful attempt to turn her birthplace into an accusation. But votes should be earned by what politicians do and what they promise to accomplish.
Which brings us, finally, to Yusuf. "Do you understand what's happening?" he asked.
Perfectly.
We are watching a man expose not only the absurdity of his own politics, but the grubby little fraud at the heart of Reform: dress prejudice up as patriotism, find a brown man - or woman - to sell it, and hope nobody notices the joke.
Unfortunately for Yusuf, he is the joke.
