Hanuman Ansh is on an unstoppable run. The film collected just Rs. 1.07 crores in Week 1 and then dropped to Rs. 50 lakhs in Week 2. Surprisingly, it then earned Rs. 11.09 crores and a whopping Rs. 62.15 crores in its third and fourth week, respectively. Many expected the film to drop in the fifth week. Instead, it has collected Rs. 49.51 crores in the fifth weekend, with the fifth Sunday collections being Rs. 22.73 crores. As of September 6, it has earned Rs. 124.32 crores. We asked trade experts about this unbelievable box office performance of the historic film.
Trade experts talk about Hanuman Ansh’s HISTORIC run: “Abhi toh bas shuruaat hai. Even Rs. 300 cr or Rs. 400 cr lifetime can’t be ruled out…it can collect more in Week 6 than Week 5”
Trade veteran Taran Adarsh said, “Look at the jump. It collected Rs. 9 lakhs on day 1 and now has crossed Rs. 100 crore mark. The first week was bad, while the film had a total collapse in the second weekend. I am sure the producers were so disheartened, looking at the second week numbers. They must have thought ki film ka pack-up ho gaya. But then it picked up and how.”
On Friday, Bollywood Hungama reported that on the day of release, the makers had to resort to a BOGO (Buy One Get One) Ticket offer. Taran Adarsh explained, “What option did they have? Now they don’t need it as it’s running on the basis of the content. The audience has become the brand ambassadors and they are carrying it forward.”
He added, “There were hardly any pre-release promotions. The makers are now visiting cinema halls. However, it is purely riding on content. As a child, my mother and I went to see Jai Santoshi Maa (1975). Many people had come with the pooja ki thali and some of them left their shoes outside the auditorium. During the song ‘Main Toh Aarti Utaaru Re’, people used to sing along, clap, or fold their hands. For Hanuman Ansh, I saw similar visuals – some people were barefoot and standing in devotion. It’s a rare phenomenon.”
Girish Johar, producer and film business analyst, revealed when he realized Hanuman Ansh is a sleeper success, “I realized in the middle of the second week. Despite low collections, the film was hanging in theatres. The producers were pushing the word of mouth. The third weekend did the trick, after which there has been no looking back.”
Distributor and exhibitor Raj Bansal, meanwhile, replied, “I realized it in the third week. In the first week, no one cared about the film. In the second week, its trending caught attention. But in the third week, I realized that it’s going the Mahavatar Narsimha (2025) way. I was also reminded of Jai Santoshi Maa.”
Lifetime predictions
After the fifth weekend’s collections, trade experts believe it won’t be a surprise if Hanuman Ansh collects more in Week 6 than Week 5. Taran Adarsh opined, “Yes, there’s a possibility. Now it’s in the hands of the public. Where the public takes it now is up to them. It’s a case study.”
Trade analyst Atul Mohan said, “It may collect more next week than this week. Abhi toh bas shuruaat hai. It can go anywhere – Rs. 200 crores, Rs. 300 crores and even Rs. 400 crores lifetime can’t be ruled out. Now, several schools are planning to take kids to watch the film.”
Raj Bansal explained, “It’s difficult to predict for such films. The sky is the limit. Who would have imagined that it would collect Rs. 20 crores plus on the fifth Sunday? There’s a lot of demand and urgency to see the film. I get so many calls requesting for tickets because its shows are sold out in every theatre here.”
Girish Johar said, “It all depends on how it tracks during the weekdays. But anything can happen in today’s times. When an Obsession can do such numbers, why not Hanuman Ansh? So why restrict it to Rs. 200 crores? At the same time, why even burden it with such numbers? At the end of the day, it’s making a huge ROI, making profits for everyone concerned. It’s getting the audiences back to the theatres. That’s critical.”
To conclude
Atul Mohan hinted that devotional films are having a dream run at present, “Two years ago, Hanuman (2024) also worked. Mahavatar Narsimha was a hit. Laalo (2025) was a sleeper blockbuster. And now, Hanuman Ansh is on a historic run.”
Girish Johar signed off by saying, “It’s a beautiful film that rests on emotions. It once again shows that emotion is the critical element the audience wants, be it in any genre – action, horror, romance, animation, etc. If the audience connects with that emotion in a film, they don’t mind who the actor, director or producer is.”

The Backlash Against Data Centers
The Atlantic staff writer Josh Tyrangiel joined for a special edition of Washington Week With The Atlantic to discuss the future of AI.
On a special edition of Washington Week With The Atlantic, the Atlantic staff writer Josh Tyrangiel joined for a discussion about the future of AI and what, if anything, the U.S. government plans to do to address the rapid development of the technology.
Across the country, massive data centers are being built, and they’re “landing themselves without a whole lot of conversation” in American towns, Tyrangiel said last night. “It’s natural that all the fears about AI—about it taking your jobs, about it rendering human beings obsolete, about the values it changes—all are focused on” these data centers, he argued. “And politicians have been incredibly late to wake up to the anger around AI.”
“I don’t think people believe that they are going to partake in the wealth that comes from data centers in their community,” Tyrangiel continued. “Every community is going to make different choices, but what I’m sensing is that, particularly from Trump, the politics are out of line with where people are.”

Another Apple event is almost here, though this one will likely feel a little different than the September events of lore. It’s the first Apple event since CEO Tim Cook’s departure, and might be the first time the public gets a taste of how the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, can slip into those shoes.
The event will be livestreamed on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern). You can watch the stream right here on this page, or on Apple’s website and YouTube channel. Apple will also stream the event on its Apple TV devices and Apple TV+ streaming service. Leaks and rumors have left just about everyone expecting news about Pro-level iPhones and a long-awaited Apple foldable device.
Since the Covid pandemic, Apple has eschewed live presentations, instead inviting media and employees to the Apple campus to watch prerecorded videos of all its product announcements. WIRED will have reporters on the ground—you can follow along with all the action on our live blog, which will go live the morning of the event. WIRED will also have a roundup of everything the company announces for your perusal right after the event.
What to Expect
Thanks to leaks from sources like Bloomberg, the event is widely expected to be the moment Apple finally announces its long-rumored foldable iPhone. It’s bound to be pricey, with rumored estimates sitting around $2,000.
Apple is also expected to focus on premium products, chiefly the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4. That means Apple may push the launch of its base iPhone 18 to the spring of 2027. The move likely stems from increased manufacturing costs and limited product availability due to the ongoing memory crisis. It's also an effort to build hype for Apple’s more premium—and expensive—products, and maybe entice customers to sign up for the company’s new iPhone leasing program. We’ll likely see the mid-tier iPhone 18e at that spring event, alongside a second-gen iPhone Air.
New AirPods may also be on the table, though Apple’s heavily rumored AirPods Pro with cameras—designed to be the “eyes” of Siri for AI-powered visual assistance—could be delayed to later this year or to 2027.
If you’re hoping for new iPads, Macs, or home devices, well, you may have to wait a little longer. Apple announced a new Mac Mini and Mac Studio at the end of August, but the company may debut new home products, a new iPad Mini, and new MacBooks during events in October.
As for snagging devices right after Apple announces them this week, unconfirmed reports suggest the company will open iPhone preorders on September 12, a day later than it usually offers them, out of respect for the victims of 9/11. The following week is likely when the company will drop the final, official versions of its software, like iOS 27 and macOS 27.

Leicester City sink to new low in League One but can Russell Martin turn it around?
Leicester City find themselves sat 17th in League One after an embarrassing 4-0 home defeat against Oxford United on Saturday; Russell Martin is already under pressure after just one win in their first five games.
Monday 7 September 2026 15:14, UK
A decade ago in September 2016, Leicester City were getting ready to play in the Champions League.
Now? They sit 17th in League One, the lowest position in the club's history since they entered the Football League in 1894.
Russell Martin has led the Foxes to just one win in their first five games, and on Saturday they were battered 4-0 at home by Oxford United.
Leicester fans were chanting 'you're getting sacked in the morning' at Martin at the King Power Stadium, who would have been desperate for a good start to turn his reputation around after a dismal end to his time at Southampton, and then a gruelling spell at Rangers.

"There's a big expectation to deal with, but I think he's more than comfortable doing it."
Meanwhile, Reading co-CEO Joe Jacobson believes the inexperience in the squad is hurting their progress this season.
"They've got a really young team at the minute," he said. "You look at the players they're bringing off the bench and they're taking off experienced players and bringing on younger ones.
"It's difficult for those young players, who will feel the pressure and feel the atmosphere in the stadium. The fans are waiting to turn because of what's happened over the last couple of years. It takes a long time for a fan base to turn and get right behind their team again.
"They have a really tough job on their hands and Russell Martin will know that. He knows exactly what he wants to do and how he wants his team to play. Sometimes that causes division within the fan base, but I'm sure he'll be knuckling down on exactly what he wants to do with his team.
"It reminds me of when he was at Southampton. They lost four games in a row in September and then didn't lose a league match until February. If he can turn the ship, he might start to get a tune out of some of those players."
Jacobson also feels that the disconnect between the club and the fans is also causing an issue, especially since the owners announced Leicester was up for sale, having had a similar recent experience at Reading.
"It's been difficult at Reading because of what happened previously with the ownership there. We've felt it as well. It has taken a long time to get the fans to buy into what you want to do, and the ownership have done amazing things there over the years," he added.
"But when they recently came out and talked about wanting to sell the club and actively looking for a buyer, straight away the fans almost say, 'Well, you don't care now. You just want out. That's your main focus.'
"If the ownership are openly saying they want to sell, it's really difficult for the fans to buy into that. But I still think they're going to have a really successful season.
"Once these players get time on the training field with the manager, I'm sure they'll come good. At the minute, there's that anxiousness and a divided fan base. They want to support their club, but they also want to feel that everyone is pulling in the right direction."
Next up for Martin and Leicester is a trip to Stockport County on Saturday, who are currently sat third in League One.
A decade ago, the Hatters were in National League North. Now they welcome the Foxes to Edgeley Park as favourites for victory.

Dev Benegal‘s “English, August” almost didn’t survive to be restored. Its original camera negative had melted. The dupe was gone too. All that was left were two surviving 35mm prints – and, it turned out, a box of DAT tapes nobody expected to matter three decades later.
“It’s really sad that when I saw the original camera negative, it had melted. It was in terrible condition,” says Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, founder of the Film Heritage Foundation (FHF), the organization that took on the restoration. FHF was left to rebuild the film from whatever prints remained.
What remained were two 35mm release prints: one Benegal had personally kept and donated to FHF, the other preserved by the NFDC-National Film Archive of India, the government body that houses India’s official film archive. “There was no other material, so we had to look at both these materials, do the comparison and use these particular prints,” Dungarpur says. Both prints, he says, were in decent condition – a stroke of luck given how little else of the film had survived.
Popular on Variety
Released in 1994, “English, August” follows Agastya Sen, a young, Westernized trainee nicknamed “August,” sent to a remote provincial town for a year of civil-service training in India’s elite administrative cadre. Adrift among Bob Dylan records, Marcus Aurelius and a bureaucracy he can barely stomach, Agastya finds himself a stranger in a country that is technically his own. The film is adapted from Upamanyu Chatterjee’s 1988 novel of the same name, a book that became a defining portrait of a certain post-colonial, urban Indian generation.
Benegal says the screenplay only became the film in the editing room. “This is a film which was truly written on the editing table. I am a firm believer that’s where movies are actually written,” he says. “While we were editing, Upamanyu asked me, ‘Why did we even write a screenplay? We are writing the film right here.'”
The soundtrack turned out to be the restoration’s unlikely triumph. Benegal recalls the constraints under which the film was originally mixed. “Vikram Joglekar had recorded the sound in digital. Ignoring industry advice not to do that!” he says. “In 1994 we did not have the money to create a stereo mix. Those were days of the License Raj, where we had to secure special permission to import six reels of Kodak Optical Sound Negative. Even after that we only had outdated equipment to make a flat mono mix.” What survived instead was a set of DAT tapes Benegal had quietly kept for thirty years. “Back in 1994, DATs were the cutting-edge digital recording medium, and I kept them in my personal archive purely out of my obsession with audio – never imagining they would save the film three decades later when the original 35mm sound negatives vanished,” he says. “Going back to those tapes with Vikram Joglekar was like opening a time capsule.” Dungarpur confirms the tapes gave FHF something restorers rarely get. “We went back to the studio, and Vikram Joglekar, who was the sound recordist, brought back Satish P.M., the sound engineer, to work on restoring these tracks,” he says. “We had the unmixes, so it was great.”
Color grading brought its own rhythm to the process. Dungarpur says the palette was set by cinematographer Anoop Jotwani, who tested a single reel before the rest of the film followed his lead, with Benegal weighing in throughout from New York as the restoration work itself took place at L’Immagine Ritrovata, the film lab in Bologna, Italy. “You had Dev Benegal working almost daily on it. He did the English subtitles. We were talking daily about the look of the film, the way it was restored in Bologna, the grains and the color tone,” Dungarpur says. “There was a constant flow between Bologna and Dev Benegal, who was sitting in New York. He actually booked a suite to look at the grading, to look at the colors, to hear the sound.” Rahul Bose, who made his feature debut as the film’s lead, also came in to see part of the process, Dungarpur says.
Benegal is unequivocal about why Bose was right for that role. “Rahul Bose understood that Agastya wasn’t someone the audience needed to like; he needed to be truthful,” Benegal says. “He wasn’t trying to perform alienation – he simply inhabited the character with remarkable honesty. He also had the confidence to do very little. That’s much harder than it sounds.”
Not everything about the soundtrack could be fully reconstructed. Benegal says the production had gone to unusual lengths at the time to license its music. “Back in the day the producing team worked tirelessly to license and pay for music rights – something virtually unheard of then in India,” he says. One piece of paperwork never made it. “The paperwork documenting the Miles Davis’ “‘Round Midnight” clearance was lost in a torrential monsoon flood,” he says. The gap has created its own folklore among fans, he adds: “Some people have made a mix tape in their minds, from the box of tapes Agastya carried with him to Madna. Those tracks were never actually part of the original theatrical mix. Memory has a curious way of creating its own version of a film.”
For Dungarpur, the restoration answered a demand that had been building for years. “There was a great demand by people who wanted, were looking for, something to watch it back on the big screen and to see a restoration of this,” he says of “English, August.” “There are many people coming from around the world” eager to see the film again, he adds, calling it one of the independently produced films FHF exists to bring back “into a different time” for new audiences – including at Venice where the restoration premieres. It’s also FHF’s third consecutive year premiering a restoration at the festival, following Girish Kasaravalli’s “Ghatashraddha” in 2024 and Bimal Roy’s “Do Bigha Zamin” in 2025.
Watching “English, August” again more than 32 years after making it, Benegal finds the film’s portrait of isolation has only sharpened. “What feels familiar is the uncertainty,” he says. “India in the early 1990s was beginning to open up economically and culturally, but the old structures still shaped everyday life. There was a generation caught between inherited institutions and emerging freedoms. That sense of being in transition still resonates.” What has changed entirely, he says, is the texture of being alone. “The film unfolds in an India before mobile phones, social media and constant connectivity. Agastya is left alone with his thoughts… In 1994, if you were exiled to a small district town, you were genuinely off the grid. Agastya’s isolation was spatial and physical; today, isolation is algorithmic.”
Benegal argues the character’s alienation was never really about the West. “Agastya isn’t alienated because he listens to rock and jazz or reads Marcus Aurelius. He’s alienated because he’s searching for authenticity in a role that feels imposed upon him. That’s a condition that transcends both geography and time,” he says. He sees that same restlessness in a different uniform today: “The modern Agastyas aren’t just urban civil servants reading Marcus Aurelius in small towns – they are scrolling through curated, globalized lives on their phones from anywhere. The absurdity hasn’t disappeared; it’s just been upgraded to high-speed internet.”
The film’s satire of Indian bureaucracy has aged in a similar direction, according to Benegal. “Three decades later, the language of bureaucracy may have been digitized, but the core absurdities – the performance of power and the gap between official intent and ground reality – remain unchanged,” he says. “If anything, the satire feels almost prescient today.”
Benegal is candid that the film could not be made the same way now. “‘English, August’ succeeded precisely because it fit into zero existing boxes – it rejected that one prescribed way of making films,” he says. The five languages spoken across the film famously baffled censors at the time: “English, August has five languages, and that stumped the Indian censors who insisted, ‘a film can only have one language.'” Distribution came down to one gamble. “I have to give a huge shout out to Sunder Kimat Rai, who was country head of 20th Century Fox at that time, who took the gamble to distribute the film. He said, ‘the demographics match.’ I had no idea what ‘demographics’ even meant,” Benegal says. He doubts that kind of bet would be made today. “While we have streaming platforms and festival infrastructure, we also have hyper-calculated algorithms. Everything gets filtered through target demographics, pitch decks, and comparative commercial comps. The tools to shoot and edit are democratized, but the willingness of financiers and distributors to take a gamble on pure, unclassifiable tone is far rarer.”
Asked what a 20-year-old watching the film today might see that 1994 audiences couldn’t, Benegal points to something less generational than it first appears. “I hope they watch it as a portrait of someone asking timeless questions: Who am I? What kind of life do I want? What happens when the expectations of society don’t align with your inner life?” he says. “A young audience today may recognise mental and emotional states that weren’t discussed as openly in 1994. Agastya’s uncertainty may feel less like aimlessness and more like an honest search for meaning.”
Benegal is already looking past the restoration to his next project. “I’m working on ‘A Love Supreme’ a contemporary re-imagining of the epic Shakuntala – a story of a resilient, enigmatic woman whose path defies societal norms to become an autonomous woman,” he says. “But, the impulse remains the same as it was in 1994 – finding the humor, absurdity, and humanity in spaces where people feel out of place.”

Out in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms. Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.
Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.
One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.

Natalie Harp was by Trump’s side during weekend of AI slop at Bedminster: report
Harp has been dubbed the ‘human printer’ and is reportedly a key staffer involved in his social media communications
Natalie Harp, the White House staffer who has attracted attention for her extreme devotion to President Donald Trump, was reportedly around the Republican over the weekend at his golf club in New Jersey as he fired off countless unusual social media posts, such as an apparently AI-generated cartoon of himself attacking Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and multiple threats to rename New Mexico.
Harp was photographed by journalists on Friday boarding the presidential helicopter around the same time as Trump as it headed to Bedminster National Golf Club. She later appeared in a photo shared on Sunday from pro-Trump media personality Michael Solakiewicz. In the image, she appears to be typing on a tablet behing the president as he dines at Bedminster.
The Independent has contacted the White House for confirmation on Harp’s whereabouts and whether she was involved in the posts.
Harp, a former anchor on the right-wing One America News Network, has been dubbed the “human printer” because she frequently prints out hard copies of various messages and social media posts for the president.
The president is also known to dictate posts out loud to Harp, who often manages his day-to-day social media output,The Independent has previously reported.
That said, the president’s signature late-night posting sprees areoften his own doing, a former White House and campaign staffer from Trump's first term once told The Independent.
Others have described using Harp, who is known to work just outside the Oval Office, as a conduit to get messages onto the president’s social media feed and in front of the American people.
Homeland security adviser Stephen Miller, the architect of much of the president’s hard-line immigration policies, is reportedly among them.
Miller has used Harp’s closeness with the president “at least a couple” of times to get ideas before Trump, a source told Zeteo.
After Miller reportedly showed videos to Harp, they soon appeared on the president’s Truth Social page, the source said.
“I wanted the president to post something about crypto, so I [asked Natalie], and it worked,” another unnamed source told the outlet.
The president’s golf weekend may be over, but his eye-catching posts have continued.
On Monday, he fired off a post showing a map where the United States covered all of continental North America and Greenland.

US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”
He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.
He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.
“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.
In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.
This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.
Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.
“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.
“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.
Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”
“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.
Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage.
Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”
The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.
“Probably not,” he said.
The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

The Telluride Film Festival casts a wide net, as almost all festivals of its ilk do, but if it has had any speciality that stands out among many, it might be the well-earned tearjerker. There is as much crying at Telluride every year as there isn’t in baseball, but with the festival’s emphasis on top-line prestige fare, returning patrons look forward to going through some emotional catharsis in the mountains every Labor Day weekend. Among the 2026 lineup, probably no film got passholders any deeper in their feels than “Elsinore,” starring Andrew Scott and directed by Simon Stone. Their remarkable film dramatizes the true-life story of a well-known British actor — Ian Charleson, of “Chariots of Fire” fame — who died at the peak of the AIDS crisis in 1990, but who spent his last months and weeks staying alive long enough to achieve the life goal of playing Hamlet at the National Theatre.
There won’t be a dry eye in the house when this goes wide, as the cliche goes, but there also won’t be an untickled funny bone, given a performance by Scott that’s almost as drolly funny as it is passionate and heartrending (with no small help from writer Stephen Beresford). And there won’t be any un-warmed hearts among any viewers with a deep love for the life of the theater, since the movie serves as a love letter to stagecraft and community, on top of of most obviously being an ode to the seeming indomitability of Charleson as he bravely forestalled his final bow.
Popular on Variety
Stone’s long history as an actor before he became a premier stage director in Australia and then London — before finally moving into film — deeply informs every legit-loving moment of “Elsinore.” Variety spoke with him the day after his new film unspooled in Telluride, where he enjoyed a crowd waiting to give him and Scott yet another ovation in the lobby, some time after the credits rolled. Under his direction, Scott is an instant contender in the best actor face, and Stone may be up for some contending himself.
You told the crowd at the premiere that “Elsinore” was hot off the presses. How recent was it?
We finished on Wednesday of last week, so it’s a week and a half old. It’s very fresh. I think we were very lucky. Focus happened to have a slot that was unoccupied in their fall slate. And I think of course they recognized what Andrew’s doing in the movie is kind of undeniable (for awards consideration), and also that it’s a film that really resonates with audiences. I think that when you’re dealing with studios who still believe in watching movies in the theater, a film like this is like catnip. It’s specially made as an advocate for the theater-going experience. And I think all that catapulted us into a schedule that meant that we had to go fast, because we had to get to here (Telluride). We’re releasing in November, and when we release the movie, it will have been about 10 months from when we shot it. That’s lightning.
I’m not sure of comparable stories about how quickly a film turns around, and that is a testament to the work of everyone who told that story, and how prepared Andrew was. I guess we were all. I’d directed “Hamlet” on stage; Andrew had played Hamlet on stage; I had directed at the National Theatre. We knew all of these environments and this community. When you live that life for a long time, you want to be true to it, so there was an insistence on veracity and honesty that held true.
We all probably could have guessed that Andrew had done “Hamlet” on stage.
He had to relearn all the soliloquies, and I dadidn’t know exactly what scenes what bits were from, so I had to remind myself. But I essentially directed that production of “Hamlet” live, and we shot a documentary of me directing it, essentially, but I had an avatar of Johnny Flynn pretending to be me. But nobody knew when they walked into that rehearsal room on those days how it was gonna be staged. I staged it live, the way you would in a rehearsal room. What you’re watching in all of those rehearsal sequences is Andrew genuinely improvising. I mean, he knew his lines, but the idea of how he does it and where he does it, how it… That thing where Johnny (as the director) goes, “Don’t be afraid of intimacy. Hold each other,” those are all lines that I, a minute before we rolled, had fed into Johnny’s ear. Because I direct plays all the time, so I was like, “Well, this is the easiest way of us shooting this — for me to just direct this play.”
What were the other actors in the “Hamlet” scenes told about the story or about what to do?
They knew the backstory because in London, Ian’s story is one of those myths that is really meaningful, and a lot of his friends were in the film. And it’s a love letter to what theater is — it’s right there. They all wanted to do that, and to make it genuine, as opposed to like… You see so many depictions of theater as this over-the-top, self-centered, performative thing, and I wanted to show it as a crucible, as a shelter, as a safe place.
There is a scene when Ian starts coming clean about his illness with the rest of the “Hamlet” cast, and a viewer might wonder if, in a scene like that, there will be one token person who seems uncomfortable after learning he has AIDS, but they appear uniformly supportive. It does show what theater buffs hope the inner theater community is really like.
That’s right. I also think the theater community is a group of outsiders. It’s a bunch of freaks and geeks, and the reason we got into it was to share a common humanity, despite not being an average human being. There are a lot of parallels with the gay community at that time, and there is a distinct overlap, obviously. There are a lot of gay kids that ended up in theater because it was a place to express things that they felt that they couldn’t express elsewhere. So I think it’s a kind of rallying cry for acceptance and truth. And when we screened it last night, so many people were so heartfelt in really trying to express how moved they were by having felt seen or having felt someone in their life was seen by this film. That’s worth a million reviews or a million articles. It’s just a single person saying “That meant so much to me,” and I think Ian would feel really happy that that’s his legacy.
You must know what you’ve got on your hands. Did you expect the kind of reaction you’ve gotten in Telluride?
I would never have the hubris to assume that my reaction to something is gonna be someone else’s reaction to something. But I do know that I’ve made it in the spirit of heartfelt positivity about the joy we can find in life in the face of adversity. I think we’re living in a time in history where things feel so insecure geopolitically, socially — so divisive, so much difference. We’re focused on difference all the time in the media or in politics, like what separates us. I knew that people would really appreciate a film which is about no matter how different we are, we have to be together, otherwise all is lost…. The final scene seems like a triumph of an individual, but it’s not. It’s a group of people saying, “You are one of us.” The final scene is a flashback, because by the time you see the final scene, he’s already passed. So what you know is that you’re being let into what might have been his last memory as he disappeared, and it’s a memory of being with a group of people who said “We love you.”
Where do you think we’re at now in terms of people doing stories about “the AIDS era”? In terms of major films, it’s receded a bit.
Well, like all of these things, I think they need to recede. You know, thank God people aren’t making so many World War II movies. Every second movie in the ’50s was about the Second World War, and it had to be, because it was the big reckoning. When I was growing up, most multiplexes had one Second World War film in it at any point. And if you chart the history of Hollywood, you realize that becomes less and less and less and less. And, and there, of course, is the danger because at the end of the day, it was an important kind of reckoning, and it was an important catharsis. Then, of course, people go, “Well, that can’t be the only thing we’re focusing on,” because at a certain point it becomes fetishistic. I do think that that’s the same thing with any cataclysmic event: It needs a real analysis, but then it also needs the catharsis, which is we’ve explored — what it was about us that we got wrong. In the AIDS epidemic, it was very much a marginalization of a group of people that we thought that that was their problem rather than ours. I hope that we have learnt the lesson from that.
I also think that it’s because unless you’re in certain parts of the Third World, you’re not dealing with the idea of fatality if you get an HIV diagnosis. So all of these things mean that it kind of becomes less immediately relevant or immediately urgent. But that doesn’t mean that it doesn’t represent all sorts of lessons that we can learn about ourselves now. And I think that what’s great about this film is that AIDS is a context in the film. It’s a situation. In the same way that Martin’s film (Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” also showing in Telluride) is (set) in the ’70s…. The idea of American intervention in overseas political environments, that’s a context. But at the same time, (“Wild Horse Nine”) is a conversation about what happens when arrogant white men think that they can tell other people how to live, and that then suddenly feels relevant to now.
And I think that we found an equivalent thing with this. AIDS is a context, but it’s a conversation about divisiveness in communities, about the endless attempts to separate ourselves from each other and to create taboos in minority communities about what’s acceptable and what’s not acceptable. And I think that this film is is about: stop looking for everything that’s different about you and find something that’s similar. Find the common ground. Ian did that so beautifully in his life.
So I think it’s a very long-winded answer to your question about the relevance of the AIDS movie. But I think that the great triumph is that when “Philadelphia” was made, it had to be the only topic of that film, and we’ve got to a point where it’s one of five strands. And that’s an achievement. That’s a triumph.
Dealing with a terminal illness is closer to universal than not. People die unexpectedly, of course, too, but for the most part…
Yeah facing the end of life is a pretty common thing. The beauty of what he does in the movie is that he looks into the abyss and he finds hope. And weirdly, I was talking to some people where it was like, “Last night I was crying my eyes out, but today I feel really good.” I was like, that’s a common response to people who watch the film, because it’s true catharsis. It’s like a good session with your therapist. It’s like, yeah, it was painful to witness for a second, but at the end of the day, what it gave you was hope, and that’s a great thing to have. Because he faced the end willingly and with beauty, and that grace is extraordinary.
You said it was Andrew’s performance that put Focus into a hurry in wanting to get this out at a premium time this fall. What does his work on this mean to you, as his director?
Well, I mean, Andrew is one of those actors that I think we took for granted for a long time, thinking that he’ll always turn up and he’ll always be amazing. And I think this is one of the first projects where we had to be as amazing as he was — that he wasn’t just in the service of what we were doing. I think we as an industry have done that a lot. We’ve hired him to be in the service of what we need to do, and he’s always turned up, he’s delivered, he’s been brilliant. But this is the first one that’s been really 100% about what can we do to be in the service of you, Andrew, and he deserves the movie in the same way that Ian deserves this portrait of him. And I feel so honored to have kind of been a priest of that temple.

The story so far: India’s food regulator has proposed a red, hexagonal warning label on the front of packaged foods high in added sugar, saturated fat or salt, in a move aimed at giving consumers a simple, at-a-glance signal about unhealthy products.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), in an affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on August 28, has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages.
The proposal comes after years of debate over front-of-pack labelling and intervention by the Supreme Court. The Court is scheduled to consider the affidavit on September 10.
Also Read | FSSAI’s proposed warning labels could let unhealthy foods escape scrutiny, says expert
How the proposed system is expected to work?
FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages.
In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase.
The thresholds are proposed to be based on the Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024. However, the FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat.
Single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey, are also proposed to be exempt.
Also Read | Supreme Court slams FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products
What do critics say about the proposed change?
Nutrition advocates say the biggest concern is the decision to initially require a product to be high in two nutrients before it attracts a warning. A product that is high in sugar but low in salt and fat, for instance, could escape a warning altogether.
“This defeats the purpose of a warning label,” Arun Gupta, convenor of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPI), told The Hindu. He has argued for a simpler principle: if a product is high in sugar, salt or saturated fat, it should carry a warning.
Also Read | Why the FSSAI is also putting liquor under the scanner
The distinction could matter particularly for products such as sugary beverages, which may be high in added sugar but contain little or no fat or salt and could therefore fall outside the warning requirement in Phase I.
Dr. Gupta has also raised concerns over the use of “added” rather than total sugar and fat, the size of the proposed warning and the absence of a firm deadline for Phase II. He has called for the warnings to be available in Hindi and English, arguing that language and visibility are essential if the labels are to reach consumers across the country.
He has urged the Court to examine the proposed nutrient thresholds, definition of high-fat/sugar/salt foods, warning size, language requirements and exemptions to ensure that the system remains visible and scientifically robust.
Also Read | From Bournvita to ‘100% Pure’: Why is FSSAI tightening the rules on food claims?
Why is this significant?
Front-of-pack warning labels have been under discussion in India since at least 2018. Draft regulations on high fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods were proposed in 2022, but did not become law.
The issue returned to the centre of the public-health debate in 2026 after the Supreme Court directed FSSAI to move towards interpretive warning labels for unhealthy packaged foods.
The regulator’s approach has also evolved rapidly in recent weeks. An earlier proposal placed before the Court in August relied on displaying nutritional information against recommended daily limits. Following the Court’s intervention, FSSAI returned with the red-hexagon warning framework in its August 28 affidavit.
Also Read | FSSAI proposes front-of-pack red pictorial warnings for foods high in fat, sugar, salt
For consumers, the proposed red hexagon is intended to make it harder for marketing claims such as “natural” or “multigrain” to obscure the nutritional profile of a product.
For the food industry, mandatory warnings could increase pressure to reformulate products by reducing sugar, salt and saturated fat. FSSAI has said the phased approach would give industry time to reformulate.
But the proposal is not yet a notified regulation. The immediate question before the Supreme Court is whether the framework provides a clear and meaningful warning or leaves products high in a single nutrient outside the net for an unspecified period.

The anger was impossible to miss.
As television reporters walked into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and adjoining protest sites to cover the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, many were greeted with chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’. Several journalists carrying microphones or wearing lanyards bearing the logos of prominent television channels — including NDTV, News X, ABP News, and Times Now — found themselves surrounded by protesters questioning their coverage of the movement. In some instances, reporters were heckled. In some instances, the confrontation turned physical: Times Now reporter Dev Kotak was roughed up by the crowd at Jantar Mantar, and video of the aftermath circulated widely. A Zee News reporter was filmed in Mumbai standing in the rain as youth protesters around him jeered.
The mood was most poignantly captured, perhaps, by a banner at the protest site. It contained the mugshots of six senior mainstream media journalist-cum-anchors: Arnab Goswami of Republic, Sudhir Chaudhary of DD, Chitra Tripathi of ABP, Anjan Om Kashyap of Aaj Tak, Amish Devgan then of News 18, and Rubika Liyaquat of Times Now Navbharat. Above their photos, the banner said, “India’s worst enemies — More dangerous that terrorists or anti-nationals”.
Taken together, the scenes that unfolded in Delhi raise the important question: Why did a large section of young protesters reserve some of their sharpest criticism not for politicians or police, but for television news channels?
Television Crew Faces Public Anger
The protests that erupted in Delhi in June-July brought together thousands of students and young people from across the country, turning a satirical political collective called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) into the nucleus of a wider youth-led movement. What began as a mobilisation around the NEET-UG paper leak and concerns over the examination system expanded into a broader expression of anger against the government, with protesters demanding accountability from those in charge. The demonstrations grew in scale over weeks, drawing sustained public and media attention and eventually contributing to Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.
As the protests grew, major television networks deployed reporters to cover the events. Instead of the routine interactions that often accompany live reporting, many ground reporters encountered open hostility from sections of the crowd.
Slogans of “Godi Media” were raised during a gathering in the national capital Delhi. pic.twitter.com/oyZpCVz0EY
— The Nawakadal (@thenawakadal) July 20, 2026
Videos shared widely on social media show protesters chanting ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ — a phrase originally coined by journalist Ravish Kumar, roughly translating to ‘lapdog media’ — as reporters prepared to go live. In one video, a protester says he stopped a News18 vehicle from being damaged despite his own anger towards the channel. “I am a Muslim myself. I protected their vehicle from being damaged. Though I know this evening, they will again do a Hindu-Muslim debate,” he said.
GODI MEDIA IS DEAD!

Traditional Mainstream Media has COMPLETELY LOST Gen Z’s Trust!
Lakhs of Students who hit the streets got EVERY piece of Real Information from Social Media — not your Biased Propaganda Boxes.… pic.twitter.com/zLIOM5GXP1
— তন্ময় l T͞anmoy l (@tanmoyofc) July 21, 2026
As reporters started being identified by the brands they represented, some began using unbranded microphones instead. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor and Vishnu Som, and India Today’s Preeti Choudhry were among those.
The outbursts were not confined to a handful of isolated incidents. Numerous videos from different locations captured similar confrontations, while comments beneath those videos echoed the protesters’ criticism of mainstream television news. Smaller outlets perceived as pro-government were heckled as well, suggesting the hostility was directed at a type of coverage rather than at legacy television alone.
At the same time, several incidents crossed the line from protest into intimidation. Videos also emerged showing journalists being pushed, chased or physically heckled by sections of the crowd.
This andhbhakti of CJP is now crossing all limits. You can tell godi media to walk away, raise slogans, but you can’t physically push, grope or beat them.
Wonder whether these are genuine protestors or lumpen elements.https://t.co/Xo4bTJ1DgX
— 🍉 (@DelhiIsNotFar) July 21, 2026
In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.
You are the most vile, most pathetic, most disgusting person @sudhirchaudhary
I always agree to disagree, never hate anyone but you are really a bad person.
You are now labelling innocent students for your propaganda.
Shame on you! pic.twitter.com/lYj5cNlURk
— Arpit Sharma (@iArpitSpeaks) July 21, 2026
Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.
ALSO READ: Op Sindoor: As Indian media made false, outrageous claims, PIB looked the other way
Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.

A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.

The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
हमारे जवान तो जंग के लिए तैयार हैं, लेकिन क्या आप मन से तैयार… pic.twitter.com/spQrwxqbTm
— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

Zee TV’s fiction show Jagadhatri has completed 300 episodes, marking a milestone for the series and its cast and crew. The show, led by Sonakshi Batra as Jagadhatri and Farman Haider as Shivaay, has continued its run with a mix of drama, action, romance and emotional conflicts.
Jagadhatri completes 300 episodes; Sonakshi Batra and Farman Haider reflect on the show’s journey
The current storyline has taken a dramatic turn following the death of Rudra, played by Ayushh Shrivastava. His death has left Jagadhatri facing accusations, while the narrative moves towards secrets and revelations that are expected to further impact the characters.
As the show reaches the 300-episode mark, Sonakshi Batra reflected on her experience of playing the titular character and the response to the series. She said, “I have always said that Jagadhatri is a very special show for me. It is a very different show and Jagadhatri is a very different character from anything I have done before. In many ways, this character gives me strength even in real life. The way Jagadhatri is strong, smart, fearless and hardworking, she inspires me every single day. This show has given me so much, new lessons, beautiful learnings, the love of the audience and, of course, so many memorable experiences. Completing 300 episodes is a very big milestone for me and the entire team. When we started this journey, I had never imagined that we would receive this much love. Today, seeing so many fan pages and people talking about Jagadhatri, her action sequences, her fights and her journey makes me incredibly happy. I love that the show gives me the opportunity to explore so many shades, action, romance, drama and emotions and play such a layered character. I am truly grateful for everything Jagadhatri has given me. As we celebrate 300 episodes, I only want to say that I will continue to work harder and give my best to the show. I hope we continue to receive the same love and blessings from our audience and keep celebrating many more such milestones together. Happy 300 to us!”
Farman Haider, meanwhile, spoke about playing Shivaay and the experience of being part of the show. He said, “I absolutely love working on Jagadhatri because it is such a unique show. It has drama, action, romance, emotions, fun and so many unexpected turns, and that makes it exciting for both the audience and us as actors. Playing Shivaay has been a wonderful experience because the character has so many layers, and as an actor, getting the opportunity to explore different shades within one character is something very special. Completing 300 episodes is a huge milestone for all of us, and it makes me extremely happy and proud. This journey has been possible because of the hard work of everyone, both on screen and behind the scenes. Our entire team has worked tirelessly to make the show bigger and better with every episode, and seeing the audience shower us with so much love and blessings makes all the effort worth it. I am truly grateful to everyone who has supported Jagadhatri and Shivaay and made them a part of their lives. I am super excited about this milestone, and I am sure this is just the beginning. We will continue to work harder, entertain our audience and hopefully celebrate many more milestones together. As Shivaay, I promise to keep giving my best and keep entertaining our fans with everything we have. Happy 300 to us!”
With the story continuing to build around Jagadhatri and the aftermath of Rudra’s death, the show is set to move into its next phase. Jagadhatri airs every day at 10:30 p.m. on Zee TV.

An experimental gene therapy for Angelman syndrome from Ultragenyx failed in a Phase 3 study, STAT reports. The medicine showed no benefit compared to a sham treatment in the rare disease, which causes severe intellectual disability and developmental delays. The drug, called GTX-102, had shown powerful results in early trials, raising the hopes of families affected by the devastating condition. The trial failure is also a significant blow to Ultragenyx’s business, and the company said it’s now planning “significant expense reductions.”
Just a week after the landmark U.S. approval of a game-changing drug for advanced pancreatic cancer, the same therapy is showing promise against the world’s biggest cancer killer, Nature tells us. In a small trial in non-small cell lung cancer, the drug, Revolutions Medicines’ Rasonque, shrank tumors in more than 30% of participants. Each patient had tumor-promoting mutations in a member of the RAS family of proteins, and had previously tried other therapies. A larger study in which participants with non-small cell lung cancer are randomly assigned to receive either the drug, also called daraxonrasib, or standard chemotherapy is underway.

The kharif sowing season is closing the gap with last year’s pace, though key crops remain under pressure. Farmers planted 108.63 million hectares as of 4 September, only 1.6% below the same period last year, according to agriculture ministry data. This is nearly in line with the ministry’s normal benchmark of 110.45 million hectares. The headline number masks sharper declines in rice, maize, soybean and cotton, which together form the backbone of India’s food and fibre supply. Rice acreage, at 42.18 million hectares, is down 3.7% from last year, raising concerns for government procurement and food-security programmes, including the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, that feed 80 crore people. Pulses have provided some relief, as acreage has risen 1.6% to 11.71 million hectares, led by gains in Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Telangana. Coarse cereals and oilseeds have slipped marginally, while cotton and sugarcane are also trailing last year’s levels. The uneven monsoon remains a risk. Rainfall is 13% below normal and patchy across regions, leaving crops at critical growth stages vulnerable. Analysts warn that while the overall acreage gap is small, the crop-specific shortfalls could weigh on foodgrain, edible oil and cotton supplies in the months ahead. Karnataka, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand and Maharashtra led the decline in rice acreage. Assam and Odisha reported higher acreage, according to the ministry's statement. “The 1.6% gap in overall kharif acreage by itself is not alarming, but the 3.7% decline in paddy acreage needs closer attention because of its implications for foodgrain availability and procurement. The increase in pulses acreage provides some comfort, but the final output will depend on rainfall during the remaining crop cycle,” said Binod Anand, agricultural economist and member of the Union government’s high-powered committee on Minimum Support Price (MSP). In pulses, the increase was led by Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, which more than offset declines in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Odisha. Acreage under Shri Anna and coarse cereals stood at 18.14 million hectares, down marginally from 18.25 million hectares a year earlier. The decline was mainly due to lower acreage in Karnataka and Maharashtra, as well as reductions in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Oilseed acreage declined marginally to 19.20 million hectares from 19.31 million hectares last year. Lower acreage under soybean and groundnut offset gains in crops such as sesamum and sunflower. Cotton acreage was also marginally lower at 10.92 million hectares, compared with 10.99 million hectares a year earlier. Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab reported declines, while Telangana and Gujarat recorded higher acreage. Sugarcane acreage at 5.85 million hectares was marginally below the 5.89 million hectares recorded a year ago, while jute and mesta acreage increased to 634,000 hectares from 624,000 hectares. The narrowing sowing gap comes despite a below-normal monsoon season so far. India received 13% less rainfall than normal between 1 June and 4 September, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The rainfall distribution has also been uneven across regions. IMD has forecast subdued rainfall activity over peninsular India in the week ahead, while several parts of central and eastern India are expected to receive rainfall. The uneven rainfall pattern could remain important for crops that are now at critical stages of growth. Rice, soybean, maize and cotton have all recorded lower acreage than last year, making the distribution of rainfall in the remaining monsoon period important for crop conditions and eventual yields.
