A landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles by Jamaican over slavery reparations, aiming to confront historical crimes that still disadvantage former British colonies, the Caribbean nation’s culture minister has said.
The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.
“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.
“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so.”
First announced in June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.
It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.
Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.
Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to the Americas and sold into slavery.
Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery, that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.
“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.
“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.
“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.
He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.
There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.
In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbean launched a manifesto outlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmer resisted pressure from member states to include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.
Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.
On Sunday, the delegation will host a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum, to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.
She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.
“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”

Chelsea agree £47.1m move for Monaco's Camara
- Published
Chelsea have agreed a £47.1m deal to sign Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara.
The 22-year-old is set to undergo a medical after Chelsea complete the sale of Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City in a deal that matched the £125m British transfer record.
Chelsea had been reluctant to complete a transfer for Monaco's asking price but they are believed to have dropped their demands when striker Folarin Balogun's move to Everton from the French club came into renewed doubt.
It was expected the Blues would continue with their current midfielder options despite sanctioning Fernandez's exit but an opportunity to sign one of their primary targets at a lower price was taken up.
They had also held talks with Roma's Manu Kone and another unnamed Premier League option.
The signing is not viewed as a like-for-like replacement for Fernandez, with Camara offering a different profile in midfield. However, Chelsea believe the deal will help maintain the strength of new manager Xabi Alonso's squad.
One of the club's aims this summer was to emerge from the transfer window with a stronger squad despite selling Fernandez to a direct rival.
Chelsea believe they have achieved that after signing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa in a club-record £117m deal, centre-back Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace and, most recently, goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa.
The club have also recruited strikers Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck, winger Geovany Quenda, midfielders Jordan Henderson and Valentin Barco, as well as full-backs Marco Palestra and Pep Chavarria.
Alonso's side have won all three of their matches this season, beating Fulham and Brighton in the Premier League, and have also reached the third round of the Carabao Cup with victory over Luton Town.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

I Found the Best Kindles to Take Your Library Anywhere
Featured in this article
There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.
I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.

Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?
Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only the recent Kindle Scribe models with the original price tag. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. It's interesting that none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it's also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.
Here are all the increases, including Signature versions:
- Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)
If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I'd wait until Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday to shop when they're on sale. It's likely the sale prices will only bring the Kindle down to be the price it was before, but better than paying more.
What About the New Kindle Scribes?
Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There's now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.
All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, slightly slimmer form factor, and updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.
Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities, but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
Accessories for Easier Reading
If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.
Cases and Covers
Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don't forget that the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.
About Those Older Kindles
Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.
Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.
Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.
Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.
Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for under $200 on eBay.
Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.
Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.
FAQs
Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?
As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.
The following Kindle devices are impacted:
- Kindle 1st Generation
- Kindle 2nd Generation
- Kindle DX
- Kindle DX Graphite
- Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
- Kindle 4
- Kindle Touch
- Kindle 5
- Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation
What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?
Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.
Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.
How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?
If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.
If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.
If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:
- Get a library card for your local branch.
- Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
- Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.
If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.
What Else Can a Kindle Do?
Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.
Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.
While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.
When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.
Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.
There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.
How Do You Update a Kindle?
When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.
What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?
Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.
Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?
The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.
You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.
Are Kindles Good for Students?
Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.

On Feb. 24, 2025, the Food and Drug Administration did something it arguably should have done long ago: It removed the elaborate monitoring program that has governed one of psychiatry’s most important drugs, clozapine, for more than 30 years. For anyone who treats serious mental illness, this is welcome news.
But I want to say something more complicated about it, because I have spent a large part of my career prescribing this drug (or trying to) to the most vulnerable population there is: children with psychosis. The paperwork was never really the problem.
Very few things in all of medicine have struck me as close to miraculous. Vaccines. Antibiotics. And, in children with childhood-onset schizophrenia, clozapine. That will not surprise anyone who has worked with it in schizophrenia.
Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic we have for the sickest patients: the roughly 1 in 3 people with schizophrenia whose illness does not yield to other medicines. It is the only drug approved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, the only one shown to reduce suicide, and it is associated with lower death rates than the alternatives. When nothing else has worked, clozapine can, sometimes, give a person back to themselves. I have watched it happen in children, in the carefully controlled trials my colleagues and I ran, where young people who had been lost to relentless psychosis began, within days, to return to their families.
And yet it is one of the most underused drugs in all of medicine. In the United States, only about 4% of people with schizophrenia receive clozapine, though perhaps a third could benefit, and the figure should probably be higher still in childhood-onset schizophrenia, which tends to be even more treatment-resistant. There is, in plain terms, a proven, lifesaving, sometimes life-restoring treatment that American medicine mostly declines to give.
For years, simply to prescribe clozapine, a clinician had to enroll in an FDA-mandated registry. Patients submitted to regular blood draws, which are weekly at the start, with each result logged into a national database before a pharmacy could release the next supply. The goal was to catch the small number of patients in whom clozapine can sharply reduce the white cells that fight infection.
Whatever caution it began in, there is good evidence it also kept the drug from people who needed it. That is the very program the FDA has now retired, perhaps influenced by advocacy efforts, including those by parents.
But the deeper barrier was fear. Clozapine carries a fearsome reputation: the blood tests, the long list of side effects, the rare but genuine danger. This has scared clinicians; they just don’t want to take the risk. And the FDA can remove the registry, but cannot make the fear go away.
This is especially true when dealing with children, in whom neutropenia tends to be more common than in adults. I have watched capable, caring clinicians steer around clozapine for years, reaching for a fourth or fifth less-effective medication rather than the one most likely to work, because avoiding it simply felt safer. Recently I could not find a single child psychiatrist across four academic centers willing to start clozapine in a child with childhood-onset schizophrenia.
When I first started using clozapine, I was afraid as well. But it soon became clear that it was not a particularly difficult medicine to work with. Yes, you have to monitor the side effects carefully, but the benefits simply made the risk worth taking. And as I started seeing the benefits of clozapine, the fear quickly went away.
After all, in other areas of medicine, we treat children with many risky medications (such as chemotherapeutic drugs) because we know they are lifelines for those illnesses. We need to approach clozapine the same way when it comes to schizophrenia.
In my experience, parents were rarely the problem. They understood, they were desperate, had often done the work of getting over their fear, and were ahead of the curve. They typically had already heard and read about clozapine and were ready to be on board as soon as we were ready, partly because they had tried everything and nothing had worked. I used to say, after seeing what I saw at the National Institute of Mental Health, “If someone in my family was diagnosed with schizophrenia, I would want them on clozapine yesterday.”
The cost of our avoidance of clozapine is invisible but enormous, measured in people who stay sick, and in lives that end early, for want of a drug already sitting on the shelf.
I do not mean to minimize the side effects of clozapine. The risks are very real. My colleagues and I ran into them at the NIMH every now and then. We went on to study how often it happened in our children, and who was most at risk. The problem is concentrated in the first months of treatment, and it never quite reaches zero.
But we found ways through: We showed, for instance, that adding lithium could lift the neutrophil count enough to keep a child safely on clozapine, and we published it. Its other side effects, too, can be managed, and there is ample literature, including from our own group, on how to do that in children. In fact, as we published more, we began to notice something new: Some of the children referred to our study arrived already on clozapine, something we had never seen in the study’s earlier years.
Those of us who worked closely with clozapine had argued for years that its monitoring was stricter than the evidence justified; that a rigid, uniform schedule, largely unchanged for decades, treated every patient as though the danger were constant and equal, when in truth it was concentrated in the early months, foreseeable, and, in most cases, manageable. The FDA’s recent decision, in that sense, is less a reversal than an overdue acknowledgment of what the people closest to the drug had been saying all along.
Notably, the FDA still recommends the blood tests; it has simply stopped forcing them. This is a welcome change, and it means the responsibility that used to live inside a federal registry now lives where it probably always should have: in the judgment of the clinician and the informed choice of the patient.
That is the real opportunity in this decision, and the real test of it. Lifting the program is not permission to be careless; it is an invitation to be wise, and better informed.
Ideally it will empower clinicians to reach for clozapine sooner, for the people most likely to be saved by it, including the young. The worst outcome would be to lose the bureaucratic barrier and go on avoiding the drug anyway, only now without even a rule to blame.
And perhaps, and this is my real hope, it will move us to reach for clozapine earlier, rather than only as a last resort. To my colleagues who care for the youngest and sickest patients, I would put it as plainly as I can: Do not let fear make this decision for you. We have spent three decades treating clozapine as the door you open only after every other has failed. The science has never justified waiting that long. The government has now removed one of our excuses. Whether we use this moment to actually reach the patients who need it, or simply find a new reason to look away, is up to us. It always was.
Nitin Gogtay, M.D., is a psychiatrist, physician-scientist, and author of “The Vanishing Children” (HarperCollins, January 2027). He spent almost two decades studying and conducting blinded clinical trials of clozapine on childhood-onset schizophrenia at the National Institute of Mental Health.

In Summary
- The CMF Buds Neo are the latest TWS from Nothing’s sub-brand, CMF.
- The new buds come in attractive colors, in true CMF tradition, and punch above their price point in terms of specs and features.
- At Rs 1999, the CMF Buds Neo are the most affordable TWS in CMF’s audio portfolio, and have also been called the most accessible entry point to the CMF ecosystem. They do face a lot of competition, though.
While it is hard being a new smartphone in this tech climate, we believe it is harder being a new pair of TWS. The number of new TWS, as well as increasingly competitive prices and features across a wide range of price brackets, make it quite a task for a new pair to make its mark in the tech world. The latest addition in this lineup comes from Nothing’s sub-brand CMF, the CMF Buds Neo. Priced at Rs. 1,999, the Buds Neo are positioned as the most accessible entry to the CMF ecosystem. They come with an impressive feature list and a quirky design. But is that enough to help the CMF Buds Neo make space for itself in the TWS market?
CMF Buds Neo Appearance and Design: Typically CMF, Geometry with some flair
CMF, like its parent company Nothing, speaks a very distinct design language. A language no one else in the industry has adopted (yet) – a very smooth blend of Nothing’s industrial design combined with CMF’s bright colored flair. The CMF Buds Neo speak this language. Their square-shaped case comes with soft, rounded edges that make it sit very comfortably in one’s hands. The top left corner has a tactile, round dial. This is not just a design touch but also has some utility – it can be used to attach a lanyard that will keep your Buds Neo from getting lost.
The buds come in three different colors: Black, White, and Dark Blue. The Dark Blue and White color options bring very vibrant color contrasts with green and orange ear tips and tactile dials, respectively, while the Black is all black. The white variant, whose white case comes with a super bright orange tactile dial, is perhaps the most distinct. There is a small ‘CMF by Nothing’ badge in orange on the front as well. The cases have a matte finish while the dials are glossy.
The case has a very tiny LED light on the front and a USB Type-C port on the back. Flip the case open, and you find the buds resting nicely inside, with a ‘Buds Neo’ branding slightly above the earbuds. The buds come with a typical TWS design – a bulbous head attached to a long pill-shaped stem. The eartips bring the pop of orange to the white buds, while the texture of the overall buds is a mix of glossy and matte.
There is a small glossy dot on the head of the stem of the right bud and a thick, slightly raised circle on the stem of the left bud. The buds are comfortable to wear and come with one set of eartips attached and two others in the box. We used the medium-sized eartips, and they fit snugly. Speaking of snug fits, the buds also attach magnetically to the case.
The CMF Buds Neo case itself is quite compact – it is square, with length and breadth both at 54.3 mm, and is a little thick at 23 mm. It weighs 50.3 grams, while the buds weigh just a little over 4 grams each. The case is very pocket-friendly, and the buds are light on the ear. The buds come with an IP55 rating, making them good enough for sweaty gym sessions, while the case has an IPX rating, making it splash-proof, which is handy (most TWS cases still do not have splash resistance).
The white case does get dirty very easily (it caught dirt marks in our bag), but all in all, the design of the CMF Buds Neo is very eye-catching and definitely something not-so-usual. If you are not into pops of color, you can choose the black variant. Those who want to be right between these two extremes can go for the blue variant, with its flash of green eartips and disk.
CMF Buds Neo Specs and Controls: Very impressive at this price point
The CMF Buds Neo come with impressive specs for their price. They have 12.4 mm dynamic drivers with a 20 Hz- 20 kHz frequency response, two mics per earbud (for a total of four), Bluetooth 6.0, support for AAC and SBC codecs, and ANC of up to 35 dB. There is also support for spatial audio, and you get six EQ presets. All of these features are accessible through the NothingX App. The case comes with a 460 mAh battery with support for fast charging, and each earbud has a 45 mAh battery in it as well. The buds support Google Fast Pair, Microsoft Swift Pair, and also Dual-Device connectivity.
Pairing the CMF Buds Neo is simple: you flip the case open, wait for the buds to appear in your device’s Bluetooth list, and select them. To get the buds in pairing mode to connect with other devices, you can simply tap and hold the stem of the buds for five seconds, then select them from your device’s Bluetooth list. The controls on the buds are basically a series of taps- double-tapping on either bud will take you to the next track or reject a call; triple-tapping will take you to the previous song, while tapping and holding will let you switch between ANC and transparency mode.
No action is assigned to the double-tap-and-hold, but one can assign it to increasing or decreasing the volume or summoning the voice assistant. Apart from the call functionality, these controls can be customized using the Nothing X app. Interestingly, there is no option to map a control to a single tap, perhaps out of concern for accidental touches.
CMF Buds Neo Performance: Good audio, decent ANC and very good calling
The 12.4 mm dynamic drivers on the CMF Buds Neo come with a titanium-coated PET dome and a flexible PEEK and PU surround. This, as per Nothing, adds a bass-ful punch to the audio while ensuring vocals do not get muddied. The buds certainly deliver on both these fronts. The audio is full-bodied, and while it does focus a bit on bass, it does not drown out the treble or vocals. It is not balanced in a way that would give an audiophile an eargasm, but we seldom see that at this price anyway. On the other hand, they will impress casual listeners in a heartbeat, delivering a thoroughly enjoyable experience in pop, Bollywood, R&B, and hip-hop, and similar genres.
The Nothing X app comes with six EQ presets, and each one offers a distinct sound profile, which sometimes is not the case in this price segment. There is also the option to create an EQ based on one’s own preferences. The buds provide a reasonably spacious sound, which is usually not very easy for TWS to achieve, especially at this price point. The sound obviously does not feel as immersive as some of the high-end audio gear available on the market, but for the price, it is a hit in our books. The vocals are sharp enough to listen to hour-long podcasts or watch content.
The CMF Buds Neo also come with ANC. There are four options – low, medium, high, and adaptive. We mostly stuck to the ‘high’ setting. It will not cancel out very loud noises, but the snug fit of the buds combined with effective ANC does kill environmental noise with ease. It managed to drown out noise in a crowded cafe very effectively. We could not hear our friend sitting across from us with ANC on. The transparency mode brings back awareness to what would otherwise be a very isolating experience – the conversation we were not able to hear earlier became clear with transparency mode.
The call quality of the buds is very good as well – a pleasant surprise at this price point. We did not have any issues hearing the caller and did not get any complaints about our voice quality either. There is a low latency mode for games, but we had to turn it on manually, which was a bit of a pain.
The controls of the CMF Buds Neo are easy to remember but take some serious getting used to. We often found we had to tap harder than we are used to in order to register a command. The buds also lack wear detection, which means the audio does not automatically pause when one takes the buds (one or both) out. While this is a feature not often found at this price point, its absence was inconvenient.
Battery is another strong suit of the CMF Buds Neo. The buds promise 11 hours of listening time with ANC off, with 52 hours of total playback with ANC off, including the case. With ANC on, the numbers become 5 hours for the buds, and 30 hours with the case. We found the buds’ actual performance to be close to these numbers. With mixed use (ANC/ transparency mode on and off) at 70 percent volume, the buds easily lasted for around 9 hours. The buds also have a fast charging feature in which 10 minutes of charging gives one 5.5 hours of play time with ANC off . However, there is no cable in the box, which is a bit of a letdown.
CMF Buds Neo App: NothingX remains as clean and easy to use as ever
The NothingX app is the perfect accompaniment to the CMF Buds Neo – simple, clean and easy to use. We did have some trouble adding our Buds Neo to the app, but after a little struggle, the buds were added to the list of our other CMF devices. There is one main page, and you can scroll down to access all the functions and features. ANC, Spatial Audio, controls, bass enhancement, equalizer settings, low lag mode, dual connection, and firmware updates can all be accessed through the app. One also gets the exact charge percentage left in each earbud, although rather oddly, not that of the case. The app is easy to use and remains one of our favorites.
CMF Buds Neo Review Verdict: Superb value for the price
The CMF Buds Neo come with a price tag of Rs. 1,999, which is quite competitive for the performance and specs they offer. The similarly priced OnePlus Nord Buds 3r bring a comparable spec sheet, as do the Realme Buds T200 Lite, but both come with Bluetooth 5.4, marginally less playtime, and are not even close to the Buds Neo in the design department.
The CMF Buds Neo are near-perfect entry-level TWS options. Their audio, ANC, and battery performance give them an edge over the competition, and the distinct design is the cherry on this TWS cake. If you do not want to burn a hole in your pocket and still want a good pair of feature-packed TWS, the CMF Buds Neo are the perfect pick.
- Distinct design
- Enjoyable audio
- Good ANC
- Super call quality
- Very good companion app
- Good battery life
- Controls take some getting used to
- No charging cable in the box
- The white coloured case attracts scratches and smudges easily

Hockey parents already pay $400 for sticks. Trump’s tariffs could make it worse
Hockey families in the U.S. are feeling the pinch from rising equipment costs
In St. Paul, Minnesota, Kelly Rand’s twin teenage sons are going through constant growth spurts, forcing their family to buy replacement hockey equipment almost constantly.
The financial strain is obvious: a goaltender's helmet that ran $400 in 2022 now sells for $1,000, while a chest protector purchased a year ago for $465 currently costs $900.
For a sport where families already face mounting costs for ice time, gear, travel, and coaching, the recent 50% tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump's administration on Canadian goods present an unwelcome added burden, threatening to push prices even higher.
"If a kid on the ice breaks a stick, every other parent is looking at that mom or dad going, ‘Ahhh oh, no!’" Rand said. "You feel for them. How many $400 sticks can you afford in one season?"
Hockey sticks and skates feature among more than 550 items hit by the White House tariffs. According to John Merola, e-commerce director at B&R Sports, custom goalie gear and specialized skates made in Canada by companies such as True Hockey fall directly under these trade rules.
Merola noted that standard sticks now average $200, with top-tier models reaching up to $400. He added that major brands including Bauer, CCM, and True continue to manufacture a significant portion of their custom lines in Canada.
"This not a minor blip by by any means," Sports & Fitness Industry Association CEO Todd Smith said. "Even if manufacturers have moved over the last several years from Canada to other countries, there’s still healthy amount being manufactured in Canada and, yeah, this 50% tariff is a big deal."
When Rand’s family bought a complete custom goalie package a few years ago, the setup cost $3,300. Historical data from HockeySkates DB shows that skate prices, which ranged between $80 and $900 in 2016, now span from $200 up to $1,230.
Widespread inflation and tariffs applied to other trading partners have driven up gear costs in recent years. A sales report from the Sports & Fitness Industry Association indicates that US spending on hockey equipment surged 45.4% from 2020 to 2025, rising from $228.9 million to $332.9 million alongside rising participation.
Data from the U.S. International Trade Commission, which combines ice and field hockey products, shows Canadian imports made up approximately 8.5% of total equipment imports last year. That puts Canada fourth behind China (52.7%), Vietnam (13.2%), and Thailand (9.5%).
Of the 2.1 million sticks imported last year, over 1.5 million (74.1%) came from China and 268,000 (12.8%) from Mexico, compared with 18,909 (0.9%) from Canada.
Chris Douglas, an economics professor at the University of Michigan-Flint, considers an immediate 50% jump in stick prices across the board unlikely given Canada's small market share, but he cautions that price pressure could build if demand shifts.
"Maybe that causes the price of hockey sticks to rise somewhat — maybe by $50 or something like that," Douglas said. "Hockey is expensive with the equipment, ice time and so forth, so maybe there’s a family right on the margin where $50 or $100 in additional cost causes them not to enroll their kids at hockey any longer."
Reflecting on previous trade actions against China, Merola noted those tariffs had a broader commercial effect, though the impact was not immediate.
"Bauer, CCM — the big, heavy hitters in the market — came in and said: ‘We’ll absorb these costs. Don’t worry about it,’" Merola said. "And then as nothing happened, they kind of came back and said, ‘We can’t cover this, so we’re gonna have to increase pricing.’"
A similar wait-and-see strategy could take place now, delaying how soon manufacturers and retailers pass costs along to consumers. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade negotiations could resume if Washington shows a serious interest in discussions.
Douglas noted that much depends on how long businesses expect the duties to remain in force.
"It’s hard to form expectations of the current tariff regime where tariffs are changing basically every day, it seems like," Douglas said. "But if there’s an expectation that tariffs are going to be permanent or at least in place for the long term, then I think prices rise pretty instantaneously because the cost of production has risen and that gets passed on to consumers via a higher price."
Merola believes persistent tariffs will prompt brands to shift further production to the US, Asia, or other regions. However, Roustan Hockey—the last major stick producer operating in Canada—reaffirmed last week that it intends to maintain domestic manufacturing.
"We remain committed to our employees, our customers and our manufacturing operations here in Canada," founder W. Graeme Roustan said in a statement after hosting federal minister Evan Solomon for a tour of the facility in Brantford, Ontario.
The Sports & Fitness Industry Association is calling for an end to the tariffs, highlighting a 7% rise in US hockey participation over the past three years driven by events like the 4 Nations Face-Off and the Winter Olympics.
While acknowledging that the National Hockey League, USA Hockey, and local teams provide free equipment and ice time through learn-to-play initiatives, Smith remains concerned about the long-term impact of trade duties.
"This has, obviously, the potential to really stunt that growth," he said. "It couldn’t be a worse time for tariffs to hit in terms of really having the having the possibility to increase costs."

Do you hate being middle-aged? NPR's Alllison Aubrey wants to change that
Do you hate being middle-aged? NPR's Allison Aubrey wants to change that
Ailsa Chang turned 50 this year. She planned her birthday party "with the intensity of a heat-seeking missile," determined to prove to the world, and maybe to herself, that she was thrilled about the decade ahead. She still isn't sure if that was genuine excitement or a defiant performance. Probably both.
That tension got her excited to talk with her NPR colleague Allison Aubrey, whose new book, "Your Turn: How to Create a Midlife You Love," argues that the years after 50 can bring renewed purpose instead of decline. Aubrey joined Chang in person at NPR West in Culver City to discuss it.
Redefining midlife
Aubrey has a wider window in mind than most people picture when they hear the word "midlife." She puts it at 50 to 75, she said, pointing to a Pew Research Center projection that 3.7 million people worldwide will be over 100 by 2050.
At a time when a century-long life is possible, Aubrey said, then turning 50 doesn't mean winding down. It means roughly half a lifetime is still ahead, with room to look past parenting and paychecks and ask a harder question: What is my purpose now?
To find answers, Aubrey interviewed more than 150 people making what she calls a "third turn," a phrase she borrowed from her grandfather's "Kentucky Derby wisdom," about the unexpected opportunities to surge ahead in the third quarter of life. She found a pattern in the stories that struck her most: people who took the skills and instincts built over a career and pointed them toward something more personal, something closer to legacy than to a job title.
The Mid-life Pivots to Inspire
These stories are at the heart of "Your Turn": A lawyer who closed her practice and opened a bookshop. A nurse practitioner who started singing lead vocals in a band that tours up and down the coast of Maine. And a former magazine editor, Joanne, who Aubrey describes as a "buttoned-down and a committed perfectionist," who signed up for her first improv class in her late 50s.
Joanne is in her 60s now and performs improv in Washington, D.C. She told Aubrey that improv gave her a new script for life: saying "yes, and" to whatever came next. Chang said the story pushed her to consider her own leap, singing lessons and an acting class, which she committed to on the air.
What the science says about play and connection
Chang asked Aubrey how two reporters who spend their careers in hard news should think about making room for play. Aubrey pointed to a study she covered earlier this year out of University College London. Researchers found that people who regularly engage with the arts, through singing, dancing or going to the theater, appeared to age more slowly at the cellular level than people who don't.
The effect on biological aging, which is a person's rate of aging compared to peers, Aubrey said, appeared as strong as the effect of exercise.
Friends as an anti-aging formula
Chang, who isn't married and doesn't have children, said her friends function as her family, and Aubrey's book convinced her they're also keeping her healthier. Aubrey agreed and offered two reasons.
First, emotions are contagious. They spread between people, she said, so surrounding yourself with creative, optimistic people tends to make you more of the same. Second, after interviewing more than 150 women who made compelling career pivots, Aubrey said she noticed a formula, that mirrors a curriculum on midlife learning program developed by Marc Freedman, an aging expert and founder of the nonprofit CoGenerate: Go inward first, back to whatever lit you up as a kid, whether that was singing or drawing or something else entirely. Then go outward and find the group or organization built around that interest.
Writing the book changed Aubrey, too
Chang asked whether writing "Your Turn" reflected Aubrey's own third turn. It did, Aubrey said.
As a science reporter, she trusts the scientific method to answer a question with evidence. But the questions she found herself asking in the mirror, about identity, her changing body and her purpose, don't resolve that way. Writing the book taught her to make room for both, she said: the evidence-based tools she still relies on, and the wisdom and intuition that can help us listen to our hearts and move forward to a next chapter full of adventure, joy, purpose and play.

Germany's far-right AfD says 'democracy demands' parties work with them after state election win
- Published
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections for the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.
While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say I do not accept the vote of the people".
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was "deeply shocked" by the result, describing it as "seismic... not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously".
His party, the conservative CDU, saw its share of the vote almost halved to 17.2% in the state's preliminary results.
Merz said it was not possible to return to "business as usual", adding that the country needed "profound reforms" and the CDU needed to "reach people at an emotional level.
"This election result is a seismic result not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously," he said.
No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.
Von Storch said the state's results "were on the table and now democrats have to talk to [one] another. This is what democracy demands".
She added that if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".
Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".
The state's defeated premier, the CDU's Sven Schulze, also said the mandate to govern Saxony-Anhalt "now lies with the AfD".
Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.
The party's plans for Saxony-Anhalt, which include segregating child refugees into special classes and setting up a task-force to help detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, are highly controversial within Germany.
Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude.
"We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.
The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.
Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".
One idea being floated is whether there could be informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.
The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas.
The AfD has signalled an openness to talk with other parties but all - apart from the BSW - refuse to co-operate with the far-right.
The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.
They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.
Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally.
Commentators and political opponents called AfD's victory a watershed and break with the past.
"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters overnight. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the state's projected results on his Truth Social platform. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev then took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".
Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.
Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".
Asked about those who had expressed fears over the far-right party gaining power in the state, deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC that its supporters were afraid of "losing our economy, they are afraid of losing our inner security".
She said conservative voters were turning to alternative political parties because they were not being listened to".
She added that the party's detractors should: "Wake up and realise what happened in several other European states... The conservative parties will disappear from the landscape as it happened in Italy, as it's about to happen in the UK, as it might also happen in France".

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.
