What’s the Matter With Moderation?
Hoping to break a 94-year losing streak, Kansas Democrats have turned to Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor whose mood may not match his party’s.
One simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right.
And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter.
Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. Full of himself even by senatorial standards (one Republican Senate colleague described him to me as a “know-it-all”), Marshall is leery of public forums where he might hear from protesters and tends to speak before thinking—a hazard of his appetite for cable-TV appearances. In nearly six years as a constituent of the senator, I have traveled from one end of Kansas to the other, and I have concluded that passionate supporters of Roger Marshall are the electoral equivalent of jackalopes: If they exist, I have never found one.
Should Hamilton break the Senate’s longest GOP win streak, he would score more than an enormous off-year upset; his influence on 2028—a free-for-all to define post–Donald Trump politics—could be even larger. Because Hamilton seeks to vindicate the belief, beleaguered in today’s culture, that moderation is a good thing, not just as an electoral strategy, but as an approach to life.
In Texas, James Talarico’s Christianity seems, at times, to dovetail with uncanny precision with the agenda of secular progressivism. Hamilton’s rhetoric suggests that his Democratic revival tent would be roomier, but at the same time he has so far faced relatively little pressure to translate his disposition into details. He is motivated by “compassion, a belief in safety nets for vulnerable people,” he told me, and also by “fiscal responsibility, limited government, and strong defense.”
Such inoffensive straddling may be out of step with today’s politics. “People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad,” El-Sayed explained to Michelle Goldberg of The New York Times. A roiling left has risen to match Trump’s raging right. To win, Hamilton must not only persuade independents and Republicans to vote for him—he must also motivate angry progressives in this time of throat-cutting.
If El-Sayed and others like him are the furious faces of the Democratic future, perhaps Hamilton is a DINO. When I asked him if Democrats should seek to impeach Trump a third time, he ventured his belief that “the impeachments in the first term did not accomplish anything”—a claim that dismisses the expression of righteous anger as a political imperative in itself. Hamilton likes to talk about the good that he could accomplish in partnership with the well-liked Senator Jerry Moran, the senior Republican from Kansas. But maybe that’s not what the people, who truly are pissing mad, really want.
Emporia is the seat of Lyon County, which in 2024 gave 56 percent of its votes to Donald Trump and 41 percent to Kamala Harris. Yet Hamilton was not in hostile territory when he visited one late-August morning. Gravel City Roasters is a combination coffee shop and art gallery located directly across Emporia’s main drag from the county Democratic headquarters. There is a Pride flag on the wall with Refugees welcome superimposed on its rainbow stripes. The chai, served in mismatched mugs, is excellent.
But the comfort zone is narrow here for a 21st-century Democrat. The little city with its college campus is surrounded by farmland that has historically bred beasts, grains, and discontent. In its heyday—the era of William McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt—Emporia was home to the journalist William Allen White, whose Gazette newspaper was a sort of proto-Substack. Readers around the world vibed to his grumbling, which often had to do with the eternal sense of Kansas as undervalued and overlooked. “Go east and you hear them laugh at Kansas; go west and they sneer at her; go south and they cuss her; go north and they have forgotten her,” White wrote in his career-launching screed, dated 1896 and titled “What’s the Matter With Kansas?”
Thirteen decades later, an Emporia pharmacist, John Schmidt, picked up the theme, telling me at the coffee shop of the town’s beef processing plant (closed), its Michelin rubber-track factory (downsized), its maker of plastic ice scrapers (victim of a bankrupt holding company), and the nearby drugstore (battered by low reimbursements). The area’s future, too, feels festooned with pink slips.
A few dozen people awaited Hamilton, who arrived in a blue blazer and an open-collared white shirt. He immediately went to work shaking hands and nodding thoughtfully. After watching Hamilton campaign half a dozen or so times, the best description I can manage is “pastoral.” Fair enough, I suppose, for a 62-year-old pastor. Hamilton has a soft voice, and his gaze is gentle, intent, and framed by horn-rimmed glasses. His head moves constantly in tiny yeses and no’s, like a seismograph needle registering each quick conversation.
After working his way to the rear of the shop—pausing to autograph a woman’s copy of his book on the Holy Spirit—Hamilton used a wireless microphone to tell a joke about hypocritical politicians pretending to know the Lord’s Prayer. “I am a Democrat who actually knows the Lord’s Prayer,” he said. “When it says, ‘give us this day our daily bread,’ it’s reminding us to make sure that people have enough to eat.”
A sturdy little stump speech rolled out from there, befitting a man who has been crafting sermons since Seinfeld was new. He said he is a fifth-generation Kansan who married his sweetheart a week after high-school graduation and wants to give his granddaughter “a better country.” He said he built a church from nothing to 24,000 members. He said he prayed a year and a half ago that Trump would govern “with wisdom, grace, and compassion,” but found himself watching something quite different. Somebody’s got to do something became Maybe I should do something.
Rather than take on Trump directly, however, he aimed the balance of his fire at Marshall, who, Hamilton noted, “has voted for nearly everything the president has done.” Hamilton said he is against tariffs because they hurt farmers, against the Iran war because it drives up fuel prices, against Medicaid reductions because they threaten rural hospitals, and against cuts to food aid because more than 14,000 Kansas children need that support. “Since when did it become woke to care about your neighbor?” he asked rhetorically, aware that his audience was already seeing attack ads trying to tie him to left-wing ideas, and that Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas used an X post to denounce one of Hamilton’s sermons as “heretical.”
Don Duncan was part of that audience, having driven to town from nearby Chase County to have a look at the candidate. In the primary, a local Democrat, Christy Davis, drew 113 votes in Chase County, leaving Hamilton with eight; on the Republican side, Marshall got 479. Duncan, a self-described “Democrat who leans independent,” told me he did not think things are as bleak for Hamilton as that would suggest.
“It’s just a matter of people getting to know him,” said the retired school administrator and coach. “We need someone to get us back together.”
Could that be Marshall? I asked. “I can’t say we ever talk about him,” Duncan answered.
About 100 miles north and east, amid the big houses and busy shops of Kansas City’s southern suburbs, stands Hamilton’s monument to open minds, the “church for thinking people” that he founded in 1990. The main sanctuary of Leawood’s United Methodist Church of the Resurrection is visible from all directions, an elliptical edifice clad in glass and stainless steel, vaguely reminiscent of Disney’s Space Mountain. Rising 100 feet above a 77-acre campus of auxiliary buildings and parking lots, it features the largest fused-stained-glass window in the world, a work roughly the size of a basketball court. Nine satellite churches in greater Kansas City—four in Kansas; five in Missouri—carry the COR brand to sites around the area and beyond.
If the words megachurch pastor conjure images of hellfire oratory and $400 haircuts, Hamilton comes as a surprise, as mild as Jake from State Farm. Yet his success stands in contrast to the decline of mainstream Christianity in his lifetime.
Born in 1964 and raised by divorced parents in Prairie Village, one of those same southern suburbs, Hamilton came of age in a time of Protestant crisis. Perplexed by the social upheaval of the 1960s, Hamilton’s United Methodist denomination lost more than 10 percent of its membership in the 1970s and a further 5 percent in the 1980s. What energy there was in American Christianity came from conservative movements energized by opposition to abortion, homosexuality, scientific modernism, and a grab bag of philosophical attitudes derided by evangelicals as “secular humanism.”
Even as a teen, Hamilton found this alienating. Drawn to church for its social possibilities—“I didn’t believe in God, but I believed in girls,” he likes to say—the God he eventually embraced was one who delighted in discovery and gloried in progress. God gave us a brain for a reason, he thought, taking to heart the biblical admonition to worship with all of one’s “heart and soul and mind.”
In college at Oral Roberts University in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Hamilton “grew more and more interested in the parts of the Gospel that evangelical churches were leaving behind,” he told me during a July interview at a barbecue joint across the state line in Kansas City, Missouri. “I began focusing on scriptures dealing with social justice, ‘rolling down like waters,’ as Amos has it; the caring for widows and orphans; the story of the Good Samaritan. And I noticed that our churches were great at helping the people who came to church, but not so much with the people who were outside.”
Trained as a pastor at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Hamilton returned with his young family to Kansas City in the late Reagan years. He soon persuaded his regional bishop to let him start a new congregation for people turned off by what Christianity had become. Though United Methodism suffered a further 29 percent drop in membership from 1990 to 2020, Hamilton’s congregation grew from fewer than a dozen people meeting in a funeral-home chapel to the largest mainline Protestant congregation in America.
He credits an idea known to theologians as the via media, the “middle way,” which has roots in ancient philosophy and scholastic Christianity, but had its flowering in Elizabethan England. At its core the idea involves a belief that truth is not to be found on the extremes and that compromise in pursuit of worthy aims is a virtue. Society as Hamilton envisions it is a sort of Newton’s cradle, the toy that is composed of a line of metal balls suspended by threads. When the ball on one end is lifted and released, it swings into contact with the pack, where its energy is conducted to the ball on the other extreme, which swings away in reaction. Energy might come from extremism, but stability lies with the center.
COR is that stable center, Hamilton maintains, “roughly equal parts Democrat, Republican, and independent,” where inevitable conflicts among freethinking people can be respected and accommodated in pursuit of shared missions. “I am wired to see both sides,” he told me, “which is not the same as saying that all issues are 50–50. I believe cutting Medicaid and closing rural hospitals is just wrong. Making it harder for public schools to serve special-needs students is wrong, and I am willing to talk with anyone to explain why I think so. But I don’t expect everyone to agree with me all the time.”
Hamilton hasn’t shied from hard issues as a pastor. When a faction of American Methodists joined forces with culturally conservative congregations in Africa to try to pass anti-LGBTQ ordinances for the denomination, he led the opposition. Criticizing what he saw as a misguided focus on a few biblical verses over a larger Gospel of inclusion and acceptance, Hamilton ultimately concluded that a schism was inevitable, and he was instrumental in negotiating the many details of separation.
The thing to notice about that story, as Hamilton tries to turn from pastor to lawmaker, is that the via media was the road not taken by Hamilton and the Methodists when the chips were down. There was no middle ground, and now there are two denominations where there used to be one.
Hamilton would likely run into an even more challenging divide in Washington, where the two factions cannot go their separate ways. Can moderation really be an agenda? In the biblical story of King Solomon, when confronted with a seemingly unresolvable impasse, the wise solution was not to split the baby, but for one combatant to surrender for the greater good. That’s not the Washington way.
Electoral politics is, in some ways, just second-grade math: addition and subtraction. Candidates seek to add votes in Column A while subtracting votes from Column B. All of the money, overt or dark; all of the advertisements; all of the pandering and polarizing; all of the door-knocking, the text messages, the awkward TikToks, the yard signs, the stilted visits by candidates to factories, diners, fairgrounds, living rooms, nursing homes, colleges—it’s all about addition and subtraction.
For Hamilton, the problem pencils out at around 80,000 votes. Any combination of addition and subtraction that hits this target, whether raising the Democratic vote share or reducing Marshall’s compared with his 2020 victory, will get the job done. That’s a big number in a state the size of Kansas, where about 1.3 million people voted in 2024, but so is the number of people who cram the pews of Hamilton’s sanctuaries each Christmas and Easter: around 100,000 per holiday.
As shown by the August 4 results, his stronghold is in Johnson County, home to his church and to about a quarter of the state’s voters. Once a bastion of chamber-of-commerce Republicanism, the county turned purple during its explosive growth in the Baby Boom years and has, in the Trump era, become a relatively safe base for Democratic Representative Sharice Davids.
Driving up turnout in Johnson County and other metro centers—working-class Wyandotte County (Kansas City, Kansas), liberal Douglas County (Lawrence, home to the University of Kansas), booming Sedgwick County (Wichita, still the state’s largest city)—will be the keys to Hamilton’s addition problem.
As for subtraction, meet Marshall. A retired ob-gyn who calls himself “Doc”—a nickname that hasn’t caught on with Kansas voters—he has distinguished himself as one of Trump’s most obsequious acolytes, though not always the most on-message. Marshall’s ready-fire-aim approach to public speaking has left his candidacy riddled with self-inflicted wounds. Asked whether he’s okay with Iran having ballistic missiles (the program Trump was promising to destroy), Marshall said, “I would prefer they didn’t. But I don’t think that’s the key issue here. I think that they have to be able to defend themselves.” Of rising gas prices triggered by the war: “Freedom is not free. Americans are going to have to make some sacrifices.” When Kansans died on a plane that collided with an Army helicopter over Washington, Marshall blithely blamed their deaths on DEI, a theory unsupported by crash investigators.
Having sold his house in central Kansas shortly after being elected to the Senate, Marshall is dogged by allegations that his status as a Kansas resident is largely fictitious. He lists as his residence a roughly 1,200-square-foot cabin on a family ranch property, but for several years his congressionally paid travel plans included frequent stops at his “vacation” home in Florida, which he says has been uninhabitable since suffering severe hurricane damage in 2024. Marshall’s campaign did not respond to my requests to discuss the race for this article, but in a recent social-media post he wrote, “Over the last six years, I’ve averaged 185 days per year in D.C. doing the work you sent me to do, 130 days per year in Kansas with over 300 stops per year across the state, about 35 days of official travel, and 20 holiday/personal days.”
When he does visit Kansas, Marshall has avoided open meetings with the public ever since a crowd in a rural community jeered him in March 2025 during Elon Musk’s DOGE fiasco. “The town halls just became non-productive and dangerous,” Marshall told a newspaper in Hays, Kansas.
The odor of weakness around the incumbent helped inspire the GOP-dominated legislature this year to spitball easing Marshall out of office in favor of an appointed successor whose term they would extend through 2028. Voilà! No election needed. The scheme died amid criticism that the Constitution doesn’t allow states to change the length of a Senate term, no matter how lame their senator might be.
With no choice but to defend Marshall, the GOP is probing for Hamilton’s vulnerabilities. A Massachusetts-based super PAC spent a reported $600,000 on a TV ad that pieces together phrases from sermons to portray Hamilton as “mega-woke.” “Black Lives Matter,” Hamilton says in the ad, “marching for righteousness.” In another moment, marked with an ellipsis on-screen, he says, “By virtue of being white … I have to repent.” The Kansas City Star dug up the June 2020 sermon from which the clip is taken and found Hamilton saying “I have certain benefits by virtue of being educated, white, and male, right?” adding, almost a minute later, “Before I can do anything to help anyone else, I have to have a conversion. I have to repent.”
Ted Cruz’s X post avowing that Hamilton held “heretical” views relied on a sermon in which Hamilton says that non-Christians might enter heaven. Marshall thanked Cruz in his own post and added, “Wait until you hear about the ‘hundreds of mistakes in the Bible’ my opponent claims to have found.” In response, the Hamilton campaign shared a quote from Joshua Leu, a pastor of a church in Great Bend, Kansas, where Marshall once served on the board. HuffPost had asked Leu about Hamilton. “I would say that he’s a middle-of-the-road pastor who is willing to listen to all sides, and then based on his understanding of the gospel, try to make the best decision,” Leu said.
Attacking Hamilton as a fellow traveler of the progressive left, a democratic socialist in gossamer disguise, might work in Kansas. But there are reasons why even Kansans who reject that portrait as grossly inaccurate might still say no to his candidacy. The party of Lincoln still has deep resonance in a state where people were battling years before Fort Sumter. Bob Dole’s success at amassing power in Washington and using it to funnel money to the state taught lessons in the value of seniority that are still remembered. Western Kansas is not only overwhelmingly Republican, but it is also suspicious of what it regards as the citified East, where Hamilton is from. And not even all of his Johnson County congregation’s members are Hamilton supporters, by the candidate’s own assessment. As the church has grown, some members have griped that Hamilton has become less accessible—an issue that his Senate campaign is likely to exacerbate, to say nothing of actually serving in the Senate. He’s taken a leave from sermonizing for now, but would stay on as senior pastor and preach at least a dozen times a year if elected.
A Kansas Democrat starts out in such a deep hole in a Senate race that Hamilton considered running as an independent, but the recent example of the failed independent Greg Orman (who lost a race for Senate in 2014 and governor in 2018) convinced the pastor and his advisers that only a Democrat could unseat Marshall. When voters ask, as they frequently do, how Hamilton would deal with pressure from party leaders, he told me his answer is: “I won’t work for Chuck Schumer; I’ll work for the people of Kansas.”
But other candidates in the region—Dan Osborn in Nebraska, Brian Bengs in South Dakota—have chosen the middlest of ways by running as independents. Perhaps Hamilton’s decision to step off the via media by allying himself with one of our nation’s two political parties is a concession to the reality of politics. Before Hamilton can be as nettlesome for Schumer as, say, West Virginia’s Joe Manchin was during the administration of Joe Biden, he first must win in November. Well-intentioned concessions, however, are the beginning of another, much more famous, road.
With money continuing to pour in from more than 16,000 donors, Hamilton can answer the attacks. And he has another shield in his armory. A prolific author of books on scripture, prayer, and Seeing Gray in a World of Black and White, Hamilton has created texts and instructional videos that are staples at Bible studies and Sunday-school classes in at least 500 Kansas churches, he told me. This makes him something of a known commodity in rural communities that might otherwise be leery of a big-city candidate.
As he calculates, 500 churches averaging 50 people each represents a small army of 25,000 people at least partly inoculated against anti-Hamilton attack ads. He doesn’t expect to win them all in counties where Democrats sometimes number in single digits, and he doesn’t need to. Maybe a handful in each precinct, in the secrecy of the voting booth, stung by the price of tractor fuel and fertilizer, will mark his name, or simply skip Marshall’s.
Hamilton is not a dynamic political performer; he doesn’t suck the oxygen from the room. The son of a service-station manager, a husband and father by the end of his teens, Hamilton instead relies on approachability, on his feeling for life as ordinary people live it: sometimes messy; sometimes painful. He seems to genuinely believe that what people have in common matters more than their differences. You can build a church on that. But can you build a campaign?
Jim Hightower, the former Texas agriculture commissioner turned liberal pundit, used to say, “There is nothing in the middle of the road but yellow stripes and dead armadillos.” But Kansas has—or had—something of a tradition of moderate Republican senators in the not-so-distant past. Nancy Kassebaum, the daughter of former Governor Alf Landon, the Republican Party’s 1936 presidential nominee (even Kansas went for Franklin D. Roosevelt that year), died last month. She served three terms in the Senate, from 1978 to 1997. She was a Republican who worked on health care, voted to ban assault weapons, and opposed, for nearly all of her career, a constitutional amendment to balance the budget. “We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution,” she said. Hamilton might anger partisans on the left and right—in his pews and beyond—by adhering to the middle way. He will need to make compromises in order to win, or, should he win, in order to govern. Politics inevitably sullies religion. But Jesus, in the Gospel of Matthew, also recommends the narrow road instead of the wide and easy one.
As a student of the via media, Hamilton surely knows what came for Queen Elizabeth’s moderate vision. The elegant span she championed connecting Catholic structures and rituals to Protestant individualism proved a bridge to nowhere. The decades after her death belonged to the extremists. Rivers of blood flowed across Europe as Catholics and Protestants waged their Thirty Years’ War. In England, sectarian Puritans staged a regicidal revolution. Refugees from religious violence poured into the Americas.
Some eras in history are like that, obstreperous and irreconcilable. Hamilton likes to point out that Kansas contains the geographical center of the lower 48 states, and he hopes to find America’s political midpoint too. The risk is that, like so much of the Farm Belt, the center has been hollowed out.

China is getting first crack at a British technology that might change how mobile games are made and played. Today, the Xiaomi 18 Fold launches in mainland China with an Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX graphics processor inside its custom Xring O3 chip. What’s so special about that? After five years of development, Arm now has an AI gaming graphics accelerator inside its GPU.
First Xiaomi, then the world: why Arm might give phone gaming a huge graphics boost
Arm’s DLSS for Android is imminent.
Arm’s DLSS for Android is imminent.
By following Nvidia’s playbook, Arm-powered phones are about to have PC-like technologies to make games run faster, at higher resolution, with advanced lighting techniques, all without using more power than they do today. The jagged edges you see in the mobile versions of popular games might begin to go away.
And these advancements won’t just be locked to Chinese phones. The chips, devices, and games are already inbound.
“You will be able to buy it; you will be able to get it in phones next year, you will be able to get it in other types of larger screen devices, whether that be tablets or Chromebooks,” Arm’s Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI, tells The Verge in an interview.
While he can’t say which other devices will contain the Mali G2-Ultra NX, he hints that some of Google’s upcoming Googlebooks might use this graphics tech as well.
“We think it’s going to be huge,” Bergey tells me.
DLSS for Android
There are two ways to look at Arm’s new Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX. One is that it’s stronger than prior mobile GPUs, period, with an alleged 85-percent performance increase over the GPU that Xiaomi was using previously, and a 14 percent increase over Arm’s previous flagship in “non-AI gaming.”
But the other, more important way is that it enables a suite of hardware-accelerated graphical techniques that sound very similar to Nvidia’s DLSS, including AI upscaling (where it imagines a higher-resolution image), frame generation (where it generates new “fake” frames between existing ones), and even ray reconstruction like Nvidia’s DLSS 4.5.
Arm is calling all of these techniques “neural graphics,” but it doesn’t mean quite the same thing as when Nvidia uses that term — we’re not talking about enhancing faces by reimagining how light and shadow work, at least not just yet.
Instead, these improvements are about speed, offering what Arm claims is up to four times the framerate when “Neural Super Sampling,” “Neural Frame Rate Upscaling” and “Neural Denoising” are all applied simultaneously, because each technique lets the system do less work rendering actual pixels and frames, counting on AI to fill in the rest.
Note that games likely won’t feel four times faster, though, even if they look that way. Half of the boost is because your phone will imagine new frames between existing ones — and when Nvidia, AMD, and Intel do “frame generation,” it typically comes with the cost of additional latency.
Regardless, these techniques won’t all arrive immediately. “The first titles will largely be super sampling,” says Bergey, with frame gen coming in early 2027 and denoising “soon after that.”
But when you put them together, he says a phone can now genuinely play an experience like this Neural Dawn technology demo, below — and without draining your battery fast. “It might be like, hey, you can now play 1080p, 60 frames per second for three hours,” Bergey tells me. “In the past, it was 30 minutes.”
With the Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, which pairs Arm’s GPU with a larger battery, screen, and surface area for cooling, may offer even more performance. The Chinese company is showing off 3.2K resolution at 120 frames per second.
Bergey says that an entire phone with these chips will consume no more than 2.5 watts, with only 1.5 watts allotted to the GPU. “That’s basically what you want for real sustained gaming where it’s not getting warm in your phone, you’re not like ‘Oh, where’s my charger,’ that kind of thing,” says Bergey.
Or, he says, device and chipset makers can run this GPU at lower wattage to last longer. It’s not just for gaming phones: “This is not overclocking, this is mainstream,” he says. “This is about AI replacing traditional rendering; anywhere you can use it, you will use it,” he says.
It’s not just for premium phones and tablets, either: “While Mali G2-Ultra NX targets flagship smartphones, neural graphics will also be available across the Premium and Pro configurations, bringing the technology to a broader range of mobile segments and tiers.”
Arm isn’t the only one attempting to push these speed-boosting PC technologies into the mobile realm. The developers of the graphically intensive Stellar Blade, for example, recently revealed they’re making their game run at 60fps on the Nintendo Switch 2 by using both Nvidia’s DLSS and a version of AMD’s frame generation technique. The Switch 2 has an Arm-based mobile chip too, though it contains a custom Nvidia GPU.
Like with the most advanced versions of Nvidia, AMD, and Intel’s techniques, game developers will need to integrate Arm’s features into their games, though participating game engines like Unreal Engine and Unity can help. Bergey doesn’t think it’s a switch gamers will be able to flip for just any game they like.
Where Winds Meet, Infinity Nikki and Arena Breakout: Infinite are the first three games confirmed to take advantage of Arm’s new graphics accelerator, and Bergey tells us more games are on the way. Some will be announced in the coming weeks, he says — he’s just not allowed to reveal them quite yet.

Suruchi Phogat first held a pistol in 2019, at the age of 13. She did so because there were no rifles at the Guru Dronacharya Shooting Academy in Bhiwani and because her father was determined to make her a sportsperson.

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has dismissed concerns that the Centre’s push to expand private participation in the space sector will result in its privatisation or diminish its role. In a statement shared on X, the space agency termed reports and speculation about its future role “baseless and incorrect”. “ISRO will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished,” the agency said, adding that it would remain India’s principal institution for advanced space research, technology development, national and strategic missions, space science, exploration, and critical capabilities. The clarification came after key ISRO employee associations wrote to chairman V Narayanan, seeking assurances over the institution’s future role, safeguards for its existing workforce, and the impact of the reforms on recruitment. The concerns followed remarks by IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka that ISRO would eventually stop manufacturing launch vehicles, with such activities being undertaken by private companies or PSUs. Responding to the concerns, ISRO said greater private participation is aimed at expanding the country’s space ecosystem instead of replacing the government agency. “Industry, startups and academia are being enabled to participate across the space value chain, complementing and multiplying ISRO’s capabilities. The reforms should therefore be seen as ecosystem expansion and capability multiplication, not privatisation,” it said. ISRO added that transferring a mature technology does not mean it is withdrawing from the corresponding domain. Instead, such transfers allow industry to undertake large-scale production and commercialisation, while freeing the agency’s scientific and technical workforce to focus on advanced research and complex national missions. Industry To Scale Production Under the proposed division of responsibilities, the production of mature launch vehicles, routine satellites, and other established systems will increasingly be undertaken by private companies or PSUs through competitive processes. ISRO, meanwhile, will focus on frontier R&D, advanced payloads, sensors, propulsion systems, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions, and strategic capabilities. The transition has already begun with the transfer of Small Satellite Launch Vehicle technology to Hindustan Aeronautics. IN-SPACe has also initiated the process of involving private players in the end-to-end realisation, operation, and commercialisation of Launch Vehicle Mark-3. ISRO said the institutional framework established following the space sector reforms gives each entity a distinct role. The Department of Space will provide policy direction, while ISRO will lead advanced research, technology development, and national missions. IN-SPACe will facilitate and authorise the participation of non-government entities, while NewSpace India will commercialise mature technologies and capabilities. Goenka also addressed the concerns on X yesterday, saying a “misleading narrative” had emerged around ISRO’s future role. “Let me say it unequivocally: ISRO’s role is by no means diminishing. It will remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector,” he said. Goenka said industry would increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites, and other systems, allowing ISRO to focus on advanced R&D, scientific and strategic missions, new technologies, and complex infrastructure. “The direction is not a smaller ISRO. It is a larger Indian space ecosystem, with ISRO pushing the technological frontier,” he added. Spacetech Startups Take Off The number of Indian spacetech startups has grown from single digits in 2019 to more than 400 by early 2026. These startups are building capabilities across launch vehicles, satellites, propulsion, payloads, ground infrastructure, Earth observation, and space-data services. Skyroot Aerospace emerged as India’s first spacetech unicorn after raising $60 Mn at a valuation of $1.1 Bn in May 2026. Two months later, the Hyderabad-based startup launched Vikram-1, marking India’s first private orbital rocket mission. GalaxEye launched its maiden Mission Drishti in May this year to deploy an OptoSAR satellite combining optical and synthetic aperture radar imaging. However, the startup lost communication with the satellite following an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic storm. Earlier today, Pixxel raised $100 Mn in the largest single investment round for an Indian spacetech company. ISRO said private capital, manufacturing capacity, entrepreneurship, and access to global markets would be essential to increase the size of India’s space economy from around $8.4 Bn currently to $44 Bn by 2033.

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.
Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.
“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”
Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.
During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.
He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.
The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.
“There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”
Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”
His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.
He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.

France’s wine harvest devastated by heatwaves as Champagne production halves
France will likely produce it’s lowest wine harvest in 30 years after recording its hottest summer ever
France is facing one of its poorest wine harvests in 30 years, with output in the Champagne region set to halve from 2025, the farm ministry said on Monday.
The shortfall follows shrinking vineyards alongside severe heat and drought that damaged vines and grapes.
In its initial estimate for this year's production, the world's second-largest producer behind Italy projected 33.9 million hectolitres – equivalent to about 4.5 billion standard bottles. This is 6 per cent below last year and 17 per cent down on the 2021 to 2025 average.
France recorded its hottest summer yet in 2026, as scientists say human-made climate change makes extreme weather events more intense and more frequent and Europe experiences the fastest warming of any continent.
A hectolitre is equivalent to 100 litres or 133 standard wine bottles. The figures mark France's third consecutive weak wine harvest, following low output in 2024 and 2025.
Although spring conditions had initially supported a better harvest outlook, summer drought and heatwaves damaged vines and reduced yields, the ministry said. In addition to the challenge from the weather, the industry was last year hit by U.S. tariffs, and consumption is at its lowest in over 60 years as economic pressures, changing tastes and health concerns have deterred drinkers.
French agriculture being hit hard
Wine output in Champagne is expected to be 49% down on 2025, and 47% below the five-year average.
Bourgogne-Beaujolais is forecast to be down by a third and Val de Loire and Charentes by 12% and 6% respectively. Languedoc-Roussillon, France's largest producing basin, should rise 5% from last year's weak harvest thanks to better yields, though output remains below average.
Bordeaux is also expected to rebound 10% from 2025 after late-August rain helped offset drought stress, but production remains well below its five-year average. Most wine producers in France - like other European countries - started harvesting grapes unusually early this year as a result of extreme heat, the ministry said.
France is traditionally the world's largest exporter by value. The production area fell 2.5% this year. Oversupply in the face of falling wine consumption has prompted winemakers to uproot a portion of their vineyards in past years.
Beyond the wine sector, most French agriculture producers have been badly hit by this summer's record heatwaves that devastated crops, pastures and water supplies. France on Friday announced an emergency aid package for farmers of more than €1 billion ($1.16 billion).

- The claim that Canada assisted China in avoiding U.S. tariffs by reselling Chinese steel as Canadian is still under investigation.
- U.S. businesses and the U.S. government have accused Canadian companies of acting as a "backdoor" funneling Chinese steel into the United States. President Donald Trump's administration also has accused Canada of being one of China's "biggest enablers" in efforts to avoid tariffs in general.
- In May, the Department of Justice reached a settlement with two Canadian companies accused of falsely labeling Chinese steel as Canadian to avoid customs duties. However, the companies did not admit fault as part of the settlement.
- Some trade experts have expressed skepticism that Canada is enabling Chinese efforts to avoid tariffs on steel. Canada's government also has enacted a number of measures in an attempt to prevent Chinese steel from flooding the Canadian market.
- We have not rated this claim due to a lack of verifiable evidence. We reached out to offices of the U.S. and Canadian trade representatives and will update this story if we hear back.
In the fall and summer of 2026, social media users claimed that Canada resold Chinese steel as Canadian to help China avoid U.S. tariffs.
The rumor spread on Facebook and X (screenshot, screenshot). Snopes readers also contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
It is true that American businesses have accused Canadian companies — not the country's government — of skirting tariffs by selling Chinese goods, including steel, as Canadian. In an August report, Trump's administration also accused Canada of being one of "China's biggest enablers" in helping evade tariffs in general through "transshipment," or the shipment of goods from one country to another via a stop in yet another country.
In May, the Department of Justice reached a $19 million settlement with two Canadian companies over allegations that they "knowingly and improperly" failed to pay duties owed on steel manufactured in European and Asian countries, including China. The defendants denied the allegations and the settlement is not an admission of fault, but it also does not mean the United States' allegations were unfounded, according to the court documents (Page 2).
Snopes relies on independent verification and primary evidence for all of our conclusions. As of this writing, the courts have not determined that any Canadian company or government official has attempted to evade tariffs or help China avoid tariffs through this supposed scheme. Furthermore, there is not enough publicly available evidence that such a scheme has happened or is happening. As such, we have not rated this claim.
We reached out to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Canada's trade minister for the U.S., Dominc LeBlanc, for more information and await a response.
It is also worth noting that the claims connected these allegations to the breakdown in U.S.-Canada trade talks in late summer 2026. That may be because Greer reportedly raised concerns to Canadian officials about the transshipment of Chinese steel through countries Canada is seeking new free-trade deals with.
Here's what we know about the allegations:
US businesses accuse Canadian firms of avoiding tariffs
In December 2025, American industry leaders accused Canadian and Mexican firms of using cheap Chinese materials in ways that undercut U.S. businesses during a public hearing on the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade 
For example, here's what Brandon Farris, vice president of the Steel Manufacturers Association, said, according to Page 135 of the official transcript for the Dec. 4, 2025 hearing:
Some producers of steel-intensive goods in both countries continue to rely on steel sourced from non-market, excess capacity nations such as China. From 2020 to 2024, Mexico's steel imports from China rose by 59 percent, while Canada's increased by nearly 75 percent. Just as Canada and Mexico have experienced rising imports from countries with chronic excess steel capacity, the U.S. has faced its own surge of steel products from both neighbors.
Michael Salmon, CEO of Specialty Steel Works in Indiana, said that "China in particular continues to use Mexico as back door access to key U.S. markets, including steel" (Page 139). And Bob Wahlin, CEO of Stoughton Trailers, an American trailer manufacturer, said the United States must "close loopholes in the agreement" allowing "highly subsidized" Chinese steel to "enter the U.S. market from Canada and Mexico" (Page 244).
DOJ, US government accusations against Canada
The best publicly available evidence that at least some Canadian firms may be skirting tariffs on Chinese steel appears to be the previously mentioned Department of Justice settlement with two Canadian companies, Farjess and Royal Canadian Steel.
According to the Justice Department's complaint, the same people oversee Royal Canadian Steel and Farjess. Royal Canadian Steel imported steel into Canada and supplied that steel to Farjess (PDF pages 4 and 5).
The DOJ alleged that Farjess and/or Royal Canadian Steel personnel removed labels on steel referencing a Chinese company in order to conceal the origin of the steel from customs officials (PDF pages 13 to 15). Allegedly, the companies replaced the Chinese labels with their own. Evidence submitted in court included scans of those labels (see Exhibits 7 and 8).
While this scheme may have helped Chinese companies avoid tariffs, the Justice Department's allegations focused on the benefits to the two Canadian firms — specifically, that they experienced "windfall profits" from the allegedly fraudulent activity (PDF Page 22).
Skepticism of US claims and Canada's response
CBC reported in 2025 that Eric Miller, an expert on Canada-U.S. trade policy with the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, said Canada is "nowhere near as much of a back door for Chinese steel as the American companies make it out to be."
Miller reportedly said Canada is "quite militant" about prevention of Chinese transshipment because it wants to protect its own access to the U.S. market.
"Any objective look at Canada's track record would say that repeatedly over the last decade, Canada has seriously put in place measures to try to control imports of Chinese steel," the CBC quoted Miller as saying.
Indeed, in July 2025, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced measures to restrict and reduce foreign steel from entering the Canadian market amid fears from Canada's steel industry that it would be overwhelmed by an influx of Chinese steel newly subject to U.S. tariffs.

Swiss deeptech startup Jaipur Robotics has raised €4.3 Mn (around ₹48 Cr) in a seed funding round co-led by EquityPitcher Ventures and High-Tech Gründerfonds (HTGF), with participation from existing investors. The latest round takes Jaipur Robotics’ total funding to nearly $6 Mn. The startup previously raised $1 Mn in a pre-seed round led by TiVentures, with participation from Techstars, in 2025. Jaipur Robotics plans to use the fresh capital to accelerate product development, expand its international sales presence, and grow its team. It will also develop new features and integrations for waste-to-energy (WtE) plants, with crane automation emerging as a key focus area. “The first purpose is to scale the product and grow the product. We have a very clear roadmap in terms of product features and a clear goal for what we want Jaipur Robotics to become for our clients,” founder and CEO Ermes Zamboni told Inc42. Founded in 2024 by Zamboni and Nikhil Prakash, Jaipur Robotics develops AI-powered computer vision systems for WtE plants. Its technology uses industrial cameras and sensors to monitor waste piles, identify hazardous or oversized objects, and alert crane operators before such material reaches a furnace. The startup also featured in the August 2026 edition of Inc42’s flagship ‘30 Startups To Watch’. Building An ‘Intelligence Layer’ WtE plants typically store waste in large bunkers before cranes move it into furnaces. However, these piles can contain concrete blocks, metal parts, gas cylinders, and other material that can damage equipment, block furnaces, and lead to costly shutdowns. Jaipur Robotics’ system identifies such objects and pinpoints their location, enabling operators to remove them before they cause damage. It also assesses the composition and calorific value of waste, helping operators determine which sections of a pile should be fed into a furnace to maintain stable combustion. “We are essentially building an intelligence layer for these plants,” Zamboni said. Building this layer requires the startup’s technology to analyse waste in far more complex conditions than a conventional conveyor-based sorting system. Inside WtE bunkers, waste is piled together and may be crushed, buried, or partially obscured. Jaipur Robotics claims its AI models have been trained on more than 50 Mn labelled waste images and are customised for conditions at individual plants. The startup is now extending its technology from waste detection to crane automation. Its system can map waste piles, estimate the location and volume of different materials, and determine what should be removed or fed into a furnace. “We want to move from an object-detection company to a full-stack OS-type company for these facilities,” Zamboni said. Rather than replacing existing cranes, Jaipur Robotics is developing a software layer that can be integrated with a plant’s existing infrastructure. The startup believes automation can also help address a shortage of trained crane operators by enabling them to supervise automated systems instead of manually controlling cranes. While its crane-automation capabilities remain under development, Jaipur Robotics’ waste-detection technology is already deployed commercially. The startup claims the technology can detect hazardous material with up to 99% accuracy. Its systems currently analyse more than 5 Mn tonnes of waste annually across over 35 facilities in Europe. India Expansion On Radar While Europe remains Jaipur Robotics’ primary market, the startup is also eyeing India for expansion. The startup already has an engineering team in Bengaluru and plans to establish an Indian legal entity by the end of 2026. It is also in discussions with potential customers in the country. Jaipur Robotics is looking to tap WtE plants in India, where waste handling and crane operations remain heavily dependent on manual intervention. The startup believes its computer vision and automation technology can help such facilities improve operational efficiency and safety. India’s WtE market was valued at $1.56 Bn in 2025 and is projected to reach $1.97 Bn by 2034, according to IMARC Group.

German chancellor faces pressure after far-right party wins in state election
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has doubled down on pushing through unpopular reforms to Europe’s largest economy after a far-right party surged to a landslide victory in a regional election, with a very good chance of forming the first far-right stat...
BERLIN -- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz doubled down Monday on pushing through unpopular reforms to Europe’s largest economy after a far-right party surged to a landslide victory in a regional election, with a very good chance of forming the first far-right state government since the Nazi era.
Merz said his center-right Christian Democratic Union was “deeply shocked” by what he called “the most serious election defeat that the CDU has had for years, for decades.” But he indicated that he's determined to stay at the helm and said that “giving up is not an option for me.”
The anti-migration and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany, or AfD, fell just short of a majority in Sunday’s vote in Saxony-Anhalt, a small eastern state that gained outsized prominence as AfD eyed power there. Its regional branch is one of several considered a proven right-wing extremist group by Germany's domestic intelligence agency.
AfD's victory is a major distraction for Germany and Merz at a time when Europe faces several challenges, including Russia’s continued aggression against Ukraine, a suspected sabotage campaign targeting NATO countries, and difficult dealings with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Merz said he wanted to assure Germany’s allies that “our institutions are resilient and stable” and the country will stick to its values and constitution after the AfD win. “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history,” he said.
He vowed that he won't “budge one millimeter from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia now.” Germany is one of Ukraine's biggest supporters in its war against Russia.
Because of Germany’s Nazi past, far-right movements have always come under strong scrutiny. Other major parties have refused to cooperate with AfD in a so-called “firewall.” Unlike many countries in Europe, modern Germany hasn’t yet had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government.
Merz vowed to weaken AfD before he came to power last year, but instead has seen the party's support increase.
The governing coalition of his Union bloc and the center-left Social Democrats has developed a reputation for squabbling and become deeply unpopular, as has Merz himself. The government has struggled to persuade voters that it can get the country’s chronically sluggish economy moving, through potentially painful reforms, including to the pension system.
But Merz insisted Monday that “we need fundamental reforms in Germany.” He said it's a question of “nothing less than the future of our country and the opportunities of our children and grandchildren, and we must not squander those. That is why my determination to continue the reform course is unbroken.”
He acknowledged a need to “justify them, not just rationally but also emotionally."
Germany faces another two regional elections on Sept. 20 — in Berlin and in another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where AfD is also strong.
While Merz continues to push back against resistance to reforms, AfD — whose victory was cheered by far-right parties across Europe — faces potentially tricky maneuvering to put its candidate for governor in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, in power.
Siegmund had pushed for an absolute majority in the state legislature that would allow AfD to sidestep mainstream parties' shunning of it. After the vote, he signaled that AfD still isn't willing to make compromises, insisting that “we don’t want to become like the parties that were punished” by breaking pre-election promises. He also rejected the idea of a minority government.
But he said that it has "a very clear mandate to form the government,” and that his party would reach out to other groups in the legislature and even to individual lawmakers. “Our goal now is to build precisely this stable majority in the coming days and weeks,” he said.
AfD is three seats short of a majority. It could reach out to the hard-left BSW party, which won five seats. The two parties share a Russia-friendly course and oppose immigration but disagree on some other issues.
BSW has criticized the “firewall” against AfD and signaled again Monday that it could allow Siegmund to become governor by abstaining in a potential third round of voting for a new governor in the state legislature, in which a simple majority would suffice.
It’s also possible that newly elected lawmakers from other parties could defect to AfD, which would only need three to break ranks.
Forming a government excluding AfD would only be possible if all the other parties in the legislature worked together. However, an alliance of any kind between those parties is improbable and would be prone to instability.
Billionaire Elon Musk congratulated the party on its election victory with a “Well done!” on his online platform X. Siegmund immediately thanked him for his support.
Trump posted a screenshot of the election projection on his Truth Social platform without any comment.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev on X described the outcome of the election as a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD that will put migration under control.” Dmitriev also said that “AfD will restore Germany and Europe by leading the common-sense approach that migrant-friendly, warmongering Biden-think EU politicians tried to eradicate.”
The leaders of right-wing populist parties in Spain and Portugal also congratulated AfD.
The Polish prime minister was critical. “In Poland, only idiots or traitors could rejoice the AfD triumph in Germany,” Donald Tusk wrote on X.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, whose country faces a presidential election next year in which the far right is a leading contender, said that “AfD’s platform is a betrayal of the European spirit” and that “our first responsibility is to resist the normalization of far-right ideas.”
Among voters who didn't back AfD, the reaction was one of deep dismay. Horst Walter Boerner, an 86-year-old from Magdeburg born during World War II, expressed shock.
“It’s terrible for us,” he said, saying the election was “fear-driven.” He said AfD's victory was foreseeable because of the crowds it drew during the campaign, but he said “this should have never happened.”

Associated Press journalists Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, and Kerstin Sopke in Magdeburg, Germany, contributed to this report.

Zerodha does not want to go public itself. But it wants to be involved in almost everything that happens when another company does. “To run a brokerage firm is to live with contradictions,” Zerodha cofounder Nithin Kamath had written on Substack last month. “These contradictions have become harder to live with since the business took off post-2020. At least until then, the pursuit of revenue and profits made some of these contradictions easier to rationalize,” Kamath added. It’s in this light that we need to study Zerodha’s new direction. Zerodha Corporate Advisors received a nod from the market regulator SEBI on September 1 to operate as a Category-I merchant banker. The subsidiary can now advise companies on IPOs, follow-on issues and other capital-market transactions, putting Zerodha in a business dominated by names such as Axis Capital, IIFL Capital, Kotak Investment Banking and Nomura. The company is expected to start its merchant banking operations over the next couple of months, with equity capital markets, including IPOs and follow-on issues, set to be the initial focus. For Zerodha, the move opens up a new source of fee income at a time when its core broking business is facing pressure from lower retail derivatives activity and regulatory changes. But merchant banking is a completely different business from what Zerodha has built its name around. Zerodha has millions of investors on its platforms. It now needs to build relationships with founders, CFOs, institutional investors and other capital market participants. That will determine whether the new business becomes a meaningful part of Zerodha’s revenue base or remains a small adjacency. New Dawn For Zerodha Zerodha’s success in broking was built largely around technology, pricing and ease of access. A customer could open an account online and start investing without needing a traditional broker. Winning an IPO mandate is an entirely different ball game. Merchant bankers have to build relationships with promoters and management teams well before a company reaches the public markets. This is the part that Zerodha’s core brokerage business never had to pay much attention to. As a merchant banker, the company would also need to lean on experts around regulatory processes, investor relations, pricing discussion, roadshow execution and then selling the issue. Established investment banks have spent years building these relationships. “Merchant banking can certainly become a meaningful new vertical for Zerodha, although I would not look at it as a direct substitute for brokerage revenues over the next three to five years,” Deepank Bhandari, founder of S45, an AI-native investment bank, told Inc42. The economics of the two businesses are different. Broking is a high-frequency business supported by a large customer base, while investment-banking revenue is transaction led and can be uneven. “Building a meaningful merchant banking franchise also takes time because the pipeline, team and execution track record have to compound over multiple transactions,” Bhandari said. Zerodha has said it wants to bring its low cost approach to merchant banking. Mohit Mehra, whole-time director at Zerodha Corporate Advisors, said the company wants to bring the tried-and-tested “low cost, no-hard selling approach” to the merchant banking world. That could help Zerodha win some mandates in the early stages of the business, particularly among companies looking for a different proposition from established banks. But fees are negotiated deal by deal, and a lower quote will not by itself overcome a gap in relationships or execution experience. The early mandates will therefore be important in establishing Zerodha’s credibility. Does Zerodha Hold Any Cards? Zerodha does have one advantage that most new investment banks cannot build quickly: access to a large retail investor base. For an IPO that can help with investor awareness and retail participation. “For certain IPOs, particularly consumer facing or new age companies, having a large retail investor ecosystem can help with awareness, investor education and participation,” Bhandari said. Zerodha’s investor base also gives it an existing distribution channel. A company that appoints Zerodha Corporate Advisors to manage its IPO could potentially reach a large pool of retail investors already using Zerodha’s platforms. But the retail investors are only one part of an IPO. Institutional investors, mutual funds, insurers, AIFs, foreign investors and anchor investors can have a major role in determining demand and pricing. “Established players such as Axis Capital, IIFL Capital, and Nomura have built these relationships and execution capabilities over many years. Zerodha will have to build its own institutional franchise over time,” Bhandari said. That is likely to be one of Zerodha’s biggest tasks as it enters the business. Its retail network gives it a head start. It does not give it an institutional distribution franchise. Can Zerodha Turn Tech Into Another Advantage? Zerodha could have another opening with new age companies. The startup has spent years building technology products for investors and has been active in India’s startup sector through Rainmatter. Its brands are also closely associated with product-led businesses and a focus on keeping financial products simple. That could help it connect with founders of technology and consumer internet companies looking to list. “Zerodha’s technology-first DNA is definitely an advantage, particularly when dealing with founders of new age businesses,” Bhandari said. Besides this, the company’s familiarity with the startup sector could help it understand how these companies think about products, customers and growth. That may give it a different pitch when competing for IPO mandates. Both Nithin and Nikhil Kamath have invested in dozens of startups in their personal capacity and when it comes to the startup ecosystem, Zerodha stands apart for its bootstrapped story and as Nithin Kamath wrote last year, “ethical compass”. But this advantage has its limits. Companies also look for senior judgement, regulatory experience, institutional investor relationships, sector understanding and confidence that the team can execute through difficult market conditions, Bhandari added. Zerodha will therefore have to prove that its technology background can translate into investment banking execution. The first few transactions will be of great importance here. A successful IPO gives a merchant banker more than a fee. It creates a track record that can be taken to the next issuer. And so far, Zerodha has no track record in this context. A New Revenue Stream Having said that, Zerodha’s merchant banking business is unlikely to move the needle on revenue immediately. The company is said to have closed FY26 with close to ₹8,800 Cr in revenue, while brokerage revenue is said to have fallen to ₹2,738 Cr. That may be precisely why Zerodha is adding the business. Its brokerage revenue has fallen from ₹3,066 Cr in FY25 to ₹2,738 Cr in FY26, as regulatory changes in the derivatives market have reduced trading activity among retail investors. Merchant banking will operate on a very different revenue model, with fees tied to individual capital-market transactions rather than the steady flow of retail trades. “Traditional merchant banking and IPO advisory rely on lumpy, deal-dependent fee structures,” said Avinash Gorakshakar, founder of Avinash Mentor Research. He expects the business to contribute a low single digit percentage of Zerodha’s overall revenue over the next three to five years. That also means the business will be more exposed to the fundraising cycle. A strong IPO market can produce a large pipeline of mandates, while a weak primary market can sharply reduce deal flow. The timing and size of individual transactions will also make revenue less predictable than a brokerage. The company has also entered other businesses in recent times to reduce its dependence on F&O activity, including margin trade funding, lending and asset management. Merchant banking takes that diversification a step further, moving Zerodha into the corporate side of capital markets. SEBI-registered investment analyst, Gorakshakar, expects the firm to target mid-market companies and startups with a lower-cost advisory and underwriting proposition. If Zerodha can price mandates below traditional investment banks while keeping its cost base lean, it could put some pressure on fees in this segment. Still, the near term financial contribution is likely to remain modest. Merchant banking needs a steady flow of mandates before it can build into a meaningful business, and each transaction can take months to complete. Bhandari sees the same distinction. “I would therefore see it as diversification and a long-term adjacency rather than an immediate counterweight to broking,” he said. For Zerodha, the initial goal may therefore be less about adding another large revenue stream and more about establishing a presence on the issuer side of the capital markets. If that franchise expands from IPOs and follow-on issues into a broader set of capital-market transactions, the economics could become more meaningful over time. Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi
- Published
A residential building in the Indian capital Delhi has collapsed with dozens of students feared trapped inside.
Eyewitnesses told local media that as many as 50 people were inside the five-storey building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi when it came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday.
At least one person was killed and two others are in a critical condition, NDTV reports, citing local police. Six people were said to have been rescued so far.
There had been construction work going on in the basement of the building, Hostel Daze, which sits a short distance from the Delhi University campus.
Many of the students staying there were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday.
A legislative assembly member said at the scene that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble.
Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed.
Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure".
"Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added.
Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old.
The owner of a nearby shop told news agency ANI that it was under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to increase their income.
"They strengthened the upper building, but the pillars below were weak," he said, noting that the construction workers had also been buried.
The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account.
"Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said.
Police are searching for the owner of the building, Times of India reports.

Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?
Aftershocks of party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt will ripple across Germany, with two more state elections this month
Germany is reeling from the biggest far-right victory in a state election since the Nazi period after voters in Saxony-Anhalt in the former communist east gave the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party a thumping first-place finish of 44%, just short of an absolute majority.
What happened and why is it significant?
For the first time since the second world war, a German state is on the brink of electing a far-right government after a big win in Saxony-Anhalt, described by the news magazine Der Spiegel as a magnitude 9.0 “political earthquake”.
Coming in nearly 27 points ahead of the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), the conservative party of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, the AfD pulled off a coup whose aftershocks will ripple across Germany and beyond its borders. The AfD will have broad powers over education, culture and domestic security if it manages to take power in the state. Among other policies, it has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms. It now has a strong wind at its back for the two state elections yet to come this month.
Its triumph also raised doubts whether the unpopular Merz could hold on in the face of such a clear rejection of his policies and leadership after just 16 months in power. The AfD co-leader Alice Weidel told reporters in Berlin that her party was targeting a 40% result at the next general election, scheduled for 2029. It is currently polling in first place at 28%.
Alice Weidel (right, with Ulrich Siegmund, centre, and her AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, left) said the AfD was targeting a 40% vote at the next general election. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA
What might happen next?
The AfD’s national leaders and the chief candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, the media-savvy former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, said the state’s voters had given the party a clear mandate to govern. However, without an absolute majority in the state parliament, the party would need partners or supporters to either join a coalition or “tolerate” a minority government. Siegmund said repeatedly before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority. The remaining parties ruled out playing kingmaker to Siegmund by lending formal support. However, the BSW, a small “left-conservative” populist party which narrowly cleared the 5% hurdle to representation, has hinted at tacit cooperation.
Prior to the election, some Christian Democrats in the state openly questioned the “firewall” policy. Siegmund indicated he would spend the coming days and weeks “with an outstretched hand”, testing the hitherto resolute opposition to helping the AfD into power. If Siegmund fails to build a coalition, he suggested holding a new election, something that would require a two-thirds majority in the state legislature.
1:24
'We should have learned more from history': Germans react to AfD win – video
What does the result say about the firewall approach?
The stunning outcome in Saxony-Anhalt has underscored doubts about the viability of the policy of mainstream parties to exclude the AfD from power. The only other time the AfD won in a state, in neighbouring Thuringia in 2024, its victory was less decisive, allowing the remaining parties to cobble together an ideologically awkward, cross-spectrum coalition. Given the AfD’s margin of victory in Saxony-Anhalt, it is difficult to imagine how the humiliated CDU could form such a “Frankenstein” alliance of disparate parties this time. The state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged the party no longer had a mandate to try.
Siegmund has suggested a new election if he fails to build a coalition. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA
What does the result mean for the CDU and Friedrich Merz?
Sunday’s election amounted to a stinging rebuke of Merz and his CDU. The stony-faced chancellor admitted he was “deeply shocked” by the result. Exit polls showed voters were furious about his broken promises to revive the economy and shore up fiscal discipline. Energy prices, stoked by inflation and the Iran war, have hit voters hard in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany’s poorest state. Cost of living issues appeared to far outweigh immigration, the AfD’s trademark call to arms, as a mobilising issue. Although support for the AfD has been strongest in the ex-communist east, the party also made strong gains in two elections in western states earlier this year amid fears over deindustrialisation.
The Social Democratic party (SPD), a junior partner in Merz’s alliance, indicated on Monday it would be willing to water down planned changes to Germany’s costly and creaking social welfare system in order to placate disgruntled voters. Merz insisted the measures to shore up the healthcare and pension systems were necessary and vowed to remain and fight for them “in the interest of our children and grandchildren”.
Friedrich Merz has been ‘deeply shocked’ by the result. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA
What about the next two state elections?
Voters in the German capital, Berlin, and the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, two of Germany’s 16 länder, will go to the polls on 20 September. The obvious momentum for the AfD, as well as widespread German dissatisfaction with Merz and his right-left government with the SPD, mean those polls are also fraught with risk for the parties in the federal coalition. The AfD currently has a narrow lead ahead of the co-ruling SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but for now looks unlikely to win an absolute majority. The situation in Berlin – once divided between east and west – looks muddled, with the CDU, far-left Linke and the AfD all jockeying for first place. Even if the CDU managed to hold on to its lead on election day, it would struggle to form an ideologically coherent coalition, dealing Merz and his party another stinging blow that could further destabilise his government.
