The Best Alexa Speakers I’ve Tried
Featured in this article
Amazon started the smart speaker game, but finding the best Alexa speaker has only gotten harder as the company launches more and more devices. Amazon has the largest range of smart speakers and displays by a long shot, which can be overwhelming to dive into. The most recent were launched late last year: the Echo Dot Max, the Echo Studio (2nd Gen), the Echo Show 11, and the Echo Show 8 (4th Gen). But Amazon has plenty of older, cheaper models available, too.
If you're looking for something small and simple to control your home, either an Echo Dot ($80) or the Echo Dot Max ($120) is your best bet. The Dot Max has really impressive sound for its compact size and is my overall favorite Alexa speaker, but if you're only going to use it for voice commands rather than jam sessions, you can get away with the older, cheaper model, especially if you want to buy a few to place around your home. For anyone looking for a smart display, the Echo Show 11 ($250) is the best of Amazon's newest smart displays that come designed for the updated assistant, Alexa+. The older third-generation Echo Show 8 ($150) is still a great value if you want something cheaper.
Read on to see every Alexa speaker I've tried (hint: it's all of them) and what I think after testing each one. You can also learn more about Alexa+, and we've got guides on setting up your Echo speaker, creating Alexa routines, and the best tricks an Echo Show can do.
Updated September 2026: I've updated this guide with Amazon's increased pricing that affected several models, and details about the price hike.
Comparing the Best Alexa Speakers
| Model | Speaker Array | Screen Specs | Camera Specs | Other Features | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon Echo Dot Max | One 2.5-inch woofer; one 1-inch tweeter | None | None | Tap controls; smart home hub | 
| Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) | One 1.73-inch speaker | None | None | None | 
| Amazon Echo Show 11 | One 2.8-inch woofer; two full-range drivers | 11-inch display with 1920 x 1200 resolution | 13-MP camera with auto-framing | Zigbee smart home hub that supports Matter and Thread; spatial audio; Dolby Atmos | 
| Amazon Echo Show 8 (3rd Gen) | Two 2-inch speakers | 8-inch display with 1280 x 800 resolution | 13-MP camera with auto-framing | Zigbee smart home hub; spatial audio | 
Honorable Mentions
While I wouldn't call these smart speakers my absolute favorites from Amazon, they have some excellent qualities that make them stand out among the vast lineup of Echo models.
The Echo Studio (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for sound quality. This is the second version of the Echo Studio to be our audiophile pick. The current version is a similar size to the old Echo (4th gen), but the musical power on this speaker is almost ridiculous. It filled my entire second floor's long great room with music, and I didn't even need to reach the highest level of volume to pull it off. Honestly, I'm almost afraid to use it at full blast. Not only was it loud, but clear and delivered a nice amount of bass, beautifully playing soft tones of Tracy Chapman's “Fast Car” and the piano riffs of “Dark Blue” by Jack's Mannequin with its three 1.5-inch drivers, plus a 3.75-inch woofer. The harmonizing of “What Is This Feeling?” by Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo sounded beautiful, too. If you're looking for big sound in an Alexa box, this is it. It's a similar size to the Apple HomePod, but I like the sound much better and it's cheaper, too. You'll also get a built-in smart home hub, spatial audio and Dolby Atmos, tap controls like the Echo Dot Max, and early access to Alexa+ right away.
The Echo Spot (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for bedside tables. The Echo Spot returned in 2024 after a few years of discontinuation, and it's a great little bedside companion thanks to its half-circle screen that displays the time, plus any alarms you have set are also visible under the main time. You can customize the clock with a couple of different color and face options, and the screen dims nicely when the lights are out to a gentle red that's easy to read without lighting up the room. I like asking for alarms set to my latest playlist or some lo-fi jams, and it's easy to set that up with a voice request. Unlike the Echo Shows, it doesn't have a distracting, constantly moving slideshow that would be annoying for the bedroom, nor does it display ads or have a built-in camera. (Nobody wants a rogue camera in their bedroom.) It does not have fantastic sound, but it's plenty loud for an alarm or casual listening while you get dressed in the morning.
The Echo Dot Kids (5th Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for kids. Do your kids really need their own Alexa speaker? That's up to you. This special edition of the Echo Dot is nearly identical to the fifth-gen Dot above, but it has easy-to-use parental controls that allow you to set time limits, filter explicit content, and review activity. The owl- or dragon-themed sphere comes with a year of Amazon Kids+, which includes thousands of Audible books and other special games and features. After that, you'll be charged $3 per month. Alexa can help your kids spell, play their favorite music, or—via another speaker in your house—remind them of dinner time.
More Alexa (and Alexa-Compatible) Speakers
There are a lot of Echo devices out there, and some third-party speakers that are Amazon Alexa–compatible. Here's every Alexa smart speaker we've tried and what we thought of it. Some of these speakers didn't raise in price like the models above, which might make them more appealing than before if you're looking to spend less.
Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) With Clock for $60: I like this version of the older Echo Dot that adds an LED clock to the front of the speaker, and was thrilled to see it in stock again last year. The LED clock can also display information like the weather when you ask Alexa questions. It's once again temporarily out of stock as of this writing, and has had spotty availability (it's out of stock right now, but Amazon says it's temporary). Still, it's a good find when it's available.
Amazon Echo Hub for $180: The Amazon Echo Hub is similar to an Echo Show, but without the speaker. Instead it's a thin device that feels a bit like a tablet, designed to be mounted on the wall (or placed on a separately purchased stand, which is how I used it) and used to control your smart home devices. It's a great choice for anyone who wants something focused on smart home control only. You can still ask Alexa questions and even play music, but the thin speakers aren't worth playing music from. But you can tell your Echo Hub to play music on a different set of speakers, and even set up default speakers to work with it. It's a great companion device if you already have a smart home setup.
Amazon Echo Pop for $40: The Echo Pop is a perfectly fine little speaker, and the cutest one in Amazon's lineup. Does it have great sound? No. It's fine enough for background tunes or if you're limited to a dorm room, but you'll get much better sound for a similar size from the Echo Dot (but you'll pay a little more, and you won't get as cute of colors)!
Amazon Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen) for $100: This smart display is another just-fine option, but it's too small to be a great display, and the included camera makes it a no for a bedside table; better to go with the above Echo Spot or an Echo Dot. This model did raise in price by $10.
Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $200: I usually love an Echo Show 8, but this model didn't have the same sound quality as the older model. If you're going to get one of Amazon's new displays, you're better off getting the Echo Show 11 ($220) for the same experience with a slightly larger screen (while it's a 3-inch difference, it doesn't feel that big) and better sound. This smart display raised in price by $20.
Amazon Echo Show 15 (2nd Gen) for $350: This smart display is a good display, but it clearly wants to double as a TV and isn't very good at it yet. I'm hoping we see better TV-related performance in the future to make it worth adding to a kitchen or office. It does a great job with widgets, though, thanks to the massive 15.6-inch screen. There's also the larger Echo Show 21 ($500), which is essentially the same thing but larger. Both of these large displays rose in price—the Show 15 went up $50, while the Show 21 went up $100.
JBL Authentics 200 for $380: This JBL smart speaker supports both Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa, letting you switch between them for different tasks without changing your preference in the app. That makes this speaker particularly appealing for folks with a sprawling collection of smart products from both.
Sonos Era 100 for $219: If you're looking for a speaker that can talk to Alexa but isn't necessarily made by Amazon, the Sonos Era 100 is a great option. We just wish we liked the Sonos app better. You can catch our entire guide to the Sonos ecosystem here.
Why Did Amazon's Prices Increase?
Amazon increased many of its prices last month for its products, affecting the Amazon Echo line as well as Kindles, Fire TV streaming sticks, and Eero routers. It's not a huge surprise after other companies have done the same this summer, claiming rising costs and chip shortages. Amazon made a similar claim, with a spokesperson blaming increased storage and memory costs. Still, it's disappointing to see and will lead to a fall sale season with prices that won't be as impressive as earlier this summer.
Amazon's Echo devices saw increases from anywhere between $20 and $100, with the larger price increases being for the Echo Shows. The following Echo speakers all faced a price increase:
- Echo Dot (5th Gen): $80 (up $30)
- Echo Spot (2nd Gen): $110 (up $30)
- Echo Dot Max: $120 (up $20)
- Echo Show 8 (4th Gen): $200 (up $20)
- Echo Show 11: $250 (up $30)
- Echo Show 15: $350 (up $50)
- Echo Show 21: $500 (up $100)
What’s Alexa+?
Amazon has rolled out the new-and-improved Amazon Alexa, named Alexa+, which is built on generative AI and promises a more powerful assistant that can handle more conversational topics and requests. It's available for a free 30-day trial; after that, you either pay a $20 monthly fee or become a Prime member. Being a Prime member is the better deal, likely by design. Neither my colleagues nor I have been impressed enough by Alexa+ to say it's worth paying for on its own. I do like the updated, more conversational voice, and Alexa+ did a good job answering all kinds of questions quickly and thoughtfully. Check out our early access hands-on for everything I thought while testing.
Alexa+ has brought some changes, even for those not using it. It now requires that all voice recordings be sent to Amazon for processing, which wasn't required before. Amazon has changed its features to support this, and now all recordings with regular Alexa go to Amazon, too. There used to be a “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” privacy feature you could select to have voice requests processed locally, but it was discontinued on March 28, 2025, per an email Amazon sent to current users.
FAQs
What’s the Difference Between an Echo and an Echo Show?
A regular Echo is a smart speaker, or a speaker with microphones in it so it can hear you speak to it and respond. An Echo Show is a smart display, which has a screen and a camera to let you make video calls, stream content, and see your questions answered on a screen. Both have similar capabilities when it comes to smart home control, answering questions, and playing music, but Echo Shows have extra abilities thanks to the screen. All Echo Shows have a camera and come with a physical camera cover for privacy.
When’s the Best Time to Buy an Echo?
The best time to buy any Amazon speaker is during a major sale event like Black Friday or Amazon Prime Day, when there are often steep discounts. You'll often see the cheaper speakers for around 50 percent off, and the larger speakers see some nice sale prices too.
How and Where Should You Set Up Your Alexa?
Alexa speakers get the best use in spaces you're in often. I like setting mine up in my kitchen and living room—usually a display in the kitchen, so I can pull up a recipe or the weather while I make my morning cup of tea, and a speaker in the living room so I can play music and command the lights without a screen to distract from the TV or playing with my son. You can also set one up in the bedroom to use as an alarm clock, but make sure it's a model without a camera for the best privacy.
Ultimately, what's most important is that the speaker is somewhere it can hear your commands. Where that will be will vary based on your home, but think about where you'll be when you ask for the weather or to dim the lights, and place your speaker accordingly.
You'll set up Alexa speakers using the Alexa app, which allows you to manage multiple Alexa speakers if you own more than one through your Amazon account. Third-party speaker setup methods may vary.
Is Alexa Always Listening?
Alexa is always listening, to a certain extent. It's designed to only listen for its wake word and shouldn't be recording or processing any audio unless it hears that word. But Alexa can sometimes mishear a word and think it's the wake word, or it might hear a word similar enough to activate the speaker. If you've owned an Alexa, there have likely been times when the assistant suddenly responds when you weren't speaking to it. Once it hears the wake word (or what it believes to be the wake word), it will start listening to everything in an attempt to hear what you need and respond.
Alexa+, the latest version of Alexa, will also remain on for a little bit after you ask a question to listen for follow-up questions, no wake word required. Both Alexa and Alexa+ light up in some fashion (regular speakers will turn the light ring blue, while the displays will have a blue bar appear on the screen) to let you know the assistant is listening. Most Echo devices also have a physical mute button and will display a red light or red bar to let you know when the mute is activated.
How Do You Remove Ads and Spam From an Echo Show?
If you're using an Echo Show device, you've likely noticed there is a ton of default content the device will show you. Sports scores! Local news! A recipe you might be interested in! It makes the device exhausting and annoying to be near.
Here's how you can control what you see:
- Swipe down from the top of your Echo Show to pull up the menu, and select Settings.
- In the Settings menu, choose Home Content.
- There are more than 40 options you can toggle on and off on this menu, and you should remove as many as you can that you don't use. I usually remove all but weather forecasts and recently played audio.
While you're able to turn off interest-based ads from third-party skills (this is under Alexa Privacy in the Settings menu), it won't stop all ads. The only setting that is ad-free is choosing Photo Display mode, which can use either Amazon's included library of photos or your own. The downside is that it turns it into a digital photo frame, so you won't even see a clock or features like widgets.
Can I Have My Alexa Requests Locally Processed, or Do They Have to Go to the Cloud?
There used to be a privacy feature called Do Not Send Voice Recordings that let you have all your voice requests processed locally on your Alexa device instead of being sent to Amazon's cloud storage. That feature was killed in March 2025 to support Alexa+, and even if you continue to use the old Alexa, you don't have access to that feature any longer.
How Does WIRED Select Smart Speakers to Test? How Are These Speakers Tested?
For this guide, we specifically test speakers that are compatible with Amazon Alexa. It's a big limitation and narrows down the options significantly, especially compared to speaker options you'll see in our other guides like the Best Bluetooth Speakers. That's mainly Amazon's own ecosystem of speakers, and while there are third-party options, the best options tend to be of Amazon's own design to work with its own voice assistant.
Each speaker gets installed in a tester's home for day-to-day use, to see how the microphone performs, how the speaker sounds with different types of music, how well the smart home control features work with compatible devices such as smart lights and video doorbells, and to test other features as necessary (e.g., streaming features on smart displays).
How Does WIRED Get Models? What Does WIRED Do After Testing Them?
We acquire review units usually as a press sample, though we will also independently purchase samples if need be. All review units in this guide were provided as press samples with no obligation to cover or promises for what that coverage would be.
After testing, we keep most of our picks either installed for long-term testing in our homes or in storage to compare against updated models and new speakers that come out. If the sample becomes irrelevant or unnecessary to keep, we donate it locally.

Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
- Published
Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators.
A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg.
"We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government.
"All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told."
The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted.
Mofokeng is now part of a legal case set to be announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.
At least 69 protesters were shot dead by police on that day in 1960, becoming a pivotal event in the history of the anti-apartheid movement.
Though Sharpeville may be a place name rich in historical resonance, it scarcely looks like a site that symbolises the struggle: the township is slowly crumbling.
The once tarred roads of this area south of Johannesburg are returning to dirt. Many of the houses are still the small, brown-faced brick homes built under the apartheid-era government. The earth is dry and barren - heaps of rubbish are piling up throughout the neighbourhood.
While the legalised system of racism was buried in 1994 when the country held its first democratic election and elected Nelson Mandela as president, its scars remain.
There have been attempts at redress - not least through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) - set up by Mandela's government to investigate crimes committed during the apartheid era.
But the Sharpeville survivors feel they have not seen justice.
Sharpeville's local memorial park, the Human Rights Precinct, tells the story of how the streets of township became the scene of a bloodbath.
Inside the park stand 69 white pillars, one for each life lost.
The victims were killed while demonstrating against the racist pass laws.
At the time, black people were forced to carry a document known as a passbook, known as "dompas" in Afrikaans, which restricted their freedom to move around the country.
A person could be beaten and jailed if found without it - or if found in a "whites-only" area without permission.
Many heeded the call from the leaders of the Pan Africanist Congress in March 1960 to march in protest against the dompas, including then-20-year-old Mofokeng.
"The life we were living under apartheid was a life of oppression. We could not move around freely. We ended up planning to march to the police station against these passbooks that were being used to oppress us," he says.
Thousands turned up to what they thought would be a peaceful protest.
"[The police] had rifles, machetes, even shields. We explained to the police that we didn't want the passes anymore and we were prepared to go to prison. There was a commotion, then all hell broke loose when the police started shooting."
Mofokeng was among the more than 200 people injured and recent estimates by South African researchers have revised upwards the number who died to as many as 91.
Another survivor, Larazus Magotsi - now 90 - walks along the long row of graves in the cemetery where most of those who died are buried. Among them is a headstone marking where a 12-year-old was laid to rest.
Magotsi's eyes are filled with tears as he struggles to compose himself.
"We heard gunshots and ran and hid inside a store, peeping to see what was happening outside," he says.
"People were lying on the ground. When we looked out again, we saw that some were trying to get up, but the police were just shooting at them.
"Others were using machetes to strike the heads of people who were still moving."
It is thought that more than 1,300 bullets were shot into the crowd. Archive photos show policemen walking among the corpses, lying where they fell, in the immediate aftermath of the massacre.
The only legal case that followed the killings was a failed attempt to charge the protesters with affray.
Now, survivors and relatives of those who were killed are hoping to overturn the law they say prevents them from getting justice.
The 1961 Indemnity Act was passed by the apartheid government in the wake of the massacre and protected the police and government from having criminal charges or even civil claims brought against them in relation to what happened at Sharpeville.
Despite more than 30 years of democratic rule, that law remains on the statute books.
But now South African non-governmental organisation Lawyers for Human Rights, together with UK-based law firm Leigh Day, has filed a case at the High Court arguing that the law is unconstitutional under the new constitution that came into effect in 1994.
"Apart from the individual damages, what the community's looking for is basically reparations to enable their healing. They feel as though Sharpeville is a forgotten community," says Charne Tracey, one of the lawyers on the case.
Part of their court application includes getting a class action certified - if approved this would mean that for the first time dozens of victims and relatives of those killed could collectively sue the state. It could also possibly lead to criminal charges being brought against the alleged perpetrators, if any are still alive.
"Nothing has been done that assists with their healing and improvement of their quality of life, or remedy the long-term effects of what they've suffered," Tracey says, adding that 70 people could be involved in the class action.
Constitutional law expert Prof Frans Viljoen believes having the old law repealed is important because it would help to "clean up" the legislation and "close a chapter on the past".
"Although South Africa has a very transformative constitution… The principle of continuity of statehood still applies, which is why the case can be brought against the current state," says Viljoen.
"So if there were laws in our statute book in 1994, the constitution explicitly says they remain in force until parliament repeals them, abolishes them or changes them," he adds.
But he backs attempts to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional "to cleanse us of that past".
The TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was generally praised for bringing together victims and perpetrators who were granted amnesty as long as they, among other conditions, fully disclosed what they had done.
But the greatest criticism of the process was that it did not bring about justice for some as people were not jailed for their acts and no police officers applied for amnesty for the Sharpeville shootings.
The government told the BBC it had supported apartheid victims over the years, and would continue to do so, but did not oppose survivors and families pursuing legal remedies.
When it comes to reparations the justice department said 560 TRC-recognised victims of apartheid-era violence had received individual grants amounting to some $31m (£23m) and though not all Sharpeville survivors and relatives had been identified it encouraged them to come forward.
For many in the community of Sharpeville, there is hope that restitution will help heal decades of lingering trauma.
"Apartheid is dead and buried. A win would bring complete healing, not just for us, but for future generations as well," says Mofokeng.
"Considering how people died, many have not completely healed."

- The Sift is an entirely new dimension in Minecraft Dungeons 2, featuring strange landscapes and unusual creatures.
- Players can reach The Sift by travelling through the Deep Dark portal.
- The dimension forms part of the adventures that players would venture on in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
While Minecraft Dungeons took players through familiar Minecraft-inspired locations, the sequel is taking a much bigger swing by introducing a strange dimension. The brand-new dimension in Minecraft Dungeons 2 is called The Sift. All gameplay trailers and demos have shown us glimpses of all the mysterious threats and beautiful landscapes you can find here. So, dive right in to learn everything about The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
What is The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2?
The Sift is a new dimension in Minecraft Dungeons 2 that is said to appear due to the mysterious rift formation throughout the Overworld. The Minecraft Dungeons 2 trailer reveals how the team of four heroes reaches The Sift that sits beyond the Overworld.
What makes this realm interesting is that it sits alongside the Overworld adventures in the ARPG sequel. This won’t be a one-way ticket or a side mission that you would complete and forget. Mojang has specifically described The Sift as a place containing new mobs, bosses, beautiful landscapes, and mysteries waiting to be uncovered.
What Does the Sift Look Like?
The visual style of The Sift is dramatically different from the familiar Minecraft biomes in the original game. The gameplay footage shows the Minecraft Sift dimension dominated by red and orange tones, while also having traces of green vegetation and striking water pools, originally named ‘Ouch Water.’
Mojang emphasizes that the environment represents both beauty and danger. The landscape almost looks quite peaceful until you encounter the hostile creatures that remind you it’s still an action RPG game.
The terrain is also not a simple flat battlefield. The gameplay reveals how the heroes move through elevated areas, platforms, waterways, and uneven terrain to fight various enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
How to Enter The Sift Dimension in Minecraft
The most obvious doorway to reach the Sift dimension is through the mysterious rifts that keep appearing throughout the Minecraft Dungeons 2 world. Although the trailer shows the rifts appearing automatically, we also learn that Grand Illusioner’s staff can create these rifts at will.
Apart from the mysterious rifts, you can also reach The Sift dimension by traveling through the Deep Dark portal. Yes, the same secret Ancient City portal in the Minecraft vanilla game that we have been eyeing all these years. Although the mechanics to activate that portal have not been revealed yet, the end moments of the Minecraft Dungeons 2 demo trailer hint at Note Block usage.
All Minecraft Dungeons 2 Mobs, Enemies, and Bosses You Can Find in The Sift
Every new dimension in Minecraft, whether it’s a dungeon crawler or the original game, has plenty of inhabitants. The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2 is no different from them. This realm is associated with several unusual creatures, including the Sifters, Singers, Echo Golems, Blubs, Sprouts, and more.
Below is a breakdown of all the known Minecraft Dungeons 2 Sift enemies and bosses, including their attacks and behaviors that we know so far:
Baby Sifter
The Baby Sifter is a small hostile creature found during the early stages of exploring The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2. Despite its appearance, you should not treat it as a cute creature, since it can perform melee attacks by biting.
Bearded Sifter
The Bearded Sifter is a ranged hostile mob that attacks the heroes from a distance. It has a particularly bizarre animation as the creature rapidly shakes its head to shoot projectiles from its chin. These projectiles can even track you before locking on and then travel in a straight line.
Blub
The Blub is a passive creature in The Sift and can be described as a glowing rabbit-like animal that hops around the realm. You might have already seen it in the gameplay trailer where the hero picks up a Blub, and it makes adorable squeaking sounds. So, if you want one as a pet, make sure to lock in your Minecraft Dungeons 2 pre-order before the game releases.
Echo Golem
The Echo Golem is one of the important beings connected to the dimension’s lore. These golems are powered by soul blocks that were created by the Singers. Unlike the hostile mobs in the Minecraft Dungeons 2 Sift dimension, Echo Golems help the heroes progress through the story.
Licker
The Licker is another unusual passive mob found in The Sift. We saw this creature appearing in one of the promotional materials uploaded by Mojang on their socials. Currently, its behavior is unknown apart from the only activity it does, as its name suggests.
Nester
The Nester is a hostile Sift-native mob that prefers melee combat. When it spots a hero, it will rapidly bound toward them before lunging forward to deliver a bite. Once the melee attack ends, a cooldown starts, making it stay near the hero until it’s ready to attack again.
Singer
The Singer is one of the most mysterious inhabitants of The Sift dimension in Minecraft Dungeons 2. The leaks from the latest Minecraft Dungeons 2 novel, The Rift, suggest that the Singers communicate through song and are closely associated with the portals to reach The Sift.
They are also supposedly responsible for creating Echo Golems and can use their music to pacify the Minecraft Wardens. Singers have a distinctive appearance with pale green bodies, shaggy fur, tiny faces on their elongated necks, pale antlers, short legs, and long arms.
Sprout
The Sprout is a flying hostile enemy in The Sift, having a strange tentacle-like appearance. While the ground-based ranged enemies can force you to reposition yourself in combat, these flying mobs will add another layer of difficulty in the new dimension.
Tall Sifter
The Tall Sifter is a hostile ranged enemy in The Sift that keeps its distance from the heroes and shoots projectiles from its mouth. Unlike the Bearded Sifter, these projectiles can land near the heroes and then explode after a short delay. To make matters worse, these explosions can leave behind yellow goo on the ground that constantly depletes your health.
Trill
Trills are an unusual entity appearing in groups inside The Sift dimension. They can fly through the skies, adding a bit of strange life to the dimension’s atmosphere.
Sculk Slasher
The Sculk Slasher is a hostile sculk creature equipped with long claws that can slash the heroes during a fight. The mob is particularly dangerous for melee fights, since it can reposition itself by dashing backward and leaving behind a spectral afterimage.
Sculk Dancer
The Sculk Dancer is a large hostile mini-boss in the Sift dimension of Minecraft Dungeons 2. Its attacks include swinging its arms and spinning its body. Getting too close can be dangerous since it performs some massive AoE attacks rather than targeting a single point. Similar to the Slashers, Sculk Dancers can also leave spectral afterimages that mimic their movements.
Sculk Monstrosity
The Sculk Monstrosity is one of the major bosses you can find in the Minecraft Dungeons 2 Sift. Some of its major attacks include dashing towards the heroes with a shoulder charge and unleashing a burst of souls during the boss fight. It can also summon Sculk Cubes that roll toward players to perform short melee attacks.
Sprout Boss
The Sprout boss is a massive variant of the ordinary Sprout encountered in The Sift. We have received a short glimpse of this boss during the end moments of the gameplay trailer, so the details of how this boss attacks are yet unknown.
The Sift’s Story and Connection to Deep Dark in Minecraft Dungeons 2
With all the information available about The Sift dimension, we know that it has a strong relationship with the Deep Dark biome, the Singer mobs, soul blocks, Echo Golems, and the High Council.
At the same time, it also raises an important question of whether the dimension would eventually drop in the main game. The possibility can’t be ignored, because the Deep Dark portal has been in the vanilla Minecraft Ancient Cities ever since the Wild update. However, it is important to note everything that has been shown officially and what the community wants.
Is The Sift Connected to Minecraft Deep Dark Biome?
Yes, the Sift has a clear connection to the Deep Dark biome in Minecraft Dungeons 2. The two settings are linked through the portal and the Singer’s abilities alongside the Echo Golems.
The Deep Dark biome introduced the sculk blocks in Minecraft, the Warden, and hints of an ancient civilization. Minecraft Dungeons 2 builds on that idea by showing that the Singer’s music abilities were used to open the Deep Dark portal to reach the Sift, as suggested by The Rift novel.
Will The Sift Come to Vanilla Minecraft?
For now, there is no official confirmation that The Sift is coming to vanilla Minecraft. Mojang has specifically presented it as an entirely new dimension for Minecraft Dungeons 2.
Mojang’s Chief Creative Officer, Jeb, also explains that adding a full dimension to vanilla Minecraft is a bigger task, and it affects the whole community connected to it. He also chooses not to say anything about future updates, thereby making the argument strong for ‘no new dimension in vanilla Minecraft.’
So, that is all about the brand new dimension: The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2. Which Sift mobs are you excited to meet first once the game drops on September 29, 2026? Tell us in the comments below.
How to get to the Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2?
The Sift is accessed through the Deep Dark portal in Minecraft Dungeons 2 and also through the mysterious dimensional rifts created using the Grand Illusioner’s staff.
Is The Sift coming to vanilla Minecraft?
There is currently no official confirmation that The Sift dimension will be added to the main Minecraft game.

Why Nepal floods should worry India
- Published
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders.
India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts.
Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood.
And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side.
Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system.
How many Nepal rivers flow into India?
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges.
Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border.
A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep.
Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).
India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers.
Which Indian states are most exposed?
Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone.
Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala.
But the risk extends beyond Bihar.
Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected.
Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda.
"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD.
Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk.
When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate?
Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists.
First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily.
Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments.
Second, the river.
Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels.
Third, when the water meets India.
How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain.
So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India.
The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood.
So how much depends on Nepal v India?
"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction.
How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk
The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration.
Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river.
According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained.
"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha.
The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal.
How much warning can India get from Nepal?
For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream.
Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara.
Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours.
A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours.
India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts.
But important gaps remain, says Sanyal.
They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment.
And then there's, crucially, the last mile.
A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger.
For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time".
What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India?
A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists.
Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal.
The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate.
But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India.
Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India.
"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal.
Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment.
"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal.
Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream.
The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management.
So what should worry India the most?
"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha.
In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine.
Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger".
"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says.
A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path.
That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure.
It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material.
And then there's climate change.
Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts.
High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast.
And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border.
They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

Liam Farrell: Wigan Warriors captain on retirement, fond memories, and next steps after Super League career to remember
Liam Farrell joined Sky Sports' The Bench podcast to discuss his decision to retire, what comes next, and if we will see him in a Wigan Warriors shirt again; The regular Super League season concludes with Round 27 from Thursday September 10 live on Sky Sports
Monday 7 September 2026 14:35, UK
Wigan Warriors captain Liam Farrell says he is not sure if he will play for the club again after he announced he will retireat the end of the 2026 Super League season.
The 36-year-old, who has only ever played for the Warriors, will call time on a career which has spanned 17 professional seasons. Farrell has captained Wigan since 2023 and been capped 12 times by England.
He has totalled 428 appearances for Wigan and scored 151 tries, winning six Super League titles, five Challenge Cups and two World Club Challenge successes during his illustrious career.
Farrell has not featured since June with an ongoing neck issue and with just three potential matches remaining in the season for his club, the chances of him featuring again for his boyhood club are in doubt.
That third match, if Wigan were to make it, would be the Super League Grand Final at Old Trafford on October 3, live on Sky Sports.
Of course, it would be a dream for Farrell to lead his team out once again at the Theatre of Dreams, but he remains aware that not every career concludes with a fairy-tale ending.
"It is one of them - who knows," Farrell told Sky Sports' The Bench podcast.
"I have still got to see the specialist again and see what he recommends and there will be a decision made in the near future.
"That is all I have got for now. Careers don't always end how you want them to end.
"Don't get me wrong, I would love it to end that way, but I'll wait and see what the next few weeks bring.
"Regardless of how it does end up, I have done more than I ever wanted to achieve and I would be happy whichever way it goes.
"I am at peace with that. It would have been nice to maybe just play one more game but like I said, things don't always finish the way you want them to.
"We will just wait and see what the decision is in the next few weeks."
While time will tell on whether we will see Farrell in a Wigan jersey one more time, he remains adamant that pulling on the cherry and white just once would have been enough.
"I have lived a lot of my dreams. I think one thing I said to the lads over there: my goal was always one game for Wigan. If I'd have come off the bench, played once, I'd have been happy and retired there," he added.
"But to have had the career I have had and the success I have had. The teams I have been involved in, the trophies I have won, I have been unbelievably lucky. It is a dream come true for myself."
Joining the 'performance side' of things
While this season marks the end of Farrell's involvement at Wigan as a player, he will now move over to the performance setup, a job he has been working towards in the background for a number of years.
"I got all my qualifications for that a few years ago," Farrell said. "So, that has just been in the back pocket for when the time came of retiring. It is something I'm excited about.
"It is something I want to get into and slowly build into it as well."
The regular Super League season concludes with Round 27 from Thursday September 10 live on Sky Sports.

GM's breakup with CarPlay and Android Auto has one exception
Is Cadillac’s Lyriq EV an exception to the rule, or a sign of things to come?
Car manufacturers are turning away from Android Auto and Apple CarPlay in favor of native infotainment systems. The trend has generated a fair bit of controversy, with critics labeling it as an industry-wide pivot toward subscription models and data-related cash grabs. Executives, meanwhile, have billed the move as providing a more seamless, functional in-car experience.
One of the companies most invested in this move is General Motors. Last year, CEO Mary Barra confirmed that GM would phase out Apple CarPlay and Android Auto from its gas-powered vehicle lineup, doubling down on the controversial decision to drop the popular entertainment systems from its EVs in 2023. In its place, the company is upgrading its in-house infotainment, replacing its built-in Google operating system with Google's AI assistant, Gemini. In an April press release, the company stated that it hopes to deliver "a custom-built AI assistant, fine-tuned with proprietary vehicle data to help anticipate your every need" by the end of 2026.
However, not every vehicle in GM's lineup will be losing access to third-party infotainment systems. Reportedly, the 2027 model of Cadillac's luxury EV, the Lyriq, will continue to support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The decision to preserve the Lyriq's access to phone mirroring systems is surprising, given GM's recent transition toward native applications in EVs like the Chevy Silverado EV Work Truck and GMC Hummer EV, both of which saw their CarPlay and Android Auto functionalities removed earlier this year. As it stands, the electric SUV will be the only GM EV sold in North America compatible with both infotainment systems.
Exception or the rule?
While GM's transition from Apple CarPlay and Android Auto might be controversial, company executives have stated that it will ultimately lead to a stronger product. In an interview with Nilay Patel on The Verge's Decoder podcast, Barra stated that the company had received customer feedback that "it was very clunky" moving between GM's in-house system and third-party applications. Now, GM is banking on customers preferring an AI-driven system with a host of verbal commands and smart features, ranging from smart route planning and curated entertainment systems to hands-free texting and streaming applications.
With this in mind, GM's logic behind the Lyriq is puzzling. In a CarBuzz report on the luxury EV's infotainment options, a Cadillac representative explained that the company preserved the Lyriq's access to phone mirroring applications "based on customer feedback." However, it's unclear why this logic has not applied to GM's other models, or whether it is a signal of moves to come.
In prioritizing its own application, GM has made efforts to grant access to key non-native applications — a commonly cited impetus for consumers hesitant to migrate to their car's in-house infotainment system. In December of last year, for instance, GM announced that Apple Music would be available on its in-car software platform for all 2025 and 2026 models. Tim Twerdahl, GM's VP of global product management, touted the addition as "the latest example of how we're expanding entertainment choices built directly into our vehicles." With its new Gemini-powered system, GM's Google compatibility gives you access to Google Maps and other popular applications available on the Google Play Store.
For drivers of non-Lyriq GM EVs who prefer their phone mirroring application, the EV Play LT is a nifty workaround. Capable of providing wired and wireless phone mirroring for Chevy, GMC and Cadillac EVs, the EV Play LT is a third-party product that will deliver Apple CarPlay and Android Auto functionalities in infotainment systems without the popular phone mirroring apps. At $199.99 and with no subscription fees, the product might be just what the infotainment doctor ordered.

Andrew Garfield, 43, said his ideal day off involves a lot of lying down and looking out the window.
Speaking on Monday's episode of the "Smartless" podcast, the actor said he was happy to do very little after nearly a year of nonstop work.
"I can do it for a couple of months. I really can," Garfield said.
He spent 11 months moving between dramatically different roles: Sam Altman in "Artificial," a grieving farmer who leads a rebellion against King Richard II in "The Uprising," and magician Roy Horn in the upcoming Apple TV+ series "Wild Things."
Constantly switching between the characters felt disorienting, he said.
"You get to the point sometimes where you're so deeply resentful of the work that you love to do so much, and that's kind of where I'm at," Garfield said.
By the end of it, Garfield said he was ready to take a break, adding that some of his favorite ways to unwind include reading books, watching "dumb TV," and "literally looking out" the window.
"I have a lovely window in my house, and there's a beautiful tree that I just stare at," he said.
"Again, it's like the most valuable commodity outside of live performance is quiet, and time, and space, and not having our attention snatched by the things that are always snatching our attention," he said.
Garfield said he also values time with friends and family, who help keep him grounded.
"One of the gifts of being raised the way I was is that it was made very, very clear to me by osmosis that there was no way that I could ever allow myself to drink my own Kool-Aid enough to lose myself," he said.
That perspective has also made him more conscious of the personal cost of spending months away from home for a job.
"I'm thinking about that more as I get older. In my 20s and 30s, it was like, I'll go anywhere any time, and I'll devote myself to this in a way that's probably a little unhealthy," Garfield said.
But now, he feels that "time is ticking" and has become more aware that "it's not forever," he said.
Other celebrities have also spoken about how they enjoy their downtime.
Hilary Swank has said that exercise helps her decompress when she's stressed.
"Ultimately, working out for me is about stress relief. I really like resistance training, and I try to do it twice a week. It really helps me cope with stress and I find it also makes me sleep better," she told Business Insider in 2024.
Keke Palmer has said some of her favorite ways to unwind involve "doing things solo."
"I love journaling, prayer, and any type of fitness, such as Pilates, yoga, and hiking. All of that stuff brings me immense joy," she told Business Insider in 2025. "I love bingeing comfort TV. It doesn't even have to be the most interesting thing."

Opening summary: race to rescue tunnel workers
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.
China said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal: the highest number was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for.
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” said the home minister, Sudan Gurungd. More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
Here’s the other main developments:
- 
  Four days after the disaster, authorities said some bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition. They would be buried after legal formalities because of health risks and a fear of disease outbreaks. “DNA samples will be collected, and the bodies will be buried in an open space,” the Chitwan district administration said in a notice.
- 
  The foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said Nepal required specialist assistance to rescue people trapped in tunnels; restore transport and communication lines where bridges had been destroyed; identify bodies; conduct DNA testing; and store bodies for longer periods.
- 
  A team of Indian tunnel experts arrived in Nepal on Saturday, Khanal said. China’s Xinhua news agency reported Beijing had dispatched five tunnel experts to support rescue efforts, with four more due to join them.
- 
  The US will provide $3.6m in humanitarian aid to Nepal, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households,” the state department said in a post on X.

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore
- Published
Kimi Antonelli's stunning victory in the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid will go down in Formula 1 folklore - and, remarkably, his team boss Toto Wolff said that he had seen it coming on Saturday.
After Sunday's race, Wolff said that beforehand he thought that one of his two drivers was going to be standing on the top of the podium.
It was an eye-opening statement given they started the race 17 places apart on the grid, George Russell on the front row alongside shock pole winner Pierre Gasly's Alpine; Antonelli on the penultimate row.
"I thought one of the two is going to win," Wolff said. "Either George, because he was on the front row, or Kimi because he's going to walk over water, here at Monza. And I felt that yesterday also."
Wolff was asked to explain why he felt a performance he was comparing to a miracle was on the cards.
"It's been a while that I've seen drivers," he said. "Energy levels, mindset or behavioural pattern. I knew that was his mission today, to win the race. I chatted with his father yesterday. The father also saw that coming.
"These are the moments where you can see how a weekend is panning out through the sessions that a special moment can come."
- Antonelli takes stunning Monza win from 19th on grid 
  - Published49 minutes ago
- Antonelli extraordinary as Gasly has superb weekend - driver ratings 
  - Published2 hours ago
For the Mercedes drivers, this race was all about the context of the weekend.
Antonelli knew coming in that he would be starting at the back because of a grid penalty for using too many engines this year.
Russell knew that he had to make the most of this opportunity and cut as much as he could out of his team-mate's 59-point championship lead.
Fifth or sixth was the general consensus for what might be realistically possible for Antonelli, who himself said after the race that he had "thought a podium was possible".
What changed everything was his remarkable progress in the early laps of the race, which brought to mind another Biblical miracle, the parting of the Red Sea.
Antonelli was 14th after a relatively conservative first lap, then 12th at the end of lap two, when Charles Leclerc crashed his Ferrari to bring the race to a temporary halt.
"With the red flag, I was already P12," Antonelli said. "And then I knew that I could have a shot at it."
A lap after the restart, he was up to eighth, and on the back of the leading group of cars running nose to tail. Seventh a lap later, after dispatching Lando Norris' McLaren.
By now, Russell was in the lead, having wasted little time dispensing with Gasly. But the Briton sensed trouble.
"A great race from the neutral perspective," Russell said. "As soon as I saw Kimi up to P5 after a handful of laps, I knew he was going to be in the fight with us. That was clearly a very impressive opening few laps."
Wolff said: "The differentiator today was the ability to go through the traffic. We've seen it with other great ones in the past. Lewis (Hamilton), who did it in some of the races. That's what he's shown today. When a driver and a car are one, then there's nothing that can stop them."
Antonelli in no mood to obey a computer algorithm
Briefly, for a few laps, Russell and Max Verstappen threatened to break away in the lead while Antonelli was finding a way past Gasly, the two McLarens and Hamilton's Ferrari.
But Russell and Verstappen were fighting at the front, costing each other time, and Antonelli was up to third by lap 13, just 1.8secs off Verstappen in the lead, with Russell between them.
Three laps later, the Mercedes drivers were running one-two, and starting to swap places themselves, until, with Russell leading, it was suggested by that team that they give it a rest and try to break away from Verstappen.
If Russell could not do so, they said, they would "invert the cars" - put Antonelli into the lead to try himself. But slowly they began to inch clear.
At this point, coming up to half-distance, the race victory was still up in the air. There was a virtual safety car (VSC), called when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin broke down at the first corner.
Mercedes called Antonelli for new tyres - a decision they had to make as he had switched to the medium compound at the red flag and that would not make it to the end. Russell continued on his hard tyres.
"It was the right thing to split the strategies," Wolff said, "because we didn't know what the better one would be. In the morning meeting, we said the hard tyre is going to go forever. You can start on it and finish on it. And you can see with George, it was a forever tyre.
"At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead, that two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."
Antonelli was in no mood to obey a computer algorithm. Rejoining 14.3secs behind Russell, with 24 laps to go and four cars between them, winning was not an easy task. But he made it look like it.
Antonelli caught Russell with five laps to go and the win now looked inevitable. There was a hiccup when he ran off the track at turn one with four laps to go after Russell blocked his attack on the inside, and Antonelli lost grip on the loose rubber off line and slid into the gravel trap.
That dropped him to 1.7secs off again, but a lap and a half later, he drove past Russell on the straight between the second Lesmo corner and Ascari, and that was that.
The home fans, with split loyalties before the race between Antonelli and Ferrari, screamed with delight as he crossed the line, 60 years since the last time an Italian won his home race.
"It's one that I will remember forever," Antonelli said. "Definitely the fans gave that little bit extra to push more. The support has been great this weekend.
"Definitely seeing the grandstand cheering every lap it gave that little bit of extra to push more and to try and do even better to win it."
- Far too late for title fight priority - Hamilton 
  - Published2 hours ago
'Circle closes' after 'everyone doubted' Antonelli in 2024
The win, Wolff said, was "how the circle closed" after Antonelli's difficult introduction to F1, when he crashed in a one-off outing in free practice at this race two years ago, a moment Wolff said was "probably the toughest moment in his career. For himself and his family. A moment where everyone doubted, including himself.
"Two years later, it's the biggest glory, the biggest moment of his career (so far). That's probably going to be one of his biggest (ever)."
A maiden season in F1 last year followed in which Antonelli showed flashes of promise but little that indicated what has happened this year would follow.
"When you talk about the complete driver, there's the aspect of experience that needs to come," Wolff said.
"There is also that he has this easiness of a young man that helps to overcome difficult moments. That also helps in managing not getting ahead of himself when having these glorious moments.
"There is the fact of is he capable of maturing, of staying the personality that he is, humble, with a lot of introspection, self-criticism, in order to develop. And that only the future is going to show - whether he is like a few drivers before him a complete deal.
"But it is still surprising and amazing to see how quickly he develops. For me, it's like an AI agent that continuously self-improves and learns. That's the speed. And there also, his age is for sure beneficial. The ability, cognitively, intellectually, to constantly become better."
Russell hurts with title almost a lost cause
After the race, Russell tried to put a brave face on it, but it was impossible not to see how much it was hurting him.
Speaking in the news conference, sentences ran out of steam, his voice was on the point of breaking at times.
Russell gently pointed out, in not quite so many words, that without the VSC he probably would have won - "it would have been very interesting to see how the race would have panned out if there was no VSC".
But he was well aware of what Antonelli's stellar performance meant. The strategy, he said, "takes nothing away from Kimi's drive altogether".
And the championship, he now knows, is almost a lost cause. Antonelli's win moves him 66 points clear.
Russell talked about "taking the positives", about how, after a "very tough run" in the early summer, since the season re-started in the Netherlands two weeks ago, "every lap, every session, I've been sort of in the mix of the top three positions, similar to where I was at the start of the year".
That's true. But there has not been a hint all year of Russell being able to put together a run of results where he consistently beats Antonelli, which is now his only hope.
"It's definitely Kimi's in control of it," Russell said. "And, you know, he's deserving to be in control of it.
"For me personally, I'm not even thinking about a fight or a comeback or anything. I'm just focused on taking it race by race and trying to maximise every single weekend.
"He's performing incredibly well. It's going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap. So I'm just sort of accepting that is what it is."

When shopping for an electric vehicle, affordability is becoming a more common trait. But affordable and energy efficient is truly a rare breed. Often you have to sacrifice one for the other. Want something affordable? Great, here’s a range loser. Want something that goes the distance? Be ready to pay the price.
Audi’s new A2 E-tron is its most affordable and efficient EV yet
Unfortunately it won’t be making it’s way to North America any time soon.
Surprisingly, here comes Audi to split the difference. The German automaker’s new A2 E-tron compact crossover is inexpensive, starting at just £32,200 (about $45,000). And it absolutely impresses with an ultra low drag coefficient and a range of battery and drivetrain options that, when configured correctly, can produce a range of up to 401 miles.
Unfortunately for us Yanks, this rear-wheel drive compact car is just for the European market for now. But perhaps Audi will eventually see the error of its ways, or Americans will get their heads out of their tailpipes long enough to see the real advantages of a highly efficient, compact EV with an Audi badge.
Efficient is often synonymous with aerodynamic, and the A2 E-tron certainly confirms that. Flush door handles, cool air intakes, a fully enclosed underbody, and gap reducers around the wheel arches help reduce the drag coefficient down to 0.24, a first for Audi. Another first is bidirectional charging, which will help support vehicle-t0-load via an outlet in the trunk, or vehicle-to-home with the right compatible DC wall box.
With the right motor and battery setup, the A2 E-tron consumes just 12.8 kWh per 62 miles (100 km), while the real mile-eater of the lineup manages up to 401 miles (645 km) on the European WLTP cycle. Inside, the A2 E-tron features a standard curved MMI panoramic display that combines an 11.9 inch digital gauge cluster with a 12.8 inch center touch screen.
There’s also plenty of clever storage thanks to a Fidlock magnetic fastening system that allows owners to click things like cupholders and charging cable bags into dedicated points around the cabin and trunk. Cyclists may be familiar with the tech that can keep their water bottles attached to their bike without a cage, but Audi says this is the first time it’s making an appearance in a production car.
While Audi gave up on its EVs-or-bust pledge last year, the automaker is leaving the door open for a mix of gas, hybrid, and electrification. The A2 may not be appearing alongside its brethren like the impressive S6 Sportback E-tron at the dealership anytime soon, but nothing is set in stone.

This could be year I win Ballon d'Or, says Mbappe
- Published
Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe says this could be a good year for him to win the Ballon d'Or for the first time.
The 27-year-old scored 42 goals in 44 games for his club last season but they did not win any trophies.
He won the World Cup Golden Boot with 10 goals, taking his career tally at World Cups to a record 22 - although France finished fourth.
"I think when you play for Real Madrid, the best club in the world, people associate you with this award," he said.
"There are many people that speak about me and the Ballon d'Or. Of course I've made history in the most important competition. Maybe it's a good year for this but people can vote according to what they think."
He added: "I always think I'm the best [player in the world] but everyone has their own opinion.
"Maybe people think different ways. I don't think it's a discussion we need to have.
"Of course this year could be good for me to win the Ballon d'Or. But journalists vote."
The highest Mbappe has finished in the Ballon d'Or rankings is third in 2023, when he was a Paris St-Germain player.
Three players are given shorter odds with the bookmakers to win the Ballon d'Or, which will be awarded on 26 October.
England captain Harry Kane is odds-on to win, after a club-record 61 goals in 51 games for German double winners Bayern Munich last season. He also scored six times at the World Cup.
Lamine Yamal, who won La Liga with Barcelona and the World Cup with Spain, is second favourite - followed by his club and international team-mate Rodri, formerly of Manchester City.
'I really don't care' - Mbappe on PSG success after his exit
Mbappe, who started his career at Monaco, is the all-time top scorer for both PSG, with 256 goals in 308 games, and France, with 66 in 106.
He has netted 90 goals in 107 matches for Real Madrid but is yet to win a major trophy in two years at the Bernabeu.
On a personal basis, he has won eight consecutive league golden boots - six in Ligue 1 and two in La Liga - plus two in World Cups and another two in the Champions League.
He won the 2018 World Cup with France, but on a club level he has yet to win the Champions League.
PSG, who had never lifted the trophy before, have won it both seasons since Mbappe departed.
"I can't change it," he said of his former club's success without him.
"The truth is that I really don't care. I know how to analyse football, I know why.
"I don't know everything about football but I know more than most."
Speaking about Real's lack of recent trophies, he added: "My experience with Real Madrid says I shouldn't think too long-term because a lot can change.
"I want to think how I can be ready, to help my team to win the game and to start the Champions League in a good way."
