Minecraft Dungeons 2 is going to reveal a mysterious new dimension called The Sift and introduce new locations, enemies, weapons, and a broader action-RPG experience. This sequel is packed with some of the familiar faces from the vanilla Minecraft mobs, along with some unique entities with powerful abilities. So, check this complete list of Minecraft Dungeons 2 enemies before taking them on inside the game.
Minecraft Dungeons 2 Enemies List
The regular enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2 cover a surprisingly broad range of combat styles. While some may rush toward you with their weapons drawn out, others might prefer to stay at a distance and shower your group with serious damage-dealing projectiles. So, here’s a complete list of all the standard enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2:
| Enemy | Description | 
|---|---|
| Baby Sifter | A small hostile creature native to the Sift | 
| Baby Zombie | A smaller, faster zombie variant that charges at heroes | 
| Bearded Sifter | A ranged Sift creature that fires tracking projectiles from its chin | 
| Cave Spider | A fast cave-dweller that attacks with poisonous bites | 
| Chicken Jockey | A baby zombie riding a chicken that charges toward heroes | 
| Copper Cube | Small cube enemies that spawn from the Copper Monstrosity boss | 
| Creeper | An explosive enemy that detonates when it gets close to a player | 
| Enchanter | A magical Illager that strengthens nearby allies with enchanted buffs | 
| Escavator | A pickaxe-wielding Illager that attacks heroes at close range | 
| Flame Construct | A fiery construct that explodes and can breathe fire | 
| Geomancer | A spellcasting Illager that creates stone pillars and explosive formations | 
| Husk | A hostile undead mob | 
| Nester | A Sift creature that rapidly bounds toward players and bites them | 
| Pillager | A ranged Illager that uses a crossbow and retreats when approached | 
| Ravager | A large creature that charges through mobs and heroes | 
| Royal Guard | An armored Illager equipped with a mace and shield | 
| Sculk Cube | A summoned creature that rolls toward heroes and explodes | 
| Sculk Slasher | A Sift monster with long claws that charges and slashes heroes | 
| Skeleton | A ranged undead enemy that uses bows and Powerbows at higher tiers | 
| Slime | A hopping enemy that comes in multiple sizes and splits when defeated | 
| Spider | A web-shooting enemy that slows players before attacking | 
| Spider Jockey | A skeleton riding a spider that attacks with a bow | 
| Sprout | A flying, tentacled creature native to the Sift | 
| Tall Sifter | A ranged Sift enemy that spits explosive projectiles | 
| Vindicator | A fast, axe-wielding Illager | 
| Zombie | A slow undead enemy with different tiers and equipment | 
Baby Sifter
Baby Sifters are the beginner-level enemies that you will encounter once you step into The Sift dimension. The creature first appeared in the key art, and later we got a clearer view in the Minecraft Dungeons 2 gameplay trailer.
Right now, we know that the combat behavior of this mob includes short melee attacks that deal minimal damage to the heroes.
Baby Zombie
Baby Zombies are famous for being one of the most notorious mobs in Minecraft, and they’re returning in this action RPG sequel. Unlike their adult counterparts, these smaller zombies move quickly towards the heroes and can produce swift melee attacks. They’ve been spotted in the Deep Dark, so keep an eye out for these speedy nuisances.
Bearded Sifter
The Bearded Sifter is another unusual addition to the list of enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2. These are native to the Sift dimension and can attack with blue colored projectiles from a safe range.
Now, the Bearded Sifter’s ranged attacks are not their only strong point. But when you encounter them, you’ll see the projectiles follow the target before eventually travelling in a straight line. The mob remains idle for a few seconds after the attack is over, so you must take advantage of this situation and defeat it right then.
Cave Spider
The Cave Spider is a fast-moving version of the regular Spider mobs that inhabit the Deep Dark. The biggest threat is their poisonous bite and their swift speed. Since these mobs rush towards the players at high speeds, it can get really messy to deal with a situation when the Cave Spiders surround your party on a bridge.
Chicken Jockey
The Chicken Jockey is one of the rarest mobs in Minecraft since it combines two familiar faces into one irritating package. These enemies can rush toward the heroes and attack them with swift melee attacks. Although the mob briefly walks away in another direction before making its next attack, its swift mobility is what will annoy you the most during the runs.
Copper Cubes
While fighting the Copper Monstrosity boss in Minecraft Dungeons 2, it will spawn some minion mobs to break your momentum. These small cube enemies that spawn during the boss fight are called Copper Cubes and can attack you with their melee fighting moves.
Creeper
The Creeper needs little introduction. This iconic enemy in Minecraft Dungeons 2 will run towards you and explode, dealing some serious damage. But there’s a useful trick to deal with it. Once it starts glowing, move away from its range and try to take it down with your ranged weapons in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
Enchanter
The Enchanter is a magical Illager that focuses less on directly damaging the heroes. Instead, it buffs up two other Minecraft Dungeons 2 enemies in range. When linked, the affected enemy becomes larger, gains health, and deals more damage. Since the Enchanter stands idle at a distance, make sure to defeat that mob first to break the links.
Excavator
The Excavator is an underground Illager armed with a pickaxe. It acts as a Vindicator, rushing towards you and swinging its pickaxe once it gets close enough. It can also slam the pickaxe on the ground, dealing more damage, but leaving itself exposed for a brief period.
Flame Construct
The Flame Construct is basically a walking brazier with an unhealthy attitude. These enemies can spawn in the Deep Dark and also while fighting the Twisted Warden boss. Usually, you will find these mobs embedded in the ground, but once a player approaches, the mob activates. It then jumps on the ground, creating a large explosion that sets the nearby mobs on fire.
Geomancer
The Geomancer is a magic-wielding illager that prefers fighting from a distance. It uses magic to make stone pillars erupt from the ground around heroes. Some of these pillars can create barriers and restrict movement, while others can explode after a short delay.
Husk
The Husk is one of the confirmed enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2, as shown in the latest gameplay trailer. Similar to the Zombies, they will run toward you and attack using their hands.
Nester
Nesters are native to the Sift, and their combat style is pretty straightforward. They will run close and bite the targets. Once the attack is on cooldown, they briefly remain idle before making chaos again. Although it may not sound serious, a pack of Nesters can make your run troublesome.
Pillager
You might remember the Pillagers from Minecraft Raids. A similar concept is introduced here, as these enemies appear with crossbows in their hands. The Pillagers can appear in the mountainous regions and in the Deep Dark.
These enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2 will keep firing with their crossbows, but once they start to load, grab the opportunity to use your melee weapons and finish them off.
Ravager
The Ravager is a large hostile mob that looks like a bull and solely relies on brute force. The signature move of the Ravager is to charge forward, ramming through the targets in front of it.
When one starts charging, getting out of the way is probably the best counter rather than drawing your sword. You can later use bows and crossbows to deal with it from a safe range or use the War Hammer to inflict critical blows.
Royal Guard
The Royal Guards are heavily armored Illagers equipped with a mace and a durable shield. This combination of armor and the shield makes them a strong frontline. So, I would prefer using the War Hammer to break the defense first and then use your ranged weapons to finish them off.
Sculk Cube
The Sculk Cubes are small hostile minions summoned by the Sculk Monstrosity during its boss fight. These cubes will roll towards you and attack with a melee fighting style.
Sculk Slasher
The Sculk Slasher is a Sift-native creature equipped with long claws. It can slash at heroes from a distance and also charge towards them, leaving behind a spectral image afterwards.
Skeleton
The Skeleton remains a staple of the undead lineup of Minecraft Dungeons 2 enemies. They use bows and can spawn with different equipment depending on their tier. The higher-tier enemies can be more dangerous, as some can even come equipped with the Powerbow and some armor on their body.
Slime
The Slimes return from the vanilla game due to their unique ability to divide into several smaller Slimes. When a large Slime is defeated, it splits into two medium Slimes that can further divide into two smaller Slimes each. So, yes, ranged weapons are the way to go for countering them before they surround you.
Spider
Spiders take a more tactical approach than simply running towards you. The Spiders can fire webs that can catch the players and their companions, thereby making you slow down. So, make sure to take them down fast, before hordes of spiders spawn and fire webs all over the arena to slow down your movement.
Spider Jockey
The Spider Jockey takes the already irritating Spiders and adds a Skeleton on top. So, the Skeletons, now having obtained a mount, will roam around the arena, firing arrows at your party.
Sprout
Sprouts are flying tentacled creatures that belong to the Sift dimension. Although we have spotted them in the key art and the recent gameplay trailers, there are not enough details about what their attack moves are.
Tall Sifter
The Tall Sifter is a bizarre ranged enemy you can find in the Sift. It will keep a safe distance from the heroes and spit large glowing projectiles at you. The projectiles form globs and, after roughly three seconds, the globs explode, leaving a large yellow goo in the blast area.
Vindicator
Vindicators are fast-moving, axe-wielding Illagers that will rush directly towards the heroes. Although they may seem like a simple threat, the Vindicators can come equipped with a helmet or pieces of armor at higher tiers to increase the difficulty.
Zombie
In the list of Minecraft Dungeons 2 enemies, we finally have the humble Zombies that can attack the players with their hands. But you should not take them lightly, because at higher tiers they can come equipped with swords, melee weapons, and even strong armor, thus taking longer to deal with these undead mobs.
Minecraft Dungeons 2 Mini Boss List
The regular enemies are only a small part of the problem since there are some mini-bosses in Minecraft Dungeons 2 that demand a little more attention and better dodging skills. Encountering these mini-bosses will pop up a health bar, and each of them will showcase unique abilities. So, these are the mini-boss enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2:
| Mini-Boss | Description | 
|---|---|
| Warden | A powerful Deep Dark mini-boss that uses melee attacks, burrowing, and sonic boom | 
| Sculk Dancer | A large Sift creature that attacks with sweeping movements and spectral afterimages | 
Warden
The Minecraft Warden has always been one of the most intimidating enemies in the vanilla game. Now that it returns as a mini-boss enemy in Minecraft Dungeons 2, it will surely put up a tough fight.
The Warden can choose any random hero to focus on, temporarily ignoring others in the party. One of its main attacks is the sonic boom that can create a large AoE blast. However, after using it, the Warden stands still for a while before attacking once again.
Other abilities of this mini-boss include burrowing underground and appearing behind a player. It can also charge at you, unleashing melee attacks with its hands.
Sculk Dancer
The Sculk Dancer is apparently the only hostile mini-boss in Minecraft Dungeons 2 that can fly. It appears in the Sift dimension and attacks by swinging its arms and spinning its body. One of the most interesting parts of its attacks is that, similar to the Sculk Slashers, it can leave behind an afterimage after its attacks.
Minecraft Dungeons 2 Boss List
And now, we are heading to some of the biggest problems: the bosses in Minecraft Dungeons 2. These enemies are ready to turn the combat dial up several notches. These bosses can unleash powerful AoE attacks, control the arena with rapid attacks, and more. So, here is the list of all bosses in Minecraft Dungeons 2:
| Boss | Description | 
|---|---|
| Copper Monstrosity | A copper golem boss that uses electricity and summons copper cubes | 
| Redstone Monstrosity | A massive boss that fires explosive Redstone projectiles | 
| Sculk Monstrosity | A Sift boss that charges heroes, unleashes souls, and summons Sculk cubes | 
| Sprout Boss | A gigantic Sprout variant encountered in the Sift | 
| Twisted Warden | A colossal soul-corrupted Warden with devastating sonic and soul-fire attacks | 
Copper Monstrosity
The Copper Monstrosity is a massive creature made out of copper, and it is one of the main bosses in Minecraft Dungeons 2. Unlike the cute little copper golems in Minecraft that are completely passive, the Copper Monstrosity seems to take on some highly contrasting features.
While the boss fight is on, the Copper Monstrosity can fire lines of electricity from its hands and also create a damaging electrical ring around itself. While it does melee attacks, the boss can also summon Copper Cubes that can roll towards the players and reduce their health.
Redstone Monstrosity
The Redstone Monstrosity boss in Minecraft Dungeons 2 was first showcased in the reveal trailer. Its signature moves involve firing volleys of Redstone blocks and breathing out flames from the mouth.
Sculk Monstrosity
The Sculk Monstrosity is a massive golem-like boss that you can find in the Sift dimension. It can charge toward heroes and release a burst of souls. Additionally, it can summon Sculk Cubes that roll towards the players, inflicting little damage.
Sprout Boss
The Sprout Boss is a giant variant of the Sprout enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2. Although revealed in the latest gameplay trailer, the full attack pattern and mechanics have not been fully shown yet.
Twisted Warden
Finally, one of the main bosses in Minecraft Dungeons 2 that has constantly been shown in the official artwork and promotions is the Twisted Warden. It seems like someone took the regular Warden and filled it with twisted Souls.
This colossal creature can appear from the ground and start hitting you by swinging its enormous arms in wide arcs. These melee hits can deal serious damage and knock down the targets.
The ranged attack is even nastier because the Twisted Warden can unleash a sonic boom with a larger AoE effect. It can also fire tracking soul projectiles during the attack. Furthermore, the boss can pull souls from the surroundings and blast them onto the floor to create patches of soul fire.
Finally, during the boss fight, the Twisted Warden can summon Skeletons, Excavators, and Flame Constructs to turn the arena into a full-sized mob brawl.
And that completes the whole list of all enemies and bosses you can find in Minecraft Dungeons 2. So, which of the above are giving you a hard time? Tell us in the comments below.
Where do Minecraft Dungeons 2 enemies appear?
Enemies in Minecraft Dungeons 2 can appear across several biomes, including the mountains, Taiga, Deep Dark, and the Sift.
What is the strongest enemy in Minecraft Dungeons 2?
Among the Minecraft Dungeons 2 bosses, the Twisted Warden seems to be the strongest one due to its massive damage-dealing abilities.

Following the devasting flash floods in Nepal on August 26, which claimed over 1,200 lives and caused massive destruction, a video has gone viral on social media, purporting to show the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) phenomenon. It displays footage from a search helicopter, ostensibly showing the breach of a glacial lake in China. Users on social media have widely shared the clip, claiming that this was the immediate trigger to the Nepal floods.
X user Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) posted the clip on August 27, with the hashtag #NepalFloods. At the time of this article being written, the post garnered 2 million views, and was reshared close to 2,000 times. (Archive)
A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood #GLOF can happen when a glacier-dammed lake suddenly breaches. 🌊🧊
Pressure and fractures create a pathway for the trapped water to escape, sending a massive surge of water and debris downhill at terrifying speed#GlacialFlood #NepalFloods #Nepal pic.twitter.com/0zrw0SIEqO
— Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) August 26, 2026
Also Read: Nepal floods: Unrelated videos of past disasters, AI visuals falsely viral
A journalist with Dainik Bhaskar, Ashish Rai (@journorai) also posted the clip on X, which received 2 million views and close to 4,000 reshares. (Archive)
Several other X users, like former MLA Rajpal Singh Sekhawat (@Rajpal_BJP), Dr. Kiran J Patel (@kiranpatel1977), Pradhyumn Sharma (@pradhyu78651514), AH Siddiqui (@anwar0262) and (@greatandhranews) posted the clip with the same claim. (Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Fact Check
To check whether the claims surrounding this viral clip are authentic, we broke it down into keyframes, then ran reverse image searches on the keyframes. This led us to an Instagram reel, uploaded by an user with the handle (@helipilotleigh), on August 22. It contains the exact same footage as the viral clip.
View this post on Instagram
In the caption, the user, whose name is Leigh Coates, explains what a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, or GLOF is, and mentions that the video shows one happening over the Columbia Glacier in Alaska.
The description on her YouTube channel states that she is a helicopter pilot based in the United States, who specialises in ferry flights and advanced training for mountain flying, as well as airport landings.
We noticed that she had uploaded similar videos of glacial outbursts on her Instagram profile, and her YouTube channel.
In conclusion, the video that went viral recently in the context of the Nepal flash flood, showing a glacial outburst — purportedly in China — is actually from the Columbia Glacier in Alaska. It was uploaded by a helicopter pilot named Leigh Coates on her Instagram handle, a few days before the flash flood in Nepal. Thus, the claim that the phenomenon shown in this video was a direct trigger for the August 26 Nepal floods is false and misleading.

Online stockbroking platform Upstox has launched US stock investing on its platform, weeks after receiving approval from the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA). The offering will allow Indian investors to access more than 8,000 US-listed stocks and over 2,000 ETFs. This includes shares of companies such as Apple, Tesla, Amazon, and Google parent Alphabet. Users can begin investing with as little as $1 through fractional investing, which allows them to purchase a portion of a share instead of an entire share. The service will operate through the GIFT City framework. Global investment services will be provided by the IFSC branch of Upstox Securities Pvt Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of RKSV Securities India Pvt Ltd and an IFSCA-authorised broker-dealer. Investments will be routed under the RBI’s Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), which allows resident Indians to remit up to $250K per financial year across all permitted overseas transactions. Upstox users can fund their accounts in ₹ through supported Indian bank accounts, with the amount converted into US dollars. The platform will also allow users to place after-market orders outside US trading hours, which will be queued for execution after the market opens. “International investing represents the next significant phase of growth for India’s wealth ecosystem, and launching US stocks feels like a full-circle moment,” said Upstox cofounder and CEO Ravi Kumar. The launch comes less than three months after Upstox, along with Zerodha, Groww, and Angel One, received IFSCA approvals to offer international investment products through GIFT City. Upstox joins platforms such as INDmoney and HDFC Securities, which already enable Indian investors to access US-listed securities. Last week, the company received SEBI’s approval to operate as a merchant banker through its wholly owned subsidiary Zerodha Corporate Advisors Pvt Ltd, with initial focus being on equity IPOs. Meanwhile, Upstox’s domestic broking rivals Zerodha, Groww, and Angel One are preparing their own international investment offerings after securing IFSCA approvals. Zerodha had begun working on a US stock investing product last year, but founder and CEO Nithin Kamath said its launch had been delayed by regulatory and remittance-related challenges. The push towards global investing comes as Indian brokerages diversify beyond their core equity and derivatives businesses amid regulatory changes and pressure on transaction-linked revenue. Brokerages are expanding into areas such as asset management, lending, insurance, wealth management, and investment banking. Last week, Zerodha received SEBI’s approval to operate as a merchant banker through its wholly owned subsidiary Zerodha Corporate Advisors. Groww, meanwhile, has been expanding across wealth management, lending, asset management, commodities, and global investing. For Upstox, the launch comes as it explores a public market debut. The Tiger Global-backed company has reportedly begun preliminary discussions with investment banks for an IPO that could raise up to $400 Mn through a combination of fresh shares and an OFS. Founded in 2009 by Ravi Kumar, Raghu Kumar, and Shrini Viswanath, Upstox offers products across equities, derivatives, mutual funds, IPOs, commodities, and insurance.

UK government expected to announce restrictions on trade with West Bank settlements
- Published
The UK government is to set out new restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the BBC understands.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to outline the measures in the Commons on Tuesday, which could include restrictions on trade in agricultural products from settlements.
Last week, Miliband said he would unveil a "comprehensive reset" of the British government's policy on Israel.
The Israeli government has previously warned it would retaliate if any new measures were introduced.
Settlements are illegal under international law, and recent months have seen a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers.
One minister told the BBC: "The statement will be a complete reset of the nature of our Israel-Palestine relationship. It will all feel very different.
"It is not just about sanctions. We hope that this will finally achieve what those of us who have been working towards for two years over the Middle East have been working on."
BBC News has not seen the full details of the measures.
But Labour MPs who have been briefed on the plans believe the sanctions will target trade with illegal settlements. They believe that means the sanctions would cover both goods and services.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed to Labour MPs at their weekly parliamentary meeting on Monday night that Miliband would be making the statement, according to a number of MPs present.
The prime minister is also said to have told the meeting that he had briefed international leaders about plans in phone calls on Monday afternoon.
Burnham spoke to US President Donald Trump over the phone on Monday, during which the prime minister stressed the importance of a two-state solution in the Middle East.
An official account of the call released by No 10 did not specify that Burnham had briefed Trump on the sanctions, while the US - which is likely to strongly oppose the proposals - has not commented.
Speaking in July, Stephen Doughty - who was then Europe minister but has since been appointed Middle East minister - told the business select committee that existing powers to impose restrictions on settlements did not go far enough.
He said: "At the moment, we can sanction where there is evidence of it being linked to settler violence, but not, for example, in relation to a contractor working on the settlements. We need to expand our sanctions powers."
While ministers are said to recognise that banning a relatively small quantity of mostly agricultural products is a largely symbolic gesture, the government is expected to frame this announcement as a major reset in Britain's wider policy on Israel.
The expected announcement by the UK government comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.
Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.
Speaking in his first address to Parliament as foreign secretary last week, Miliband said those plans were "illegal under international law", and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's announcement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.
Tuesday's expected intervention will come almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.
The government believes the prospect of a two-state solution is being jeopardised by the rapid expansion of settlements.
The proposal for an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital, to exist alongside Israel has received international backing over several decades.
Israel rejects a two-state solution. The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

In a quiet summer garden, a caterpillar perches on a branch, munching serenely on leaves. A moment later it freezes. It senses danger—and just in time. From behind, a wasp approaches, sizing up its prey.
Tobacco hornworm caterpillars don’t look like they have ears, and yet they’re able to sense predators such as wasps. How does the caterpillar know a wasp is approaching?
Scientists do not fully understand how this caterpillar’s senses work, but we are part of a team of biologists and engineers who want to figure it out. Our ongoing research suggests that tobacco hornworms can hear using tiny, supersensitive hairs on their body.
Understanding the intricate biological mechanisms that allow this organism to perceive and interact with its environment would help solve a mystery of the natural world. It could also help scientists design new, cheaper microphone technology.
Because the hornworms’ hairs are so sensitive, we have to study them in complete silence. And where better to study hearing than in the complete silence of an anechoic chamber?
What Happens in the Anechoic Chamber
What happens outside the anechoic chamber stays outside the anechoic chamber, because it is meticulously built that way. Anechoic chambers are some of the quietest places in the world. They are engineered specifically to block the entry of any undesired sounds. Heavy-duty steel springs support the “floating” chamber and keep it from touching the ground. This detachment isolates the space from outside vibrations or noise.
In such a chamber, we studied the caterpillars’ responses to vibrations. Every day for a year, we set up a caterpillar on a platform and sent vibrations toward the platform at a variety of intensities.
To measure the movement and precise vibrations that traveled through the platform the caterpillar sat on, we used a device called an accelerometer. In response to vibrations, we sometimes saw the caterpillars jump; at other times they twitched or even shuddered from the sheer physical force.
Through our observations, we pinned down the specific threshold where the caterpillars stopped reacting to vibrations. Any vibration weaker than that magnitude, and the caterpillar wouldn’t visibly react at all.
After noticing this consistent pattern, we decided to test more caterpillars inside the anechoic chamber, but this time using airborne sound as the stimulus. The idea here was that if the caterpillars are more sensitive to sound than they are to vibrations, they are probably hearing airborne sounds independent of any vibrations.
Sound is broadly defined as a form of vibration or energy that becomes audible, meaning you can hear it with your ears. But here’s the catch: Sound also causes objects to vibrate. To make sure the caterpillar wasn’t just sensing the sound’s vibrations through the platform, we also used the accelerometer to measure the vibrations that the platform experienced from the sound. Our goal was to compare the platform vibrations produced in two distinct scenarios: when sound through the air was used as the stimulus versus when just direct vibrations were used as the stimulus.
We noticed that this time the caterpillars continued reacting to the sound even beneath their threshold of response to the direct vibrations. This finding suggested that they were hearing the airborne sounds.
Finding the Caterpillars’ “Ears”
So, where are their “ears?” Or rather, what are their “ears?”
There are two ways of hearing sound: from the sound waves’ pressure and from the velocity of the particles making up the sound waves.
For the longest time, scientists have associated hearing with tympanal organs. A tympanal organ in most mammals is a membrane that vibrates in response to pressure from sound waves. Its vibration moves the bone structures adjacent to it as well.
In most insects that respond to sound pressure, the structure analogous to the tympanal organ is a sac filled with air. They perceive any vibrations to this sac as sound.
But caterpillars pose a challenge to this typical hearing system, because they can hear but do not have obvious tympanal membranes. After digging into some past research and examining the caterpillars under the microscope, we spotted the distinctive hairs on their bodies.
Thus, our next project began. We removed their hairs and compared their responses to sound before and after the hair removal. Sometimes we surgically removed all the hairs by plucking them with tweezers under the microscope, and sometimes we strategically targeted a few.
The result was striking: The caterpillars’ defensive reactions decreased dramatically across various sound frequencies depending on which specific hairs were removed. While our research continues, and we haven’t yet published our results in a journal, this work is allowing us to piece together the caterpillar hearing puzzle and investigate which of these hairs are tuned to register different sound frequencies.
This line of research into how insects hear sounds using specialized, microscopic hairs could inspire a new generation of acoustic tools. Standard microphones are devices that contain membranes within them that can detect sound pressure levels. By mimicking these biological systems, such as using structures like these hairs in place of membranes, future microphones could be designed to instead measure the air particle velocity caused by sound, alongside the sound pressure levels.
Microphones that can detect air particle velocity would also be able to determine the direction of origin of the sound wave. In the case of microphone designs for hearing aids, a microphone that is able to track both sound pressure and air particle velocity could provide the user with information on both volume and direction of the sound wave. And studying caterpillars’ hearing systems and imitating how their “hearing hairs” work could inspire such directional microphones.

A new Elizabeth Holmes documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim is coming from A24
It looks unsettling, to say the least.
In case you haven't gotten enough of the Elizabeth Holmes saga, there's a new documentary about the Theranos founder from A24 and it sure looks... unsettling. You Can See Everything is the latest bizarre chapter in Holmes' story from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.
After two previous documentaries and a Hulu miniseries, you might think there's little new to add to Holmes' story. But You Can See Everything is apparently a bizarre coda to the events that ultimately led to her downfall. It was filmed in 2023 in the days before she reported to prison to serve out an 11-year sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. And Holmes apparently gave Fielder and Oppenheim extensive access "in an effort to clear her name," according to The New York Times.
The result is a three-hour long documentary that looks as strange and uncomfortable as you might expect from the startup founder who once claimed her blood testing startup would revolutionize healthcare. Fielder, known for his comedic roles, features prominently in the teaser released by A24.
"Why would I deceive you," Holmes asks in a close-up shot while staring unsettlingly into Fielder's eyes. "There's no reason for me to do that."
The teaser doesn't give much away, but the film reportedly features some "innovative recreations" in addition to Holmes' intense conversations with Fielder, according to The NYT. There's also, apparently, a conversation in which Holmes and her partner discuss plans "to launch a new and improved Theranos." Okay then!
Given the public's past fascination with Holmes and Theranos, the latest chapter will likely draw its share of curious viewers. And, in case you were wondering, Holmes herself seems more enthusiastic about this portrayal than others. The startup founder, who has turned into a somewhat prolific poster on X in the last year, shared the trailer from her account (which she describes as featuring "mostly my words," though she relies on others to help post.) "I'm always being real," she wrote.
You Can See Everything will get a theatrical release sometime in October.

'It's incredible,' Winnipeg man says after car blows over onto lawn in Sunday night storm
Some power outages for roughly 4,000 Hydro customers could stretch into Tuesday
A Winnipeg man says the damage left by Sunday night's thunderstorm was "overwhelming" after his vehicle rolled into the front yard of a nearby home.
High winds and heavy rains led to downed power lines and trees, particularly in Winnipeg's Westwood and River Heights areas, Hydro spokesperson Peter Chura told CBC News on Monday morning.
Sometime during the storm, Darryl Gervais says the wind pushed his Pontiac Vibe, which rolled over into a nearby lawn on Lindsay Street in the River Heights area.
Gervais said he had just finished repairs on the vehicle and left it for his son to use right before the storm hit.
"It looked wonderful, and now it doesn't," he told CBC News on Monday. "The windows are smashed, the roof is crumpled, and there's a trail of parts along the lawn."
But Gervais is glad no one was hurt, saying if the vehicle had rolled another three metres, it would have hit a house.
"It's incredible, the force of the wind that can pick up a 3,000 pound vehicle," he said.
"Yesterday, I was working on it, figuring it would last another two years."
Preliminary numbers from Environment Canada show winds in the city reached 83 kilometres per hour on Sunday night, while 35 millimetres of rain hit Winnipeg's airport and The Forks got about 63 millimetres.
'Pretty scary'
Robyn Canicula, who lives nearby on Lindsay Street, says her family may be staying in a hotel for the next few days after the storm damaged her home just before her children head back to school.
"We can't go in the backyard because there's a power line down," Canicula told CBC News on Monday. "Our trampoline's gone, our pergola's up in a tree down the road."
The storm left destruction all over the neighbourhood, including downed power lines and trees, as well as power lines that were cut in half, she said.
"It feels like we're in a movie. It's pretty scary."
Canicula is thankful the community has come together in light of the damage, she said.
"We've had a lot of neighbors reach out," she said. "Actually, somebody's been helping my husband put a tarp on our roof and our neighbour's roof, so it's been really nice, all the support we've been getting from the community."
About 4,000 customers in Winnipeg were without power on Monday morning, Hydro's Chura said.
Although crews worked through the night to repair damage and restore power to some, people in areas that suffered severe damage should expect "extended outages today and likely into tomorrow," Chura said.
"We'll assess the damage and concentrate on the damage that's going to restore the most customers to power at once, and then work our way down from there," he said.
"There's more severe weather in the forecast, so that could complicate repairs and cause further hazards for people."
Hydro is urging the public to stay away from downed power lines and to report them to 911, said Chura.
"And remember, a downed tree can also be hiding other hazards, so stay away from those as well."
The storms began near Moose Jaw, Sask., on Sunday morning and moved eastward over southern Manitoba, resulting in "quite an interesting dinner hour" for Winnipeg, Environment Canada meteorologist Dan Fulton said.
"It was a lot of precipitation, but it pretty much all fell within an hour or two," he told CBC News on Monday.
Storm damage reported near the community of Elie, which is just west of Winnipeg, points to a potential tornado, Fulton said.
"If it was [a tornado], it would be probably a pretty brief tornado, but I mean, it can't be ruled out."
More rain is expected to hit southern Manitoba on Monday night, including Winnipeg, but Fulton said he doesn't expect "we'll see anything in Winnipeg other than that rain."
The only potential complication would be if severe weather develops in the province's southwest and clips Winnipeg on Monday evening, he said.
Rainfall warning in southwestern Manitoba
A yellow rainfall warning has also been issued for parts of southwestern Manitoba as heavy rain and thunderstorms are expected to bring upwards of 50 millimetres of rain in some places on Monday.
The cities of Brandon and Dauphin, as well as the towns of Swan River, Virden and Melita, are included in the weather agency's advisory issued shortly after 4 a.m.
Rainfall amounts are expected to be highly variable, but widespread amounts are predicted to be between 30 to 50 millimetres, while local amounts could be higher than 50 millimetres, Environment Canada said.
Water is likely to pool on roads and low-lying areas. Visibility is also likely to suddenly reduce at times.
The weather agency is warning people not to drive through flooded roadways, to allow extra time for travel and to avoid low-lying areas.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods hit parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction (here, here, and here). In this context, a video showing an avalanche is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it depicts the first visuals of the floods in Nepal. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video depicts the first visuals of the floods in Nepal.
Fact: The viral video does not show floods in Nepal. The visuals actually show an avalanche at Lake Humantay in Cusco, Peru, from July 2026. This was available online before the Nepal floods. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
On conducting a reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video, we first found the same video uploaded on the Facebook account of a Mexican user on 27 July 2026. The post contained hashtags including Peru.
Further, we found a video featuring the same visuals on the Instagram account of a Spanish media page, uploaded on 30 July 2026. The accompanying caption stated that the video showed an avalanche captured by tourists at Lake Humantay in Cusco, Peru, and credited Instagram user @memomtz88. We noticed that the credited user was the same Mexican user whose Facebook account had uploaded the video on 27 July 2026. We then found the same video uploaded on @memomtz88’s Instagram account on the same day.
Several Spanish media outlets reported this incident with the same visuals (here, here). We also compared the scenes in the viral video with photographs of Lake Humantay in the Cusco region of Peru available on Google Maps and found that the surroundings in the footage match those of the lake. A comparison of the viral visuals and the Google Maps images can be seen below.
To sum up, an old Avalanche Video from Peru is being falsely shared as Nepal flood visuals.

How Do Automatic Litter Boxes Work?
Automatic litter boxes vary depending on the brand and litter type. Generally, they have sensors, either by motion or weight, to tell when a cat has entered or exited the device. Usually customizable and controlled via app on your phone, or on a more rudimentary timer system, the cleaning cycle will begin a short time after the cat has used the box. With dome-shaped litter boxes, the cleaning will happen via a cycle where the litter spins and rotates around the spherical interior; the bigger soiled clumps will be deposited into the waste basket while the clean granules pass through the grates and get recycled back into the box.
The Petkit PuraMax 2, for example, rotates backward and then forward (rather than a clock-wise/counter-clockwise spin cycle) to sift the clumps from the clean litter, depositing the larger clumps into the waste basket. The Pet Zone Smart Scoop is the most rudimentary design we tested, simply using a rake attachment to scoop the bigger clumps into a waste receptacle in the back.
Are Automatic Litter Boxes Safe?
Pet owners should always do research and make an informed decision regarding which box is best for them and their cat. We only tested automatic litter boxes that remain open during cycling to ensure that if for some reason the weight sensors didn't pick up on a cat being inside, the cat could jump out. We don’t recommend devices that close completely because of the potential that the machine could not sense the cat and kill it during its automatic cycle.
These automatic boxes use sensors—some only needing 1 pound of weight to detect your cat—where the cycle will automatically stop no matter where it is in the cleaning process. Many also have anti-pinch sensors. For added security, the devices on this list have customizable schedules, including “do not disturb” modes. If you're a neurotic helicopter cat mom like me, you could only run the clean cycles when you choose, like when you're in the room to observe the cycle (although if you do that, the box won't stay clean for as long).
Where Should I Put the Automatic Litter Box?
All of these automatic litter boxes require electricity, so they will need to be near an outlet. Since cats will generally take a little while to get comfortable with their new potty, I recommend that you keep your old litter box until they use the device regularly. It helps to put the new automatic litter box near the old boxes to familiarize your cat with it. Adding in litter attractant and using old litter from the previous box also encourages your cat to use the new model.
As a general rule, for old-school litter boxes, you should have one box for each cat, plus one. With automatic models constantly cleaning, there is less need for multiple options, but we recommend leaving your old litter box out for an extended period to ensure the cat has acclimated to the new automatic box.
What Should You Look for When Shopping?
After testing around a dozen automatic litter boxes, I look for several things that make day-to-day life with the device easier for you and your pet. First, the connected app. This is what you'll be checking daily, so it's important that it works well. This is one of the reasons the Litter-Robot 4 was our top pick for a long time: its connected app is intuitive, simple to use, and reliable. I absolutely love the Petkit models we've tested, but the app is subpar, overcrowded with ads for other products and poorly translated. I also look for anything that makes filling litter easier: I love the Litter-Hopper attachment, which refills litter for you on Litter-Robot models, the self-filling litter reservoir on Homerunpet, and the self-sealing waste bags of the newest Petkit models. You'll also want to keep the cat's size in mind. My two cats are large, so I tend to opt for something with an extra-large, front-facing hole. Which box you choose depends on litter type and compatibility—if you're using tofu litter, make sure you get a model that is compatible with your preferred type. Budget is also a factor, with some models as low as $150 or as high as nearly a grand.
How Does WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?
I do a lot of research, looking up other reviews online, including our competitors, to see which are getting buzz. Since I'm the pet tech writer here at WIRED, I also have knowledge from other pet tech brands I love for things like automatic feeders and pet water fountains. Most of these brands also have automatic litter boxes, which I always try to test among their lineup of new pet tech. I also talk to other cat-parents to see what they're using (and liking). I aim to test a wide range of styles and price points for every type of budget and cat.
How Does WIRED Acquire the Boxes?
Sometimes we reach out to brands we're excited about and receive samples for potential review; other times we will buy a model we're interested in and expense it.
What Does WIRED Do With Them After Testing?
We keep some models on hand for long-term testing to see if they hold up over time. This is especially useful for our former top pick, the Litter-Robot 4, whose Litter-Hopper attachment eventually stopped working, or the Petkit models, whose AI starts falling flat without a Care+ subscription. Keeping some devices for longer-term testing helps ensure that we are giving our readers a comprehensive review. Most boxes we test for several weeks and donate locally upon completion.
History of the Automatic Litter Box
Rudimentary automatic litter boxes have been around since the late ’80s. These early models featured an automatic rake attachment (much like the Pet Zone Smart Scoop box) but had problems with reliability and loudness. It wasn’t until the 2010s that the devices started incorporating advanced tech like Wi-Fi and app control. In the decade since, that technology has continuously grown and improved, with most devices providing insight into your cats’ habits and health—truly becoming an asset in understanding your feline friends even better.
What I'm Testing Next
My cats are currently testing the Petkit Purobot Max 3, the newest model in beloved brand Petkit's automatic litter box lineup; and the Bissell CleanWell Self Cleaning Litter Box, the first automatic litter box model in the cleaning titan's new pet tech category.

Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
- Published
A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.
Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.
It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.
"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."
That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.
Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.
"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.
Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.
The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.
Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.
The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.
That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.
A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.
But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.
Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.
And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.
The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.
"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.
"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."
He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.
But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.
"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.
Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.
Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.
The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.
"There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital.
He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday.
"The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more."
Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes.
Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them.
Puntland authorities have been more outspoken.
Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast.
The BBC has not independently verified his allegations.
The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operation… in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out.
Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say.
There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed.

Logic clearly dictates that the needs of the penne outweigh the needs of the stew, or the bun. While this would have been a gloriously fan-faithful reason for Le Creuset, the French-Belgian maker of colorful cookware for more than a century, to materialize its new limited-edition Star Trek collection, the range is being launched in celebration of 60 years of the cult sci-fi show.
No matter, because when you have such stellar items as Vulcan oven mitts, shuttlecraft baking dishes, and—perhaps best of all—a cheese grater in the shape of the classic Trek communicator (which has somewhat wonderfully been nicknamed the “Communi-grator” by Le Creuset's design team), there's only cause for celebration in the cosmos.
Going on sale today, to coincide with the space series' 60th anniversary, the limited-edition collection has actually been in development for years after Le Creuset approached Paramount to collaborate on the kitchen kit in time for the landmark birthday. Le Creuset is no stranger to fun mashups, with its recent 2024 Pokemon collection being snapped up almost instantly (those looking to get pieces now have to scour the likes of eBay for items way over original retail prices).
As well as the 15 cm Communi-grator for $68, foodies looking for Federation-themed gear might appreciate the $500 Enterprise round casserole pot complete with Starfleet insignia knob, or the $450 Klingon shallow casserole dish with trefoil "Heart of Virtue" knob—both in cast iron. Inside the Enterprise NCC-1701 pot is the legend “to boldly go”, while the Klingon dish offers up an encouraging “Qapla!” (“success” in Klingon), handy for experimental cooking.
Carrying culinary adventures into the unknown comes the Le Creuset x Star Trek: Galileo shuttlecraft casserole dish ($150), which has a roomy 1.6 liters of space inside. Vulcan votaries are well catered for with the $35 Spock ear mug (perfect for Vulcan spice tea), complete with gold detailing along the rim as a nod to the Starfleet uniform; the $55 Spock hand spoon rest; and the whimsical Vulcan salute “live long and prosper” oven mitt, resplendent in signature Star Trek baby blue for $40.
Not merely content with digitally launching the collection online, Le Creuset engaged Sent Into Space to boldly send its Enterprise casserole dish where no pan has gone before—more than 111,000 feet above the Earth, atop 99.5 percent of the planet’s atmosphere. While obviously a blatant (albeit fitting) marketing stunt, there's actually some considerable logistics to overcome in sending a cast-iron pot to the edge of space.
Sent Into Space co-founder Chris Rose had the task of launching the pot in the stratosphere via a space-capable balloon taller than the height of The White House, where it stayed for 1 hour, 19 minutes, and 4 seconds enduring temperatures down to -63.4°C (-82.12°F). “Because of the weight, we had to give some serious consideration to how we were going to hold things, making sure everything was very balanced,” Rose tells WIRED. Rose and his team also have to rely on simulations to take into account considerations such as where will the pot land as it's parachuted back down to Earth, as well as how to avoid bodies of water and built-up areas, for example.
“The legal authorities within the aviation community need to know. We can't have a Le Creuset casserole dish floating past the window of an airborne A380 as it makes its way off to some destination,” Rose says. “So we are in constant communication, both from a flight-clearance perspective before this ever leaves leaves the ground, to onboard systems for telemetry and communication.” Indeed, in the early stages of reentry, Rose says the Enterprise casserole dish reached speeds in excess of 300 mph before slowing and landing safely in Lincolnshire, England.
Back on terra firma, the Le Creuset x Star Trek collection should serve cadets and captains alike, provided you can secure your selections before stock vanishes like a cloaked Bird-of-Prey.

Boy with shattered kneecap left waiting 6 days for RFDS flight from Karratha
In short:
10-year-old Noah Ross shattered his knee in an accident at a skate park in Karratha.
He has spent six days waiting in the local hospital to be flown to Perth for specialised treatment.
What's next?
RFDS WA chief executive Judith Barker says crews are working to transfer him as quickly as possible.
A 10-year-old boy with a shattered kneecap has been left waiting in serious pain for almost a week with no RFDS flights available to transfer him from Karratha to Perth.
Kayla Ross was called to the local skate park last Wednesday to find her son Noah on the ground after a scooter accident.
Noah has needed around the clock pain medication and has been unable to leave his bed since arriving at Karratha Hospital's emergency room.
"We got into the ER and we've been at Karratha Hospital ever since, waiting for an RFDS flight to Perth for surgery," she said.
Noah said the wait had been difficult.
"Really bad because I can't move out of bed," he said.
"I haven't seen sunlight for days and I can't do anything so its really painful and annoying."
There has been no confirmation yet of when Noah will be flown to Perth.
"We were initially told it might be a couple of days and every day it's just carried on and we're just waiting," Ms Ross said.
"Yesterday there was a flight for us. Unfortunately the plane broke down."
A commercial flight is not an option for Noah to be transferred to Perth due to his pain level and being unable to lower or bend his leg.
The WA Country Health Service (WACHS) said Karratha Hospital was experiencing "unusually high" demand for patient transfers.
"As a result some retrievals are taking longer than usual as aircraft are prioritised to the patients who need them most urgently," said WACHS acute retrieval and ambulance director Fred English.
"There are currently five patients awaiting retrieval in Karratha. All remain in a stable condition.
"It is clinically appropriate for these patients to continue receiving care locally, they're in capable hands."
City vs country divide
The RFDS remains the only option for urgent medical transfers for people living outside a safe driving distance from Perth.
The service maintains a fleet of 17 turbo prop aircraft, 3 jets and 2 helicopters, transporting an estimated 29 people each day.
Having lived in Karratha with her family for three years, Ms Ross said she was surprised by the wait for the transfer.
She said local hospital staff also wanted to get Noah to Perth.
"If we were in Perth we would've had the surgery and he would've been home by now recovering," she said.
"Instead it's prolonging that recovery period.
"The hospital staff here have been brilliant. They can feel our frustration and they're frustrated as well,. They want to get us out of here."
With Noah's surgery scheduled for Perth Children's Hospital, Ms Ross said the repeated calls from PCH staff for updates on her son's location were adding to to the stress of the situation.
"It's worrying for us … because what's the outcome if we get there later? You know, the healing process? How does that all work?" she said.
The family is not criticising RFDS and said they do not blame the organisation for the delay.
"They're doing a good job," Noah said.
"But we just need more people to fundraise for them so they can get more people onto their planes and to help."
High demand for transfers
RFDS WA chief executive officer Judith Barker has acknowledged it has been a difficult time for Noah's family but said crews are working to transfer him to Perth as quickly as possible.
"The RFDS works closely with the WA Country Health Service to prioritise patient transfers right across WA to ensure the patients who need care most urgently are retrieved as quickly as possible," she said.
Ms Barker said the service's teams worked around the clock every day to ensure transfers happened as quickly as possible.
Noah's mother said the RFDS was in need of more support to cover regional areas of WA.
"Obviously they're doing brilliant work, they're a charity … but there needs to be something [more] because this really isn't good enough," Ms Ross said.
"If we're living here there needs to be support for us. We need to be able to get care."

'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
- Published
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."
The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.
"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.
It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.
Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."
About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.
She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.
Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.
But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.
Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."
She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".
Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.
Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.
Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.
Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.
Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.
"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."
Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.
Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.
When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.
The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.
They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.
Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
One security consultancy estimates that kidnappers across Nigeria collected nearly $5.8m (£4.3m) in ransoms over the past year as the number of abductions surged. SBM Intelligence estimates that 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase on the previous year.
The increase in bandit activity appears to be a key driver in this trend.
Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".
Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.
As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.
Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.
- The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria 
  - Published28 November 2025
Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.
At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.
But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.
This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.
Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.
After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.
The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.
"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.
"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.
Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.
The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.
A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.
President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.
In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.
But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.
The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".
"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.
One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.
He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.
"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".
"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.
He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.
"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."
He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.
Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.
"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."
She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.
The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.
Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.
"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

In 2020, Margo Fairchild built a tiny home on her own, despite having no professional background in home construction.
To take on the project, she relied on a mix of YouTube videos and homebuilding forums. She also created an Instagram page to document her progress, where architects and builders from around the world reached out to offer advice when she had questions.
It took her 15 months to build her 240-square-foot, one-bedroom, one-bathroom tiny home. The $43,779 project cost more than she anticipated, but it has paid off. The home has been featured on tiny-home YouTube channels and local news outlets, leading to other opportunities for Fairchild, including a hosting role on HGTV's "Worst Yard on the Block."
"Building this tiny home has changed everything about my life," Fairchild told Business Insider. "It completely changed my perspective on how I look at perfectionism, and taught me so much about resilience, tenacity, and pushing through."
Here are five things she says to consider before building a tiny home.
1. Plan for unexpected costs
Tiny homes, which are typically under 400 square feet, can cost between $30,000 and $60,000 to build, according to Rocket Mortgage. But that estimate may not include expenses like permit fees, utilities, or hiring an architect or builder.
Fairchild had to dip into her savings to finance her home.
"Basically, any paycheck I had during that time went toward construction," she said. "Almost immediately, my budget flew out the window."
Her advice to prospective tiny-home builders is to try to list every cost before getting started, from how much wood they'll need down to the screws and nails. They should also realize they might be missing some.
"When people are building these things by themselves, there are just all of these tiny miscellaneous costs that are going to add up that you just wouldn't have even anticipated," she said.
2. Decide whether a tiny home on a foundation or wheels is right for you
Tiny-home rules can vary widely by state and local jurisdiction, determining how they can be built and placed, and whether permits are required.
In some places, a tiny home on a foundation may not be allowed, while a tiny home on wheels may be. Fairchild said prospective builders should research local ordinances early and choose the type of home that best fits their needs.
"There are pros and cons to both," she said. "With one on wheels, you can sometimes get insurance for it, and, depending on local rules, you may face fewer zoning and permitting hurdles. But then you have to consider where you'll park it, whether you'll be charged rent for the land, and what utilities you'll need to retrofit so that you can be off-grid if necessary."
3. Will your tiny home align with your lifestyle?
Fairchild designed her tiny home around a few nonnegotiables, including ceilings high enough for her to exercise comfortably.
"I like to work out," she said. "There's a gym down the street, but if it's snowy or rainy and I don't want to go, I need room to work out in my house."
She said it's important to design a tiny home around the way you actually live.
"How do you live? What are the things that you like to do inside your home every day that you don't want to give up?" she said. "I would say incorporate the things you absolutely cannot live without, so you don't feel like you're giving up anything. You have to be happy."
4. Be realistic about downsizing
Before moving into her tiny home, Fairchild lived in a normal-sized home and had to let go of many of her belongings, including furniture and clothes.
While her home largely fits her needs, its small size means she keeps some belongings — including winter clothes and craft supplies — in a storage unit or at her mother's home.
"People are often downsizing from a regular-size house, and they have a lot of stuff," she said. "Instead of just designing a tiny house and thinking, 'Oh, this looks cute,' set out all the things you think you'll need in your home. I'm not kidding, measure the cubic footage of your stuff."
5. Make sure you can comfortably share a small space
Sharing a small space with someone can bring frustrations, so it's something to consider from the start, Fairchild said.
"If you're building a life with someone and you're going to be living together, make sure your relationship is rock solid, or learn tactics for being kind and patient with each other and taking space when you need it," she said.

Cricket Australia has agreed to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

Sanjay Dutt recently found himself in an amusing moment on stage when Maharashtra Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik asked him to speak in Marathi. The actor, known for his candid sense of humour, responded with a joke about his own experience and quickly moved past the request.
Sanjay Dutt responds to Maharashtra Minister’s request to speak in Marathi: “6 saal jail mein raha, tab bhi nahin seekh paaya”
At a recent event in Mumbai, Sanjay Dutt shared the stage with Pratap Sarnaik. Videos from the event have surfaced on social media, showing the actor and the minister along with other dignitaries. During the event, Sarnaik said, “Aajkal main sab logon ko Marathi sikha raha hoon (These days, I am teaching everyone Marathi).”
The minister was referring to a recent requirement concerning autorickshaw drivers in Mumbai, under which they are expected to have a functional understanding of Marathi phrases. Sarnaik then suggested that Sanjay Dutt should also speak in Marathi, saying, “So I thought after his entry, let us all get Sanjay Dutt to talk in Marathi. He speaks in Hindi, but all of us understand Marathi.”
Responding to the request, Sanjay Dutt took the microphone and said, “Pratap bhai, main 6 saal jail me raha, Yervada mein. Tab bhi Marathi nahin seekh paaya. Main thoda seekha tha.”
“Marathi pride 🔥”… but only if you’re a taxi driver, auto-wallah or street vendor with no bodyguards and no film-industry connections.
