Education-focused SaaS platform Meritto’s parent NoPaperForms filed its updated draft IPO papers with market regulator SEBI for a proposed public issue comprising a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹375 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 3.8 Cr equity shares. Investor Info Edge will be the only one to participate in the OFS via its holding arm Startup Investments (Holding) Ltd, which holds a 47.93% stake in the SaaS startup on a fully-diluted basis. Info Edge initially invested in NoPaperForms in 2017, acquiring a 27.92% stake. It increased its stake further to almost 48% when it led its ₹28 Cr Series B funding round in 2018. Cofounder, managing director and CEO Naveen Goyal owns 30.19% shareholding in the company on a fully-diluted basis. Fellow cofounder and chief strategy officer Suraj Sapra also holds 4.7 Lakh shares or 0.22% in the startup. The remaining 17.6% stake is owned by NoPaperForms Solutions Employees Stock Option Plan Trust. Founded in 2017, NoPaperForms offers two software products: Meritto and Collexo. The flagship platform, Meritto, is a SaaS-based enrolment automation and CRM tools for educational institutions, helping them manage student admissions and fee collection. In FY26, the platform served 1,183 customers, centralised 148.76 Mn student enquiries and processed ₹3,179.85 Cr in education fee. Under Collexo, it offers fee-collection and payments-related solutions for educational institutions. Its Pixi brand, under Collexo, also sells co-branded cards to students. The startup also enables educational organisations to deploy AI agents across student-facing and institutional workflows with its Mio AI suite. NoPaperForms filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route back in November 2025. The markets regulator approved the public listing in March. On the financial front, NoPaperForms saw its net profit jump 6.3X to ₹11.9 Cr in FY26 from ₹1.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue rose 25% to ₹115.7 Cr in the year under review, compared to ₹92.3 Cr in FY25. The startup reported an operating revenue of ₹44.8 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) against a net profit of ₹6 Cr in the quarter under review. A Break Down Of NoPaperForms’ Leadership Deck Board of Directors Naveen Goyal Goyal is the cofounder, chairman, managing director and CEO of NoPaperForms. Prior to founding the venture, he headed Careers360 as a director and chief strategy officer for almost five years. Previously, he also founded Edukriti Learning Solutions in 2009 and led the business as its chief executive for 18 months. He was paid a remuneration of ₹58.8 Lakh in FY26. Suraj Sapra Sapra is the cofounder, whole time director and chief strategy officer of NoPaperForms. He takes care of strategy, growth, market expansion, customer success and strategic initiatives at the SaaS platform. Prior to this, he was a senior manager at Info Edge for nearly seven years till 2017. NoPaperForms paid Sapra a remuneration of ₹47.4 Lakh in FY26. Naresh Chand Gupta Gupta, founder and CEO of asset management company AccuraCap, has been an independent director on NoPaperForms’ board since August 2025. Besides NoPaperForms, he is also on the board of data analytics company eClerx Services. Neha Clovia cofounder Neha has been an independent director on NoPaperForms’ board since August 2025. Previously, she was associated with FCB ULKA Advertising, Living Media India, and Smile Sales. Additionally, she also serves on the board of companies like BlueStone. Siddhartha Pahwa Pahwa is founding partner at private equity (PE) firm Ocimum Partners, and has invested in companies such as Woovly, Beautywise and GluedIn. He joined as an independent director on NoPaperForms’ board in August 2025. Priyank Shanker Garg India Angel Network’s Garg joined as an independent director in August 2025. He is also currently associated with NextVerse Ventures as a member. Key Managerial Personnel Sumit Kejariwal CFO Kejariwal joined the startup in July 2022. With more than two decades of experience under his belt in finance, he was previously associated with Macquarie Global Services, Price Waterhouse Coopers, and Rahul Kapoor and Associates. NoPaperForms paid Kejariwal a remuneration of ₹34.6 Lakh in FY26, including salary, reimbursements and contribution towards pension plans. Upasana Srivastava Srivastava joined NoPaperForms in September 2025 as the company secretary and compliance officer. She is a fellow member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India. Prior to the IPO-bound startup, she also worked at ixigo, IndiGo and OMC Power and Lanco. In FY26, the remuneration paid to her was ₹ 18.3 Lakh.

Mumbai has seen a surge in H1N1 (swine flu) cases over the last three months, as the number of cases have jumped to 441 this year from 62 during same period last year. This marks a 612% rise, while for malaria the cases have seen a 20% rise.
According to Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)’s monsoon data for June, July, and August, 441 cases of H1N1, and 4,485 malaria cases were recorded between June and August as compared to 3,733 last year.
To curb the surge of swine flu, BMC has been screening suspected H1N1 patients, and prescribing Oseltamivir. Further, surveys are being conducted in the affected regions, where the H1N1 positive cases have been located.
The BMC said suspected H1N1 patients are being screened and treated with oseltamivir wherever required. Close contacts of infected patients are being monitored for 10 days, while door-to-door surveys are being conducted in affected areas. BMC also clarified that they have prepared ventilators, PPE kits, reserved beds and medicines to manage patients for hospitalisation.’
Mumbai’s E-ward, K-West ward, G-South ward, F-South ward, and H-West ward have so far recorded the highest cases of malaria. To combat the vector-borne disease, BMC has increased the field-level monitoring in most affected areas. They have surveyed 52,197 potential breeding sites for malaria control. Anopheles mosquito breeding sites were detected at 8,055 locations, along with 12,55,469 potential mosquito breeding sites for dengue control, and Aedes mosquito breeding at 27,352 areas.
Decline in monsoon related illnesses.
Mumbai saw a decline in dengue cases,leptospirosis cases, COVID-19 cases, Chikungunya, and Gastroenteritis. According to BMC data, COVID-19 cases dropped drastically by 77% this year, as 151 cases were recorded compared to last year’s 668. For dengue the fall has been by 20% — 1,563 patients recorded this year in June, July, and August. For chikungunya, cases have dropped from 370 to 46, a decrease of 87%.
Leptospirosis cases declined by 37% — from 406 to 255, while gastroenteritis cases dropped from 2,197 to 1,954, this year.

- The claim that U.S. Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr. once testified that brain damage prevented him from holding a job remains under investigation.
- The rumor stems from a 2024 New York Times report that cites a 2012 deposition Kennedy reportedly gave in the context of divorce proceedings from his second wife, Mary Richardson Kennedy, who died by suicide that year.
- The Times' story said Kennedy argued in his deposition that his alleged brain damage caused cognitive issues that impaired his ability to make a living. It's worth noting that the report did not state that Kennedy specifically claimed he could not hold a job.
- According to the Times, Kennedy said in his deposition that a parasitic worm ate part of his brain. He appeared to confirm this in an X post he shared during his 2024 presidential campaign. Further, his campaign reportedly confirmed he had a dead worm in his brain but had made a full recovery.
- While we found a document that appeared to be part of the aforementioned divorce proceedings, we could not find the deposition The New York Times referenced in its 2024 story. For this reason, we've left the claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if and when additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services for comment and await a response.
In late summer 2026, a rumor circulated that U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. once sought to avoid paying alimony by claiming during divorce proceedings that severe brain damage prevented him from holding a job.
The claim appeared on Threads and Facebook. One post on X said Kennedy had asserted he "was too brain damaged to work so therefore couldn't pay alimony." (archived):
Snopes readers also searched the website and emailed us to confirm the veracity of the rumor.
The claim stemmed from a 2024 New York Times report that cites a 2012 deposition Kennedy reportedly gave in the context of divorce proceedings from his second wife, Mary Richardson Kennedy, who died by suicide that year.
According to the newspaper, Kennedy said in his deposition that his brain damage "was caused by a worm that got into my brain and ate a portion of it and then died."
We found one document that appeared to be part of these divorce proceedings, but we could not find the deposition the New York Times referenced in its 2024 story. While we have no reason to doubt the veracity of the Times' reporting, Snopes relies on primary evidence, including documentation, to rate claims. For this reason, we've left the claim unrated until we learn more.
We reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services for comment and await a response. We also asked the Times to direct us to the deposition and will update this story if we hear back.
The Times' story said Kennedy argued in his deposition that his cognitive issues impaired his ability to make a living. It's worth noting that the report did not state that Kennedy specifically claimed he could not hold a job. The report stated:
Some of Mr. Kennedy's health issues were revealed in the 2012 deposition, which he gave during divorce proceedings from his second wife, Mary Richardson Kennedy. At the time, Mr. Kennedy was arguing that his earning power had been diminished by his cognitive struggles.
Kennedy appeared to confirm there was a worm in his brain in an X post (archived) he shared during his 2024 presidential campaign. However, his post boasted that his cognitive state was still superior to that of his competitors — then-former President Donald Trump and then-President Joe Biden.
"I offer to eat 5 more brain worms and still beat President Trump and President Biden in a debate," he wrote.
Further, his campaign reportedly said he had a dead worm in his brain but had made a full recovery.
The document we found was a 2011 affidavit by Kennedy in which he alleged his second wife had physically abused him, stolen from him, abused his children from a previous marriage and threatened to commit suicide. However, this document, which was published by Newsweek, did not include any information about Kennedy's alleged brain damage affecting his earning power.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated numerous quotes attributed to Kennedy, including the claim that he once said infertility was genetic.

Every year around this time, Apple announces new iPhones. The products go on sale soon after, usually ranging from a base model to more premium and more expensive Pro models. But this year will likely be different—not just because the company has a brand-new CEO.
Apple’s iPhone event will be held on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern), announced last week with the title “Surprise and Shine!” If you tune into the livestream, expect the announcement of an iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and, if all the rumors and widely held analyst expectations are true, the first look at an Apple foldable device.
Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill and its decent track record for figuring these things out, Apple is expected to prioritize its more expensive, premium devices this year and hold off on announcing its base model iPhone 18. That cheaper model is rumored to launch in the spring of 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and maybe a second-generation iPhone Air.
Why the drastic change in strategy? It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage, which has made just about everything more expensive. Apple hasn’t been spared. In June, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with manufacturing costs.
“Our assumption is that they're going to be launching three models in the fall, the premium side of the models of the 18 series,” says Nabila Popal, a senior director of data and analytics at IDC. “Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.”
Popal says it's a smart strategic move because Apple is aiming to spread out its revenue between a usually very strong fourth quarter and a typically much weaker spring quarter the following year. Apple’s portfolio has also expanded, and the iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup are more enticing for people already prepared to spend the money on a new iPhone.
When components become more expensive, companies have three real options: Eat the costs, raise prices, or, as Apple seems to be doing, lean into it. By moving its cheaper options to a later date, Apple can drum up excitement for its bigger, better, pricier offerings. When it charges more for those, it is likely to be less off-putting than making a cheap phone even more expensive. It’s part of a “premiumization” of devices, as Popal calls it, that Apple hopes to leverage and build hype for its pricier options.
Shawn DuBravac, chief economist at the Global Electronics Association, tells WIRED he is optimistic about what these kinds of rising prices ultimately mean for customers.
“Throughout the history of time, the deflationary pressures of technology have always flowed to the consumer,” DuBravac says. “I'm confident that will be the case again. It just will take some time for the markets to solidify.” In other words, new technologies launch with a high price, but manufacturing efficiencies and competition inevitably drive costs down for consumers.
That may not be the case anytime soon for folding phones, which are seeing higher prices than ever. Samsung’s entire 2026 Galaxy Z folding smartphone range saw price increases, as did Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and Motorola’s Razr 2026 models. Apple’s folding iPhone is rumored to cost around $2,000.
To help mitigate those high costs, Apple is turning to financing options and trade-in programs. In July, the company launched an iPhone leasing program that lets people pay a monthly fee to rent the newest iPhones, then swap them out when a new device releases. The program will undoubtedly help more people afford the newest devices, but ownership advocates have criticized it, saying it keeps you from truly owning and managing your device. It also fits Apple’s broader effort to turn all of its products into a subscription service.
“The way most consumers buy Apple phones is through financing or trade-in programs,” Popal says. “We can expect a lot more aggressive trade-ins to help cushion that.”
Thanks to the memory crisis and price increases, all smartphones are getting more costly to make. Less expensive phones become less appealing for manufacturers to prioritize, and leading smartphone brands have started to see them as far less economical to produce.
On the flip side, demand for refurbished devices has been climbing for a while now, with sales of used devices growing even as new phone sales slow down. More people are looking to save money or purchase more eco-friendly products.
“The days of the cheap smartphone are over,” Popal says.

Abdul El-Sayed is trying to win over undecided Jewish voters in Michigan — without compromising his substantive positions on Israel or disavowing his most radical allies.
The Jewish Democrats trying to get to “yes” on Abdul El-Sayed
A Democratic fundraiser on how the candidate’s charm offensive is going.
During both his primary and general election campaigns, El-Sayed’s opponents have portrayed him as insensitive to Jewish concerns, if not outright antisemitic. These charges have often rested on falsely equating El-Sayed’s opposition to Zionism (he is not committed to Israel’s existence as a majority Jewish state) with a hostility for Jewish people.
But in recent weeks, two other concerns came to the forefront. One was El-Sayed’s response to an antisemitic attack on a Michigan synagogue. In March, a 41-year-old named Ayman Mohamed Ghazali drove a truck into Temple Israel’s Jewish preschool. Days later, El-Sayed condemned the attack, while also noting that Ghazali had recently lost family members to an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon. El-Sayed suggested that these events illustrated how “hurt people hurt people” and that “violence is a cycle,” one that had led Ghazali to perpetrate “an evil act of displaced rage.”
Separately, El-Sayed had campaigned with the far-left streamer Hasan Piker during his primary campaign. This had always sat poorly with many Jewish and centrist Democrats in Michigan. But Piker made his association with the Democratic Senate candidate more conspicuous in late August. During a broadcast, Piker lambasted Jeremy Moss, a pro-Israel Jewish Democrat running for Congress in Michigan who had not endorsed El-Sayed but was in active conversations with the candidate about how to bridge lingering divides with Jewish voters. More explosively, Piker said, among other things, that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually somebody is going to come around and take action, not against the State of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” He subsequently insisted he was merely spotlighting the hazards of portraying all Jews as ardent Israel supporters, not making some kind of veiled threat, as his detractors alleged.
Nonetheless, this triggered a new round of calls for El-Sayed to both disavow Piker, and to take other measures to reassure Michigan Jews that he cares about their safety.
These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally.
El-Sayed declined to disown the streamer. But he did defend the right of all Americans “to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” saying this was “particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.”
Some Jewish Democrats found this insufficient. In an open letter Wednesday, 400 Democratic Jewish Michiganders — including donor Rob Orley — announced that they would be supporting Republican Mike Rogers in their state’s Senate race.
Days earlier, El-Sayed had sought to mend fences with such voters at a summit held by the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus. During his appearance there, he apologized for his remarks following the Temple Israel attack, saying “I should have issued a statement, of course condemning it, and it just should have been the full stop.”
Among those in attendance was Charles Gaba, a healthcare analyst and major Democratic fundraiser; Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow has called him “the biggest powerhouse democratic donor wrangler that nobody has ever heard of.”
Gaba was a strong supporter of Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. And he has expressed serious reservations about El-Sayed, even while committing to voting for him and raising money for his candidacy.
These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally: over how far Democrats can and should go in criticizing Israel, whether the left takes antisemitism seriously, and if centrists are using allegations of anti-Jewish bigotry to stigmatize legitimate dissent.
To explore these debates — and clarify the concerns of “Sayed-skeptical” Jews in Michigan — I spoke with Gaba this week.
Our conversation has been edited for clarity and concision.
From your vantage point, what are undecided Jewish Michiganders’ biggest reservations about El-Sayed — and how many are actually addressable by his campaign?
I’d say that there’s probably four main ones. Two are connected to his comments about the Temple Israel attack. And he definitely addressed one of those complaints with his statement: that it was awfully timed. In other words, that days after the attack was not a good moment to raise other issues instead of simply condemning the violence full stop.
But the larger issue to me — and to a lot of other folks I’ve spoken with — is he seemed to be under the impression that timing was the only problem. That it was just too soon and if he’d waited a month and then made the exact same comments about “context,” that would have been fine. He doesn’t seem to get that trying to put it in context at all is the larger problem. Because a bunch of preschoolers at a synagogue in Michigan have absolutely nothing to do with a military conflict overseas, just nothing. If a family member of someone who died in the September 11th attacks had gone and attempted to kill Muslim children, their loss wouldn’t be relevant context. You couldn’t say, “Oh well, but he was upset about that attack.”
I think an El-Sayed supporter might say: There’s a difference between explaining an abominable act and excusing it. In his original statement, El-Sayed did say explicitly that “there is never a justification for attacking innocent people or houses of worship” and described the violence as “heinous” and “evil.” Taken literally, he was arguing that the strike that had killed Ghazali’s family members led to his act of antisemitic terrorism, even as nothing could possibly justify it.
There was just no reason to try to put it in context at all. Pretty much everyone understands that the Israel-Hamas war has brought emotions to a fever pitch for a lot of people.
I don’t think we needed someone to say, “Hey, that whole mess in the Mideast might have inspired this!” Yeah, no shit. Who was the audience for this? Who was he trying to give context to? Certainly the Jewish community understands the situation. I think the Muslim community understands the situation. And so does everyone else. I don’t think it served any purpose other than to upset and offend a bunch of people. So he was lecturing to no one essentially, in my view. Which I get; I have a tendency to do that myself sometimes in other ways. But it isn’t helpful. And shifting the timing wouldn’t have made it helpful.
So, what are the other two big sticking points for Jewish Democrats not sold on El-Sayed?
The third is this Hasan Piker guy. The media certainly seems to be pretty focused on that. If memory serves, El-Sayed seemed to be trailing Mallory McMorrow and Haley Stevens in the primaries up until around March. And then it was announced that he was going to be rallying with Piker at Michigan State and the University of Michigan.
A combination of that and the reaction to it — namely the McMorrow campaign heavily criticizing him for the rally — generated a bunch of attention and certainly raised Abdul’s profile tremendously. I don’t know how much credit to give Piker, but it made some difference. And next thing you know, he’s kind of running in the lead.
So, it’s pretty clear that Piker was brought in specifically to help him win the primary with a very young, progressive crowd. To that effect, it worked. But that doesn’t mean he’s helpful for winning a general election.
So, why do you think El-Sayed refuses to distance himself more explicitly from Piker, if the influencer’s support is not helpful in the general election?
I don’t know. Maybe he thinks that he’s being noble or something by not throwing him under the bus. But the guy just seems to be kind of an asshole, and I would not want to be associated with him in either the primary or the general. And so associating himself with Hasan Piker makes me think less of Abdul.
And I have a lot of respect for Abdul. I’ve met him about a half-dozen times or so, back when he ran for governor and then several times during this campaign. And we’ve also been in contact a few times in between to discuss healthcare policy. And I know he’s a very intelligent guy, very thoughtful guy, and very passionate about universal healthcare. I respect him for all of that. But I think less of him for associating with Piker. And I think a lot of Jewish Michiganders feel that way.
So, what’s the fourth issue?
Well, this is not so much about Abdul specifically as it is about the left. A lot of progressives get that you should condemn antisemitism, or bigotry against the Jewish religion. But many don’t seem to grasp that Judaism is not just a religion; it is also a people. And we do have a several thousand-year connection with the land of Israel — not the leadership, not the current government — but with the land itself. And so that makes the distinction between antisemitism and anti-Zionism complicated. You know, to try to say, “Well, as long as you give up Israel, then Judaism is fine” — many of us can’t do that because it’s an intrinsic part of who we are.
Is there not a distinction between recognizing Jews’ historical and religious connection to Israel — and being committed to the maintenance of a majority Jewish state in the Middle East?
In other words, there are anti-Zionists who deny Jews’ roots in Israel — or the right of Jewish Israelis to live in the region. But I think most progressive anti-Zionists would dispute neither of those things. Rather, they’d argue that Israeli Jews have a right to live in their land — but that maintaining a majority Jewish Israel should not take precedence over allowing Palestinian refugees and their descendants to return to their ancestral territories.
It’s definitely true that there’s more than one type of anti-Zionism. I think there’s several groupings and different shades between them. And that also holds true on the Zionist side. There are right-wing extremists like [Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar] Ben-Gvir who say, “We should annex both the West Bank and Gaza.” And then there’s others that go even more extreme and say that Israel should dominate the entire region, including Lebanon and Egypt.
And then, at the other end, there’s Hamas and other extremists who literally want to either kick out or slaughter every Jew in the region.
And those extremes have led people to think that Zionism means “Jews get to take over the region” and that anti-Zionism means “Jews have to be kicked out.”
I think for most people, it’s somewhere in between. I’ve started calling myself a “small-z Zionist,” which is basically a more mainstream, two-state solution type. I don’t know how feasible that solution is. There’s only a slim chance these days. But the odds of a two-state solution are still better than those of creating a single “kumbaya, let’s all live together in peace” nation, in my view.
How were El-Sayed’s remarks to Michigan’s Jewish Caucus received, from your vantage point?
They were better received than I expected, to be honest. Although, I suspect that those most opposed to him probably didn’t show up at the event at all, since they’ve made up their minds.
Having said that, I did have discussions with several people afterwards, and there was definitely still concern about the whole “context” thing. People were polite and it was a reasonably warm reception. And to his credit, he did stick around afterwards and had one-on-one personal conversations. He was there for quite a while, so I give him credit for that.
From a purely electoral perspective, how much does El-Sayed actually have to lose, if he fails to consolidate the Jewish vote? In demographic terms, the bloc of Jewish voters who are open to voting for El-Sayed — but still need to be persuaded — would seem to be tiny. After all, we’re talking about a small minority of small minority; Jews account for only about 1.4 percent of Michigan’s electorate. So, what’s at stake here politically?
In terms of activism, organizing, and donations, the Jewish community punches far above our weight.
But yeah, we’re a fraction of a fraction. I think the biggest thing is just reassuring moderate Democratic voters in general. Basically, if the headlines start to read, “Jewish leaders seem reassured by Abdul apology,” then some non-Jewish folks — who aren’t sure about El-Sayed — might say, “Oh, well, if the Jews signed off on this guy, I guess he’s okay.”
Update, September 3, 3:30 pm ET: This piece was originally published on September 3 and has been updated with new developments and later clarified Charles Gaba’s title.

The trope of the lone action hero with near-superhuman strength gets a gender switch in “No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman,” a visually impressive drama about a resourceful female Peshmerga sniper. Although selected as Iraq’s submission for the Best International Feature Oscar, the third fiction feature from Norwegian-Kurdish helmer Halkawt Mustafa (“Red Heart,” “El Clásico”) may fall between two stools for Western viewers: There’s not enough action for genre fans and the narrative’s blend of melodrama and earnestness may turn off highbrow arthouse viewers. But it’s a different story in MENA territories where Sony/Empire has already nabbed distribution rights. Regional and Kurdish diaspora audiences should appreciate the strong visual and technical craftmanship used in this harrowing tale.
The narrative centers on Vyan (striking London-based Kurdish thesp Avan Jamal, impressive), a 24-year-old Kurdish émigré to Norway who is visiting Iraqi Kurdistan with her parents and younger sister Helin in 2014, when Islamic State (IS) launches an attack. Their parents are murdered and Vyan and Helin are sold as IS sex slaves. Ever resilient, Vyan manages to kill the man who bought her and make her way to Peshmerga territory. There, she joins an elite unit of female fighters as a sniper.
Popular on Variety
As Vyan’s poetic voiceover narration states, Peshmerga means “before death” and its fighters enter combat out of strength, not out of fear. Certainly, Vyan is fearless. She reckons that she has killed more than 100 of the enemy in three years. Given that, as the title notes, IS fighters believe that there is “No Paradise If You Are Killed by A Woman,” it’s no wonder they have placed a million-dollar bounty on her head.
After heroically preventing an IS suicide truck bomber in an armored vehicle from attacking her unit’s base, the heavily wounded Vyan returns to Norway to recover. There, a government official (Thorbjørn Harr) offers her a difficult choice: accept a new identity and government protection (they fear the fact that she is an IS target could endanger other Norwegian citizens) or be prosecuted for fighting for another country. Luckily, Norwegian civilians don’t have to worry. A phone call to the family’s old landline confirms that Helin remains trapped in Mosul, in the clutches of an IS fighter known as the Swedish sniper. Loyal Vyan prepares for what may be her final mission: to singlehandedly rescue her sister.
The last half of the film feels as if it could easily be adapted into a tense video game as it follows Vyan silently creeping through tunnels and crawling through the aftermath of IS carnage. It certainly gives a more detailed picture of how a sniper operates, and the lonely patience required for the job, than Clint Eastwood’s “American Sniper” ever did. Vyan uses logic and the help of friendly Kurdish commander from the Iraqi government forces in Mosul to locate the IS snipers preventing civilians from leaving the devastated city.
Research for multi-hyphenate Mustafa’s 2015 TV project “The Women ISIS Fears” and his time as a war photographer seeing strong female fighters inspired “No Paradise,” which he dedicates to his daughters. Like the helmer’s previous features, it proudly incorporates Kurdish customs and traditions, from the “singing” that Vyan’s rifle performs to the traditional tunes sung by her Peshmerga captain and the Kurdish commander in Mosul.
Highlights of a polished technical package include the prowling camerawork of Norwegian DP John Erling H. Fredriksen and the film’s use of actual Mosul locations. The shocking ruins of what was once a thriving population center attest to a brutal military campaign to liberate the ancient city from IS. Also worthy of special mention in a film where the main character spends much of her time in silence is the tension-building sound design by Mattias Eklund and Jan Kasskawo.

Smaller ball for women makes it 'harder to do my job'
- Published
England will play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in the next three weeks and, like all the world's top women's players, they have some new equipment: a smaller ball.
During September and October's WXV Global Series, World Rugby is trialling a size 4.5 ball - about 3% smaller than the size five used in the men's game, but the same weight.
Their introduction has not been without controversy and for England hooker May Campbell, responsible for throwing the ball in at the line-out, told BBC Sport it can go "a bit skew-whiff".
One of England's kickers, Helena Rowland, has found a much bigger margin for error with the smaller ball, saying: "If you get it slightly wrong, the difference is massive."
The fly-half says England players have noticed passes "dying", falling to the floor earlier than expected, "which they wouldn't have done previously".
Not all feedback has been negative. Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.
The thinking behind the trial is that the smaller ball will suit women's physiology and improve their skillset. In other sports, like basketball, women use a smaller ball, and in athletics sprint hurdles are lower for females.
But Rowland says she has never felt "hindered" by playing with the same size ball as in men's rugby.
'Harder to do my job'
Players with a specific skillset may find the change harder than others. Hookers must throw in at a line-out, scrum-halves are the most frequent passers and fly-halves the most regular kickers.
Rowland explained: "We've learned for however long how to kick with a size five.
"So I've had 13-odd years of doing that and training my routine and trying to nail that and get as much consistency as I can.
"So it's about, I suppose, trying to pack all those years of training and all those kicks into a four- or five-week block to get used to it, to then go out on to the world stage."
Rowland added that she has not "necessarily seen any positives", saying: "I know some of the girls have said that from an offload perspective, it's maybe made them more confident.
"But for me, it hasn't. I don't think there's enough of a change in the ball for me to be able to be running around with it in one hand and offloading left, right and centre.
"I haven't necessarily found any of the positive impacts. I've just found it a bit harder to do my job."
A World Rugby spokesperson said everyone involved in the WXV Global Series, including players, coaches and match officials, would have their views taken into account "with equal value" through surveys.
- Smaller balls for women's rugby 'worst decision ever' 
  - Published6 May
John Mitchell, England's head coach, has said "it's too early" to judge the impact of the smaller ball, and conclusions would have to be drawn after the world champions' opening three Tests in September.
Some England players were given a size 4.5 ball to practise with in the off-season and Campbell says "there's no point in complaining about it", given every side in the WXV Global Series will be in the same position.
But she adds: "I feel like a lot of us don't know how it's going to change the game, and kind of the reason behind it changing and the data behind it.
"It's just this decision has kind of just happened that we're now trialling it at the top level."
Inconsistency in shape
One area of concern for the England players is the ball changing shape.
Campbell says they "played around" with how much the ball was blown up, adding: "In previous weeks it was actually a bit fatter, and then this week it definitely feels smaller."
Rowland agrees, saying: "There needs to be a bit more done in terms of how the balls are made. We had some new balls today versus the ones we've had for the last three weeks [and the difference] is massive.
"If you've been training with an old ball that's fat to then go into a game and it's a completely different shape, actually that makes a massive difference as well, which I think is something that you don't necessarily find so much in the size five."
The ball has already been trialled in the Under-18s and Under-20s Women's Six Nations as well as the HSBC Sevens Series.
Rowland says she would "love to see the data on if it actually has made a difference".
It seems a fair request, and is one that BBC Sport put to World Rugby, but we did not receive any data.
A spokesperson said: "The balls haven't been used in the international XVs environment yet so there isn't directly comparable data to share with players either directly or via their unions.
"Once we've built up a large enough data set of player responses, match official responses and game data, we'll publish the results, so it'll be available to players, unions, the International Rugby Players Association, coaches, match officials, the media and everyone else."
Some players are frustrated as they feel they have become guinea pigs on the global stage. To compound that frustration, they will then return to their clubs where the league season will be played with a size five ball once again.
BBC Sport asked World Rugby when the trial period is likely to conclude, and were told: "We'll be able to assess our position on women's 15s once the international window has started.
"This will allow for completion of the WXV tournaments and full analysis in early 2027. The evidence to date suggests that further exposure produces greater results."
While it looks like players and coaches will get to see the data in early 2027, any wider outcomes or decisions might take longer.

War criminal Mladic buried with military honours in Serbia despite EU warnings
Thousands of mourners gather to attend his funeral in Belgrade, defying EU warnings against glorification of war criminals
Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb commander who died while serving a life sentence for war crimes, was buried on Monday with military honours and crowds attending as Serbia defied European Union warnings against allowing public homage to the man found guilty of the continent’s first case of genocide since World War II.
Thousands of mourners started arriving early at the small Serbian Orthodox Church of St. Luke in Belgrade to honour Mladic as his body lay in state.
Mladic is still viewed as a hero by many Serbs. His military officer’s cap and sabre rested on the coffin, which was flanked by men in fatigues.
The head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, led the funeral service while Serbian army soldiers carried Mladic’s flag-draped coffin at the cemetery as mourners clapped and a military orchestra played. Pro-government media broadcast the ceremony live.
Bosnian Serb nationalist leader Milorad Dodik and the Russian ambassador in Serbia, Alexander Botsan-Kharchenko, were among those present at the funeral.

How Long Should A Laptop Battery Last On A Single Charge?
And how you can help it perform at its best.
Laptops are at their most convenient when not plugged in — where their portable nature can really shine. To maximize that convenience, you'll want to make sure your laptop is lasting as long as it should. While there are many different types of laptops, each specialising in its own niche, there are still ways to figure out whether your laptop is receiving the proper mileage.
You shouldn't need one of the best laptops on the market to see a decent battery duration. By knowing how long a given laptop's battery should last on a single charge, you can avoid having to replace a battery early in your laptop's life. While most laptop batteries can be replaced without being brought into a repair shop, and warranties can sometimes cover premature battery death, generally replacing batteries is an expensive process that can often require niche tools (such as niche, specialized screwdriver heads). It's best to know ahead of time if you're getting your money's worth, as well as how to optimize battery life by changing settings and knowing which activities will drain power the fastest.
How to tell how long your laptop should last
To start, it's important to look at the type of laptop you have. The general range for modern laptops will lie somewhere between four and 12 hours from a single charge, but that's a pretty wide net. Premium-thin and Ultrabook laptops will last near the upper end of that tier (at eight to 12 hours, with some even reaching 15 under optimal conditions), whereas more standard laptops will last about six to 10 hours — or four to seven hours if it's a budget-friendly machine. Gaming laptops will drain significantly faster, and you should only expect about two to four hours from them.
A laptop's niche is only part of the equation, though, as the type of charger you're using can also subtly affect battery life. Aftermarket chargers in particular may not deliver the precise voltage you need and could end up stressing your battery. Though an aftermarket charger isn't a complete recipe for disaster, it's ill-advised if you want your battery to reach its full potential.
To reach that full potential for each of these bounds, you'll need to optimize things. There are some key settings to change for extended laptop battery life, such as turning down display brightness, closing background apps and tabs, and lowering your display's refresh rate. You could also switch to a power-saving mode in your laptop's power management settings, though you may need to switch out of this mode to carry out a demanding task.
How to keep your laptop battery healthy
On the subject of demanding tasks, it's not only important to keep an eye on your laptop battery through settings, but also through how you use your laptop. Gaming's the obvious one, as even laptops explicitly designed for it run out of power quickly — but video editing, video streaming and 3D rendering are all quite intensive. If you know you'll need to engage with one of these activities, it's important to plan ahead — whether that's by getting a solid power bank or by making sure you can reach a socket.
You'll also want to keep your laptop in the right conditions. Chiefly, you'll want to maintain an ideal moderate temperature of 68 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit. Extreme heat (temperatures of 95 degrees Fahrenheit and above) could cause permanent damage to lithium-ion batteries, while cooler temperatures (about 32 degrees Fahrenheit and below) will make those batteries temporarily less efficient.
Furthermore, you should avoid using all of that battery up at once. Letting your battery run out multiple times could cause permanent damage to your laptop battery due to continued cell drain. Similarly, try not to keep your laptop plugged in too long when fully charged, as this could also lead to degradation of the battery. For this reason, it can be good practice to follow the 40-80 rule, where you start charging at 40% battery and stop at 80%, thereby avoiding either extreme — though this is certainly not strictly necessary and not always achievable.

September has arrived, bringing the first hints of fall: cooler days, changing leaves, and the urge to revisit comfort watches. Below, The Atlantic’s writers and editors recommend six films that put them in an autumn spirit.
When Harry Met Sally (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
There’s the cornucopia of cable-knit sweaters, a chocolate-brown velvet bowler hat, the fog of bright-orange leaves streaming through the glass wall at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Autumn in New York is the backdrop of When Harry Met Sally, but that doesn’t fully account for the place that Nora Ephron and Rob Reiner’s classic occupies in my life: For me, it’s the chicken noodle soup of movies. I have my personal reasons for considering it the ultimate comfort watch. Maybe it’s my affinity with Sally (played by Meg Ryan), the curly-haired journalist determined to have life happen to her, though her job is to “write about things that happen to other people.” Or the movie’s love for my hometown, which forms the bedrock of so many of Ephron’s films. Or the weirdly specific fantasy of having your date unwittingly quote to you something you wrote in a magazine.
This time of year, I’m far from the only person who considers a When Harry Met Sally rewatch as inevitable as digging my denim jacket out of the back of my closet. If there’s a universal magic to the movie, maybe some of it comes from magic in real life. The original script saw Sally and Harry’s (Billy Crystal) story ending bittersweetly, with the two apart. But midway through making the film, Reiner fell in love with his wife, Michele Singer. This fall—our first without Reiner and Singer—I’ll be revisiting the movie in large part for the ending he decided on instead: perhaps the most memorable, and certainly my favorite, in the romantic-comedy genre.
— Marie-Rose Sheinerman, assistant editor
Michael Clayton (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Fall is not really about melancholy and the inner life, as the poets would have you believe. It’s that period, after summer’s frivolities, when things get serious again. Michael Clayton, a film I first saw at the urging of my friend and colleague James Parker—and which we both regularly rewatch—is charged with that urban, autumnal, overcoated feeling of things getting serious.
The people in it are grown-ups. If they’re not, as with Timmy—Michael Clayton’s brother, whose feckless behavior leaves Michael exposed to loan sharks—they’re basically ignored. Sydney Pollack? What a performance! What an impeccably serious guy! Tom Wilkinson, Tilda Swinton—they’re brilliant in this. And George Clooney, playing the titular character, is haunted by his own rotting, inky-eyed charm and stymied at every turn, despite his good intentions. He’s at his best in the scene where Michael, working as his law firm’s fixer, advises an affluent, arrogant client who has just committed a hit-and-run. The client, thinking it’s still unfettered summer, throws a childish tantrum. Michael, in his best autumnal mode, sets him straight: “There’s no play here. There’s no angle. There’s no champagne room. And I’m not a miracle worker; I’m a janitor.”
— Sebastian Smee, staff writer
Little Women (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Fall is a happy-sad season: The sunlight is golden (but that’s a sign that the days are getting shorter), the leaves are ochre and maroon (a sign that they’re dying), and the air is crisp (a sign of impending winter). And to me, Greta Gerwig’s 2019 adaptation of Little Women perfectly embodies this feeling. The story follows the four March sisters through the different seasons of their life. Their childhood flashbacks are scenes captured in warm, autumnal tones, and adulthood flash-forwards are shot in cooler, harsher light, to reflect the girls’ feelings about the passage of time.
Jo March wants to grow up, and yet she clings to girlhood, panicking as those around her—such as her sister Meg, who gets married—seem content to let the past go. In one pivotal scene, Jo tells her mother that she wishes she could still want what she wanted as a child, when simply being with her family was enough. Now her aspirations for a career and romantic love seem at odds, and her sense of independence has become inextricable from an acute sense of loneliness. For those of us who also cling to the past (even if that past is just “summer”), this film will comfort you and remind you that change is inevitable.
— Nancy Walecki, staff writer
You’ve Got Mail (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
The first 30 minutes of You’ve Got Mail are an unabashed ode to autumn. “Don’t you love New York in the fall?” the film’s romantic hero, Joe (Tom Hanks), writes in an email to the heroine, Kathleen (Meg Ryan). When Kathleen arrives at work a few minutes later with a perfect orange pumpkin under her arm, she breathlessly repeats the question: “Don’t you just love New York in the fall?” And how could you not? The film shows children bobbing for apples at a street fair, a tree with copper leaves set against a row of brownstones, and characters walking around the Upper West Side in good knits, blazers, and fleeces.
Even when the movie shifts to winter and then spring, You’ve Got Mail still feels autumnal. That feeling goes beyond the scenery: It’s a wistful movie, and at times a sad one. Characters major and minor express regret over lost loves, broken family relationships, and unrealized dreams. Kathleen and Joe spend most of the film in relationships with people they clearly do not love. These notes of melancholy make it a perfect romantic comedy to turn to as the days get shorter.
— Eleanor Barkhorn, senior editor
Point Break (streaming on Peacock)
I grew up in Los Angeles, and as a result, I do not really understand seasons, weather, or people’s fear of being seen perspiring. Since I moved to the East Coast eight years ago, I have found autumn to be a cute but unwelcome reminder that winter is real and, even worse, that I will soon be forced to experience it.
The 1991 action thriller Point Break is also about Angeleno men who do not condone the end of summer. In the movie, they take this aversion one step further, robbing banks to fund the travel necessary to never stop surfing under the hot sun. The dialogue is clunky, albeit quotable, and almost nothing about the plot is believable. And yet, it’s so fun to watch these guys, and the FBI agent who tails them, try to make one summer weekend last forever. That is how I will be spending the fall: in denial, doing as much hiking, paddleboarding, and swimming as possible, until I am forced to stop.
— Marc Novicoff, staff writer
Silent Friend (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Silent Friend is a meandering film that has nudged me toward accepting slowness and inevitable change. The historical drama follows three environmentalists at a German university across three epochs as each tries to uncover the secret life of plants: In 1908, Grete navigates sexism and her own position as one of the first female students in the university’s botany department; in 1972, a young man named Hannes, immersed in his college campus’s Cold War–era counterculture, develops sensors to understand how a potted geranium perceives him; and in 2020, a neuroscientist runs an experiment connecting a tree’s electrical activity with his own after the COVID lockdown cuts off his access to human subjects.
At the center of it all is a nearly 200-year-old ginkgo tree that provides quiet solace to the three characters. The tree becomes a central figure in the story, observing, listening, and breathing alongside its subjects. Its presence embodies the spirit of the film, which is more sensory-driven than narrative-driven and makes it easy to lose yourself in the foliage. Now every time I see a leaf change color, I’m reminded to pay closer attention to the natural world around me and all of the life that brims within it.
— Kim Jao, assistant editor

The Measles-Stricken Mother Who Lost Her Newborn Son
By Tom Bartlett
When the Amish man emerged from his barn to greet me, he had no idea that his newborn son’s death had become national news. The man wore a straw hat, black trousers, and suspenders over a long-sleeved blue shirt; one of his similarly dressed sons was guiding a horse-drawn plow in a nearby field.
The man told me that, like most Amish people, he and his family don’t watch TV or use the internet. They don’t read the newspaper either. So they didn’t know until I told them that last Tuesday, Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, held a press conference to announce the first two “measles-associated” deaths in the state in 35 years.

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields.
To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.
Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".
"David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said. "They shouldn't be written off."
"I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.
"Nothing good was supposed to come out of me."

Indian Embassy in China asks families for DNA samples to identify victims
The Embassy will forward the data to the concerned Chinese authorities for comparison.
The Indian Embassy in China on Monday urged families of Indians missing since the August 26 flash flood in the Tibet-Nepal border region to provide DNA samples to help identify them.
The Indian mission made the request after Chinese authorities confirmed that they were now able to receive DNA samples from families of Indian nationals listed as missing in the disaster, an Embassy press release said.
Families willing to provide DNA information have been asked to submit the relevant data in the internationally recognised CODIS format, it said.
The Embassy will forward the data to the concerned Chinese authorities for comparison.
"The Embassy will be notified, and will in turn inform the family, should a match be confirmed", it said.
"Blood samples can be collected from the parents of the missing foreign national or the spouse and children (samples from multiple children should be collected wherever possible)," the Indian mission said.
"If the missing person has no living parents or children, kindly collect blood samples from siblings (collecting samples from all siblings is preferred)," it said.
The Indian mission said that if necessary, samples can be collected from other maternal relatives (e.g., cousins on the maternal side) and paternal relatives (e.g., cousins on the paternal side) with specified details of the relationship.
"DNA STR data for the aforementioned samples is required; for males, Y-STR data must also be included. Data should be stored in the internationally recognised CODIS format", it said.
The embassy said that the samples should be well labelled with the nationality, name and passport number of the missing person, name and passport number of the family member and sample ID number.
"Families may contact the Embassy of India at the following for further guidance: Telephone: 86 18514284905 Email: cons1.beijing@mea.gov.in", it said.
The disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, sending a massive surge of water and debris downstream through the Bhotekoshi River and devastating settlements in northern and central Nepal.
On Sunday, Chinese officials updated the death toll to 43, with 519 others remaining missing.
The missing include 261 foreigners, of whom 49 are from India.
Most of the dead and missing foreigners were on both sides of the ill-fated immigration building when it was devoured by the flood.

India stands at a defining moment in its journey towards the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Under the Healthcare for All pillar, the government has rightly prioritised strengthening Ayushman Bharat, expanding primary healthcare, reducing out-of-pocket expenditure, and promoting preventive care. Yet there is one element that cuts across all these ambitions and determines their success: mental health.
Mental health is not a niche concern. It influences educational attainment, workforce participation, social cohesion, and physical health outcomes. A healthier and more productive India cannot be built without placing mental well-being at the centre of public health.
Major implications
The scale of the challenge is substantial. Mental illness affects one in seven Indians, with nearly 200 million people living with a diagnosable mental health condition. The contribution of mental disorders to India’s total disease burden has doubled over the past three decades. Yet the national treatment gap remains 84.5%, meaning that more than four out of five people who need care do not receive it. The reasons are well known. India has only 0.3 psychiatrists per 1,00,000 population, alongside significant shortages in clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers, and psychiatric nurses. These shortages are the result of decades during which mental health received insufficient attention, both in India and globally.
Mental disorders significantly increase the risk of chronic diseases, while chronic diseases in turn increase the risk of mental illness. More than 60% of people attending primary care facilities have a diagnosable mental disorder. Rates of anxiety and depression are substantially higher among people living with diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS. Ignoring mental health, therefore, undermines efforts to control non-communicable diseases and reduce healthcare expenditure.
The economic implications are equally compelling. A 2025 modelling study by researchers from PGIMER and NIMHANS estimated that integrating universal depression screening into India’s primary healthcare system could generate net savings of ₹291 billion to ₹482 billion annually, equivalent to as much as 0.32% of GDP. Mental health is not a social welfare issue alone — it is also a human capital investment and an economic growth strategy.
The encouraging news is that India has already built many of the foundations required for transformation. More than 1.73 lakh sub-centres and primary health centres have been converted into Ayushman Bharat Arogya Mandirs, with mental healthcare included among the essential service packages. The District Mental Health Programme now covers more than 90% of districts. Tele-MANAS, launched in 2022, has expanded across all States and Union Territories.
Three main priorities
The task now is not to start from scratch. It is to build on this foundation at scale.
First, one must empower frontline health workers to become the backbone of community mental healthcare. India’s one million ASHA workers represent the world’s largest community health workforce. Evidence from Madhya Pradesh and other States demonstrates that, with appropriate training and supervision, ASHAs can successfully identify, support, and refer individuals with common mental disorders. Expanding this model through validated screening tools, digital learning platforms, and performance-linked incentives could expand access to care.
Second, India must invest more systematically in community-based care. Models such as Zimbabwe’s Friendship Bench, Atmiyata in India, and programmes implemented by The Live Love Laugh Foundation demonstrate that trained community workers can bridge the gap between awareness and treatment, particularly in rural and underserved populations. These approaches improve access and reduce costs, and deserve wider adoption and funding. Third, the country must fully realise the promise of financial protection. Extending outpatient mental health benefits under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana and strengthening the implementation of insurance parity as per the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, would make mental healthcare affordable for millions who currently go without care.
If India is to become a truly developed nation by 2047, mental health must move from the margins of public policy to its centre.
Indu Bhushan is the founding CEO of India’s National Health Authority and Ayushman Bharat; Anisha Padukone is the CEO of The Live Love Laugh Foundation

Is your average airport security experience a quick walk through the screening area, or does the line often snake around multiple stanchions? The answer depends on where you're flying out of.
At the top 50 busiest airports in the US, the average security line wait time is 9.9 minutes, but TSA data shows that passengers can wait almost three times as long at some airports and as little as a few minutes at others.
The Trump administration is pushing to privatize airport security by expanding the TSA's Screening Partnership Program (SPP), which allows airports to use private contractors for screening instead of federal TSA officers.
The push comes as the agency has faced retention and workplace challenges, exacerbated by government shutdowns in 2025 and 2026 that forced TSA officers to work without pay for weeks.
Travel website Travel Bulletin examined the 50 busiest airports in the US to determine the ones with the longest and shortest average wait times. Travel Bulletin analyzed eight weeks of wait-time estimates from the MyTSA app and passenger-volume data from the FOIA Electronic Reading Room, covering mid-June to mid-August 2026.
Passengers traveling through San Francisco and Kansas City — the only two major SPP airports among the 20 total using private screeners — spend among the least amount of time in line.

Flight recorders recovered from 'devastating' Amazon cargo plane crash
- Published
Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from the Amazon cargo plane that crashed at Miami International Airport, but the priority remains the recovery of victims, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has said.
Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway shortly before 14:00 local time (19:00 BST) on Sunday.
The plane hit two vehicles, including a white van carrying seven people within the airport perimeter, and a Toyota with three passengers.
NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it was too early to draw conclusions about what caused the crash, with investigators still in the "fact finding stage".
Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.
The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.
It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla, coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.
Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating", with debris from the aircraft, vehicles and airport fencing scattered across the area.
"It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well," she said.
She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait."
The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation.
Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene.
Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing.
The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation.
Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots.
The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation.
Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said.
"Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again."
Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash. Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews.
The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US.
Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities.
21 Air, the company operating the aircraft, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation.

How To Legally Download YouTube Videos
How can you compile videos for your Cutest Cat Compilation of 2026 roundup?
YouTube has introduced many user-friendly features over the years — whether it's the "Jump Ahead" button that quickly skips sponsored segments, or the mobile update to timestamped comments, which flashes them to the top of the pile when the relevant point in the video plays. However, like many of its fellow video-sharing platforms, YouTube does not allow users to fully download videos, leaving only one legal option to do so. And while the rollout of YouTube Premium (formerly YouTube Red) arrived with the promise of a download feature, that option comes with a big catch.
Downloadable videos have long been a feature of YouTube Premium, though they were previously locked to the mobile version. Luckily, following YouTube testing video downloads on computers in 2020, the feature is now available across different YouTube platforms. On the less fortunate side of things, those looking to use this feature to download videos for creative use, such as to edit into a different video (as is standard practice for commentary and reaction channels), will be disappointed, as videos downloaded in this way can only be used in-application.
How to download videos with YouTube Premium
Using YouTube Premium's download feature is quick and simple, and you can download any video with YouTube Premium or download almost any video with YouTube Premium Lite (though Lite won't allow you to download Shorts or music content). The process is the same across both mobile and desktop: Simply click the three dots to the right of the Like, Dislike, and Share buttons. From there, just select the Download option, and your video will begin to download.
Downloading a video via YouTube Premium sends it to the Downloads section of your YouTube account, available in the left menu on desktop and at the bottom of the Library section on mobile (below "Recents" and any playlists you've made). It's worth noting that your downloaded videos are purely in-app; you do not receive a video file downloaded to your device. Moreover, downloads aren't the same across devices, regardless of whether you're using the same account — so, for instance, videos you have downloaded on mobile won't be automatically downloaded on desktop. YouTube tested a way to sync downloads across devices back in 2018, but it never came to fruition.
YouTube Premium is flawed, but there's not much of an alternative
YouTube's download function does grant the benefit of offline viewing, but is otherwise not ideal when it comes to video downloads. Not only do you lose these downloads when you lose your subscription, but they're also only available offline for 29 days. After that, you'll need to reconnect your device to the internet to restart that timer and make them available offline again. While most users will likely remain constantly connected, that highlights the biggest drawback: You can't bring those videos outside the application. You don't receive a video file that you can edit or transmit to other devices, just the option to view a video offline.
What's more, there are very few alternative solutions to downloading YouTube videos. There are YouTube video downloaders online, where you can insert a link to a video and receive a downloadable file in return, but many of these are riddled with adware and spyware. You'll also be circumventing Google's platform rules — which are very much against the practice. There have historically been sites with no spyware kept afloat by donations, but Google has taken most of those down — and it's not recommended to dive into the sketchy sites that remain. YouTube's Terms of Service (under Permissions and Restrictions) prohibit downloads of this sort, or the use of screen recording on videos, without permission from the rights holder, YouTube, and/or any applicable law.

Female employees at the Eiffel Tower were asked to step out of sight during a visit by a Hindu religious delegation at the weekend, according to union representatives, prompting a staff protest and an investigation by Paris city authorities.
The monument was closed late on Monday (September 7, 2026) as employees held a meeting over the incident, which has angered staff and drawn criticism from French politicians.
On Saturday, a delegation of about 100 people linked to the Hindu group Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha, or BAPS, made a private visit to the Eiffel Tower.
“As the delegation passed through, women were asked to leave their workstations so that men could take their places,” Diane Davoine, a union representative, told Reuters.
“Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again,” she said.
Signs at the base of the tower on Monday read: “The opening of the Eiffel Tower is delayed for operational reasons.”
Ms. Davoine said management apologised to staff over the incident.
Paris Mayor reacts to the incident
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said that an investigation would be launched “as soon as possible”. In a post on social media platform X, he said he was aware of the employees’ anger and agreed their dissatisfaction was legitimate.
“It is urgent that all light be shed on the facts that led to this protest,” Mr. Gregoire wrote.
BAPS, whose representatives were in France for festivities related to the inauguration of a Hindu temple in the Paris suburbs, said in a statement that the visit to the Eiffel Tower was arranged at the start of opening hours to avoid disrupting others, due to the size of its delegation.
“To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for any pain or inconvenience caused,” the statement said.
A spokesperson for SETE, the company operating the monument, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Yael Braun-Pivet, the president of the National Assembly, wrote in a post on X: “Welcoming others never means giving up our values. In France, women are fully present in public life. No one tells them to become invisible.”

No new striker, no worries - Havertz and Odegaard torment Chelsea
- Published
Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.
Former Manchester City goalscorer Julian Alvarez was on their radar but remains at Atletico Madrid, while the Gunners were also interested in Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Vinicius Jr.
While Rogers opted for London rivals Chelsea, Barcola moved to Liverpool and Vinicius Jr has stayed at Real Madrid.
Yet reigning champions Arsenal have started this season as strongly as they finished 2025-26, when they celebrated their first Premier League title for 22 years.
After wins over Coventry City and Aston Villa, they came from behind to beat big-spending Chelsea 2-1 in a thrilling derby on Sunday - thanks to goals from two familiar faces.
Kai Havertz, an Arsenal player since 2023, and Martin Odegaard, who joined in 2021, scored as they passed their first big test of the campaign against opponents who have spent close to £350m since the end of last season.
A maximum nine points from three games, one goal conceded and big players stepping up.
"I can't see anyone stopping Arsenal," former Premier League winner Chris Sutton told BBC Sport.
'Our mentality is to keep fighting'
It is surely too early in the season to get carried away, and there are likely to be bigger tests ahead for Mikel Arteta's side.
But Arsenal have set down an early marker as they chase back-to-back Premier League crowns.
Along with Manchester City, they are one of only two clubs with a maximum nine points from three games.
After sweeping aside Coventry on the opening day of the season, they produced a mature performance to come away with all three points at Villa.
Against Chelsea, they had to find a different way to win after £117m signing Rogers fired Chelsea into a second-minute lead.
"Our mentality is to keep fighting. We have shown that many times," said captain Odegaard, who scored the 50th-minute winner after Havertz had equalised before half-time.
"We never want to concede early, but the reaction is top. We got our reward in the end and the response was brilliant.
"We showed our quality with and without the ball and the result reflects that."
Odegaard has scored three goals in four appearances in all competitions this season, after netting only once in 36 last term.
"It was a big game, massive game, tough opponent, and we got there in the end, so brilliant," he said.
Former Manchester United and England player Ashley Young said Odegaard's form will be key for Arsenal this season.
"He's just a joy to watch," Young told BBC Sport.
"He's exciting when he gets on the ball, he's allowing other players to get on the ball.
"The connection down the right side between him, Bukayo Saka and Havertz - it's just good to see when you've got players that know each other and build relationships in that way.
"Riccardo Calafiori has been brilliant from last season. He seems to me like he's the one that's got a free role in the team.
"It was his run, and he played it precisely, for the winning goal. He goes quickly, takes people out of the way. It's just clever. Arsenal deserved all three points."
Havertz said Odegaard was back to his "very best".
"He's an unbelievable player - we have seen that over the last years," said the Germany forward.
"He's going to help us a lot this season."
'Arsenal are a powerhouse'
Sutton said Arsenal are still ahead of the rest, despite their rivals spending hundreds of millions of pounds during the transfer window.
"They're such a powerhouse," said the former Blackburn and England striker.
"Chelsea are a good team, but Arsenal always find a way to win. Can you stop Arsenal? I don't think they [other Premier League teams] can."
Arsenal have won their opening three games of a top-flight campaign while conceding fewer than two goals (1) for the third time - after 1924-25, when they finished 20th, and 2003-04, when they went the season unbeaten.
They have also won eight league games in a row stretching back to last season.
Having seen off big-spending Chelsea, their next league match is at Sunderland on Saturday.
Before that Arsenal launch their Champions League campaign at Napoli on Wednesday.
Havertz said Arsenal will head to Italy with confidence high with after seeing off his former club Chelsea.
"Chelsea have an amazing squad, but so do we," said Havertz, who scored the winning goal for the Blues against Manchester City in the 2021 Champions League final.
"We knew it was going to be tough. They scored early, so it's not easy for us, but we believed in ourselves and changed the game around."
