Atomberg Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg began as a B2B supplier of energy-efficient BLDC fans before entering the D2C segment in 2016. It has since expanded to manufacture mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances. The startup designs and manufactures its products in India and sells them via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. Backed by names such as Steadview Capital, Jungle Ventures and A91 Partners, Atomberg has raised over $126 Mn in funding to date. Taking the first step towards its public listing, the D2C appliance brand, in July 2026, converted into a public entity and changed the name of its parent entity from Atomberg Technologies Pvt Ltd to Atomberg Technologies Ltd. In August 2026, the startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an OFS of up to 7.65 Cr shares. The startup is also considering raising up to ₹90 Cr through a pre-IPO placement. On the financial front, Atomberg’s losses widened 26.5% to ₹149 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹117.8 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 34.8% to ₹1,293.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25. AVPL International (AITMC Ventures) Founded in 2016 by Preet Sandhuu and Deep Sisai, AITMC sits at the intersection of agriculture and drones. It manufactures drones, offers drone-as-a-service, and runs more than 70 drone training centres across 16 states. In July 2025, AITMC once again kicked off its IPO plans as the company’s board approved a proposal to increase the fresh issue size of its IPO to ₹200 Cr from ₹125 Cr previously. AITMC then filed its draft papers with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in October 2025. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. Notably, this marks its second attempt at going public. Previously in December 2023, the company was eyeing an NSE Emerge listing, which comprised solely of a fresh issue of up to 2.1 Cr shares. That earlier plan was shelved after AITMC signed a term sheet in January 2025 for a strategic merger with BSE SME-listed DroneAcharya, a deal that ultimately fell through. On the financial front, AITMC Ventures’ net profit climbed 59% to ₹14 Cr in FY25 from ₹8.8 Cr a fiscal earlier, while operating revenue zoomed 87% to ₹87.5 Cr as against ₹46.8 Cr in FY24. boAt Founded in 2016 by Aman Gupta and Sameer Mehta, boAt is a D2C consumer electronics brand that sells headphones, smartwatches, speakers, and other audio wearables. The company has raised over $171 Mn across multiple rounds from investors such as Warburg Pincus, Qualcomm Ventures, Malabar Investments, Innoven Capital, and Fireside Ventures. boAt has pursued an IPO for several years now. It first filed its DRHP with SEBI in 2022 for a ₹2,000 Cr public issue, but later shelved the plan amid challenging market conditions. Taking a second shot, the boAt’s parent, Imagine Marketing, pre-filed its DRHP confidentially with the SEBI in April 2025, and secured SEBI approval in August. In October 2025, boAt filed its updated DRHP for an ₹1,500 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to ₹500 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹1,000 Cr. On the financial front, boAt saw its revenue from operations grow 10.7% YoY to ₹628.1 Cr in Q1 FY26, while profit stood at ₹21.3 Cr compared to a ₹31 Cr loss in Q1 FY25. C5i Founded in 2000 by Ashwin Mittal, C5i (formerly known as Course5 Intelligence) is an enterprise AI company that helps large businesses automate tasks and turn data into actionable insights. Backed by names such as Nuvama Asset Management and 360 ONE, the startup has raised more than $55 Mn in funding to date. The platform first attempted to go public in 2022, targeting a ₹600 Cr IPO, but later shelved the plans due to weak market conditions. Reigniting its IPO ambitions, the startup once again filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in July 2026. C5i is now looking to raise about ₹1,000-1,200 Cr via the public issue. On the financial front, C5i’s consolidated net profit declined 15% to ₹48.3 Cr in FY25 as against ₹56.7 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile its operating revenue surged 26% to ₹545.3 Cr from ₹431.4 Cr in FY24. Curefoods Founded in 2020 by Ankit Nagori, Curefoods is a cloud kitchen unicorn that manages brands like EatFit, CakeZone, Nomad Pizza, Sharief Bhai Biryani, and Frozen Bottle. It claims to operate over 200 cloud kitchens and offline outlets across 70 Indian cities. The startup has raised over $175 Mn from backers including Iron Pillar, Accel, Three State Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, and ASK Finance. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Curefoods filed its DRHP with SEBI in late June 2025 and received markets regulator’s approval in late October. As per the DRHP, the proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to ₹800 Cr and an offer-for-sale of up to 4.85 Cr equity shares. However, in June 2026, the startup took a U-turn and put its IPO plans on hold amid the turmoil in the Indian equities market and concerns over its potential valuation. As per reports, mutual funds were not aligned with the ₹4,000 Cr (about $419 Mn) valuation sought by Curefoods during its roadshows. On the financial front, Curefoods' net loss remained steady at ₹169.9 Cr in FY25 as against ₹172.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 27.4% to ₹745.8 Cr compared to ₹585.1 Cr in FY24. Fibe Founded in 2015 by Akshay Mehrotra and Ashish Goyal as EarlySalary, Fibe initially offered salary advances and small-ticket personal loans to young working professionals. Since then, it has evolved into a diversified consumer finance platform. Today, it offers personal loans and purpose-driven financing solutions across sectors such as education, insurance, healthcare, rooftop solar and travel. It claims to operate a merchant network spanning 10,387 touchpoints across India, and claims to have ₹8,603 Cr in assets under management as of March 2026. It has raised more than $266 Mn from a host of marquee names such as TPG, Norwest Venture Partners, Eight Roads Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, TR Capital, and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). In June 2026, the lending tech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of over 4 Cr shares. On the financial front, Fibe saw its net profit more than double to ₹257.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹113.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue surged 31% to ₹1,584.6 Cr from ₹1,208.9 Cr in FY25. Garuda Aerospace Founded in 2015 by Agnishwar Jayaprakash and Rithika Mohann, Garuda Aerospace manufactures over 30 types of drones, while also offering drone-as-a-service (DaaS) solutions. It claims to have trained over 1 Lakh drone pilots, serving more than 100 government agencies along with over 500 enterprises. The startup currently operates a fleet of over 400 drones and has a manufacturing capacity of up to 15,000 units annually. Backed by cricketer MS Dhoni, Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle and Ocgrow Ventures, Garuda Aerospace has raised more than $37.1 Mn in funding to date. It was last pegged at a post-money valuation of $250 Mn during its last fundraise last year. The company first signalled its intent to go public in 2023. At the time, Jayaprakash told Inc42 that the company would list on the bourses within two years. Eventually in April 2026, the Chennai-based dronetech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. While the exact size of the IPO is yet to be determined, the company’s board, in March, approved a proposal to raise up to ₹750 Cr via fresh issue of shares and an undisclosed OFS component. The startup bagged SEBI’s approval for its IPO in August 2026. On the financial front, Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹11 Cr in H1 FY26 against an operating revenue of ₹41.2 Cr. InCred Holdings Founded in 2016 by Bhupinder Singh, InCred Group runs three distinct business verticals. InCred Finance handles lending, InCred Capital is focussed on wealth and asset management, while InCred Money specialises in retail bonds and alternative investments. The company boasts backing from heavyweights like Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), OAKS, Investcorp, Moore Capital, and Elevar Equity, among others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in September 2025, InCred Holdings, the parent of InCred Financial Services, sought shareholder approval to raise up to ₹ 1,500 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. By November 2025, InCred Holdings filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. The startup received the markets regulator's nod for its IPO in February 2026. In May 2026, the company filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a public issue, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,250 Cr and an OFS of up to 9.9 Cr equity shares. InCred Holdings reported a 5.3% jump in net profit to ₹290 Cr in 9M FY26 from ₹275.5 Cr during the same period last fiscal. Operating revenue also surged 38.6% to ₹1,848.9 Cr from ₹1,333.9 Cr in 9M FY25. Infra.Market Founded in 2016 by Souvik Sengupta and Aaditya Sharda, Infra.Market runs a B2B marketplace that helps customers procure construction materials like concrete, steel, pipes, fittings, and chemicals. The startup has raised over $415 Mn till date from investors such as Tiger Global, Accel, and Nexus Ventures. In October 2025, Infra.Market confidentially pre-filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI for a nearly ₹5,000 Cr ($563.3 Mn) listing. It received SEBI’s go-ahead in January 2026. However, the platform now appears to have ditched plans for a standalone IPO and is exploring a reverse-listing route via its listed subsidiary Shalimar Paints. In August 2026, the paint manufacturing giant proposed that it would acquire shares and CCPS of Infra.Market through a swap, involving securities worth around ₹10,545 Cr. The two companies are also exploring a potential “unification” at a later stage, subject to applicable laws and requisite approvals. Infra.Market’s net profit dwindled 42% to ₹219.7 Cr in FY25 from ₹378 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, revenue from operations rose 27% to ₹18,472 Cr versus ₹14,530.2 Cr in FY24. Kuku Founded in 2018 by Lal Chand Bisu,Vikas Goyal and Vinod Kumar Meena, Kuku is an audio-centric OTT platform that hosts audiobooks, podcasts, and original shows under Kuku FM in multiple Indian languages. It also operates a vernacular short-video app under Kuku TV brand and a microlearning platform Guru. The startup claims to have raised more than $156 Mn in funding to date and is backed by marquee names such as Vertex Ventures, Krafton, IFC and Paramark Ventures. In December 2025, reports first emerged that the OTT soonicorn was looking to list on the bourses. The company is said to have appointed Kotak Mahindra Capital, Axis Bank and Morgan Stanley as bankers to helm its potential IPO. In June 2026, Inc42 reported that Kuku filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr to ₹3,500 Cr (about $261 Mn to $366 Mn) through its IPO. The startup is targeting a valuation of up to ₹15,000 Cr (about $1.8 Bn) for the public listing. The IPO will comprise both a fresh issue of shares and an offer-for-sale component. Kuku FM’s net losses soared 59% to ₹153 Cr in FY25 from ₹96 Cr the prior fiscal, while operating revenue soared 175% to ₹242 Cr from ₹88 Cr in FY24. MakeMyTrip Launched in 2000 by Keyur Joshi, Rajesh Magow, and Deep Kalra, MakeMyTrip is an online travel aggregator (OTA) that operates an end-to-end platform for booking flights, hotels and holiday packages. It also offers ancillary services such as forex cards and travel insurance. Over the years, it acquired rivals such as Goibibo and redBus to complement its primary business of air ticketing and hotels. More recently, it also acquired a minority stake in Visa processing platform Atlys and holiday packages business Flamingo Transworld. Since its inception, the company claims to have processed over 8.7 Cr transactions for retail consumers and onboarded 77,000 SME and large corporate customers. It was also one of the first Indian startups to list on Nasdaq in 2010. After Nasdaq, the travel tech major is now eyeing an Indian IPO. In April 2026, reports surfaced that the company appointed Axis Capital, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan as advisers for the IPO. Subsequently in July 2026, the travel tech major filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route for a $1 Bn OFS-only listing. On the financial front, MakeMyTrip reported a nearly 46% YoY decline in its net profit to $51.7 Mn in FY26, while operating revenue rose a mere 6.7% YoY to $1.04 Bn during the fiscal under review. NoPaperForms A brainchild of Naveen Goyal and Suraj Sapra, Meritto parent NoPaperForms helps educational institutions and edtech businesses automate student enrollment and fee collection processes. Founded in 2017, the startup catered to 1,183 educational institutions, including Manipal University, Shiv Nadar University and PhysicsWallah, in FY26. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Meritto turned into a public entity in May 2025 after its board and shareholders passed a resolution to approve the conversion. Subsequently, in November 2025, the company filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential route for an IPO, and received approval from the markets regulator to go ahead with its IPO in March 2026. In September 2026, NoPaperForms filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹375 Cr and an OFS component of up to 3.8 Cr equity shares. On the financial front, NoPaperForms reported an operating revenue of ₹115.6 Cr in FY26, up 25.2% from ₹92.3 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, the startup’s profits surged 534% to ₹11.9 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹1.9 Cr in FY25. Moneyview Founded in 2016 by Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview started off as a personal finance platform before pivoting to digital lending. Today, it offers services such as UPI payments, gold SIPs, fixed deposits, digital gold, home loans, BNPL and insurance. The company claims to manage over ₹19,800 Cr in AUM and has raised more than $250 Mn in funding. It competes with players like listed fintech MobiKwik, IPO-aspirant Navi, and MoneyTap. Moneyview entered the unicorn club in 2024 after a ₹38.6 Cr infusion from Accel India and Nexus Ventures. In March 2026, the fintech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹1,500 Cr and an OFS of up to 13.61 Cr equity shares. It received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in late-June 2026. Moneyview clocked a revenue of ₹2,409 Cr in the nine month period ended December 2025 against a net profit of ₹245 Cr. OYO (PRISM) Founded in 2012 by Ritesh Agarwal, OYO, rebranded as PRISM in 2025, is a travel tech major that operates budget hotels, vacation homes, casino hotels, coworking spaces, and corporate stays. After postponing its IPO plans multiple times, the hospitality giant’s parent entity PRISM secured shareholder nod in December 2025 to raise up to ₹6,650 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. Days later, the company confidentially pre-filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI. It eventually received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in June 2026. Right after, the hospitality major filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a ₹6,650 Cr IPO, which will comprise entirely of a fresh issue of shares. The company is targeting a valuation of $7 Bn to $8 Bn and has appointed ICICI Securities, Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs, and Citibank to helm the issue. OYO's IPO journey has been a turbulent one so far. It first filed its DRHP in September 2021 for a $1.2 Bn public issue, but later shelved the plans amid market volatility. It once again filed its DRHP via the confidential route for a $600 Mn IPO in 2023, but later withdrew the papers again in May 2024. On the financial front, PRISM reported a profit of ₹748 Cr in 9M FY26, almost 3X of the ₹245 Cr profit it reported in the full year FY25. Its operating revenue stood at ₹6,941 Cr in 9M FY26, up from ₹6,253 Cr in FY25. PhonePe Founded in 2015 by Sameer Nigam, Rahul Chari, and Burzin Engineer, PhonePe is India's leading digital payments platform. It regularly accounts for nearly half of all Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions processed in the country. Originally focussed on digital payments, the fintech giant has since evolved into a comprehensive financial services provider, offering insurance products, broking services, and more. PhonePe was acquired by Flipkart in 2016. Six years later, US retail giant and parent Walmart spun it off as a separate entity from Flipkart. The fintech major redomiciled back to India in late 2022, setting the stage for its eventual listing on the Indian exchanges. In January this year, the fintech major filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for its IPO, which will comprise solely of an OFS component. Walmart, Tiger Global, Microsoft and General Atlantic will offload their stakes as part of the offer for sale. However, raking a U-Turn, the fintech major, in March 2026, temporarily paused its IPO plans amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia and volatility in the global equity markets. While the company plans to restart the IPO process once global capital markets regain stability, sources told Inc42 that PhonePe has pushed the IPO till at least June 2026. Financially, PhonePe’s net loss widened by 62% to ₹2,792 Cr in FY26 as against ₹1,727.4 Cr reported in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25. PlaySimple Games Founded in 2014 by Siddharth Jain, Siddhanth Jain, Preeti Reddy, and Suraj Nalin, PlaySimple Games is a casual mobile gaming studio. It operates a portfolio of 30 live mobile games across five categories – search, crossword, anagram, other word games, and non-word puzzles. It claims to have a presence in more than 110 countries. The startup was acquired by Swedish gaming company MTG for more than $360 Mn in 2021. Prior to the acquisition, PlaySimple raised $4.5 Mn in funding from the likes of Elevation Capital and Chiratae Ventures. None of the original cofounders remain with the company today, and it is currently led by MTG's Yoav Ecker as MD and CEO. In April 2026, PlaySimple filed its DRHP with SEBI for a public issue which will comprise solely an OFS component of ₹3,150 Cr. MTGx Gaming Holding AB will be the lone seller during the listing. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in August 2026. If listed, PlaySimple will become the second gaming company to go public in India, after Nazara Technologies. On the financial front, PlaySimple reported an operating revenue of ₹2,259.8 Cr in CY2025, up 20% YoY. However, net profit declined 31% YoY to ₹359 Cr, largely due to a 54% surge in advertising and sales commission costs. Purple Style Labs Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury house of brands featuring fashion labels like Pernia's Pop Up Studio & Shop, Wendell Rodricks, and Hemant Trevedi. It operates over 12 Pernia's Pop-Up Studio experience centres across India. Backed by Alchemy Capital Management, Bajaj Holdings and Investment, and Minerva Ventures, the startup has raised more than $78 Mn to date. In September 2025, the D2C brand filed its DRHP with SEBI for its public issue and received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. It then filed its RHP with SEBI in August 2026 for a public issue, which consists entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. It has also set a price band of ₹546 to ₹575 per equity share for its IPO, valuing the company at ₹4,604 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. Subsequently, Purple Style Labs wrapped up its public issue with an oversubscription of 1.29X, receiving bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. It will now tentatively list on the bourses on September 7. On the financial front, the startup’s consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 as against ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25. Razorpay Founded in 2014 by IIT-Roorkee alumni Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar, Razorpay has evolved from a simple payment gateway to an omnichannel fintech giant for payments, banking, SME payroll, lending, insurance, and more. It claims to process an annualised total payment volume (TPV) exceeding $180 Bn and caters to a majority of India’s unicorns. Kicking off its IPO plans, the company reverse flipped back to India in May 2025 by merging its US-based entity with its Indian arm Razorpay Software Pvt Ltd. In February 2026, the fintech major roped in Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi as investment bankers to helm its upcoming IPO. In June 2026, the unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. The startup is said to be looking to raise anywhere between $500 Mn to $700 Mn at a valuation of $5 Bn to $6 Bn, lower than its last private valuation of $7.5 Bn. Razorpay has so far raised nearly $740 Mn from heavyweights such as Y Combinator, Tiger Global, Peak XV Partners, Lone Pine Capital, Alkeon Capital, and GIC. The startup’s net profit skyrocketed 365% to ₹33.5 Cr in FY24 from ₹7.2 Cr in the year-ago period, even as operating revenue shot up a mere 9% to ₹2,475 Cr from ₹2,283 Cr in FY23. Razorpay claimed that it slipped into the red in FY25 due to an ESOP expense of ₹1,209 Cr and tax payments linked to its reverse flip to India. Meanwhile, operating revenue is said to have surged 65% YoY to ₹3,783 Cr in FY25. RentoMojo Founded in 2014 by Geetansh Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo is an omnichannel rental platform to lease appliances, furniture, and furnishings. The startup operates an app, website and physical stores. It operates 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. Backed by Accel, Chiratae Ventures and Bain Capital, the startup has raised over $45 Mn in funding to date. Hopping on the IPO bandwagon in September 2025, RentoMojo enlisted IIFL and Motilal Oswal enlisted as bankers for its IPO. A few months later in March 2026, the rental platform filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO and received SEBI’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026. In September 2026, the startup finally filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.7 Cr shares. It has also set a price band of ₹384-₹404 per share for its upcoming public issue, which will value RentoMojo at around ₹4,206 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. The IPO will open for bidding on September 9 and close on September 11. Meanwhile, right before RentoMojo filed its draft papers, its cofounder and former COO Nain filed a petition before the NCLT’s Bengaluru bench to stall the IPO proceedings. Alleging oppression and mismanagement, the plea claimed that incomplete or inaccurate information was shared with him and sought to declare his 2023 sale of 2,223 shares void ab initio. On the financial front, RentoMojo reported a profit after tax of ₹104.3 Cr in FY26, up 142% from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr during the year under review from ₹266 Cr in FY25. Table Space Founded in 2017 by the late Amit Banerji and Karan Chopra, Table Space offers enterprise managed workspace to companies across multiple Indian cities. It counts the likes of EY, Dell, Fujitsu, AMD, Shell, and JCI among its clients. The startup has so far raised $407 Mn from the likes of Hillhouse Capital, Rava Partners, and Alta Capital. The Bengaluru-based startup first attempted to go public in 2025, but the plans were delayed after cofounder Banerji passed away in January 2025. In the aftermath, it appointed cofounders Chopra and Mehra as co-CEOs. Reigniting its listing plans, the managed workspace provider, in August 2026, filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹800 Cr and an OFS of up to 6.55 Cr shares. On the financial front, Table Space managed to narrow its loss by 74% to ₹402.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,555.4 in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 66.3% to ₹2,262.3 Cr from ₹1,360.5 Cr in FY25. Tonbo Imaging Founded in 2012 by Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D'Souza, Tonbo Imaging is a defence tech startup that designs and builds advanced imaging and sensor systems. Its product portfolio includes smart thermal weapon sights, see-through armors, AI-based seekers, and gun shock simulators. The company has raised over $59 Mn to date from investors such as Artiman Ventures, Celesta Capital, and Qualcomm Ventures. It was last valued at $175 Mn during its $20.4 Mn pre-IPO fundraise in April 2025. With presence across Europe, APAC region, the US, Australia, and Israel, the startup counts NATO, US Navy SEALs, Israeli Defense Forces (IDF), the defence ministries of India and Armenia, among others, as its customers. Tonbo Imaging’s IPO plans came to light in May 2025 after CEO Lakshmikumar, in May 2025, said that the startup was looking to file its DRHP with SEBI for up to ₹1,000 Cr IPO. The company filed its draft papers a few months later in December. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026. In August 2026, the company refiled its DRHP with the markets regulator, with the offer size largely unchanged from the previous DRHP. Tonbo’s net profit declined 30% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in the previous year. Operating revenue slumped 22.7% to ₹299.9 Cr from ₹374.3 Cr in FY25. Travelstack Tech Founded in 2014 by Vaibhav Aggarwal and Adarssh Mnpuria, FabHotels runs a chain of 1,379 budget hotels across 50 Indian cities. TravelPlus counts names such as Eternal, Infra.Market, Zepto, Titan Company, and UnifyApps as customers. Both verticals operate under the consolidated entity Travelstack Tech. Kicking off its IPO process, Travelstack filed its DRHP with SEBI in mid-December 2025. The company received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in March 2026. The proposed IPO will comprise a fresh issue of up to ₹250 Cr alongside an OFS of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Fresh proceeds will fund working capital, repay borrowings, and support general corporate purposes. Financially, Travelstack posted a net profit of ₹32.2 Cr in H1 FY26, driven by a ₹37.4 Cr deferred tax gain, on an operating revenue of ₹400.4 Cr. For the full FY25, the company slashed its net loss by 95% to ₹6.3 Cr from ₹114.1 Cr in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue surged 31% to ₹716.4 Cr from ₹547.8 Cr in FY24. Zepto Founded in 2021 by Aadit Palicha and Kaivalya Vohra, Zepto is a quick commerce startup that delivers groceries and other essentials. Backed by Y Combinator, Nexus Venture Partners, Glade Brook Capital, and Motilal Oswal AMC, the quick commerce unicorn has raised nearly $2.5 Bn to date. The quick commerce major has been planning its IPO for some time now, with no clear timeline in sight. It was first planning to list on the bourses in 2025 but paused the plans in June 2025 for a year to trim cash burn and improve profitability. The startup revived its IPO ambitions in November 2025 and confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO. The quick commerce major then received SEBI’s approval to float its proposed IPO in May 2026, and subsequently, it filed its updated DRHP in July 2026. As per its UDRHP, Zepto’s public offering was supposed to comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹8,010 Cr and an OFS component of 11.35 Cr shares. However, taking another U-turn, Zepto once again put its IPO plans on hold in August 2026. Cofounder and CEO Palich internally told employees that the startup was now aiming to list on the bourses between February 2027 and May 2027. In the meantime, the quick commerce major plans to raise $105 Mn via a pre-IPO funding round and fix its cash burn problem. On the financial front, Zepto’s net loss widened 26% to ₹5,905.2 Cr in FY26 as against ₹4,699.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue more than doubled to ₹22,623.6 Cr during the year under review from ₹11,109.9 Cr in FY25. Zetwerk Founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan, Rahul Sharma and Vishal Chaudhary, Zetwerk operates a B2B platform that connects manufacturers with vendors and suppliers of industrial machine components. The unicorn has so far raised over $793 Mn to date from the likes of Greenoaks Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Mars Growth Capital and Peak XV Partners. Kicking off its IPO plans in February 2025, the unicorn began lining up bankers for a $500 Mn IPO at a likely valuation of nearly $5 Bn. Zetwerk later dialed back the plans, saying that it would list on the bourses in 2027. By November 2025, Zetwerk reversed its course again and appointed six bankers to helm its IPO. In Summary
- A decade ago, Indian brands commanded a large chunk of the Indian smartphone market. In Q2 2016, three of the top five smartphone brands were Indian ones.
- The arrival of Chinese brands and changes in the market led to the decline and exit of many Indian phone brands. Today, while brands like Lava and AI+ exist, their market shares are nothing compared to Indian brands of the past.
- Rising smartphone prices and memory costs seem to have opened the door for Indian smartphone brands, with new brands emerging and old ones looking to make a comeback, with encouragement and support from the Government. But is this just a temporary phase, or will Indian brands win back the market dominance they lost almost a decade ago?
When I first started covering technology, the Indian smartphone market looked extremely different from what it does today. Today, there are barely any Indian brands among the major smartphone brands in the Indian market – Counterpoint’s report on Q2 2026 showed not a single Indian brand among the top eight smartphone brands in the Indian market. Yes, some Indian smartphone brands do exist, such as the persistent Lava and the newcomer AI+, but they do not command significant market shares.
The story was extremely different a decade ago.
It may be hard to believe, especially for those who have started following smartphone trends in India since 2017, but in mid-2016, Indian tech brands were not just surviving but ruling the smartphone charts. IDC’s report for Q2 2016 placed three Indian brands in the top five smartphone brands in the country – Micromax, Intex and Reliance Jio (this was around the time of the 4G revolution).
And this was not because of a lack of competition. The Indian market was home to a number of high-profile foreign smartphone players like Apple, Samsung, HTC, BlackBerry, LG, Sony, and Motorola were very much present in the Indian market, and the likes of OnePlus, Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo had also arrived in the market. Still, Indian brands like Micromax, Intex, Spice, and Karbonn dominated sales charts for multiple and sometimes even consecutive quarters. In fact, in Q2 2014, Micromax even overtook Samsung to be the number one smartphone brand in the country in terms of shipments. It was a time when we carried a story on how Micromax deserved to be shown more respect.
Ghosts of the Indian smartphone market past: Why Indian brands ruled, and how the Chinese brands beat them
There was a reason for this dominance. At that point of time, Indian smartphone brands mainly catered to the budget segment, mostly under Rs. 15,000 (or even Rs 10,000), which comprised a large chunk of the smartphone market. While international brands had tried to enter this segment, they had very limited success, as they could not match the price-to-spec ratio that the Indian brands were offering. Big displays, big batteries, and decent processors (often from the more affordable MediaTek) and a small price tag made phones from the likes of Micromax, Intex, and Karbonn the perfect pick for anyone looking to pick up an entry-level smartphone. The likes of Apple, Samsung, HTC, Sony, and BlackBerry were largely operating in the mid/ upper mid and premium segment.
The tech climate changed as Chinese brands began to make their presence felt. Xiaomi, OnePlus, Vivo, and Oppo all stepped into the Indian market in 2014. Oppo and Vivo seemed to be playing in the premium segment, while brands like Xiaomi and OnePlus initially seemed to focus on flagship killers (a term OnePlus popularised). However, given India’s demography, it did not take a long time for these brands to realize that real numbers were actually in the budget and mid segment.
Even as Indian brands struggled with inventory issues as the 4G revolution hit India, the Chinese brands shifted focus and brought in smartphones with prices and spec combinations that matched and, in many cases, even eclipsed what Indian brands were offering. That was not all.
With the mobile Internet becoming more accessible thanks to extremely affordable 4G rates (pioneered mainly by Reliance Jio), these brands also opted for a very unconventional plan of action, going for flash sales, online only sales, often with little to no advertising in mainstream media, and building communities online. These not only cut expenses, but built greater brand loyalty (something Indian brands had been unable to do, as they had focused mainly on price). This combination of pricing and communications affected all the other brands in the market, but hit the Indian brands particularly hard, as it took away their biggest USP – a low price tag. The years that followed saw not just Indian brands fade, but even the likes of LG, Sony and HTC bid farewell to the Indian market.
The Indian Smartphone Market Today: Rocked by a steep price rise
In the last ten years, the Indian smartphone market has changed completely. Many Indian brands that had seemed almost invincible have packed their bags and left, although some like Lava have managed to stick around, in spite of not being the force they once were. But the tech stars in the tech universe move in different ways, and the way in which they have been aligning in recent times makes me think that the time is ripe for Indian smartphone brands to make a comeback in their own market.
Hear me out before you think I am talking through my hat. We have seen a very steady shift happening in the tech world in 2026. Many brands that earlier ruled the budget, mid, and lower-mid segments have been climbing up the price ladder for a while now, seeking larger profit margins. Indeed, the number of phones available in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment has been shrinking in recent times, with many brands seemingly inching towards vacating it altogether.
The likes of Motorola, OnePlus and Xiaomi are also no longer organizations with lean portfolios and small, focused teams but have become tech behemoths with large-scale operations, huge marketing budgets, multiple sub-brands and extensive product portfolios. This has, of course, affected their ability to offer the extremely competitive price-spec combo that made them popular in the first place.
The dramatic increase in the price of memory has now made it even more difficult for existing brands to offer good devices at lower price points. Devices with specs that used to be seen in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment are now being seen at prices in the range of Rs 25,000 or more. Options at lower price points are either vanishing or are coming with relatively modest specs.
And Indian brands are suddenly appearing on the horizon again.
Guess who’s back, back again… Indian smartphone brands
White Lava had never left; it seems to have got a new lease of life. AI+ is increasingly aggressive, and Fire-Boltt, a brand known more for its wearables and hearables, has entered the smartphone market. Even as this is being written, Mivi, a mainly audio brand, has announced plans for a smartphone with a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor for under Rs 15,000, and there is also talk of Micromax returning to the market, and Boat (which, like Fire-Boltt, is known mainly for audio and wearable products) is also planning to sail in smartphone waters. And from what we know, all these brands are targeting the sub-Rs 15,000 market, from which many brands have moved products to higher price points and/ or releasing new devices with much more modest specs in the past.
The Indian Government is also making efforts to build a smartphone brand that it can call its own. On August 21, it officially sent out a notification, as per which the Union Cabinet approved a budget of Rs. 62,500 crore for a Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) to build globally competitive, native smartphone brands. The scheme offers a number of incentives and rewards for Indian brands. To qualify, a company must be registered in India, keep its ownership and trademarks in India, have more than 51 percent Indian shareholding, be controlled in India, and have its products designed locally without outsourcing. This is a massive push and is likely to encourage more Indian entrepreneurs to enter the smartphone market.
Welcome back, Indian brands, but this time, please stay!
But making a comeback will not be enough. The smartphone world has changed a fair bit since the time Indian brands ruled the charts. And the new ones or those making a comeback would need to adopt a fundamentally different approach to ensure that the second innings of Indian brands in the smartphone market is a long one, and does not end as abruptly as the first. Being an ‘Indian brand’ has to have a different connotation than it did in the past.
Indian brands have struggled with offering good after-sales service and good software, and have tended to compete mainly on price and specs. That needs to change. The new and not-so-new native brands have to ensure they not just deliver a smartphone at a competitive price, but follow through on the whole process that comes after. Easy access to repairs and spare parts, timely OS updates, and improved, new-age marketing strategies are all necessities for these brands to actually establish themselves in this competitive market for the long run.
Native brands also need to shed their image of merely assembling and/or importing devices from outside and rebranding them for the Indian market. Authentic and good quality products backed up with a solid sales and service system are both needed to make consumers associate Indian brands not just with low prices, but also with high quality.
As of now, Indian brands are knocking on the door of their nation’s smartphone market once again. Just how well they will do, only time will tell. While I am hoping their second coming will be a successful one and they will win back lost ground (more local brands are always welcome in any market, and the big five out there need competition), there is no way of knowing how things will actually work out. Who knows, if I am still here, covering tech a decade later, I might be telling you a completely different story altogether.
A decade is a VERY long time in tech. Stay tuned.

Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem
- Published
Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity to India and Bangladesh.
But the very glaciers and mountains giving Nepal this massive natural advantage are succumbing to global warming - and last Wednesday's deadly floods have laid bare the risks to the nation's hydropower ambitions.
More than 1,300 people were killed, while thousands more are still missing.
The floods, which destroyed entire villages near the border of Nepal and Tibet, severely damaged 12 hydropower plants in the Trishuli River basin and knocked out more than 10% of Nepal's total power generation capacity. Operators tell the BBC they don't yet know if any of these facilities can be brought back to operation.
The state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority, which owns six of the 12 damaged facilities, has assured Nepalese households that supply remains adequate. But its spokesman Rajan Dhakal acknowledges that with climate-related disasters becoming more frequent, "the time has come for a rethink of our hydropower policy".
Only two-thirds of people in Nepal had access to electricity in 2010, and even connected households would face power cuts for up to 16 hours a day.
An expansion of hydropower infrastructure alongside efforts to tackle corruption and boost energy imports from India to fill seasonal gaps meant that by 2018, most of Nepal was enjoying 24 hours of power supply per day.
At present, there are 225 hydropower plants across Nepal with more than 3,900MW of installed capacity, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority - capable of powering some three million households simultaneously.
Hundreds more such facilities are either being constructed or in the pipeline. Most of them are built high up in the mountains, where they can seize fast-flowing currents to generate power. These projects require little to no storage system.
However, with the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warming 50% faster than the global average, they face greater environmental risks. Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier and its bedrock as the cause of last week's flash flood.
While scientists say it is too soon to draw any firm links to climate change, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority previously said more than nine in 10 disaster events recorded between 2018 and 2024 were "related to climate".
Nepal's former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising, who called the catastrophic deluge a "once-in-a-century" event, says it holds lessons for designing plants and picking sites where they are built.
"We need to design the plants [to be more] resilient to the floods and, most importantly, adopt early-warning systems as well as robust emergency evacuation measures," he told environmental news outlet Mongabay.
Potentially hundreds of hydropower labourers, engineers and residents are thought to be trapped inside the mud-filled tunnels of these plants since the floods hit.
A "rethink" of Nepal's hydropower strategy could involve reservoir-based plants that need not be situated up in the mountains, says Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority. These could allow water to be stored and released as needed, but would also involve significant economic and environmental costs.
'All our eggs in one basket'
Some question if Nepal has been too reliant on hydropower.
"We should not be putting all our eggs in one basket in these dangerous times," says renewable energy expert Kushal Gurung, who founded the clean tech firm WindPower Nepal.
"We need to seriously embrace other alternatives as well, like solar and wind. And for that we will need to revise our energy policy that is at the moment very pro-hydropower," he says.
The claim is echoed by Vivek Shastry, researcher at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who argues that "meaningful additions of wind and solar generation is a resilience strategy that can limit single-point or interconnected electricity system failures in the future".
A report from the German aid agency suggests the technical potential for energy production from solar power in Nepal is around 10 times larger, external than that of hydropower.
Puspa Sharma, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore's Institute of South Asian Studies, agrees Nepal has to diversify its energy sources, but warns this can be done "only to a limited extent".
"While there is untapped capacity in wind and solar, hydropower really is the one that gives Nepal massive competitive advantage vis-a-vis its South Asian neighbours," he says, citing various studies comparing renewable energy potential in the region.
Hydropower continues to dominate large-scale investments in Nepal, and some climate activists say the funding has continued despite known disaster risks.
The Upper Trishuli-1 project, which has been all but destroyed after last week's floods, was one of Nepal's largest foreign direct investment ventures, valued at about $647m. Its backers include the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.
The Upper Trishuli 3A, which has also been severely hit, was funded by China's Export-Import Bank.
Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says international lenders were "acutely aware of the extreme danger to which they were exposing thousands of labourers, officials, residents, rivers, infrastructure and landscape".
"Their own reports repeatedly highlighted it. But they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur," he says.
History has already shown the Trishuli River basin to be volatile, Thakkar says, pointing to how it had been hit by floods in the last two years. In September 2024, an unprecedented cloudburst over the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river basins sparked flash floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading - settlements by the river that are also among the hardest hit from last week's floods.
Then in July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet's Gyirong county burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least 11 people. That flood damaged critical infrastructure and halted trade along the busy Nepal-China corridor. The border crossing was shut for nearly six months and had only reopened on 1 January this year.
Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority admits that even if climate risk assessments were carried out correctly, "the designing of the plants may not have been done accordingly".
"Clearly we will need to improve in the way we build and operate our hydropower plants," he adds.
Private operators are already feeling the financial impact. Insurers have paid out around $40m for flood-related damage to more than 20 privately owned plants over the past three years, according to Uttam Bhlon Lama from the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.
He warns insurance premiums are rising significantly and making the cost of doing business "unfeasible".
This disaster shows climate risks are international and cannot be managed by Nepal alone, suggests Manjeet Dhakal, a member of the country's climate delegation at the UN Climate Change Conference.
Governments and international organisations must share data, assess impacts and develop early-warning systems together, he urges.
"Nepal is among the least responsible for the greenhouse emissions that led to these exacerbated risks.
"Ironically, our hydropower industry is an attempt to reduce our already minimal emissions... We cannot, and should not, be made to respond to these risks alone."

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is the next massive installment in the franchise. The latest Modern Warfare 4 title comes bundled with a variety of game modes. Infinity Ward has developed completely new modes for MW4, and several classic ones are returning as well. So, if you are eager to play the upcoming CoD title, check out all the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game modes here.
Full List of Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Game Modes Coming at Launch
In line with the previous CoD titles, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 will feature different modes, from Campaign to the revamped DMZ. So, let’s go over all the game modes available in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4:
Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Mode
Of course, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 includes a campaign mode at launch. Get ready to experience an interwoven storyline in MW4. As Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is set in South Korea, players will take on the role of Private Park Hyun Jun (played by Young Mazino), a rookie South Korean soldier experiencing the horrors of war during North Korea’s invasion.
On the other hand, Captain Price and Ghost also return in the Korean setting. Now, as an outlaw, Captain Price operates in the shadows and is on the hunt for a weapon of mass destruction. If you are looking for the official synopsis of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, it is as follows:
“War erupts on the Korean Peninsula as North Korea launches a full-scale invasion that threatens to destabilize the world. A young squad of South Korean soldiers fights to survive on the collapsing front lines, while half a world away, a vengeful Captain Price wages a personal war from the shadows as he stays one step ahead of those hunting him.”
As usual, CoD players can expect globetrotting action-adventure in MW4 as Infinity Ward has revealed that players will experience trench warfare in Korea, close-quarters combat in New York, high-octane chases through Paris, SAS night raids in Mumbai, and many more city-wide assaults.
Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Multiplayer Modes
On the multiplayer side, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 features a total of 17 modes. More new modes will be added to the game post-launch. For now, here are all the confirmed Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer modes:
Respawn
- Team Deathmatch: Two teams compete, and whoever secures the most kills or reaches the target score wins.
- Domination: Two teams engage in a fierce battle to capture three distinct objective areas on the map. Whoever takes control of the most objectives and earns enough required points wins the match.
- Hardpoint: Each team now has to compete to take control of an objective area that keeps changing throughout the match.
- Kill Confirmed: It is very similar to TDM mode, with one big change: players need to collect the defeated enemy’s dog tag to confirm the kill.
- Free for All: Players won’t be assigned to any side and are on their own, and the player who secures the elimination target score first wins.
- Counter Attack: A brand-new mode focused on counter-attacking, and the well-performing team takes home the win.
- Inflation: A bounty-style spin on Kill Confirmed. Kill enemies and loot their bodies to collect money. The team that collects the most money wins!
- Hijack: The attacking team needs to carry a Data Spike and plant it at an enemy Comm Station, whereas defenders need to prevent them from planting the device.
- Frontline: 6v6 pure elimination-focused mode where finishing off opponents outside their base offers you more points.
Round-Based
- Search and Destroy: One team needs to plant a bomb, and the other needs to stop them at all costs.
- Gun Fight: A 3v3 fight; each player receives the same randomized set of weapons and equipment, offering a fair fight.
- Gun Fight 10v10: Players receive randomized loadouts each round, but this time each team has a total of 10 players.
- Arms Deal: Collect money by securing kills and wrapping up objectives. Use the money to get limited weapons and equipment each round.
Big War
- Combat Outpost: Capture, hold, and reinforce outposts. Reinforcing captured outposts unlocks valuable team rewards.
- Frontal Assault: Features a large-scale map, infantry and vehicle combat, and more
Party
- Gun Game: Each player is handed a weapon at the start and receives a new weapon as they begin eliminating others. The first player to swiftly secure eliminations and complete using all the given weapons wins the Gun Game.
- Drop Zone: Teams fight for their lives to capture and control the Drop Zone. Capturing the special zone unlocks temporary killstreak-esque buffs.
Training
- Mobility Course: A training mode with numerous levels to help players master the new movements introduced in MW4.
Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 DMZ Mode
DMZ, Call of Duty’s extraction shooter mode, is also returning in Modern Warfare 4. Players will be dropping in Hajin, and the mode has also received significant changes, including a new bodycam view specially made for the DMZ mode in MW4.
In addition to being tasked with completing Dynamic Operations (multi-step objectives), players are pitted against both human opponents and AI enemies.
DMZ features a dynamic weather system. Sudden rain, fog, or storms will affect your gameplay. Furthermore, players receive tactical tools such as night vision for navigating the pitch-dark locations within the exclusion zone.
Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Warzone
Lastly, the fan-favorite battle royale mode, Warzone, is also available in Modern Warfare 4. The Hajin Exclusion Zone from DMZ mode will also be a main map of Warzone in CoD Modern Warfare Season 1. In addition, there is a new map called Zodiac for the Resurgence matches available as part of Warzone.
And that’s everything you need to know about the various game modes in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Let us know which is your favorite MW4 game mode in the comments below
How many game modes will be available in Modern Warfare 4?
Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 will feature 4 game modes at launch: Campaign, Multiplayer, DMZ, and Warzone.
What are the new multiplayer game modes in Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4?
Counter Attack, Inflation, Hijack, Combat Outpost, Frontal Assault, etc, are the new multiplayer game modes in Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4.

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

Researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras (IIT Madras), and Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore, have developed a set of AI-based tools designed to assist in the early detection and assessment of kidney diseases, a press release said.
The team has developed three technologies that complement each other. The first is a machine learning model that uses clinical and laboratory information to predict the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD). This CKD prediction model is implemented in a user-friendly prototype interface to facilitate future clinical translation.
The second is a deep learning system that automatically analyses CT scans and classifies them into four categories: normal kidney, kidney cyst, kidney stone, and kidney tumour. The image classifier has been trained with over 12,000 images and can distinguish healthy kidneys from cysts, stones, and tumours.
And the third is a 3D imaging platform that recreates kidneys from CT scans to precisely assess tumour volume and the percentage of kidney involvement. The 3D imaging framework was developed using open-source software and is a step toward the development of a kidney ‘digital twin’, integrating AI-assisted image analysis with patient-specific 3D anatomical models for personalised clinical decision-making.
Kidney diseases are often asymptomatic in their early stages and are not diagnosed until substantial damage has occurred. The AI tools aim to assist physicians for earlier diagnosis, which could help slow the disease process and reduce the need for expensive interventions like dialysis.
The research was led by G.L. Samuel, department of mechanical engineering, IIT Madras, and Jennifer Delighta, research scholar, IIT Madras, in collaboration with Santosh Varughese from the department of nephrology, CMC Vellore. The research received institutional support from IIT Madras and the SPARC (Scheme for Promotion of Academic and Research Collaboration) project, the press release said.

Abdul El-Sayed has become one of the political right's favorite foils since campaigning for and winning the Democratic Party nomination for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan in 2026.
Online rumors about the progressive firebrand and epidemiologist have targeted his politics and background as a Muslim with Egyptian immigrant parents.
For example, Snopes has debunked a claim that El-Sayed said America "deserved" the 9/11 attacks and unpacked misleading allegations about his mother's supposed ties to terrorist groups.
Here are four claims we've looked into about El-Sayed:

Stop Calling AI Companies ‘Labs’
The term lends an air of scientific rigor to what are really billion-dollar corporations.
When did AI companies become AI labs? That term, and the image of studious, exacting white-coated scientists that it conjures, has become curiously entrenched as a descriptor for the businesses swiftly escorting the world into an existentially unsettling future. AI companies themselves have embraced the label: When Chris Olah, a co-founder of Anthropic, addressed the pope earlier this year, he repeatedly referred to his company, one of the most powerful AI enterprises in the world, as a lab. Industry press releases, technology commentators, and news publications have all picked up the word too. You’ll see the term on transit advertisements in San Francisco and in the pages of The New York Times (and, yes, The Atlantic).
Here is my proposal: Everyone, please stop. This term has gone too far. Although AI companies do invest heavily in research and development, using a word typically associated with groups of truth-seeking scientists is misleading, odd, and too favorable to these companies’ own ends. As a software engineer working in tech, I’ve seen little evidence that AI companies’ research practices differ significantly from those of the rest of the tech industry. Google and Microsoft, for example, have robust research divisions, but we still call them companies. So why has the laboratory term become so deeply enmeshed with AI?
Part of the reason is historical. Over the past century, research laboratories have played a crucial role in computer science. Studies performed at Bell Labs, one of America’s first industrial labs, resulted in the development of the transistor and the cellular network. In the 1970s, scientists at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science pioneered the foundations of modern cryptography. As the Harvard historian Steven Shapin writes in his book The Scientific Life, countless innovations such as these that originated in corporate labs during the 20th century helped change the public’s perception of science. No longer simply knowledge for knowledge’s sake, science became viewed as a key engine of societal and economic progress.
In their early years, OpenAI and Anthropic mainly performed research, similar to other industrial labs. Since then, however, they have commercialized rapidly: Each company is now valued near $1 trillion and generates billions in quarterly revenue. Holding on to the lab label seems to have the obvious PR benefit of allowing both companies to lean into their scientific legacy. Because of concerns about child safety, privacy, and job displacement, Americans largely hold a negative perception of the industry—and tech as a whole. That’s translated into popular opposition from politicians, data-center activists, and religious leaders who are concerned about the outsize influence of these companies: Spending on AI as a share of U.S. GDP now rivals defense spending. Meanwhile, scientists remain relatively popular. A 2026 Pew Research Center poll found that more than 75 percent of Americans trust scientists to act in the public interest, but the majority do not trust business leaders to do the same. These positive connotations associated with scientific research help the AI industry signal altruism while downplaying their profit-making ambitions. OpenAI and Anthropic’s leaders write at length about how AI’s risks and perils must be carefully studied for the sake of humanity. Research is portrayed as essential to this mission: OpenAI says it treats “safety as a science,” and Anthropic writes that “providing trustworthy research” will improve policy outcomes.
The problem is, these companies act much more like private enterprises than bastions of science. Much of the research listed in the Publications section on both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s websites are not peer-reviewed papers accepted by scholarly outlets. I examined 100 recent pieces of research from both companies’ Research pages; the overwhelming majority had no corresponding peer-reviewed paper accepted by a conference or journal. It’s unclear whether these were submitted to academic venues and, if so, whether they were rejected, are under review, or are forthcoming. (Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic responded to requests for comment.)
Legal risks and long peer-review cycles are typically cited as reasons that fast-moving tech companies seldom share data or engage in peer review. And to its credit, the industry doesn’t always choose research topics that paint its products in a positive light. Anthropic has conducted studies on its models’ undesirable behaviors, such as disempowerment and sycophancy.
Even so, Anthropic has a habit of landing on ambiguity about the fallout of its technology. In its education report, for instance, Anthropic, the entity best equipped to observe whether students are using Claude to cheat, concludes that the question of “How much are students using AI to cheat?” is “hard to answer.”
The practice of assuming scientific authority while exercising potentially biased research practices has more in common with quasi-scientific advocacy organizations than it does with traditional laboratories. Take, for example, the George C. Marshall Institute, a think tank founded in 1984 whose leaders worked closely with the Reagan White House. The institute, whose publications defended oil interests and the tobacco industry, operated under the motto “Science for better public policy.” As the historians Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway reported in the book Merchants of Doubt, the institute strategically refused to publish in journals subject to independent peer review. Instead, it disseminated reports and briefings to policy makers that merely reproduced the “trappings of scientific argumentation—graphs, charts, references, and the like.”
If Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI giants want to keep referring to themselves as labs, they should adhere to scientific best practices: open-sourcing code, preregistering studies, and, most important, subjecting research to independent peer review. Ultimately, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI aren’t tweedy labs doing arcane research—they’re industry-defining corporations reshaping our workplaces, our schools, and our communities. Holding them accountable could start with calling them out for what they are—and what they aren’t.

Man charged with murder after woman found dead in Canberra house fire
A 27-year-old man has been charged with murder and arson after a woman was found dead in a unit fire in Canberra's north earlier this year.
Emergency services were called to Wallcliffe Flats on Osborne Place in Belconnen about 6:40am on May 18, with crews finding a ground-floor unit alight.
Kylee McHugh, 46, was found inside but could not be saved.
On Monday, police arrested a 27-year-old Canberra man who is due to face the ACT Magistrates Court today.
ACT Policing's Detective Acting Inspector Chris Watson said the accused was known to Ms McHugh, describing it as an "association" rather than a "relationship of any kind".
"We believe that in the early hours of the 18th of May he did murder Kylee and subsequently set the house on fire,"
Detective Acting Inspector Watson said he could not speak on a possible motive, but confirmed that the accused was known to police.
He said the man was known to "transit the area" where Ms McHugh was killed, and police were investigating whether drugs could have been involved.
Detective Acting Inspector Watson did not say how Ms McHugh died.
He encouraged anyone with further information to contact Crime Stoppers.
"At this point in time [the 27-year-old] is the only suspect but we do believe there are other people that have more information and that can assist us," he said.
"They may have information that isn't known to us and may be able to provide further insight into events that happened after her death."

Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to the Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.
Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.
This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.
The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.
Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s (Celsius; high 90s Fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

Morning opening: What now after AfD's election triumph?
Jakub Krupa
Europe wakes up this morning to final results of the Saxony-Anhalt state election in Germany, with the far-right Alternative für Deutschland confirmed as the winners – but without a majority in the state parliament.
Cue chaotic discussions about what’s next, including theoretical scenarios with defections, a minority government backed on issue-by-issue basis by the far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, or even… a snap election to resolve the deadlock.
We areexpecting to hear from the embattled German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, around lunchtime. With German media running grainy pictures of Merz looking glumly on the backseat of his car, it is probably fair to say that the pressure on him will only increase.
There are also lots of political reactions from across Europe, with no doubt more to come.
I will bring you all the latest here.
Separately, I will keep an eye on Ursula von der Leyen’s trip to Greenland amid renewed US interest in the territory, and on the funeral of Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić.
It’s Friday, 4 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
AfD's gain in Germany will be seen as a worrying sign ahead of 2027 election marathon - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
The Saxony-Anhalt election has been closely watched – as will be the other two upcoming German state election in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern – ahead ofa number of key elections in the next 12 months which could see right and far-right parties making further gains across Europe.
Starting from Sweden this weekend, we will also see Latvia and Bulgaria go to the polls this autumn, but then the focus shifts to the 2027 French presidential elections, and key parliamentary races inFrance, Italy, Spain, Greece and Poland next year.
Italian government split in reactions to AfD's win
Italy’s foreign minister Antonio Tajani called the election result “terrible news … because it concerns a political force that is antithetical to the liberal and western values,” Corriere della Sera reported.
But Italy’s deputy prime minister in the same government Matteo Salvini was delighted with the outcome of the vote, calling it “a resounding success that highlights the strong demand for change, security, and jobs.”
“In the face of those on the left who stoked fears and catastrophic scenarios. Fear? Terror? Danger? No, it’s called DEMOCRACY. Another Europe is possible.”
For what it’s worth, Giorgia Meloni has yet to respond to the election result.
We are also getting first reactions from European ministers.
Donald Tusk, the prime minister of Poland, said:
“In Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany.”
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski called the AfD’s win “a very worrying” signal for Europe.
France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, described the win as “a serious moment in Europe”, warning that “nationalism and xenophobia will never be a solution”.
“We must listen with humility to the anger, the concerns, the fears, and respond to them,” he added. “We cannot forget our history. That is the meaning behind the choices made by France and Germany.”
French finance minister Roland Lescure joined in his warnings, saying Europe faced “a major challenge in the face of a populist wave” across the continent.
But former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán celebrated AfD’s win, saying it was “a huge night for Germany and Europe!”
Russian presidential aide praises 'historic' win for 'pragmatic' pro-Russian AfD
Russian presidential envoyKirill Dmitriev took a screen grab of US president Donald Trump’s post on Saxony-Anhalt and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”.
AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.
AfD state leader thanks Elon Musk for support after Saxony-Anhalt win
On Sunday night, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, thanked Musk on X “for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time”, adding: “I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation”.
Siegmund wrote his comments after Musk said “Well done!” in German to AfD co-founder Alice Weidel, when she posted about the projected win.

The Motion Picture Association signed two declarations at the Lumière Summit, aimed at deepening international collaboration and investment in audiovisual sector, protecting intellectual property and strengthening the creative economy.
The MPA joined government and private sector partners in signing the Lumiere Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image and the Declaration on Strengthened International Cooperation in the Fight Against Film and Audiovisual Piracy at the conclusion of the Summit.
MPA Chairman and CEO Charlies Rivkin also attended roundtables with Summit co-chairs, French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
Rivkin joined President Lee and MPA member CEOs for a business roundtable focused on the industry’s commitment to partnering with Korea’s creative sector. He also participated alongside MPA member CEOs in a separate business roundtable with President Macron on the future of the industry and opportunities to deepen collaboration with France’s creative sector.

Nail the basics, speak up, keep learning, and meet in person.
JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon and AT&T CEO John Stankey shared those four pieces of career advice during a recent, wide-ranging interview hosted by LinkedIn.
LinkedIn posted text and video highlights of the conversation between the two corporate titans on its platform.
Here are the four key takeaways from what the pair said:
1. Fundamentals matter
Dimon, who has led America's biggest bank by assets for more than 20 years, said young people have different ambitions and goals than previous generations, and are likely to have more complex, varied, and faster-moving careers.
But he said the "basic principles" of getting ahead at work will stay the same: "Treat people fairly, work hard, earn your respect every day, be curious, learn a lot, have a little heart, have a little grit."
Dimon said those core values will remain relevant even as AI and other technologies remap how the world works, because humans won't fundamentally change.
2. Embrace conflict
"Get the dead cat on the table," Dimon said.
The billionaire banker said he was describing "when people are conflict avoidants, they're sitting around a room" and waiting for someone else to speak up, or worrying he won't like to hear what they have to say.
"We fail when we avoid conflict," Dimon said, adding that he views open discourse not as conflict, but as bringing up a problem and figuring out how to solve it.
3. Stay up to date
Stankey — who's worked at AT&T for over 40 years and has been CEO for the past six — said that when he doesn't know "what the heck" a colleague is talking about during a meeting, he'll make a note on a card about what they spoke about.
"I pull the card out at night right before I go to sleep," he said, "and I have a conversation with my chatbot to educate me a little bit about what the subject is."
"Just being disciplined about how you learn is really, really critical," Stankey added.
The telecoms veteran also said he spends time with a "reverse mentor" — someone in their 20s who helps him understand what people in that age group are doing, what's important to them, and how they're using technology.
4. Work alongside others
Stankey said he recognizes the value of remote-working tools such as Zoom, but the downside is they've "flattened relationships" and "made them a bit disposable or categorizable."
The AT&T chief said the path to solving hard problems and having "deeper, richer, more constructive relationships" is to understand your coworkers, and working next to them helps greatly with that.
"You can understand if something's going on in their life that you intuitively pick up at a table that you can't get across a video screen," he said.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei on Monday (local time) criticised Canada for what he described as its support for US-Israeli military aggression, amid escalating tensions between Tehran and Washington. In a rather lengthy post on X, Baqaei accused Ottawa of displaying "strategic confusion." He wrote, "On the very day the U.S. president, in blatant contempt for Canada’s sovereignty and independence, portrayed the entire country as part of the United States, Canada’s foreign and finance ministers chose to further appease their bullying neighbor—this time by targeting Iran with a statement that distorts every fact about the situation in our region." The post further read, "Canada cannot credibly present itself as a champion of “peace and security,” “freedom of navigation,” and “international law” while simultaneously backing U.S. military aggression and Washington’s illegal, interventionist actions in our region." Elaborating further, Baqaei said the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global energy route, had remained open and secure before the US and Israel launched their war against Iran on 28 February. Taking a dig at the recently strained US-Canada ties, the foreign ministry spokesperson added, "If freedom of navigation is truly the issue, why does Canada - having itself experienced American bad faith and knowing that U.S. signatures are 'written in pencil' - choose to support U.S. military aggression and economic terrorism instead of calling for an end to American aggression, blockade, and economic warfare?" The strongly worded post from Tehran came after Canada's Foreign Minister Anita Anand and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne issued a joint declaration in which they condemned Iran's regional actions and maritime threats. In a statement issued on 6 September, Ottawa leaders wrote, "Canada condemns and calls on Iran to immediately end its destabilizing activities in the Middle East. Iran's actions, including its continued threats to vessels seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, its pursuit of illicit nuclear activities and its support for regional proxy groups, continue to undermine global peace and security." The joint statement added, "Canada is working closely with partners, including within the G7, to maintain significant pressure on Iran. This includes support for efforts led by the United States, as well as France and the United Kingdom, to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and continued sanctions on Iran, such as those announced under U.S.-led Operation Economic Outcast. Canada continues to support efforts aimed at disrupting Iran's ability to finance terrorist activities." Further, the Canadian ministers vowed that Ottawa will pursue additional measures in coordination with its allies to push for peace and security in the region, while maintaining pressure on Tehran to end its "malign behaviour." Since 2010, Ottawa has sanctioned at least 492 Iranian individuals and entities through the Special Economic Measures Act (SEMA) and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (JVCFOA). Canada's condemnation of Iran's regional actions comes at a time when several US allies are now rallying support behind Washington, after initially rejecting US President Donald Trump's request to assist in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the South Korean government said it was considering assisting the US' security efforts in the Strait of Hormuz by deploying military assets.
