12 pilgrims killed as vehicle hits divider, overturns on UP's Eastern Peripheral Expressway
The pilgrims were returning to Budaun after a pilgrimage to Bagad Dham in Rajasthan when the accident took place, the police said.
At least 12 people were killed and more than 16 injured after a canter carrying pilgrims overturned on the Eastern Peripheral Expressway in Uttar Pradesh’s Baghpat district late on Sunday, police said on Monday.
The pilgrims were returning to Budaun after a pilgrimage to Bagad Dham in Rajasthan when the accident took place, the police added.
The accident occurred at around 1am between Basi and Bada villages in the Khekra Kotwali area, around 15 km from Baghpat district headquarters. The canter, carrying 32 devotees from Budaun, reportedly hit a divider before overturning, triggering panic and cries for help.
Police and emergency personnel reached the spot soon after receiving information and rushed the injured to the district hospital. Doctors there declared six people dead.
According to a doctor at the district hospital, 22 injured people were brought to the hospital for treatment. Eighteen of them were subsequently referred to a higher medical centre in Meerut. Six more people later died while undergoing treatment at a medical college in Meerut, taking the toll to 12, SSP Rai Suraj Rai confirmed.
The deceased were identified as Munni Devi, 55, Sugadpal, 40, Sadhu, 60, Rameshwar Yadav, 60, Premsingh, 40, and seven-year-old Jitendra. Authorities were working to establish the identities of the remaining victims.
One of the injured passengers, Kunwarpal, said most of the passengers were asleep when the vehicle suddenly overturned.
“We were all sleeping in the vehicle when there was a loud impact and the canter suddenly overturned. There was screaming and chaos at the spot,” he said.
According to Kunwarpal, the driver told the passengers that a vehicle approaching from behind had collided with their canter, causing it to lose balance and overturn. Police, however, are investigating the circumstances and the exact cause of the accident.
Bagad Dham, also known as Gogamedi, is a prominent pilgrimage site in Rajasthan’s Hanumangarh district and is associated with Jaharveer Baba Goga Ji Maharaj, also known as Goga Nath Ji. Large numbers of devotees visit the site during August and September.
The pilgrims had travelled together from their village in Budaun to Rajasthan and were returning home when the accident occurred in Baghpat. According to Vimlesh Kumar Yadav, all the passengers belonged to the same village.
He said villagers had been undertaking pilgrimages to Rajasthan for nearly two decades and their previous journeys were generally completed without any major incident. This time, however, the accident has left several families devastated.
Baghpat District Magistrate Asmita Lal and Superintendent of Police Suraj Rai visited the district hospital. They met the injured and directed medical personnel to ensure that they received proper and timely treatment.

The Republican mayor of Oswego, New York, Robert Corradino, has rejected the renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” a change enacted by US President Donald Trump through an executive order on August 27. While Google and Apple Maps have already adopted the new name for US users, Corradino said his community is “taking the renaming very personally” and will continue to use Lake Ontario in all signage, tourism materials, and official communications. According to a report by National Post, Corradino emphasized that Lake Ontario is central to Oswego’s identity, citing its economic importance through charter boats, cruise ships, and tourism.
The renaming of ‘Lake Ontario’ and local pushback
Corradino emphasized that Lake Ontario's name is rooted in a Huron Indigenous word meaning "lake of shining waters," predating the province of Ontario itself, which took its name from the lake in 1867. “Lake Ontario is in the DNA of Osweganians. Everything that we are emanates from the lake,” he said. The mayor also noted that Canadian tourism, vital to local businesses, has dropped substantially following the breakdown of US-Canada trade negotiations last month.
 Statistics Canada data shows Canadian travel to the US fell 10.6% in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025.
Corradino reaffirmed Oswego’s stance: “Lake Ontario has carried its name for hundreds of years. It is a name rooted in history, geography, and the shared identity of the communities that surround it. The city of Oswego will continue using the name that reflects our history and honors the generations who have lived, worked, and built their lives along its shores.”
A Bipartisan and cross-border backlash
Recently, Oswego County legislators from both parties passed a resolution rejecting the renaming, citing rebranding costs for taxpayers and businesses. MapQuest also refused to adopt the "Lake America" name, boosting its app store rankings.
Trump's order has drawn criticism well beyond Oswego. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton responded to the renaming with a brief rebuttal on X, while Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders said the American public has no appetite for calling the lake "Lake America."
North of the border, Carney noted on social media that the name Lake Ontario derives from the Wendat word "Ontari'io," meaning the lake is beautiful and big, and that it predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence by more than 400 years. He argued that acknowledging reality means continuing to call it Lake Ontario. Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre echoed the sentiment, saying the lake was never Trump's to rename on a whim.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford went a step further on Saturday, unveiling a new "Lake Ontario" sign in Winona, Ontario, declaring in a video posted to X that the lake carried that name long before Trump and would continue to carry it long after he's gone.

‘We saw him happy, now we see his dead body’: Families mourn students killed in Delhi PG collapse
A five-storey boys’ PG accommodation in Delhi’s Satya Niketan collapsed on Sunday, killing five students and two labourers.
“Arpit had big dreams and was working hard to make them come true. He wanted to study in a big city and we sent him to Delhi. He was his mother’s favourite,” his father said.
In a matter of minutes, the hopes and dreams of five students came crashing down after a five-storey paying guest accommodation for boys collapsed in south-west Delhi’s Satya Niketan on Sunday. One labourer, as well as one man who still has to be identified, were also killed in the incident. At least two people are currently critical at AIIMS.
The incident, which took place near the heart of Delhi University’s south campus, has sent shockwaves in the city, reiterating the fragility of the Capital’s infrastructure, the lack of proper regulatory norms, and laxity in the enforcing the ones that exist.

Arpit Jahaj, 18 – Student
Arpit had returned to the city from his hometown in Dewas, Madhya Pradesh, just hours before the building came down. “We had just celebrated Rakshabandhan holiday together, saw him happy and playful, and now we are seeing him as a dead body,” said his father, Bhupendra Jahaj, who works as a cab driver.
The 18-year-old was preparing for the Chartered Accountancy examinations and was a second-year student at the Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma (ARSD) College.
“We got a call from Arpit’s friend on Sunday night about the building collapse and by the time we reached here, nothing was left and he was gone,” his father recalled, standing outside the mortuary of AIIMS trauma centre, waiting to receive his son’s last remains.

His friends searched all night for him in the remains of the building and only later did they learn that he had died. The hospital said they had received a body matching the identity. “But when we went to identify him, we could not because the body was badly injured. Around 6.30 am (on Monday), the family reached the hospital and his mother identified him by his birth marks,” his friend Yuvraj told HT.
Arpit had been living in the PG for nearly one-and-a-half years. “Everyone is telling us how bad the condition of the PG was. I wish my son had told me before,” his father said.
Following the postmortem, Arpit’s family donated his corneas at the hospital. “Maybe he will be able to see the world, even after he is not with us.”

Yuvraj Soni, 20 – Student
Like Arpit, Yuvraj was also a CA aspirant. He was a second-year student at Motilal Nehru College.
He had been living in the north campus till a few days ago. “Yuvraj had just moved to this PG and it took him away from us,” said his friend Aryan.
His sister Nikki and his brother Vivek were at the hospital, but all they could do was express their shock and disbelief. They had no words left with which to share the impact of the tragedy.

Volcano eruption triggers flight suspensions at Indonesia's main airport
- Published
A volcanic eruption has halted hundreds of flights at Indonesia's main international airport, stranding tens of thousands of passengers.
Authorities said 209 flights were suspended after ash from Mount Anak Krakatoa was detected in airspace near Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Sunday morning.
The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said.
More than 22,000 people have been impacted by the suspension of flights, which has been extended until 13:30 (0630 GMT).
The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks.
Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where there is high volcanic and seismic activity.

India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
- Published
In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations.
Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations.
Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research.
But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own.
In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister.
In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system.
For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu.
A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented.
The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses.
Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink.
BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible.
"Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC.
"We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres."
But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says.
Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government.
"When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains.
Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed.
Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages.
Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says.
"Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains.
Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places.
India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University.
"This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says.
For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation.
Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak.
"It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said.
The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures.
"The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again."
Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs.
The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects.
Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September.
"I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?"
Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether.
Educationists argue that scrapping the agency would not solve the underlying problem.
The NTA needs deep structural reform to address recurring failures, but abolishing it is not the answer, said M Jagadesh Kumar, former chairman of India's universities regulator.
"A single national testing body offers common security standards, technology, candidate services and result procedures. Creating many new agencies could duplicate costs and produce uneven safeguards," he told PTI news agency.
Rao agrees.
"It is not a case of all bad news. The body has conducted several exams successfully, where we did not hear of any leaks," he said.
What is needed, he argues, is a statutory institution staffed by specialists with the academic, technical and operational expertise to run a secure examination system.
Yet for some experts, the debate ultimately goes beyond the NTA itself.
Aiyar says the bigger issue is not just stopping the next paper leak, but whether a highly centralised testing system can cope with the intense competition for limited educational opportunities.
The NTA may be able to make exams more secure, she says. "But it cannot, at least on its own, change a system in which millions of students compete for a limited number of seats and a single exam can shape their future."
Some experts say reform must go beyond the NTA itself: India needs an exam system less reliant on one-off, high-stakes tests, gives students multiple chances and can better withstand disruptions.
Rao remains optimistic that the task force led by Nilekani will help plug gaps in the existing system.
But for many students, another committee offers little reassurance unless it produces changes they can actually see.
"I am studying for my university entrance examination next year," said a 16-year-old Grade 12 student.
"In my head I am prepared that there might be a leak. But what can we do about it? I will prepare and hope for the best."

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

Captain Ishan Kishan (270, 334b, 30x4, 7x6) made a resplendent double-century to help East Zone place one hand on the Duleep Trophy 2026 after another dominant day against South Zone at the M.A. Chidambaram Stadium here on Monday.
Returning from 111 not out overnight, the 28-year-old ground the South Zone bowling down in a clinical, chanceless innings as he became the third East Zone batter to score 200 after Arun Lal and Saba Karim. He reached his second First-Class double-ton (and his maiden Duleep Trophy century) off 270 deliveries in an innings that lasted 522 minutes in total.
After a bruising first day in the field, South Zone opted to take the new ball just 13 balls into the morning, and while its seam contingent produced a more disciplined showing, it was unable to reap the rewards of its pressure.
Kishan and Kumar Kushagra (101, 132b, 8x4, 5x6) negotiated the first hour with caution before opening up to extend their union beyond 200 runs. Kishan drove Mohammed Siraj and MD Nidheesh each for consecutive boundaries on his way past 150 before Kushagra – who was 63 not out overnight – raised his sixth FC ton.
The Jharkhand batter maturely negotiated some early challenges from Nidheesh and CV Milind before moving into the nineties with a pair of handsome boundaries off the back foot against Shreyas Gopal. He finally reached three figures off 128 balls with a single to leg against Gopal.
However, Kushagra would find himself back in the dugout three balls later courtesy of a miscued pull off Tripurana Vijay, and Anukul Roy, his replacement at the crease, looked uncomfortable initially. He has given out leg-before in the same over from Vijay but survived on review and wore a pair of Siraj bouncers on the helmet and glove. However, he showed enough gumption to make it to Lunch.
The pressure was taken off by Kishan, who cut loose and found his full flow. He showed particular relish in taking down Gopal, who he sent mercilessly to the boundary through the day, and added 79 from 69 balls after the second session.
By midway through the second session, South Zone skipper Tilak Varma was left with no option but to turn to the part-time spin of Devdutt Padikkal and Shaik Rasheed to make up the overs, and it was former who Kishan dispatched through the offside to reach 200 to wild applause from another strong crowd.
The most danger either batter appeared in through the afternoon was when Kishan reached 250 via a straight drive drilled into Anukul’s midriff. Kishan, who felt the effects of the sweltering Chennai heat, retired hurt a ball later while Anukul’s essay ended five shy of a half-century after he was trapped in front by Rasheed on the stroke of Tea.
That was but small consolation for South Zone though, as Mohammad Kounain Qureshi and Mohammed Shami prolonged their misery with a stand of 54 through a laboured final session.
When Shami finally lost his stumps to Gopal on 28, it seemed less like a breakthrough and more like an opportunity to allow the returning Kishan to bask in the glory of what he had achieved through the day.
It was only fitting then, that it was Kishan that brought up the 700 before he found long-on on 270, as the East Zone innings wrapped up on 708 all out.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet after an ice-and-rock avalanche triggered a surge of water and debris through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. The disaster destroyed homes, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and other infrastructure. As of 04 September, at least 1,252 people have died in Nepal, and more than 4,200 remain missing. Search and rescue operations are continuing, with two hydropower workers rescued alive from a tunnel on 4 September, nine days after the disaster (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this, a photo is being widely shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a young girl being protected by her brother, who were victims of the Nepal floods. Let’s verify the truth behind the photo in this article.
Claim: The photo shows a young girl being protected by her brother, who are victims of the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Fact: The photo is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods. Vietnamese photojournalist Na Son Nguyen took it in October 2007 in Can Ty, a remote village in Hà Giang province, Vietnam. The photo shows two Hmong siblings, with the boy comforting his younger sister while their parents were away working in the fields. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A Google Lens search of the viral photo led us to a BBC report (archived) dated 4 May 2015 featuring the same photo, confirming that it predates the 2026 Nepal floods. According to the report, Vietnamese photographer Na Son Nguyen took the photo in October 2007 in Can Ty, a remote village in Ha Giang province, Vietnam. Talking to the BBC, he said the photo shows two Hmong siblings, with the boy comforting his crying sister while their parents were away working in the fields. He also said this was his most-shared photo, but unfortunately, it was repeatedly circulated online in the wrong context.
We also found (archived) an Instagram post by Vietnam-based photojournalist Na Son Nguyen featuring the same photo, published on 2 April 2015. The post states that Nguyen captured the photo in October 2007 in a mountainous village in Hà Giang province, Vietnam. He said the photo shows a young boy comforting his younger sister while their parents were away working in the fields. This confirms that the viral photo is unrelated to the recent floods in Nepal.
To sum up, this viral photo does not show children affected by the August 2026 Nepal floods; it was taken in Vietnam in 2007.

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes
- Published
England selection should no longer be restricted to players based at domestic clubs, according to cap centurion Courtney Lawes.
The 37-year-old is back in contention to add to his 105 England appearances, having signed a one-year deal with Sale after two seasons at Brive in the French second tier.
A clutch of English talent - notably Toulouse star Jack Willis - remain across the Channel and out of reach for England head coach Steve Borthwick.
"I can see why they do it because they don't want all their players playing abroad, but I don't think that's necessarily going to be the case anyway," said Lawes.
"It's important that you have the best players available for selection. If we want the game to develop and more people to watch it, I think it has to develop.
"I just reckon you make your best players available and by any means necessary.
"I don't see why you'd limit yourself."
In addition to Willis, who was voted the best player in France in 2024-25 and could well retain the award after a player-of-the-match performance in the Top 14 final in June, Willis' brother Tom, Kyle Sinckler, Manu Tuilagi, David Ribbans, Billy Vunipola, Lewis Ludlam and Junior Kpoku also ply their trade in France.
England have better access and control over players who are at Prem clubs. The clubs, in turn, benefit from central payments from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) and more chance of retaining their biggest stars, who face international exile with a move overseas.
Other nations, such as New Zealand, France and Ireland, have a policy of picking home-based players, but some of England's other rivals, such as South Africa, Australia and Scotland, lean heavily on players based abroad.
Borthwick has opted not to include either Lawes or Joe Marchant, his new Sale team-mate who has spent the past three seasons at Stade Francais in Paris, in his first training camp of the season, asking them to prove themselves in the Prem first.
The England coach adopted a similar approach when Owen Farrell returned from Racing 92 at the start of last season.
"I spoke to Steve a little bit," said Lawes, who played 80 minutes in a 50-28 win over Bath in the Prem Rugby Cup on Sunday, to Rugby Union Weekly.
"It was just what I would expect - he knows I'm coming back and he's going keep an eye on me, but he wants to see me play in the Prem first and I think that's a good idea.
"I've spent two years away, let's see how I go in the Prem first, I'm not really thinking about England before I can get up and running for Sale so that's there's no point."
Lawes, who initially retired from Test rugby after the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final defeat by South Africa, said his return to England was not something he expected when he departed boyhood club Northampton in the wake of lifting the domestic title the following year.
"Probably not, no [I didn't expect to be back]," he added.
"All options were on the table last season - potentially staying at Brive, potentially coming back or retiring. They were all on the table but you're a long time retired and I can still move really well so, why not when you've still got it in your legs?"
Watching from afar, he believes England have the talent to improve on an erratic 2025-26 campaign.
"It's obviously been pretty up and down more recently," he added. "They had an unbelievable autumn and then struggled in the Six Nations.
"It is hard to know exactly what's going on in camp, but obviously there's some issues otherwise they'd probably be playing a bit better than they are.
"With the squad they've got they should be doing quite well."

From factory floors to corner offices, women's roles in the workplace have undergone many reinventions over the past century.
By the 1920s, decades of industrialization had drawn growing numbers of women into the workforce.
Then, as men were sent off to war, more women entered the wartime effort in factories and other professions previously dominated by men.
Women's equality movements throughout the 1960s and 1970s gave working women more opportunities, and in recent years, the gap between men and women in the workforce has been closing, according to data released by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
These vintage photos show how women's roles in the workforce have evolved over the last 100 years.
In the wake of the Industrial Revolution, more women than ever began to leave the household and go out to work.
Jobs commonly held by women included postal clerks, who sorted letters and packages. While it wasn't uncommon for women to work in post offices, very few women actually delivered mail.
The US Postal Service reported that in 1920, only 5% of the nation's 943 village carriers were women.
As local postal delivery was gradually phased out in favor of larger city delivery, most of the remaining women village carriers either resigned or were transferred to clerk positions.
Many women also began working in factories.
The US Department of Labor reported that in 1920, women made up about 20% of the labor force, an increase from previous generations.
Many of them were involved in the production and manufacturing of clothing, food products, and tobacco products.
Women of color, on the other hand, were largely employed in agriculture and domestic service work for much of the early 20th century.
During World War I, women held occupations in domestic and personal service, clerical occupations, and factory work.
Many women took typing courses to secure higher-paying jobs as secretaries or typists in clerical offices rather than working in factories.
The Encyclopedia of Chicago reported that working conditions, wages, and hours in clerical work were seen as the best at the time.
Clerical work attracted young, literate, mostly white women who would work as typists until they were married, only to be replaced by other young unmarried women when they left their jobs to raise their families.
The government also began paying greater attention to women's working conditions. In 1920, Congress established the Women's Bureau.
As the popularity of silent films began to rise, women also found work behind the scenes on movie sets.
The Women Film Pioneers Project wrote that a 1923 edition of "Business Woman" published a list of 29 different jobs that women held in the film industry, apart from actresses.
Job positions included those of a typist, secretary to the stars, executive secretary, costume designer, seamstress, telephone operator, hairdresser, script girl, film retoucher, title writer, publicity writer, musician, film editor, director, and producer, among others.
Women also held jobs as blacksmiths and worked on vehicles.
However, most occupations were seen solely as a precursor to marriage.
Among married white women of both native and immigrant backgrounds, only around 10% were in the workforce, History reported.
It was more common for married women of color to hold jobs outside the home, however.
Unemployed women during the Great Depression could join "SheSheShe" camps.
Inspired by the Civilian Conservation Corps, which only allowed men to join in exchange for free room and board, Eleanor Roosevelt campaigned for so-called "SheSheShe" camps to help women gain employment in environmental conservation, The Corps Network reported.
Many families during the Great Depression were able to achieve middle-class status by adding another working member to the household — in many cases, a woman.
Many women during the Great Depression found work as secretaries, teachers, telephone operators, and nurses.
Women also earned incomes by sewing clothes in Works Progress Administration (WPA) sewing rooms. The rooms manufactured products such as men's trousers, boys' coveralls, baby clothes, women's dresses, and diapers.
In the 1930s, women made 25% less than men for some government jobs.
A 1933 law called the National Industrial Recovery Act established the National Recovery Administration, which oversaw industry codes that set standards including minimum wages and maximum hours. Just over a quarter of the codes set lower minimum wage rates for women than for men.
In 1942, during wartime, the War Labor Board ruled that women would be paid the same as male workers who were now away at war.
However, the war ended before they could receive equal pay.
With no laws to protect female workers from pay inequality, female workers in the 1940s earned around 60% of what their male counterparts made, MarketWatch reported.
By 1943, women made up 65% of the US aircraft industry's workforce.
Before the war, women were largely in traditionally "female" fields such as nursing and teaching.
After Pearl Harbor, many women entered the armed forces at astonishing rates. In 1943, more than 310,000 women worked in the US aircraft industry, making up 65% of the industry's total workforce, History reported.
Before the war began, women made up just 1% of the industry.
By 1945, one in every four married women worked in jobs outside the home.
During World War II, women assisted in manufacturing wartime necessities like gas masks.
Forbes reported that between 1940 and 1945, women's participation in the US workforce increased from 27% to nearly 37%.
Women were largely seen as "supplemental" workers in the 1950s, meaning their income was secondary to their husbands'.
Even though there were technically more women in the workforce in 1952 than during the war, women were often paid less and given jobs with less upward mobility than their male counterparts.
After the war, women returned to stereotypically "feminine" jobs. In some cases, jobs were advertised for women only.
Many women were forced to give up the jobs they had worked in during wartime, giving them to male soldiers returning home.
The most popular jobs for women during the 1950s were secretaries, bank tellers or clerical workers, sales clerks, private household workers, and teachers, The Week reported.
Female secretaries in the 1950s gained a reputation for being young and attractive.
In fact, a 1959 quiz from a secretarial training program in Waco, Texas, reposted by The Atlantic, asked women if they have what it takes to be a secretary, including "smiling readily and naturally" and being "usually cheerful" among its requirements.
The 1950s marked the beginning of the "jet age," and many young women found work as flight attendants, then called "stewardesses."
Flight attendants during the 1950s became symbols of the golden age of flying — when traveling by air was seen as the height of sophistication and glamour. However, with this "glamorous" career also came a host of sexist protocols.
Condé Nast Traveler reported that women were not allowed to work as flight attendants after they reached the ages of 32 to 35, while male flight attendants could work well into their 60s.
In 1957, Trans World Airlines dropped its no-marriage rule for female flight attendants. However, many airlines continued to only hire non-married female flight attendants.
While many women joined the workforce, they were nevertheless expected to fulfill their duties at home, in what would be coined "the second shift."
After women returned home from their secretarial or office jobs, they had another job to do: caring for the children, doing the housekeeping, and, of course, putting a hot dinner in front of their husbands.
This became known as the "second shift." If women didn't hold office or other jobs during the day, they were relegated to being "housewives."
In the 1950s and 1960s, women found creative ways to make their own incomes from their homes.
Many suburban women began selling Tupperware out of their own homes in what became known as "Tupperware parties."
"Tupperware ... took those moms out of the kitchen where they were 'supposed to be' and let them enter the workforce, and let them have something outside the home," Lorna Boyd, whose mother Sylvia was an at-home Tupperware seller in the 1960s, told the Smithsonian Institution.
Women were also making history in their careers.
In the 1960s, Barbara Walters was a broadcast journalist working in New York City. In 1976, she would become the first woman to anchor a nightly newscast, Variety reported.
Many other women were also joining the journalism field as coverage of the Vietnam War became increasingly widespread.
While technology-based and other computer programming jobs may now be dominated by men, they were considered "women's work" in the 1960s.
Smithsonian Magazine reported that "computer girls" became a term for "savvy young women" pursuing careers in computer programming.
Computer programming was seen as "easy" work similar to typing or filing, so many women ended up building the field that would come to be known as software development.
From the '40s to the '60s, women played a major role in the development of computer programming.
Women were among the earliest computer programmers in the US, working on projects including the ENIAC computer during World War II, but programming was often treated as routine work.
"Women were seen as an easy, tractable labor force for jobs that were critical and yet simultaneously devalued," technology historian Marie Hicks said in her book "Programmed Inequality," which detailed a similar phenomenon in Britain, The Guardian reported.
But as computing became more prestigious and lucrative, the field became increasingly male-dominated. By the mid-1980s, the share of computer science bachelor's degrees earned by women in the US had begun to decline.
In the 1960s, multiple pieces of legislation were passed to protect women in the workplace from discrimination.
Title VII was added to the Civil Rights Act of 1964, protecting workers from employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
In 1963, the Equal Pay Act of 1963 was passed in order to protect men and women who perform "substantially equal work in the same establishment" from sex-based wage discrimination.
These measures were especially beneficial to women of color. Up until the 1970s, women of color could be openly discriminated against in the hiring process and were often assigned to providing 
"domestic service work" to white families, The Economic Policy Institute reported. 
During the 1970s, computing work gained more prestige as the industry realized how valuable computers would become.
It meant women were no longer welcome in many computer programming offices.
"They weren't going to put women workers – seen as low-level drones – in charge of computers," Hicks told The Guardian.
Female computer workers, or "computer girls," were gradually phased out and replaced with men, who received higher salaries and more prestigious job titles.
By the 1970s, many women were still fighting for better workplace conditions, equal pay, and more job opportunities.
The Atlantic reported that from 1972 to 1985, the number of women working "professional" jobs increased from 44% to 49%. The number of women working "management" jobs nearly doubled, rising from 20% to 36%.
However, in 1970, women still did not earn equal wages to men holding the same positions.
In the 1970s, education became more important than ever for securing a well-paying job.
After measures were passed that prevented universities and institutions from discriminating against students on the basis of sex, more women were admitted into medical school than in past generations, according to a study published by the British Medical Bulletin.
Other strides were made for women in the late 1970s.
In 1978, the Pregnancy Discrimination Act was passed as an amendment to Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibited pregnancy-based employment discrimination.
Women in the workforce in the 1980s continued to make strides, but there was still a way to go.
The Atlantic reported that, in 1985, half of all college graduates were women. However, only 41% of women between the ages of 25 and 44 held full-time year-round jobs.
Even in the mid-1980s, women themselves saw their own careers as inferior to their husbands'.
The Atlantic also cited a 1985 Roper survey that showed only 10% of women said that a husband should turn down a "very good job" in another city "so the wife can continue her job."
However, women of the 1980s made history in their fields. Dr. Mae Jemison was among 15 new astronauts named by NASA and became the first Black female shuttle flyer.
In 1984, at the Democratic National Convention held in San Francisco's Moscone Center, Geraldine Ferraro became the first woman nominated as vice president by a major political party.
Women were encouraged to "do it all" — meaning, hold a successful job as well as maintain a happy and healthy marriage and raise children.
In the 1990s, women overwhelmingly began to be employed in offices and earned higher salaries than before.
Computers became increasingly prevalent, reducing the need for secretaries, bank tellers, and retail workers.
Some women were also postponing marriage and children until later in life.
For most earlier decades, women would be married between the ages of 20 and 22, Time reported.
The median age for women to get married rose to 24 in 1990, and by 1997, it was 25.
In 1995, nearly half of all women surveyed for a report by the National Center for Education Statistics said they earned half or more of their total family income.
In recent years, women have held more jobs than men in the US.
Fortune reported that at the start of 2020, 109,000 more women were working than men, and women in the US made up 50.4% of the labor force.
Sectors that traditionally hire women, like healthcare and education, were growing, and other industries previously dominated by men were also hiring more women than ever before.
Forbes reported that 13.8% of mining and logging jobs were held by women, and more women were employed in manufacturing and transportation than in years past.
The COVID-19 pandemic caused the women's labor force participation rate to hit a 33-year low, with 2.3 million women in the US leaving the labor force between February 2020 and January 2021.
By 2025, however, nearly half of all US employees were women, some of whom chose to start their own businesses and chose entrepreneurship over traditional careers.
Between July 2025 and July 2026, women's labor-force participation fell from 57.6% to 56.4%.

There is much to be said for the extraordinary women living ordinary lives, who nonetheless shaped India. Women have changed public life in the country far more than their presence in formal politics would suggest.
And so, as India marked its 79th birthday over the weekend, I found myself reflecting on the multitude of people’s movements, big and small – as well as the women who helped shape them. During India’s struggle for freedom from British rule, women organised boycotts of British goods, made contraband salt and marched to confront the police, taking on roles usually dominated by men. In the 1970s Chipko movement, protesting deforestation, women put their bodies on the line, wrapping them around trees to stop them being felled, turning a local struggle into a national reckoning over environment and development. More recently, grandmothers in Shaheen Bagh sat to protest the citizenship law, which critics have denounced as discriminatory, creating space for dissent when many thought none existed.
Today, routes into public life for women have multiplied, with social media enabling people without political links to be in the public eye. But not all barriers have disappeared. Electoral politics remains notoriously hard to break into, especially for women. Almost half of all female parliamentarians and state legislators come from political families, while for men it is 18%, a 2025 analysis by Association for Democratic Reforms showed.
What makes a woman leading an ordinary life suddenly want to put her head above the parapet to change things for everyone? I spoke to women thrust into the spotlight in the recent student movement, who have stepped in front of vans, starved themselves and had abuse hurled at them in the process – to find out why they do it.
‘Politics is not just slogans and protests’: Neha Bora, 29
The president of the leftwing All India Students’ Association, Bora fasted for 23 days, demanding accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of the Education Minister during the Cockroach Protests. Now, she is touring the country as part of a Gen Z Rising outreach campaign on education reforms.
“I am a PhD student at Jawaharlal Nehru University in theatre and performance studies. My family’s political understanding is very different from mine. I ended up joining politics because that was the only way I could make sense of the times that I was living in – to not be … completely helpless in the decisions that are made for me, that should be made by me. To have a say in what I do, how I do it and what gets done around me. What is tolerable, what is good, what is injustice – all these definitions made sense to me through politics. Theatre was the first thing that taught me that politics is not just slogans and protests. Politics is the very language in which you talk to yourselves, the thoughts you formulate in your head, the relationships you have with your friends, family and peers. Student politics reaffirmed this idea.
Freedom as a student means the ability to study in a university where the model of education has not been turned into an opportunity for profit. Where education is something that helps societies move forward from dogmatism, conservatism and orthodoxy.”
‘Freedom for me is to have a voice – and not be ashamed’: Rhiya Ahir, 27
A model, actor and theatre artist from Mumbai, Ahir made the split-second decision to physically block a police van holding detained protesters – an act that exposed her to an organised hate campaign.
“I started doing theatre when I was four and a half. It taught me empathy and understanding other people’s pain, even people I don’t know. I’ve always been raised with the belief that if you see something wrong you have to step in.
Freedom for me is to have a voice, to put it across confidently and to not be ashamed. I was trolled for a photo in a swimsuit. But what about the uncles who wear chaddis at the Ganga ghat? My clothes are not my character. My clothes cannot overshadow the point or the fact that I was there, and I helped 20 students get back home safely that day. So, my clothes are just my clothes.
The hate did make me second-guess myself. The first two days [after the Mumbai protest] were very difficult because I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. They couldn’t find fault with my argument, so they started questioning my character. They went through my Instagram and found that I was a model. They talked about what I wear. They said she’s doing it for the camera.
When the hate started pouring in I was like, ‘What did I do to offend someone? Did I do something wrong?’ Then I realised this doesn’t change my reality. This doesn’t change who I am as a person. I don’t have to prove myself to anyone.”
‘The police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me’: Danish Ali, 24
Ali was among the student activists on hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. A member of the Jawaharlal Nehru University student union, she faces a year-long suspension for dismantling a facial recognition system at the campus library. For her, freedom is deeply personal and rooted in her identity as a Muslim woman.
“I come from a very small town in Madhya Pradesh. No one in my family had even visited the city, so going to Delhi for higher education was almost like going abroad for education. Since the protest, the police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me. They called my father, asking him to tell me to focus on my studies.
As a student activist, freedom means to be able to critique the government openly and say that we don’t like their policies. Freedom is being assertive about your individuality and not caring what the society would says, what your parents might say or what the state might do to you.
Freedom also means being an equal citizen in this country. Muslims in this country are being made to feel as if they are secondary and that they don’t have any right to express their religious or cultural identities. I am an equal citizen and I don’t want anyone to tell me otherwise.”
‘What used to work … won’t work with the youth’: Ratna Singh, 31
She traded a career in the law and journalism to join the Cockroach Janata party, where she now serves as the legal head. She felt drawn to the protests, seeing her work reflected in the students’ demand for accountability. Initially hesitant to become its public face, she stepped forward as spokesperson when they needed female voices.
“When I was in law school, most of my classmates would go to law chambers for internships but I would spend the summers teaching children at NGOs. Education has been something I have been very sensitive towards, and I believe every child should have access to it.
A lot of people were criticising us [and calling us] an impatient generation. We are impatient because we want to see change. We can’t be protesting and be OK with not getting answers from the government. We are also just done with divide and rule politics on the basis of religion. Political parties need to understand that what used to work for a certain mindset of people – it won’t work with the youth.
There are so many protests which have begun in different parts of the country. The fear of speaking up is gone. We are seeing a lot of leaders coming up in their own districts. They are starting their own initiatives. I think that’s giving us all hope to keep going.”

Last month, I injected myself with a GLP-1 drug and became my own lab rat for three weeks.
As a fitness coach with my weight well under control, I didn’t need this. And yet, I took it. Why?
I work with people to treat their metabolic disease — obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, PMOS, metabolic syndrome. GLP-1 medicines, including semaglutide (the drug in Ozempic) and tirzepatide (the drug in Mounjaro), are among the tools we use. My job is to guide users to a healthy lifestyle (the right kind of activity, better food, improved sleep), while my medical team monitors their health markers. Our goal is to get them off the drug, with their health intact.
For the last 15 years, I’ve coached thousands of people on their strength and health. The single biggest pattern, which shows in their urgency and commitment to the cause, is the trigger moment. A doctor check-up, a wedding, or even a small event like finding themselves unable to bend down and tie their shoelaces helps them prioritise their health and wellness. As they get stronger and start building good lifestyle habits, good things happen.
But for a large percentage, the struggle with weight is real. And it never really ends. While people who lose weight see improvement in their quality of life across the board, maintaining that weight is an uphill struggle, especially when the reality and demands of life hit. As work mounts and stress amplifies, many of these habits crack, especially given the tremendous strain on our time and mental health and the way the environment is structured around us. You may have the best intentions, but you may still end up skimping on sleep or reaching for junk food.
Which is where GLP-1 drugs come in: this new tool in a weight loss toolbox, which I recently tried firsthand – something I always do, even when it comes to designing training plans. I always test-drive anything I recommend for my clients to coach well; I don’t know any other way.
How it went
I’ll start with a caveat: do not do this yourself. While I had no prescription and did not medically need the drug, I did this systematically. I tracked my vitals daily and weekly and reported my subjective and objective experience nearly every day to my doctor and my dietitian.
The drug I opted for was Mounjaro, the most advanced GLP-1 drug on the market today, opting for a starter dose of around 2.5 mg/ week, after consulting with my doctor. Honestly, I did not expect much, since my baseline lifestyle is good. I eat well 85% of the time; I’m active five or six days a week; my sleep hygiene is decent (even if my sleep, lately, hasn't been). But the experience surprised me more than I expected.
Food noise — the constant background hum of thinking about food — simply disappeared. I wanted simple, sattvic food, finding anything greasy immediately unappetising. Over-eating was not possible, whether it was my favourite dessert or the potato chips with my rice. The ease with which I could move through a world of hyper-palatable food, whether I was eating out, ordering in, or eating home-cooked meals, was mind-blowing.
That is the beauty of these drugs: they allow for mindful eating, making that admittedly woo-woo term accessible to all. I wasn't constantly thinking about food or tempted by the package of cupcakes being passed around at work, and I made sensible, adult decisions about food quite naturally, indulging in my favourite snacks without overeating.
In fact, I naturally wanted to eat more nutritious meals because they make me feel good. And I paid attention to my body and how it responded. Also, because I simply could not overeat, my energy levels started to improve, making it a truly liberating time.
Add a doctor, diet and activity
Dr Arun Raghavan, diabetologist and co-founder of Chennai’s Revivo Clinic, which focusses on metabolic care for obesity and diabetes, explains that GLP-1s in India are for adults with a BMI of 30 or higher who have at least one weight-related condition, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or Type 2 diabetes. “They work alongside diet and activity. They are not a stand-alone fix,” he cautions.
And yes, some people should not touch them at all, he adds: anyone with a personal or family history of certain thyroid cancers or a rare inherited hormone disorder, and those with a history of pancreatitis or gallbladder disease. “Most bad reactions come down to the wrong patient, no baseline work-up, or no monitoring.”
The side effects are mostly gastrointestinal and are worse when starting or increasing the dose. His real warning is about stopping. “Come off the drug without having built the lifestyle, and the hunger returns. People lose muscle and regain the weight, often as fat.”
Battling the side effects
It was not all rosy. For the entire three weeks I was on the medication, I had a mild headache and low-grade nausea. It eased after the first week, but it never fully left. My resting heart rate climbed 15%. My heart rate variability — a marker of recovery, where higher is better — dropped 15%. I had frequent palpitations and a mild brain fog, all symptoms that I discussed with Dr Arun Raghavan.
While there is nothing particularly abnormal about these patterns, these were indeed high costs for someone who did not need the drug. For someone who does, going unmonitored is a gamble.
So, did it work?
The results of all this weren’t insignificant: my muscle mass increased by 1.2 kg (a lot!), and fat decreased by 3.2 kg. I was active six days a week, following a hybrid (strength plus conditioning) protocol I developed, which translated to about four 4-hour sessions a week. (Disclaimer: These measurements were taken with a high-end body composition machine, and while the data is reasonably accurate, what we can look at are trends only)
The downside, however, was that my sleep was affected a fair bit, especially at first. Practising some pranayama helped, and it did get better once my body got used to the drug, but the first few days were a struggle.
So, will I recommend this to my clients? It depends.
For people who struggle with weight loss, the first step is to understand the underlying reason for their struggle, whether it be environment, lifestyle, psychological, or an underlying health condition. Only then can an action plan be structured, and GLP-1 could be a valid tool for some people. While you are on the drug, you need to do physical activity, get enough sleep and manage nutrition.
Sure, the last may become easier than before, but it still requires discipline – adding adequate protein, avoiding junk food, increasing your vegetable intake and drinking enough water. And during this window (we see this as a six- to 24-month window, depending on the person), shift your lifestyle to one that is sustainable and significantly better.
Shedding that old lifestyle and identity is a relevant part of this metamorphosis. It is not possible to undergo a simplistic change, i.e. take the drug, lose weight, be happy forever and ever. That isn’t going to happen, because there is a very high chance you will put it back on.
Is using Mounjaro a short cut?
I see a lot of moral dilemmas around taking this drug. Do I want to use a crutch? Do I want others to know that I use a crutch? How will this affect my social life? And of course, the wariness in taking a drug in a world where trust in Big Pharma is rightfully eroding.
I understand and empathise with most of these dilemmas. After all, would I trust a drug to only do positive things for me? I don’t think so. But if it serves the purpose and there’s no long-term cause for concern, then I would use the tool for the job. Because every day with subpar health is affecting you: that’s my simplistic thinking.
I also see people taking the drug and not seeing results because they refuse to take responsibility for their actions and lifestyle. These are people that no drug or coaching can help, until they choose to help themselves.
Most of us eat too much. We think about food too much. We have too many options. Year on year, our weight-loss resolutions don’t change. And neither does our weight. We don’t struggle with knowing what to do. The people I’ve coached over 15 years struggle with food noise. With an environment that makes it hard to be healthy. And life getting in the way — work, stress, kids, the usual.
The drug silences that noise, and that’s why it feels like magic. It’s also why selling only the drug is dangerous: the day you stop, the struggle comes back. The injection is the simple part, but life isn’t always that way. Even Johann Hari, a journalist who took these drugs, lost 20 kilos, and wrote a book about them, refuses to call it a miracle. He calls himself one of the “guinea pigs” in a “mass experiment.”
It is a tool.
I profit from saying this, but I’m saying it anyway: the people selling you only the needle are selling a return ticket and calling it a journey. It buys you a window. What you build in that window is everything.
Disclaimer: This is a first-person account of a three-week self-experiment. It is not medical advice or a recommendation to use GLP-1 medicines without a prescription or medical supervision.
Arvind Ashok has coached strength and fitness for over 15 years. He is co-founder of The Quad and of Revivo Clinic, a metabolic-health practice that pairs medical care with lifestyle change.

Bengalis can eat meat: Bengal BJP chief pushes back on Dhirendra Shastri's veg call
West Bengal BJP chief Samik Bhattacharya rejected Dhirendra Krishna Shastri's appeal to avoid non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja, saying Bengalis are free to eat what they choose. He said Shastri could advocate vegetarianism but not impose his views on Bengalis.
West Bengal BJP chief Samik Bhattacharya on Monday pushed back against Bageshwar Dham chief Dhirendra Krishna Shastri's appeal to Bengalis to avoid non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja, saying no religious figure or political party could dictate what people in the state should eat or wear.
Bhattacharya sought to assure Bengalis that food choices were a matter of personal freedom and that West Bengal's traditional food habits could not be changed at the behest of a visiting religious figure. "We eat what we eat," he said.
"What one eats or wears is a personal choice. Bengal's food culture is diverse, and everyone has the freedom to follow their own preferences. Won't Bengalis have fish or mutton? Even Swami Vivekananda approved of it. No saint, leader, or anyone else has the right to decide what you should eat. Personal choice must remain personal," Bhattacharya said.
During his recent visit to Howrah, Shastri, popularly known as Bageshwar Baba, had appealed to people to avoid non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja and described those who consume it during the festive season as pakhandis (hypocrites).
Responding to the remarks, Bhattacharya said Shastri had the right to advocate vegetarianism, but his views could not be imposed on Bengali society.
"We cannot say much about a saintly figure. His kathas are famous across the country and hundreds of thousands of people went to Howrah to listen to him. Anyone can advocate for vegetarianism and that doesn't make it a crime or a sin. However, if someone uses a word like hypocrite, we do not endorse that," he said.
Bhattacharya said traditional Bengali food practices included non-vegetarian offerings and meals during religious festivals. "I am a political worker. What a sadhu says here or a maulvi says there – what does that have to do with us?" he said, adding that Durga Puja was approaching and Bengalis traditionally eat luchi (poori) on Ashtami and kochi patha (goat meat) on Navami.
"Here, goat meat is offered as an offering to Maa Kali," Bhattacharya said, arguing that West Bengal's religious traditions themselves do not conform to a blanket vegetarian prescription.
The remarks came days after Shastri's visit to West Bengal, where he held religious programmes across the state. His visit had also acquired political overtones, with the Bageshwar Dham chief able to hold programmes under the BJP government despite allegations that he had faced difficulties in obtaining permission during the previous Trinamool Congress regime.
Before Shastri's avoid 'non-veg during Durga Puja' call, the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) urged Durga Puja organisers in West Bengal to preserve traditional practices and keep non-vegetarian food away from pandals. But, the outfit clarified that it was not seeking a ban on non-vegetarian food.
Bhattacharya's intervention makes clear that the BJP government in West Bengal does not endorse any blanket prescription on vegetarianism during Durga Puja.
State minister Dilip Ghosh echoed Bhattacharya's remarks, saying that offering meat to Goddess Kali has been a long-standing tradition for decades.
"The situation in Bengal is different. People here are devotees of Goddess Kali, and animal sacrifices are offered to Her, as well as to many other deities. Sacrifices are even offered to Goddess Durga on Navami, and the meat is consumed as prasad. Fish is even offered to the deity as prasad. This is a long-standing tradition that has persisted for ages," he said.
SANJEEV SANYAL REACTS TO SHASTRI'S VEG CALL
Noted economist Sanjeev Sanyal also weighed in on the controversy without naming Shastri. In a post on X, Sanyal said meat was "core to Shakta Hinduism" and was offered to Maa Durga and Maa Kali as part of ancient rituals.
"The prasad eaten by the devotees on Navami/Dasami at Durga Puja is meat. Any interference in this sacred ritual will not be tolerated," he said.
The controversy has opened a wider debate in West Bengal over the intersection of religious observance, personal food choices and the state's distinctive cultural traditions, where fish and meat have long formed an integral part of the Bengali diet.

A closely watched cardiovascular drug from Novartis failed in a pivotal study, the company said Friday, a major blow to the firm and to efforts to target a common heart disease risk factor.
The drug, called pelacarsen, had shown in earlier trials that it could drastically lower levels of what’s called Lp(a), a little blob of lipids and proteins that at elevated concentrations increases the likelihood of severe heart problems.
But Novartis said that in the Phase 3 HORIZON trial, pelacarsen failed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death or emergencies like heart attacks or stroke compared to placebo.
