If you opt for an Android phone over an iPhone, there are certain features you get as standard as part of Android. Then there are other features specific to certain manufacturers, as each Android phone maker puts its own spin on the software.
Pixel phones, for example, get the Now Playing widget on the home screen and lock screen that works like an instant Shazam. It'll tell you the name of the song playing in your environment before you've even searched for it.
With Samsung phones, one of the best perks isn't as widely known about or used as it should be. It's called the Edge Panel, and it works like a customizable shortcut bar that gives you speedy access to the other parts of your phone.
If you own a Galaxy device and have never come across the Edge Panel, or you used it once but have since forgotten about it, here's what it's capable of now—and how you can make the most of it to optimize your mobile experience.
How the Edge Panel Works
You can think of the Edge Panel as being a little bit like the Start menu on Windows, or the dock on macOS. It provides something that Android doesn't have by default, which is a user-configurable launcher for collecting your favorite apps and feature shortcuts.
When it's enabled, the Edge Panel appears as a faint line along the side of the screen, and you can swipe across it to open the pane. If you don't see it, head to Settings and choose Display > Edge Panels to turn it on (via the toggle switch) or customize what the panels show (by tapping the menu entry).
There are actually seven different types of panel to choose from, as you'll see when you start to customize the feature: Apps, People, Tasks, Weather, Tools, Clipboard, and Reminder. You can have just one of them active, or all seven, or something in between (once you've got the Edge Panel up, swipe across it to switch between the different types).
The names of these panels give you some idea of what they can do. You can use the Apps panel to access the apps you use the most, without having to hunt for them in the main app drawer or having them clutter up your home screen. You can also jump to your most important people on the Contacts panel in the same way.
The Clipboard panel gives you quick access to the phone clipboard, while Tasks features shortcuts such as taking screenshots, adding new calendar events, adding alarms, and taking a screenshot. Having these shortcuts on the Edge Panel means you don't have to dig through menus or remember key combinations for the same functions.
Tools is actually just a single tool: a compass that tells you your current location and points you north, south, east, or west. Weather is pretty self-explanatory, while Reminder syncs information from the Reminder app that comes preinstalled on Galaxy devices.
Customize the Edge Panel
The Edge Panel works fine in its default state, but to make the most of it you really need to set it up to suit you and the way you use your phone. From the main Settings menu, choose Display, then tap Edge Panels.
First, select Panels to pick which panes are shown. Put a check next to the panes you want to have available. If you tap the three dots (top right) then Reorder, you're able to choose the order they appear in as well—place the panes you use most often furthest to the left, as they'll be available in fewer swipes.
You can also tap the three dots then Hide on Lock screen if you don't want the Edge Panel to appear before you've unlocked your phone. Bear in mind that you might not want some information—such as the contents of the clipboard or your reminders—being available to anyone who picks up your handset.
With Apps, People, and Tasks, you can customize what's included. Just tap the Edit button underneath the pane. In each case, there are more available options than there are slots on the Edge Panel, so you need to prioritize accordingly.
Back on the Edge Panels screen, there are a couple of other options worth knowing about. If you pick Handle, you can set the properties of the little onscreen strip that Edge Panel is activated through. Pick the size and transparency level of the handle, its color, and which side of the screen it appears on.
Finally, there's the Show in landscape mode toggle switch; disable this if you don't want to see the Edge panel when you're using your phone in its landscape orientation. This mode is mainly used for watching videos and playing games, in which case the Edge Panel and its handle might distract you.

Drones force Amritsar airport shutdown, send 7 flights to Delhi, Chandigarh
As per the standard operating procedure (SOP) for drone sightings, a committee was formed to assess if the drone activity could pose a threat
Operations at Amritsar airport were suspended for more than an hour on Sunday night after drones were spotted over the airport, forcing seven aircraft holding for landing to be diverted, officials aware of the matter said.
According to people aware of the matter, the airport was closed for operations at around 9.50pm after the Indian Air Force (IAF) informed the Air Traffic Control (ATC) about drone activity across the airfield.
“Around seven flights thus had to be diverted, to Chandigarh and Delhi because planes scheduled to land at Amritsar were already holding near the airport area,” an Airports Authority of India (AAI) official said.

“Two of the flights were diverted to Chandigarh and five of them were diverted to Delhi. These five included two flights each of Air India, IndiGo and one of Air India Express,” a Delhi airport official said.
As per the standard operating procedure (SOP) for drone sightings, a committee was formed to assess if the drone activity could pose a threat to aircraft movements.
After assessing the situation, the committee decided to temporarily suspend the flight operations at the airport at around 9.50 pm,” the AAI official added.
Another official aware of the development said, “The committee reviewed the situation around 11 pm because no more drones were seen or reported around the airport. The airport was thus cleared to resume operations at 11.15pm.”
Five of the seven diverted flights later returned to Amritsar.
One of the passengers posted on X and said, “ #Amritsar airport was apparently closed for landings for almost 2 hours tonight. Our Dubai → Amritsar flight kept circling overhead before eventually being diverted to Delhi. We’ve now landed in Delhi… and the latest update is that the same aircraft will apparently fly back to Amritsar once the airport reopens. What a night. And honestly, full credit to the Air India Express crew — they handled the whole situation incredibly calmly, kept everyone updated and never let the uncertainty turn into panic. The airport closure is a story. The crew’s handling of it deserves an appreciation post.”
An airline official said that the airline had enough fuel to hold for over an hour.
“The flight IX 138 was scheduled to land in Amritsar at 10.40pm. It had to be diverted to Delhi, however, it landed back in Amritsar.”
The Dubai - Amritsar is one of the busiest routes for the airport. Apart from Delhi and Mumbai, the airport has regular flights between the two destinations.

The response
While I appreciate Drs. MacKenzie and Rajput for helping to shine a light on the bias and unfair challenges graduates of osteopathic medical schools face in residency placements, the answer is not for D.O. grads to surrender and give up the principles and practices that they bring to the health care system. While it may be hard for some M.D. physicians to understand, the separate pathways are more than just logistics. Organizations, examinations, accreditation systems, and professional structures matter, but they are not what makes osteopathic medical education worth preserving.
We need to preserve something much more fundamental: the cognitive architecture of osteopathic medical education. By cognitive architecture, I mean the intentional organization of knowledge, experiences, scientific disciplines, and professional values to shape how physicians perceive, reason through, and solve clinical and health system problems. Every allopathic medical school (M.D.) teaches biomedical and clinical science. Increasingly, they teach health systems science as well. The distinction between allopathic and osteopathic education is not whether these subjects exist elsewhere. The distinction is how they are intentionally integrated.
Osteopathic principles and practices are more than just an add-on elective. Osteopathic medical education intentionally integrates biomedical, clinical, health systems and biomechanical sciences, and concepts aligned with complexity science into a coherent framework for physician formation. Osteopathic philosophy serves as the integrative lens through which these domains influence clinical reasoning. For the D.O. community, the result is physicians who strive to excel at both promoting and maintaining health and treating disease; who value relationships as well as diagnoses; who recognize that structure and function are linked; who appreciate context, adaptation, prevention, and community; and who use medical, surgical, manual, behavioral, and social interventions as complementary tools in patient care.
Given the incredible growth of osteopathic medical education, this philosophy and these principles are resonating with prospective medical students and patients in record numbers. Today, about 30% of all medical students in the U.S. are educated at a college of osteopathic medicine, and that percentage is growing every year. Those students deserve equal opportunities, and that is why the American Association of Colleges of Osteopathic Medicine is working with our peers in the medical community and why we’re supporting the Fair Access in Residency (FAIR) Act. The answer to our nation’s physician shortage crisis is to fully open the doors to residency for all qualified candidates, not to close the door on those who choose the osteopathic pathway.
— Robert Cain, American Association of Colleges of Osteopathic Medicine
The response
Excellent article and well researched. Most of my colleagues never knew or cared that I was a D.O. They cared more about the care I offered and whether I could accept constructive criticism when it was due. I completely agree with the article, but I think the credentialing boards generate so much revenue that they are reluctant to combine (and possibly line their pockets a little less) and work together. Perhaps we even do away with the maintenance of certification altogether. Isn’t passing boards and maintaining continuing medical education credits, along with the threat of lawsuits always looming, enough to ensure we keep up with the science?
— Sharon McKelvey
The response
There are more differences in the training of M.D. students and D.O. students than just the modality of osteopathic manipulative treatment. The entire approach to the patient is different. Holism (a term that has been grossly overused and misunderstood) is a tenet that stresses a more global understanding of a patient and all that influences their health and well-being. This approach begins in year one and continues throughout all (usually) four years. D.O. training focuses heavily on history and physical diagnosis and tends to create a higher percentage of primary care providers because of this broad approach. All facets of scientific evidence-based medicine and surgery are taught and complementary, and alternative medicine is not avoided. In fact, osteopathic manipulative medicine focusing on circulation and innervation is a central modality during training.
Most of us who have spent careers as osteopathic physicians in a largely allopathic American health care system have learned to value and embrace these unique aspects. Vive la différence!
— Alfred Sassler, University of Cincinnati Medical Center/UC Health
The story
“AI won’t enhance physician autonomy. It will further diminish it,” by Frances Mei Hardin
The response
Thank you for this article. I couldn’t agree more that “lack-of-autonomy creep” has been happening for a long time. It would be OK if the new structures and “tools” were mostly in the service of better patient care, but let’s be honest, most new “advancements” are not. As the author points out, our autonomy has been removed from us piece by piece. The power is in the hands of the owners of the means of production, and that is not the doctors. We are the workers, not the factory owner, albeit well-paid ones, which is one reason we don’t complain. How can money-driven incentives improve patient outcomes?
Let’s be honest about that. Venture capital couldn’t care about patient outcomes as much as we do. AI will be deployed for cost savings primarily. The AI we happily use for our notes will be the loser to the AI the insurance companies use to tell us we have “overcoded.” Physicians are suffering from a history of autonomy that is currently an illusion. This long-defunct echo prevents us from organizing and exerting the power we do have to influence our destiny. I am by no means a Marxist, but in this case the metaphor is apt. We have gone from being respected autonomous experts to unempowered, well-paid “factory workers.” The attribution of liability that the author references is but one example.
The answer is to not passively accept what is given but to organize to make our voices heard. And sorry, our professional organizations as they currently exist are not the answer, as they are in bed with corporate (insurance, pharma) interests, something almost too obvious to have to state.
— Jody Whitehouse, M.D.
The story
“Whale songs: the sounds of love and loss as heard by an OB-GYN,” by Caroline Cherston
The response
These observations rang true to me because of my experience working in the pit right after Sept. 11. My therapy dog and I accompanied grieving families to ground zero in the days following the attacks. Mothers accompanied by their adult children would arrive at the still burning disaster, still in denial that their child had been killed. Once there, staring at the devastation, there was no denying the reality of death. These women would scream a very distinctive wail, something I had never heard before and will never forget. As a park ranger living with brown bears in Alaska, I have witnessed what I interpret as grief when a sow loses a cub. Now I work at a national park where we teach our visitors about whales. Grief is human, grief is universal. Would that we studied it more and embraced its process.
— Naomi Boak, National Park Service
The story
“The Lindsay Clancy case shows the limits of postpartum psychiatry,” by Jamie Maguire, Lauren M. Osborne, and Jennifer Payne
The response
The authors are right on the mark arguing that scientific knowledge on postpartum psychopathology is lacking, and that this gap is likely to have played a role in the tragic Clancy case. I agree with their argument whereby the major flaw of extant knowledge is lack of precision, particularly concerning risk factors for developing severe, even lethal, conditions. Most importantly, by focusing on science, the authors steer the discussion away from (unsubstantiated) claims about psychiatry’s negligence and toward where we, collectively (science, mental health services, policymakers, and the public) should head to prevent such tragedies. I particularly identify with the article’s ending, which suggests that ultimately, precision enables compassion.
One aspect, however, is conspicuously absent from the authors’ vision: the role of clinical psychological science in achieving such precision. The past four decades have seen a proliferation of methodologies enabling increasingly precise assessment of risk and protective factors in psychopathology, including psychometrically sophisticated self-report measures, investigator-based semi-structured interviews, computerized tasks targeting cognitive-affective processes, and the validation of these methodologies against neural processes and overt behavior.
Perhaps the most intriguing risk factor for psychopathology gleaned from clinical psychological science, and one that is particularly relevant to the assessment and treatment of postpartum psychopathology, is malignant self-criticism. Defined as the tendency to set impossibly high self-standards and to adopt a punitive self-stance once these standards are (inevitably) unmet, self-criticism emerged as a robust predictor of virtually all forms of psychopathology, including suicide and violent behavior. Self-criticism has also been shown to derail evidence-based psychotherapeutic and psychopharmacological treatment of depression, even though more recent studies have shown that self-criticism responds well to distinct forms of treatment.
Importantly, such research demonstrated the formidable risk associated with self-criticism for postpartum depression and anxiety, as well as for disruptions in mother-child communication, which might exacerbate postpartum psychopathology.
Of course, we cannot know the extent to which malignant self-criticism played a role — if any — in the Clancy case. Other psychological risk factors may be in play. The bottom line, however, is that psychiatry and psychology should not compete over markers. Rather, they must join forces, in science and practice, in identifying a wide spectrum of factors that increase vulnerability to the chilling outcome manifested by the Clancy case and other tragic ones. The aim, therefore, is biopsychosocial precision in mental health science and practice.
— Golan Shahar, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev
The story
“8 steps to making surrogacy more ethical for everyone involved,” by Arthur Caplan
The response
The problem is with the very concept of “surrogacy,” which means acting on behalf of someone else. Our ideas of surrogacy are based on a patriarchal notion that the essence of the baby is in the seed. While the original idea was that men had the seeds, medicine eventually had to acknowledge that women have seeds too, and babies are thus “half his and half hers.” Our society, and this discussion, claim that the real, the meaningful relationship is with the seed, and the pregnant woman is just a place, a spot you plant the precious seed. (In ordinary English we refer to the earth itself as dirt, soil in which we plant seeds.)
But pregnancy is not a location — it is a relationship. Babies are born recognizing the language the pregnant woman spoke. The comfort “rocking” offers a baby is its duplication of the walking motion. Hiring someone to be the location disregards the relationship. Can I hire someone else to be the wife for a husband, live with him, interact physically and socially — and then fire her, take him back, claim she was only a surrogate? We need to acknowledge and respect the relationship that is pregnancy.
— Barbara Katz Rothman, City University of New York
The story
“Medical aid in dying and the burden of choosing to live,” by Monika Piotrowska
The response
I am 82 years old and still healthy, but — let’s face it — for how much longer? The analogy the author makes between a student learning that they are not doing well academically and facing the inevitability of dying does not work for me at all. The author speaks of autonomy, and I don’t understand that, either. Because my husband has died of dementia with no autonomy at all and it wasn’t pretty. Because I want to be able to decide I am ready to die and I know that I soon will be ready to die (but still hoping to outlive Trump). I have had a long and really wonderful life and I am content. What I fear is burdening others with my care. I don’t want to impose that on my children. I want to be able to make the choice about the timing of my death so as to retain my autonomy and my ability to make choices, to have quality, not quantity of life. MAiD promises this to me, and is such a tremendous relief.
— Nora Staffanell
The story
“AI has created a shadow medical system,” by Arya Rao and Marc Succi
The response
In their recent essay on AI and the “shadow medical system,” Arya Rao and Marc Succi close with the 1979 IBM assertion that “A computer can never be held accountable, therefore a computer must never make a management decision.” Applied to health care, that claim has been outdated at least since 2018. That was the year LumineticsCore received the first FDA de novo clearance for an autonomous medical diagnosis — diabetic retinopathy — and began carrying malpractice insurance for its no-clinician-in-the-loop system. And just this year, Doctronic launched a prescription-renewal pilot that has some physician oversight, but not over every clinical decision made by the AI. Accordingly, Doctronic also carries a malpractice policy holding the system to physician-level accountability.
The problem of AI accountability for health decisions is real and important. It is no longer accurate to say it is unsolved.
— Joel Selanikio, M.D., futurehealth.live
The response
While the article makes several insightful points about AI assuming clinician responsibilities, the bigger picture should be on who is accountable for those decisions. Rao and Succi correctly identify accountability as the dividing line between a useful medical tool and a functioning medical system. Accountability is more complicated than ensuring a physician remains nominally involved. “Human oversight” becomes meaningless when responsibility and authority are separated.
We’ve seen this problem with clinical decision support for years. Technology identifies an abnormality or recommends action, while the difficult question — who owns the next step? — remains unanswered. AI makes that long-standing design failure much more consequential. If the default is to lay accountability at the clinician’s feet, we are in danger of creating an unsustainable system. A clinician cannot meaningfully be accountable for AI decisions if they did not select the model, cannot interrogate its reasoning, cannot see its underlying data, or do not have a realistic opportunity to intervene.
The American Medical Association has called for transparency, accountability, physician oversight, regular auditing, and clearer standards around AI-enabled clinical decision support. It has also argued that liability should be appropriately apportioned rather than automatically falling on physicians. “Human in the loop” is not an accountability model. Requiring a clinician to approve an AI-generated recommendation may create the appearance of oversight without giving that clinician genuine control. “Clinicians must review an AI output” is closer to a disclaimer than a governance policy unless an organization clearly defines where human judgment is required and leaves space for clinicians to exercise that judgment.
That thinking applies to the shadow system. A click, signature, or brief review should not magically transfer responsibility from an AI developer or platform to a physician. Accountability has to extend beyond the diagnosis to the care loop. Technology often succeeds at identifying a problem while failing to establish who owns what happens next. We must design clinical systems around explicit responsibility and completion of the care process, rather than merely generating alerts or recommendations. This idea maps to Rao and Succi’s concern about AI correctly identifying abnormal lab values and the trail of questions that follow: Who confirms it? Who determines its significance in context? Who ensures follow-up occurs? Who recognizes when the algorithm missed the dangerous alternative diagnosis? That’s where “answering a medical question” becomes practicing medicine.
— Craig Joseph

How St Helens let Super League success become long-term stagnation - the flap of a wing!
Sky Sports' Megan Wellens dissects how St Helens succumbed to their worst-ever Super League finish in 2026; the regular Betfred Super League season concludes with Round 27 from Thursday September 10 live on Sky Sports
Monday 7 September 2026 13:48, UK
The dust has settled on the fact that St Helens have missed out on play-off rugby for the first time after their seventh-placed finish in Super League.
The analytical dissection of how this happened has been ongoing by fans and pundits for the best part of two years. Some supporters would say longer.
The next 12 months will give an indication of how long those with power inside the four walls of the club have realised that their trajectory has been downwards.
The famous question posed by meteorologist Edward Lorenz back in the 1970s was 'can the flap of a butterfly's wing in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?'
Can the smallest of changes lead to significant outcomes in the most complex of systems?
If this low ebb for Saints is their tornado, what exactly was the flap of the wing? What exactly caused the chaos?
For that, we need to rewind to 2019, when they picked up their first Super League title in five years.
2019: The start of a run like never before
Midway through 2018, St Helens were sitting mid-table and made the decision to part ways with head coach Keiron Cunningham and bring in Justin Holbrook.
After a Luke Gale drop goal saw Saints heartbreakingly fall in the semi-finals in 2018, 2019 marked the year when they were simply the best team around.
The Saints obliterated the competition in 2019, losing just three matches and cantering to the top of the league.
Their 23-6 win over Salford Red Devils in the Grand Final was the moment that cemented that St Helens were here once again.
It was a star-studded team with the likes of Jonny Lomax, Tommy Makinson, Alex Walmsley and Lachlan Coote all in their mid-to-late 20s and in their prime. A mix of homegrown talent and hand-picked Australian superstars was running the show.
They had to then overcome a change of head coach but, under Kristian Woolf, success would continue...
2020-2023: Four in a row leads to climbing Everest
Woolf has spoken openly about the fact that the season shutting down due to Covid potentially saved his job.
Woolf's team had just lost to Huddersfield Giants and Castleford Tigers when the season went on hiatus.
By the time it returned, he had spoken with his playing group about what more they wanted from him and how they wanted things to run. A collaboration between a stern coach and a group striving for success - and continuing to achieve it - was born.
Jack Welsby scored one of the best Grand Final tries ever seen in 2020 and then two more Super League wins followed. Not only that, they won a Challenge Cup and a League Leaders' Shield.
Then they do the unthinkable...
World Club Challenge: Everest complete
When St Helens headed down under for the World Club Challenge in 2023, no one believed they could beat Penrith Panthers.
Hometown head coach Paul Wellens moved from captain and player to assistant coach, and after over 10 years in the coaching game at the club, he had stepped up to the top job.
Then, Lewis Dodd sent over a golden-point drop goal that is lauded as one of the most seismic moments in the sport in this country.
They had climbed to the top of Everest and planted the St Helens flag.
You have won it all, your players have provided every success you have asked for.
So what is the next task? Is it starting a transition period? Is it trusting this same group of players to provide once again? Is it a mix of both?
St Helens went for option B...
Salary cap bites
Big players were winning big and getting their reward, deservedly so. But in a salary-capped sport, there comes a time where that may start to bite.
By this point, the likes of Makinson, Lomax, Walmsley, Mark Percival, Louis McCarthy-Scarsbrook and Sione Mata'utia had brought unprecedented success. They were also now mostly in their 30s.
Naturally, with that, comes upgraded contracts. Simply put - you win more you deserve to earn more.
But, if contracts are being upgraded year on year, the space on a salary cap dwindles. Your chance to bring in big names dwindles. Your room for youngsters to be earning well dwindles.
A sum of £2.1m only stretches so far and you need to be ruthlessly pragmatic. Or players need to be willing to earn less than what they were receiving in their 20s. A tough sell!
Over the next three seasons under Wellens, St Helens would make just 11 signings to replace the likes of Regan Grace, James Roby, Will Hopoate, Makinson, Lewis Dodd and Mata'utia.
Those signings were Tee Ritson, Wesley Bruines, Daryl Clark, Waqa Blake, Kyle Feldt, Tristan Sailor, Lewis Murphy, Moses Mbye, Matt Whitley, Shane Wright and Deon Cross.
Wright and Cross only became available due to the financial collapse of Salford Red Devils.
Some would argue those big boots have still not been filled. Or if they have been filled, the successor has not matched up to their predecessor.
Moneyball gone wrong?
Back in 2025, former St Helens CEO Mike Rush described the club's recruitment strategy as 'Moneyball'.
Moneyball is a term coined from Michael Lewis' book which analysed how, in 2002, Oakland Athletics and their general manager Billy Beane used a statistical approach that saw them sign players whose skills might be being undervalued on traditional methods of scouting.
You sign players to fulfil particular roles, for example making lots of tackles or making metres, knowing they lack in other areas, so that you can still compete despite being hampered by a budget.
"We're always going to get stuff wrong because whether it's an overseas player or not, you take risks and you gamble," Rush told Sky Sports.
"Context is, and without divulging personal business, it's a salary-cap sport. You're putting certain numbers on players' heads that you believe they're worth.
"Without people knowing the salary-cap value, it's very difficult. It's where that person sits on our cap [that determines] if we get value.
"It's much more detailed than just picking a certain player and saying, 'is he playing well?'
"Waqa Blake played in an NRL Grand Final. That doesn't make him a great player, but for what we had available in our cap or for what we valued the player at, it was worth a chance to do."
So, you gamble and sign what you think is value for money. But did that mean St Helens built a cost-effective squad of players who did not deliver what was asked of them?
One thing that is for sure is that they did not replace like for like.
"I've said it a number of times but Saints' recruitment has been shocking," Sky Sports' Jon Wilkin said.
"It's been terrible. They've made convenient and short-term recruitment choices. They've not replaced like for like and they need to rethink their recruitment strategy.
"There's a lot of young guys who have gone out into Super League who aren't ready. I'm loving that, it is great for them and for their future.
"But the reason they're out there was because you had an old squad at the start of the year that wasn't durable enough to get through a year, and then you signed shoddy replacements for guys who moved on."
Not only that, St Helens are not the spending force they once were. It is not just the 'Super League giants' with cash to burn. Obviously, Wigan have got richer, but Wakefield now have money, as do York, Leigh and more.
More clubs are offering better and Saints are being outcompeted in the wage stakes.
Wellens to Rowley to Walters...
If quality drops, senior players age and suffer injuries, and more is asked of youngsters, then naturally, outcomes of seasons will change.
Lomax and Percival have managed just 14 games between them in 2026. They do not offer what they once did.
Wellens, Roby and Rush also all left the club in a quick span of time. That is three people who have had eyes on St Helens' successes and failures, consistently since the 1990s.
They lost stalwart and skipper Matty Lees to injury early in the season and have not had him as the enforcer on the pitch. They also lost their other enforcer in Morgan Knowles to the NRL.
St Helens fans did not enjoy the attritional approach to rugby under Wellens that brought them third, sixth and fifth-placed finishes that saw them make the play-off semi-finals twice in those three seasons.
The club decided that those results, with the roster available, were not good enough and change was needed. With that, they brought in Paul Rowley to turn the club's fortunes around on a three-year deal.
Rowley lasted less than a season at Saints before being sacked ahead of the fixture against rivals Wigan Warriors in Round 20 back in July.
It is unknown how the season in full would have shaped under Rowley given the raft of injuries that St Helens faced and the clear signs that his systems were not embedding into a club that has a very specific DNA.
What we do know is they finished seventh.
Now they have turned to Australia head coach Kevin Walters to get things back on track.
St Helens legend James Graham said on his podcast, The Bye Round, that he had sent Walters a YouTube video of all of Saints' greatest wins to show him just why they have the tagline 'Never write off the Saints'.
Walters is renowned for maintaining strong environments and being an advocate for his players. He is already teasing big signings he is making.
The noises from St Helens are that they are now reverting to splashing the cash to ensure the quality on the field matches the expectations off it.
Chaos theory...
The question posed was what was St Helens' 'flap of a wing'. What were the small, incremental changes made that ended in this tornado.
Frankly, it seems that what caused their tornado in 2026 is that they spent four years not flapping their wings at all.
They say in sport, if you are not evolving you are falling behind. Those at St Helens can say they could not see this outcome occurring.
But this is not a random outcome. It was predetermined when option B was chosen - the option of standing still and attempting to not cause disruption by flapping your wings.

Singapore ministers set for pay rise up to US$1.4 million entry benchmark
First pay update since 2012 aims to stop political salaries ‘falling further behind’ market rates, the prime minister says
The entry-level ministerial salary benchmark will rise to S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) from S$1.1 million, while the prime minister’s pay benchmark will increase to S$3.6 million from S$2.2 million, in line with recommendations made by an independent committee.
Wong said during a ministerial statement in parliament on Tuesday that he would donate the increase in his salary to “suitable good causes” but did not expect other political office holders to follow suit.
As prime minister, he said he held the “ultimate responsibility” for the salary framework. “So I want to be clear about how I will personally handle the increase and why I am taking these changes forward, because I believe they are in Singapore’s interests.”
The review was conducted by an eight-member committee formed in January, after a deferment amid geopolitical uncertainty arising from the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. The review, which is held once every five years, was initially set for 2023.
Wong said the government had accepted the committee’s recommendations, but it did not intend to implement them all at once.

Arunachal Pradesh – A Living Treasure of Biodiversity
Arunachal Pradesh is one of India’s most biologically diverse states, where forests, rivers, wetlands, mountains and communities are part of one interconnected ecological landscape. Its extraordinary range of habitats supports thousands of plant and animal species, including several rare, endemic and threatened species.
The State’s biodiversity is shaped by its remarkable variation in altitude and climate. From tropical forests in the foothills to temperate forests, alpine meadows and high-altitude ecosystems, Arunachal Pradesh offers a continuous range of habitats within a relatively compact geographical area.
With more than 80 per cent of its geographical area under forest cover, the State plays an important role in maintaining the ecological balance of the Eastern Himalayas. It is also part of the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, one of the world’s globally recognised regions of exceptional biological richness and conservation importance.
A Landscape of Remarkable Ecological Diversity
The geographical diversity of Arunachal Pradesh is reflected in its forests. Depending on altitude and climatic conditions, the State has tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, moist deciduous forests, subtropical broad-leaved forests, pine forests, temperate forests, coniferous forests, sub-alpine vegetation and alpine meadows.
This remarkable transition from the warm foothills to the high Himalayas creates habitats for species with very different ecological requirements.
The State is home to more than 5,000 species of flowering plants, around 600 species of orchids, about 75 species of rhododendrons, 45 species of bamboo, 17 species of cane and hundreds of medicinal plants. Arunachal Pradesh is particularly renowned for its orchid and rhododendron diversity.
The forests also support a remarkable variety of mammals, including the tiger, leopard, clouded leopard, snow leopard, golden cat, marbled cat, Asiatic elephant, red panda, takin, hoolock gibbon and several other rare and threatened species.
A Paradise for Birds
Arunachal Pradesh is equally celebrated for its avian diversity. Its forests and mountain ecosystems provide habitats for hundreds of bird species, making the State one of the most important birding regions in India.
The Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary in West Kameng is one of the best examples of this extraordinary richness. Located within the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, Eaglenest is home to a wide variety of hornbills, pheasants, kingfishers and other birds. The sanctuary is also known for the discovery of the Bugun liocichla, a bird named after the Bugun community that lives in the region.
Protecting Arunachal’s Wildlife
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is protected through an extensive network of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, tiger reserves and other conservation landscapes.
The state is home to important protected areas such as Namdapha National Park and Tiger Reserve, Kamlang Tiger Reserve, Pakke Tiger Reserve, Mouling National Park, Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, Sessa Orchid Sanctuary, Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, among others.
These landscapes support an exceptional range of wildlife, from high-altitude species such as the snow leopard and red panda to tropical forest species including the clouded leopard, hoolock gibbon and numerous birds, reptiles and amphibians.
Recent wildlife surveys have continued to expand scientific knowledge of these ecosystems. A 2024 WWF-India survey in Arunachal’s high-altitude rangelands recorded six wild cat species, including photographic evidence of the elusive Pallas’s cat, marking the first such photographic record from the state. The survey used 136 camera traps across 83 locations, covering approximately 2,000 sq km.
The Orchids of Arunachal Pradesh
Among the many botanical treasures of the State, orchids hold a special place.
Arunachal Pradesh has one of the richest orchid assemblages in India, with hundreds of species occurring across its varied habitats. The Sessa Orchid Sanctuary in West Kameng was established in 1979 to conserve and study orchids in their natural habitats. The sanctuary has recorded a remarkable diversity of orchid species, including epiphytic and terrestrial orchids.
The Orchid Research and Development Centre at Tipi further strengthens conservation and research efforts. Its facilities include orchid species houses, natural orchidaria, a herbarium, tissue culture laboratory, museum and hardening units. These initiatives support both ex-situ conservation and the rehabilitation of orchids in their natural habitats.
Glaw Lake: Arunachal Pradesh’s First Ramsar Site
A landmark development came in August 2026, when Glaw Lake, located within the Kamlang Tiger Reserve in Lohit district, was designated as India’s 101st Ramsar Site and became Arunachal Pradesh’s first Ramsar Site.
Situated at an elevation of around 1,168 metres, Glaw Lake covers approximately 82 hectares and forms part of the catchment of the Kamlang, Lang and Lati rivers, which flow into the Lohit River. The lake is recognised by the State Forest Department as an important repository of aquatic biodiversity.
Its Ramsar designation gives international recognition to the ecological importance of the wetland and strengthens the focus on its conservation and sustainable management. The recognition is also significant for Arunachal Pradesh’s wider efforts to protect wetlands and the ecosystems and communities that depend on them.
A State Where New Discoveries Continue
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity story is still being written.
Recent scientific discoveries demonstrate how much remains to be documented within the State’s forests and mountains. The rare plant Vaccinium piliferum, a relative of the wild blueberry that had not been documented for nearly 188 years, was rediscovered in Vijoynagar in Changlang district recently.
New orchid species have also been identified in different parts of the State, while researchers have recorded new cascade frog species from Arunachal Pradesh. In 2026, scientists also identified a new butterfly species, Euthalia zubeengargi, from Basar in Leparada district.
Such discoveries are a reminder that Arunachal Pradesh is not merely a repository of known species. Its forests and mountains continue to offer opportunities for scientific research and the discovery of life forms that may not yet be fully documented.
Biodiversity and Indigenous Knowledge
For generations, the indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh have lived closely with their natural surroundings. Forests provide food, medicinal plants, fibres, fuel and other resources, while traditional knowledge has helped communities understand seasonal changes, plants, wildlife and sustainable use of natural resources.
Today, this relationship is increasingly important to conservation.
A recent example comes from West Kameng, where indigenous communities are sustainably harvesting Zanthoxylum, locally known as Khagi, a wild Himalayan spice. The initiative has reportedly involved around 200 families while contributing to the protection of approximately 100 square kilometres of forest and generating livelihood opportunities.
Such efforts demonstrate that conservation and livelihoods can move together when local knowledge and sustainable practices are placed at the centre of biodiversity management.
Conservation: Protecting a Living Legacy
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is a natural asset of national and global importance. At the same time, ecosystems across the world are facing growing pressures from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, invasive species and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources.
Protecting Arunachal’s biodiversity therefore requires more than creating protected areas. It calls for habitat restoration, scientific research, responsible tourism, community participation, sustainable livelihoods and greater awareness among citizens.
The State’s protected areas, community conservation initiatives, biodiversity documentation programmes and institutions dedicated to research and conservation all contribute to this larger effort.
Looking Ahead
The story of Arunachal Pradesh is inseparable from its forests, rivers, mountains and wildlife. Its biodiversity sustains ecosystems, supports livelihoods, enriches traditional knowledge and strengthens the ecological security of the Eastern Himalayas.
From the orchids of Sessa to the forests of Namdapha, from the bird-rich landscapes of Eaglenest to the wetlands of Glaw Lake, every ecosystem adds another chapter to the State’s natural heritage.
The recent recognition of Glaw Lake as a Ramsar Site is an important milestone, but it is also a reminder of the responsibility that comes with being home to such extraordinary natural wealth.
Arunachal Pradesh is a living treasury of biodiversity and conserving it is not only about protecting nature today, but ensuring that its forests continue to breathe, its rivers continue to flow, and its remarkable species continue to thrive for generations.

The numbers speak for themselves: Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), a party that dabbles in Nazi imagery, distinguishes between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and is too extreme even for France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, nearly doubled its score in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt to 43.8% of the vote.
Meanwhile, the centre-right CDU of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, collapsed to 17.2%, less than half its total in the same race five years ago, and the centre-left SPD – Germany’s other main party of government for the past 60-odd years – scraped 9.3%. The least that can be said is that the centre did not hold.
It is not yet clear whether the AfD, whose local branch in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as “confirmed rightwing extremist”, will be able to form a government: it has 39 lawmakers in the 83-member parliament, just short of an outright majority.
But the score is the party’s strongest-ever state result and puts it closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since the second world war. It has sent shock waves round Europe, with nationalists cheering a “historic win” that is “just the beginning” and mainstream leaders warning of a “grave moment” for Europe.
Sweden holds legislative elections next weekend. France faces a crunch presidential ballot next spring. Key parliamentary races will follow there, as well as in Italy, Spain and Poland, later in the year. Far-right parties are polling strongly in all of them, and Europe’s centre fears a continent-wide nationalist wave.
It would be wise not to read too much into one election result in one quite particular German state. Saxony-Anhalt, analysts note, is home to barely 1.8 million voters and has long been a far-right stronghold: in federal and state elections over the past decade, support for the AfD there has consistently been double the national average.
“A far-right party winning a regional election in Germany is not more scary than a far-right party winning a regional election in France, the UK or the Netherlands,” said Tarik Abou-Chadi, a professor of European politics at Oxford University. “Saxony-Anhalt should not be the basis for sweeping conclusions about the electoral sociology of the AfD.”
Nonetheless, the AfD leads in national polls. It is also ahead – although in a far tighter race, with the SPD – in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where state elections are due later this month, and it is lying second even in liberal Berlin. Its rise is part of a decade-long march by far-right parties across Europe.
Almost one in four voters in Europe now cast their ballot for far-right parties, according to research led by Matthijs Rooduijn, a political scientist at the University of Amsterdam, a proportion that has grown nearly fivefold since the mid-1990s and climbed particularly steeply over the past three years.
This analysis, by more than 150 political scientists in 31 countries, found that the proportion of Europeans voting for a far-right party in their country’s most recent national elections had risen in 2026 to more than 23%, from about 10% a decade ago and roughly 5% in 1995.
Far-right populist parties are now in government as part of ruling coalitions in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, propping up a rightwing minority government in Sweden, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany (and, until very recently, the UK).
They have also suffered recent defeats, including in the Netherlands, where Geert Wilders’s Freedom party (PVV) lost nearly a third of its seats to finish second last year, and Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz was comprehensively beaten by his centre-right rival in April.
But the trend seems clear. As Cas Mudde of the University of Georgia, a leading expert on Europe’s far right, put it after Orbán’s defeat: “The far right is here to stay, and many of its parties are as established as the (former) ‘mainstream’ parties. Like other parties, their electoral support fluctuates.”
That steady electoral advance has been achieved despite a refusal by mainstream parties in countries such as France and Germany to collaborate with far-right parties, prompting some commentators to argue that the “cordon sanitaire” or “firewall” has now failed, or even been counterproductive.
By keeping the AfD out, they argue, Germany’s mainstream parties have actually boosted it: the party has been protected from the compromises and failures inherent in government. At the same time, the centre has been “hollowed-out”: forced into uncomfortable, unstable alliances that agree on and – vitally – accomplish little, further frustrating voters and driving support for the extremes.
“There’s a self-reinforcing political dynamic that feeds the AfD’s rise,” said Mujtaba Rahman, of the Eurasia Group risk consultancy. “The weaker the election results, the less common ground in the coalition, the fewer the policy results. The fewer results, the bigger the frustration in the electorate, the bigger the AfD’s share of the vote.”
Many political scientists, however, say blaming the firewall is an excuse, and data suggests far-right parties do not in any case get weaker when they are in government, but become stronger: one recent study of more than 1,300 different governments in 57 countries found far-right parties that entered government averaged a score six percentage points higher come the next election.
Besides the persistent inability of mainstream governments to deliver for disillusioned voters hit by a spiralling cost of living crisis, it is above all the gradual mainstreaming and normalisation of the far right’s ideas that has driven – and continues to drive – its steady advance, political scientists argue.
Research suggests voter attitudes towards core far-right themes such as immigration have not changed significantly over time, but have become much more significant in their voting decisions: normalisation by the media and by mainstream parties that readily embrace far-right framing have legitimised far-right views.
“The entire debate about whether the cordon sanitaire is ‘successful’ or contributes to strengthening the far right completely misses the point,” said Gabriela Greilinger, an Austrian-Hungarian political scientist. “Far-right politics and policies already constantly take centre stage, whether or not the far right is in power. There is no cordon around their ideas.”

Kazakhstan, Hong Kong ‘can build biotech unicorns by linking talent and capital’
Top academic tells SCMP event there’s real opportunity to connect capital, ideas and state support across the two regions
Kazakhstan and Hong Kong could partner to build biotech unicorns – private start-ups valued at US$1 billion or more – by linking the Central Asian country’s strong tech workforce with the city’s global financial network, a top academic has said.
Huck-Hui Ng, dean of the school of medicine at Kazakhstan’s Nazarbayev University, said the nascent biotech sector in the country has already produced several start-ups in areas including artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health, and could build a “substantial” ecosystem with the right policies and government support.
Ng made the remarks on Monday at the South China Morning Post’s inaugural “China Conference: Central Asia 2026” in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana.
“There is a real opportunity to connect entrepreneurs with capital, ideas and government support across the two regions,” Ng said during a panel. “If we can bring those elements together, I believe many things can happen.”
Kazakhstan is pushing to become a regional healthcare hub, with the nation’s drug regulator in April becoming the first in Central Asia to win World Health Organization certification for meeting global standards.
The country has also attracted manufacturing investments from overseas drug makers, including companies in China, and it is rolling out AI to help with diagnosis at clinics nationwide.

Queiroz returns as Ghana head coach
- Published
Carlos Queiroz has been reappointed as head coach of Ghana's men's national team.
The 73-year-old, who had two spells as assistant manager at Manchester United under Sir Alex Ferguson, took charge of the Black Stars in April and led the side to the last 32 at this year's Fifa World Cup, where they were beaten 1-0 by Colombia.
Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat, but the Ghana Football Association (GFA) has decided to re-engage him for another spell in charge following internal discussions.
The GFA has not announced the length of his new deal but said he will prepare the team for "a successful new phase on the international stage".
"The GFA believes Queiroz's extensive international experience, technical expertise and knowledge of the Black Stars position him strongly to lead the team into this next chapter," a statement added.
Queiroz has previously led Iran, Portugal and Egypt at major tournaments and has had stints in charge of South Africa, Colombia and Qatar.
Further details on his mandate will be announced by the GFA in due course.
Queiroz said the chance to continue in the role gave him "immense pride and honour".
"Serving Ghana is far more than coaching a football team," he added in a post on Instagram.
"It is a privilege, a responsibility and a mission to honour one of Africa's greatest football nations and its incredible and passionate football people.
"Our ambition is clear: improve every day, unite the nation, make Ghana stronger and fight for every victory with passion, humility and pride. The mission continues."
Queiroz will begin his second spell in charge of the West Africans with qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, which begin later this month.
The Black Stars are yet to announce the dates and venues for their first two fixtures in Group C, where they have been drawn alongside Ivory Coast, The Gambia and Somalia.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Antonelli extraordinary as Gasly has superb weekend - driver ratings
- Published
Kimi Antonelli pulled off one of the fightbacks of the ages as he fought from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix.
The 20-year-old's stunning victory came after he caught and passed his team-mate George Russell with three laps to go.
Russell, who had started second and battled for the lead with Antonelli earlier in the race before holding on to first until the closing stages, is now 66 points behind in the drivers' championship.
Meanwhile, it was a difficult day for Ferrari in front of the tifosi, with Charles Leclerc enduring a high-speed crash at the Parabolica early on while Lewis Hamilton was forced to settle for sixth.
Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Monza.
Kimi Antonelli - 10/10
What more could you ask for? Started 19th because of an engine penalty and sliced his way through the field to win his home Grand Prix. A trip through the gravel while hunting Russell was the only scare in an otherwise extraordinary drive.
George Russell - 9/10
Fastest in both FP2 and FP3, missed pole by just 0.060 seconds and led a huge chunk of the race. The strategy ultimately swung things Antonelli's way but Russell hardly put a foot wrong himself.
Max Verstappen - 8.5/10
Another very strong Sunday after Red Bull struggled more over one lap. Briefly led the race and fought hard with both Mercedes drivers before bringing home a podium despite reporting problems with the rear of the car.
Lando Norris - 7.5/10
Qualifying ninth wasn't where Norris wanted to be as McLaren struggled with its brakes, but he recovered well on Sunday. Beat Piastri in their late fight to take fourth and continued his strong run of form.
Oscar Piastri - 6.5/10
The speed was clearly there with third in qualifying, but the penalty for impeding Lawson dropped him back on the grid. He fought forwards throughout the race but ultimately lost out to Norris late on.
Lewis Hamilton - 7.5/10
A much better weekend than sixth place suggests. Quick throughout practice and almost identical to Leclerc in qualifying, before being forced into the gravel during their first lap fight and having to recover from outside the points.
Pierre Gasly - 9.5/10
One of the performances of the season on Saturday to put an Alpine in pole position on pure pace. He simply didn't have the race speed to keep the quicker cars behind on Sunday, but seventh still completed a superb weekend.
Arvid Lindblad - 8.5/10
Another hugely impressive rookie weekend. Qualified in the top 10 and then converted it into eighth place, comfortably leading Racing Bulls home and once again showing he belongs at this level.
Franco Colapinto - 7.5/10
Excellent qualifying to put the Alpine eighth but overshadowed by Gasly. Even found himself running fourth after the red flag. A big trip through the gravel cost him heavily, but recovering all the way back to ninth salvaged a deserved points finish.
Yuki Tsunoda - 6.5/10
A much tougher weekend than Zandvoort, particularly with 17th in qualifying while Lindblad reached Q3. Recovered nicely to score the final point, although lining up incorrectly for the restart was an unnecessary blemish.

Gabriel Bortoleto - 7/10
Missed Q3 by just one thousandth of a second and again had the edge over Audi team-mate Hulkenberg. Just missed out on the points on Sunday but there wasn't much wrong with his weekend.
Nico Hulkenberg - 6/10
Couldn't quite match Bortoleto in qualifying or the race. He remained in the fringes of the points fight but ultimately finished behind his team-mate in 12th.
Carlos Sainz - 6/10
Williams never looked particularly comfortable at Monza. Sainz at least made Q2 and brought the car home in 13th, but there was little opportunity to make an impact further up the order.
Liam Lawson - 7/10
A difficult weekend to judge given the grid penalty and subsequent pit-lane start. His qualifying was also hurt when Piastri impeded him, so fighting back to 14th was a respectable effort on his second successive weekend at Red Bull.
Oliver Bearman - 6/10
There were encouraging signs from Haas' major upgrade and Bearman looked strong on Friday. Twelfth in qualifying was solid but slipping to 15th on Sunday meant the promising pace didn't translate into points.
Esteban Ocon - 5/10
Always looked to be facing a difficult weekend without the same upgraded Ferrari power unit as Bearman. Qualified behind his team-mate and finished behind him too in a fairly anonymous race.
Alex Albon - 5.5/10
His qualifying was compromised by both an engine penalty and helping Sainz with a tow. Made a little progress from the back on Sunday but Williams simply didn't have enough pace for him to get much further.
Sergio Perez - 4.5/10
Another difficult weekend for Cadillac, although Perez at least beat Bottas in the race. Started near the back and never really threatened to make meaningful progress.
Valterri Bottas - 4/10
Out-qualified Perez but slipped behind him during the Grand Prix and finished two laps down. Cadillac remained well off the midfield throughout the weekend.
Lance Stroll - 3.5/10
Qualified last and there was little to suggest Aston Martin had the pace to achieve much more. A hydraulics problem eventually brought a miserable weekend to an early end.
Fernando Alonso - 4/10

Charles Leclerc - 4/10

Every summer evening, Gulshan follows the same routine. She washes the floor of her one-room home several times so it cools a little for her four children to sleep on. Last summer, the family saved enough to buy a desert cooler, which uses evaporation as a cheaper alternative to air conditioning.
The family uses the appliance cautiously to save on energy costs. But even when it is on, Gulshan, who does not use a surname, has to dampeneveryone’s clothes before sleeping. The 39-year-old and her children now have rashes and one has a skin infection from the wet cloth against their skin.
This summer, Gulshan started jotting down these coping strategies in a garmi khata, or heat registry. “I feel relieved that at least somebody might read my family’s experiences,” she says.
They are one of 40 households in Sunder Nagri, a slum in north-east Delhi, documenting their experiences of surviving the city’s increasingly longer and more frequent heatwaves.
Over the last few years, cities across India have begun drawing up heat action plans – agreements formulated by a municipality or district administration on how to prepare for and respond to extreme heat.
While some incorporate data such as satellite-derived land surface temperatures to identify heat hotspots, there are still significant gaps in information on people, making it difficult to understand how heat is experienced differently across communities.
Aravind Unni, an urban planner and researcher in Delhi, says: “Experiences of heat are vastly different depending on geography, income, occupation, gender, caste, class.
“While we have some meteorological data on heat, what’s absolutely missing is people, community – what they feel, what they experience.”
Most data collated in heat planning is usually just meteorological, such as air temperatures and heatwave thresholds.. The idea for the heat diaries was to “move beyond just the numbers”, says Nibedita Saha, a Greenpeace India researcher who worked on the project.
Aakiz Farooq, a senior campaigner at the group, says the team contemplated how best to encapsulate experiences and thought: “What if they become their own storytellers, they write their own evidence, they write their own testimonies?”
Arshi, 19, who lives in one room with five other family members, is a distance-learning student at Delhi University. She also works at home making decorative tassels for trucks.
She makes about 150 rupees (£1.17) working with her mother and sister for a day. “Sometimes I go to the college library just to sit in the air-conditioned space for a while. But I have to come back home so I can help my sister and mother,” she says. These experiences are part of Arshi’s diary.
The diaries, which ask about daily routines, work, home, mood and families, are intended to serve as comprehensive journals of residents’ daily lives.
Arshi’s small brick house is extremely humid, and while the temperatures are lower after rain, the combination of heat and humidity means everyone is sweating profusely.
The ambient air temperature insideis 29.3C (85F), but with relative humidity at 84.6%, the “feels-like” temperature is 36.3C (97F).
Raja, a 21-year-old street vendor, experiences temperatures as high as 45C during peak summer months as he sells vegetables from his pushcart. The fresh produce spoils quickly, leading to losses, and he has noticed a drastic drop in numbers of people on the street, which also reduces his income.
Every night, he returns to a home with limited ventilation and no cooling source beyond a ceiling fan. As the gap between day and night temperatures narrows year after year in Delhi, people in homes such as Raja’s get no respite, even after the sun sets. “I started sleeping out on the roof in May so I could feel some air,” he says.
Workers such as Raja, Unni says, could be better protected by public policy if the state knew of their experiences at a micro-level and establish systems to provide compensation.
When Sunder Nagri’s residents set out to map heat indices within their neighbourhood, they found that some streets, including where Raja sells vegetables, reflected temperatures on the ground of more than 54C (129F). The residents are attempting to find pragmatic solutions, such as shade, water sources or increased greenery.
This summer, satellite analysis found striking differences across Delhi. For instance, an analysis by the news magazine India Today found an average land-surface temperature of nearly 44C in the south-west district of Mahipalpur, by the airport, compared with about 37C just 2 miles (3km) away in the leafy, upmarket suburb of Vasant Kunj.
Unni feels the diaries and community heat mapping can help form urban resilience policy, but says a big stumbling block is that “Indian cities do not have the administrative capacity or infrastructure to have decentralised action”.
The diaries have now been submitted to India’s National Human Rights Commission, urging it to recognise extreme heat as a human rights issue and recommend measures to protect people.
Farooq says the team also plans to share the testimonies with ministries, policymakers and MPs to push for more targeted measures to protect people from extreme heat.
He says they are also working to develop the testimonies into evidence of impacts and injuries that could be used for lawsuits to increase accountability, given the supreme court’s 2024 ruling that protection from the most adverse impacts of the climate crisis forms part of the right to life.
On 4 August, India’s government added heatwaves to the list of nationally notified disasters, allowing states to access emergency relief funds.
Unni and Farooq say it “would be ideal” if the decision meant funds could support local action guided by community participation.
Arshi also feels more hopeful after the new guidelines. “Even if the government sees something as small as our rising medical and electricity costs and tries to help with that, it would feel like a win for me. At least they would have seen what we are going through,” she says.

Serielizados, Spain’s second largest audience-driven film/TV festival after San Sebastián, has unwrapped its main competition programs at this year’s edition, set to unspool onsite over Oct. 19-28 in Barcelona and a month later on streaming service Filmin,
Headlining the official national competition as a world premiere is the second season of Movistar Plus+’s and 100 Balas’ “Celeste”, one of Spain’s most successful TV shows which won best screenplay at Serielizados 2024 after triumphing at Series Mania Panorama with a best series plaudit plus best actress win for Carmen Machi.
The latter who wooed viewers with her portrait of tax inspector Sara Santano, returns here with a new tax evasion case. “Celeste”’s creator Diego San José and director Elena Trapé, both behind Serielizados’ best screenplay winner “Jakarta in 2025, will be back in Barcelona together with Machi.
Popular on Variety
Co-produced with Arte France, and one of the most anticipated of new shows from Movistar Plus, “Killing a Bear” (“Matar a un oso”) will also bow in the national competition, with top showrunners Jorge and Alberto Sánchez-Cabezudo and cast on hand.
Inspired by real events, the six-parter centers on the first criminal investigation in Spain into the killing of a wild animal, following the death of bear Cachou in the Pyrenees’ Aran Valley in 2020. In the title roles are Eduard Fernández, María Rodríguez Soto, Miki Esparbé, Pol López, Nora Navas and Àlex Monner.
	Both “Killing a Bear” and “Celeste 2” will compete against the previously announced national entries “In Vitro” from HBO Max-3Cat, which is the fest’s opening title, and “Segunda Temporada” from Filmin.
Toplining Serielizados’ second biggest showcase – the six-title international competition – is the French-German-Dutch co-production “Etti” with star creator Hagai Levi (“In Treatment,” “Scenes from a Marriage”) expected at the Catalan premiere. 
	
Based on the diaries of Dutch writer Etty Hillesum, Arte France’s banner drama turns on a young woman’s turbulent affair with her psychologist against the background of a contemporary Nazi-occupied Amsterdam which promotes Hillesum to take a extraordinary and exemplary ethical stand. It will arrive in Barcelona after festival runs in Venice -out of competition- and Series Mania.
Strongly repped at Serielizados, Arte France will also showcase the buzzy French series “Camarades” for which Manon Kneuzé earned a best actress prize at this year’s Series Mania. The satire from creators Benjamin Charbit (“Zorro”) and Dominique Baumard (“The Bureau”), is set during the May 1968 student uprisings. The premiere on arte.tv is set for Sept. 16.
	From the U.K. are two high-end drama entries already picked up by Spanish streaming services.
BBC comedy “Ann Droid,” about a self-help robot, would well conquer Serielizados and Filmin viewers with “its irreverent yet touching take on grief and human relationships,” the festival says in a statement. The show, starring and created by Emmy-nominated Diane Morgan (“Mandy,” “Cunk”) was recently renewed by the BBC on the back of its 7.6 million views for the opening episode, making it the U.K. pubcaster’s second biggest new scripted launch of 2026.
In another genre, “Dirty Business” to be showcased in Spain on Movistar Plus, is a factual drama ordered by Channel 4, in which David Thewlis and Jason Watkins play two unlikely detectives, investigating an environmental disaster.
	German drama “A Better Place” combines suspense and social commentary about the failing of the prison system. The first German TV show produced by Studiocanal’s German TV arm, Studiocanal Series, teaming with Komplizenbfor WDR/ARD Degeto, will be repped in Barcelona by co-creator Alexander Lindh.
Also under the ARD-WDR banner is “Naked,” A bold series about sex addiction and the limits of desire to be repped on-site by creator and co-writer Silke Eggert.
	Presiding over the international competition is prominent Spanish director Rodrigo Sorgoyen, shortlisted to represent Spain at the Oscars with his Cannes competition contender “The Beloved.” He will be joined by hot Spanish showrunner comedian Victoria Martín behind Movistar Plus+’s “Se tiene que morir mucha gente,” one of Spain’s biggest TV hits of the year.
Claire-Marine Pietriga from Canneseries and Berlinale Series advisor Rowan Woods will be joined on the national competition jury by Roosa Toivonen, a Finnish producer and co-head of the Tallinn Black Nights Film festival’s industry series arm TV Beats.
	
Commenting on the competition lineups, Serielizados co-head Betu Martínez who viewed with his selection committee over 200 shows for consideration, said the festival motto for this year could be “life through series” as every selected show “mirrors current societal anxieties, with a strong authorial voice.”
Trend-wise, he emphasised the “strong shift towards European production, particularly from Northern and Central Europe,”, and the expanding role of public broadcasters as cultural gatekeepers and risk takers, “backing bold, out-of-the-box auteur series like “Naked” or “A Better Place.”
Martínez also underscored Serielizados’ equally crucial goal to defend “series that truly matter.” This year’s festival motto “An Eye For It,” referring to the event’s cultural curation remit. “In an era of overabundance driven by algorithms, a festival’s core job is editorial curation. we act as a filter,” he insisted.
Other festival highlights of Serielizados’ 13th edition include a talk with Catalan nouvelle cuisine trailblazer Ferran Adrià about the 3Cat drama “Genesis,” set to play on Netflix in Spain after its airs on the Catalan pubcaster.
A prime showcase for Catalan productions and co-productions, the festival will screen the Finnish-Italian-Spanish heavy metal animation show “Belzebubs,” ahead if its premiere on 3Cat, and the U.S. episodic sci-fi from Marc Martínez Jordán, “Future Manifest.”
Committed as well to new talent and formats, the festival will also stage a Catalan-language Microseries Showcase, organised with Igualada’s Zoom Awards and EVA platform.
Spain’s other fast-expanding regional hub for top talent and indie productions, the Basque Country, already spotlighted at the festival in 2025, will bring two shows from pubcaster EITB: the female-driven “Aloka(h)iru” co-helmed by Alba Lozano and Nitya López, and “Estu” from the artistic collective Arriguri.
Other sections focus on immigration, with Belgium’s “The Best Immigrant” and Germany’s “All Heroes Are Bastards” as well as comedy in all its shapes.
Making their Spanish debut are NBC’s US sports mockumentary “The Fall and Rose of Reggie Dinkins,” Focus Features’ “Lorne,” about Saturday Night Live’s creator Lorne Michaels, and TVNZ’s parody of spy pics “New Zealand Spy.”
Serielizados saw single visits soar 80% in 2025 to 16,000 on-site visitors and 194,000 viewers on the streamer Filmin. It will soon release the program of its industry days Serielizados Pro headed by festival co-founder Víctor Sala.

A claim that federal officials approved a plan to change the name of the state of New Mexico to "New America" spread online, with one popular post going so far as to claim U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the state's name in early September 2026.
The claim emerged following a real order Trump signed Aug. 27, 2026, to change Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in the United States.
X user @DailyNoud shared the claim on Sept. 1 that New Mexico's name also would be changed (archived), writing: "Donald Trump has signed an executive order to change the name of New Mexico to New America." The post received more than 2.7 million views, as of this writing:
Variations of the claim also spread on Instagram, Threads and Facebook. Some people seemed to interpret it as true, and Snopes readers contacted us in search of more information.
To investigate the claims legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo and Bing. If officials in Trump's administration had really approved plans to change the state's name — or if Trump had signed any such executive order — these searches would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting about an official move to change the name of New Mexico.
We identified the claim's original source: satirical social media account Casper Planet, which describes its output as "Snews that doesn't matter." This post didn't explicitly say Trump signed an executive order, rather — it claimed that "federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America." (X user @DailyNoud also was a satire account.)
The Facebook page Casper Planet shared the related claim (archived) on Aug. 29, 2026:
New Mexico To Be Renamed New America Following Federal Geographic Naming ChangesWASHINGTON - Federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America, continuing a recent effort to update geographic names across the country.According to officials familiar with the change, the word "Mexico" was identified during a routine review of American maps and was determined to be geographically confusing.The change is expected to affect highway signs, government documents and approximately 14 million souvenir coffee mugs.Residents will officially become New Americans, while people born there before the change will reportedly be allowed to continue identifying as New Mexicans during a two-year transition period.Mexico has not been consulted.
In addition to a location tag on "Satire Street," its Facebook bio reads (archived):
Delivering the Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up
We reached out to the page owner for comment in January 2026 regarding a claim about AI-generated images of massive snow bank on Wyoming's Devils Tower. The account's administrator, Justin Hathaway, told Snopes over the phone: "I just love doing this satire stuff, it's such an outlet for me." He continued: "Another reason is people don't really read things fully anymore, and it's a good way to educate people on reading stories fully if they sound somewhat unbelievable."
Other Casper Planet posts Snopes has debunked include a claim that Yellowstone National Park rangers warned the public that ravens had learned to open car doors and another that a man received a DUI while riding a bear.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work.
