There is a bacterium called Streptococcus pneumoniae. It comes in at least a hundred different forms, or serotypes, and lives in the tissue lining our nose and throat. S. pneumoniae is normally harmless. But when your body’s immune system becomes weaker, for example when you have a viral fever, these bacteria may invade your lungs and cause pneumonia, your brain and spinal cord to cause meningitis, and your bloodstream to cause sepsis.
These diseases are called pneumococcal diseases, and fortunately, they can be prevented by vaccines. Each of these vaccines contains a unique sugary substance called a capsular polysaccharide, aimed at each serotype of S. pneumoniae. That is, they offer protection specific to each serotype.
And the current crop of pneumococcal vaccines protect against only a subset of the 100-odd serotypes. To increase coverage, scientists need to include additional serotype-specific capsular polysaccharides in the vaccine. And covering all the serotypes in a single shot would be extremely challenging, not to mention extremely expensive as well.
Sugary shot
Recently, a team of British scientists reported an important first step in this direction. They did two things: first, they switched the polysaccharide with proteins and, second, they adopted an approach called reverse vaccinology.
Basically, two kinds of pneumococcal vaccines are available today. One is a mix of purified capsular polysaccharides from multiple serotypes. Pneumovax 23 is an example. It does not work well in infants and offers short-lived protection.
To help boost the effects as well as the durability of the immune response, scientists have linked the polysaccharides to a carrier protein. Such vaccines are known as pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs). Typical examples include PCV10 and PCV14; the numerals denote the number of serotypes included.
When these vaccines target and eliminate some serotypes of S. pneumoniae, it also opens the door for other serotypes to mount an infection. These non-vaccine serotypes also face less biological competition for space and resources, so they multiply and eventually replace the vaccine-targeted serotypes, rendering the vaccines obsolete.
Second, many non-vaccine serotypes either possess antibiotic resistance genes or can acquire them from their resistant counterparts. This leads to the rise of both vaccine- and antibiotic-resistant serotypes.
Thus, scientists are looking for a universal pneumococcal vaccine that can target all serotypes and prevent these outcomes, which keep the threat of pneumonia, meningitis, and other pneumococcal diseases alive in the population.
An intense search
Reverse vaccinology starts from the germ’s genome to identify proteins that can be included in vaccines. Scientists demonstrated an example of this in the recent COVID-19 pandemic: once the virus’s genome was sequenced in early 2020, scientists around the world could analyse it and zero in on the spike-protein gene to make COVID-19 vaccines. The approach completely bypassed the need to culture the germs in large bioreactors and purify molecular components from them to make the vaccine.
The S. pneumoniae genome encodes more than 2,000 genes. Of them, around 1,300 are common across serotypes. The genomic data of more than 20,000 S. pneumoniae isolates across nearly a hundred serotypes are also available in the public domain. The scientists deployed extensive computational analysis using an arsenal of bioinformatic tools to analyse these sequences.
They reasoned that the best candidate genes for creating their universal vaccine would need to encode for proteins with three attributes: (i) it must be located on the surface so that the immune system can easily access it; (ii) it must have low or no similarity to human proteins, so that the immune system does not attack the body’s tissue, and (iii) it must be capable of eliciting a robust and durable anti-pneumococcal immunity.
The team shortlisted some candidates and further whittled the list down based on their predicted shapes and stability. From this, the team picked three candidate genes. They were: zinc metalloprotease B (Z), pneumococcal adherence virulence factor A (P), and a protein which the scientists designated YfhO-like (Y) due to its similarity to another bacterial protein.
The team produced proteins Z, P, and Y in the laboratory and made an experimental vaccine by mixing them together. They also added two non-protein immune response boosters: a small piece of synthetic DNA called CpG and a sugary polymer called chitosan. They named this formulation ZPY-CpG-Ch.
Potent antibodies
To test whether the vaccine could elicit protective anti-pneumococcal antibodies, the scientists vaccinated laboratory mice. After some time, they exposed the mice to a lethal dose of S. pneumoniae serotype 1, which is known to be hypervirulent. Compared to unvaccinated mice, all of which succumbed to the lethal dose, vaccinated mice showed 80-100% survival. Importantly, the scientists found that the level of protection offered by ZPY-CpG-Ch was comparable to that of PCV13.
The team also found that antibodies from the mice vaccinated with ZPY-CpG-Ch could help kill S. pneumoniae bacteria in a test tube. When injected into unvaccinated mice, the antibodies could also protect them against a lethal dose of serotype 1.
Third, ZPY-CpG-Ch fully protected vaccinated mice exposed to lethal doses of two non-vaccine serotypes, 11A and 33F. It also offered 50% protection against a third non-vaccine serotype, called serotype 8.
In all mouse experiments, measures of the vaccine’s protective effect based on the bacterial load in lungs and blood mirrored the rodents’ survival rates. However, the ZPY-CpG-Ch vaccine did not reduce the load of pneumococcal bacteria in the upper respiratory passages of vaccinated mice. That is, despite being protected, vaccinated mice have the ability to still spread the infection to uninfected mice.
Worthy goal
Finally, the team also reported that vaccinating mice with ZPY-CpG-Ch stimulated a subset of immune cells that are implicated in pneumococcal immunity.
The results from this work are too preliminary for ZPY-CpG-Ch to be a universal pneumococcal vaccine. It has also been tested against a very small subset of serotypes, four to be precise. Vaccine data from laboratory mice also may not truly reflect the human situation.
Nevertheless, this work represents a baby step towards the worthy goal of developing a universal pneumococcal vaccine.
S. Swaminathan is a retired professor of biology at BITS-Pilani, Hyderabad, and a former scientist at ICGEB, New Delhi.

German company Isar Aerospace has successfully launched Europe’s first entirely commercial orbital rocket. It attempted to achieve the feat last March, but that lasted all of 30 seconds before the vehicle crashed into the sea and exploded. This time the company managed to get the two-stage Spectrum into low Earth orbit from a Norwegian spaceport.
Europe has its first commercial orbital rocket
Isar Aerospace gives the continent more options to “buy European” for space launches.
CEO and Co-Founder Daniel Metzler said in a press release:
“Today, Isar Aerospace opened space from Continental Europe. Launch continues to be the largest bottleneck for the global space industry and from today on, there is a true alternative for commercial and institutional customers … Europe now has sovereign access to space. We have entered into a new chapter for European spaceflight.”
Until now, Europe has been largely reliant on Arianespace and Avio, which are largely funded by governments. The current global political climate makes the accomplishment particularly important for European countries that might view the United States as a less reliable partner at the moment and that have been cut off from Russian Soyuz rockets by the country’s invasion of Ukraine. The European Space Agency has also made “buy European” a cornerstone of its policies.

Stephen Fuhr was mocked for opposing the purchase of F-35s. Now he's in charge of Canada's defence procurement
Ex-fighter pilot who has long been critical of U.S. jets could oversee dramatic increase in defence budget
Stephen Fuhr got his "Picasso" nickname back in his days as a fighter pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF).
He'd been ordered to produce detailed attack maps, but his abstract scribbles earned him a call sign inspired by the cubist master, according to former military officials.
Today, the 57-year-old holds a more serious title: Canada's secretary of state for defence procurement.
In this role, he leads the Defence Investment Agency, an organization created last year by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to speed up the procurement of tens of billions of dollars worth of military acquisitions.
- Canada announces Defence Investment Agency to manage purchase, delivery of military equipment
- Canada joining international program to build next generation of fighter jets
It's been a quick rise for the former CF-18 pilot who, after retiring from the Armed Forces in 2009, drew mockery from members of the military community by vigorously opposing the purchase of American F-35 aircraft.
Multiple sources indicate that relations remain strained to this day between Fuhr and the RCAF, whether over fighter jets, radar planes or helicopter replacements.
In an interview with CBC News, Fuhr said he is always ready to fight for his convictions.
"I'm not afraid to stand out on the hill by myself," he said. "It's just a principled place to be. And sometimes it's lonely, but that's just the way it is."
CBC News spoke with a dozen people who have interacted closely with Fuhr over the years. Some requested confidentiality to avoid harming commercial relations with the government, or were not authorized to speak publicly.
Fuhr — who is from Edmonton but now lives in B.C.'s Okanagan Valley and is MP for Kelowna — first became interested in aviation when his grandfather took him to model airplane competitions. He never lost his taste for speed and flight.
In addition to his pickup truck, he enjoys getting behind the wheel of his sporty Porsche 911 or flying his own aircraft, a two-seater Van's RV-8 featuring a shark mouth on the nose.
Sitting in the cockpit in a hangar at the Kelowna airport, he tells CBC News this plane is his "happy place."
But he rarely gets time to fly over the nearby mountains. After travelling the world in recent months, his summer schedule was once again disrupted by wildfires in the area. Fuhr's house in West Kelowna was burned to the ground by a wildfire in 2023 and was only recently rebuilt.
Now, his political career is set to become even more demanding. Under the Liberal government's Bill C-31, he could soon inherit new powers as head of the Defence Investment Agency to award sole-sourced contracts in order to protect Canada's "economic security."
The measures proposed in Bill C-31 would create a "super minister" in charge of military procurement, said Justin Massie, a defence expert at Université du Québec à Montréal.
"He would have more power than Mélanie Joly at industry or [David] McGuinty at national defence, because he would combine many of the powers that were usually or historically delegated across several departments," Massie said.
Fuhr is in line to oversee a dramatic increase in Canada's defence budget, amid a promise to reshape the military relationship between Canada and the U.S.
He says he's aiming for a sweeping transformation of the military procurement system, either by producing more equipment in Canada or by finding new global partners.
"We are going to become less reliant and more resilient," he said.
"The good news is we have friends in every time zone. And everybody wants to work with Canada."
Fuhr gets an obvious political boost from being a former CF-18 pilot. Being a member of Canada's select "top gun" club is an enviable calling card.
Still, sources said Fuhr is seen as an outsider by many prominent members of Canada's fighter pilot community.
During his four years in a CF-18 squadron at CFB Cold Lake in Alberta, from 1999 to 2003, he was known for standing up to his commanding officer and his career had its share of ups and downs, according to several sources.
Fuhr did not wish to comment on personal issues during the interview.
Some former pilots argue Fuhr lacks "operational credibility" within their community, having never been part of deployments in conflict zones.
He counters by pointing to a defining moment of his piloting career after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, in which airliners were turned into missiles. He said he had trained for war, but not the scenario in which he took to the skies to protect North American airspace as commercial planes were redirected to Canada.
"When you've got hundreds of civilian airliners full of people coming your way, and that is now a threat you have to work through, that's a different mind space," he said.
After leaving CFB Cold Lake, he worked in Winnipeg managing Canada's fighter fleet and then training pilots and instructors. He retired from the RCAF after 20 years with the rank of major.
Fuhr made more of a name for himself after returning to civilian life in the early 2010s.
While many in the fighter pilot community were tireless supporters of the F-35, he became a fierce critic.
"It may be a great airplane, it's not the right plane for Canada," he said on CBC's Power & Politics in 2011.
Friends and former colleagues speak of his fixation against the Lockheed Martin aircraft, which had been chosen by the Stephen Harper government to replace the CF-18s.
F-35 proponents say the aircraft is superior to any other Western fighter jet due to its stealth capabilities and the extraordinary amount of data it can process.
Still, Fuhr objected to the purchase for Canada, citing the project's staggering costs, numerous delays and some of the technical difficulties faced by some air forces. His opinion was based on a thorough review of every major study on the aircraft, including various public reports from the U.S. and Canadian governments on the program's failures.
He knew by publicly attacking the F-35, he was taking on many of his former air force colleagues.
"From the fighter pilot community, the F-35 has basically been considered the be-all and end-all," said Mike Reyno, a military magazine publisher and friend of Fuhr.
"What Stephen has done, and this is all with publicly available documentation, is [point out] the F-35 has actually failed to meet almost every critical point along its development."
A former supporter of the Conservative Party of Canada, Fuhr ran as a Liberal Party candidate in the 2015 federal election alongside Justin Trudeau, drawn in part by the Liberal promise to cancel the F-35 purchase.
He won the Kelowna-Lake Country seat but lost it to the Conservatives in 2019. He then became a consultant for Boeing, among other roles, and continued to criticize the F-35, describing the aircraft as "unaffordable" in 2021.
Two years later the Trudeau government announced the purchase of 88 F-35s, signing a firm contract for 16 aircraft.
Fuhr returned to politics last year, this time alongside Carney, who responded to growing tensions with the U.S. by subjecting the F-35 purchase to a review.
There is no doubt Canada will integrate F-35s into its air force, but the real question is how many aircraft the government will ultimately buy, and whether it will decide to add Swedish Gripen fighters to its military arsenal.
Easygoing and approachable, Fuhr is a fixture at defence trade shows, announcements, business trips and media interviews.
He is a prime target for lobbyists and executives hoping for a share of the new defence investments.
"He talks to everyone," said a lobbyist whose clients find it easier to get meetings with Fuhr than the defence minister.
Numerous procurement files are moving ahead much faster than expected under his leadership, including Swedish GlobalEye radar planes, German-Norwegian submarines and the purchase of over 60,000 assault rifles from Colt Canada.
- Carney chooses German submarines for Canadian navy fleet
- Canada fast-tracks army rifle upgrade with $307M initial order
But Fuhr has ongoing tensions with the RCAF regarding the diversification of equipment supply sources.
"The Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Navy have welcomed the change," said Reyno. "I would say that the air force hasn't been as welcoming to that because the Royal Canadian Air Force basically wants to operate everything the Americans operate."
Fuhr is not closing the door to new mixed fleets of aircraft or helicopters, while the RCAF has stated its objections to the purchase of Gripens.
"Many of our allies … run a mixed fleet with fighters," says Fuhr. "I don't necessarily subscribe to the fact that we can't do it. We certainly can and we've done it and our allies do it now. So it's a function of 'do we want to do this or not?'"
Despite disagreements on the matter, a former pilot says he wishes Fuhr the greatest success in his bid to modernize Canada's sclerotic military acquisition process.
"Stephen Fuhr has to succeed. Whether anyone likes him personally or not, it is crucial for Canada to procure the right equipment to do the right job in a timely manner," they said.
Fuhr is aware he carries the reputation of an unyielding politician who holds firm views on various procurement projects. He says he is always ready to change his mind — but only if he is given compelling evidence.
"That evidence better actually bring something to the table and be credible. And if it doesn't do those two things, then I don't see a reason anyone should change their position," he said.
Throughout the interview, Fuhr made an effort not to speak directly about the F-35, a particularly sensitive topic given the trade and diplomatic tensions with the U.S.
Still, he smiled as he was asked about recent comments by U.S. Gen. Gregory Guillot, the commander of NORAD, who said F-35s weren't necessarily the best aircraft to protect the Canadian and American borders.
"He is the commander of NORAD. So I think what he says, I take him at his word," Fuhr said, breaking into a laugh.

Lines stuns Zhao in English Open first round
- Published
Oliver Lines stunned Zhao Xintong with a 4-2 win over the world number one in the first round of the English Open.
China's Zhao, the 2025 world champion, made two century breaks as the tie was level at 2-2 following the first four frames.
But England's Lines, 31, compiled breaks of 77 and 84 to win the next two frames and set up a last-32 meeting with Yuan Sijun in Brentwood.
"You know you have to raise your game," said Lines.
"You try not to think about it, but you know if you don't play somewhere near your best then you are going home."
Elsewhere, world number four Neil Robertson was beaten 4-3 by China's Luo Zetao.
But former world champion Kyren Wilson beat Poland's Mateusz Baranowski 4-1 and China's three-time UK Championship winner Ding Junhui sealed a 4-3 win over Michael Holt.

Multiple people injured as armed man lunges at Democratic candidate during campaign event
The man ‘aggressively shoved his way through the crowd’ and was armed with two pistols, the sheriff says
Multiple attendees at a Democratic campaign event in Ohio were left injured after an armed man lunged at a gubernatorial candidate.
The incident unfolded on Sunday as Dr Amy Acton, who is running to replace outgoing Republican Governor Mike DeWine, spoke at the Mahoning County Democrat Booth at the Canfield Fair.
The county’s Sheriff Jerry Greene identified the attacker as 38-year-old Patrick Havas to CBS News, telling the network that the individual had “aggressively shoved his way through the crowd toward Acton while holding a cell phone up”.
Havas was armed with two pistols and brass knuckles, Greene said, and allegedly knocked over two older people on mobility scooters - one of whom fell to the ground.
Addie Bullock, the communications director for Acton’s campaign, confirmed the incident in a public statement.
“While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr Acton, injuring multiple people,” Bullock said. “Dr Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured.”
Bullock added, “This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against each other.”
Greene told CBS News that Havas has been charged with two counts of misdemeanor assault and one count of disorderly conduct.
Wayne Penny Jr, an Ohio democrat, revealed more about Havas’ alleged attack to the network.
“He literally bull-rushed through the crowd, knocked our volunteers down, ran through, pushed and knocked the elderly gentleman over with Parkinson's, and the gentleman hit his head and fell,” Penny Jr said.
Journalist Henry J Gomez later shared a picture of Acton helping to one of the injured attendees at Sunday’s event.
DeWine, who has endorsed fellow Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the gubernatorial race, shared his own statement thanking law enforcement for responding to the incident.
“Fran and I are thankful Dr Amy Acton was not hurt, and we send our thoughts to those who were injured,” DeWine wrote. “We spoke to Dr Acton this afternoon, and she said to share with Ohioans that she is okay.”
The outgoing governor added, “We are grateful for the quick work of the Ohio State Highway Patrol and other law enforcement on the scene at the Canfield Fair today when a man tried to forcefully push himself toward Dr Acton as she was speaking and injured other attendees at the Mahoning County Democratic booth.”
The Independent has contacted the Mahoning County Sheriff Office for comment.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Some Target baskets carry a Bluetooth Low Energy Beacon that transmits its location to "smart" lights in the store. The lights can interact with the beacons and Target's app to find a shopper's location, help them navigate around a store or send location-specific offers. Because the basket-mounted beacons transmit only locations and do not collect information about the shopper, it is technically Target's app that tracks shoppers, not the beacons.
In August and September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that the retailer Target used a Bluetooth device on its baskets that tracked shoppers in store.
The claim came from an Aug. 29 TikTok video in which a person who appeared to be a Target employee claimed the retailer fitted its baskets with trackers that followed shoppers throughout the store.
The alleged employee said:
Hello, I just want to make a PSA: You are now being tracked at Target. These baskets, this thing, that's a tracker, so they're now tracking shoppers at Target, at your local Target, for, supposedly, "consumer habits."
Other users shared similar claims about Target's alleged tracking on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), X (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim.
In short, Target does track shopper locations using the basket-mounted Bluetooth beacon that the TikTok user showed in their video. The beacon transmits its location to Target's "smart" overhead LED lights, which in turn can communicate location information to its app.
Acuity Brands, which Target said supplied its LED lights, explained in a news release in 2017 that by using its lights and beacons attached to items such as shopping carts it could deliver "highly accurate, real-time positioning services for customers" through a retailer's app. Acuity Brands said Target renewed a multiyear deal for products including its indoor location services in 2020.
According to its privacy policy, Target still used LED light and Bluetooth technology to track shoppers in-store in August 2026. The policy advised that customers who did not want to share their store location data could disable location sharing on their device or in the Target app.
We contacted Target to confirm how it collected and used data about customers in store using Bluetooth beacons, as well as how customers could opt out of tracking. We await a reply to our query.
What we know about Target tracking
The TikTok user who shared the video about Target's basket-mounted beacons on Aug. 29 shared another video (archived) the day after, identifying the exact product Target used to track shoppers as a Bluetooth beacon from Acuity Brands. A Reddit user who posted (archived) about the device six months earlier showed a device with the same FCC ID as the one the TikTok user identified.
The Federal Communications Commission grants FCC IDs to products that meet the necessary regulatory standards for wireless communication.
The product's user manual said it is a Bluetooth Low Energy Beacon that "communicates its position to Atrius Assets," the software that Target has used since at least 2020 for indoor location services.
Bluetooth Low Energy Beacons are small devices that send out radio signals that can be picked up by nearby devices. Beacons can only transmit — not receive — data, so they generally rely on apps to interpret and use the data they are sending.
In terms of tracking, if many beacons are sending their location, a device can interpret those signals and triangulate the location of an individual beacon, or individual shopper holding a basket fitted with a beacon. Target wrote in its news release in 2019 that its lights interacted with its app to find customer locations, suggesting that the basket-mounted beacons sent their signals to the lights.
It was unclear from the available information whether Target used the data it gathered about individual shoppers' routes through their stores beyond providing location-based offers through the app or guiding customers to specific products.
Target used Bluetooth beacons since at least 2015
The technology publication TechCrunch reported that Target and other retailers have used beacon technology to track shoppers in store and send them location-based offers since at least 2015 and that the retailer added Bluetooth beacon-driven indoor mapping to its app in 2017.
Target appeared to still use this technology in 2026. Its privacy policy in August 2026 said Target might use location information shared by customers' phones to "help you find nearby Target stores; or, in-store location through the use of your phone's blue tooth signal, LED light chip technologies or other technologies will permit Target to find nearby products for you, get you real-time deals, auto-sort your shopping list and more."
Target said in its privacy policy that shoppers who wished to opt out of sharing their in-store location could prevent their devices from sharing their location with Target "by adjusting the permissions on your mobile device or within the relevant app."
It did not appear from the beacon's manual that shoppers could turn the device off themselves, meaning Target would still collect information about where the basket traveled if a shopper used it, but could not connect that data to a specific phone or customer if the device's owner turned off location sharing or did not use the Target app.
